# Core3 Codebase Guide

Reference notes on how this SWG "Core3" emulator server (C:\Companion\Core3) is
put together, compiled from a full architectural survey. Companion System
specifics (STF/TRE/IFF binary formats, skills.iff, trainer conversation
wiring, the full profession-box-leak investigation) live in
`docs/companion_system/NOTES.md` and its `tools/` scripts -- this document
covers the rest of the engine: items, creatures, quests, buildings/dungeons,
resources/harvesters, commands, SUI dialogs, object menus/radials, skills/XP,
combat, database persistence, zones/planets, and factions/groups. Sections:

1. Items / Object Templates
2. Creatures / Mobs
3. Screenplays / Quests
4. Buildings, Cells, and Dungeons/Caves/Bunkers
5. Resources & Harvesters
6. Commands (slash-command dispatch pipeline)
7. SUI (server-driven dialog boxes)
8. Object Menus / Radial Wheel
9. Skills & XP
10. Combat Basics
11. Database Persistence
12. Zone / Planet / Region Fundamentals
13. Factions/GCW and Groups
14. Build & Deploy Workflow (recap)
15. Loot & Treasure System
16. Missions / Bounty Terminals
17. Guilds & Player Cities
18. Vehicles & Space/Ships
19. Chat, Mail & Social Systems
20. Crafting & Manufacturing

Two-layer architecture throughout: a **C++ core** (compiled, defines object
classes/behavior via `.idl` files under `MMOCoreORB/src/`) and a **Lua data
layer** (`MMOCoreORB/bin/scripts/`, loaded at server startup, no recompile
needed) that instantiates and configures those classes with concrete game
content. Almost everything in "make new X" work happens in the Lua layer;
C++ changes are only needed for genuinely new *behavior*, not new *instances*
of existing behavior.

---

## 1. Items / Object Templates

**Data location:** `MMOCoreORB/bin/scripts/object/tangible/*`, `object/weapon/*`,
`object/draft_schematic/*`, `object/factory/*`.

Every item is a Lua table built from a `shared_*` template (points at the
client-side mesh via `clientTemplateFileName`) plus a server template that
sets stats and registers itself:
```lua
object_..._belt = object_..._shared_belt:new{ templateType = ARMOROBJECT, ... }
ObjectTemplates:addTemplate(object_..._belt, "object/tangible/.../armor_..._belt.iff")
```
The second string arg to `addTemplate` is the item's global template ID,
referenced everywhere else (schematics' `targetTemplate`, loot's
`directObjectTemplate`, `/object create`).

**C++ hierarchy:** `TangibleObject` (`src/server/zone/objects/tangible/`) →
`WeaponObject`, `WearableObject` → `ArmorObject`. New *item type behavior*
needs a new `.idl` + Implementation + a `SharedXObjectTemplate` C++ class
(`src/templates/tangible/`). A new *instance* of an existing type (new sword,
new belt) is pure Lua.

**Schematics:** `bin/scripts/object/draft_schematic/<category>/*.lua`,
C++ base `DraftSchematic.idl`. Field `targetTemplate` points at the crafted
item's `.iff` path -- this is the schematic↔item link.

**Loot:** `bin/scripts/loot/items/*.lua` (`directObjectTemplate` = item path)
and `bin/scripts/loot/groups/*.lua` (`lootItems = {{itemTemplate=..., weight=...}}`).
Creature Lua templates reference a group by name via `lootGroups`.

**Recipe -- add one new item:**
1. New file under `object/tangible/.../my_item.lua`, built from an existing
   `shared_*` template (reuse client art unless you have new mesh assets),
   `ObjectTemplates:addTemplate(..., "object/.../my_item.iff")`, and
   `includeFile(...)` it into that category's include list.
2. (Craftable) copy a sibling schematic Lua, point `targetTemplate` at the
   new item, `includeFile` it.
3. (Lootable) add a `loot/items/*.lua` entry, add it into a `loot/groups/*.lua`
   group, reference that group name from a mob's `lootGroups`.
4. Restart the server (no rebuild).

**Condition/decay/repair (applies to any `TangibleObject`, not just
weapons):** `maxCondition`/`conditionDamage` are set at craft time from the
schematic's rolled stats (`armor_integrity`/`hitpoints` etc., section 20's
math). `isBroken()` (`TangibleObject.idl:824-827`) is simply
`maxCondition < 2 || conditionDamage >= maxCondition`. Below full break,
there's a **graduated performance penalty** most people miss:
`getConditionReduction()` (`TangibleObject.idl:829-841`) returns 0 until the
item is 75% damaged, then ramps linearly to a 50% stat penalty once fully
broken -- a weapon's `getMaxDamage()`/`getAttackSpeed()`
(`WeaponObjectImplementation.cpp:492-558`) both subtract this before combat
ever sees the number, so a badly-damaged-but-not-yet-broken weapon is
quietly weaker well before it visibly breaks. `TangibleObjectImplementation::inflictDamage()`
(`.cpp:993-1044`) is the single choke point everything routes through
(weapon self-decay on hit, armor/PSG condition chip on absorbing damage,
repair-tool use-count). `repair()` (`.cpp:1334-1444`) is roll-based
(skill/tool-quality/station-proximity vs. shock wounds/complexity) and, on
anything short of a perfect roll, **permanently shrinks `maxCondition`**
(e.g. weapon repair: `<25` roll sets `maxCondition=1`, `<50` -> ×0.65,
`<75` -> ×0.80, else ×0.95) -- repair is not free/lossless even at high
skill. `hasAntiDecayKit()` fully bypasses all of this for items with an
anti-decay kit applied.

**Weapon attachments (`PowerupObject`) -- weapon-only, one socket, no armor
equivalent:** a `PowerupObject` (`objects/tangible/powerup/PowerupObject.idl:19-103`)
is crafted like an ordinary item (its own `DraftSchematic` category,
`object/draft_schematic/item/item_powerup_weapon_*.lua`), holding percent
stat modifiers (`primaryAttributes`/`secondaryAttributes`, capped ~33%/16%)
and a `uses` charge counter. `WeaponObject` has a single `powerupObject`
slot (`WeaponObject.idl:62`); `ApplyPowerupCommand.h` is the drag-and-drop
handler (type-matches ranged/melee/thrown/mine, refuses default/Jedi
weapons, refuses if a powerup is already socketed -- one at a time). Every
weapon stat getter conditionally adds the powerup's stored bonus; each
successful non-force attack calls `decreasePowerupUses()`
(`WeaponObjectImplementation.cpp:687-710`), auto-removing and destroying the
powerup at 0 uses. **Armor has no equivalent socket/attachment mechanism**
in this codebase -- craft-time-only `Component` ingredient slots
(section 20's `applyComponentStats`) are the only way armor stats get
combined from sub-parts, and those are baked in at assembly, never
post-craft-insertable.

## 2. Creatures / Mobs

**Base Lua class:** `mobile/creatures.lua` defines `Creature = {...}` with
defaults (`objectName, mobType, level, chanceHit, damageMin/Max, baseHAM,
armor, resists[9], templates{}, lootGroups{}, primaryWeapon/secondaryWeapon,
primaryAttacks/secondaryAttacks, optionsBitmask, conversationTemplate`).
Register with `CreatureTemplates:addCreatureTemplate(obj, "name")`.

Examples: `mobile/tatooine/bantha.lua` (simple animal), `.../alkhara_bandit.lua`
(combat NPC, `primaryAttacks = merge(brawlermid, marksmanmid)` pulling named
skill-group tables from `mobile/creatureskills.lua`), `mobile/trainer/trainer_1hsword.lua`
(conversational humanoid, `optionsBitmask = INVULNERABLE + CONVERSABLE`,
`conversationTemplate = "..."`).

**C++ hierarchy:** `CreatureObject` → `AiAgent` (`src/server/zone/objects/creature/`
and `.../ai/`). AiAgentImplementation (~4900 lines) owns pathfinding, aggro
timing, combat weapon/damage rolls, and behavior-tree execution
(`.../ai/bt/`). Stats, loot, attack lists, faction, taming are all
data-driven from the Lua template -- no C++ needed for a new mob unless it
needs genuinely new AI behavior.

**AI is a real behavior tree, not a state machine.** Node classes live under
`ai/bt/` (`node/{Selector,Sequence}.cpp` incl. `RandomSelector`/
`ParallelSelector`, `decorator/{If,Not,LookForTarget,LookForPlayer,...}`,
~120 total `leaf/Checks.h` conditions + `leaf/SimpleActions.h`/
`FollowActions.h` actions). Trees are **authored in Lua but built from these
C++ classes** — `AiMap::registerBehaviors()` (`managers/creature/AiMap.h:379-508`)
registers every node class by string name; `addAiTemplate()` reads a Lua
table of `{id, name, pid, args}` rows and wires up the real tree (e.g.
`scripts/ai/default.lua:289`, `rootDefault`, a 34-node tree). Each mob's tree
is assigned per-slot (`MOVE, HEAL, TARGET, ATTACK, AWARE, IDLE, ...`,
`AiMap.h:313`) via `AiAgentImplementation::setAITemplate()`
(`AiAgentImplementation.cpp:3171`), which resolves slots by an exact
`customAiMap` string key first, then falls back to an `ObjectFlag` bitmask
default. **Modular override via `TreeSocket`** (`bt/TreeSocket.h:40`): a mob
can override just one slot (e.g. only `AWARE`, for a different aggro-scan
pattern) while inheriting the rest of `rootDefault` — see
`enclaveSentinel`/`villageRaider`/`crackdown` entries in
`managers/creature/templates.lua:13-37`.

**Tick loop:** `AiAgentImplementation::runBehaviorTree()`
(`AiAgentImplementation.cpp:3045`) runs the root tree roughly once/second
(`ai/events/AiBehaviorEvent.h`, base 1000ms `Task`, re-scheduled every run);
the tree's own Selector/Sequence structure is what branches into
combat/aware/idle each tick, not an explicit switch.

**Aggro & targeting is a real threat table, not nearest-target.**
`isAggressiveTo()`/`isAggressive()` (`AiAgentImplementation.cpp:4148-4290`)
decides *whether* to engage (baby-creature exemption, pet-vs-owner,
GCW/faction via `FactionManager::isEnemy()`, carnivore/herbivore, player
faction-standing < -3000). Once engaged, **which player stays the target**
is tracked in `server/zone/objects/tangible/threat/ThreatMap.h` — per-attacker
accumulated damage/heal/aggro, `getHighestThreatAttacker()`. Initial target
*acquisition* (before combat starts) is different again:
`bt/decorator/LookForTarget.h`/`LookForPlayer.h` shuffle the agent's nearby-object
cache and try each candidate in randomized order, gated by faction/LOS/invis
checks — so "who gets aggro'd first" is randomized-order/first-valid, while
"who stays the active target during a fight" is damage/threat-based.

**Pathfinding:** `managers/collision/PathFinderManager.h` — Recast/Detour
navmesh (`dtNavMeshQuery`) for outdoor terrain, a separate triangle/floor-mesh
graph for indoor cells. Both patrol waypoints (`generatePatrol()`,
`AiAgentImplementation.cpp:3215`) and combat chase/flee destinations
(`findNextPosition()`, `:2691`) funnel through the same
`PathFinderManager::findPath()` — the only difference is what destination
gets fed in.

**Giving a new mob genuinely different behavior — no C++ needed for most
cases:** set `customAiMap = "someKey"` on the creature template (checked
before the `ObjectFlag` bitmask default) to point one or more slots at an
already-existing alternate tree (`templates.lua:13-37` has real examples:
`cityPatrol`, `crackdown`, `villageRaider`). To build a genuinely *new* tree,
author a new `.lua` file composing the ~120 already-registered node classes
via `addAiTemplate(...)`, hook it into `templates.lua`'s `customMap`, and
point a template's `customAiMap` at it — still zero C++. A real "boss phase
change" example (`scripts/screenplays/dungeon/death_watch_bunker/deathWatchBunker.lua:1078-1114`)
is done as a ScreenPlay watching HAM% and swapping in a whole different
creature template at the same spot — not a BT branch. **Only a truly novel
condition/action** (nothing in the existing leaf catalog can express it)
requires a new `bt/leaf/` or `bt/decorator/` C++ class registered in
`AiMap::registerBehaviors()` — the one case in this whole system that needs
a rebuild.

**Spawning (3-tier chain):**
1. **Lair template** -- `mobile/lair/creature_lair/<planet>/*.lua`:
   `mobiles = {{"creature_template_name", weight}}`, `addLairTemplate(...)`.
2. **Spawn group** -- `mobile/spawn/<planet>/*.lua`: `lairSpawns` array of
   `{lairTemplateName, spawnLimit, minDifficulty, maxDifficulty, numberToSpawn,
   weighting, size}`, `addSpawnGroup("groupName", obj)`.
3. **Region binding** -- `managers/planet/<planet>_regions.lua`: tuples of
   `{"name", x, y, {shape,size}, SPAWNAREA, {"spawnGroupName"}, maxSpawnLimit}`
   -- the actual map coordinates.

**Recipe -- add one new mob:**
1. New Lua file under `mobile/<planet>/my_beast.lua` (model on `bantha.lua`),
   `templates = {"object/mobile/<existing_iff>.iff"}` (reuse existing mesh),
   `CreatureTemplates:addCreatureTemplate(my_beast, "my_beast")`, `includeFile(...)` it.
2. New lair file referencing `mobiles = {{"my_beast",1}}`, `addLairTemplate(...)`.
3. Reference that lair from an existing (or new) spawn group's `lairSpawns`.
4. If new spawn group: add/adjust a region tuple in `<planet>_regions.lua`.
5. Restart the server (no rebuild).

## 3. Screenplays / Quests

**Base class:** `screenplays/screenplay.lua` -- `ScreenPlay = Object:new{...}`.
Minimal pattern:
```lua
MyQuest = ScreenPlay:new{ numberOfActs = 1 }
registerScreenPlay("MyQuest", true)  -- true = autostart at server load
function MyQuest:start() self:spawnMobiles() end
```

**Folder layout** under `screenplays/`: `tasks/<planet>/` (most real quests,
plus `epic_quests`, `hero_of_tatooine`, `defector_quests`, `misc`),
`quest_tasks/` (reusable objective modules: `go_to_location`, `escort`,
`patrol`, `encounter`), `dungeon/`, `caves/`, `poi/`, `trainers/`, `sui/`, `tutorial/`.

**C++ Lua bridge:** `src/server/zone/managers/director/DirectorManager.cpp`
exposes: `registerScreenPlay`, `includeFile`, `createEvent`/`createServerEvent`,
`createObserver`/`dropObserver` (event constants like `KILLEDCREATURE`,
`OBJECTDESTRUCTION`, `ENTEREDAREA`, `CONVERSE`), `spawnMobile`/`spawnSceneObject`/
`spawnActiveArea`/`spawnBuilding`, `createLoot`/`createLootSet`, `giveItem`,
`spatialChat`, `setQuestStatus`/`getQuestStatus` (shared-memory state),
`awardSkill`, `sendMail`.

**Two separate quest systems:**
- **Mission terminals** (bounty/crafting/entertainer/combat) --
  `src/server/zone/objects/mission/*.idl` (`MissionObject`,
  `DeliverMissionObjective`, `DestroyMissionObjective`, etc.) -- unrelated to screenplays.
- **Datapad journal** -- native `PlayerObject` methods: `activateJournalQuest`,
  `activateJournalQuestTask`, `completeJournalQuestTask`, `completeJournalQuest`,
  `addWaypoint`. Backing data is client-format IFF: `datatables/player/quests.iff`
  (schema in `managers/player/QuestInfo.h`), `misc/quest_crc_string_table.iff`,
  per-quest `datatables/questtask/<questname>.iff` -- same TRE/IFF/STF toolchain
  already built for the companion skill tree work (`docs/companion_system/tools/`).

**Recipe -- simple quest (no real datapad entry, shared-memory state only):**
1. `screenplays/tasks/<planet>/my_quest.lua`, `ScreenPlay:new{...}`,
   `registerScreenPlay("MyQuest", true)`.
2. `:start()` spawns quest giver + target creatures via `spawnMobile`.
3. Wire NPC conversation (same ConvoTemplate pattern as trainers) to call
   `MyQuest:giveQuest(pPlayer)`; track progress with `setQuestStatus`/`getQuestStatus`.
4. `createObserver(KILLEDCREATURE, "MyQuest", "notifyKilled", pPlayer)` to count
   kills; on completion `dropObserver`, hand out reward via `giveItem`/`createLoot`/
   `awardExperience`.
5. `includeFile("tasks/<planet>/my_quest.lua")` in `screenplays/screenplays.lua`.

**Recipe -- real "Active Quests" datapad entry:** additionally needs a row in
`quests.iff`, a CRC entry, a `questtask/<name>.iff`, and STF journal text,
repacked into a patch `.tre` (reuse `docs/companion_system/tools/`), then call
the native `activateJournalQuest*`/`completeJournalQuest*` methods from Lua
instead of ad-hoc shared-memory state.

## 4. Buildings, Cells, and Dungeons/Caves/Bunkers

**C++ hierarchy:** `TangibleObject → StructureObject → BuildingObject`.
`BuildingObject` (`src/server/zone/objects/building/`) holds
`VectorMap<uint, CellObject> cells`, `createCellObjects()`, `getCell(idx/name)`.
Player housing, guild halls, and static world buildings are the **same class**
-- difference is data-driven flags, not a separate hierarchy. `PoiBuilding`
extends it for despawn-on-no-players dynamic POIs. `CellObject`
(`objects/cell/`) is just a numbered container; cell *shape/geometry* comes
entirely from client-side `.iff`/`.pob` data -- the server only knows cell
*count and IDs*.

**Important limitation:** there is no Lua "place a new building" API for
*static world* structures. These (including every cave/dungeon shell) come
from a client-authored **World Snapshot** loaded per-zone at boot
(`src/templates/snapshot/WorldSnapshotIff.{h,cpp}`), which fixes each
building's object ID, position, and cell IDs. **This repo cannot create new
building geometry** -- that requires external client-side tools/data not
present here. (Section 21a now has a verified, byte-level breakdown of the
`.ws` format itself -- it's more tractable than this note used to imply,
including appending one new node with an *existing* model, but comes with a
real objectID-collision risk against the live database allocator that has
to be solved first; see 21a for the concrete recipe and open question.)

**Player-driven structure placement is a separate, fully generic, data-driven
pipeline -- unrelated to world snapshots.** A player places a house/harvester/
factory/guild-hall via a deed: `PlaceStructureCommand`
(`objects/creature/commands/PlaceStructureCommand.h`) does client-facing
validation (range, no-build zones) then `deed->placeStructure()` runs the
*same* `PlaceStructureComponent` for every deed type (house, harvester,
guild hall, GCW base all use the literal string
`placeStructureComponent = "PlaceStructureComponent"`), which hands off to
**`StructureManager::placeStructureFromDeed()`**
(`managers/structure/StructureManager.cpp:270-476`) for the real checks:
per-planet zone whitelist, no-build-zone/POI-distance, and a real
footprint-overlap algorithm (`getStructureFootprint()`, rotates the
template's grid footprint into a world-space box and tests overlap against
every nearby structure -- no terrain-slope check exists for buildings,
unlike mob spawning/camping which do check slope). A timed
`PlaceStructureSession` (construction delay = `lotSize * 3000`ms, with a
temporary no-build `ActiveArea` around the site) then calls
`StructureManager::placeStructure()` to actually spawn the real
`BuildingObject`/`InstallationObject` and grant the placer `ADMIN`.

**Permissions** live on every structure as a `StructurePermissionList`
(6 fixed lists: `ADMIN/ENTRY/HOPPER/BAN/VENDOR/QUEST`, cap 50 entries each) --
`isOnAdminList()`/`isOnEntryList()`/`isOnBanList()` resolve membership
(guild-wide grants fall back to checking the player's guild against the
list too). Edited via a plain slash command,
**`PermissionListModifyCommand`** (`<target> <listName> <add|remove|toggle>`)
-- not the generic `SuiListBox` pattern from section 7, a genuine deviation
-- which pushes updates live via a dedicated `PermissionListCreateMessage`
packet and, for guild grants, a `GuildStructurePermissionsTask` that updates
every online guild member's cell access.

**Decoration cap** is a hard, hardcoded limit, not the generic container
volume-limit system (cells bypass that entirely --
`containerVolumeLimit = -1` in `cell.lua`, never consulted).
`CellObjectImplementation::canAddObject()` checks
`getCurrentNumberOfPlayerItems() + count > getMaximumNumberOfPlayerItems()`,
where the max is `min(400, lots * 100)` (civic structures get a flat 250;
`MAXPLAYERITEMS = 400` is the global ceiling, `BuildingObject.idl:63`) --
so item cap is directly a function of how many lots the structure costs.
Furniture move/rotate are dedicated commands (`MoveFurnitureCommand`,
`RotateFurnitureCommand`), not a generic drag API, both requiring `ADMIN`
(or `VENDOR` list membership for vendor objects).

**Maintenance/upkeep** is a real decay simulation, not just a credit sink:
`surplusMaintenance` (a float) drains at `baseMaintenanceRate/hour` (plus a
city property-tax add-on if the structure sits in a city with
`getPropertyTax() > 0`); once negative, the *shortfall is applied directly
as condition damage* (`setConditionDamage(-surplusMaintenance)` --
maintenance debt and hitpoint decay are the same number). A weekly
`StructureMaintenanceTask` auto-pays from the owner's bank if funds allow;
otherwise the structure is condemned, and after a hardcoded **30 days**
(`getDelayDestroyHours()`) still in the hole, `StructureManager::
destroyStructure()` deletes it and wipes its contents.

**Recipe -- add a wholly new placeable structure type (reusing an existing
client model):** zero new C++ classes needed. (1) A deed Lua template
(`object/tangible/deed/<category>/*.lua`) with
`placeStructureComponent = "PlaceStructureComponent"` and
`generatedObjectTemplate` pointing at the target building/installation
`.iff`. (2) A structure template Lua (`object/building/**` or
`object/installation/**`) setting `lotSize`, `baseMaintenanceRate`,
`allowedZones`, `length`/`width` (-> footprint), and optionally
`cityMaintenanceBase`/`cityRankRequired`/`uniqueStructure` if it should be
civic/commercial. (3) Register both templates the normal way (section 1's
pattern). The one hard constraint: `generatedObjectTemplate` must point at
a client `.iff` model that already exists in the TRE data -- a genuinely
new decorative shape is still out of reach, but a new harvester variant,
reskinned house, or new guild-hall variant with different stats is a pure
data addition.

**What a "dungeon" actually is here:** a pre-placed building+cells (from the
world snapshot, fixed object IDs) that a ScreenPlay populates with mobiles,
loot, and terminals at hardcoded x/y/z/cellID coordinates. Real example:
Death Watch Bunker --
`mobile/dungeon/death_watch_bunker/*.lua` (mob templates) +
`screenplays/dungeon/death_watch_bunker/deathWatchBunker.lua` (the populator:
`getSceneObject(5996314)` to grab the pre-placed building, then
`spawnMobiles()`/`spawnObjects()` using `spawnMobile(zone, template,
respawn, x,z,y, heading, cellID)` / `spawnSceneObject(zone, template,
x,z,y, cellID, ...)`) + `deathWatchSpawnMap.lua` (pure data: coordinate/cellID
tables). Other real dungeons (`warren`, `geonosian_bio_lab`,
`corellian_corvette`) follow the identical two-file pattern.

**Recipe -- populate a new dungeon/cave/bunker (realistic without client tools):**
1. Find an existing, already-placed-in-the-world building instance with spare
   interior cells (e.g. a generic `cave_01.iff`/`cave_02.iff` shell) and its
   object ID -- reuse its cells rather than trying to create a new building.
2. New mob templates under `mobile/dungeon/<my_dungeon>/*.lua` (standard
   `Creature:new{...}` pattern) + `serverobjects.lua` registering them.
3. New loot under `loot/groups/`/`loot/items/`, referenced from the mobs.
4. New ScreenPlay `screenplays/dungeon/<my_dungeon>/myDungeon.lua`:
   `getSceneObject(<building_id>)`, then `spawnMobile`/`spawnSceneObject` calls
   at the reused building's actual cell IDs.
5. `includeFile(...)` the screenplay in `screenplays/screenplays.lua`.

Genuinely new dungeon *geometry* is out of scope for server-side work alone.

---

## 5. Resources & Harvesters

**Resource types/spawning:** `src/server/zone/managers/resource/resourcespawner/`
-- `ResourceSpawner.cpp` orchestrates spawn pools (`Minimum/Fixed/Random/Native/ManualPool`)
against a `ResourceTree`; `ResourceSpawner::shiftResources()` (driven by
`ResourceShiftTask.h`) periodically rolls new resource spawns. Resource stat
names (`res_quality`→OQ, `res_cold_resist`→CR, `res_conductivity`→CD,
`res_decay_resist`→DR, `res_heat_resist`→HR, `res_malleability`→MA,
`res_shock_resistance`→SR, `res_toughness`→UT, `res_flavor`→FL,
`res_potential_energy`→PE) map in `resourcetree/ResourceAttribute.h`.
Data: `bin/scripts/managers/resource_manager_spawns.lua` (resource
type/class/attribute definitions) and `resource_manager.lua` (global tuning:
`averageShiftTime`, `spawnThrottling`, pool membership).
Planet concentration: `ResourceSpawn::getDensityAt(zoneName, x, y)`
(`objects/resource/ResourceSpawnImplementation.cpp`).

**Extraction math (the important part):**
`InstallationObjectImplementation.cpp` (`objects/installation/`) --
`updateHopper()` (~line 392):
```cpp
float harvestAmount = (elapsedTime / 60.0) * (spawnDensity * getExtractionRate());
```
capped by remaining hopper space. `getActualRate()` = `extractionRate *
spawnDensity` (the number shown to players). Fields `extractionRate` /
`hopperSizeMax` live on `InstallationObject.idl` (defaults 100 / 10000).
**No player skill mod is currently applied here** -- adding a "faster
harvesting" skill mod would mean editing this method.

**Where the numbers come from (deed → placement):**
`StructureDeed.idl` holds a deed-level `extractionRate`, set at manufacture
time in `StructureDeedImplementation::updateCraftingValues()` from the
crafted item's `extractrate`/`hoppersize` experimental values; on placement
`PlaceStructureComponent.cpp` copies deed → installation
(`setExtractionRate`/`setHopperSizeMax`). Per-tier min/max ranges live in
deed Lua, e.g. `object/tangible/deed/harvester_deed/harvester_ore_heavy_deed.lua`:
```lua
experimentalSubGroupTitles = {"null","null","extractrate","hoppersize","hitpoints"},
experimentalMin = {0, 0, 3, 100000, 1000},
experimentalMax = {0, 0, 7, 150000, 1000},
```
(compare the personal-tier deed's much lower range).

**Recipe -- speed up harvesters:**
- **Server-wide multiplier (all tiers):** edit the `harvestAmount` formula in
  `InstallationObjectImplementation::updateHopper()` (C++, needs rebuild).
- **Per-tier boost, no C++:** raise `experimentalMin`/`experimentalMax` for
  `"extractrate"` (and `"hoppersize"`) in the relevant
  `object/tangible/deed/harvester_deed/*.lua` file. No rebuild needed.
- **New higher tier:** copy an existing deed Lua + its installation Lua,
  new `.iff` template paths, higher extractrate/hoppersize ranges, register
  both via `ObjectTemplates:addTemplate(...)`, wire into schematics/serverobjects.

### Hot spots -- the actual concentration/density mechanism

This is the part that answers "how does a survey tool show rich patches on
the map" -- it's a real 3D Simplex noise field, not a lookup table, generated
fresh every time a resource spawns:

- **`SpawnDensityMap`** (`src/server/zone/objects/resource/SpawnDensityMap.h`)
  wraps `SimplexNoise::noise(x, y, z)` (`simplexnoise/SimplexNoise.h`).
  `initialize()` (lines 128-153) picks a random `seed`, a spatial `modifier`
  (`0.00015f` for ore-type resources, `0.0006f` for everything else -- smaller
  modifier = broader, smoother hot spots; larger = tighter/noisier), and a
  `density` ceiling drawn from one of three tiers:
  - `HIGHDENSITY`: 90-99%
  - `MEDIUMDENSITY`: 75-95%
  - `LOWDENSITY`: 50-75%
- **`getDensityAt(x, y)`** (`SpawnDensityMap.h:106-115`) normalizes the
  coordinate against the zone's bounding box, samples the noise field, clamps
  negative values to 0 (dead ground) and scales positive values by `density`
  -- the resulting float *is* the "hot spot" value a survey ping shows.
- **Which tier a resource type gets** --
  `ResourceSpawnImplementation::getConcentration()`
  (`ResourceSpawnImplementation.cpp:144-158`): `chemical`/`gas_inert`
  (and anything JTL) -> HIGH; `ore`/`water`/unlimited solar/wind -> LOW;
  everything else -> MEDIUM. **This is the one function to edit to change how
  rich a resource class's hot spots run.**
- **Survey tool query chain** (client ping -> server density lookup -> radar
  blips): `RequestSurveyCommand.h` -> `SurveySessionImplementation::startSurvey()`
  -> `ResourceManagerImplementation::sendSurvey()` -> `ResourceSpawner::sendSurvey()`
  (`ResourceSpawner.cpp:798-893`) builds an N×N grid (3-6 points per side,
  range from the survey tool's own stats) centered on the player, samples
  `getDensityAt()` at every grid point, drops a waypoint on the strongest hit
  (`maxDensity >= 0.1f`), and packages every sample into a `SurveyMessage`
  packet -- that packet's per-point float values are literally what paints
  the client's radar-blip UI. Sampling/harvesting (as opposed to scanning) is
  the same density value consumed by `ResourceSpawner::sendSampleResults()`.
- **Spawn lifetime / rotation:** each `ResourceSpawn` has a `despawned` unix
  timestamp (`inShift()` checks it); `ResourceShiftTask`
  (`managers/resource/ResourceShiftTask.h`) fires every `averageShiftTime` ms
  (config, default 2h) and calls `ResourceSpawner::shiftResources()`, which
  walks all 5 pools (`Minimum/Fixed/Random/Native/ManualPool`) and replaces any
  expired spawn with a brand-new type + a **freshly-seeded** `SpawnDensityMap`
  -- this is why hot spots move around over a server's lifetime rather than
  staying fixed.
- **GM tools for testing new resource types without waiting for a shift:**
  `/gmcreatespecificresource <type> [attrib,value ...]` and
  `/gmcreateclassresource` (both -> `ResourceSpawner::manualCreateResourceSpawn()`,
  `ResourceSpawner.cpp:419-477`) instantiate immediately (still with an
  auto-generated density map) with attribute overrides you specify, slotted
  into the `manualPool`. `/resource despawn <name>` forces an existing spawn
  to expire so the next shift replaces it; `/resource info <name>` dumps its
  expiration/pool/attribute values; `/resource find <class> <attr> gt|lt
  <value>` locates live spawns matching a filter.

**Recipe -- add a new resource type / tune its hot spots:**
1. New type/class needs a row in the client `resource_tree.iff` datatable
   (`datatables/resource/resource_tree.iff`, loaded by
   `ResourceTree::buildTreeFromClient()`, `ResourceTree.cpp:29-133`) -- class
   chain, min/max pool (how many planets), attribute min/max ranges. This is
   client-format binary data; reuse the IFF/TRE tooling in
   `docs/companion_system/tools/` (`iff_datatable.py` is a generic DTII codec,
   not skill-specific) to patch it.
2. Put its name in the right pool-include table in
   `bin/scripts/managers/resource_manager.lua`
   (`minimumpoolincludes`/`randompoolincludes`/`fixedpoolincludes`/`nativepoolincludes`),
   or leave it pool-less and only spawn it via the GM commands above.
3. To change richness tier, edit `ResourceSpawnImplementation::getConcentration()`
   (C++, rebuild); to change hot-spot shape, edit the `modifier` constants in
   `SpawnDensityMap::initialize()` (C++, rebuild).
4. Restart (Lua/datatable changes only need a restart; the two C++ tweaks
   above need a rebuild first).

## 6. Commands (slash-command dispatch pipeline)

**Base class:** every slash command (`/hpet`, `/attack`, `/invite`, ...) is a
C++ class extending `QueueCommand`
(`src/server/zone/objects/creature/commands/QueueCommand.h` -- corrected
path, previously mis-stated here as `objects/scene/`) or, for combat
abilities specifically, `CombatQueueCommand` (see section 7 of the combat
writeup above). Real non-combat example from this project:
`src/server/zone/objects/creature/commands/HpetCommand.h` and its four
siblings (`CompanionFollowCommand.h`, `CompanionStayCommand.h`,
`CompanionPatrolCommand.h`, `CompanionStoreCommand.h`).

**Full dispatch loop, click/type to execution** (confirmed by direct read,
2026-07-13): a typed/clicked command becomes a `CommandQueueAction` pushed
onto a per-creature `CommandQueue` (`server/zone/objects/creature/
CommandQueue.cpp`) via `enqueueCommand()` -- capped at 5 queued actions for
an AI agent, 15 for a player. `getNextAction()`/`handleRunningState()`
select the next action by `QueueCommand::getDefaultPriority()`
(`IMMEDIATE` jumps the queue unless the creature `hasAttackDelay()`,
`FRONT` jumps normal-priority actions but not other immediates, `NORMAL`
waits its turn) and hold off on anything with `addToCombatQueue()==true`
while a posture-change or attack delay is active. The actual dispatch call
is `ObjectControllerImplementation::activateCommand()`
(`managers/objectcontroller/ObjectControllerImplementation.cpp:71`) --
this is where the `characterAbility` gate lives
(`playerObject->hasAbility(characterAbility)`, the exact mechanism the
companion macro-list commands' `command_table.iff` `characterAbility`
column relies on), where admin-command permission is checked, and where
`doQueueCommand()` finally gets invoked. On success, `onComplete()`
clears the client-side queue entry; on any non-`SUCCESS` return,
`onFail()` maps the error code to a system message and clears the queue
instead.

**Entry point:** `int doQueueCommand(CreatureObject* creature, const uint64&
target, const UnicodeString& arguments) const` — this is where all the real
logic goes. Standard opening guards: `checkStateMask(creature)` and
`checkInvalidLocomotions(creature)`, both inherited, return `INVALIDSTATE`/
`INVALIDLOCOMOTION` early if the player can't currently act (e.g. mid-combat,
sitting, dead). Return codes are the `int` constants defined on `QueueCommand`
itself (`SUCCESS`, `GENERALERROR`, `INVALIDPARAMETERS`, ...).

**Registration:** every command class must be registered by name in
`src/server/zone/managers/objectcontroller/command/CommandConfigManager{2,3,4}.cpp`:
```cpp
commandFactory.registerCommand<HpetCommand>(String("hpet").toLowerCase());
```
The registered name is what both `/hpet ...` typed in chat *and* a skill's
`COMMANDS` field in `skills.iff` (see section 9) refer to — a command exists
in the engine the moment it's registered here, but a *player* can only use it
once some skill they've learned lists it in that skill's `COMMANDS` column
(comma-separated list of command names). `companion_master_novice`'s own
`COMMANDS="hpet,companionfollow,companionstay,companionpatrol,companionstore"`
is the real example already in this codebase.

**Recipe — add one new non-combat slash command:**
1. New header `src/server/zone/objects/creature/commands/MyCommand.h`
   extending `QueueCommand`, modeled on `HpetCommand.h` — constructor takes
   `(const String& name, ZoneProcessServer* server)`, implement
   `doQueueCommand()`.
2. `#include` it and add
   `commandFactory.registerCommand<MyCommand>(String("mycommand").toLowerCase());`
   in `CommandConfigManager2.cpp` (or 3/4, they're just split for compile-time
   parallelism, no functional difference).
3. Grant it to players by adding `"mycommand"` to some skill's `COMMANDS`
   field in the relevant `skills.iff` patch (own custom profession) or an
   existing one if you're extending stock content.
4. Rebuild (`ninja -C build/unix/ninja-debug core3`), restart.

**Pattern for N near-identical command variants (avoid N hand-written
classes):** `CompanionAbilityCommand.h`
(`objects/companion/commands/CompanionAbilityCommand.h`, added for the
companion macro-list pass) is one single `QueueCommand` class registered
under 36 different names (`CommandConfigManager2.cpp`); it derives which
underlying action to invoke *at runtime* from its own registered name
(`getQueueCommandName()`, strip a known prefix, hash the rest) rather than
having 36 separate classes each hardcoding one action. Reuse this shape any
time you need many thin command variants that all reduce to "look up X from
my own name, then dispatch the same way" -- one class, many
`registerCommand<T>(name)` lines, instead of a class-per-name.

## 7. SUI (Screen UI) — server-driven dialog boxes

Every non-trivial "click a button, get a list/prompt/confirmation" UI (train
lists, confirmation dialogs, the companion dialogue menu) is a **SUI box** —
a server-constructed dialog the client renders generically, not a
client-authored UI resource. Real, fully-worked examples in this project:
`server/zone/managers/companion/CompanionSkillTrainer.cpp`'s
`sendDialogMenu()`/`sendTrainList()`/`sendHelpSheet()`.

**Construction pattern** (`SuiListBox`, `SuiInputBox`, `SuiMessageBox` etc.
all live under `src/server/zone/objects/player/sui/`):
```cpp
ghost->closeSuiWindowType(SuiWindowType::MY_WINDOW); // avoid stacking dupes
ManagedReference<SuiListBox*> sui = new SuiListBox(player, SuiWindowType::MY_WINDOW);
sui->setPromptTitle("@my_stf:my_title");
sui->setPromptText("@my_stf:my_text");
sui->setCancelButton(true, "@ui:cancel");
sui->setOkButton(true, "@ui:ok");
sui->setCallback(new MySuiCallback(player->getZoneServer(), someArg));
sui->addMenuItem("@my_stf:option_one"); // index 0
sui->addMenuItem("@my_stf:option_two"); // index 1
ghost->addSuiBox(sui);
player->sendMessage(sui->generateMessage());
```
All prompt/button/menu-item text is an STF key (`@table:key`), same STF
tables/TRE toolchain as everything else client-visible
(`docs/companion_system/tools/`).

**Full SUI box catalog** (all under `src/server/zone/objects/player/sui/`,
all extend `SuiBox`, box-type constants at `SuiBox.idl:70-82`):

| Class | Purpose | Real usage |
|---|---|---|
| `SuiListBox` | scrollable option list (the one shown above) | throughout this project's companion dialogs |
| `SuiInputBox` | single text-entry prompt, optional char-filter mode | `StructureManager.cpp:1085` (rename), `GuildManagerImplementation.cpp:486` (guild name) |
| `SuiMessageBox` | plain confirm/info, no input | `VendorManager.cpp:223`, `GroupManager.cpp:652` |
| `SuiTransferBox` | two-pane quantity transfer with ratios | `InstallationObjectImplementation.cpp:205` (harvester energy), `CityManagerImplementation.cpp:604` (city treasury) |
| `SuiBankTransferBox` | transfer box hardwired to cash↔bank credits | `BankTerminalMenuComponent.cpp:67` |
| `SuiColorBox` | color-palette picker, `skillMod`-gated | `ArmorObjectMenuComponent.cpp:81` (dye), `GogglesObjectMenuComponent.cpp:59` |
| `SuiKeypadBox` | numeric keypad entry | `SuiManager.cpp:727` |
| `SuiSlotMachineBox` | extends `SuiListBox`, adds gambling payout box ID | `GamblingManagerImplementation.cpp:90` |
| `SuiFireworkDelayBox` | extends `SuiTransferBox`, per-event delay tuning | `FireworkShowModifyEventSuiCallback.h:57` |
| `SuiCharacterBuilderBox` | extends `SuiListBox`, walks a menu-node tree | `CharacterBuilderTerminalImplementation.cpp:56` (GM/dev tool) |

**Callback pattern** — subclass `SuiCallback`
(`src/server/zone/objects/player/sui/SuiCallback.h`):
```cpp
void run(CreatureObject* player, SuiBox* suiBox, uint32 eventIndex, Vector<UnicodeString>* args) {
    if (eventIndex == 1 || player == nullptr) return; // eventIndex==1 == Cancel
    int selection = Integer::valueOf(args->get(0).toString()); // list-box selection index
    ...
}
```
Real worked example: `server/zone/managers/companion/callbacks/CompanionDialogMenuSuiCallback.h`.

**Window-type registry:** every SUI window needs a unique ID in the
`SuiWindowType` enum (`src/server/zone/objects/player/sui/SuiWindowType.h`).
Custom features should claim a small contiguous block rather than scattering
IDs — this project's convention (companion system reserved `1200-1210`) is
worth following for any new subsystem.

**Recipe — add a new list/confirmation dialog:**
1. Reserve a new `SuiWindowType` value (pick an unused block, e.g. the next
   free 10-value range after `1210`).
2. New callback header under an appropriate `callbacks/` folder, extending
   `SuiCallback`, implementing `run()`.
3. A `sendMyDialog(CreatureObject* player, ...)` method somewhere sensible
   (a manager or the object itself) building/sending the `SuiListBox`/`SuiInputBox`
   as above.
4. Add any new prompt/option STF strings via the TRE toolchain if the text is
   new (`docs/companion_system/tools/`).
5. Call `sendMyDialog()` from wherever the player triggers it (a command, a
   radial option — see section 8).

## 8. Object Menus / Radial Wheel

The right-click radial menu on any object is a **client/server hybrid**, and
the split matters: the client proposes its own default radial items based on
the object's `gameObjectType` (baked into the `ObjectMenuRequest` packet the
client sends, with **zero server-side validation** of what it claims to
offer), and the server's `ObjectMenuComponent` only ever **appends** extra
items on top — it never removes or overrides client defaults. Full ID enum:
`src/server/zone/managers/radial/RadialOptions.h` (234 values). **Correction:**
reserved custom slots for new server-only options are actually
`SERVER_MENU1..10` (ten generic values after `SERVER_DIVIDER`,
`RadialOptions.h:82-93`) — not 4. Real objects needing more than that (like
the companion device, which reuses `SERVER_MENU4` for two mutually-exclusive
states depending on object state) have to get creative or add real new
context to disambiguate. Also note: radial IDs are only unique *per
component instance*, not globally — `BankTerminalMenuComponent`
(`.../components/BankTerminalMenuComponent.h:15-22`) defines its own private
enum (`JOIN=71, WITHDRAW=68, ...`, aliasing the SERVER_MENU numeric range on
purpose) and attaches them as children of radial ID `20` (`ITEM_USE`) rather
than using `RadialOptions::SERVER_MENU*` at all — a component is free to
invent its own local numbering as long as its own
`fillObjectMenuResponse()`/`handleObjectMenuSelect()` pair agree with each
other; they don't have to come from the shared enum.

**Component hierarchy** (`src/server/zone/objects/scene/components/` and
subtype folders): base `ObjectMenuComponent` (generic pickup/rotate for
furniture-like objects) → `TangibleObjectMenuComponent` (adds Slice/View
Components, the generic tangible default) → `PetMenuComponent extends
TangibleObjectMenuComponent` (real pet in-world menu). **There is no
`IntangibleObjectMenuComponent`** — intangible objects (control devices,
etc.) have `objectMenuComponent == nullptr` by default unless explicitly set
via `setObjectMenuComponent("SomeComponentName")` (either from the object's
Lua template's `objectMenuComponent` field, or at runtime in C++, e.g.
`CompanionControlDeviceImplementation::spawnObject()` calling
`companion->setObjectMenuComponent("CompanionMenuComponent")`).

**The pair every custom component implements**
(`src/server/zone/objects/companion/components/CompanionMenuComponent.{h,cpp}`
is a complete real example):
```cpp
void fillObjectMenuResponse(SceneObject*, ObjectMenuResponse* menuResponse, CreatureObject* player) const;
// menuResponse->addRadialMenuItem(RadialOptions::SERVER_MENU1, 3, "@my_stf:my_label");
int handleObjectMenuSelect(SceneObject*, CreatureObject* player, byte selectedID) const;
// switch(selectedID) { case RadialOptions::SERVER_MENU1: ... }
```
**Known gotcha (root-caused this project, see `docs/companion_system/NOTES.md`):**
the client does not necessarily send the ID your own component thinks is
canonical for "the base action" (e.g. `ITEM_ACTIVATE`) — for many
`gameObjectType` categories the client's own baked-in default sends a
specific literal ID (e.g. real `PetControlDevice` handles literal `44`/`59`,
`RadialOptions::PET_CALL`/`PET_STORE`, never `ITEM_ACTIVATE`). Always check
what a close real precedent object of the same/similar `gameObjectType`
actually checks for in its own `handleObjectMenuSelect()`, don't assume.

**Recipe — add a custom radial option to an existing object type:**
1. Confirm/create the object's `objectMenuComponent` (Lua template field or
   runtime `setObjectMenuComponent()` call).
2. New/edit `<Type>MenuComponent.{h,cpp}` under
   `src/server/zone/objects/.../components/`, add the item in
   `fillObjectMenuResponse()` using one of the 4 `SERVER_MENU1-4` slots (or a
   documented real ID if you're intentionally matching client-default
   behavior for that GOT), handle it in `handleObjectMenuSelect()`.
3. Register the component name in `ComponentManager.cpp` (`#include` +
   `components.put("MyMenuComponent", new MyMenuComponent());`) if it's a
   brand-new component class.
4. Rebuild, restart.

## 9. Skills & XP

**Schema:** every skill/profession is a row in `datatables/skill/skills.iff`
(client-side binary datatable, patched via the TRE toolchain — see
`docs/companion_system/NOTES.md` for the full binary-format writeup and
`docs/companion_system/tools/build_companion_content.py` for a complete
worked example authoring 20 real rows). Key columns: `NAME`, `PARENT`
(tree-graph edge for layout, **not** prerequisite — see the PARENT-vs-
SKILLS_REQUIRED note in `build_companion_content.py`), `GRAPH_TYPE` (only
`1`=single-branch-chain, `4`=four-branch-tree, and `5`=pyramid are ever
used by any real profession), `IS_PROFESSION`, `IS_TITLE` (grants a player
title, needs a matching `skl_t.stf` entry), `SKILLS_REQUIRED`/
`SKILLS_REQUIRED_COUNT`, `XP_TYPE`/`XP_COST`/`XP_CAP`, `COMMANDS`
(comma-separated command names granted — see section 6), `SKILL_MODS`
(comma-separated `name=value` pairs, see below), `SEARCHABLE`.

**Display strings** — every skill/profession needs matching STF entries
(same `string/en/` TRE location as everything else client-visible):
`skl_n.stf` (box display name, **required** or the box shows raw `@skl_n:key`),
`skl_t.stf` (player title, only for `IS_TITLE=1` rows), `skl_d.stf`
(description shown in the skills window), and if it grants new commands,
`cmd_n.stf`/`cmd_d.stf`. `exp_n.stf` separately names whatever `XP_TYPE`
pool the skill draws from (only needed once per distinct XP type, not per
skill).

**C++ side** — `src/server/zone/managers/skill/SkillManager.{h,cpp}`:
`awardSkill(skillName, creature, ...)` grants a skill (checks prerequisites
via `canLearnSkill()`/`fulfillsSkillPrerequisites()`/
`fulfillsSkillPrerequisitesAndXp()`), `creature->hasSkill(name)` checks
possession, `surrenderSkill()` removes one. XP itself is granted via
`PlayerManager::awardExperience(player, xpType, amount, ...)` — a skill's
`XP_COST` is checked against however much of that `xpType` pool the player
has accumulated; `xp_limits.iff` sets each pool's overall cap.

**Skill Points are a separate pool from XP, and the 250 total is hardcoded,
not data.** A skill box costs *both* `pointsRequired` (col 8 of `skills.iff`,
`Skill.h:96-119`) *and* `xpCost` simultaneously, deducted together in
`awardSkill` (`SkillManager.cpp:329,369,372`). The player's SP field is a
flat int (`PlayerObject.idl:224 protected int skillPoints`) with **no stored
max** — `awardSkill`/`surrenderSkill` instead recompute
`int totalSkillPointsWasted = 250;` and subtract every learned skill's cost
each time (`SkillManager.cpp:436-450, 724-735`), logging a mismatch warning
and self-correcting if it drifts. **250 is a hardcoded C++ constant, not a
datatable value** — changing the real per-character SP budget needs a code
change, not a data patch.

**Two `skills.iff` columns are parsed but dead — don't rely on them.**
`preclusionSkills` (mutual-exclusion trees) and `apprenticeshipsRequired`
are both read into `Skill` (`Skill.h:39,105,148-152`) but **never checked**
anywhere in `SkillManager::fulfillsSkillPrerequisites()`
(`SkillManager.cpp:995-1045`) — mutually-exclusive skill lines are not
server-enforced today despite the schema supporting it.

**XP types are just arbitrary strings, not a fixed enum** — whatever
`XP_TYPE` values appear in `skills.iff` (plus a handful of hardcoded
combat/crafting types in `PlayerManagerImplementation.cpp`) become keys into
`PlayerObject.idl:128 experienceList`/`:122 xpTypeCapList`. Caps are the
**max** `XP_CAP` across every skill box a player owns for that type
(`SkillManager::updateXpLimits`, `SkillManager.cpp:879-926`, recomputed on
every skill grant/surrender), falling back to `xp_limits.iff`'s default, or a
hardcoded `2000` if the type appears nowhere (`PlayerObjectImplementation.cpp:754-762`).
Any `prestige_`-prefixed type is uncapped. XP over a newly-lowered cap is
immediately clawed back.

**Skill mods stack additively within a source category, then additively
across categories — there is no override precedence.**
`SkillModList::add()`/`getSkillMod()`
(`objects/creature/variables/SkillModList.h:76-91, 150-170`): same-named
mods from the same category (`SKILLBOX`, `WEARABLE`, `BUFF`, `STRUCTURE`,
`CITY`, `DROID`, `ABILITYBONUS`, ...) sum together and get clamped to that
category's min/max (`WEARABLE` ±25, `BUFF`/`STRUCTURE`/`ABILITYBONUS` ±125,
`DROID` ±110 by default, `SkillModManager.cpp:80-92`; `SKILLBOX`/`CITY` are
unbounded) — then **all categories' clamped totals are summed** for the
final value `creature->getSkillMod("name")` returns. So e.g.
`melee_accuracy` from a skill box + worn armor + a food buff + a city
specialization bonus all land in separate buckets and simply add up.

**Adding a real elective profession needs zero C++** — the trainer-NPC path
mirrors what the companion trainer already imitates:
`scripts/screenplays/trainers/trainerData.lua` maps a trainer "type" string
to an ordered list of skill-box names (`trainerSkills["trainer_<name>"] =
{...}`); `trainerConvHandler.lua`'s `handleConfirmLearnScreen` checks credits
then calls `LuaSkillManager:awardSkill(...)` — the real transaction, fully
generic over any `skillName`. A new profession needs: `skills.iff` rows +
STF strings (as above) + one new `trainerSkills[...]` entry + one
`createTrainerConversationTemplate(name, "trainer_<name>")` call
(`screenplays/trainers/trainer_conv.lua`) + one trainer NPC Lua file
(model on the real `trainer_1hsword.lua`/`trainer_companion_master.lua`).
Only a **selectable-at-character-creation** base profession additionally
needs a `creation/profession_defaults.iff` row (separate binary file,
loaded by `PlayerCreationManager::loadProfessionDefaultsInfo`,
`PlayerCreationManager.cpp:112-146`, supplies starting HAM/items/novice
skill) — still data, no C++. For testing without building the conversation
tree, `/grantSkill <name>` (`GrantSkillCommand.h:19-59`) is the real
admin-only direct-grant command, bypassing money/XP/trainer entirely.
**`SKILL_MODS` are purely informational unless something explicitly reads
them** — `creature->getSkillMod("name")` is the consumer-side call; if
nothing in the C++ source calls `getSkillMod()` with your mod's exact name,
it renders correctly in the skill sheet but does nothing (confirmed real
example of both states in this project: `companion_threat_response`/etc.
are still decorative, while the Resilience branch's effect was hand-wired
into `CompanionControlDeviceImplementation::handleCompanionDeath()` by
directly counting `hasSkill("companion_master_resilience_0N")` ranks rather
than via `getSkillMod()` — both patterns are legitimate, `getSkillMod()`
is for stackable numeric mods, direct `hasSkill()` rank-counting is simpler
for small fixed tiers).

**Recipe — add one new skill box to an existing tree, granting a command:**
1. New row in the relevant `skills.iff` patch: set `NAME`, `PARENT` (tier-1
   rows parent to the profession itself; tier-2+ parent to the previous
   tier), `GRAPH_TYPE` matching the tree's existing value, `SKILLS_REQUIRED`
   = the prerequisite skill, `XP_TYPE`/`XP_COST`, `COMMANDS`/`SKILL_MODS` as
   needed.
2. Matching `skl_n.stf` entry (required); `skl_t.stf`/`skl_d.stf` entries if
   `IS_TITLE=1` or you want a real description instead of blank.
3. If it grants a new command name, that command must already be registered
   in C++ (section 6) — `COMMANDS` only grants *access*, it doesn't create
   the command.
4. Rebuild/redeploy the patch `.tre` via `docs/companion_system/tools/`,
   restart both server and have players reconnect with a matching client
   `.tre` copy.

### 9a. Jedi / Force System

**Not stripped down — a full Force-sensitive Village/FRS questline is the
active progression mode.** `JediManager` (`managers/jedi/JediManager.{h,cpp}`)
is a thin C++→Lua dispatcher; the real logic is `VillageJediManager`
(`scripts/managers/jedi/village_jedi_manager.lua`, selected via
`jediProgressionType` in `jedi_manager.lua:14` — a simpler
`HologrindJediProgression` alternate mode also exists but isn't active).
Unlock path: badge-quota-triggered "glowing" (`screenplays/village/intro/glowing.lua`)
→ a real multi-phase quest chain (~70 Lua files under
`screenplays/village/{intro,phase1..4,outro}/`) → `awardSkill(pPlayer,
"force_title_jedi_novice")` + `PlayerObject::setJediState(1)`. Real
holocron items (`jedi_holocron_{light,dark}`) route through
`JediManager::useItem()` mid-questline. `isJedi()`/`isJediLight()`/
`isJediDark()` are just `jediState` int thresholds (`PlayerObject.idl:1876-1888`:
`≥2`/`==4`/`==8`). A separate **Force Rank System** (`managers/frs/Frs*`) —
Light/Dark council membership, arena duels, vote-based rank maintenance —
is a live endgame PvP ladder layered on top of being Jedi, not vestigial
(confirmed by real GM debug tools like `unlockFRSForTesting()`).

**Two extra gates beyond the generic `skills.iff` prerequisite system:**
(1) every skill row has a `jediStateRequired` column (col 19), checked
generically in `fulfillsSkillPrerequisites()` — usable by any skill, not
just Force ones. (2) `force_`-prefixed skill names additionally defer to
`JediManager::canLearnSkill()`
(`village_jedi_manager.lua:102-122`), which enforces things `skills.iff`
can't express: `force_sensitive_*` branch boxes require a **quest-reward
unlock flag** (`ScreenPlayState` per named branch, 16 branches), the "Jedi
Rank 01" title requires **≥24 learned force-sensitive skills**
(`SkillManager::getForceSensitiveSkillCount()`), and "Jedi Rank 03"
(Knight) requires a hardcoded **2 fully-mastered `force_discipline_*` trees
+ ≥206 cumulative points spent in them** (`SkillManager::
villageKnightPrereqsMet()`, `SkillManager.cpp:1064-1095`). Surrendering is
also specially blocked mid-progression (can't drop below the 24-skill
floor, can't break Knight prereqs, dropping mid-trial fails the trial).

**Force powers run through the same command pipeline as any attack/buff**
(section 6), just with a **dedicated Force Power resource pool**
(`PlayerObject.idl` `forcePower`/`forcePowerMax`, separate from HAM mind).
Attack-type powers extend `ForcePowersQueueCommand` → `CombatQueueCommand`
(same `CombatManager::doCombatAction()` pipeline as weapons); self-buffs
extend `JediQueueCommand` directly. Force cost is FRS-modified
(`getFrsModifiedForceCost()`, scaled by `force_manipulation_light/dark`
skill mods). Regen is a real scheduled `ForceRegenerationEvent`
(base 5/tick, ×3 while meditating, interval tuned by
`jedi_force_power_regen`/`force_control_*` skill mods) — not a passive
HAM-style tick. Per-power numeric tuning (cost, damage, FRS modifiers) is
pure Lua data under `commands/<name>.lua`, same pattern as any other
command config (section 6).

**Lightsaber crafting is the standard crafting pipeline (section 20) plus
one bespoke crystal class.** Assembly/schematics are ordinary
`DraftSchematic`s with crystal slots marked as component slots — nothing
saber-specific in the crafting system itself. The real complexity is
`LightsaberCrystalComponent` (`objects/tangible/component/lightsaber/`):
plain color crystals (0-11) are cosmetic only; `color == 31` marks a "real"
Force crystal (or the rarer, strictly-better Krayt Dragon Pearl) that rolls
actual stats (damage, HAM costs, attack speed) from an `itemLevel`-driven
quality tier (`POOR`→`FLAWLESS`). Real crystals can be permanently "tuned"
to one player (requires Jedi Rank 01, costs Force Power) and, if destroyed,
either subtract their stat bonuses back out of the weapon or — for a
cosmetic crystal — force the saber to auto-unequip as unusable until
recolored. **The C++ loader only recognizes two hardcoded crystal names**
(`LootManagerImplementation.cpp:188-199`, fetches `lightsaber_module_force_crystal`
and `lightsaber_module_krayt_dragon_pearl` by literal string, doesn't
iterate the Lua stat table generically) — adding a third stat-rolling
crystal tier needs a C++ change, not just data; plain color crystals need
none.

**Death penalty: exactly one Jedi-specific mechanic, no permadeath.** No
character/rank loss on death anywhere in the source. The one real penalty
is an XP clawback on cloning (`PlayerManagerImplementation.cpp:1891-1907`):
`-5%` of the player's `jedi_general` XP cap, floored so cumulative
`jedi_general` XP can never go below **-10,000,000**. The only other
Jedi-specific rule is that Jedi robes can never be insured (`isInsurable()`
excludes them), so they always take the standard uninsured-death condition
hit. `/resetJedi` is a GM-only manual punishment command (force-surrenders
all `force_` skills, resets `jediState` to 0) — not an automatic mechanic.

**Recipe — new Force power:** needs C++ regardless of how similar it is to
an existing one, because `CommandConfigManager::addCommand()` silently
no-ops on any command name never registered via
`commandFactory.registerCommand<T>(name)` — there's no way to introduce a
new ability name from Lua alone. New/reused C++ class → register in
`CommandConfigManager{2,3,4}.cpp` (rebuild) → new `commands/<name>.lua` for
all tunables (no rebuild for balance tweaks) → grant via a skill's
`COMMANDS` field (same section 9 recipe, `force_`-prefixed names also need
to satisfy `canLearnSkill()` above). Retuning an *existing* power's numbers
is pure data, no rebuild. **New lightsaber crystal:** a new plain color is
pure data; a new stat-rolling tier needs the C++ change described above
(new named fetch in `LootManagerImplementation.cpp`) plus new Lua stat
data.

## 10. Combat Basics

**Core manager:** `MMOCoreORB/src/server/zone/managers/combat/CombatManager.{h,cpp}`
(singleton). Entry point `CombatManager::doCombatAction(CreatureObject*
attacker, WeaponObject* weapon, TangibleObject* defenderObject, const
CreatureAttackData& data)` (`CombatManager.cpp:211`).

**Command → attack flow:** every combat ability is a C++ class extending
`CombatQueueCommand` (`src/server/zone/objects/creature/commands/CombatQueueCommand.h`,
itself a `QueueCommand` -- see section 6). `CombatQueueCommand::doCombatAction()`
(`CombatQueueCommand.h:149`) validates range/weapon-type/LOS/faction-flagging
then calls `CombatManager::instance()->doCombatAction(...)`, which flows
`doTargetCombatAction` → `creoTargetCombatAction`/`tanoTargetCombatAction` →
`getHitChance()` (roll) → `calculateDamage()` (number) →
`getArmorReduction()`/`applyDamage()` (mitigate + apply).

**Hit/miss roll:** `getHitChance()` (`CombatManager.cpp:2072`) sums
`accuracySkill + accuracyWeapon + accuracyPosture + accuracyBonus` vs.
`defenseSkill + defensePosture`, feeds the difference into
`hitChanceEquation()` (`CombatManager.cpp:2238`, `toHitBase=75`,
`toHitStep=25`, `toHitScale=50`), then `System::random(100) <= toHitChance`
decides hit/miss. A hit still rolls against the defender's weapon-type
`DODGE/BLOCK/COUNTER/RICOCHET` (`getWeaponDefendResult()`, `CombatManager.h:282`).

**Damage number:** `calculateDamage()` (`CombatManager.cpp:1109`) starts
from `weapon->getMinDamage()` + `System::random(range)`, applies the
command's `damageMultiplier`, a flat ×1.5 PvE / ×0.25 PvP scaler, melee
×1.25, knockdown ×1.5, then `getDefenderToughnessModifier()` and (force
attacks) `force_defense` skill mod reduction.

**Weapon fields** (item Lua template, section 1 pattern):
`src/templates/tangible/SharedWeaponObjectTemplate.{h,cpp}` --
`minDamage`/`maxDamage`/`attackSpeed`/`damageType`
(KINETIC/ENERGY/ELECTRICITY/STUN/BLAST/HEAT/COLD/ACID/LIGHTSABER)/
`weaponType` (bitmask, `CombatManager::WeaponType`)/`maxRange`/
`certificationsRequired`.

**Armor/resist reduction:** `getArmorObjectReduction(ArmorObject*,
damageType)` (`CombatManager.cpp:2332`) reads the matching resist getter
(`getKinetic()`, `getEnergy()`, ...) off the `ArmorObject`;
`getArmorReduction()` (`CombatManager.cpp:2442`) orchestrates, applies
`weapon->getArmorPiercing()`, and picks NPC/vehicle/turret variants by
defender type.

**Special attacks -- Lua + C++, tightly coupled:** the command *name* must
exist in the client-shared `datatables/command/command_tables_shared*.iff`
(ships only inside client `.tre` archives, same TRE-toolchain caveat as
quest journal data -- section 3). A C++ class (e.g. `Berserk1Command.h`,
`BodyShot1Command.h`) registers against that name via
`commandFactory.registerCommand<T>("bodyshot1")` in
`CommandConfigManager2/3/4.cpp` (section 6's pattern). `bin/scripts/commands/<name>.lua`
sets tuning knobs (`damageMultiplier`, `speedMultiplier`, `accuracyBonus`,
`poolsToDamage`, `weaponType`, `animation`, `combatSpam`, ...) and calls
`AddCommand(MyCommand)`, which `CommandConfigManager::addCommand()`
(`CommandConfigManager.cpp:843`) reflects onto the matching C++ setters.
Bespoke logic (e.g. Berserk1's self-damage-for-buff) overrides
`doQueueCommand()`/`doCombatAction()` directly in the `.h`; most specials
just call the base `doCombatAction()` and let Lua-configured multipliers do
all the work.

**Deeper mechanics (beyond the summary above):**
- **Accuracy is layered, not one sum:** `getAttackerAccuracyModifier()`
  (`CombatManager.cpp:1949-1991`) sums weapon-type skill mods + their
  `private_`-prefixed twins, applies a **flat -15 penalty if the total is
  0** (fully unskilled), plus a `dead_eye` buff scaler; a **separate**
  `getAttackerAccuracyBonus()` (`:1993-2005`) adds `private_attack_accuracy`/
  `private_accuracy_bonus` (this is the bucket a command's own Lua
  `accuracyBonus` field feeds). Defense (`getDefenderDefenseModifier()`,
  `:2011-2045`) starts from defender level + weapon-type defense mods,
  **hard-caps at 125** before PvP-only `private_defense` and
  group/food-buff bonuses are added *after* the cap.
- **Secondary defense (dodge/block/counter) is a contested roll**, not a
  flat chance: attacker `random(499)+1` vs. defender `random(199)+1`,
  compared against `accuracyTotal+roll <= evadeTotal+roll`
  (`CombatManager.cpp:2166-2180`); `getDefenderSecondaryDefenseModifier()`
  returns 0 outright if the defender is intimidated/berserked/a vehicle.
- **Damage stacking order** (`applyDamageModifiers`, `CombatManager.cpp:1308-1368`
  + the outer scalers in `calculateDamage`, `:1109-1235`): weapon damage mods
  → `private_damage_multiplier` (full multiply, only if set) →
  `private_damage_divisor` → **self-inflicted reduction while
  stunned/intimidated** (`private_damage_divisor_stun`/`_intimidate`, set by
  the state-buff itself, see below) → PvE ×1.5 / force-vs-NPC
  ×(2+random(1)) → melee ×1.25 → knockdown ×1.5 → `getDefenderToughnessModifier()`
  (CM/Toughness skill-mod line) → force_defense divide → **PvP ×0.25** →
  floor at 1. A lair target with 3+ already-spawned mobs takes an
  undocumented ×3.5 damage bonus (`CombatManager.cpp:1225-1235`) to
  encourage killing lairs early.
- **Armor piercing is exponential, not linear:** `getArmorPiercing()`
  (`CombatManager.cpp:2647-2672`) is `pow(1.25, piercing-rating)` if the
  weapon out-pierces the armor, else `pow(0.50, rating-piercing)` -- small
  rating differences swing damage a lot. `weapon->isBroken()` zeroes
  piercing to 0; broken armor loses its rating lookup entirely.
- **The "combat queue" from section 6's `addToCombatQueue` column** is
  enforced by `CommandQueue` (`server/zone/objects/creature/CommandQueue.{h,cpp}`,
  one instance per creature): `enqueueCommand()` pushes onto `queueVector`
  (capped 5 AI / 15 player); `getNextAction()` picks by
  `QueueCommand::getDefaultPriority()` (IMMEDIATE jumps the queue unless
  the creature `hasAttackDelay()`, FRONT jumps normal-priority but not
  immediates); `handleRunningState()` blocks any `addToCombatQueue()`
  command while `hasPostureChangeDelay()`/`hasAttackDelay()` is active --
  this is the actual "combat actions serialize behind the attack-speed
  timer, chat/social commands don't" behavior. Stun/knockdown/`NEXTATTACKDELAY`
  all set one of those delays, which is what "interrupts" the queue.
- **Combat states are Buffs with concrete skill-mod penalties baked in**
  (`CreatureObjectImplementation.cpp:2720-2915`), not abstract flags:
  stunned = `private_melee/ranged_defense -50` + 20% self-damage reduction;
  blinded = `private_attack_accuracy -60`/`private_dodge_attack -60`;
  intimidated = `private_melee/ranged_defense -20` + 50% self-damage
  reduction; berserk = `+20` accuracy/`+75` melee damage but `-60`
  defense both types; cover = forced prone + `private_defense +10`/
  `ranged_defense +25` layered on top of the posture table below.
- **Posture is a real lookup table**, not a simple bonus:
  `CreaturePosture` (`src/templates/params/creature/CreaturePosture.h:131-224`)
  has separate ranged-attack/ranged-defense/melee-attack/melee-defense
  tables keyed by locomotion, e.g. ranged defense STANDING -10, KNEELING 0,
  PRONE +25, RUNNING +45; melee attack STANDING 0, PRONE -90, RUNNING +25.
  Both terms feed into `getHitChance()` as plain additive accuracy/defense
  values, not a separate multiplier stage.
- **DoTs**: `CombatManager::applyDots()` (command-configured DoTs) and
  `applyWeaponDots()` (weapon-innate, e.g. grenades/flamethrowers, consumes
  a weapon "dot use" charge) both feed `DamageOverTimeList::addDot()`
  (`server/zone/objects/creature/damageovertime/DamageOverTimeList.cpp:114-223`),
  resist formula `random(100) >= clamp(potency*80/(100+defense), 5, 95)`,
  duration shrunk by `dissipation_<type>` skill mods (capped 90%
  reduction). Ticking piggybacks on the same periodic HAM-regen loop
  (`activateStateRecovery()`/`activateHAMRegeneration()`), not a separate
  DoT scheduler.

**Recipe -- add one new weapon special attack** (reusing an already-existing
client command-table row is the realistic path; a truly new command name
needs the TRE toolchain):
1. Confirm the command name already exists in the client-shared command
   table (or repack a patch `.tre` if genuinely new).
2. New header under `.../creature/commands/`, extend `CombatQueueCommand`,
   model on `BodyShot1Command.h` (or `Berserk1Command.h` for bespoke logic).
3. Register in `CommandConfigManager2/3/4.cpp`.
4. `bin/scripts/commands/mySpecial.lua` (copy `bodyShot1.lua`), `AddCommand(...)`,
   add to `commands.lua`'s `RunSlashCommandsFile(...)` list.
5. Rebuild, restart; grant it to a profession via that skill's `COMMANDS`
   field (section 9).

## 11. Database Persistence (`@json` / save-load pattern)

**What `@json` actually does:** an IDL annotation that additionally
generates a `writeJSON(nlohmann::json&)` method and a lightweight `...POD`
snapshot/DTO class (`Optional<T>`-wrapped fields, its own
`writeJSON`/`readObject`/`writeObject`) -- see
`src/autogen/server/zone/objects/companion/CompanionObject.h:334,451` for a
real generated example. **Every** `.idl` class, `@json` or not, already gets
the real save/load machinery for free from `ManagedObject`/
`DistributedObjectServant`: `readObject(ObjectInputStream*)`/
`writeObject(ObjectOutputStream*)` (binary). `@json` is strictly additive --
it's for JSON *export* (admin tooling, the web status API via
`src/server/web/APIProxyObjectManager.cpp`, offline dumps via
`src/odb/ObjectDatabaseCore.cpp`'s `dumpObjectToJSON()`), **not** the
gameplay save path. It's the default expectation for any new persistent
class though -- 202 files project-wide use it (buffs, missions, buildings,
installations, `GroupObject.idl:20`, most tangible subtypes), not a
companion-specific pattern.

**Actual save mechanism -- periodic sweep, not per-field-write, not
logout-only:** `MMOCoreORB/utils/engine3/MMOEngine/src/engine/orb/db/DOBObjectManager.cpp` /
`UpdateModifiedObjectsThread.cpp`. A background task runs every
`UPDATETODATABASETIME` ms (`DOBObjectManager.cpp:49`, default **300000ms =
5 minutes**, overridable via `ObjectManager.updateToDatabaseTime` in
`config.lua`). Each sweep collects objects touched since the previous sweep
across worker threads (`collectModifiedObjectsFromThreads`), and a thread
pool calls `commitUpdatePersistentObjectToDB(object)` for each one that
`isPersistent()` (`UpdateModifiedObjectsThread.cpp:105-121`), inside a
Berkeley-DB-backed transaction (`CommitMasterTransactionThread`). Creation
and forced saves (shutdown) drive the same path, just triggered explicitly
instead of on the timer.

**Correction/clarification (2026-07-13, verified by tracing the actual
shutdown call chain):** "forced saves drive the same path" does **not**
mean shutdown saves every live object unconditionally -- it means
shutdown reaches the exact same dirty-objects-only collection as the
periodic sweep. `ServerCore::shutdown()` calls `objectManager->
createBackup(SAVE_FULL | SAVE_REPORT)` →
`DOBObjectManager::updateModifiedObjectsToDatabase()`
(`DOBObjectManager.cpp:414`), whose input set always comes from
`collectModifiedObjectsFromThreads()` (`:350`) -- which only collects
objects some code path already explicitly marked dirty via
`_setUpdated(true)`, `SAVE_FULL` vs `SAVE_DELTA` only changes *how* an
already-collected dirty object is written, not *which* objects get
collected. **An object that was never marked dirty is not saved at
shutdown either.** This matters for any class whose mutators are all
hand-written `native` methods that never call `updateObjectToDatabase()`
themselves (see the caveat two paragraphs up) -- there is no "shutdown
saves everything anyway" safety net for such a class. Real example:
`docs/companion_system/NOTES.md`'s "New finding #2" writeup on
`CompanionObject`.

**Follow-up correction (2026-07-13, drafting a fix for that finding):**
the exact primitive to call for explicit dirty-marking needed a second
look. `SceneObject::updateToDatabase()` -- the convenience method the
"real call sites" list above uses (`BuffList.cpp:52`, etc.) -- has an
**empty generated body in every single class in this codebase**
(`ManagedObjectImplementation::updateToDatabase() { }`,
`SceneObjectImplementation::updateToDatabase() { }`, confirmed by
grepping the entire `autogen/` tree for a non-empty override -- zero
matches). It appears to be dead/vestigial, not a working dirty-marking
call, for any class -- whether those other call sites persist correctly
through some other mechanism or share this same latent gap is an open
question this pass didn't chase down (out of scope for a companion-
focused session). **The call that is fully, unambiguously confirmed to
work is `zoneServer->updateObjectToDatabase(object)`**
(`ZoneServerImplementation.cpp:702-704` → `ObjectManager::
updatePersistentObject()`, `ObjectManager.cpp:494-498` → real, direct
`object->_setUpdated(true)`, traced end to end with no forwarding-chain
ambiguity) -- prefer this form over `updateToDatabase()` in any new code
until/unless the latter is independently confirmed to do something.

**Also confirmed (same pass): `ObjectManager.saveMode` (default off, not
set anywhere in this repo's `config.lua`) does NOT disable persistence**
-- it only gates a performance optimization (per-thread incremental dirty
tracking, avoiding a full object-directory walk every sweep). With it
off, `DOBObjectManager::updateModifiedObjectsToDatabase()`'s default
branch calls `executeUpdateThreads()` →
`runObjectsMarkedForUpdate()` (`DOBObjectManager.cpp:964`), which walks
**every live object in RAM** (`localObjectDirectory`) and saves anything
with `_isUpdated()==true` -- so `_setUpdated(true)`
(`updateObjectToDatabase()`) is correctly picked up regardless of
`saveMode`, at both the periodic sweep and shutdown. Worth knowing before
anyone reads the `saveMode` early-outs in `DistributedObject.cpp`/
`DOBObjectManager.cpp` and assumes persistence is broken by default --
it isn't; that code path is just the (unused, in this repo) fast path.

**Fresh boot:** the server does **not** bulk-load the database.
`ZoneServerImplementation::initialize()`/`startGroundZones()`
(`ZoneServerImplementation.cpp:200-289`) boots zones/managers; individual
persistent objects are fetched **lazily by object ID** the first time a
`ManagedReference` to them is dereferenced -- the ORB layer transparently
reads the Berkeley-DB row and reconstructs via the same
`readObject(ObjectInputStream*)` used to write it, firing
`notifyLoadFromDatabase()` (`ManagedObject.cpp:282`). Players load in when
their client connects and their character object ID is looked up.

**Recipe -- add a new persistent field to an existing object type:**
1. Add the field to the `.idl` (protected field + `@read`/`@preLocked`
   accessors), mirroring `CompanionObject.idl`'s `vitality`/`maxVitality`
   pattern. Keep `@json` on the class for JSON-dump tooling, not required
   for the save itself.
2. Rebuild -- regenerates `readObjectMember`/`writeObjectMembers`
   automatically, no manual serialization code.
3. Implement the setter body in the `Implementation.cpp` if `native`.
4. Nothing else to wire up -- persistence is structural, not opt-in per
   field; the object is included in the next sweep (or immediately on
   creation) automatically.

**Important correction/caveat -- "structural, not opt-in" is only true for
plain idlc-generated accessors, NOT for hand-written `native` setter
bodies.** Dirty-tracking itself is a plain in-memory flag
(`DistributedObject::_setUpdated(true)`, `engine/orb/object/DistributedObject.h:31-60`)
that appends the object to the *current worker thread's own* modified-object
list (`Thread::addModifiedObject`) -- that's what the periodic sweep actually
drains. Ordinary generated field setters flip this automatically. But a
`native` method you hand-implement in an `Implementation.cpp` does **not**
get this for free just because the field is `.idl`-declared -- concrete,
real proof already sitting in this codebase:
`CompanionObjectImplementation::setVitality()`
(`server/zone/objects/companion/CompanionObjectImplementation.cpp:22-32`)
mutates the persistent `vitality` field directly and never calls
`_setUpdated`/`updateToDatabase()` anywhere in its body -- mutating it alone
does not, by itself, get the object queued for the next save sweep. The
pattern used everywhere else in this codebase for a native setter that
should actually persist its change is an **explicit** call to
`zoneServer->updateObjectToDatabase(object)` (`ZoneServerImplementation.cpp:702-704`,
→ `ObjectManager::updatePersistentObject()`, `ObjectManager.cpp:494-498`, →
`_setUpdated(true)`) somewhere in the native method body -- real call sites:
`PlayerManagerImplementation.cpp:1114/1152`, `ContainerComponent.cpp:363/455-456`,
`BuffList.cpp:52`, `MissionObjectImplementation.cpp:255`. **Bottom line:** if
you add a new persistent field and give it a `native` setter (rather than
letting idlc generate a plain one), you must call
`updateObjectToDatabase()` yourself inside that setter, or the field will
silently never save.

**Real-world scope of this gap, not just a one-off example:** a 2026-07-13
pass checked how far this applies to `CompanionObject` specifically and
found the *entire* class is exposed to it -- every single mutating method
declared on `CompanionObject.idl` is `native` (`setVitality`,
`healVitality`, `grantSkill`, `removeSkill`, `recalculateCombatLevel`,
`setCompanionState`, `addExperience`, and more), and there are zero
`updateObjectToDatabase()`/`_setUpdated()` call sites anywhere in
`objects/companion/`. The only thing that incidentally saves companion
state today is `setMaxVitality()` (the one plain/generated setter, called
on every summon/store), which piggybacks a full snapshot. Full writeup
with severity assessment and a proposed fix shape:
`docs/companion_system/NOTES.md`, "New finding #2 -- companion state...
may not reliably survive a server crash mid-session".
