## 12. Zone / Planet / Region Fundamentals

**Zone vs Planet vs ZoneServer:** `ZoneServer` (`ZoneServer.idl`/
`ZoneServerImplementation.cpp`) is the top-level process object -- holds
`zones`/`spaceZones` maps (`String zoneName -> Zone*`), owns every singleton
manager, boots at server start. `Zone` (`Zone.idl`) is **one per planet** --
`GroundZone`/`SpaceZone` extend it. There's no sub-planet zone sharding: a
whole planet (`tatooine`, `corellia`, ...) is a single `Zone` holding every
object in an octree/quadtree. `Zone` owns a `PlanetManager`
(`getPlanetManager()`) -- "Planet" isn't a separate class, `PlanetManager`
is the manager attached to a `Zone` handling planet-specific spatial data
(regions, spawn areas, travel points).

**Coordinate → zone:** there's no router needed -- x/y is only meaningful
relative to whichever `Zone` an object's own `zone` reference already
points at. `ZoneServerImplementation::getZone(zoneName)`
(`ZoneServerImplementation.cpp:584`) is a simple name→`Zone*` lookup.
Sub-planet subdivision (city limits, PvP flags, spawn density, POI
triggers) is the **Region** system, loaded from Lua at zone boot --
`PlanetManagerImplementation::loadRegions()` (`PlanetManagerImplementation.cpp:909`)
runs `scripts/managers/planet/<planet>_regions.lua`, the same file already
referenced in section 2's mob spawn-area tuples.

**Moving between zones (shuttle etc.):**
`SceneObjectImplementation::switchZone(newTerrainName, x, z, y, parentID, ...)`
(`SceneObjectImplementation.cpp:1049`). Real example:
`BoardShuttleCommand.h:106-226` -- resolves the travel ticket's
`arrivalPlanet`/`arrivalPoint`, `server->getZoneServer()->getZone(arrivalPlanet)`,
finds a `PlanetTravelPoint` via `arrivalZone->getPlanetManager()->getPlanetTravelPoint(name)`,
computes a landing `Coordinate`, calls `creature->switchZone(...)` -- just
reassigns the `zone` reference and repositions; no "boundary crossing"
concept.

**Where zone/planet lists live:** which zones this server currently runs --
`MMOCoreORB/bin/conf/config.lua`'s `ZonesEnabled = {...}` (`config.lua:95-127`)
and `SpaceZonesEnabled = {...}` (`config.lua:129-147`); ~15 dev/test zones
are commented out by default. `ConfigManager::getEnabledZones()`
(`ConfigManager.h:493`) is what `startGroundZones()` reads at boot. World
geometry is still the client-authored World Snapshot limitation from
section 4 (`src/templates/snapshot/WorldSnapshotIff.{h,cpp}`).

**Recipe -- enable an existing-but-disabled zone** (adding a genuinely new
planet needs client terrain/snapshot data not present here):
1. Uncomment/add the zone name in `config.lua`'s `ZonesEnabled` (and
   `SpaceZonesEnabled` if applicable).
2. Confirm `scripts/managers/planet/<planet>_regions.lua` exists (every
   shipped planet already has one).
3. Confirm the referenced client `.tre` data actually contains that
   planet's terrain/snapshot.
4. Restart -- `startGroundZones()`/`startSpaceZones()` iterate
   `getEnabledZones()`/`getEnabledSpaceZones()` and deploy automatically, no
   C++ changes.
5. Add travel-point/shuttle entries if players should reach it by starport;
   add the planet to any spawn/quest Lua that should cover it.

---

## 13. Factions/GCW and Groups (Parties)

**Faction/PvP fields** live on `TangibleObject.idl` (inherited by
`CreatureObject`): `faction` (CRC of a string like `"rebel"`/`"imperial"`),
`factionStatus` (`FactionStatus.h`: `ONLEAVE=0`/`COVERT=1`/`OVERT=2`),
`pvpStatusBitmask` (`ObjectFlag::ATTACKABLE`/`OVERT` bits). Getters:
`getFaction()`, `getFactionStatus()`, `getPvpStatusBitmask()`.

**Attack eligibility gate:**
`TangibleObjectImplementation::isAttackableBy(CreatureObject*)`
(`TangibleObjectImplementation.cpp:1466`) -- checks `pvpStatusBitmask &
ATTACKABLE`, no-combat-area, pet-ownership/faction-pet special cases, then
player-vs-player faction/duel/TEF rules. Called from
`CombatManager::doTargetCombatAction` (`CombatManager.cpp:346`) as a hard
pre-check *before* any hit roll -- not folded into the accuracy math.
Covert↔Overt field transitions happen in
`CombatQueueCommand::doCombatAction()` (`CombatQueueCommand.h:174-218`,
`ghost->doFieldFactionChange(...)`), gated by
`ConfigManager::instance()->useCovertOvertSystem()`.

**Groups:** `GroupObject.idl` (also `@json` -- cross-reference for section
11) holds `groupMembers`, `lootRule` (default `GroupManager.FREEFORALL`),
`masterLooterID`, `groupLevel`. `addMember()`/`removeMember()` are native
methods on the object itself (`GroupObject.idl:81,84`), invoked by
`GroupManager` (`joinGroup()`/`createGroup()`, `GroupManager.h:78,93`), the
command-facing entry point for `/invite`-style flows.

**XP/loot split on a kill:**
`CreatureManagerImplementation::notifyDestruction()`
(`CreatureManagerImplementation.cpp:572`) builds a per-attacker damage
`ThreatMap`, finds `getHighestDamageGroupLeader()` to decide loot ownership
(group ID if grouped, else top-damage player -- lines 629-639,
`setContainerOwnerID(ownerID)` at line 698), fires `KILLEDCREATURE`
observer notifications to every online group member (this is what quest
kill-counters from section 3 hook into), and calls
`playerManager->disseminateExperience(destructedObject, &copyThreatMap)`
(`PlayerManagerImplementation.cpp:1937`) which splits XP **proportionally
to damage share**, not equally per head.

**Recipe -- how a group kill already works end to end (stock behavior, no
code changes needed for the common case):**
1. `/invite` → accept → `GroupManager::createGroup()`/`joinGroup()` →
   `GroupObject::addMember()`.
2. Any member attacks normally (section 10); `CombatManager` accrues
   per-attacker damage into the target's `ThreatMap` regardless of grouping.
3. On death, `notifyDestruction()` reads the group off the `ThreatMap`
   automatically -- no explicit "is this a group kill" flag anywhere.
4. XP splits by damage share; loot ownership goes to the group and is
   distributed per the `GroupObject`'s `lootRule`.
5. To change loot behavior, the lever is `GroupObject::lootRule`/
   `masterLooterID`, not the kill/XP path itself.

### 13a. PvP / GCW Warfare Deep Dive

**TEF (Tactical Engagement Flag)** is four independent rolling 5-minute
timers on `PlayerObjectImplementation` (`lastGcwPvpCombatActionTimestamp`,
`lastBhPvpCombatActionTimestamp`/implicit via `hasBhTef()`,
`lastPvpAreaCombatActionTimestamp`, `lastCrackdownGcwCombatActionTimestamp`
+ `crackdownFactionTefCrc`; `PlayerObject.idl:260-274`), combined by
`hasTef()`/`hasPvpTef()`/`hasGcwTef()`/`hasBhTef()`/`hasCrackdownTef()`
(`PlayerObjectImplementation.cpp:2888-2915`). `FactionManager::TEFTIMER =
300000`ms (`FactionManager.h:22`) — every qualifying hit *refreshes* the
window rather than starting a fresh flat timer.
`CombatManager::checkForTefs()` (`CombatManager.cpp:3486-3549`) decides
per-hit which sub-flag to raise (cross-faction attack, active bounty
target, resisting a crackdown scan); `QueueCommand::checkForTef()`
additionally TEFs a *healer* who heals a hostile-status target.
`PvpTefRemovalTask` self-reschedules to the soonest remaining timer and
only clears `ObjectFlag::TEF` once all four are expired. OVERT status is
literally the in-fiction "Special Forces" label (terminal text checks
`getFactionStatus() != OVERT` directly) and carries a 5-minute
`declare_overt_cooldown` before you can flip back.

**GCW rank is a separate numeric ladder (0-15) from covert/overt status**,
`CreatureObject::getFactionRank()`/`setFactionRank()`, data-backed by
`datatables/faction/rank.iff` (name/cost/delegate-ratio per rank). Killing
an enemy player is a **flat, not damage-scaled**, standing award
(`FactionManager::awardPvpFactionPoints()`, `FactionManager.cpp:238-257`:
+30 own faction / -45 enemy faction, both sides). Standing is capped at
`max(1000, currentRankCost * 20)` — you must periodically spend it to keep
earning more. Promotion is a manual purchase at a faction recruiter NPC
(`recruiterConvoHandler.lua:78-99`: spend `getRankCost(nextRank)` standing,
`setFactionRank(rank+1)`), not automatic. Rank gates real things elsewhere:
crackdown-scan detection odds, HQ terminal menu options, donation ratios.

**GCW base sieges are a real 9-state machine**, tracked on a
`DestructibleBuildingDataComponent` attached to the base building:
`INVULNERABLE → VULNERABLE → BAND → JAMMED → SLICED → DNA → OVERLOADED →
SHUTDOWNSEQUENCE → REBOOTSEQUENCE`. Real OVERT bases open a vulnerability
window periodically (`vulnerabilityDuration`/`vulnerabilityFrequency`,
defaults 3h every 48h); PvE/non-OVERT bases are effectively unsiegeable
long-term (uplink-jam auto-resets in 24h, never destructs). Enemy-faction
attackers must clear, in order: an uplink code-guessing minigame, a
security-terminal slice **gated behind the `combat_smuggler_slicing_01`
skill** (fail → alarm + spawns real base-security NPC patrols), a
DNA-strand-matching minigame, then a switch-puzzle power-regulator
overload — only then does a 10-minute, broadcast, un-skippable destruction
countdown start (`BaseDestructionTask`, one line printed per minute),
which the owning faction can still abort (subject to the same
`declare_overt_cooldown` gate) via a reboot sequence. This is all in
`GCWManagerImplementation.cpp` — a genuinely deep, already-built minigame
chain, not a stub.

**Dedicated always-PvP zone flags exist and are wired into combat, but
currently ship unused.** `ActiveArea` supports `PVPAREA`/`OVERTAREA`/
`REBELAREA`/`IMPERIALAREA`/`NODUELAREA` bits (`ActiveArea.idl:43-45`,
`regions.lua:19-20`). `isAttackableBy()` checks `isInPvpArea()` on both
combatants *before* the faction/covert-overt branch — if both parties are
in a flagged PvP area they're mutually attackable regardless of faction or
TEF (`CreatureObjectImplementation.cpp:3759-3801`), with the same
sticky 5-minute timer so leaving mid-fight doesn't grant immunity. **No
planet's `_regions.lua` currently uses these flags** — the hook is fully
functional but dormant, meaning adding a Restuss-style always-PvP zone to
an existing planet is a single new region-table row, zero C++.

**Duels are a separate, TEF-exempt, opt-in 1v1 system.** No accept
command — dueling is symmetric: both players must independently `/duel`
each other (`requestedDuelTo()` true on both sides) before
`areInDuel()`/mutual attackability kicks in. `NODUELAREA`-flagged zones
refuse challenges. Every TEF/GCW-standing check in the codebase explicitly
excludes duel partners first (`!areInDuel(...)` guards in both
`QueueCommand::checkForTef()` and `CombatManager::checkForTefs()`) — duel
combat generates no faction points, no TEF, and works between any two
factions/neutrals.

**Recipe — new PvP zone on an existing planet:** add one row to
`scripts/managers/planet/<planet>_regions.lua` with the `PVPAREA` (and
optionally `NODUELAREA`) bit OR'd into the region's flags int — pure data,
no rebuild, the combat-eligibility check already consumes it.
**Recipe — new base-siege objective type:** needs a new state constant on
`DestructibleBuildingDataComponent` plus new native `GCWManager.idl`
methods modeled on the existing DNA/power-regulator minigames (rebuild),
then a Lua terminal template + spawn-coordinate entries in
`gcw_manager.lua` (data).

## 14. Build & Deploy Workflow (recap)

- Lua changes (creatures, items, loot, screenplays, quests via shared-memory
  state, deed stat ranges): **no rebuild** -- just restart the server
  (`kill` / `r` in the running `gdb ./core3` session, or `cd bin && gdb ./core3`
  then `r` if it's not running).
- C++ (`.idl`/`.cpp`/`.h`) changes: from `MMOCoreORB/`,
  `touch <changed file>` (WSL2 `/mnt/c` mtime lag workaround) then
  `ninja -C build/unix/ninja-debug core3`, then restart.
- Client-visible text/data changes (skill trees, STF strings, datatable
  quest journal entries) require rebuilding `companion_patch.tre` via the
  toolchain in `docs/companion_system/tools/` and redeploying it to both
  `C:\Companion\tre\` (server) and the SWG client install folder -- see
  `docs/companion_system/NOTES.md` for the full binary-format writeup.

**`.idl` changes regenerate their `autogen/` pair automatically -- but only
when the `.idl` file's own mtime is newer than its already-generated
`.cpp`.** `MMOCoreORB/CMakeLists.txt`'s `option(BUILD_IDL ... ON)` is on by
default; `MMOCoreORB/src/CMakeLists.txt`'s `BUILD_IDL` branch adds one
`add_custom_command` per `.idl` file (`OUTPUT` the generated `.cpp`,
`DEPENDS` the `.idl` only) that invokes the real `idlc.jar`
(`IDLC_JAVA_ARGS`, defined in `cmake/Modules/FindEngine3.cmake:158`) via
ordinary CMake dependency-checking -- so ninja only re-runs `idlc.jar` for a
given file when that file's `.idl` is genuinely newer than its last
generated output. Practical effect: a hand-patched `autogen/*.h`/`*.cpp`
file with no matching change in its source `.idl` is stable indefinitely,
*until* someone later touches that same `.idl` for an unrelated reason --
at that point the next build silently regenerates the file via real
`idlc.jar` from scratch and discards any hand-edit that isn't also
reflected in the `.idl`. Also note: `ENABLE_ERROR_ON_WARNINGS` is on by
default (`-Werror`), so new code needs to be warning-clean, not just
error-free, for a "clean build" to mean anything. (First found and detailed
in `docs/companion_system/NOTES.md`'s "IDL/autogen + build mechanics
confirmed" dated section, in the context of the `CompanionObject`
`isCompanionObject()` `const` bug -- recorded here too since it applies to
any `.idl`-backed class in this codebase, not just the companion system.)

**A brand-new `.idl` or `.cpp` file needs a real `cmake` reconfigure before
`ninja` can see it at all -- editing an existing file never does.**
`MMOCoreORB/src/CMakeLists.txt`'s `BUILD_IDL` branch builds its whole file
list via `file(GLOB_RECURSE idls "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/src/*.idl")`, and the
ordinary source list a few lines below via
`file(GLOB_RECURSE zone3_sources "server/zone/*.cpp")` -- **both globs run
once, at `cmake` configure time**, not at `ninja` build time. A new file that
matches the pattern is invisible to the already-generated `build.ninja`
until `cmake` is re-run, and adding a new file does **not** trip CMake's own
"reconfigure if `CMakeLists.txt` changed" safety net (no `CMakeLists.txt`
changed). Symptom: `fatal error: '.../SomeNewClass.h' file not found` from
whatever includes it (often the umbrella `objects.h`), even though the
`.idl` and hand-written `Implementation.cpp` both genuinely exist on disk --
`ninja` re-running any number of times, with or without `touch`, cannot fix
this because its own dependency graph has no rule for the file at all.
Fix: re-run `cmake` against the *existing* build dir (safe, non-destructive
-- reuses the cached `CMakeCache.txt` for every other option, just re-globs
and regenerates `build.ninja`), matching whatever args
`MMOCoreORB/Makefile`'s own `build-*` target already used, e.g. for
`ninja-debug`:
```bash
cd MMOCoreORB/build/unix/ninja-debug
cmake -G Ninja -DRUN_GIT=ON -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug ../../..
cd MMOCoreORB && ninja -C build/unix/ninja-debug core3
```
Quick diagnostic before assuming a code bug: `git status` for untracked
`.idl`/`.cpp` files, or compare a suspect `.idl`'s mtime against
`build.ninja`'s own mtime. (Hit for real on 2026-07-13, root-caused in
`docs/companion_system/NOTES.md`'s matching dated section -- the file
involved that day, `BuildingTool.h`, belonged to an unrelated build-mode
prototype, not the companion system, which is why this fact is recorded
here rather than only in the companion notes.)

---

## 15. Loot & Treasure System

**Runtime pieces:** `LootManager` (`src/server/zone/managers/loot/LootManager.idl`
/ `LootManagerImplementation.cpp`, a `ZoneServer`-owned singleton reached via
`zoneServer->getLootManager()`) performs the actual roll at kill time.
`LootGroupMap` (`.../managers/loot/LootGroupMap.h`, itself a `Singleton`) is
the static in-memory registry of every loot item/group template, built once
at boot from Lua (`itemTemplates`/`groupTemplates` `HashTable`s,
`LootGroupMap.h:30-31`; populated via the Lua-callable statics
`addLootItemTemplate`/`addLootGroupTemplate`, `LootGroupMap.h:79-80`).

**Data layer** -- two parallel Lua trees under `bin/scripts/loot/`:
- `loot/items/<category>/*.lua` -- one `LootItemTemplate` per lootable
  instance: `directObjectTemplate` (the item's registered `.iff` path from
  section 1), optional `craftingValues = {{"statName", min, max, precision}, ...}`
  (rolled stat ranges, same shape as a schematic's `experimentalMin/Max` from
  section 20), `customizationStringNames`/`customizationValues`, `skillMods`.
  Registered via `addLootItemTemplate("name", table)`. Real example:
  `loot/items/creature/rancor_bile.lua`.
- `loot/groups/<category>/*.lua` -- one `LootGroupTemplate` per weighted
  pool: `lootItems = {{itemTemplate="name", weight=N}, ...}` or
  `{groupTemplate="name", weight=N}` (groups can nest other groups to
  arbitrary depth). Registered via `addLootGroupTemplate("name", table)`.
  Real examples: `loot/groups/creature/rancor_common.lua` (simple, weights
  even at 2,500,000 each) and `loot/groups/junk.lua` (29 items at weight
  285,500 plus 3 nested sub-groups). Weights are **not** percentages -- the
  roll is `System::random(10000000)` against cumulative weight
  (`LootGroupTemplate::getLootGroupEntryForRoll()`, `LootGroupTemplate.h:46-61`),
  so a fully-covered pool's weights should sum to ~10,000,000.

**Mob -> loot wiring:** a creature Lua template's `lootGroups` field (parsed
by `CreatureTemplate::readTemplateData` calling
`lootgroups.readObject(&lootCollections, level)`, `CreatureTemplate.cpp:187-188`,
into a `LootGroupCollection`) is a list of "collections", each shaped
`{chance=N, groups = {{group="lootGroupName", chance=N}, ...}}`. If a
collection's `chance` is omitted it defaults to `2,000,000 + level*20,000`
(`LootGroupCollectionEntry.h:41-42` -- 20% + 0.2% per mob level). Real
example, `mobile/tatooine/alkhara_bandit.lua:32-38`:
```lua
lootGroups = {
    { groups = { {group = "alkhara_tier_1", chance = 10000000} } }
},
```

**The roll, end to end** (fires from the same kill-resolution function
already documented in section 13's XP/loot split --
`CreatureManagerImplementation::notifyDestruction()`,
`CreatureManagerImplementation.cpp:685-704`, which also rolls a separate
flat credit drop via `lootManager->calculateLootCredits(level)` at line 689):
1. `LootManagerImplementation::createLoot(trx, container, AiAgent*)`
   (`LootManagerImplementation.cpp:656`) pulls the dead mob's already-parsed
   `LootGroupCollection` and calls `createLootFromCollection()`.
2. For each collection entry: roll 1 (`System::random(10000000)` vs. the
   entry's own `chance`) decides whether this collection wins anything at
   all; roll 2 walks the entry's `groups` list, accumulating each named
   group's `chance` until it exceeds the roll, picking that group
   (`LootManagerImplementation.cpp:695-744`).
3. `createLoot(trx, container, lootGroupName, level)`
   (`LootManagerImplementation.cpp:757`) resolves the winning name: if it is
   itself a `LootGroupTemplate` (nested group), it rolls again inside
   `LootGroupTemplate::getLootGroupEntryForRoll()` (up to 32 levels of
   nesting) until it bottoms out at a real `LootItemTemplate`.
4. `createLootObject()` instantiates the actual `TangibleObject` from the
   item template's `directObjectTemplate`, rolls any `craftingValues` stat
   ranges, and (barring the `isRandomResourceContainer()`/`isShipComponent()`
   special cases) transfers it into the mob corpse's `inventory` container.

Also present: `LootManager::createLootSet()`
(`LootManagerImplementation.cpp:815`) for spawning a *fixed count* of
guaranteed rolls from one group (chests/quest containers, not per-mob-death
loot), and the Director/screenplay-facing `createLoot`/`createLootSet` Lua
bridge functions already noted in section 3.

**Recipe -- add a new lootable item to an existing mob:**
1. New `loot/items/<category>/my_item.lua`: `directObjectTemplate` pointing
   at an existing (or new, per section 1) item `.iff` path, `craftingValues`
   if it should roll stats, `addLootItemTemplate("my_item", my_item)`,
   `includeFile(...)` it into that category's include list.
2. Either add it directly into an existing group's `lootItems` list
   (`{itemTemplate = "my_item", weight = N}`, adjusting sibling weights to
   keep the pool near 10,000,000 total), or create a new
   `loot/groups/.../my_group.lua` and nest it into an existing group via
   `{groupTemplate = "my_group", weight = N}`.
3. If attaching to an existing mob, edit that mob's Lua `lootGroups` field
   to add/adjust a `{group = "...", chance = N}` entry inside its collection.
4. Restart the server (pure Lua, no rebuild).

## 16. Missions / Bounty Terminals

**This is the mission-terminal system explicitly separated from
screenplays/quests in section 3** -- native `.idl` classes under
`src/server/zone/objects/mission/`, not Lua-authored content. Core singleton:
`MissionManager` (`.../managers/mission/MissionManager.idl` /
`MissionManagerImplementation.cpp`). `MissionObject` (`MissionObject.idl`) is
the datapad/mission-bag item a player holds; each has an associated
`MissionObjective` subclass (one `.idl`/`Implementation.cpp` pair per
mission type) that drives the actual gameplay hook once accepted:
`DestroyMissionObjective`, `DeliverMissionObjective`,
`CraftingMissionObjective`, `SurveyMissionObjective`,
`EntertainerMissionObjective`, `HuntingMissionObjective`,
`ReconMissionObjective`, `BountyMissionObjective` -- all under the same
`objects/mission/` folder. `PlayerBounty.idl` tracks a player character that
has become a live bounty target (used only by the bounty flow).

**Terminal -> type mapping:** `MissionTerminal` (`objects/tangible/terminal/mission/MissionTerminal.idl`)
holds a single `terminalType` string field set from the Lua template's
`missionTerminalType`, and exposes `isBountyTerminal()`/`isGeneralTerminal()`/
`isArtisanTerminal()`/`isEntertainerTerminal()`/`isScoutTerminal()`/
`isImperialTerminal()`/`isRebelTerminal()`/`isNewbieTerminal()`/
`isStatueTerminal()` (`MissionTerminal.idl:76-123`), each a trivial string
compare. Real Lua example, `object/tangible/terminal/terminal_mission_bounty.lua:44-49`:
```lua
object_tangible_terminal_terminal_mission_bounty = object_tangible_terminal_shared_terminal_mission_bounty:new {
    templateType = MISSIONTERMINAL,
    missionTerminalType = "bounty"
}
```
Sibling files (`terminal_mission_artisan.lua`, `_entertainer`, `_scout`,
`_imperial`, `_rebel`, `_newbie`, `_statue`) are the same pattern with a
different `missionTerminalType` string -- there is no C++ per-type subclass,
just this one string field switched on everywhere.

**List request -> populate -> accept, end to end**
(`MissionManagerImplementation.cpp`):
1. Player clicks the terminal -> `handleMissionListRequest()` (line 163):
   range/cooldown/city-ban checks, bounty terminals additionally require
   `combat_bountyhunter_novice`, then ensures the player's `mission_bag`
   container has enough empty `MissionObject` placeholders (line 222,
   `server->createObject(0x18e19914, 1)` -- "empty mission") before calling
   `populateMissionList()` (line 589).
2. `populateMissionList()` dispatches on terminal type to one of
   `randomizeGeneralTerminalMissions()` / `...ArtisanTerminalMissions()` /
   `...EntertainerTerminalMissions()` / `...ScoutTerminalMissions()` /
   `...BountyTerminalMissions()` / `...FactionTerminalMissions()`
   (lines 595-608), each of which fills the placeholder `MissionObject`s by
   calling a `randomizeGenericXMission()` helper (destroy/deliver/survey/
   crafting/entertainer/hunting/recon/bounty, lines 616-803).
3. `randomizeGenericDestroyMission()` (line 805) is the representative
   example: it calls `getRandomLairSpawn()` to pick a real
   `LairSpawn`/`LairTemplate` (the exact same spawn-group data documented in
   section 2's 3-tier mob spawning chain), derives a difficulty band, and
   picks a mission "building" target and reward from
   `LairTemplate::getMissionBuilding(difficulty)`.
4. Accepting a listed mission -> `handleMissionAccept()` (line 232):
   validates the mission bag/datapad chain, caps a player at 2 active
   missions (only 1 of which may be a bounty), and for bounty missions locks
   `playerBountyListMutex` and calls `addBountyHunterToPlayerBounty()`
   before transferring the `MissionObject` into the player's `datapad` and
   calling `createMissionObjectives()` (line 293), which `new`s the correct
   `XMissionObjective` subclass for the mission's `TypeCRC`
   (`createDestroyMissionObjectives()`/`createBountyMissionObjectives()`/etc.,
   lines 298-434) -- this is what actually starts the tracked gameplay
   (spawning the destroy-target lair, arming the bounty hunter droid, etc.).

**Bounty targets specifically** -- `randomizeGenericBountyMission()`
(line 1048) either rolls a **player** target from the live
`playerBountyList` (`Vector<PlayerBounty*>`, gated behind
`combat_bountyhunter_investigation_01/03` skill tiers raising the odds) or,
far more commonly, an **NPC** target picked from
`bhTargetsAtMissionLevel` (`VectorMap<uint,Vector<String>>` keyed by mission
level 1-3, loaded in `loadLuaSettings()` from
`bin/scripts/managers/mission/mission_manager.lua`'s
`bh_targets_at_mission_level` table, lines 24-65). Every entry in that table
is an ordinary **creature template name** -- real examples: `"bh_bodyguard"`
(`mobile/mission/bh_bodyguard.lua`), `"bh_tusken_warlord"` -- registered via
the exact same `CreatureTemplates:addCreatureTemplate()` pattern documented
in section 2, just conventionally placed under `mobile/mission/` and named
with a `bh_` prefix. `bh_target_zones` (line 11-22) is the separate planet
list used only for level-3 (hardest) NPC bounties to pick a random remote
planet via `getRandomBountyPlanet()`.

**Recipe -- add a new NPC bounty target:**
1. New creature Lua under `mobile/mission/bh_my_target.lua`, modeled on
   `bh_bodyguard.lua` (ordinary `Creature:new{...}`, section 2's pattern --
   pick a level appropriate to the tier you're targeting),
   `CreatureTemplates:addCreatureTemplate(bh_my_target, "bh_my_target")`,
   `includeFile(...)` it via `mobile/mission/serverobjects.lua`.
2. Add `"bh_my_target"` to the appropriate `level1`/`level2`/`level3` list in
   `bin/scripts/managers/mission/mission_manager.lua`'s
   `bh_targets_at_mission_level` table.
3. Restart the server (pure Lua + creature template, no rebuild).

**Recipe -- add a new mission *type* (C++, heavier lift):** new
`MissionObjective` subclass (`.idl` + `Implementation.cpp`) modeled on the
closest existing type (`BountyMissionObjective` for target-tracking,
`DeliverMissionObjective` for fetch/carry, `SurveyMissionObjective` for
scan-and-report), a `createXMissionObjectives()` method added to
`MissionManagerImplementation`, a `randomizeGenericXMission()` roller wired
into `populateMissionList()`'s per-terminal-type dispatch, and (if it needs
its own terminal category) a new `missionTerminalType` string plus Lua
terminal template following the section pattern above. Requires a rebuild
(`.idl` change).

### Letting the player pick a category + level before missions generate

Today there is **no player-facing filter at all** -- `populateMissionList()`
picks category purely from which physical terminal object was clicked
(`terminalType` string, immutable per placed terminal), and difficulty/level
for the combat-flavored types (destroy/hunting) is fully automatic:
`randomizeGenericDestroyMission()`/`randomizeGenericHuntingMission()` call
`PlayerManagerImplementation::calculatePlayerLevel()`
(`PlayerManagerImplementation.cpp:4398-4417`, derived from the player's
equipped-weapon combat skill mod, capped at 25) and `getRandomLairSpawn()`
(`MissionManagerImplementation.cpp:1820-1930`) restricts candidates to
`playerLevel ± 5`. Crafting/entertainer/deliver/survey/recon/bounty missions
never consult player level at all today. The native "List Missions" client
panel is **not** a server-composed SUI -- it's a stock client window driven
by baseline `MissionObject` messages, and the radial IDs for it
(`MISSION_TERMINAL_LIST`/`MISSION_DETAILS` in `RadialOptions.h`) are handled
entirely client-side (never reach `ObjectMenuSelect.h`), so you cannot hook
that specific radial click server-side.

The **exact chokepoint** every "List Missions"/"Get More Missions" request
already passes through is `MissionManagerImplementation::handleMissionListRequest()`
(line 163) -> `populateMissionList()` (line 589). The cleanest insertion
point is here, not the radial menu:

**Recipe:**
1. Add a per-player pending-choice field to `MissionManager.idl` -- model
   directly on the existing `playerBountyList`/`playerBountyListMutex`
   `VectorMap` + `Mutex` pair already on that class (same idiom, e.g.
   `VectorMap<uint64, pair<int,int>> playerMissionPreference` for
   category/level, guarded by its own mutex). Requires a rebuild.
2. Add two new SUI callback classes under
   `server/zone/objects/player/sui/callbacks/`, modeled line-for-line on
   `InstallMissionTerminalCommand.h`/`InstallMissionTerminalSuiCallback.h`
   (`objects/creature/commands/InstallMissionTerminalCommand.h:19-60` and its
   sibling callback) -- that command already does exactly this shape of
   "`SuiListBox` of named options -> callback stores the selected index" for
   terminal *installation*; category/level selection at generation time is
   the same pattern applied one step later. First SUI lists categories
   (`general`/`artisan`/`bounty`/`entertainer`/`scout`/faction, matching the
   real `missionTerminalType` strings from the section above); its callback
   stores the choice and opens a second `SuiListBox` of level/difficulty
   bands; that callback stores the level and finally calls
   `handleMissionListRequest(...)` (or a new overload) to actually generate.
3. In `handleMissionListRequest()` (line 163), before the existing
   `populateMissionList()` call at line 229: check the pending-preference map
   for this player; if empty, pop the category `SuiListBox` and return
   *without* generating anything yet.
4. Thread the stored category/level through `populateMissionList()` (line
   589) so it can call a specific `randomizeGenericXMission()` directly
   instead of switching on the terminal's own `terminalType`, and through
   `randomizeGenericDestroyMission()`/`randomizeGenericHuntingMission()` /
   `getRandomLairSpawn()` (lines 825, 1878, 1893-1899) so the chosen level
   replaces the automatic `calculatePlayerLevel()` result (clamp it to a sane
   admin-configured band so players can't demand max-difficulty/max-reward
   missions from a starter terminal).
5. Rebuild (`.idl` change) and restart.

Mission type CRCs already defined, for reference:
`MissionTypes.h:5-19` -- `DESTROY`, `BOUNTY`, `DELIVER`, `CRAFTING`,
`HUNTING`, `MUSICIAN`, `DANCER`, `RECON`, `SURVEY` (`ESCORT*` are present but
effectively unused/vestigial in the current randomizers).

## 17. Guilds & Player Cities

These are two separate systems that share the same manager-per-object /
SUI-driven-terminal shape as the rest of this codebase, not a single
"social" subsystem.

**Guilds:** `GuildObject` (`src/server/zone/objects/guild/GuildObject.idl`)
is the persistent guild entity -- `guildMembers` (`GuildMemberList`),
`guildLeaderID`, `guildID`/`guildName`/`guildAbbrev`, a `waringGuilds` map
(guild-vs-guild war states, `WAR_NONE`/`WAR_MUTUAL`/`WAR_IN`/`WAR_OUT`,
`GuildObject.idl:76-79`), an election system (`candidates`/`votes`
`VectorMap`s, `ELECTION_DISABLED`/`_FIRST_WEEK`/`_SECOND_WEEK`,
lines 81-83), and a bitmask permission system on each member
(`PERMISSION_MAIL/SPONSOR/TITLE/ACCEPT/KICK/WAR/NAME/DISBAND/ALL`,
`GuildObject.idl:65-74`, checked via `hasXPermission(playerID)` natives).
`GuildManager` (`.../managers/guild/GuildManager.idl` /
`GuildManagerImplementation.cpp`) is the command-facing entry point.
`createGuild()` (`GuildManagerImplementation.cpp:632-688`) instantiates the
guild object (`ObjectManager::instance()->createObject(0xD6888614, 1, "guilds")`
-- `object/guild/guild_object.iff`), sets the creator as leader with
`PERMISSION_ALL`, and calls `createGuildChannels()`
(lines 690-713) which creates the guild's private chat room hierarchy under
`ChatManager`'s global guild room (see section 19). Real players trigger
guild creation/management through a `GuildTerminal` object
(`objects/tangible/terminal/guild/GuildTerminal.idl` +
`GuildTerminalImplementation.cpp`, SUI-dialog-driven -- section 7's pattern
-- via the `objects/guild/sui/Guild*SuiCallback.h` family), not a slash
command; `ListGuildsCommand.h`/`GuildremoveCommand.h`/
`PermissionListModifyCommand.h` are the only guild-adjacent `QueueCommand`s.

**Player cities:** `CityRegion` (`src/server/zone/objects/region/CityRegion.idl`)
is the persistent city entity -- `cityRank` (byte, grows with citizen
count/structures), `mayorID`, `zoningEnabled`, `cityTreasury`/`taxes`,
`citizenList`/`militiaMembers`/`bannedList` (`CitizenList`),
`cityHall` (a `StructureObject` reference), `structures`/
`commercialStructures` lists, mayoral election fields mirroring guild's
(`candidates`/`mayoralVotes`), and a `citySpecialization` string ("we want
to implement this with skill mods" per the class's own comment --
`CityRegion.idl:36-121`). `CityManager`
(`.../managers/city/CityManagerImplementation.cpp`) is the manager.
**A city is founded by placing a City Hall structure deed** -- there is no
`/createcity` command: `PlaceCityHallSuiCallback.h:106` (the naming-dialog
callback fired after a player places a city hall structure, section 4's
building-placement path) calls `cityManager->createCity(creature, cityName,
x, y)` (`CityManagerImplementation.cpp:196-223`), which builds the
`CityRegion`, sets `cityRank = OUTPOST`, the placing player as `mayorID`,
carves a `Region` of `radiusPerRank[OUTPOST-1]` around the hall, and mails
the new mayor a confirmation (`chatManager->sendMail(...)`, section 19's
mail API). City rank/radius grow over time via citizen-count assessments
(`scheduleCitizenAssessment`); zoning rights, tax rates, and militia
membership are all managed through further SUI dialogs off the City Hall's
radial menu (the `City*SuiCallback.h` family in
`objects/player/sui/callbacks/` -- `CityAdjustTaxSuiCallback`,
`CityToggleZoningSuiCallback`, `CityManageMilitiaSuiCallback`,
`CityMayoralVoteSuiCallback`, etc.), each a thin wrapper that reads the SUI
selection and calls the matching `CityManagerImplementation` setter.

**Recipe -- add a new city SUI action (e.g. a new city-hall menu option):**
follow section 7/8's general SUI + radial recipe: new `SuiWindowType`,
new `City*SuiCallback.h` under `objects/player/sui/callbacks/`, a
`sendMyDialog()` method on `CityManagerImplementation`, wired from the City
Hall's `handleObjectMenuSelect()`/radial menu (section 8), and a matching
setter/getter added to `CityRegion.idl` if it needs new persistent state
(section 11's persistence recipe -- rebuild required for the `.idl` change).

## 18. Vehicles & Space/Ships

**Ground vehicles are a near-exact structural cousin of the
companion/pet control-device pattern already deeply covered by this
project** (`docs/companion_system/NOTES.md`) -- same base class, same
deed-unpack-to-datapad flow, same generate/store radial pair.

**Base class:** `ControlDevice` (`src/server/zone/objects/intangible/ControlDevice.idl`)
extends `IntangibleObject`, holds a single `controlledObject`
(`TangibleObject`) reference, and declares abstract `storeObject()`/
`generateObject()`/`callObject()` (`ControlDevice.idl:14-65`) -- the exact
same base `CompanionControlDevice` extends per the companion notes.
`VehicleControlDevice` (`.../intangible/VehicleControlDevice.idl`) is the
ground-vehicle sibling of `PetControlDevice`/`CompanionControlDevice`:
`handleObjectMenuSelect()` (lines 42-69) switches on
`RadialOptions::VEHICLE_GENERATE`/`VEHICLE_STORE` to call
`generateObject()`/`storeObject()` on the held `VehicleObject`.
`VehicleObject` (`objects/creature/VehicleObject.idl:18`) **extends
`CreatureObject`** -- ground vehicles are creatures (pilotable, have a HAM
pool), same as pets/companions.

**Deed -> control device, one-time unpack (real, complete example):**
`VehicleDeedImplementation::handleObjectMenuSelect()`
(`objects/tangible/deed/vehicle/VehicleDeedImplementation.cpp:56-133`) is the
whole flow: on the deed's radial-20 ("Generate") selection, it checks the
player isn't in combat/indoors and hasn't hit
`playerManager->getBaseStoredVehicles()`, then
`server->getZoneServer()->createObject(controlDeviceObjectTemplate.hashCode(), 1)`
to spawn the `VehicleControlDevice`, `createObject(generatedObjectTemplate.hashCode(), 1)`
to spawn the actual `VehicleObject`, links them with
`vehicleControlDevice->setControlledObject(vehicle)`, transfers the control
device into the player's `datapad`, and **destroys the deed** (one-shot
consumption -- lines 116-123). `controlDeviceObjectTemplate` and
`generatedObjectTemplate` are simple Lua fields on the deed template, real
example `object/tangible/deed/vehicle_deed/speederbike_deed.lua:44-60`:
```lua
controlDeviceObjectTemplate = "object/intangible/vehicle/speederbike_pcd.iff",
generatedObjectTemplate = "object/mobile/vehicle/speederbike.iff",
```
plus the usual `experimentalMin/Max`/`experimentalGroupTitles` crafting-stat
block from section 1/20 (here rolling `hit_points` via resource attribute
`"SR"` -- shock resistance, section 5's resource-attribute codes).

**Gotcha -- vehicle speed/handling is NOT Lua-tunable in this codebase**,
unlike harvester extraction rate (section 5): `VehicleObjectTemplate`
(`templates/creature/VehicleObjectTemplate.h:6-37`) only adds
`decayRate`/`decayCycle` on top of `SharedCreatureObjectTemplate`,
whose `acceleration`/`speed`/`turnRate` setters are **commented out**
(`SharedCreatureObjectTemplate.h:158-160,226-228,238-240`) -- nothing in the
Lua load path writes them. The vehicle Lua templates even have the old
`speed={13,7}`/`turnRate={77,154}`-style values still sitting in the file,
but inside a `--[[ ... ]]` block explicitly labeled *"deprecated and loaded
from the tres, keeping for easy lookups"* (`bin/scripts/object/mobile/vehicle/objects.lua`).
The real numbers are parsed from the binary client `.iff`/TRE template
data, which isn't present in this server repo. **Net effect:** you cannot
retune an existing vehicle's speed/turn rate from server Lua the way you can
a harvester's extraction rate -- only `decayRate`/`decayCycle` and the
deed's `experimentalMin/Max` (hit points) are genuinely server-tunable
today; a new speed/handling profile would need to piggyback on an existing
client vehicle `.iff` (reuse one wholesale) rather than being authored here.

**Space/ships are structurally distinct, not a variant of the above --**
worth knowing the split exists even at orientation depth:
`ShipObject` (`src/server/zone/objects/ship/ShipObject.idl:49`) **extends
`TangibleObject` directly, not `CreatureObject`** -- ships are not
creatures. Ships still use the same control-device pattern for
storage/summoning (`ShipControlDevice` extends `ControlDevice`,
`objects/intangible/ShipControlDevice.idl:20`, with its own
`parkingLocation`/`storedZoneName`/`storedPosition` fields for where a
stored ship reappears), but everything past that point is its own subtree:
`FighterShipObject`/`MultiPassengerShipObject`/`PobShipObject` (player-owned
starship variants, `objects/ship/*.idl`), a component/slot system
(`ShipComponent.h`, `ComponentSlots.h`, `ShipChassisData.h`) instead of
armor/weapon wearables, its own AI (`ShipAiAgent`, referenced from
`LootManagerImplementation.cpp`'s ship-specific `createLoot(trx, container,
ShipAiAgent*)` overload -- section 15), and a separate `SpaceZone`
(`Zone` subtype, section 12) rather than the ground `GroundZone`. Full space
combat internals are out of scope for this orientation-level entry; start
from `ShipObject.idl`/`ShipObjectImplementation.cpp` and `ShipManager.h`
(`.../managers/ship/ShipManager.h`) if working in that subtree.

**Recipe -- add a new ground vehicle:**
1. New control-device Lua template under `object/intangible/vehicle/my_vehicle_pcd.lua`
   (copy an existing one, section 1's `ObjectTemplates:addTemplate()` pattern).
2. New `VehicleObject` mobile Lua template under `object/mobile/vehicle/my_vehicle.lua`.
3. New deed Lua under `object/tangible/deed/vehicle_deed/my_vehicle_deed.lua`
   (copy `speederbike_deed.lua`), `controlDeviceObjectTemplate`/
   `generatedObjectTemplate` pointing at the two new templates above, tune
   the `experimentalMin/Max` hit-points range.
4. Wire the deed into a schematic (section 1/20) if it should be craftable,
   or a loot group (section 15) / vendor if not.
5. Restart the server (pure Lua, no rebuild) unless genuinely new vehicle
   *behavior* is needed (new C++ `VehicleObject` subclass).

## 19. Chat, Mail & Social Systems

**There is no separate `MailManager`** -- in-game mail, spatial/tell chat,
and chat-room management (including guild chat, section 17) are all one
class: `ChatManager` (`src/server/chat/ChatManager.idl` /
`ChatManagerImplementation.cpp`, a `ZoneServer`-owned singleton reached via
`zoneServer->getChatManager()`, already used from screenplays per section 3's
`sendMail` bridge function).

**Mail:** `PersistentMessage` (`src/server/chat/PersistentMessage.idl`) is
the persisted mail object -- `senderName`, `subject`/`body` (`unicode`),
`status` (`NEW`/`READ`/`UNREAD` byte constants, lines 31-33),
`receiverObjectID`, plus `StringIdChatParameterVector`/
`WaypointChatParameterVector` for STF-templated or waypoint-carrying mail
(the mechanism section 3's quest rewards and section 17's "new city"
notification both use). `ChatManager::sendMail()` has three overloads
(`ChatManager.idl:398-407`); the core implementation
(`ChatManagerImplementation.cpp:1822-1904`) builds a `PersistentMessage`,
persists it (`ObjectManager::instance()->persistObject(mail, 1, "mail")`),
and then either delivers immediately if the recipient is online
(`mail->sendTo(receiver, false)`, after checking
`receiverPlayerObject->isIgnoring(sendername)` -- ignored senders' mail is
silently destroyed unless the sender has GM god-mode, lines 1888-1892) or
queues it in a `PendingMessageList` keyed by receiver object ID for
next-login delivery (lines 1881-1883).

**Chat rooms:** `ChatRoom` (`src/server/chat/room/ChatRoom.idl`) has a
`chatRoomType` with constants `DEFAULT`/`AUCTION`/`GUILD`/`GROUP`/`PLANET`/
`CUSTOM` (`ChatRoom.idl:66-71`). Guild chat is created per-guild inside
`GuildManagerImplementation::createGuildChannels()`
(section 17, `GuildManagerImplementation.cpp:690-713`) as a private child
room of `chatManager->getGuildRoom()`. Group chat is simpler: `GroupObject`
(`objects/group/GroupObject.idl:32`) holds its own `chatRoom` field directly,
created/destroyed via native `startChatRoom(CreatureObject leader)`/
`destroyChatRoom()` (lines 102-105) -- no separate manager call needed.
Spatial (say/emote/shout) and tell-style chat go through
`ChatManager::broadcastChatMessage()` (`ChatManager.idl:365-378`, two
overloads -- STF-templated and free-text `unicode` -- both taking a
`spatialChatType`/`moodType`/`chatFlags`/`languageID`), the same call
screenplays reach via the `spatialChat` Director-Lua bridge from section 3.

**Friends & ignore lists:** both live directly on `PlayerObject`
(`src/server/zone/objects/player/PlayerObject.idl`), not `ChatManager` --
`friendList`/`ignoreList` fields (`PlayerObject.idl:146,149`, both
`DeltaVector<string>` of character names, exposed via `getFriendList()`/
`getIgnoreList()` at lines 1548/1596) with client-driven mutation through
four `QueueCommand`s: `AddFriendCommand.h`, `RemoveFriendCommand.h`,
`FindFriendCommand.h`, `GetFriendListCommand.h`
(`objects/creature/commands/`). `isIgnoring(name)` (used by the mail-delivery
ignore check above) and `sendFriendLists()` (login-time push,
`PlayerObject.idl:1330`) are the two consumer-side entry points.

**Recipe -- add a new mail-triggered notification (e.g. from a new system's
event):** call the existing `chatManager->sendMail(fromName, subjectStf,
StringIdChatParameter, recipientCharacterName, waypoint?)` overload from
wherever the event fires (a manager, a screenplay via the `sendMail` Lua
bridge, a command) -- no new class needed; this is the same call section 17's
`createCity()` and section 3's quest rewards already use.

**Recipe -- add a new chat room type (e.g. an event-specific channel):**
add a constant alongside `ChatRoom.idl:66-71`'s existing
`DEFAULT/AUCTION/GUILD/GROUP/PLANET/CUSTOM`, then follow
`createGuildChannels()`'s pattern (`chatManager->createRoom(name, parentRoom)`,
`setPrivate()`/`setChatRoomType()`/`setOwnerID()`/`setCanEnter()`) from
whatever manager owns the new feature. Requires a rebuild (`.idl` change)
only if you need the new constant; a room reachable purely by title/parent
under `CUSTOM` needs no C++ change at all.

## 20. Crafting & Manufacturing

**Tool/session hierarchy:** a player crafts by using a `CraftingTool`
(`src/server/zone/objects/tangible/tool/CraftingTool.idl`, typed
`CLOTHING`/`FOOD`/`GENERIC`/`JEDI`/`SPACE`/`STRUCTURE`/`WEAPON`,
lines 33-39) at (optionally) a `CraftingStation`
(`objects/tangible/tool/CraftingStation.idl`, a placeable amenity that
boosts success/experimentation chance). The actual multi-step crafting UI is
driven by a `CraftingSession` (`objects/player/sessions/crafting/CraftingSession.idl`
/ `CraftingSessionImplementation.cpp`) -- this codebase's general
"player session" pattern (compare `SurveySession.idl` alongside it) rather
than a one-shot command. Client-facing steps map directly onto
`CraftingSessionImplementation` methods: `initializeSession()`/`startSession()`
(lines 36, 112) -> `selectDraftSchematic()` (line 328, creates the working
`ManufactureSchematic` + prototype, lines 392-426) -> repeated
`addIngredient()`/`removeIngredient()` (lines 532, 618) -> `nextCraftingStage()`
(line 676) -> `initialAssembly()` (line 734, the real stat-rolling step,
detailed below) -> `experiment()` (line 1007, spends experimentation points
per section 9-style skill mods) -> `createPrototype()`/`createManufactureSchematic()`
(lines 1367, 1445, the two possible end states: a one-off item, or a
mass-production blueprint). Commands
(`CreateManfSchematicCommand.h`, `CreatePrototypeCommand.h`,
`RequestCraftingSessionCommand.h`, `NextCraftingStageCommand.h`,
`SelectDraftSchematicCommand.h`, `StopCraftingSessionCommand.h`,
`CancelCraftingSessionCommand.h`) are thin wrappers that just forward into
the active `CraftingSession`.

**Schematics** (recap/extension of section 1): `DraftSchematic`
(`objects/draftschematic/DraftSchematic.idl`) is the "recipe" -- `targetTemplate`
(crafted item's `.iff`), ingredient slot definitions, and a list of
`ResourceWeight` entries (`getResourceWeightCount()`/`getResourceWeight(i)`,
`DraftSchematic.idl:111-115`). These `ResourceWeight`s are actually built
server-side from the **same** `experimentalGroups`/`experimentalAttributes`/
`experimentalMin`/`experimentalMax`/`experimentalPrecision`/
`experimentalCombineType`/`experimentalWeights`/`numberExperimentalProperties`
Lua fields already documented for items/deeds in sections 1 and 18
(`SharedTangibleObjectTemplate.cpp:441-459`) -- a schematic and a lootable
item/vehicle deed all share one experimental-attribute authoring format.
Where a schematic differs: its `experimentalProperties` entries are
**resource attribute codes** (`"OQ"`, `"SR"`, `"CR"`, etc. -- section 5's
`res_quality`/`res_shock_resistance`/`res_cold_resist`/... mapping) rather
than `"XX"` placeholders, telling the crafting math which resource stat on
the ingredient resource(s) feeds which item attribute.

**Resource quality -> item stats, the actual math**
(`CraftingManagerImplementation::setInitialCraftingValues()`,
`CraftingManagerImplementation.cpp:180-186`, delegates by
`manufactureSchematic->getLabratory()` to a `SharedLabratory` subclass --
`ResourceLabratory` for ordinary items, `GeneticLabratory` for
creature/DNA-based crafting):
1. `ResourceLabratory::setInitialCraftingValues()`
   (`.../crafting/labratories/ResourceLabratory.cpp:39-118`) iterates the
   schematic's `ResourceWeight`s; for each, it sums
   `getWeightedValue(manufactureSchematic, resourceAttributeType) * percentage`
   across every ingredient slot referencing that resource attribute
   (`getWeightedValue()`, `SharedLabratory.h:30`, reads the actual resource's
   rolled stat -- the same `res_*`/`OQ`/`CR`/... values documented in
   section 5's resource-spawning writeup -- off whatever resource item(s)
   were placed in the schematic's resource slots).
2. That weighted sum becomes a 0-100% `currentPercentage` for the item
   attribute (`getAssemblyPercentage(weightedSum) * assemblySuccessModifier`,
   line 96) which `CraftingValues::recalculateValues()` interpolates against
   the attribute's `experimentalMin`/`experimentalMax` range to get the
   final rolled stat -- this is the direct mechanism by which, e.g., a
   weapon crafted from high-Shock-Resistance metal gets a higher rolled
   `hit_points`/damage stat than the same schematic fed low-quality metal.
3. `applyComponentStats()` (lines 164-370) then layers in stats from any
   **component** ingredients (pre-crafted sub-parts placed in a component
   slot, as opposed to raw resources) using one of five combine modes on
   `AttributesMap`: `LINEARCOMBINE` (additive), `PERCENTAGECOMBINE`,
   `BITSETCOMBINE` (OR the bits), `OVERRIDECOMBINE` (component value ignored,
   schematic wins), `LIMITEDCOMBINE` (additive but clamped to
   min/max) -- the combine mode is set per-attribute by the schematic's
   `experimentalCombineType` field from section 1.
4. Player skill affects this indirectly: `experimentationPointsTotal` (how
   many points the player has to spend in the `experiment()` step nudging
   percentages up) comes from `crafter->getSkillMod(draftSchematic->getExperimentationSkill())`
   (`CraftingSessionImplementation.cpp:754`) -- the same `getSkillMod()`
   consumer pattern documented in section 9.

**The experimentation roll itself -- exact formula** (per-row spend loop,
`CraftingSessionImplementation::experiment()`, lines 1007-1199): each row the
player spends points on rolls a success **tier**, not a raw percentage --
`CraftingManagerImplementation::calculateExperimentationSuccess()`
(`.cpp:63-132`) buckets `experimentRoll = toolModifier * (luckRoll +
experimentingPoints*4)` (where `luckRoll = random(100) + cityBonus`, instant
`AMAZINGSUCCESS` if `luckRoll > 95 - foodBonus - forceSkill`) against
thresholds 70/60/50/40/30/20 into
GREAT/GOOD/MODERATE/SUCCESS/MARGINAL/OK/BARELY. A separate failure check,
`calculateExperimentationFailureRate()` (`.cpp:43-56`), rolls
`50 + (resourceMalleability-500)/40 + expPoints - 5*pointsSpent` first. The
tier then maps to a **per-point** percentage modifier via
`SharedLabratory::calculateExperimentationValueModifier()`
(`SharedLabratory.cpp:21-58`, `results *= pointsAttempted`) --
AMAZING +0.08, GREAT +0.07, GOOD +0.055, MODERATE +0.015, SUCCESS +0.01,
MARGINAL 0.00, OK -0.04, BARELY -0.07, CRITICALFAILURE -0.08 -- added to (or
subtracted from) the attribute's `currentPercentage` before the same
`experimentalMin`/`experimentalMax` interpolation from point 2 runs again. A
`CraftingTool` "force critical experiment" consumable can force
`AMAZINGSUCCESS` outright (`CraftingSessionImplementation.cpp:1098-1104`).
Spending more points per row multiplies the modifier, so dumping many points
into one attribute in one attempt is not equivalent to several smaller
attempts (tier is rolled once, then scaled by point count).

**Factories (mass production):** a `ManufactureSchematic`
(`objects/manufactureschematic/ManufactureSchematic.idl:27-39`) created via
`createManufactureSchematic()` instead of a one-off prototype can be placed
into a `FactoryObject`
(`objects/installation/factory/FactoryObject.idl`, an `installation`-type
placeable, same installation family as the harvesters in section 5) to
produce copies automatically over time, using a `FactoryBlueprint`
(embedded on the schematic itself, `ManufactureSchematic.idl:39`) as the
recipe snapshot and a `FactoryHopperObserver`
(`objects/installation/factory/FactoryHopperObserver.idl`) watching the
output hopper, mirroring the harvester hopper pattern from section 5.

**Recipe -- add a new craftable item (ties together sections 1/15/20):**
1. Item Lua template (section 1) with a real `experimentalGroups`/
   `experimentalAttributes`/`experimentalMin`/`Max`/`experimentalWeights`/
   `experimentalCombineType` block if it should roll stats from resources.
2. New/edit `object/draft_schematic/<category>/*.lua`: `targetTemplate`
   pointing at the item, ingredient slot list (raw resource slots reference
   a resource *class* by name -- section 5 -- component slots reference
   another item template), `experimentationSkill`/`customizationSkill`
   naming the skill mod consulted in `initialAssembly()`/`experiment()`.
3. `includeFile(...)` the schematic into its category's include list and
   grant it via `CraftingManager::awardSchematicGroup()` (called from a
   skill's grant path, or directly) so a player's crafting tool actually
   lists it.
4. Restart the server (pure Lua, no rebuild) unless the item needs a new
   C++ object type (section 1's item-type-vs-item-instance distinction still
   applies here).

---

## 21. Client TRE/Asset Pipeline — Reality Check

This section consolidates what's genuinely patchable with this project's own
tooling vs. what still requires reverse-engineering, now that the question
has actually been tested against real client archives rather than assumed.

**A full client data mirror exists one directory above this repo**, at
`C:\Companion\tre\` (~8.3GB, 80+ real `.tre` archives — `bottom.tre`,
`patch_00..14_*.tre`, `data_sku1_*`, `mtg_patch_*`, `mtg_planets.tre`, etc.),
sibling to `Core3/`. The Core3 repo itself ships no real client `.tre` data
— only this project's own output (`docs/companion_system/tools/companion_patch.tre`).
Confirmed by direct extraction: terrain `.trn`, world snapshot `.ws`,
`resource_tree.iff`, and the vehicle mobile template `.iff`s **all
physically exist** in that mirror for every stock planet (plus several
non-stock ones in `mtg_planets.tre`) — none of the "blocking" formats below
are actually missing bytes; the real gap is tooling coverage.

**Proven, working codecs today** (`docs/companion_system/tools/`, each with
a documented byte-exact round-trip in `docs/companion_system/NOTES.md`):
`iff_datatable.py` (generic DTII DataTable — `COLS`/`TYPE`/`ROWS` chunks),
`stf_codec.py` (STF string tables), `tre_reader.py`/`tre_writer.py` (TRE
archive container), `core3_hashcode.py` (the `String::hashCode()` port used
as the TRE lookup key).

**Correction — `resource_tree.iff` is NOT client-only/unreachable, it's
already-solved format.** `ResourceTree::buildTreeFromClient()`
(`ResourceTree.cpp:29-40`) loads it via the exact same `DataTableIff` C++
class `SkillManager::loadClientData()` uses for `skills.iff`
(`SkillManager.cpp:71-80`) — it's a plain DTII table, real copies exist in
8+ archives in the mirror (`patch_03/04/09/10/11_00/12_00/13_00/14_00.tre`,
`mtg_planets.tre`, all at `datatables/resource/resource_tree.iff`). **New
resource classes/attribute ranges are patchable today** with the identical
`iff_datatable.py` + `tre_writer.py` recipe already proven for
`skills.iff`/`command_table.iff`/`xp_limits.iff` — no new reverse-engineering
needed. (Other datatables sharing this same `DataTableIff` loader and likely
reachable the same way, unconfirmed by direct test: `datatables/player/quests.iff`,
`misc/quest_crc_string_table.iff`, `datatables/questtask/*.iff`.)

**The other three blocking cases, re-ranked after direct byte-level testing:**
1. **`resource_tree.iff`** — not actually blocked (see above).
2. **World snapshot `.ws`** (new buildings) — verified tractable, easiest of
   the remaining two, but with one real non-format risk. See §21a.
3. **Vehicle `SharedCreatureObjectTemplate` speed/turnRate** — two separate
   problems. The client `.iff` files exist (`shared_speederbike.iff`, etc.,
   `patch_05/07/08/11_02/13_00.tre`) and use a moderate-complexity named-chunk
   format (`parseVariableData(varName, chunk)`, one chunk per field, with
   template inheritance) — readable in principle. But even once read, it's a
   dead end **today** regardless: `setAcceleration`/`setSpeed`/`setTurnRate`
   are commented out in `SharedCreatureObjectTemplate.h:158-160,226-228,238-240`
   (see section 18) — applying the values needs a C++ change, not just a
   Python codec.
4. **Terrain `.trn`** (new planets) — hardest, confirmed by direct extraction
   and full parser reading, not just the header. See §21b.

**Practical ceiling right now:** any client **DTII DataTable** (proven:
`skills.iff`, `xp_limits.iff`, `command_table.iff`, `resource_tree.iff`;
likely: `quests.iff`/questtask tables), any **STF string** table, and
**TRE packaging/patching** at correct load priority are all solved,
proven problems for this project today. Terrain, world snapshots, vehicle
object-template chunks, and mesh/animation formats remain unsolved —
terrain being by far the hardest of the four, world snapshots the most
approachable next target (with one open risk, see §21a), and vehicle stats
blocked by a C++ gate even after parsing.

### 21a. World snapshot (`.ws`) — verified by direct extraction

Extracted a real file (`snapshot/yavin4.ws` from `patch_00.tre`, 135,117
bytes — the smallest real snapshot found; `tatooine.ws` runs 1.37MB).
**Correction to the earlier "flat node list" guess: it's actually a
recursive tree**, not flat. Confirmed container:

```
FORM 'WSNP'
  FORM '0001'
    FORM 'NODS'
      FORM 'NODE' -> FORM '0000' -> DATA(52 bytes)   [+ optional child NODEs]
      ... (996 top-level NODEs)
    OTNL chunk                                        [317 object-template path strings, at end of file]
```

Same big-endian FORM/DATA nesting `iff_datatable.py` already handles for
DTII tables (`IffStream::loadMainChunks`,
`MMOEngine/src/engine/util/iffstream/IffStream.cpp:92-104`) — no
hash-sorted lookup table like `.tre` needs. Parser:
`src/templates/snapshot/WorldSnapshotIff.cpp:14-56` (top-level: `WSNP` →
version form `'0001'` → `NODS` → node count is implicit,
`nods->getChunksSize()` → then `OTNL`, an int count + that many
null-terminated strings). Per-node: `WorldSnapshotNode.h:62-108` — a fixed
52-byte `DATA` record (`objectID`, `parentID`, `nameID` [index into OTNL],
`cellid`, quaternion `qw/qx/qy/qz`, position stored as `x,z,y` not `x,y,z`,
a float `gameObjectType`, one unknown u32), **then recurses** for
`versionForm->getChunksSize() - 1` more child `NODE`s — this recursion is
exactly how a building (`objectID=0x0007255d`,
`object/building/yavin/shared_temple_blueleaf.iff`) owns 2 interior-cell
children, one of which owns 4 more (furniture/loot-crate placements) —
depth-3 nesting observed in the real file. 96% of the 1,369 total nodes are
still leaves (buildings/structures with children are the minority).

**Tractability:** yes — a Python reader is ~60 lines, mechanically the same
kind of walk as `iff_datatable.py`. A writer needs to bump the declared
big-endian size of every ancestor `FORM` after an insert (`NODE`→`0000`→
...→`NODS`→`0001`→`WSNP`, plus `OTNL`'s own size/count if a new template
path is needed) — the same category of bookkeeping `tre_writer.py` already
does, just more nesting levels. **Appending one new building is genuinely
append-only** — parent/child linkage is entirely by `objectID` *value*
lookup (`PlanetManagerImplementation.cpp:574`,
`zoneServer->getObject(node->getParentID())`), not by array position or byte
offset, so a new node can be added as the last child under `NODS` without
touching any existing bytes.

**The real risk isn't the file format — it's `objectID` collision.**
`PlanetManagerImplementation::loadSnapshotObject`
(`PlanetManagerImplementation.cpp:557-620`) hands the file's `objectID`
straight to `zoneServer->createClientObject(hash, objectID)` (`:579`) as the
object's **permanent, live, database-persisted** object ID — the exact same
ID space `ObjectManager`'s own runtime counter
(`getNextFreeObjectID()`/`nextObjectID`, `ObjectManager.cpp:407-444`)
allocates from for every object created dynamically at runtime. This pass
did not establish where the safe boundary between "IDs baked into stock
snapshot files" and "IDs the live counter will hand out" actually is — that
has to be resolved (e.g. picking new IDs from a clearly-unused high range,
or querying the DB's current high-water mark before authoring) before
hand-adding a node is safe, independent of the (solved) file-format
mechanics.

### 21b. Terrain (`.trn`) — verified by direct extraction

Extracted a real file (`terrain/tatooine.trn` from `patch_00.tre`,
**1,188,188 bytes**). A generic FORM/DATA chunk walker with **zero
per-tag special-casing** (same big-endian tag+length convention as
`iff_datatable.py`) parses the entire file end-to-end with zero errors:
**7,090 total chunks, 54 distinct tag names, max nesting depth 21.**
Top-level shape: `FORM 'PTAT'` → `FORM '0014'` → a flat `DATA` block
(terrain file path + global params) + `FORM 'TGEN'` (the
`TerrainGenerator`, 139KB, 7 sub-groups) + `FORM '0001'` (`TerrainMaps`,
1.05MB — two raw 512×512 baked bitmap blobs, `WMAP`/`SMAP`, no internal
structure). So **the container itself is exactly as chunk-walkable as
DTII** — this part is not the hard part.

**The hard part: ~40-50 leaf chunk types, each with a bespoke, undocumented
byte layout that must be hand-transcribed from C++, one at a time — there
is no DTII-style self-describing schema for any of them.**
`layer/Layer.cpp` (304 lines) is the real recursive core:
`parseAffector` is a 21-case switch on tags (`ACCN/ACRF/ACRH/AENV/AEXC/
AFDN/AFCN/AFDF/AFSC/AFSN/AHCN/AHFR/AHTR/APAS/ARCN/ARIV/AROA/ASCN/ASRP` +
3 dead cases), `parseBoundary` a 6-case switch (`BPOL/BREC/BCIR/BPLN` + 2
dead), `parseFilter` a 6-case switch (`FHGT/FBIT/FDIR/FFRA/FSHD/FSLP`), and
a `Layer` can recurse into child `Layer`s indefinitely (observed depth 21 in
the real file, 255 layers total on Tatooine). Each leaf class (e.g.
`BoundaryPolygon::parseFromIffStream`,
`layer/boundaries/BoundaryPolygon.h:293-317`: vertex count → N×(x,y floats)
→ feathering type/amount → water flag/height → shader size/name) has its
own field order with no way to infer it from bytes alone. Total subsystem
size: **82 files, 8,506 lines** (7 top-level groups, `Layer`, 5 boundary
types, 22 affector types, 9 filter types, plus fractal/family/segment leaf
classes) — versus `iff_datatable.py`'s ~150-line single generic DTII codec.

**Verdict:** a full read+write codec is realistically a multi-day port (one
leaf schema at a time, an order of magnitude bigger than any format solved
so far) — but not a blind reverse-engineering project, since every leaf's
exact layout is already handed over by the C++ parser (no fuzzing/guessing
needed), and nothing observed is compressed/checksummed at the leaf level,
so byte-exact round-trips look achievable. **A much cheaper realistic
middle path exists today: since the generic walker already gives exact
tag/offset/length for all 7,090 chunks, most content can round-trip as
opaque unchanged bytes — you only need per-field knowledge for the
specific leaf types you actually intend to mutate** (e.g. one `AHCN` height
constant, one `SFAM` shader filename, one `BPOL`'s vertex list), not the
whole format. **A read-only "list what's in this terrain file" introspection
tool is cheap and effectively already built** in this pass (the zero-error
generic walker itself) — e.g. "this planet has 255 layers, 256 circle
boundaries, 56 polygon boundaries, 87 height-constant affectors, 15 shader
families" comes for free before any leaf-level decoding work.
