## 22. Character Creation, Badges & Titles

**Entry point:** client `ClientCreateCharacter` packet (CRC `0xB97F3074`)
→ `ClientCreateCharacterCallback` → `PlayerManager::createPlayer()` (one-line
forward) → **`PlayerCreationManager::createCharacter()`**
(`managers/creation/PlayerCreationManager.cpp:317-634`) — this one function
is the entire real flow, everything below is steps inside it.

**Sequence:** per-galaxy character cap + name validation → resolve
`PlayerCreatureTemplate`/`RacialCreationData` from the chosen race →
**Jedi is silently unselectable at creation**: if the profession string
contains `"jedi"` it's rewritten to `"crafting_artisan"` (`:365-366` — Jedi
is earned in-game only, see section 9a) → height clamped to template
min/max → appearance/hair applied and validated (`ImageDesignManager`,
`HairAssetData`) → flat hardcoded starting cash/bank (**100 / 1000**,
configurable via `player_creation_manager.lua`'s `startingCash`/
`startingBank` globals) → skill points set from the same Lua config →
**three additive item/skill layers**, all inside `addProfessionStartingItems()`/
`addStartingItems()`/`addRacialMods()`: profession layer (novice skill +
per-attribute HAM mods from `profession_defaults.iff`/`profession_mods.iff`
+ profession clothing/items), common layer (`default_pc_equipment.iff` +
universal `commonStartingItems` Lua table), racial layer (additive racial
HAM mods from `racial_mods.iff`/`attribute_limits.iff` + species-specific
starting skills/items, e.g. Wookiee bonuses).

**No player-chosen attribute allocation exists server-side** — HAM totals
are 100% deterministic from the profession+racial mod addition above; the
client packet has no per-attribute distribution field, and the
`getMaximum/MinimumAttributeLimit()` accessors are read-only display data,
never consumed in the write path.

**Starting city/location is NOT decided at creation**, despite the client
packet carrying a `location` field (parsed, never read). Every new
character is unconditionally dropped into a newbie tutorial building/zone
first (`createTutorialBuilding()`/`insertIntoSkippedTutorialBuilding()`).
Real city selection happens **later, in-world**, via
`NewbieSelectStartingLocationCommand` reading `datatables/creation/
starting_locations.iff` and teleporting the player out of the tutorial
zone — a `StartingLocationTerminal` object inside the tutorial hall is what
presents the city list.

**Rate limit:** one character creation per hour per account, enforced via
an in-memory map + DB fallback query.

**Badges — real, generic, not stubbed.** Data: `datatables/badge/
badge_map.iff` (client binary, same TRE-only situation as `skills.iff`),
loaded by `BadgeList::loadData()` into rows with a `TYPE` from a closed set
(`ACCUMULATION/INTEREST/EXPLORATION/MASTER/EVENT/CONTENT`). Storage: a
160-bit (`5×uint32`) bitmask + per-type counters on `Badges`
(`objects/player/badges/Badges.h`). **Award is fully generic** —
`PlayerManagerImplementation::awardBadge(ghost, badgeId)` sets the bit,
fires `ObserverEventType::BADGEAWARDED`, and auto-cascades into milestone
meta-badges (total-count and exploration-count thresholds) purely by name
lookup, no per-badge hardcoding. Exposed to Lua (`ghost:awardBadge(id)`),
used by ~9 real screenplays (dungeons, world events, theme parks). **Area-
triggered badges are a real object type** (`BadgeActiveArea`, auto-awards
on `notifyEnter()`), placed as plain `{name,x,y,cellID,radius,badgeID}`
Lua-data rows per planet (~50 real exploration spots across all planets).
**Real mechanical effects exist, not just cosmetic tracking**: a set of
"Ace Pilot" badge triples each add +1.0 to a real space-combat XP
multiplier; a badge gates one faction-recruiter conversation branch;
mastering certain professions auto-awards a mastery badge. Rough scale:
160-badge bitmask ceiling, real indices referenced in source run to ~138,
consistent with vanilla SWG's historical badge count.

**Collections — confirmed absent.** No `Collection`/`CollectionManager`/
collection-slot concept exists anywhere in `src/` (the only near-name-hits,
`LootGroupCollection`/`ForageAreaCollection`, are unrelated loot-table
grouping classes). `PlayerObject.idl` has no collection field. This is a
hard gap, not a stub to extend — building it would mean a new datatable
schema, new `PlayerObject` storage, a new client-facing response message,
and a new manager from scratch.

**Titles beyond skill titles — none.** `setTitle()`
(`PlayerObjectImplementation.cpp:1661-1677`) hard-requires the title string
to resolve to a `skills.iff` row with `IS_TITLE=1` that the player actually
holds (section 9's mechanism) — badges never call `setTitle()` anywhere in
the source. So the skill-title system is the *only* player-title mechanism
in this codebase; badge display is entirely separate
(`BadgesResponseMessage`, sent by `/requestBadges`).

**Recipe — new badge:** reusing an existing unused badge ID/name in
`badge_map.iff` is pure code, zero data changes:
`ghost:awardBadge(id)`/`playerManager->awardBadge(ghost, badgeId)` from any
screenplay/command, no rebuild. A genuinely new badge row needs a
`badge_map.iff` patch (same TRE `iff_datatable.py` recipe as `skills.iff`)
plus a matching `badge_n`/description STF entry — still no C++ rebuild. A
place-triggered badge is one more `{name,x,y,cellID,radius,badgeID}` row in
the relevant planet's Lua manager file. **New collection slot: not
applicable** — there's no framework to extend; this would be new C++ from
scratch, not a small addition.

---

## 23. Entertainer / Performance System

**Data model:** each dance/song is one row of a client-binary datatable,
`datatables/performance/performance.iff` (same TRE-only situation as
`skills.iff`/`badge_map.iff`), loaded by `PerformanceManager::
loadPerformances()`. Fields include `requiredDance`/`requiredSong`/
`requiredInstrument` (ability-string gates, same `hasAbility()`/`COMMANDS`
mechanism as any other granted command — section 6/9), `actionPointsPerLoop`,
`loopDuration`, `baseXp`, `flourishXpMod`, `healMindWound`/`healShockWound`,
and animation/flourish names.

**Session:** `EntertainingSession` (a `Facade`, same pattern as
`SurveySession`/`CraftingSession` from sections 5/20) attached via
`addActiveSession(SessionFacadeType::ENTERTAINING, ...)`. `/dance <name>`/
`/music <song>` start it; a self-rescheduling 10-second tick task
(`EntertainingSessionTask`) drives per-cycle Action-point drain, patron
healing, and XP award for the whole performance duration. Music has a real
15-second **outro** window on stop (`stopMusic(skipOutro=false)`
broadcasts a flourish, delays the actual stop by 15s) — dance stops
instantly.

**Audience:** `/watch <target>`/`/listen <target>`
(`PlayerManager::startWatch()`/`startListen()`) require line-of-sight,
reject NPC targets (except droids with a playback module for `/listen`),
and are continuously range-checked every tick (60m) — wandering out of
range auto-drops you as a patron, it's not a one-time join check.

**Two independent per-tick effects on patrons**, both in
`doEntertainerPatronEffects()`: (1) **wound/shock healing** — a real
Medic-adjacent mechanic gated by `healing_dance_wound`/`healing_music_wound`/
`healing_dance_shock`/`healing_music_shock` skill mods, healing MIND/FOCUS/
WILLPOWER and shock wounds specifically (never HAM health/action — a clean
split from the Medic profession), scaled by `(flourishCount+1)`; (2) **stat
buffs** (`performance_enhance_music_focus/willpower`, `_dance_mind`) — only
granted to patrons who are grouped with the entertainer or are their
explicit `/setPerform` target (passive bystanders get healing but not the
buff), requiring ≥1 minute of continuous watch/listen, strength/duration
accruing tick-by-tick capped at ~2h10m total.

**Flourishes are real and mechanically load-bearing, not animation-only.**
`FlourishCommand` (index 1-8, gated by a `"flourish+N"` granted ability)
drains Action points, plays the real animation/packet, immediately re-runs
the patron buff-tick out of cycle, and adds to `flourishXp` (capped per
tick: only the first few flourishes count, tuned by loop duration).
`BandFlourishCommand` propagates one flourish to every in-range grouped
bandmate (including droid playback modules). Separate "special effect"
abilities (Dazzle/Distract/Spotlight/etc., `PerformEffect.h`) are a
distinct cosmetic mechanic, not flourishes, and don't feed XP.

**XP formula** (`awardEntertainerExperience()`, every tick):
`xpAmount = ceil((flourishXp + baseXp) * (1 + groupBonus*0.05 +
min(audienceSize,50)/50 + min(applause,100)/100))`. **Applause is the only
"tip" mechanic — there is no credit-based tipping in this codebase**:
targeted applaud/cheer/clap social emotes from bystanders increment a
capped counter that only feeds the XP bonus above, no currency changes
hands. A separate location+time `EntertainerMissionObjective` (10-minute
timer while performing inside a mission-generated area) uses the normal
mission-reward path instead.

**Instruments are ordinary crafted items** (`DraftSchematic`s under
`object/draft_schematic/instrument/`, standard resource/ingredient slots —
section 20's pattern applies directly); 10 real instrument types exist in
a hardcoded C++ enum/switch (`PerformanceManager::getInstrument()` etc.).
**Dances/songs are fixed authored content, not player-composable** — no
Lua API or SUI exists to create a new one; they only come from
`performance.iff` rows filtered by the player's granted ability list. The
one real "creation" mechanic is a droid **playback/recording module**
(`DroidPlaybackModuleDataComponent`) that records a live performance's
index and replays it later — a jukebox, not song authoring.

**No "Group Dance" mechanic exists** as a distinct feature (confirmed
absent by exhaustive grep) — group-adjacency only matters for shared-crowd
XP splitting and buff eligibility, not a single combined heal/buff action.

**Recipe — new instrument (reusing an existing model):** pure data, a new
`DraftSchematic` Lua file; a genuinely new instrument *category* needs a
C++ enum + switch-statement change (`PerformanceManager.cpp`, hardcoded,
not data-driven). **New dance/song:** requires a `performance.iff` patch
(TRE toolchain) referencing already-shipped client animation names (no new
animations can be authored here) plus a `COMMANDS`-style ability grant via
`skills.iff` (the same column that grants slash-commands, confirmed
dual-purposed) — three fallback performances are hardcoded directly in
`SkillManager` as always-granted because they're missing from the
datatable, a real precedent for bypassing the datatable-grant path
entirely if needed. **New flourish slot beyond 8:** needs a C++ change
(`FlourishCommand.h` hardcodes the 1-8 range); reusing existing slots for a
new dance is pure data.

---

## 24. Vendor / Bazaar / Auction System

**Player vendors:** `VendorDataComponent` (extends the shared
`AuctionTerminalDataComponent` also used by plain bazaar terminals).
Listing an item is **not a server SUI** — the client sends a native
`CreateAuctionMessage` packet directly (price, duration, description) →
`AuctionManagerImplementation::addSaleItem()` → validation
(`manage_vendor`/`vendor_item_limit` skill mods, a flat 99,999,999 price
ceiling) → the item is converted into a persisted `AuctionItem` record and
**removed from the world** (it only becomes a real object again on
retrieval). Buying (`doInstantBuy()`) is a real credit transfer — **bank
credits only** — with city sales tax backed out of the seller's proceeds
into the city treasury if the vendor sits in a taxed city (section 17).
Both parties get real in-game mail with a waypoint.

**Bazaar/commodity search is real and genuinely galaxy-wide, not a
per-vendor stub.** `AuctionTerminalMap` is a real 3-level index (planet →
region/city → vendor → sorted item list) with a 4-tier location scope
(`LT_GALAXY/LT_PLANET/LT_REGION/LT_MARKET`) that falls through to a true
"search every terminal in the galaxy" query when no scope is given. Search
supports category filters, min/max price, and case-insensitive substring
name matching, and runs on its own async task queue (never blocks the main
thread) — this is a fully working Galactic-Trade-Network-equivalent, not
placeholder infrastructure.

**Auctions are real, with one confirmed gap.** `AuctionItem.auction` flags a
timed auction (vs. fixed-price instant-buy); bidding supports real
eBay-style **proxy bids** (auto-outbid up to your stored max, previous
bidder refunded + mailed); expiry is a scheduled `ExpireAuctionTask`.
**Confirmed bug (2026-07-13, read `expireAuction()` in full,
`AuctionManagerImplementation.cpp:2169-2286`): the seller is never paid
for a won timed auction.** The winning-bid branch (`playername` non-empty,
lines 2205-2285) transfers item ownership (`updateAuctionOwner()`,
:2216 — confirmed by reading that function too, :2343-2362, it only
updates ownership/commodity-limit bookkeeping, no credit transfer
anywhere in it) and mails both parties a "sale complete, %DI credits"
message, but **`seller->addBankCredits()` is never called anywhere in
`expireAuction()`** — grepped the whole function and its callee. Compare
the instant-buy path (`doInstantBuy()`, `:1193-1194`), which explicitly
does `seller->addBankCredits(item->getPrice())` right before committing
the transaction log. The winning bidder's credits ARE correctly escrowed
at bid time and refunded if outbid (`:1305`, `:1479`), so the money isn't
lost from the buyer's side — it just has no confirmed destination once a
timed auction actually completes. **Net effect: a seller who lists a
timed auction (as opposed to instant-buy) and it sells via bidding likely
never receives payment**, despite getting a mail saying the sale
succeeded. Not yet fixed, no source touched (research-only finding) — if
addressing, the fix is almost certainly a one-line
`seller->addBankCredits(item->getPrice())` added to the winning-bid
branch of `expireAuction()`, mirroring `doInstantBuy()`'s existing
pattern, plus a `TransactionLog` entry for parity with every other credit
movement in this file. Worth a direct in-game test (list something via
timed auction, let it expire won, check seller's bank balance) to confirm
before trusting this system for anything real.

**Draft fix, ready to apply, not yet applied** (research-only chat,
2026-07-13 — no source touched): the winning-bid branch of
`expireAuction()` needs the same seller payout `doInstantBuy()` already
does at its own lines 1193-1195, adapted for the fact that a timed
auction's buyer already paid at bid time (escrowed via the existing
proxy-bid logic at lines 1305/1479, refunded from there if outbid), so
unlike `doInstantBuy()` there's no `player->subtractBankCredits()` needed
here — only the missing seller-side credit, inserted right after
`updateAuctionOwner(item, buyer);` at line 2216:

```cpp
		item->setStatus(AuctionItem::SOLD);
		updateAuctionOwner(item, buyer);

		// ADD: pay the seller -- doInstantBuy() does this at its own
		// lines 1193-1195 via seller->addBankCredits(); expireAuction()'s
		// winning-bid branch never did, despite telling both parties by
		// mail that the sale completed. The buyer's credits were already
		// escrowed at bid time (see the proxy-bid logic above in this
		// same file), so only the seller-side payout is missing here.
		ManagedReference<CreatureObject*> seller = pman->getPlayer(sellerName);

		if (seller != nullptr) {
			Locker slocker(seller, item); // item already locked by caller; cross-locks seller safely
			TransactionLog trx(seller, TrxCode::AUCTIONBID, item->getPrice(), true);
			seller->addBankCredits(item->getPrice());
			trx.commit();
		} else {
			// Same "seller not found" shape doInstantBuy() already
			// handles at its own lines 1181-1189 -- log it, don't
			// silently drop the credits without a trace.
			error() << "expireAuction(item=" << item->getObjectID()
				<< "): winning-bid seller not found [" << sellerName
				<< "], credits not paid out.";
		}

		// Waypoint to Vendor / bazaar
```

Uses the exact same `TransactionLog`/`Locker` idiom the rest of this file
already proves out, and the same `TrxCode::AUCTIONBID` constant already
used for the proxy-bid refund path a few hundred lines up in the same
file (a more specific `TrxCode` may exist for a completed sale
specifically — worth a quick check of the full `TrxCode` enum before
applying, but `AUCTIONBID` is not a functional risk either way, just a
labeling choice for the transaction log). **Not yet applied to source.**
Needs a rebuild (`.cpp`-only change, no `.idl` change) and the same
in-game test described above before this can be considered resolved.

**Vendor upkeep is a separate credit pool from structure maintenance**
(section 4) — `VendorDataComponent::maintAmount`, its own SUI-driven
pay/withdraw, its own hourly drain (**15cr/hour base**, -20%/-40% by
merchant skills, **+6cr/hour** if registered/searchable on the map). Same
"maintenance debt = condition damage" pattern as structures, but tracked
on the vendor object itself. Running dry auto-unregisters the vendor from
search and deletes it after 100 days on strike; an empty vendor (no items)
gets deleted after 14-28 days regardless of funding.

**Two distinct commissions exist**: a flat **20-credit bazaar listing
fee** (100 for a "premium"/featured listing, reduced by merchant skills,
literally logged as `// the Galactic Trade Commission` — a pure sink, no
recipient, charged whether or not the item sells) for bazaar-terminal
listings specifically, and the **percentage city sales tax** (section 17)
which applies to any sale (vendor or bazaar) inside a taxed city, credited
to the city treasury. Regular player-vendor sales outside a taxed city
incur no fee at all.

**Recipe — new vendor cosmetic type:** pure data — the "create vendor"
flow is itself a Lua-authored decision tree (`VendorSelectionNode`,
`vendor_manager.lua`), so a new droid/terminal/NPC vendor skin is one new
object template + one new tree node line, no rebuild. **New vendor
*behavior*** (faction-restricted access, per-buyer discounts): genuinely
needs C++ — none of the purchase-path functions have any faction/reputation
hook today, and price is static at listing time, not recomputed per buyer;
adding either requires new checks inside `checkSaleItem()`/`buyItem()`/
`doInstantBuy()`. **New cross-galaxy search filter dimension** (e.g. search
by crafter name or by a rolled resource stat): the galaxy-wide *scope*
already works end-to-end, but a new *filter field* needs a code change to
the query's per-item filter block plus a matching client packet field —
real C++, not data.

## 25. Network / Packet Layer

**Outgoing message construction:** every network message is a class
extending `BaseMessage` (`utils/engine3/.../engine/service/proto/BaseMessage.h`,
itself a `BasePacket`) whose constructor manually serializes its own
fields via `insertShort()`/`insertInt()`/`insertByte()`/`insertAscii()`/
`insertStream()` calls -- there is no schema/reflection, the byte layout
*is* the constructor body. Real example, `server/login/packets/LoginClientToken.h:24-38`:
```cpp
LoginClientToken(const String& username, const String& sessionToken, uint32 accountid, uint32 stationid) : BaseMessage() {
    insertShort(0x04);
    insertInt(STRING_HASHCODE("LoginClientToken")); // the "opcode"
    insertInt(sessionToken.length() + 4);
    for (const auto val : sessionToken) { insertByte(val); }
    insertInt(accountid);
    insertInt(stationid);
    insertAscii(username);
}
```
The opcode identifying a message type is almost always
`STRING_HASHCODE("ClassName")` on the sending side, but **the receiving
side's opcode table is a fixed table of literal hex constants**
(see below) -- these must match the real SWG client's actual wire
protocol exactly, they are not something a server author can invent for
client-bound messages (the client is closed-source binary; opcodes were
reverse-engineered against it historically). Server-internal/game-logic
messages that never cross the wire to the *client* (server-to-server or
purely conceptual "Message" subclasses used with the task system) have
more latitude since nothing external needs to agree on the byte layout.

**Transport/session layer (SOE protocol):** `BasePacketHandler`
(`engine/service/proto/BasePacketHandler.h`/`.cpp`) implements the classic
SOE UDP session protocol this whole codebase (and the real 2003-era SWG
client) speaks: `doSessionStart()`/`doSessionResponse()` (handshake),
`doAcknowledge()`/`doOutOfOrder()` (reliable-UDP sequencing/retransmit),
`handleFragmentedPacket()` (large-message reassembly),
`handleMultiPacket()`/`handleDataChannelMultiPacket()` (bundling several
small messages into one UDP datagram). Every `BasePacket` carries its own
`doSeq`/`doEncr`/`doComp`/`doCRCTest` bools (`BasePacket.h:18-22`,
default sequenced + encrypted + CRC-checked, not compressed) -- these are
per-message-type transport policy flags, not something touched per
send-call.

**Incoming dispatch, opcode -> handler (the actual "add a new packet type"
mechanism):** `ZonePacketHandler::generateMessageTask()`
(`server/zone/ZonePacketHandler.cpp:223-256`) reads `opcount` (short) then
`opcode` (int) straight off the wire, then
`messageCallbackFactory.createObject(opcode, client, processServer)` --
the **exact same `registerObject<T>(id)` factory-registry idiom** already
documented for `objectFactory`/`commandFactory` elsewhere in this guide
(sections 1/6), just keyed by network opcode instead of `gameObjectType`/
command name. Real registrations, `ZonePacketHandler.cpp:127-136`:
```cpp
messageCallbackFactory.registerObject<ClientIdMessageCallback>(0xD5899226);
messageCallbackFactory.registerObject<ClientCreateCharacterCallback>(0xB97F3074);
messageCallbackFactory.registerObject<ObjectControllerMessageCallback>(0x80CE5E46);
messageCallbackFactory.registerObject<ObjectMenuSelectCallback>(0x7CA18726);
...
```
`ObjectControllerMessageCallback` (`0x80CE5E46`) is the single opcode that
funnels every slash-command/ability activation from the client into
`ObjectControllerImplementation::activateCommand()` (section 6) --
confirms the command-dispatch pipeline documented there really does start
all the way back at this one wire opcode. Each resolved `MessageCallback`
self-parses (`parseMessage(pack)`) and *is itself* a `Task`
(`generateMessageTask()`'s return type), executed via
`client->executeOrderedTask(task)` when a client session exists (guarantees
one client's packets process in-order relative to each other even though
the engine is multi-threaded) or the general `Core::getTaskManager()` for
client-less/system messages.

**Full round trip, concretely:** client sends raw UDP bytes ->
`BasePacketHandler` reassembles/deduplicates/decrypts per the SOE session
protocol -> `ZoneServerImplementation::processMessage()`
(`ZoneServerImplementation.cpp:639-662`) hands the reassembled `Message`
to `ZonePacketHandler::generateMessageTask()` -> opcode lookup in
`messageCallbackFactory` -> the matching `MessageCallback` subclass parses
its own fields and runs as a `Task` -> for the common case
(`ObjectControllerMessageCallback`) that task calls into
`ObjectController`/`CommandQueue` (section 6) -> eventually a response
`BaseMessage` subclass is constructed and sent back via
`client->sendMessage(msg)`, retracing the same transport layer outbound.

**Recipe -- add a new server-to-client message for an existing, real
opcode reused from stock content:** new class extending `BaseMessage`
under the relevant `packets/` folder, constructor serializes fields with
`insertX()` calls matching the real client-expected byte layout for that
message type (reverse-engineer from a working stock example of the same
message family -- this codebase has hundreds already, e.g.
`CommandQueueAdd`/`CommandQueueRemove` referenced in section 6), send via
`creature->sendMessage(new MyMessage(...))` from wherever the event
happens. No opcode registration needed for *outbound-only* messages (the
client already knows how to parse a given opcode -- registration in
`messageCallbackFactory` is only for messages the *server* needs to
receive and handle). Rebuild required (new `.h`/`.cpp`), no `.idl`
involved -- packets are hand-written C++, not IDL-generated.

**Recipe -- handle a new incoming client message:** realistically only
viable for an opcode the stock client already sends that this server
currently ignores (a genuinely new opcode would require a modified
client, out of scope for a server-only repo) -- new `MessageCallback`
subclass, `parseMessage()` reading fields in the client's real order,
register via `messageCallbackFactory.registerObject<T>(0x<realOpcode>)`
in `ZonePacketHandler.cpp` alongside the existing list. Rebuild required.

## 26. Space Combat Internals

**Where the real math lives (and where it doesn't):** `ShipManager`
(`server/zone/managers/ship/ShipManager.cpp`) *looks* like the space
combat manager by name but is almost entirely a **data-loading and
lifecycle** class -- loads component/chassis/weapon/missile/countermeasure/
turret/collision/pilot-AI datatables, spawn groups, handles ship
naming/re-deed/lost-items UI, `notifyDestruction()`. It contains no damage
math. The actual damage-resolution class is
`server/zone/managers/spacecombat/SpaceCombatManager.cpp`, paired with
`SpaceCollisionManager` (hit-testing) and `ShipProjectile`/`ShipMissile`/
`ShipCountermeasure` (projectile data/movement).

**Firing entry point:** the client sends a `CreateProjectileMessage`
(`server/zone/packets/jtl/CreateProjectileMessage.h`) naming the firing
weapon slot; `run()` (lines ~107-168) resolves the pilot's ship via
`pilot->getRootParent()->asShipObject()`, looks up the weapon's loaded
component CRC and `ShipProjectileData` via `ShipManager`, checks
`isComponentFunctional()`, and -- for standard weapons -- charges
capacitor energy (`energyPerShot / componentEnergyEfficiency`, no-op /
early-return if insufficient) before constructing a `ShipProjectile` and
calling `SpaceCombatManager::instance()->addProjectile(ship, projectile,
pilot)`. Missiles/countermeasures branch to `launchMissile()`/
`launchCountermeasure()` in the same file, which additionally decrement
`currentAmmo` on the weapon slot. NPC/AI ships fire the same way from
`ShipAiAgentImplementation.cpp` (lines ~1462/1529/1605) calling the same
`addProjectile()`/`addMissile()` entry points directly (no client packet
involved) -- **one shared resolution path for both player and AI-fired
weapons.**

**Projectile lifecycle (server-authoritative, tick-driven, not
hitscan):** `addProjectile()`/`addMissile()` just register the projectile
into a per-ship `projectileMap` and broadcast a cosmetic
`CreateProjectileMessage`/`CreateMissileMessage` to nearby players --
no damage yet. A periodic task (`CheckProjectilesTask`, gated by
`INTERVALMIN`) drives `SpaceCombatManager::updateProjectiles()`
(lines 781-852), which for every in-flight projectile on every ship calls
`updateProjectile()` (bolts, lines 621-661) or `updateMissile()`
(homing + countermeasure-defeat check, lines 663-740): these advance
position (`projectile->updatePosition()`), check expiry (`deltaMax`
travel-time budget), and on each tick ask
`SpaceCollisionManager::getProjectileCollision()` whether the projectile
intersects anything in `targetVectorCopy`. A `HIT` result calls
`applyDamage()` and removes the projectile; `MISS` just updates
`lastUpdateTime` and leaves it live for the next tick; `EXPIRE` removes it
with no damage. Missiles additionally scan the target's own
`projectileMap` each tick for nearby active countermeasures and roll
`counterDifficulty >= missileDifficulty` to get defeated in flight
(lines 700-728) -- this is the entire "chaff/flare" countermeasure
mechanic, no other code path implements it.

**Damage resolution layering (`applyDamage()`, lines 85-229):** base
damage is rolled once (`System::random(maxDamage - minDamage) + minDamage`,
scaled by weapon efficiency from `getComponentEfficiency()`), with a flat
**25% PvP damage reduction** when both ships are player-piloted
(`damage *= 0.75f` if both `isPlayerShip()`, line 129-131 -- a real,
easy-to-miss balance rule). Above 1 damage it also records threat
(`targetThreatMap->addDamage()`) and, for AI-piloted defenders, adds the
attacker to the AI's enemy list and possibly broadcasts a PvP-status
bitmask update. The damage is then applied through one of two mutually
exclusive branches depending on whether the bridge is targetable:
- **Bridge functional/targetable:** iterates the collision result's hit
  slots and calls `applyComponentDamage()` directly per slot (component
  armor -> component health, no separate shield/hull-armor/chassis pass).
- **Bridge down or not targetable (the normal case):** a fixed
  `HITSHIELD -> HITARMOR -> HITCOMPONENT -> HITCHASSIS` waterfall, each
  stage consuming as much damage as it can and passing remainder to the
  next (`applyShieldDamage()` 231-292, `applyArmorDamage()` 294-378,
  `applyActiveComponentDamage()` 517-561, `applyChassisDamage()`
  380-429). Front/rear shields are tracked and depleted independently
  (`result.isHitFront()`); hull armor is a two-layer armor-then-health pool
  per `ARMOR0`/`ARMOR1` slot; a destroyed component
  (`getCurrentHitpointsMap()->get(slot) <= 0`) calls
  `setComponentDemolished()`, and losing the `BRIDGE` slot specifically
  cascades directly into chassis damage. **Active-component targeting**
  (`applyActiveComponentDamage()`) is itself layered: explicit collision-hit
  slots first, then the weapon's manually-targeted slot
  (`projectile->getComponentSlot()`), then a health/weight-random fallback
  slot chosen by `getActiveComponentToDamage()` (weighted by
  `ShipCollisionData::getSlotWeight()` among all components with remaining
  health) -- so a called shot is a *preference*, not a guarantee, once the
  earlier tiers are already destroyed.

**Disable and destruction:** `applyActiveComponentDamage()` checks
`isShipDisabled()` before/after each hit and fires
`triggerDisabledObserver()` (`SHIPDISABLED` observer event, plus a 5s
`DISABLED_INVULNERABLE` grace-period flag for AI ships specifically when a
*critical* slot -- reactor/engine -- was the one that finished it off).
Chassis reaching 0 health in `applyDamage()`'s final check schedules a
`DestroyShipTask` and a `notifyObjectDestructionObservers()` callback via
the task manager (200ms delay, lock-then-notify pattern used throughout
this file for cross-object notifications to avoid holding two ship locks
across a notify chain). POB (player-owned, "capital") ships additionally
schedule `triggerInteriorDamage()` calls at every damage stage so the
walkable interior reacts to hull damage taken in space -- this is the only
place interior-damage state is driven from space combat.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) space combat has its own complete,
independent damage pipeline -- none of the ground `CombatManager`
TEF/hit-chance/mitigation code (section 10) is reused here, so a ground
combat balance fix or bug never touches ships and vice versa. (2) the
25%-PvP-damage-reduction rule is the one hidden balance lever most likely
to surprise someone extending this system. (3) "countermeasures defeat
missiles" is resolved entirely inside `updateMissile()`'s per-tick scan,
not as a separate event/observer -- a countermeasure that never gets a
tick (e.g. added and immediately expired) can never intercept anything.
(4) companions/pets have no space-combat presence at all -- `ShipAiAgent`
is a wholly separate AI hierarchy from `AiAgent`/`CompanionObject`, so
"companion rides along in a ship" is not a small feature, it would need
new linkage from scratch.

## 27. Database / ODB Internals (Deeper)

Builds on section 11 (Database Persistence) -- this section covers the
actual on-disk storage layer underneath `_setUpdated()`/the periodic save
sweep, not the dirty-tracking mechanism itself.

**Storage backend is Berkeley DB, not a SQL/NoSQL server.**
`LocalDatabase` (`utils/engine3/.../engine/db/LocalDatabase.h`) wraps
`engine::db::berkeley::BerkeleyDatabase` (a real embedded Berkeley DB
handle) directly -- there is no separate database process; the BDB
environment lives inside the zone/login server's own process and disk
files. `ObjectDatabase` (`engine/db/ObjectDatabase.h`) is the
`LocalDatabase` subclass actually used for game objects.

**Objects are split across ~25 separate named BDB databases, not one
big table.** `ObjectManager::loadDatabases()` (`ObjectManager.cpp:44-68`)
opens one physical `.db` file per logical bucket at startup --
`sceneobjects` (the vast majority: characters, items, structures, etc.),
plus dedicated ones for `playerstructures`, `buffs`, `missionobjectives`,
`missionobservers`, `cityregions`, `guilds`, `spawnareas`,
`spawnobservers`, `aiobservers`, `events`, `questdata`, `surveys`,
`accounts`, `pendingmail`, `credits`, `navareas`, `frsdata`,
`frsmanager`, `resourcespawns`, `playerbounties`, `mail`, `chatrooms`,
plus `clientobjects` (static/template-instance data, loaded separately in
`loadStaticObjects()`). Each database gets a small integer `tableID` at
registration (`ObjectDatabaseManager::loadObjectDatabase()`).

**The object ID itself encodes which database it lives in.** New IDs are
minted in `ObjectManager::getNextObjectID()` (line 953-969): the
database's `tableID` is shifted into the **top 16 bits** of the 64-bit
object ID, and a monotonically-increasing counter
(`DOBObjectManager::getNextFreeObjectID()`) fills the low 48 bits. Every
lookup path reverses this with `tableID = (uint16)(objectID >> 48)`
(`loadPersistentObject()` line 724, `deSerializeObject()`'s error-path
line 823, `persistObject()` line 670, `loadTable()` line 986) --
`databaseManager->getDatabase(tableID)` then resolves straight to the
right BDB handle with no lookup table or join needed. Practical
consequence: **an object's home database is fixed for its entire
lifetime by the top 16 bits of its own ID** -- `persistObject()` only
special-cases this when the caller explicitly requests a *different*
database than the object's current tableID, in which case it mints a
whole new object ID (`getNextObjectID(database)`) and reassigns it (line
667-680) rather than moving data between tables under the same ID.

**Serialization is the same IDL-generated `writeObject()`/`readObject()`
used everywhere else -- not a separate DB-specific format.** The write
path, `DOBObjectManager::commitUpdatePersistentObjectToDB()`
(`DOBObjectManager.cpp:224-301`): builds an `ObjectOutputStream`,
calls `managedObject->writeObject(objectData)` (the IDL-generated
per-class binary serializer -- the exact same one used for network
baselines/deltas), then **CRC-checks the freshly-serialized bytes against
`getLastCRCSave()` before writing anything** -- if the CRC is unchanged
the write is skipped entirely (`object->_setUpdated(false)`, no BDB call,
line 243-258) even though the object was selected as "marked for
update." This is a real, separate no-op-write optimization layered *on
top of* the `_updated` dirty flag documented in section 11 -- being
flagged dirty only guarantees the object gets *considered*, the CRC
compare is the actual "did anything really change" gate immediately
before the disk write. Non-root brokers (multi-process cluster configs)
skip the DB write entirely and instead forward the serialized bytes to
the root broker via `SendObjectDataMessage` (line 262-270) -- object
persistence is centralized to one process even when the game logic is
sharded across several.

**Read path mirrors this exactly:** `ObjectManager::loadPersistentObject()`
(`ObjectManager.cpp:721-798`) decodes the tableID from the requested
object ID, fetches raw bytes via `ObjectDatabase::getData()`, peeks a
leading discriminator field to decide whether this is a template-backed
`SceneObject` (`serverObjectCRC` present -> `instantiateSceneObject()`)
or a bare `ManagedObject` keyed by class name (`className` present ->
`createObject(className, ...)`), then calls the shared
`deSerializeObject()` (line 801-835) which calls `readObject()` and
**seeds `lastSaveCRC` from the just-loaded bytes** so the very first save
after load is correctly recognized as a no-op unless something actually
mutated in the meantime.

**Save cadence and the world-pause it causes:** the periodic sweep is a
self-rescheduling task, default interval **300000ms = 5 minutes**
(`DOBObjectManager::UPDATETODATABASETIME`, `DOBObjectManager.cpp:49`,
configurable via `ObjectManager.updateToDatabaseTime` in `config.lua`).
`updateModifiedObjectsToDatabase()` (`DOBObjectManager.cpp:414-520+`)
calls `Core::getTaskManager()->blockTaskManager()` **before** copying
objects into RAM for the save batch -- this blocks/pauses all game-logic
task-manager threads server-wide for the duration of that copy step (a
real, measured hitch every save cycle, logged as "waited for task
manager to stop for Nns"/"copied objects into ram in Nms"). Root-broker
instances additionally wrap the whole sweep in a real BDB
`Transaction` (`ObjectDatabaseManager::startTransaction()`/
`commitLocalTransaction()`) so a save cycle is atomic on disk even if the
process crashes mid-sweep. `ObjectManager.saveMode` (section 11) only
decides whether this sweep walks a fast per-thread "objects touched since
last save" list (`executeDeltaUpdateThreads()`) or the full
`localObjectDirectory` (`executeUpdateThreads()`/
`runObjectsMarkedForUpdate()`) -- default-off means the full walk, which
is slower per-cycle but is the one proven-correct path (section 11's
persistence-gap investigation).

**Object deletion mirrors the same tableID routing:**
`DOBObjectManager::commitDestroyObjectToDB()` (line 303-318) decodes
the tableID the same way and calls `table->deleteData(objectID)` -- a
real BDB delete, not a soft-delete/tombstone flag.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) a new persistent object *type* almost never
needs a new BDB database -- it just goes in `sceneobjects` like nearly
everything else; a genuinely new top-level database (like `buffs` or
`questdata` got) is a rare, deliberate architectural decision, not a
per-feature default. (2) Because the object ID's home database is
permanent, code must never assume "reparent this object under a
different `ManagedObject` subsystem" implicitly changes its storage
table -- it doesn't unless `persistObject()` is called again with a new
`database` argument. (3) the CRC no-op-write check means a setter that
calls `_setUpdated(true)` on every invocation regardless of whether the
value actually changed is *not* a real performance problem for disk I/O
(the CRC catches it before any write) -- it only costs the one extra
`writeObject()` serialization pass per save cycle. (4) the 5-minute
save-sweep world-pause is the operationally relevant number for anyone
tuning `ObjectManager.updateToDatabaseTime` -- shortening it trades save
recency for more frequent, all-threads-blocked pauses.

---

## 28. Pathfinding / Collision Deep Dive

**Two entirely separate pathing systems, dispatched by whether either
endpoint is inside a building cell.** `PathFinderManager::findPath()`
(`server/zone/managers/collision/PathFinderManager.cpp:55-82`) branches
on `pointA.getCell()`/`pointB.getCell()` into four cases: world->world
(outdoor, real navmesh), cell->world / world->cell (transition through a
portal), or cell->cell (indoor). Outdoor pathing
(`findPathFromWorldToWorld()` -> `getRecastPath()`, line 222+) uses a
genuine **Recast/Detour navmesh** -- `dtNavMeshQuery` (the standard
open-source Detour library, `pathfinding/recast/DetourNavMeshQuery.h`),
one query object per thread (`ThreadLocal<dtNavMeshQuery*> m_navQuery`,
`getNavQuery()` line 211-220, since Detour queries aren't thread-safe).
Indoor/building pathing (`getFloorPath()`, line 666+) is a completely
different, custom **triangle-mesh** system over each building's
`FloorMesh` (`PathFinderManager::getFloorMesh(CellObject*)`) -- doc
comment on the function spells out its return contract: `-1` same
triangle, `0` path found (`nodes` filled), `1` no path. These two systems
share no code; a building interior with a malformed/missing floor mesh
fails indoor pathing independently of whether outdoor navmesh coverage
around the building is fine.

**Navmesh data is authored offline and loaded as `NavArea` regions, not
generated at runtime.** `NavArea extends ActiveArea`
(`server/zone/objects/pathfinding/NavArea.idl`) is a real persistent
zone object carrying `getMeshBounds()`/`getMeshName()`; `RecastNavMesh`/
`RecastNavMeshBuilder` (`pathfinding/RecastNavMesh.h`/
`RecastNavMeshBuilder.h`) load pre-built Recast tile data from disk. This
means **adding walkable space in a new/modified terrain area requires
regenerating and shipping new navmesh tile data**, not just a code or
config change -- consistent with how the rest of this codebase treats
terrain/world geometry as static content, not something the server
computes from scratch.

**AI movement is driven by `AiAgentImplementation::findNextPosition()`**
(`server/zone/objects/creature/ai/AiAgentImplementation.cpp:2588-2990+`),
called once per behavior tick (section 9's `activateAiBehavior()`
interval). It is not a naive "call `findPath()` every tick" loop --
it caches the last computed path in `currentFoundPath` and only
re-queries `PathFinderManager::findPath()` when: (a) there is no cached
path yet, or (b) the agent is in a *target-following* movement state
(`FOLLOWING`/`PATHING_HOME`/`NOTIFY_ALLY`/`MOVING_TO_HEAL`/`WATCHING`/
`CRACKDOWN_SCANNING`/`LAIR_HEALING`) **and** the cached path's endpoint
has drifted more than 4m from the live target position (line 2723-2731)
-- i.e. a moving target (a fled player, a following companion's owner)
only triggers an expensive re-plan once it's wandered far enough from
where the last path was aimed, not on every tick. Speed itself is also
smoothly interpolated toward the target speed (+/-0.4 units/tick, line
2664-2671) rather than snapping instantly, and several creature states
force speed overrides: `IMMOBILIZED` halves speed, `FROZEN` nearly stops
it (0.01), crouched posture blocks movement entirely, prone forces walk
speed. Reaching the final patrol point (`endDistanceSq <= maxSquared`)
pops it off `patrolPoints`, fires `DESTINATIONREACHED` (except while
`FOLLOWING`, which never "arrives" in the normal sense), and zeroes
current speed.

**Runtime movement validation (anti-speedhack/anti-noclip) is a
separate function from AI pathing:**
`CollisionManager::checkMovementCollision()`
(`server/zone/managers/collision/CollisionManager.cpp:185-280+`) is
called against every client-reported position update. It ray-casts from
the player's last-known-valid world position to the new claimed position
in two passes: first through any nearby `NavArea` navmeshes
(`getInRangeNavMeshes()` + `PathFinderManager::getNavMeshCollisions()`/
`getRecastPath()`) to catch geometry-level illegal moves (through walls,
off the mesh), then through nearby collidable `TreeEntry` world objects
(the close-objects spatial index used throughout the engine, section
references collision-mesh intersection tests via `AppearanceTemplate`).
A ray hit or a failed recast path both fail the move and (implicitly)
snap/reject the player's claimed transform back to `lastValidWorld` --
**this is the actual mechanism stopping wall-clipping and most forms of
teleport-hacking**, independent of and unrelated to the AI pathfinding
system above even though both ultimately call into `PathFinderManager`.

**Line-of-sight is NOT pathfinding-based despite an old comment
suggesting otherwise.** `CollisionManager::checkLineOfSight()` (line
538-556) has a commented-out block that once called
`PathFinderManager::findPath()` to determine LOS between two AI-relevant
objects -- it's dead code today. The live implementation instead compares
`getRootParent()` (same building -> `checkLineOfSightInBuilding()`,
different buildings -> automatically blocked, line 557-564) and,
for the open-world case, does a direct geometric ray intersection test
against nearby collidable appearances (`getAppearanceIntersection()`).
Practical implication: **LOS and "can I walk there" are two unrelated
systems** -- a creature can have clear LOS to a target across a chasm it
can never path to, and (per the dead code) the reverse asymmetry was
apparently considered and abandoned rather than implemented.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any new large open area needs real navmesh
tile authoring/regeneration -- there's no runtime fallback that makes an
un-meshed area walkable for AI. (2) a companion or new AI archetype that
needs custom movement logic should hook `findNextPosition()`'s
call site/state machine rather than reimplementing pathing -- the
caching/re-plan-threshold behavior is what keeps AI movement from
hammering the pathfinder every tick, and bypassing it would be a real
performance regression. (3) `checkMovementCollision()` is the layer to
extend for any new anti-cheat movement rule (e.g. speed-based flagging on
top of geometry validity) -- it already has both the last-valid and
claimed position in hand. (4) don't assume fixing/improving LOS checks
touches pathfinding code or vice versa -- confirmed structurally
separate today.

---

## 29. Lua Scripting Bridge Internals

**Real embedded Lua (the standard C API, `lua.hpp`), not a custom
scripting language.** `engine::lua::Lua`
(`utils/engine3/.../engine/lua/Lua.h`) wraps a real `lua_State*` with
thin typed getters/setters (`getInt`/`getString`/`getGlobalObject`/etc.)
and `runFile()`/`runString()`. Two distinct mechanisms bridge C++ and
Lua in both directions.

**C++ -> Lua exposed functions:** plain C-style callbacks registered via
`Lua::registerFunction(name, int(*)(lua_State*))` -- `DirectorManager`'s
`initializeLuaEngine()` (`DirectorManager.cpp:~430+`) registers **dozens**
of global Lua-callable functions this way: `createEvent`/`cancelEvent`/
`createServerEvent` (scheduled-task hooks), `createObserver`/
`dropObserver`/`hasObserver` (observer-event hooks), `spawnMobile`/
`spawnEventMobile`/`spawnShipAgent`, `spatialChat`/`spatialMoodChat`,
`readSharedMemory`/`writeSharedMemory` family (see below),
`getRandomNumber`, `forcePeace`, `includeFile` (Lua-level file includes,
letting one script pull in another), `registerScreenPlay`. Each of
these is exactly the kind of primitive a screenplay/quest/spawn script
needs and can't get any other way -- this static function list *is* the
sanctioned "what can Lua content actually do" surface for
non-object-method operations.

**C++ objects exposed to Lua as userdata (Luna binding):** the second,
much larger mechanism is `Luna<T>` (`engine/lua/Luna.h`, the well-known
templated Lua<->C++ binding pattern), which wraps a real `ManagedObject`
subclass in a thin `LuaXxx` adapter class (`LuaCreatureObject`,
`LuaSceneObject`, `LuaBuildingObject`, `LuaIntangibleObject`,
`LuaMissionObject`, `LuaPlayerObject`, `LuaTangibleObject`,
`LuaAiAgent`, `LuaActiveArea`, `LuaCityRegion`, `LuaShipObject`/
`LuaShipAiAgent`/`LuaShipComponent`, `LuaConversationScreen`/
`LuaConversationTemplate`/`LuaConversationSession`, `LuaSuiManager`/
`LuaSuiBox`, `LuaSkillManager`, and ~25 more) and registers its exposed
methods so Lua code can call `object:someMethod(...)` directly on a
handle passed into a script. **~35 `Luna<LuaXxx>::Register()` calls**
happen once per Lua state during `initializeLuaEngine()`
(`DirectorManager.cpp:873-919`) -- this registration list *is* the
complete inventory of what object types script content can touch and
what methods are callable on each; a method not exposed on the relevant
`LuaXxx` wrapper is simply invisible to Lua regardless of what the real
C++ class supports.

**One independent Lua VM per worker thread, not one shared global
interpreter.** `DirectorManager::getLuaInstance()`
(`DirectorManager.cpp:3432-3471`) stores the `Lua*` in a `ThreadLocal`,
lazily creating (`initializeLuaEngine()` + `loadScreenPlays()`) one full
interpreter the first time a given task-manager thread needs one. This
means script global state (Lua globals, `require`-style caching, etc.)
is **not shared across threads** -- each thread's screenplays run in
total isolation from every other thread's Lua state, which is why the
cross-thread data-sharing primitives (`readSharedMemory`/
`writeSharedMemory`/`readStringSharedMemory`/`readVector3SharedMemory`,
all backed by `DirectorSharedMemory`, a real explicit shared-state object
distinct from Lua's own globals) exist as a deliberate, separate
mechanism -- if scripts need to coordinate across threads they must use
these functions, not Lua-level global variables.

**Hot-reload via a version counter, not file-watching.** Every thread's
Lua state also carries a `localScreenPlayVersion`, compared each call
against a single `AtomicInteger masterScreenPlayVersion`.
`DirectorManager::reloadScreenPlays()` (line 945-946) just does
`masterScreenPlayVersion.increment()` -- the next time *any* thread's
`getLuaInstance()`/`runScreenPlays()` runs, it notices its local version
is stale and re-executes `loadScreenPlays(lua)` to re-source every
screenplay file into that thread's own state (line 3457-3468). This is
the real mechanism behind any "reload scripts" GM/admin command: it's
lazy and per-thread, so a reload isn't instantaneous across the whole
server -- each thread picks it up the next time it touches Lua, and each
reload is bracketed by a Lua-stack-size sanity check
(`lua->checkStack(stackSize)`) that logs a "LUA Stack Leak" error if a
script left the interpreter stack unbalanced, a real, if coarse, safety
net against buggy scripts corrupting VM state across calls.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) exposing a new C++ method to scripts always
needs two matching changes -- the method itself, and a line in the
relevant `LuaXxx` wrapper's `Luna<T>` method table -- never just the
former. (2) a brand-new game-primitive operation that isn't a method on
an existing exposed object type (e.g. a new global helper like
`getRandomNumber`) goes through `registerFunction()` in
`DirectorManager::initializeLuaEngine()` instead. (3) any script-visible
mutable state meant to persist or be visible across zone-server worker
threads must go through `DirectorSharedMemory`'s read/write functions --
plain Lua globals or upvalues silently don't survive across threads.
(4) a screenplay/quest reload is observed per-thread on next use, not
atomically server-wide -- relevant if debugging "I reloaded but it's
still running the old script" reports, which can be entirely expected
behavior for a request handled by a thread that hasn't touched Lua since
the reload yet.

---

## 30. Login Server <-> Zone Server Handshake

**The two servers are separate processes that hand off the client via a
shared MySQL/MariaDB `sessions` table, not a direct socket/RPC call
between them** (in the default, non-`WITH_SWGREALMS_API` build --
`WITH_SWGREALMS_API` swaps this for a real external HTTP-based API and is
covered separately below). This is the single most important structural
fact about the handshake: the login server and every zone server
independently read/write the same session row in the shared game
database, and that row *is* the handoff mechanism.

**Step 1 -- client authenticates against the login server.** The client
sends a `LoginClientID` message (opcode `0x41131F96`,
`LoginPacketHandler::handleMessage()` line 48-53) containing username,
password/session-id, and client version;
`AccountManager::loginAccount()` (`AccountManager.cpp:55`) parses it and
calls `validateAccountCredentials()` (line 186+), which supports **two
login modes**: a normal username+password check against the `accounts`
table, or (if `Core3.Login.EnableSessionId` is on) a **session-ID-as-password**
re-login path that looks up an existing, unexpired row in `sessions`
joined to `accounts` -- this is how a client can silently reconnect
without re-prompting for a password (e.g. after a crash) as long as the
old session row hasn't expired. If the username doesn't exist and
`Core3.RegistrationMessage`-gated auto-registration is enabled, a brand
new account is created inline right here (`createAccount()`, same
function).

**Step 2 -- login server mints and stores a session token.** On success,
`AccountManager::loginApprovedAccount()`/the tail of `loginAccount()`
(line 135-183) generates a fresh 64-byte random session ID
(`Crypto::randomSalt<64>()`) if the account didn't already have one, then
does two things in parallel: sends it to the client immediately via a
`LoginClientToken` message (section 25's real `BaseMessage` example is
this exact class), and `REPLACE INTO sessions (account_id, session_id,
ip, expires) VALUES (..., ADDTIME(NOW(), '<duration>'))` -- default
duration **15 minutes** (`Core3.Login.SessionDuration`, format `HH:MM`).
The row is keyed to the account's *source IP* as well as the session ID
-- both must match later. It then sends the galaxy/cluster list
(`getLoginEnumClusterMessage()`/`getLoginClusterStatusMessage()`, the
server-picker list the client shows) and the account's character list
(`EnumerateCharacterId`).

**Step 3 -- client connects directly to the chosen zone server** (a
wholly separate TCP/UDP connection, no login-server involvement in the
socket itself) and re-sends its credentials as a `ClientIdMessage`,
handled by `ClientIdMessageCallback`
(`server/zone/packets/zone/ClientIdMessageCallback.h`, opcode
`0xD5899226` from section 25's registration list) carrying the same
`sessionID`/`accountID`/client `version` fields. `run()` (line 53-117)
independently re-validates by querying the **same `sessions` table**:
`SELECT session_id FROM sessions WHERE account_id = ? AND ip = ? AND
expires > NOW()` -- the zone server never talks to the login server
process directly, it just trusts whatever is currently sitting in the
shared table, matched against both account ID, source IP, and exact
session-ID string equality (line 72-113). Client version is
independently re-checked here too
(`Core3.PlayerManager.ValidClientVersion`), a second, zone-side gate
distinct from the login server's own version check.

**Step 4 -- the session token is single-use, consumed on zone
connect.** Immediately after a successful match, `approveSession()`
(line 119-177) calls `AccountManager::expireSession()`
(`AccountManager.cpp:590-606`), which `DELETE`s the row from `sessions`
(unconditionally if the in-memory `Account` object has no cached session
ID, or only expired rows otherwise -- a minor asymmetry, but the net
effect is the same token can't be replayed to connect a second zone
client). This is also where **per-galaxy bans** are enforced
(`account->getGalaxyBan(galaxyID)`, independent of any account-wide ban)
and where the character list gets filtered into allowed vs. banned
per-character (`addCharacter()`/`addBannedCharacter()`), and where
`Core3.PlayerCreationManager.MaxCharactersPerGalaxy` (default 10) is
checked to decide whether the client is allowed to create a new
character on top of connecting. The whole result -- can connect, can
create a character -- is sent back as one `ClientPermissionsMessage`.

**The `WITH_SWGREALMS_API` build variant replaces steps 2-4's raw SQL
with a real async HTTP session-approval API** (`SWGRealmsAPI::instance()
->createSession()`/`validateSession()`, both taking a callback receiving
a `SessionApprovalResult`) -- same shape (mint a session on login,
validate it on zone-connect) but delegated to an external service rather
than a shared local table; this is a compile-time `#ifdef` fork, not a
runtime config toggle, so a given server binary is permanently one mode
or the other.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) login server and zone server(s) can run as
genuinely separate, even separately-scaled processes because their only
coupling is the shared database -- there's no persistent socket or RPC
channel between them to reason about. (2) a "can't reconnect after
crash" bug report is very likely a `sessions` row/IP/expiry mismatch,
not a zone-server-side bug -- the whole reconnect story hinges on that
one row surviving with a matching IP until the client retries. (3) the
session duration (15 min default) is the real timeout window between
"logged into login server" and "must have connected to a zone server" --
a slow galaxy-select screen or client hang past that window means a
stale/expired token and a forced re-login. (4) galaxy bans and
character-level bans are two independent checks applied at zone-connect
time, not at login-server time -- a globally-unbanned account can still
be denied a specific galaxy or have specific characters hidden.

---

## 31. Buff / Debuff System Internals

**One base class, `Buff extends ManagedObject`
(`server/zone/objects/creature/buffs/Buff.idl`), covers every temporary
modifier in the game** -- combat buffs, debuffs, states (stun/dizzy/etc.
are implemented *as buffs*, not a separate system -- see below), spice
effects, trap effects, performance buffs, vehicle speed buffs, Force
power channel effects. **15 subclasses** specialize behavior:
`DurationBuff` (plain timed buff, the common case), `StateBuff`
(applies a `CreatureState` bit alongside its modifiers), `TrapBuff`,
`DelayedBuff` (activation delay before it starts), `SpiceBuff`/
`SpiceDownerBuff` (drug effects and their comedown), `PowerBoostBuff`,
`PerformanceBuff` (entertainer buffs), `ForceWeakenDebuff`,
`ChannelForceBuff` (Force-power channeling), `ConcealBuff`,
`PlayerVehicleBuff`, `PrivateBuff` (client-invisible to everyone but the
target), `SingleUseBuff`, `SquadLeaderBuff`. Each is a normal
`ManagedObject` with its own IDL/autogen pair, following the standard
codebase pattern (section 1) -- not a data-only row.

**Three independent modifier channels apply per buff, gated by one
`modsApplied` flag:** `applyAllModifiers()`
(`BuffImplementation.cpp:130-137`) is idempotent (checks `modsApplied`
first) and fans out to `applyAttributeModifiers()` (adjusts
`getMaxHAM(attribute)` pools -- health/action/mind and their
sub-attributes, `BuffImplementation.cpp:274+`), `applySkillModifiers()`
(injects entries into the **same string-keyed skill-modifier map** used
by real trained skills -- e.g. `private_speed_multiplier`/
`private_acceleration_multiplier`, meaning a speed buff and a
skill-granted speed bonus are computed through one unified lookup, not
parallel systems), and `applyStates()` (sets `CreatureState` bits).
`removeAllModifiers()` mirrors all three and flips `modsApplied` back
off. Because `activate(applyModifiers)`/`deactivate(removeModifiers)`
both take an explicit bool, a buff can be **structurally present on a
creature (in the buff list, visible to `getBuff()`) without its
modifiers currently being active** -- used deliberately (e.g. re-parsing
saved buffs after a server restart without double-applying).

**Storage and lookup:** `CreatureObjectImplementation` holds one
`creatureBuffs` member (a `BuffList`, keyed by `buffCRC`, a `uint32`
hash of the buff's name) -- `addBuff()`/`removeBuff()`/`getBuff()` are
all thin forwards to `BuffList`'s own map operations
(`CreatureObjectImplementation.cpp:3008-3082`). **State-type "buffs" are
keyed by `Long::hashCode(state)`** rather than a real buff CRC
(`removeStateBuff()`, line 3058-3068) -- confirms states (stun, dizzy,
intimidated, etc.) are just buffs whose CRC is derived from the state
bitmask value itself, letting the same duration/removal machinery serve
both without a parallel timer system.

**Secondary buffs let one buff drag others along for renewal/removal
only, not application.** `secondaryBuffCRCs` (a `Vector<unsigned long>`
on `Buff` itself) is consulted by both `CreatureObjectImplementation::
renewBuff()` (line 3017-3039) and `removeBuff()` (line 3041-3056) to
recursively renew/remove every linked secondary buff alongside the
primary -- e.g. a single "food buff" applying both a mind-pool and a
willpower-skill modifier as two separate `Buff` objects that always
expire together. This is a linkage list only, not a modifier-merging
mechanism -- each secondary is still its own independent `Buff` instance
with its own modifiers.

**Expiration is a self-scheduling `Task`, not a per-tick scan.**
`scheduleBuffEvent()` (`BuffImplementation.cpp:248-255`) creates a
`BuffDurationEvent` (`BuffDurationEvent.h`, a real `Task` subclass, the
same task-manager primitive used throughout the engine -- see sections 9
and 25) scheduled `buffDuration * 1000` ms out, holding only
**weak references** to both the creature and the buff
(`ManagedWeakReference`) so an expiring buff can never itself keep a
disconnected/deleted creature alive. On fire (`run()`, line 27-43) it
calls `buff->checkRenew()` -- an overridable hook most subclasses leave
at the base `false`, but any buff type that needs to auto-refresh itself
(rather than being explicitly renewed by outside code, e.g. an aura-type
buff that re-checks a condition each expiry) overrides it to return
`true`, causing `creature->renewBuff()` to reschedule instead of
`removeBuff()` tearing it down. `getTimeLeft()` reads the *live*
task-manager execution time for the scheduled event rather than tracking
its own countdown -- there is no separate "time remaining" state to drift
out of sync with the actual timer.

**Client sync is per-buff, explicit, and skipped for NPCs.**
`activate()`/`deactivate()` call `sendTo()`/`sendDestroyTo()` **only if
`creo->isPlayerCreature()`** (line 111, 158) -- NPC/AI buffs (e.g. an AI
enrage buff) never generate the client-facing buff-icon packets at all,
only their stat/skill-modifier effects apply server-side. Buffs also
independently support: a system-message on start/end
(`startMessage`/`endMessage`, `StringIdChatParameter`), floating combat
text (`startFlyFile`/`endFlyFile` triads with RGB), and combat-spam
broadcast text (`startSpam`/`endSpam` with `spamColor`/`broadcastSpam`)
-- three separate, independently-optional presentation channels layered
on top of the same modifier application.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) a new buff type only needs a new `Buff`
subclass (or often just a `DurationBuff` instantiated with the right
attribute/skill-modifier strings -- `parseAttributeModifierString()`/
`parseSkillModifierString()` parse simple `key=value;key=value` text, so
many buffs need zero new C++ at all) -- the activation/expiration/
persistence machinery is fully generic. (2) speed/acceleration buffs
(vehicles, states like intimidated, Jedi Force-speed, etc.) all compete
through the identical `private_speed_multiplier`/
`private_acceleration_multiplier` skill-modifier keys -- stacking
behavior for any new speed-affecting buff is governed by whatever
`VectorMap`/skill-modifier-summation logic already exists for that key,
not something a new buff type gets to define independently. (3) an NPC
"buff" that's meant to be player-visible (e.g. a companion buff aura)
needs explicit handling -- the `isPlayerCreature()` gate means a
companion's own buffs are already fine (companions likely report
`isPlayerCreature()==false`, worth verifying against the specific
companion buff use-case if the client-visible icon matters), but any
buff applied *to* an NPC/companion by design never shows a buff icon to
observers regardless. (4) `checkRenew()` is the extension point for any
"buff that renews itself under some condition" design instead of hand
building a separate periodic re-application task.

---

## 32. Image Designer / Appearance Customization

**A two-party negotiated session, not a self-service menu.**
`ImageDesignSession extends` the standard session/`Facade` pattern
(`server/zone/objects/player/sessions/ImageDesignSession.idl`/
`ImageDesignSessionImplementation.cpp`) is created by
`startImageDesign(designer, targetPlayer)` (line 50-109) and registers
itself on **both** participants via `addActiveSession(SessionFacadeType
::IMAGEDESIGN, ...)` -- self-service (designer == target, e.g. a
personal mirror/holoemote purchase) is just the degenerate case where
both references point at the same creature, not a separate code path.
Every proposed change round-trips as an `ImageDesignChangeMessage`
carrying the full slider/color state (`ImageDesignData`); nothing is
committed until `updateImageDesign()` sees `designerAccepted &&
isAcceptedByTarget()` both true (line 175-189) -- a self-design still
requires the same "accepted" flag since designer and target are the same
session object.

**Stat migration has a real, server-enforced 4-minute anti-bypass
timer** independent of the client UI. `updateImageDesign()` (line
137-171) recomputes `remainingTime = 240 - secondsSinceSessionStart`
from `sessionStartTime` (captured server-side at session creation) and
**hard-cancels the entire session** if the designer tries to accept a
stat-migration commit before that elapses -- explicitly checking for and
logging a client-side bypass attempt
(`"Player has attempted to bypass the stat migration timer in the
client"`). Stat migration itself is also gated on both parties currently
being inside a `SALONBUILDING` (checked both at session start, line
56-75, and again at commit time, line 198) and delegates the actual
stat-copy to a separate `MigrateStatsSession` facade
(`session->migrateStats()`) rather than doing it inline.

**Payment is negotiated, not fixed-price.** `doPayment()`
(`ImageDesignSessionImplementation.cpp:320-361`) takes
`max(requiredPayment, offeredPayment)` -- both are client-supplied
values from the negotiation UI, so the "price" of a given service is
whatever the two players agreed on in the session, with the designer's
`requiredPayment` acting as a floor the target must at least match. Cash
is drawn first, then bank credits make up any shortfall, each as its own
`TransactionLog` entry (`TrxCode::IMAGEDESIGN`) grouped together for
audit purposes (section on economy/logging elsewhere in this guide). A
server-side credits check (line 334-341) exists explicitly as a
"client should prevent this but just in case" backstop.

**Skill-gating is a binary unlock per customization attribute, not a
magnitude scaler.** `ImageDesignManager::updateCustomization()`
(`ImageDesignManager.cpp:26-121`) checks `imageDesigner->getSkillMod
(skillMod) < customData->getSkillModValue()` and **silently no-ops the
entire attribute change** if the designer's relevant skill mod (loaded
per-attribute from `customization_data` IFF templates via
`CustomizationData::getImageDesignSkillMod()`/`getSkillModValue()`) is
below the required threshold -- there is no partial/reduced-precision
change for a lower skill level in this code path, contrary to what
player folklore about "higher skill = finer appearance control" might
suggest; the skill check is pass/fail per feature, and once passed the
full normalized `[0,1]` slider value always maps to the complete
`min..max` range of that customization variable
(`BasicRangedIntCustomizationVariable`, sourced from the appearance
template's asset customization manager data,
`AssetCustomizationManagerTemplate::getCustomizationVariables()`).
Height/scale changes are a separate special-cased branch
(`customData->getIsScale()`, line 44-53) that directly calls
`creatureObject->setHeight()` instead of going through the generic
named-variable path.

**Hair is a real separate `TangibleObject`, not a customization
variable on the creature itself.** `createHairObject()`/
`updateHairObject()`/`removeHairObject()`
(`ImageDesignManager.h:39-43`) create/replace/destroy an actual slotted
object in the target's `"hair"` slot -- changing hairstyle means
instantiating a new object from a hair template and re-slotting it (with
the old hair's customization string carried forward where relevant,
line 226-235), not mutating a field. Color-only changes to existing hair
go through `updateColorCustomization()` instead and don't touch the
slotted object identity.

**Timeout and disconnection handling are explicit, separate
mechanisms.** `ImageDesignTimeoutEvent` is a real scheduled `Task`
armed for **2 minutes** once one party accepts but the other hasn't yet
(line 181-185) -- an accepted-but-unconfirmed negotiation doesn't hang
forever. `ImageDesignPositionObserver`
(`ImageDesignPositionObserverImplementation.cpp`) is registered on both
participants **only when both are inside a salon building** (the
stat-migration-eligible case, line 68-74) and calls
`checkDequeueEvent()` on movement -- if either party leaves the salon
building mid-session, the pending timeout event is dequeued/cancelled
(effectively voiding the in-progress stat-migration eligibility rather
than the whole session). Ordinary (non-salon) sessions don't register
this observer at all, since there's no positional eligibility to police
outside a salon.

**XP awarding is tiered by what actually changed, additively
floored, and halved for self-service.** `updateImageDesign()`'s commit
branch (line 191-311) computes `xpGranted` from the *maximum* of several
independent floors reached during that commit: base stat-migration
(2000), hairstyle change (min 100), a body/cosmetic modification
(`PHYSICAL` min 300, `COSMETIC` min 100, from
`ImageDesignManager::updateCustomization`'s out-param
`modificationType`), and a new holoemote purchase (min 100) -- then
halves the total if `designer == target` (self-service) before calling
`playerManager->awardExperience(designer, "imagedesigner", xpGranted,
true)`. This means a session that touches multiple categories awards
XP once per category floor reached, not a flat per-session amount.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) a new customizable appearance attribute is
almost always pure content -- add the variable to the appearance
template's asset customization data plus a `customization_data` IFF row
with its `skillMod`/`skillModValue`, no C++ needed, since
`updateCustomization()` is fully generic over named variables. (2) a new
*category* of skill-gated feature (like the scale/height special case)
would need a new branch in `ImageDesignManager::updateCustomization()`
-- the generic named-variable path only handles ranged-int customization
variables. (3) any bypass-timer-style anti-cheat pattern in this
codebase (stat migration's 4-minute floor is a concrete example) is
enforced from server-captured timestamps compared against
client-reported "I'm ready" signals, never trusting client-reported
elapsed time -- the same pattern to follow for any similar
time-gated negotiation feature. (4) hair changes always go through
real object creation/slotting, so a "companion appearance customization"
feature modeled on this system would need to decide up front whether
companion hair/headgear-equivalent customization is object-based (like
players) or a pure customization-variable (like most other appearance
attributes) -- these are two structurally different mechanisms in this
codebase, not a single unified path.

---

## 33. Droid Engineering / Droid Programming

**`DroidObject extends AiAgent`** (`server/zone/objects/creature/ai/
DroidObject.idl`) -- droids are a pet-like AI creature, sibling to
`CompanionObject` (section on companion architecture) rather than a
tangible item, with their own `power`/`paintCount`/`armor`/`resist`/
`hitChance`/`minDamage`/`maxDamage`/`attackSpeed` instance fields and a
huge enumerated `species` list (`ASSASSIN_DROID`, `R_SERIES`,
`PROBE_DROID`, `PROBOT`, etc., `DroidObject.idl:69-90`).

**Droid capability is entirely determined by installed *crafted*
modules, scanned from a hidden container -- not by droid type/species
alone.** `initDroidModules()`
(`DroidObjectImplementation.cpp:217-242`) reads the droid's
`"crafted_components"` slotted container, drills into its one satchel
child, and for every contained item checks
`sceno->getDataObjectComponent()->isDroidModuleData()` -- any crafted
item whose `DataObjectComponent` is a `BaseDroidModuleComponent`
subclass gets cast and added to the live `modules` vector
(`Vector<Reference<BaseDroidModuleComponent>>`). This means **droid
engineering's actual crafting output is a component item that becomes a
behavior plugin once slotted**, using the exact same
`DataObjectComponent`/schematic/crafting-station pipeline as any other
crafted item (no droid-specific crafting subsystem) -- the droid-ness is
entirely in what `initDroidModules()` does with the result afterward.

**Modules are a real polymorphic plugin interface, not data flags.**
`BaseDroidModuleComponent` (`server/zone/objects/tangible/components/
droid/BaseDroidModuleComponent.h`) declares virtuals for: attribute-list
contribution (`fillAttributeList`), radial-menu contribution
(`fillObjectMenuResponse`/`handleObjectMenuSelect`, with a
module-specific radial-ID enum spanning repair/storage/maintenance/
effects(emote)/detonate/barker(vendor)/playback/trap/harvest --
`BaseDroidModuleComponent.h:42-82`), skill-mod granting while active
(`loadSkillMods`/`unloadSkillMods`, optionally range-gated via
`skillsByRange()`), a chat-command hook (`handlePetCommand(cmd, speaker)`
-- **this is the real "droid programming" entry point**, e.g. telling a
harvesting droid what to collect, or a barker droid what waypoint/message
to store, all routed as parsed spatial-chat strings rather than a
scripting language), a per-tick power cost (`getBatteryDrain()`), and
several `isX()` capability flags (`isCombatModule()`,
`isDetonationModule()`) that let `DroidObjectImplementation` derive
whole-droid capabilities (`isCombatDroid()`/`isBombDroid()`/
`isTrapDroid()`/`hasStorage()`/`isMaintenanceDroid()`, all implemented as
"scan `modules` for any that report this flag",
`DroidObjectImplementation.cpp:367-392+`) purely from what's currently
installed. Two species (`PROBOT`, `DZ70`) are hardcoded as innately
combat-capable "regardless of module installed"
(line 376-378) -- the one deliberate exception to the fully
module-driven model.

**Power is a real consumable resource, drained per-module per-tick, not
a cosmetic meter.** `power` starts at `MAX_POWER` (1000) and every
active module reports its own `getBatteryDrain()`;
`runModulePowerDrain()` (`DroidObjectImplementation.cpp:357-365`) sums
these via `usePower()` (`DroidObject.idl:186-193`), which calls
`handleLowPower()` once power hits 0 -- a droid with more/heavier
modules installed drains faster, and running out of power is a real
state transition, not just a UI number. Recharging is itself
module/interaction-driven: `rechargeFromBattery()` (player-initiated),
`rechargeFromDroid()`/`rechargeOtherDroid()` (droid-to-droid, i.e. a
power droid recharging another droid), each a `native` method with its
own radial entry point.

**Combat stats only apply the droid's own instance fields when the
droid `isPet()` -- otherwise it falls back to the normal creature
template stat system.** Nearly every resist/damage/hit-chance getter in
`DroidObject.idl` (`getArmor()`, `getKinetic()`/`getEnergy()`/
`getElectricity()`/`getStun()`/`getBlast()`/`getHeat()`/`getCold()`/
`getAcid()`, `getDamageMin()`/`getDamageMax()`, `getChanceHit()`,
`calculateAttackSpeed()`) branches on `isPet()`: true -> return the
droid's own crafted/module-derived `armor`/`resist`/`minDamage`/
`maxDamage`/`hitChance` fields; false -> `super.getX()`, i.e. the
ordinary `AiAgent`/template-based stat pipeline used by wild/hostile
world NPCs. **This is structurally the same `isPet()`-branching pattern
already documented as the root cause of the companion TEF bug** (section
on companion combat findings) -- any hostile/unowned droid spawn in the
world (a PROBOT patrol, a security droid) never touches these
crafted-module-driven fields at all; only a player-owned, deployed droid
pet does. Worth remembering if a "droid balance" bug report turns out to
actually be two entirely different code paths depending on whether the
droid in question is tamed.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) a new droid module type (say, a new utility
behavior) is a new `BaseDroidModuleComponent` subclass plus a crafting
schematic that produces it as a `DataObjectComponent`-bearing item --
no `DroidObject` changes needed unless it needs a new whole-droid
capability flag. (2) "programming" a droid's behavior in the player-facing
sense (harvest interest, barker waypoint/message, trap settings) is
implemented per-module as parsed chat commands via `handlePetCommand()`
plus matching radial menu entries -- there's no generic droid scripting
layer to hook into, each module owns its own command grammar. (3) power
balance for a new module is just its `getBatteryDrain()` return value --
the whole-droid power drain loop is already generic and automatically
picks up any new module. (4) any droid stat/combat change must be
implemented on both sides of the `isPet()` branch (or explicitly decided
to be pet-only) to actually affect both tamed companions and hostile
world spawns of the same droid species.

---

## 34. City Specialization System

**Specializations are pure Lua content, loaded into a name-keyed map.**
`CitySpecialization` (`server/zone/managers/city/CitySpecialization.h`)
is a plain data record -- `name`, `cost`, and a `VectorMap<String, int>
skillMods` -- populated entirely by `readObject(LuaObject*)` parsing a
Lua table (`{name = "...", cost = N, skillMods = {{key, value}, ...}}`);
`CitySpecializationMap` loads the full set once at startup. **Adding a
new specialization is pure data, zero C++**, exactly like the vendor/
skill-trainer patterns documented elsewhere in this guide.

**Eligibility to select a specialization is gated by the mayor's own
trained Force/profession abilities, not by cost or a purchase
transaction.** `CitySpecializationSessionImplementation::
initializeSession()` (line 21-76) builds the selectable list by scanning
the mayor's `AbilityList` for any ability whose name
`beginsWith("city_spec")` (line 53-60) -- if the mayor hasn't personally
trained the profession/skill box that grants the matching
`city_spec_xxx` ability, that specialization simply never appears as an
option (and if the mayor has *none*, the whole menu is empty and the
session cancels with `"You need to learn a specialization skill..."`,
line 67-70). Selecting one further requires the city to be **at least
rank 3 (`RANK_TOWNSHIP`)** (line 85-88) and a **1-week cooldown**
(`city_specializationCooldown`, checked via the standard
`checkCooldownRecovery()`/`addCooldown()` cooldown-tracker mechanism
used throughout the codebase, waived for privileged/GM accounts) since
the last change (line 90-97, enforced again on the actual commit in
`CityManagerImplementation::changeCitySpecialization()` line 411-412).
The `cost` field on `CitySpecialization` plays **no role at all** in
this selection/eligibility path -- it's consumed entirely elsewhere (see
below).

**The specialization's `cost` is a recurring city-treasury maintenance
drain, not an upfront purchase price.** In the periodic city-upkeep
sweep (`CityManagerImplementation.cpp:916-930`, same cycle that charges
the base city registration/maintenance fee seen just above it at
line 905-913), if the city has an active specialization the treasury is
charged `maintenanceDiscount * spec->getCost()` per cycle
(`maintenanceDiscount` -- a separate, elsewhere-computed multiplier,
presumably tied to city rank/citizen count/tax settings). **If the
treasury can't cover it, the specialization is silently revoked**
(`city->setCitySpecialization("")`) and the region's radius is reset
purely to force every current occupant's specialization skillmods to be
stripped (`setRadius(getRadius())` -- a real re-trigger-membership-events
idiom, not a no-op, matching the "resetting the radius reinserts
everyone" comment already found on the mayor-facing change path). A
specialization can therefore lapse automatically from treasury
mismanagement with no direct player action, distinct from the
mayor-driven 1-week cooldown-gated change.

**The buff itself is a real geofenced skill-mod grant/strip pair, keyed
to physical presence in city bounds -- not citizenship.**
