`CityRegionImplementation::applySpecializationModifiers()`/
`removeSpecializationModifiers()` (`CityRegionImplementation.cpp:
872-923`) are called from the region's own enter/leave notification path
(line 240/382 -- the same ActiveArea-style enter/exit mechanism used
throughout the world-region code), applied to **any unbanned creature
physically inside the region**, not just registered citizens
(`isBanned()` check, line 882 -- banned players are excluded, but
non-citizen visitors are not). All of a specialization's `skillMods` are
granted via `addSkillMod(SkillModManager::CITY, key, value)` tagged
under one dedicated `SkillModManager::CITY` category, so removal is a
single generic `removeAllSkillModsOfType(SkillModManager::CITY)` call
rather than tracking individual mod names to undo (line 898/921) -- and
because both apply/remove run through `creature->executeOrderedTask()`
(an ordered lambda task on that specific creature, not applied inline),
the mod change is serialized relative to that creature's other queued
work rather than racing it. **One special-cased skill mod key,
`"private_defense"`, is additionally gated on active militia
membership** (`city->isMilitiaMember()`, line 905-906) even for
creatures otherwise inside city bounds and eligible for every other mod
in that specialization -- the only per-mod (as opposed to per-creature or
per-specialization) eligibility rule in the whole mechanism.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) a new specialization type is a Lua table
entry with a `skillMods` list -- no rebuild needed, following the same
"data by default, C++ only for new *mechanisms*" pattern seen everywhere
else in the content layer. (2) a new *eligibility rule* (e.g. gating a
specialization on something other than a trained ability) would need a
C++ change to `initializeSession()`'s ability-scan loop -- that loop is
specifically hardcoded to the `"city_spec"` ability-name prefix
convention. (3) any specialization-adjacent bug report about players
losing their city buff unexpectedly should check the treasury-driven
auto-revocation path first (silent, no player-facing message beyond
whatever passive tax/treasury UI they check) before assuming a region-
membership bug. (4) the `SkillModManager::CITY` tag-and-bulk-clear
pattern is a clean, reusable model for any other "grant N modifiers,
guaranteed clean removal regardless of what N currently is" feature --
notably similar in spirit to how buffs use `modsApplied` (section 31)
but implemented via categorized skill mods instead of a `Buff` object.

---

## 35. GCW Base Siege Code Walkthrough

**A strictly-ordered, numeric 8-stage hacking state machine gates
destruction -- not raw HP damage.** `DestructibleBuildingDataComponent`
(`server/zone/objects/building/components/DestructibleBuildingDataComponent.h:48-56`)
defines the stage sequence as ascending integers: `INVULNERABLE`(0) ->
`VULNERABLE`(1) -> `BAND`(2, uplink band identified) -> `JAMMED`(3,
uplink jammed) -> `SLICED`(4, security terminal sliced) -> `DNA`(5, DNA
sample matched) -> `OVERLOADED`(6, power regulator overloaded) ->
`SHUTDOWNSEQUENCE`(7) -> `REBOOTSEQUENCE`(8, the abort/cooldown state).
`isVulnerable()` is a bare `intCurrentState >= VULNERABLE`
threshold check -- because the stages are stored as one monotonically
increasing int, the whole progression is inherently linear: there is no
way in this data model to be "sliced" without having already been
"jammed," each `GCWManagerImplementation` step function
(`verifyUplinkBand`/`completeSecuritySlice`/`processDNASample`/
`handlePowerRegulatorSwitch`) is really just advancing this one integer
one notch at a time, gated by whatever player action that stage
requires. `GCWManager.idl`'s matching `isX()` query family
(`isBandIdentified`/`isUplinkJammed`/`isSecurityTermSliced`/
`isDNASampled`/`isPowerOverloaded`/`isShutdownSequenceStarted`/
`isFacilityRebooting`) is just this same integer compared at different
thresholds, not independent flags.

**Vulnerability itself is a scheduled recurring window, and only
applies to Overt-flagged bases.** `startVulnerability()`/
`endVulnerability()` (`GCWManagerImplementation.cpp:973-1052`) both
early-return unless `building->getPvpStatusBitmask() & ObjectFlag::OVERT`
-- **Covert-flagged player bases are structurally never attackable**
through this system at all, confirmed by the gate being on the exact
same PvP-status bitmask used for personal Overt/Covert GCW status
elsewhere in the codebase. Two config-driven timers
(`vulnerabilityFrequency`, the gap between windows, and
`vulnerabilityDuration`, the window length -- both loaded via
`loadLuaConfig()`) drive a `while (nextTime.isPast()) nextTime.addMiliTime(...)`
catch-up loop (line 1024-1026) so a base that missed multiple cycles
(e.g. the server was down) doesn't schedule a burst of overdue windows,
it just fast-forwards to the next real future slot. Entering the window
spawns the hacking terminals (`spawnBaseTerminals()`) and re-verifies
minefields/scanners/turrets are present (`verifyMinefields`/
`verifyScanners`/`verifyTurrets`, called on both entry and exit);
leaving despawns the terminals and resets `intCurrentState` back to
`INVULNERABLE` plus `defenseAddedThisVuln = false` (a per-window flag
tracked separately from the hack-stage integer).

**Final destruction is a real, re-triggerable, broadcast countdown
task, not instant.** `scheduleBaseDestruction()`
(`GCWManagerImplementation.cpp:2153-2182`) -- reachable once the base is
vulnerable (or via `force=true`, the GM/admin override) and not already
mid-destruction (`hasDestroyTask()`) or mid-reboot
(`isFacilityRebooting()`, which blocks re-triggering the overload with a
"you must wait for the facility to reboot" message) -- sets state to
`SHUTDOWNSEQUENCE`, broadcasts a countdown message to everyone in the
building (`broadcastBuilding()`), fires base alarms
(`activateBaseAlarms(building, DESTRUCTALARM)`), and schedules a real
`BaseDestructionTask` **60 seconds out**. `doBaseDestruction()`
(line 2194+) is itself the recurring tick: if the existing countdown
task still has time left (`dTask->getCountdown() > 0`), it just
**reschedules another 60-second tick and re-broadcasts the remaining
minutes** rather than destroying anything -- the actual countdown length
is `destructionTimer` (minutes, converted for the first broadcast at
line 2170) played out in 60-second broadcast increments, not a single
timer firing once. Static (`STATICFACTIONBASE`) vs player-owned
(`PLAYERFACTIONBASE`) bases branch differently at the very end: a static
faction base just flips ownership via a `FACTIONBASEFLIPPED` observer
notification rather than being destroyed outright, while a
`PLAYERFACTIONBASE` proceeds to real structure destruction and owner
notification.

**A separate abort path exists for the defending side, distinct from
the reboot-blocks-re-overload check above.**
`startAbortSequenceDelay()`/`abortShutdownSequence()`
(`GCWManager.idl:278-279`) let a defender interrupt an in-progress
shutdown sequence from an HQ terminal -- this is a defender action
gated by proximity to that specific terminal object
(`hqTerminal` parameter), architecturally separate from the
`isFacilityRebooting()` cooldown that blocks the *attacker* from
immediately re-triggering a fresh overload after one already
completed/reset.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the hacking sequence's step-by-step gating
is enforced purely by the single ascending `intCurrentState` integer --
any new intermediate hacking step would need to be inserted as a new
constant in the right numeric position and every downstream `isX()`
threshold check and step-handler function updated to match, not just a
new independent flag. (2) base defense (turrets/minefields/scanners) is
actively re-verified at both vulnerability-window boundaries
(`verifyTurrets()` etc. called from both `startVulnerability()` and
`endVulnerability()`) -- a base whose defenses were destroyed mid-siege
does *not* silently stay broken forever, they get re-checked/possibly
respawned each time the window opens or closes, which matters for
balancing any new defensive-structure design. (3) the destruction
countdown is genuinely interruptible at any of its 60-second ticks (both
by a defender's abort action and, implicitly, by the destroy task being
cancelled elsewhere e.g. if the building itself is deleted) -- don't
assume `scheduleBaseDestruction()` firing guarantees destruction 60
seconds later. (4) Covert-flagged bases being categorically excluded
from this whole system (not just soft-discouraged) is the single most
consequential fact for anyone reasoning about GCW base PvP exposure --
Covert is a real, unconditional immunity from `startVulnerability()`
ever running for that building.

---

## 36. Weapon Certification System

**Certification requirements live on the weapon template, checked
through two independent "do you have it" paths per required cert.**
`WeaponObjectImplementation::isCertifiedFor()`
(`WeaponObjectImplementation.cpp:668-685`) reads
`weaponTemplate->getCertificationsRequired()` (a template/IFF-sourced
string list -- pure content, no per-instance override) and requires,
for **every** entry, that the attacker satisfy it via **either**
`ghost->hasAbility(cert)` (the `PlayerObject` ability list -- the same
mechanism documented in section 34 for city-specialization eligibility,
i.e. abilities can come from something other than a trained skill box,
such as a quest reward or admin grant) **or** `object->hasSkill(cert)`
(a direct, literal trained-skill-box check on the creature). Because
it's OR-per-cert-name but AND-across-the-list, a weapon requiring
multiple certs needs all of them satisfied, but each individual cert can
be satisfied by whichever of the two mechanisms actually granted it --
there's no way to tell from `isCertifiedFor()`'s result alone which path
a given player qualified through.

**Non-player attackers are unconditionally exempt.** Every enforcement
call site in `CombatManager.cpp` (lines 1136, 1212, 1276, 1769) guards
the entire certification check behind `attacker->isPlayerCreature()` --
AI agents (including companions and hostile NPCs) never have their
weapon damage/DoT gated by certification at all, regardless of what
`weaponTemplate->getCertificationsRequired()` says for the weapon they're
using. This is a real, structural design choice (not an oversight to fix)
since certifications model *player skill training*, which AI creatures
don't participate in.

**Enforcement is a damage/effect penalty at attack-resolution time, not
an equip-time or attack-command-time block.** There is no code anywhere
that prevents equipping an uncertified weapon or that blocks the
attack command from executing -- `isCertifiedFor()` is checked fresh on
every damage calculation. An uncertified player's hit is instead
**hard-capped to a near-useless damage band** -- `minDamage = 5` (single
value, `CombatManager.cpp:1136-1137`) or `minDamage = 5, maxDamage = 10`
(ranged variant, line 1212-1215) -- overriding whatever the weapon's real
damage stats are, and **all weapon DoT effects are suppressed entirely**
(`applyWeaponDots()` returns immediately if uncertified, line
1769-1770) rather than being scaled down. The practical player
experience this produces: an uncertified weapon can still be wielded and
swung and will still land hits (accuracy/hit-chance is untouched), it
just does trivial, DoT-free damage -- a deliberately "technically usable
but not viable" state rather than a hard block, consistent with letting
players see/preview a weapon's real stats and use-case before finishing
the relevant skill training.

**Client-visible certification status is a separate, purely
informational attribute, not the enforcement mechanism itself.**
`WeaponObjectImplementation::fillAttributeList()`
(`WeaponObjectImplementation.cpp:213-224`) independently calls the same
`isCertifiedFor()` check to populate a `"weapon_cert_status"` attribute
("Yes"/"No") shown in the item's examine/attribute window -- this is
what a player actually sees confirming eligibility, computed fresh each
time the tooltip is requested rather than cached on the weapon object,
so it always reflects the player's *current* skill/ability state even
if that changed since the weapon was picked up.

**One additional, narrower call site gates item transfer specifically:**
`TransferItemWeaponCommand.h:143` checks `isCertifiedFor()` when a
player attempts to transfer/equip a weapon via that specific command
path -- worth checking directly if investigating any reported
inconsistency between "can I pick this up" and "can I fight with it,"
since this is the one place certification influences something other
than raw damage output.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) a new weapon type's certification
requirement is pure content -- one or more strings in the weapon
template's `certificationsRequired` list, matched against either
ability or skill-box names that already exist; no C++ change needed
unless the *enforcement behavior itself* needs to change. (2) granting
a certification without full skill training (e.g. a quest reward "you
may use this weapon type") should go through the `PlayerObject`
ability-list mechanism (`hasAbility()`), not by fabricating a fake
skill-box grant -- the two paths are deliberately separate and the
ability path is the lighter-weight, non-skill-tree-committing one.
(3) because enforcement is purely a damage-floor override recomputed
per-hit, there's no cached/stale-state bug class to worry about here --
finishing the relevant skill training makes the weapon immediately
fully effective on the very next swing, no relog or re-equip needed.
(4) any companion/AI-wielded weapon is exempt from all of this by
construction (`isPlayerCreature()` gate) -- a companion combat balance
tweak should never reach for the certification system, since it
structurally cannot apply to non-player attackers.

---

## 37. Housing Decoration / Customization (Deeper)

**Furniture placement, house entry, and every other container-style
access check all run through one shared, reusable ACL primitive:**
`ContainerPermissions` (`server/zone/objects/scene/variables/
ContainerPermissions.h`) packs **allow flags into the high 16 bits and
deny flags into the low 16 bits of a single `uint32` per group**
(`groupPermissions`, a `HashTable<uint32, uint32>` keyed by
`group.hashCode()`), with named bit flags `OPEN`/`MOVEIN`/`MOVEOUT`/
`MOVECONTAINER`/`WALKIN`/`MOVEVENDOR`. Evaluation
(`ContainerPermissions.cpp:87-94`) is `permission & (allow & ~deny)` --
**deny always wins over allow**, a safe-by-default resolution order.
This exact class is reused, unmodified, for house furniture placement,
ordinary item containers, crafting-component satchels, vendor placement
rights, and cell walk-in rights -- there is no house-specific permission
data type, decoration rights are just `MOVEIN`/`MOVEOUT`/
`MOVECONTAINER` permission bits on the relevant cell/building like any
other container.

**Concrete example of deliberate lockdown using this same primitive:**
the droid engineering "crafted_components" container (section 33)
denies `OPEN`+`MOVEIN`+`MOVEOUT`+`MOVECONTAINER` to **both** `"owner"`
and `"admin"` groups explicitly (`SceneObjectImplementation.cpp:
2090-2108`) -- proof this ACL system is expressive enough to lock even
the object's own owner out of a specific internal container, which is
exactly the mechanism keeping droid module storage invisible/
untouchable through normal container UI.

**Enforcement itself is a virtual, per-container-type-overridable
function (`checkContainerPermission()`), following the same component
pattern used throughout this codebase (section 1).** The generic base
just evaluates the `ContainerPermissions` bitmask; several container
*types* override it with extra domain rules layered on top --
`StructureContainerComponent::checkContainerPermission()`
(`StructureContainerComponent.cpp:12-46`) is the one governing house
furniture/entry and resolves in this order: (1) `MOVEVENDOR` is a wholly
separate special case requiring the building be public **and** the
requester either be on a dedicated `"VENDOR"` permission list or the
admin list (private structures reject vendor placement outright with a
distinct system message); (2) the building **owner or anyone on its
admin list bypasses every other check** and gets an automatic `true`;
(3) `OPEN` on a player's own client object (i.e. examining another
player) is always allowed; (4) for a real `BuildingObject`,
`isAllowedEntry(creature)` is checked and **short-circuits to `false`
for the whole permission request** if the creature isn't allowed in the
building at all (the ban/guest list gate, checked before the underlying
bitmask ACL is even consulted); (5) only after all of the above falls
through does it defer to the generic bitmask evaluation
(`ContainerComponent::checkContainerPermission()`) for finer per-group
rules (e.g. a guild-based group getting `WALKIN` but not `MOVEIN`).
**Three logically distinct permission layers exist for a house**:
owner/admin-list (full bypass), entry/ban-list (`isAllowedEntry()`,
all-or-nothing house access), and the `ContainerPermissions` bitmask
(fine-grained per-group rights for whoever gets past the first two) --
a "can decorate but can't enter certain cells" or "can enter but can't
move furniture" configuration is expressible entirely through the
bitmask layer without touching the other two.

**Other container-type overrides show the same pattern reused for
different domains**: `TurretContainerComponent`, `GCWBaseContainerComponent`
(delegates to `StructureContainerComponent` after its own siege-specific
checks, tying section 35's GCW base system into this same permission
model), `EnclaveContainerComponent`, and `WarrenDiskContainerComponent`
each layer their own domain rule on top of the identical base check --
confirming this is the one general-purpose access-control mechanism for
every "who can touch what's inside this object" question in the engine,
not something reinvented per feature.

**Decoration capacity is governed by the same generic per-container
volume limit as any container, not a house-specific item cap.**
`SceneObject`'s `containerVolumeLimit` field (`SceneObject.idl:101`,
`isContainerFull()`-style checks at lines 1194/1199) is set per
cell/container template and applies uniformly -- a house's rooms/cells
just have their own `containerVolumeLimit` values like a crate or a
player's inventory would, there's no separate "total furniture items in
this structure" counter or cap layered on top.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any new house-decoration-adjacent feature
(a new furniture interaction right, a new sub-permission) should extend
`ContainerPermissions`' flag set and plug into the existing
`checkContainerPermission()` virtual chain rather than inventing a new
ACL mechanism -- this is a mature, widely-reused primitive. (2) the
owner/admin-list bypass (`isOwnerOf`/`isOnAdminList`) happens *before*
the bitmask ACL is ever consulted -- granting someone admin-list status
on a house is a full-trust action for every container inside it, not a
scoped grant; scoped, partial decoration rights need the bitmask layer
instead, applied to a *non*-admin-list group. (3) `isAllowedEntry()`
being checked ahead of the bitmask means a banned player's
`ContainerPermissions` entries (if any accidentally persisted) are moot
-- entry denial is an unconditional short-circuit, not just another
input to the bitmask evaluation. (4) raising or lowering how much
furniture a room can hold is purely a template/content change to that
cell's `containerVolumeLimit`, no C++ needed, since the volume-limit
check is already fully generic.

---

## 38. GM / Staff Admin Command System

**Staff commands are not a separate code path from ordinary commands --
they're gated by the exact same ability-check mechanism documented in
section 6, just with a mandatory second check layered on top.**
`ObjectControllerImplementation::activateCommand()`
(`ObjectControllerImplementation.cpp:114-135`) -- the same central
per-command dispatch point from section 6 -- checks
`queueCommand->requiresAdmin()` (a per-command flag from command
config/`commandTable`, not something a command's `doQueueCommand()` body
decides for itself) and, if set, requires **both**
`ghost->hasGodMode()` (the account-level "is admin mode currently
switched on" flag) **and** `ghost->hasAbility(queueCommand
->getQueueCommandName())` -- meaning **every individual GM command's own
name doubles as an ability string** that must be explicitly granted,
separately from the blanket godmode toggle. A staff member with godmode
active but missing the specific command's ability still gets rejected
with `"@error_message:insufficient_permissions"`. Failed attempts are
logged as warnings (`adminLog.warning() << "... attempted to use ...
without permissions"`); successful ones call
`logAdminCommand(object, queueCommand, targetID, arguments)`
(`ObjectController.idl:68`) -- **every admin command execution is
audit-logged from the central dispatcher itself**, not something each
GM command implementation has to remember to do (though `SetGodModeCommand`
additionally calls it explicitly too, redundantly, right at its own
entry).

**Staff permission tiers, their command sets, and their chat tags are
pure Lua content, loaded once at startup.**
`PermissionLevelList::loadLevels()`
(`server/zone/managers/player/PermissionLevelList.h:81-126`) runs
`scripts/staff/levels/serverobjects.lua` through the same
`registerFunction()`/`Lua` mechanism documented in section 29, populating
one `PermissionLevel` record per tier: a numeric `level`, a display
`name`, a chat `tag` (the bracketed staff prefix shown in-game), a
`priviledgeFlag`, and a `skillList` -- **the exact list of command-ability
strings that tier's members are granted**. Nothing about tier
membership, command access, or display tag requires a rebuild to change
-- it's all one Lua table per level.

**Being assigned a staff tier and having active admin privileges are
two independently toggleable states, not one.**
`PlayerManagerImplementation`'s tier-assignment path (~line 3860-3901,
invoked from `/setGodMode <name> <level>`) sets `ghost->adminLevel` and
calls `skillManager->awardSkill()`/`surrenderSkill()` to grant/revoke
that tier's entire `skillList` as real skill boxes (the same skill-award
mechanism used for player skill training everywhere else in the
codebase) -- this makes the tier's command abilities *available* but
does **not** by itself turn on active admin mode. `hasGodMode()`
(`PlayerObject.idl:1386-1388`, `adminLevel > 0 && hasAbility("admin")`)
requires the separate `"admin"` ability specifically, toggled by
`/setGodMode <name> on|off`
(`SetGodModeCommand.h:73-79`, `skillManager->addAbility()`/
`removeAbility(ghost, "admin")`) -- a staff member can hold a
permanently-assigned tier (and its granted skills/abilities) while
sitting in "off" mode day-to-day, then flip `"admin"` on only when
actively moderating. `isPrivileged()` (`adminLevel > 6`) and `isStaff()`
(`adminLevel > 10`) are just higher numeric thresholds on the same
`adminLevel` field, each **also** requiring `hasAbility("admin")` --
so even a high-numbered `adminLevel` reads as non-privileged everywhere
in the codebase while admin mode is switched off.

**A strict hierarchy prevents staff from managing equal-or-higher-tier
peers.** `/setGodMode`'s own permission logic
(`SetGodModeCommand.h:33-96`) requires `hasSkill("admin_base")` just to
run the command at all (the one universal "any staff member" skill,
distinct from any specific tier), then blocks acting on a target whose
`targetPermissionLevel > ghostPermissionLevel` outright
(`INSUFFICIENTPERMISSION`) -- a mid-tier GM cannot toggle admin mode for
or reassign the tier of anyone ranked above them, including other GMs at
a higher tier. **Actually changing someone's permission *level*** (as
opposed to just toggling their existing tier's admin mode on/off)
requires the *caller* be at the specifically-named `"admin"` tier
(`ghostPermissionLevel < permissionLevelList->getLevelNumber("admin")`,
line 81-84) -- a named, presumably-top tier looked up by string, not
just "some sufficiently high number."

**Practical takeaways:** (1) adding a new GM command is entirely
standard command-authoring (section 6) plus setting `requiresAdmin` in
that command's config and giving it a distinctive ability name, then
adding that name to the relevant tier(s)' `skillList` in the staff Lua
config -- no new C++ gating logic needed, the dispatcher's existing
`requiresAdmin()` branch handles it. (2) a "staff member can't use a
command they should have access to" report should be diagnosed in this
order: is `"admin"` mode currently on (`hasGodMode()`), is the specific
command's ability name actually present in their tier's `skillList`, and
was that tier actually (re)applied since the config last changed
(tier skills are granted at assignment time, not re-synced automatically
on every Lua reload). (3) every admin command attempt -- allowed or
denied -- already has a logging hook at the dispatcher level
(`adminLog`/`logAdminCommand()`); any new staff-facing audit/reporting
feature should read from there rather than adding parallel logging
inside individual commands. (4) the tier-assignment vs. admin-mode-toggle
split means "promote this account to GM" and "this GM is actively in
admin mode right now" are genuinely different, independently-queryable
states in the data model -- useful to keep straight for any staff-facing
tooling built on top of this system.

---

## 39. Anti-Exploit / Duplication Prevention

**Every item move is a single atomic remove-then-add through one
central function, never a copy-then-delete.**
`ContainerComponent::transferObject()`
(`server/zone/objects/scene/components/ContainerComponent.cpp:206-320+`)
-- the function underneath every `SceneObject::transferObject()` call
in the codebase, including the trade system below -- **removes the
object from its current parent first** (`objParent->removeObject(...)`)
and explicitly verifies the removal actually nulled the object's parent
reference before proceeding (line 247-251: if a nullify was expected but
the parent reference is still set, the whole transfer **aborts with a
logged error** rather than continuing into an inconsistent state where
the object could end up referenced by two containers at once). Only
after that verified removal does it acquire
`Locker contLocker(sceneObject->getContainerLock())` -- **a dedicated
lock specifically for container-membership mutation**, distinct from
the general object lock -- and insert into the destination, enforcing
the destination's `containerVolumeLimit` (section 37) in the same pass.
Two additional safeguards run automatically on every transfer,
regardless of caller: `object->canBeTransferred(sceneObject)` (an
overridable per-object-type veto hook) must pass first, and **any active
slicing session on the object being moved is forcibly cancelled**
(line 221-229) -- closing off a known exploit shape where manipulating
an item's slicing-session state while it's simultaneously changing
containers could leave inconsistent state.

**Player-to-player trading requires both sides to independently and
symmetrically confirm, with the actual transfer gated on whichever
confirmation arrives second.**
`PlayerManagerImplementation::handleVerifyTradeMessage()`
(`PlayerManagerImplementation.cpp:3097-3172+`) -- reached from the
client's `VerifyTradeMessage` packet -- locks **both** trading
creatures together (`Locker clocker(receiver, player)`) before touching
any trade state, marks the sender's own `TradeSession::verifiedTrade`
flag true, then checks whether the *other* party's `TradeSession` also
already has `hasVerifiedTrade() == true`. **Only when both sides'
verified flags are true does any item actually move** -- meaning
whichever player's client happens to send its verify message second is
the one whose thread actually executes the transfer for both sides, and
because both creatures are locked together for the whole operation there
is no window where two threads could each observe "I'm the second
verifier" concurrently. `checkTradeItems()` re-validates the trade
contents immediately before committing (catching a trade window whose
contents changed or became invalid between offer and confirmation) and
aborts the whole trade (`handleAbortTradeMessage()`) rather than
partially executing if it fails. Every item transferred during a trade
gets its own `TransactionLog` entry, and **all of them share one
`trxGroup` ID** (`TransactionLog::getNewTrxGroup()`, line 3113) --
letting a GM/forensic query reconstruct an entire trade as one linked
unit after the fact rather than a scatter of individually-unrelated log
rows.

**Every credit and flagged item movement is written through a
structured, self-describing audit log, not ad-hoc logging.**
`TransactionLog` (`server/zone/objects/transaction/TransactionLog.h`)
is a real RAII object -- constructed at the point of a credit/item
change (source object, destination object, subject item, a `TrxCode`
enum value identifying *why*, and an amount where relevant), it
auto-captures the calling file/function/line via compiler builtins
(`CAPTURE_CALLER_DECLARE`), the world position/zone context, and commits
itself as structured JSON on destruction unless explicitly grouped with
another log (`trx.groupWith(otherTrx)`, the exact pattern already
documented in sections 32/24 for image-designer and auction payments).
The `TrxCode` enum (`TransactionLog.h:18-114`) has **dozens of named
reasons** spanning every credit-moving system in the game --
`PLAYERTRADE`, `INSTANTBUY`, `AUCTIONBID`, `IMAGEDESIGN`,
`ADMINCOMMAND`, `SERVERDESTROYOBJECT`, `CRAFTINGSESSION`,
`CHARACTERDELETE`, `SLICECONTAINER`, and many more -- giving every
credit/item movement in the entire codebase one uniform, queryable,
already-categorized forensic trail rather than requiring log-scraping
or per-system ad hoc records. This is the concrete mechanism behind
"how would a GM investigate a suspected dupe or credit exploit after
the fact": every legitimate credit/item path already writes to this
log by construction, so an unexplained credit/item appearance with no
corresponding `TransactionLog` entry is itself the signal something
bypassed the normal system.

**Access-control (section 37's `ContainerPermissions`) and duplication
prevention are two independent, complementary layers, not the same
mechanism.** `GiveItemCommand` (section on housing/containers) checks
`checkContainerPermission(creature, MOVEOUT)` on the source and
`MOVECONTAINER` on the destination *before* ever calling
`transferObject()` -- permission checks answer "is this move allowed at
all," while `transferObject()`'s atomic remove-then-add with the
container lock answers "even when allowed, can this move ever produce
two copies or no copies." A bug in one layer doesn't necessarily
compromise the other, which matters when auditing: a permission bypass
alone doesn't imply a duplication vector, and vice versa.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any new player-to-player or player-to-NPC
item-transfer feature should call the existing `transferObject()`
path (directly or via `ObjectController::transferObject()`, the
locked wrapper used by the trade system) rather than manually
manipulating container maps/parent pointers -- that's precisely the
class of hand-rolled transfer logic most likely to reintroduce a
duplication window. (2) any new credit-moving or valuable-item-moving
feature should wrap its transaction in a `TransactionLog` with an
appropriate (or newly-added) `TrxCode`, both for consistency with the
rest of the codebase and because it's the substrate any future
exploit-investigation tooling will assume exists. (3) the trade
system's "lock both parties together, gate on the second verification"
pattern is the concrete, reusable template for any other feature
requiring two independent parties to atomically agree before a
state change commits (a two-sided negotiated exchange, section 32's
image-design accept flow follows a similar shape). (4) `canBeTransferred()`
is the correct extension point for blocking a *new category* of item
from ever changing containers under some game-rule condition -- e.g. an
item bound mid-quest -- rather than scattering ad hoc container checks
across every command that might move it.

---

## 40. Resource Spawning / Harvesting Deep Dive

**Resource location is real 3D simplex noise, not a stored grid or a
random-point list.** `SpawnDensityMap` (`server/zone/objects/resource/
SpawnDensityMap.h`) stores only a random `seed`, a `modifier`
(spatial frequency), and a `density` ceiling -- `getDensityAt(x, y)`
(line 106-115) computes `SimplexNoise::noise(x*modifier, y*modifier,
seed*modifier)` on the fly, clamping negative noise to zero and scaling
the rest by `density`. Using the seed as the noise function's *third*
axis is the trick that gives every resource spawn its own unique,
non-repeating 2D pattern from one shared noise algorithm with no stored
per-pixel data at all -- the "map" is a formula, not a lookup table.
**Ore uses a coarser frequency than everything else**
(`modifier = .00015` vs `.0006`, `initialize()` line 128-134) -- larger,
smoother patches for ore deposits vs. tighter clustering for other
resource types, a deliberate geological-plausibility choice baked
directly into the noise parameters.

**Concentration tier sets a randomized density ceiling per spawn, not a
fixed value.** `getConcentration()`
(`ResourceSpawnImplementation.cpp:144-158`) buckets every resource type
into `HIGHDENSITY`/`MEDIUMDENSITY`/`LOWDENSITY` by hardcoded type rules
(JTL content and chemical/inert-gas always high; ore/water/unlimited
solar-or-wind always low; everything else medium), and
`SpawnDensityMap::initialize()` rolls a random ceiling *within* that
tier's band each time a new spawn is generated -- high 90-99%, medium
75-94%, low 50-74% (line 136-148) -- so two different high-density
spawns of the same resource type still won't have identical peak
richness.

**Each spawn instance picks its own random subset of planets/zones, not
"spawns everywhere."** `getSpawnZones()`
(`ResourceSpawnImplementation.cpp:160-189`) rolls a zone count between a
type's configured min/max pool size, then randomly discards zones from
the active-zone list until only that many remain (or honors an explicit
single-zone restriction if the resource type has one) -- `createSpawnMaps()`
then builds one independent `SpawnDensityMap` per surviving zone, each
with its own random seed/density roll, so the same resource type spawning
concurrently on two planets is genuinely two unrelated noise fields, not
a shared pattern.

**A resource's real total extractable pool is generated but never
enforced anywhere in the codebase.** `SpawnDensityMap::totalUnits` is
randomized to 5-10 million per zone-map at creation (line 150) and its
companion field `unitsHarvested` exists, is fully wired into
serialization (`addSerializableVariable`, JSON export) and the copy
constructor/assignment operator -- but a full-codebase search finds
**no call site anywhere that ever increments `unitsHarvested` or
compares it against `totalUnits`.** `ResourceSpawnImplementation::
extractResource()` (the only function actually invoked when a harvester
pulls resources, line 221-224) just adds to a separate,
whole-resource-wide `unitsInCirculation` counter and does nothing else.
Practically: **harvesting a location does not measurably deplete that
location or reduce its future density** in the current code -- a
resource's only real lifecycle event is timed despawn (`inShift()`
gating `getDensityAt()` to zero once a resource's shift window ends,
independent of how much was ever extracted), not usage-based exhaustion.
Worth confirming directly against a live server before relying on any
assumption that heavy harvesting measurably thins out a resource.

**Harvester extraction is a real offline-capable, time-elapsed
calculation, not a live per-tick simulation.** `InstallationObjectImplementation`'s
harvest-tick logic (`InstallationObjectImplementation.cpp:383-414`)
computes `elapsedTime` as real wall-clock time since the hopper was last
updated, capped so extraction never counts time *past* the resource's
actual despawn timestamp even if the harvester wasn't checked until
later (`harvestUntil = min(now, spawnDespawnTime)`, line 385-387) --
`harvestAmount = (elapsedTime / 60.0) * (spawnDensity * getExtractionRate())`,
a straightforward per-minute rate scaled by the location's noise-derived
density and the installation's own extraction-rate stat, capped by
remaining hopper capacity, with a **fractional remainder explicitly
carried forward** (`extractionRemainder`, line 400-402) so repeated
sub-unit ticks don't lose material to integer truncation over time. This
is what makes offline harvesting between player logins/server restarts
work correctly -- the formula is purely a function of elapsed time and
location, not something that needs to run every server tick to produce
correct results.

**Density lookups are reused identically across every resource-gathering
minigame, not reimplemented per feature.** The exact same
`ResourceSpawn::getDensityAt(zoneName, x, y)` call is used by installation
harvesters, the foraging minigame (`ForageManagerImplementation.cpp:380`),
creature milking (`MilkCreatureTask.h:121`), droid harvest-interest
modules (`CreatureManagerImplementation.cpp:815/985`, tying back to
section 33's droid harvest module), the client-facing survey tool data
packet (`HarvesterResourceDataMessage.h:49`, sent as a byte-scaled
0-100 percentage), and the generic `ResourceMap` lookup wrapper used by
admin/management tooling -- one noise-field query answers "how much of
this resource is here" for every gathering mechanic in the game.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) a new resource-gathering minigame or
installation type should call the existing `getDensityAt()`/
`extractResource()` pair rather than inventing new spatial logic -- the
noise field and its zone/density parameters are already fully generic.
(2) if a "resources should deplete with heavy use" feature is ever
wanted, `unitsHarvested`/`totalUnits` already have the exact data model
for it (per-zone harvested-vs-total tracking, already serialized) -- it
would need `extractResource()` extended to actually increment
`unitsHarvested` and `getDensityAt()` (or a wrapping check) to factor
in remaining pool, both currently missing. (3) offline harvester yield
calculations are safe to trust across server restarts/long player
absences since the formula is time-elapsed-based, not per-tick-accumulated
-- but note the resource's despawn timestamp is a hard ceiling on how
much elapsed time counts, so a harvester left running well past a
resource's shift-out earns nothing for the extra time. (4) resource type
(ore vs. non-ore) drives noise frequency, and resource type also drives
concentration tier -- both are hardcoded type-name rules in
`ResourceSpawnImplementation`, so a new resource *category* that should
behave differently spatially needs a matching branch in
`getConcentration()`/`initialize()`, not just new content data.

---

## 41. Guild System Deep Dive

**Per-member rights are one byte-wide bitmask, and "leader" is not a
separate special-cased role -- it's just whoever currently holds every
bit.** `GuildObject.idl:65-74` defines eight permission bits
(`PERMISSION_MAIL`/`SPONSOR`/`TITLE`/`ACCEPT`/`KICK`/`WAR`/`NAME`/
`DISBAND`) plus `PERMISSION_ALL = 0xFF`. `transferLeadership()`
(`GuildManagerImplementation.cpp:966-1001`) makes this concrete: it sets
`guild->setGuildLeaderID(newLeader)` **and** grants the new leader's
`GuildMemberInfo` `PERMISSION_ALL` while explicitly stripping the old
leader down to `PERMISSION_NONE` -- there is no other code path that
treats "the leader" as structurally different from any other member with
full permissions. A guild officer role is just a member with a subset of
these bits toggled on via `toggleGuildPermission(targetID,
permissionIndex, ...)`, reusing the identical mechanism.

**Guild wars are a real 4-state, per-target-guild directional state
machine (`WAR_NONE`/`WAR_IN`/`WAR_OUT`/`WAR_MUTUAL`), driven by one
toggle action from either side.** `toggleWarStatus()`
(`GuildManagerImplementation.cpp:1799-1838`) branches on the *current*
relationship to the target guild: no relationship -> declaring sets the
caller to `WAR_OUT` and the target to `WAR_IN` (an asymmetric,
one-sided declaration -- the target can immediately fight back per GCW
rules without formally accepting, since being `WAR_IN` already flags the
relationship as hostile); the target then toggling the same action
against a `WAR_IN` state (`hasDeclaredWarBy()`) is "accepting," flipping
**both** sides to `WAR_MUTUAL`; toggling while `WAR_MUTUAL`
(`isAtWarWith()`) is "rescinding," which reverts the rescinding side to
`WAR_IN` and the other side to `WAR_OUT` (mutual war doesn't collapse
straight back to `WAR_NONE` -- the original declarer's hostile status
persists until *they* also toggle it off); toggling while the caller
already has an outbound declaration (`hasDeclaredWarOn()`) cancels
cleanly back to `WAR_NONE` for both. Each real-time status flip to
`WAR_MUTUAL`/back schedules a dedicated `UpdateWarStatusTask`
(`updateWarStatusToWaringGuild()`, line 1840-1843) to propagate the
change to the other guild's members. War permission itself
(`PERMISSION_WAR`) is checked before any of this runs
(`hasWarPermission()`, line 1800) -- not every member can declare or
rescind on the guild's behalf.

**Leadership succession has two independent paths sharing one commit
function.** `transferLeadership(newLeader, oldLeader, election)`'s
`election` bool is the only thing distinguishing a leader's voluntary
handoff from an election result -- when `election == true` it skips the
player-facing "you are now the leader"/"you are now a normal member"
system messages (line 994-999), since the election flow already
communicates the outcome through its own mail/UI. The election cycle
itself (`toggleElection()`, line 2160-2186) is a real, exact **two-week**
timed process: `ELECTION_FIRST_WEEK` -> `ELECTION_SECOND_WEEK` ->
automatic tally, confirmed by the guild-wide announcement mail's own
text ("A new guild leader will be elected in exactly two weeks"). Any
full member can `registerForElection()` as a candidate and
`castVote()` for one; `viewElectionStandings()` exposes live vote
counts (`VectorMap<candidateID, voteCount>`) mid-election. A sitting
leader can `resetElection()`/close voting early via the same toggle
function, which sends its own distinct "elections closed" guild mail.

**Joining a guild is sponsorship-gated, not open application.**
`sponsorPlayer()`/`acceptSponsorshipRequest()`/`acceptSponsoredPlayer()`/
`declineSponsoredPlayer()` form a real two-sided invite flow: an
existing member with `PERMISSION_SPONSOR` nominates a player
(added to `guild->sponsoredPlayers`, a `SortedVector` distinct from the
real `guildMembers` list), and the nominated player must separately
accept -- there is no player-initiated "apply to join" path in this
API surface at all, membership growth is entirely sponsor-driven.

**Guild-wide communication and naming changes both go through
dedicated, auditable flows rather than direct field writes.**
`sendGuildMail(subject, body, guild)` is the single reusable mechanism
behind every major guild-state-change notification observed in this
research (election open/close being the concrete examples traced) --
any new guild event that should notify the whole membership should reuse
it rather than iterating members and sending individual chat messages.
Renaming (`setupGuildRename()`/`renameGuild()`) and re-abbreviating both
stage the change into `pendingNewName`/`pendingNewAbbrev` +
`renamePending`/`renamerID` fields on `GuildObject` rather than applying
immediately -- consistent with `validateGuildName()`/
`guildNameExists()` needing to run as an async/uniqueness-checked step
before a rename actually commits.

**Guild halls are a distinct transfer flow from generic structure
ownership** (section 37): `sendGuildTransferTo()`/`sendTransferAckTo()`/
`transferGuildHall(newOwner, guildTerminal)` are guild-specific
functions layered on top of the ordinary structure-ownership system
(section 24/37), not a reuse of `StructureManager::declareResidence()`'s
path -- a guild hall's ownership is tied to guild leadership/membership
state, not just whichever character's name is on the deed.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any new guild-officer-style capability is
just a new bit in the `PERMISSION_*` set plus a `toggleGuildPermission()`
call site -- no new "role" concept needed, and it automatically composes
with the existing leader-gets-`PERMISSION_ALL` model. (2) a guild-war
feature (e.g. war-zone bonuses, kill tracking) should read relationship
state via `isAtWarWith()`/`hasDeclaredWarOn()`/`hasDeclaredWarBy()`
rather than re-deriving it from the raw byte, since the asymmetric
IN/OUT states are meaningfully different from `WAR_MUTUAL` and a naive
"nonzero means at war" check would misclassify a one-sided declaration.
(3) any player-facing guild announcement should reuse `sendGuildMail()`
for consistency with how the game already communicates guild-wide
events. (4) guild membership is fundamentally sponsor-gated in this
codebase -- an "open guilds"/public-join feature would be new
functionality, not a config flip, since no code path here bypasses the
sponsor-then-accept handshake.

---

## 42. Manufacturing / Factory Crates

**A factory installation runs one schematic-driven, self-rescheduling
production loop per unit -- the same `Task`-reschedule pattern used by
buffs (section 31) and AI behavior ticks (section 9).**
`startFactory()` (`FactoryObjectImplementation.cpp:536-582`) validates
the loaded `ManufactureSchematic`'s prototype isn't sliced, doesn't have
an anti-decay kit, and (for weapons) doesn't have a powerup installed --
**a deliberate anti-exploit gate specific to factories** (ties directly
into section 39): none of those item states are something you'd want
mass-duplicated by batch production. Per-unit crafting time is a
straightforward deterministic formula, `timer = schematic->getComplexity()
* 8` seconds (line 569, overridden to a flat 30s in `DEBUG_FACTORIES`
builds for testing) -- `populateSchematicBlueprint()` then pre-scans the
factory's ingredient hopper to match up available resources/components
against the schematic's blueprint entries before the first cycle is even
scheduled. Each subsequent unit is produced by `createNewObject()`
(line 655-765), which **reschedules its own pending task**
(`pending->reschedule(timer * 1000)`, line 762) rather than running on a
fixed external interval -- production naturally pauses if
`stopFactory()` cancels the pending task for any of several reasons
below.

**Power/maintenance is checked every single cycle, using the same
elapsed-time-since-last-check model as harvesters (section 40).**
`updateMaintenance(timeToWorkTill)` (called at the top of every
`createNewObject()` cycle, line 683) determines whether the factory has
enough surplus power to keep running; if not,
`energyAmount = (elapsedTime / 3600.0) * getBasePowerRate()` is compared
against `surplusPower` to decide whether to shut down for lack of power
specifically (distinct system message) versus a generic maintenance
shutdown -- exactly the same "compute cost from real elapsed time, not
per-tick simulation" idiom documented for harvester extraction.

**Output batching is genuinely two different code paths depending on
the schematic's configured crate size, not a uniform "always crate"
model.** If `schematic->getFactoryCrateSize() > 1`, production either
finds an existing, not-yet-full `FactoryCrate` in the output hopper
(`locateCrateInOutputHopper()`) and increments its
`useCount`/`quantity` (line 722-737 -- **a factory crate is literally a
stack with a use-count**, matching `FactoryCrate.idl`'s
`setUseCount()`/`getPrototypeUseCount()`), or creates a brand new crate
via `createNewFactoryCrate()` once the current one is full or none
exists yet. If crate size is 1, `createNewUncratedItem()` produces a
standalone item directly with no crate involved at all -- **whether a
schematic's output is ever crated is a per-schematic content property**,
not a universal factory behavior.

**A manufacture schematic is a consumable with a finite total run
count, not an infinite crafting template.**
`schematic->manufactureItem()` is called once per successfully produced
unit (line 749, incrementing the factory's own `currentRunCount`
tracker too) and internally decrements the schematic's remaining-uses
counter; when `schematic->getManufactureLimit() < 1` afterward, the
schematic itself is destroyed both from the live world and from the
database (`destroyObjectFromWorld()`+`destroyObjectFromDatabase()`,
line 752-757) and the factory auto-stops with a "manufacturing complete"
notification. This closes the loop with the crafting/experimentation
system: a schematic's manufacture limit is set once at crafting time
(quality/experimentation-dependent, outside this file's scope) and is
strictly consumed down to zero by factory production, never
replenished.

**Every shutdown reason sends the owner a real, specific in-game
mail, not just a generic "factory stopped" message.** `stopFactory()`
overloads (line 600-653) cover distinct causes -- out of power, missing
a specific named resource, missing a specific component, schematic
error, manufacture limit reached -- each mapping to its own
`@system_msg:` string ID, some parameterized with the exact missing
resource/component name (`tt`/`to`/`di` fields feeding a
`StringIdChatParameter`, the same templated-mail-body mechanism used
elsewhere in the codebase) and delivered via `chatManager->sendMail()`.
A commented-out block (line 629-637) shows this mail was at some point
also meant to carry a waypoint object pointing back at the factory --
currently disabled/dead, worth knowing if "click the mail to find your
factory" is ever requested as a feature, since the scaffolding already
exists but isn't wired up.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the per-unit crafting-time formula
(`complexity * 8` seconds) is the one number to know for any
factory-throughput-related balance question -- it's schematic-complexity-driven,
not a flat rate or something installation-tier-dependent. (2) a new
item type that should batch into crates just needs its schematic
content configured with `factoryCrateSize > 1` and a `factoryCrateType`
-- no code path change needed, both branches already exist and are
fully generic. (3) any new item state that shouldn't be mass-producible
via factory (analogous to sliced/ADK/powered-up items already being
blocked) needs its own check added to `startFactory()`'s validation
block at line 555-563 -- that's the single choke point, not something
enforced per-item-type elsewhere. (4) factory shutdown-notification mail
already has per-cause specificity and even latent waypoint-attachment
scaffolding -- extending it for a new shutdown reason is adding one more
`stopFactory()` call with a new string ID, not new mail infrastructure.

---

## 43. Vehicle / Garage System

**A vehicle is a `CreatureObject` puppeted entirely by its rider, not
an independent AI entity -- structurally the direct sibling of the
companion system's `linkedCreature` pattern.** `VehicleObject extends
CreatureObject` (`server/zone/objects/creature/VehicleObject.idl:18`),
**not** `AiAgent` (contrast droids and companions, sections 8/33, which
both extend `AiAgent`) -- a vehicle has no behavior tree, no AI ticking
of its own. `isAttackableBy()` (line 190-201) makes this explicit: it
delegates straight to `linkedCreature.isAttackableBy(object)` -- the
exact same `linkedCreature` field name and delegation idiom already
documented as the companion system's established owner-resolution
accessor. A vehicle's PvP/attackability, in other words, is never its
own state at all, it's a pure passthrough to whoever's riding it.
Posture changes are explicitly suppressed (`setPosture()` is a
deliberate no-op, "vehicles should not change posture," line 94-97) and
wound/defender-vector mutations (`addWounds`/`setWounds`/`addDefender`/
`removeDefender`) are all stub no-ops too -- a vehicle has HAM-style
damage via `inflictDamage()`/`healDamage()` but doesn't participate in
the wound/defender machinery real creatures do.

**Elemental resistances degrade with vehicle condition, not armor
templates.** Every resist getter (`getKinetic()`/`getEnergy()`/
`getElectricity()`/`getStun()`/`getBlast()`/`getHeat()`/`getCold()`/
`getAcid()`/`getLightSaber()`, line 280-323) returns a fixed baseline
(30% kinetic, 25% for everything else) minus
`getConditionReduction(baseline)` -- a damaged vehicle is measurably
easier to hurt across every damage type simultaneously, derived purely
from its own condition/hitpoints rather than any equipped armor item
(`getArmor()` itself is hardcoded to always return 0, line 276-278 --
vehicles have no armor-slot concept at all).

**Summoning ("unpacking") a stored vehicle enforces a specific set of
world-state preconditions, all checked at the control-device layer, not
the vehicle object itself.** `VehicleControlDeviceImplementation::
generateObject()`/`spawnObject()`
(`VehicleControlDeviceImplementation.cpp:22-150+`) both require: the
summoning player isn't dead/incapacitated, actually owns the control
device (`isASubChildOf(player)`), is currently unparented (i.e.
standing in the open world, not inside any building/vehicle/cell) and
not in combat -- both violations share the identical
`"@pet/pet_menu:cant_call_vehicle"` message string used by the
pet-calling system, confirming vehicle-summon and companion/pet-summon
were built as parallel, string-sharing UX flows. `spawnObject()`
additionally requires a real **ground zone** (`!zone->isGroundZone()`
rejects space zones outright, line 138-140) and, if the player happens
to have an active trade session open, **force-aborts it first**
(`handleAbortTradeMessage()`, line 144-146) before summoning proceeds --
the same trade-safety pattern documented in section 39's anti-dupe
walkthrough, applied here to prevent a vehicle-summon animation/position
change from interfering with an in-progress trade.

**Parking garages exist specifically to gate vehicle *repair*, not
general summoning/storage.** `checkInRangeGarage()`
(`VehicleObjectImplementation.cpp:133-140`) wraps
`StructureManager::instance()->getInRangeParkingGarage(vehicle)` -- its
**only** call sites are the "Repair Vehicle" radial-menu-item visibility
check (`fillObjectMenuResponse()`, line 22-31: the repair option only
even appears if the vehicle is disabled/damaged **and** currently near a
garage, or the player is a privileged GM bypassing the requirement) and
the matching `RepairVehicleSuiCallback` re-validation at actual repair
time. Storing (`storeObject()`) and summoning
(`generateObject()`/`spawnObject()`) a vehicle have **no garage
proximity requirement anywhere** in this code -- garages are purely a
repair-location restriction, not a general vehicle-management
requirement, contrary to what the name might suggest.

**Rental vehicles are a distinct, finite-use variant sharing the same
class.** `rentalVehicle`/`rentalUses` (`VehicleObject.idl:21-22,
250-268`) mark a vehicle as a limited-use rental and track remaining
uses directly on the same `VehicleObject` instance -- there's no
separate rental-vehicle subclass, just these two extra fields consulted
by whatever rental-terminal logic grants/decrements them. Paint decay
(`paintCount`/`refreshPaint()`, capped at 999 charges, with a code
comment noting the cap itself changed historically from 2000 in a
"Jump to Lightspeed" balance patch) is the identical mechanic already
documented for droids in section 33 -- both share the same
`PAINTCHARGES`-style cosmetic-decay pattern.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any new vehicle-adjacent combat mechanic
should account for vehicles having zero armor-slot support and
condition-derived (not equipment-derived) resistances -- a "vehicle
armor upgrade" feature would be new functionality, not something that
plugs into the existing resist getters. (2) a "companion rides in a
vehicle" or "vehicle summons alongside a companion" feature can lean on
the fact that vehicles and pets/companions already share summon-flow
message strings and structural patterns (`linkedCreature`, the
can't-summon-here checks) -- there's real precedent to follow rather
than inventing new UX conventions. (3) "garage" in this codebase means
specifically "valid repair location," not "vehicle storage" -- don't
conflate it with the deed/control-device storage mechanism when
reasoning about or extending vehicle features. (4) the trade-abort-on-summon
safeguard is a good template for any other feature that changes a
player's position/state abruptly -- open trades should probably be
aborted rather than left to interact unpredictably with whatever the
new feature does.

---

## 44. Bounty Hunter System -- Resolution Mechanics (extends section 16)

Section 16 already covers mission-terminal listing, target selection,
and mission acceptance for bounty missions in depth. This section covers
what happens *after* acceptance for **player-target** bounties
specifically -- resolution, payout, and multi-hunter interaction --
which section 16 doesn't reach. (Note: no dedicated tracking-device/
tool class exists in `src/` under any bounty-hunter-specific name --
target-location narrowing appears to be handled entirely through the
mission objective's own waypoint mechanics already covered generically
in section 16's `MissionObjective` framework, not a separate tracking
system.)

**A live player bounty target has an eligibility gate most players
never trigger.** `MissionManagerImplementation`'s target-eligibility
check (~line 2118-2127) requires the target's `PlayerObject::
getVisibility()` meet `VisibilityManager::getTerminalVisThreshold()`
before they can even be rolled as a postable bounty target -- a
low-visibility player is simply invisible to the bounty system,
regardless of any other qualifying factor. A separate, short
**post-kill cooldown buffer** (`Core3.MissionManager.
PlayerBountyKillBuffer` config, compared against
`PlayerBounty::getLastBountyKill()`) blocks the same target from being
re-hunted again immediately after a previous bounty kill against them
resolved.

**Multiple bounty hunters can simultaneously hunt the same live
target, and it's a real race with automatic loser-resolution.**
`completePlayerBounty(targetId, bountyHunter)`
(`MissionManagerImplementation.cpp:2170-2209`) is called once, by
whichever hunter actually lands the kill. It iterates every *other*
hunter currently registered against that same `PlayerBounty`
(`bountyHunterIDs`) and calls `failPlayerBountyMission()` on each of
them automatically -- their mission objective fails
(`objective->fail()`), they get a `"failed"` system message, and (if
`Core3.MissionManager.PlayerBountyCooldown` is enabled) a fresh
per-hunter cooldown entry is recorded against that target so they can't
immediately re-accept. The **winning** hunter and every **failing**
hunter both get `ghost->schedulePvpTefRemovalTask()` called on their
behalf (line 2205, 2231) -- confirming a bounty-hunter kill is treated
as legitimate, sanctioned PvP for TEF purposes on both the successful
and unsuccessful sides of the race, not something that leaves stray PvP
flags lingering after the mission resolves either way.

**Payout has a hidden flat-rate override tied to a recurring "debuff
window," independent of the bounty's own posted reward amount.**
`getRealBountyReward(creo, bounty)`
(`MissionManagerImplementation.cpp:2321-2336`) checks whether the
target is currently within `playerBountyDebuffLength` milliseconds of
their last recorded `lastBountyDebuff` timestamp -- if so, the payout is
a **hardcoded flat reward** (50,000 credits if the target's
`getJediState() >= 4`, i.e. a fully-manifested/visible Jedi; 25,000
otherwise) **regardless of `bounty->getReward()`**. Outside that window,
the payout is whatever the bounty was actually posted for. This is the
concrete implementation of the classic "actively-hunted/revealed Jedi
pays a guaranteed bounty" mechanic -- `lastBountyDebuff` is refreshed
(`setLastBountyDebuff()`) both at kill-resolution time (if the previous
debuff window had already fully expired, line 2185-2188) and, per the
field's own gating role here, presumably by whatever periodic
Jedi-visibility/tracking-reveal process sets it during normal play
(that triggering process itself was outside this pass's scope to trace
further, but its *consumption* here -- flat 25k/50k payout during the
window -- is fully confirmed).

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any bounty-hunter-facing feature dealing
with payout amounts must account for the debuff-window flat-rate
override -- reading `bounty->getReward()` directly would silently
under/over-report the real payout during an active debuff window. (2) a
"who's currently hunting this player" query already exists ready-made
(`getHuntersHuntingTarget(targetId)`) rather than needing to scan
`playerBountyList` manually. (3) the multi-hunter race resolution (one
winner, everyone else auto-failed with their own cooldown) is the
established pattern for any other "multiple actors compete for one
outcome" mission design in this codebase, should one be wanted for a
non-bounty mission type. (4) TEF handling on both the winning and losing
sides is already automatic and doesn't need to be replicated by any
new bounty-adjacent feature -- `completePlayerBounty()`/
`failPlayerBountyMission()` are the two functions that already own
this.

---

## 45. Mail & Chat Channel Internals (extends section 19)

Section 19 already covers `ChatManager`'s ownership of mail/chat/rooms,
`PersistentMessage`'s structure, and the recipe for adding new mail/room
types. This section covers two mechanisms it didn't reach: offline-mail
reconciliation at login, and chat room entry-permission rules.

**Mail has two different storage locations depending on whether the
recipient was online at send time, reconciled into one list at
login.** `ChatManagerImplementation`'s mail-send lambda
(`ChatManagerImplementation.cpp:1941-1963`) always persists the
`PersistentMessage` (`ObjectManager::instance()->persistObject(mail, 1,
"mail")`, the dedicated `mail` BDB database from section 27's database
list) regardless of recipient state, then branches: **offline**
recipient -> the message ID is pushed onto a separate, own persistent
object, `PendingMessageList` (line 1945-1947, itself stored in the
equally dedicated `pendingmail` database, keyed by receiver object ID
via `getPendingMessages()`); **online** recipient -> the message ID goes
straight onto `ghost->addPersistentMessage(mail->getObjectID())` (the
`PlayerObject`'s own live mailbox list) and is delivered immediately
(`mail->sendTo(receiver, false)`). These are genuinely two different
lists, not the same storage viewed two ways. Reconciliation happens in
`PlayerObjectImplementation::checkPendingMessages()`
(`PlayerObjectImplementation.cpp:131-152`, called during login/object
setup): it reads every ID out of the player's `PendingMessageList`,
looks each `PersistentMessage` up by object ID via the object broker,
and for each one **re-checks the ignore list at delivery time** -- if
the player now has that sender ignored (even if they didn't when the
mail was originally sent while offline), the mail is silently
`destroyObjectFromDatabase()`-deleted instead of delivered
(line 142-145). Surviving messages get merged into the same
`persistentMessages` set the online-path uses, and the pending list is
cleared. **Practical implication: ignoring someone retroactively deletes
their unread offline mail to you at your next login** -- this is a real,
deliberate two-time-point ignore check (send time for online delivery,
login time for offline-accumulated mail), not a bug, but worth knowing
if "why did that mail disappear" ever comes up in support.

**Chat room entry permission is entirely hardcoded per `chatRoomType`,
and three of the six types have no explicit membership list at all.**
`ChatRoomImplementation::checkEnterPermission()`
(`ChatRoomImplementation.cpp:250-306`) switches on `roomType`:
`DEFAULT`/`AUCTION` always succeed for anyone; `GUILD` succeeds only if
the joining player's **current live guild** (`player->getGuildObject()`)
has an object ID matching the room's `ownerID` -- there is no separate
guild-chat membership list to maintain, membership is derived fresh from
the player's actual guild affiliation at join time; `GROUP` and
`PLANET` work identically against the player's current group/zone. Only
**`CUSTOM`** rooms use the explicit `banned`/`invited` list machinery
visible in `ChatRoom.idl` (`hasBanned()`/`hasInvited()`,
`getBannedSize()`/`getModeratorSize()`/etc.) -- and even there, **ban
always overrides invite**: `hasBanned(player)` is checked first and
short-circuits to a rejection regardless of invite status
(`INVALIDBANSTATE`, line 294-295), with private `CUSTOM` rooms further
requiring either an explicit invite or being the room's own owner
(line 296-297). A public `CUSTOM` room is open to anyone not banned.
Every rejection path returns a **distinct, documented error code**
(`NOROOM`/`INVALIDBANSTATE`/`NOTINVITED`/`FAIL`, enumerated in the
function's own header comment, line 251-257) that the client renders as
a specific message, rather than one generic "can't join" result.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) `GUILD`/`GROUP`/`PLANET` room access being
fully derived (not list-based) means leaving a guild/group or changing
zones instantly and correctly changes chat access with zero
list-maintenance code needed -- a genuinely elegant property to
preserve if this pattern is ever extended to a new derived-membership
room type (e.g. a city-chat room keyed off `CityRegion` membership would
follow the identical shape). (2) any new offline-notification system
modeled on mail should replicate the two-checkpoint ignore/permission
re-validation (at send AND at eventual delivery) rather than
checking eligibility only once at send time -- state can legitimately
change during the offline window. (3) a moderation feature (mute, kick
from a `CUSTOM` room) should be built on the existing
banned/invited/moderator list machinery already present on `ChatRoom`
rather than a new parallel structure -- the ban-overrides-invite
precedence is already established and should be preserved for
consistency. (4) `checkPendingMessages()`'s object-broker lookup pattern
(`Core::getObjectBroker()->lookUp(messageID)`) is a reusable idiom for
any other "list of deferred object IDs to resolve and process at some
later trigger point" feature.

---

## 46. Instance / Heroic Encounters -- Confirmed Absent

**No instance or heroic-encounter system exists anywhere in this
codebase.** A thorough search (`InstanceManager`, `HeroicManager`,
`Instance`, `isInstance()`, `InstanceType`, `heroic`/`Heroic`,
`privateZone`/`instancedZone`/`createInstance`/`cloneZone`) across both
`src/` and `bin/scripts/` (Lua content) turns up **zero real hits** --
the only "heroic" string matches anywhere are an unrelated furniture
item (`fountain_heroic.lua`, a decorative object) and a matching static
structure/schematic entry, plus a couple of incidental conversation-file
path matches. This is a hard gap in the same category as section 22's
"Collections -- confirmed absent," not a stub or partial
implementation to extend.

**There is no per-group/per-instance zone-cloning substrate at all.**
`Zone`/`ZoneServer` have no concept of a private or instanced copy of a
zone -- every zone is one single, permanently shared world space, which
is architecturally consistent with how this codebase treats zones
everywhere else in this guide (spawns, resource density maps, GCW bases,
guild halls -- all singular, shared, persistent world state, never
per-player or per-group copies). This matches original SWG's actual
1:1 design: "dungeons" in real SWG (Exar Kun's tomb, Axkva Min's lair,
the Death Watch Bunker, etc.) were always shared, non-instanced
world/building content that any number of unrelated groups could
simultaneously occupy and compete over -- not per-group instanced copies
in the modern MMO sense. If this server's content already includes
dungeon-style encounters, they're built entirely on the ordinary
shared-world tools already documented elsewhere in this guide: lair/mob
spawn groups (section 2), mission-terminal destroy/hunting missions
(section 16), and screenplay/quest scripting (section 3) -- not a
separate "instance" concept.

**Practical takeaway:** building true per-group instanced content (a
private copy of a zone/dungeon that only one group can enter, with its
own encounter state) would be substantial new engine work, not a
config change or a small extension -- it would need a new
zone-instantiation concept at the `ZoneServer` level (spinning up
isolated copies of a zone or a zone sub-region), group-to-instance
routing on zone transition, and instance lifecycle
management (creation on entry, cleanup on completion/timeout/last-member-leaves).
None of that scaffolding exists today. A "heroic-style tough encounter"
that doesn't require true instancing (i.e. a shared-world boss any group
can find and fight, SWG-authentic style) is achievable today with
existing tools -- a beefy `AiAgent` spawn via the normal lair/spawn-group
system, gated behind a mission or screenplay trigger -- but a genuinely
private, per-group instanced dungeon is not.

---

## 47. Observer / Event System Internals

This is the notification mechanism referenced by name in nearly every
prior section of this guide (`ObserverEventType::BADGEAWARDED`,
`SHIPDISABLED`, `FACTIONBASEFLIPPED`, `POSITIONCHANGED`, etc.) but never
itself explained -- this section is that missing piece.

**Any persistent object can be an event source (`Observable`) or a
listener (`Observer`), and both are real `ManagedObject`s, not
lightweight interfaces.** `Observable`
(`utils/engine3/.../engine/util/Observable.idl`) holds an
`ObserverEventMap` (a `HashTable<eventType, SortedVector<Observer*>>`)
and exposes `notifyObservers(eventType, arg1, arg2)`/
`registerObserver(eventType, observer)`/`dropObserver(...)`. `Observer`
(`Observer.idl`) is the matching listener base, with one method to
override: `notifyObserverEvent(eventType, observable, arg1, arg2)`.
Both extend `ManagedObject`, so observer registrations are real,
persistable, lockable object references, not a lightweight
callback-pointer system.

**The default `notifyObserverEvent()` implementation returns 1, and a
return value of 1 means "auto-unregister me" -- a real, easy-to-miss
gotcha.** `Observer.idl:21-23`'s base method just `return 1;`.
`ObserverEventMap::notifyObservers()`
(`ObserverEventMap.cpp:15-45`) calls each observer's
`notifyObserverEvent()` and, if the result is `1`, immediately calls
`dropObserver(eventType, observer)` for that pair (line 40-42) --
**any `Observer` subclass that forgets to override `notifyObserverEvent()`
silently self-unregisters after its very first notification**, since it
inherits the base class's `return 1`. This is the built-in mechanism for
legitimate "fire once, then stop listening" observers (return 1
deliberately), but it's also a real footgun for a new observer type
whose author intended persistent listening and simply forgot the
override.

**Notification snapshots the observer list under a read lock, then
releases the lock before invoking any callback.** `notifyObservers()`
copies the current eventType's observer list into a plain-pointer
`SortedVector<Observer*>` while holding `ReadLocker locker(&observerMutex)`
(line 16-31), releases the lock (line 33), and only then iterates the
snapshot calling each observer's callback (line 35-44). This means: (1)
an observer callback is free to register/drop other observers or fire
further notifications without deadlocking against the map's own lock,
and (2) an observer that unregisters itself mid-notification (the
return-1 mechanism above, or an explicit `dropObserver()` call inside
its own callback) can't corrupt the in-progress iteration, since the
iteration is already working off a stable copy.

**Notification cascades down a tree of child `Observable`s, not just
the object's own direct listener list.** `Observable::notifyObservers()`
(`Observable.idl:28-34`) fires the local `ObserverEventMap` **and then
recurses into every entry in `observableChildren`** with the identical
event/args -- `addObservableChild()`/`dropObserveableChild()` build this
parent-child propagation tree explicitly per object. A parent object
notifying an event automatically reaches every registered listener on
every one of its observable children too, without each child needing
its own separate trigger.

**Observer registrations hold real (strong) `ManagedReference`s, not
weak references.** `ObserverEventMap`'s underlying storage is
`SortedVector<ManagedReference<Observer*>>` -- a registered observer is
kept alive by the `Observable` it's registered on for as long as that
registration exists. Combined with the auto-unregister-on-return-1
convention above, this means a badly-behaved observer that neither
returns 1 nor is ever explicitly `dropObserver()`-ed is a real,
concrete object-lifetime leak (the observable holds a live strong
reference to it indefinitely) -- worth checking for on any custom
observer implementation that's supposed to be short-lived.

**`ObserverEventType` is an append-only, ordinal-value enum -- a
comment in the source says so explicitly, and it means something
concrete for persistence.** `templates/params/ObserverEventType.h:14-15`
carries an unambiguous warning comment: *"Adding Observers above the
crafting checks will cause the stored eventType on already crafted foods
to be improper -- Add new Observers to the bottom of the list."*
Because `eventType` is a bare enum ordinal (not a hashed string CRC like
most other identifier systems in this codebase, e.g. commands/opcodes/
skills), **the raw integer value gets persisted** in at least one real
case (crafted food items apparently store which event type they should
notify on) -- inserting a new constant anywhere except the very end of
the enum would silently renumber every subsequent constant and corrupt
any already-saved reference to one of them. Each entry also carries an
inline comment documenting its `arg1`/`arg2` payload contract (e.g.
`OBJECTDESTRUCTION` -- `arg1` = attacker, `arg2` = condition;
`POSTURECHANGED` -- `arg2` = new posture) -- **that comment block is the
closest thing to a canonical payload-contract reference for this event
system** and should be treated as authoritative when wiring a new
observer to an existing event type. At least one entry
(`SPECIALATTACK`) is explicitly annotated `// never notified?` in the
source itself -- a maintainer's own uncertainty about whether that event
type is dead, left in place rather than removed.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) `ObserverEventType` additions always go at
the bottom of the enum, never inserted mid-list -- this is not a style
preference, it's a real persistence-compatibility requirement per the
source's own comment. (2) any new `Observer` subclass meant to listen
indefinitely must explicitly override `notifyObserverEvent()` and return
something other than `1` (typically `0`) -- relying on the inherited
default is a guaranteed one-shot-then-silently-stops-working bug. (3) an
observer callback can safely register/notify/drop other observers
without special-casing reentrancy -- the lock-then-copy-then-release
pattern already handles it. (4) a new feature needing "notify all
related sub-objects when something happens to me" can use
`addObservableChild()` rather than manually re-broadcasting to each
child -- the propagation is already built in and automatic.

---

## 48. Task / Scheduling System Internals

This is the primitive underneath every self-rescheduling mechanism
already documented in this guide -- buffs (section 31), AI behavior
ticks (section 9), harvesters/factories (sections 40/42), the periodic
database save sweep (section 27) -- but never itself explained until
now.

**`Task` is a real priority-queue entry, not a simple timer callback.**
`Task extends PriorityQueueEntry, Runnable`
(`utils/engine3/.../engine/core/Task.h:30`) -- its `compareTo()`
(line 95-109) orders tasks by `nextExecutionTime`, meaning the
scheduler's pending-task structure is a genuine time-ordered priority
queue/heap, not a list that gets scanned. Two distinct scheduling
idioms both exist on the same class: `schedulePeriodic(delay, period)`
(a real built-in repeating-task primitive, `isPeriodic()` just checks
`period != 0`) versus the manual "call `reschedule()` again at the end
of my own `run()`" pattern -- **every self-rescheduling mechanism traced
in this guide so far (buffs, AI, harvesters, factories) uses the manual
pattern, not `schedulePeriodic()`**, likely because the manual approach
lets each reschedule computed a fresh, state-dependent delay (e.g. AI's
per-behavior-state interval, section 9) rather than a fixed period.

**The engine runs several structurally distinct thread pools, not one
generic pool.** `TaskManagerImpl`
(`utils/engine3/.../engine/core/TaskManagerImpl.h:24-137`) maintains:
plain **worker threads** organized into multiple **worker queues**
(`DEFAULT_WORKER_QUEUES` x `DEFAULT_WORKER_THREADS_PER_QUEUE`, selected
round-robin via an atomic counter) for immediate (`executeTask()`) work;
separate **scheduler threads** that own the time-ordered priority queue
and only hand a task to a worker once its `nextExecutionTime` arrives
(`scheduleTask()`/`rescheduleTask()`); a wholly separate pool of **IO
schedulers** (`scheduleIoTask()`/`scheduleInIoScheduler()`) specifically
for I/O-bound work, kept apart from the CPU-bound game-logic pool so
slow disk/DB operations can't starve tick processing; and an arbitrary
number of **named custom queues**
(`initializeCustomQueue(queueName, threadCount, blockDuringSaveEvent,
start)`, `Task::setCustomTaskQueue()`/`getCustomTaskQueue()`) -- this is
the real mechanism behind the `"slowQueue"` queue name already observed
in this guide's own mail-sending (section 45) and admin-command
(section 38) code, giving deliberately slow/blocking operation types
their own isolated thread(s) rather than competing with regular
game-tick tasks on the default pool.

**Custom queues can individually opt out of the periodic save-sweep
pause -- a real refinement to section 27's "save sweep blocks all
threads" finding.** `initializeCustomQueue()`'s `blockDuringSaveEvent`
parameter (default `true`) determines whether that specific named queue
is included in the pause/resume performed by `blockTaskManager()`/
`unblockTaskManager()` (the exact functions section 27 traced as
blocking all game-logic threads during the periodic database save
sweep). A queue created with `blockDuringSaveEvent = false` keeps
running through a save-sweep pause -- meaning **"blocks all
task-manager threads" is accurate for the default worker pool but is
not universally true of every queue in the system**; a custom queue
explicitly opted out is the one documented exception.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) a new repeating background process should
default to the manual self-reschedule pattern (matching every other
example in this codebase) unless a truly fixed-interval, no-per-cycle-
logic-needed repeat is wanted, in which case `schedulePeriodic()` is
the more direct primitive. (2) any new feature doing slow/blocking work
(network calls, heavy DB queries, anything that shouldn't share a
