thread with hot game-tick logic) should get its own named custom queue
via `initializeCustomQueue()` and tag its tasks with
`setCustomTaskQueue(name)`, following the `"slowQueue"` precedent,
rather than running on the default worker pool. (3) if that new custom
queue's work must never be paused by the periodic save sweep (e.g. it's
itself part of the save/backup pipeline, or handles something
latency-sensitive like network keepalives), pass
`blockDuringSaveEvent = false` at creation -- otherwise the default
`true` means it pauses right along with everything else. (4) `Task`
being a real object (not a bare function pointer/lambda-only construct)
is why so much of this codebase captures state directly as member
fields on custom `Task` subclasses (see `BuffDurationEvent`, section
31) rather than needing external context threading.

---

## 49. Config System Internals

This is the mechanism underneath every `Core::getIntProperty(...)`/
`ConfigManager::instance()->getBool(...)` call already referenced
throughout this guide (harvester/factory intervals, save-sweep timing,
staff levels, PvP mode, dozens more) -- never itself documented until
now.

**Config is real executed Lua, loaded from two layered files, not a
flat key=value parser.** `ConfigManager::loadConfigData()`
(`conf/ConfigManager.cpp:23-47`) runs `conf/config.lua` through a real
embedded `Lua` interpreter (the same `engine::lua::Lua` class documented
in section 29) -- a fatal, server-halting error if that file fails to
parse -- then, **if present**, additionally runs `conf/config-local.lua`
on top of it (non-fatal if missing, just logged). Because the local file
loads second, **any key it sets overrides the base `config.lua` value**
-- the standard "base config + optional local override" pattern, useful
to remember when a config edit doesn't seem to take effect (a stale/
forgotten `config-local.lua` entry is a common real-world cause).

**Nested Lua tables are flattened into dotted string keys in one flat
map, not kept as nested structure.** `parseConfigData(prefix, ...)`
(`ConfigManager.cpp:164+`) walks each Lua table recursively (max depth
5, `maxDepth` parameter), building dotted key paths like
`"Core3.MissionManager.IncludeFactionPets"` from the table nesting, and
storing each resolved leaf value as a `ConfigDataItem` in one flat
`VectorMap<String, ConfigDataItem*> configData`
(`ConfigManager.h:178`) -- every `getInt()`/`getBool()`/`getString()`/
etc. call is ultimately a lookup by that flattened dotted-string key,
regardless of how deeply nested the original Lua table was.

**Config supports live runtime mutation and hot-reload via the exact
same version-counter idiom already documented for Lua screenplay
reload (section 29) and staff permission tiers (section 38) -- this is
a real, recurring architectural pattern across unrelated subsystems,
not a one-off.** Every config change (`setInt`/`setBool`/`setString`/
`parseConfigJSON`, the latter presumably reachable via the REST port
exposed by `getRESTPort()`) calls `incrementConfigVersion()`
(`ConfigManager.h:194-196`, a plain `AtomicInteger` bump). **Dozens of
hot-path accessors** in `ConfigManager.h` (`getPvpMode()`,
`shouldUnloadContainers()`, `getMinLairSpawnInterval()`,
`useCovertOvertSystem()`, `isJtlEnabled()`, and many more) follow an
identical inline caching pattern: a local `static` cached value plus a
`static` cached version number, re-fetching from `configData` only when
`configVersion.get() > cachedVersion` -- config changes made at runtime
(via the JSON API) are picked up by these hot accessors on their very
next call, with no restart and minimal per-call lock overhead the rest
of the time. Several of these callers have their own inline comments
explicitly justifying the caching as a hot-path optimization (e.g.
`getPvpMode()`'s comment naming `CreatureObjectImplementation::
isAttackableBy()`/`isAggressiveTo()` as the reason it's cached).

**Every config lookup transparently supports a per-account override,
via one key-rewriting helper.** `withAccount(name, accountID)`
(`ConfigManager.h:198-207`) rewrites any lookup key into
`"Core3.AccountFlags.<accountID>.<name>"` whenever a nonzero
`accountID` is passed to `getInt`/`getBool`/`getString`/etc. (all of
which accept an optional `accountID` parameter, default 0/none) --
meaning **individual accounts can have config-value overrides** set
under this dotted namespace, checked ahead of (or instead of) the
global value, without any special-casing at each call site beyond
passing the account ID through. This is the concrete mechanism behind
any "flag this specific account for different behavior" admin
capability (e.g. a testing account with different limits).

**Every config value tracks its own read-count, and secrets are
redactable from dumps.** `ConfigDataItem::usageCounter`
(`ConfigManager.h:22, 36-54`) increments on every `getBool`/`getInt`/
`getString`/etc. call for that specific item -- exposed via
`getUsageCounter()`/`resetUsageCounter()` on `ConfigManager` itself, a
genuine introspection tool for confirming whether a given config key is
actually being consulted anywhere in a live server (a config key with a
usage count of zero after a full server run is either dead or gated
behind a code path that never executed). `dumpConfig(includeSecure)` and
`isSensitiveKey()` (`ConfigManager.cpp`, private) together mean a
config dump can redact secrets (DB passwords, `Core3.DBPass`/
`Core3.DBSecret`/etc.) by default, only including them if explicitly
requested -- worth knowing before ever sharing a raw config dump for
debugging purposes.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) `conf/config-local.lua` is the correct
place for environment-specific/local overrides that shouldn't be
committed alongside the base `config.lua` -- it's a first-class,
intentionally-supported second file, not a hack. (2) any new hot-path
config value (read many times per second, e.g. inside a per-tick loop
or a frequently-called combat/AI function) should follow the existing
static-cache-plus-version-check pattern rather than calling
`ConfigManager::getX()` directly every time -- there are ~15 existing
examples in `ConfigManager.h` to copy the idiom from. (3) a
per-account behavioral override (testing accounts, VIP/admin
exceptions) doesn't need bespoke code -- pass the account ID through to
the existing `getX(name, default, accountID)` overloads and set the
`Core3.AccountFlags.<id>.<name>` key. (4) `getUsageCounter()` is a ready-made
tool for auditing whether a config key is actually load-bearing before
removing or repurposing it -- worth reaching for instead of grepping
source for references, since it reflects genuine runtime consultation,
not just textual mentions.

---

## 50. ORB / Multi-Process Clustering

This extends the "root broker" concept briefly touched in section 27
(non-root brokers forwarding save data via `SendObjectDataMessage`
instead of writing to a local database) -- this section traces the
whole distributed-object architecture end to end and, critically,
confirms whether it's actually exercised by a typical deployment.

**Root-vs-remote status is decided by one config value at startup, not
a build-time or role-specific setting.** `ServerCore`'s init sequence
(`ServerCore.cpp:677-681`) calls `DistributedObjectBroker::initialize
(orbaddr, port)` where `orbaddr` comes straight from
`Core3.ORB` (`ConfigManager::getORBNamingDirectoryAddress()`, defaulting
to `""` -- an **empty string by default**). `initialize()`
(`DistributedObjectBroker.cpp:67-85`) branches on that address: empty ->
this process starts its own naming-directory service and becomes the
**root broker** (`rootObjectBroker` stays `nullptr` --
`isRootBroker()` is literally just `return rootObjectBroker == nullptr;`,
`DistributedObjectBroker.h:103-105`); non-empty -> it instead constructs
a `RemoteObjectBroker` pointed at that address/port and attaches as a
**client** of some other process's root broker. **Because the shipped
default is an empty address, a standard Core3 deployment is always a
single monolithic process acting as its own root broker** -- the
multi-process clustering capability is real and fully wired end-to-end
in the engine, but it's dormant/opt-in, not something an out-of-the-box
server setup exercises. This directly explains section 27's finding
that non-root brokers skip local database writes and forward save data
instead -- that code path exists and is correct, it's just unreachable
under the default single-process configuration.

**The distributed-object machinery follows the classic
Stub/Servant/Adapter pattern** (the same shape as CORBA/traditional RPC
frameworks): `DistributedObjectStub` is the client-facing proxy handle
any code actually interacts with; `DistributedObjectServant` is the
real local implementation when an object happens to live in this
process; `DistributedObjectAdapter` is the dispatch glue translating
method calls into either a direct local call or a network round-trip
depending on where the target object actually lives
(`DistributedObjectBroker.h:76-94`'s `deploy()`/`createObjectStub()`/
`createObjectServant()`/`getObjectAdapter()` family). `deployLocal()`/
`deployRemote()` and their `undeploy` counterparts (private, line
119-123) are the two concrete routing branches -- an object is
transparently deployed to either the local object graph or proxied to
wherever it really lives, and callers never need to know which.

**A well-known-port naming directory service is the discovery
mechanism a remote process uses to find the root.**
`NAMING_DIRECTORY_PORT = 44459` (`DistributedObjectBroker.h:57`) is the
fixed port `NamingDirectoryService` listens on; a non-root process's
`RemoteObjectBroker(address, port)` connects to the root's naming
service at that well-known port to resolve/register named distributed
objects. Remote object proxies are cached locally
(`remoteObjectCache`, a `HashTable<uint64, DistributedObject*>` wrapped
in a `DistributedObjectMap`, `DistributedObjectBroker.h:51`) so repeated
references to the same remote object don't require a fresh lookup
round-trip each time.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't assume any given `ManagedObject`
call in this codebase is guaranteed to be a same-process, in-memory
call -- the Stub/Adapter layer means it's *architecturally* capable of
being a network call, even though in the default single-process
deployment it always resolves locally. (2) if a Core3-based project
ever needed genuine horizontal scaling (splitting login/zone/database
responsibilities across separate machines), the ORB layer already
supports it via the `Core3.ORB`/`Core3.ORBPort` config pair -- this
would not require new distributed-object plumbing, just configuration
and operational setup. (3) `isRootBroker()` is the correct guard for any
new feature that should only run its "real" logic on the primary
process in a hypothetical clustered deployment (mirroring how database
persistence and the earlier-documented save-sweep already gate on it) --
default-configuration servers will always see this as `true`, so this
guard is a no-op safety net today, not something actively exercised.
(4) since the default deployment is single-process, most practical
debugging/extension work in this codebase can safely assume
same-process semantics for object references -- the multi-process path
is a real, correct, but currently-dormant capability, not the common
case to design around by default.

---

## 51. Medical / Healing Profession Internals

Traced end-to-end through `HealDamageCommand.h`, `HealWoundCommand.h`,
`CreatureObjectImplementation::healDamage/healWound/addWounds/
setWounds`, and `PlayerManagerImplementation::sendBattleFatigueMessage`.
This is a two-pool healing system (damage vs. wounds) with a shared
shock-wound ("battle fatigue") cap layered on top, plus its own
cooldown/queue mechanics separate from combat.

**Damage and wounds are two structurally distinct pools, healed by two
different item types and two different commands.** Every HAM attribute
(`hamList`) has a parallel `wounds` `DeltaVector<int>` -- wounds act as
a *ceiling reduction*, not direct damage: `maxHamValue = maxHamList -
wounds` (`setWounds()`, `CreatureObjectImplementation.cpp:1394`), so
wounding someone doesn't reduce their current pool by itself, it lowers
the maximum they can regenerate/heal back up to. `HealDamageCommand`
(stims, `StimPack`/`RangedStimPack`) restores the HAM pools themselves
via `healDamage()`, capped at `maxHamList - wounds`
(`CreatureObjectImplementation.cpp:1276`). `HealWoundCommand`
(`WoundPack`) instead reduces the `wounds` value via `healWound()`,
which raises the *ceiling* back up rather than restoring current HP --
functionally these are "heal the damage" vs. "heal the cap that limits
how much damage-healing/regen can achieve." A character can be at full
current HAM but still capped well below their true max if they're
carrying heavy wounds.

**Battle fatigue is literally `shockWounds`, a single float capped at
[0, 1000], incremented by one point per wound-causing hit and displayed
to players in three tiers.** `addWounds()`
(`CreatureObjectImplementation.cpp:1403-1442`) calls `addShockWounds(1,
true)` every time it actually applies wounds (the `doShockWounds`
parameter most callers leave `true` -- `VehicleObject.idl:135`'s stub
shows the same signature exists for vehicles too, though vehicles no-op
it). `PlayerManagerImplementation::sendBattleFatigueMessage()`
(`PlayerManagerImplementation.cpp:3266-3286`) reads `getShockWounds()`
and sends one of three tiered chat-table messages
(`shock_effect_low/medium/high`, thresholds 250/500/750 out of the
1000 cap) -- to the healer if self-healing, to the target if healing
someone else. Every heal command (`HealDamageCommand`,
`HealWoundCommand`, and by extension the other Heal*Command variants)
calls this after a successful heal, so shock-wound tier feedback is a
side effect bolted onto the heal commands rather than a standalone
system with its own tick/command.

**Both heal commands share a nearly identical validation and
self-cooldown shape, and that cooldown is a `PendingTask`, not a real
timer field.** `canTreatInjuries()`/`canTreatWounds()`
(`CreatureObject.idl:1343-1354`) are just `!getPendingTask
("injuryTreatment")` / `!getPendingTask("woundTreatment")` --
after each successful heal, `deactivateInjuryTreatment()` /
`deactivateWoundTreatment()` schedule an `InjuryTreatmentTask` under
that named pending-task key with a skill-scaled delay (`20 -
modSkill/5` seconds for damage, floored at 4s; `20 - modSkill*2/25`
seconds for wounds, floored at 3s -- `HealDamageCommand.h:30-56`,
`HealWoundCommand.h:28-49`), further modified by an active
`FOOD_HEAL_RECOVERY` buff's percentage. This is the same named-
pending-task idiom used elsewhere in the engine for other per-action
cooldowns -- there's no separate "medic cooldown manager," it's just
the generic task-queue slot mechanism reused.

**Wound healing additionally requires a qualifying location, which is
a skill-mod check, not a zone-flag or building-type check.**
`canPerformSkill()` in `HealWoundCommand.h:114-128` checks
`getSkillMod("private_medical_rating") -
getSkillModOfType("private_medical_rating", SkillModManager::CITY) >
0` -- i.e., city-granted medical rating alone doesn't count, only
non-city sources (hospitals, campsites, surgical droids) qualify --
and if standing inside a player structure specifically, requires the
`STRUCTURE`-sourced medical rating bonus be present too (so a random
player house doesn't count as a hospital even if it happens to sit in
a high-medical-rating city). Stim-based damage healing has no such
location gate; only wound healing (the "surgery"-flavored tier) does.
In-combat wound healing is blocked outright for both healer and target
(`HealWoundCommand.h:130-138`) -- stims work in combat, wound packs
don't.

**PvP/faction eligibility for being healed funnels through one shared
predicate, `isHealableBy()`, reused by both commands and (per its
`isPet()` branch) transparently delegated from a pet to its owner.**
`CreatureObjectImplementation::isHealableBy()`
(`CreatureObjectImplementation.cpp:3827+`) short-circuits true for
self-heals, false if invisible or if the target `isAttackableBy()` the
healer (can't "heal" something you could currently attack -- prevents
using heal commands as a targeting/line-of-sight probe against
enemies), same-group-in-PvP-area override, a Bounty Hunter TEF block
(`hasBhTef()`), and a link-dead-same-account gate controlled by
`Core3.CombatManager.AllowSameAccountLinkDeadBeneficialActions`
(default true) -- so by default you can still buff/heal your own
link-dead alt/main, and an operator would need to explicitly flip this
off to prevent it, which ties into the broader anti-multibox/anti-
exploit posture documented in section 39.

**Both commands support area-effect variants gated purely by the
pharmaceutical item, not a separate command/skill branch.**
`HealDamageCommand::handleArea()` fires whenever `stimPack->isArea()`
is true, iterating `getCloseObjects()` and re-running the same
`checkTarget()`/`isHealableBy()` gates per nearby ally
(`HealDamageCommand.h:260-372`) -- area stims are just stims with an
`isArea()` flag, the targeting/eligibility logic doesn't fork for
them. XP awards (`awardXp()`, both files) explicitly exclude
self-heals and pet-heals, feeding the `"medical"` XP type at `0.25x`
healed-damage for stims and `2.5x` healed-wounds for wound packs --
wound healing is intentionally weighted ~10x more XP-dense per point
than damage healing, presumably because wound pools regenerate far
slower/rarer than raw HAM damage.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) if building a custom heal-related add-on
(a new stim type, a healer companion ability, etc.), the two-pool
split matters -- "heal 50 health" and "heal 50 health wounds" are
different calls (`healDamage()` vs `healWound()`) with different
observer events (`HEALINGRECEIVED` vs `WOUNDHEALINGRECEIVED`) and
different XP weighting, not interchangeable. (2) `shockWounds` is a
single shared float per creature (not per-attribute), so any new
wound-dealing mechanic automatically feeds the same battle-fatigue
tier messaging without extra wiring -- just call `addWounds()` with
`doShockWounds=true` (the default) rather than manually touching
`shockWounds`. (3) the cooldown-via-named-`PendingTask` pattern
(`"injuryTreatment"`/`"woundTreatment"`) is worth reusing verbatim for
any new per-action-with-cooldown ability, rather than inventing a new
timer field on the creature object. (4) `isHealableBy()` is the single
correct gate to call before any new beneficial/healing action against
another creature -- it already encodes the pet-delegates-to-owner,
BH-TEF, invisibility, and attackability rules that section 39's
anti-exploit and section 16/44's bounty-hunter sections separately
document; don't reimplement PvP-heal eligibility checks by hand.

---

## 52. Beast Mastery / Creature Taming

Traced through `TameCommand.h`, `CreatureManagerImplementation::tame()`,
`TameCreatureTask.h`, `CreatureImplementation::canTameMe()/
getChanceToTame()`, and vitality handling in
`PetControlDeviceImplementation.cpp`/`PetManagerImplementation.cpp`.
This is the "creature handler" profession's core loop -- distinct from,
but structurally parallel to, the droid-engineering (section 33) and
companion (this project's own system) pet mechanics, since all three
ultimately converge on the same `PetControlDevice` abstraction.

**Only baby creatures can be tamed at all, and taming is a three-phase,
self-rescheduling `Task`, not a single roll.**
`CreatureImplementation::canTameMe()`
(`CreatureImplementation.cpp:311-319`) hard-gates on `isBaby()` --
adult wild creatures are simply untameable through the normal flow
(an admin-only `force`+`adult` override exists in `TameCommand.h:59-64`,
gated on `ghost->hasAbility("admin")`, that skips straight to success
and can tame/spawn an adult directly -- a GM/testing tool, not a player
path). A real attempt runs `TameCreatureTask`
(`TameCreatureTask.h`) through three phases (`INITIAL` ->
`SECOND` -> `FINAL`), each holding the player in place via the
`"tame_pet"` named `PendingTask` slot (the same reusable cooldown/
in-progress idiom documented in section 51 for healing) and
rebroadcasting a taming emote/chat line every 10 seconds; only on the
third tick does the actual success roll happen. Moving out of range or
losing eligibility (`canTameMe()`/`isInRange()`) at any phase boundary
cancels the attempt and restores the creature's AI state via
`resetStatus()`.

**The tame-chance formula is a flat comparison against a d100, not a
capped percentage, and skill choice matters based on the target's
aggression flag.** `getChanceToTame()`
(`CreatureImplementation.cpp:321-335`): `chance = (getTame() * 100) +
skillBonus - (creatureLevel + ferocity)`, where `skillBonus` is
`tame_aggro` if the target `isVicious()` (aggressive per its template's
`ObjectFlag::AGGRESSIVE` bit) or `tame_non_aggro` otherwise, plus a
flat `tame_bonus` skill mod always applied. The roll itself
(`TameCreatureTask.h:83-85`) is simply `tamingChance >
System::random(100)` -- since `tamingChance` isn't clamped to
[0,100] before the comparison, a sufically high skill/template
combination can exceed 100 and become an unconditional success (and,
symmetrically, a very tough creature relative to skill can go negative
and become unconditional failure). The object-menu radial option for
"Tame" is itself gated on `getChanceToTame(player) >= 15`
(`CreatureImplementation.cpp:47`), so a creature under ~15% odds
doesn't even offer the option client-side.

**Failing a tame attempt has a real combat consequence: a chance to
aggro the creature onto the player, scaled inversely by the creature's
ferocity.** On failure (`TameCreatureTask.h:87-102`), `aggroChance =
random(20 - ferocity)`; if that rolls exactly `0`, the creature
(if an `AiAgent`) immediately `addDefender(player)`s, turning what was
a passive taming interaction into a fight. Higher-ferocity creatures
have a smaller random range and thus a proportionally higher chance of
that `0` landing -- ferocity makes failed attempts both less likely to
succeed *and* more dangerous when they don't.

**Success converts the wild `Creature`/`AiAgent` into a pet through the
exact same `PetControlDevice` mechanism used by droids (section 33) and
mounts/vehicles -- there is one unified pet-control abstraction across
all pet-like systems in this engine, not three separate ones.**
`TameCreatureTask::success()` (`TameCreatureTask.h:111-243`) creates a
`PetControlDevice` (`petType = CREATUREPET`), transfers it into the
player's datapad, calls `objectManager->persistSceneObjectsRecursively()`
to establish DB persistence for the creature and its new device, then
rewires the live `AiAgent`: `setCreatureLink(player)` (the same
`linkedCreature` accessor pattern noted for companions/vehicles in
earlier sections), faction/PvP-status inherited from the owner,
`ObjectFlag::PET` bitmask, home location pinned to the player's current
position, and `FOLLOWING` movement state. XP is awarded under the
`"creaturehandler"` type, scaled `20 * creatureLevel`. A pet acquired
this way starts at `growthStage = 1` (babies grow up over time via
`PetControlDevice::growPet()`, unless the admin `adult` override forces
full growth immediately via `growPet(player, true, true)`).

**Pets have a "vitality" stat that acts as a wear-and-tear meter,
degrading specifically from combat losses against wild NPCs (not
players or other pets), gated by its own cooldown -- structurally the
same idea as droid `PAINTCHARGES` decay (section 33) but event-driven
rather than time-driven.** `PetManagerImplementation.cpp:619-623`: when
a pet is incapacitated/killed and the attacker is a non-player,
non-pet NPC, vitality drops by `2`, but only if a `"vitalityLossCooldown"`
entry on the pet's `CooldownTimerMap` has expired (reset to a 5-minute
/ 300000ms window each time it fires) -- so a pet being repeatedly
downed in a short window only loses vitality once per 5 minutes, not
once per death. `PetControlDeviceImplementation::setVitality()`
(`PetControlDeviceImplementation.cpp:1395-1452`) floors vitality at 1
(pets can never vitality-lock to zero) and applies tiered HAM-pool
penalties as it drops: `25%` penalty below 75 vitality, `50%` below 50,
`75%` below 25 -- computed against the pet's own `getBaseHAM()` and
applied as async lambda-task adjustments (via
`Core::getTaskManager()->executeTask(...)`, the same generic
task-execution idiom from section 48) rather than inline, presumably to
avoid locking issues when this fires from deep inside a kill-resolution
call stack. The same `setVitality()` code path and penalty tiers apply
identically to `DROIDPET` (`petType != CREATUREPET && petType !=
DROIDPET` is the early-return guard), confirming vitality is a shared
pet-quality mechanic across both creature and droid pets, restored via
consumable `VitalityPack` items (bio-engineer-crafted, sets vitality
back to `getMaxVitality()`) or reset to full on initial creation/
re-deed (`PetDeedImplementation.cpp`/`DroidDeedImplementation.cpp`
both call `setVitality(100)` on spawn).

**Companion pets reimplement this exact same vitality/penalty concept
independently rather than sharing `PetControlDevice`'s
implementation** -- `CompanionObjectImplementation.cpp` and
`CompanionControlDeviceImplementation.cpp` both define their own
`setVitality()` with their own persistence-fix commentary, rather than
routing through `PetControlDevice`. This is a direct, concrete
precedent worth remembering for companion-system work specifically:
the vitality *concept* (tiered HAM penalty, floor at 1, restore-to-max
on certain actions) is shared engine-wide, but the companion system's
copy is its own independent implementation, not a subclass/reuse of
`PetControlDeviceImplementation`'s version -- so a bug fix or behavior
change made to one will not automatically apply to the other.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any custom taming-adjacent mechanic (a new
tameable creature category, a custom taming item, etc.) should reuse
`getChanceToTame()`'s formula shape and the three-phase `TameCreatureTask`
scaffold rather than inventing a new roll -- the aggro-on-fail and
range/eligibility-recheck-per-phase behaviors are load-bearing parts of
the existing player experience. (2) the tame-chance formula is
deliberately uncapped past 100/below 0 -- if extending it (e.g. new
skill mods), be aware a sufficiently lopsided formula produces
guaranteed outcomes rather than a soft ceiling. (3) `PetControlDevice`
is the single real "pet" abstraction for creature and droid pets alike
-- new pet-like features should extend it rather than parallel-
implementing, unlike how the companion system currently does for
vitality specifically (a known, accepted divergence, not an oversight
to silently "fix" without checking why it was split out). (4) the
vitality-loss-only-from-wild-NPC-kills-with-a-cooldown rule means
a custom PvP-focused pet feature won't naturally interact with vitality
decay at all under the existing rules -- that's specific to PvE combat
losses.

---

## 53. Death, Cloning & Item Insurance

Traced through `PlayerManagerImplementation`'s cloning flow
(`promptCloneSelection`/`sendPlayerToCloner`/`isValidClosestCloner`/
`getInsurableItems`) plus the `INSURED` `OptionBitmask` flag. This is
the classic SWG "death penalty" package: pick a cloner, get teleported
there half-wounded, and take an item-condition decay hit scaled by
whether you bothered to insure your gear.

**Death presents a SUI list of up to three cloner choices -- nearest,
pre-designated ("bound"), and any faction/Force-gated special
facilities the player qualifies for -- built fresh on every death, not
cached.** `promptCloneSelection()`
(`PlayerManagerImplementation.cpp:~1580-1713`) scans every
`"cloningfacility"` planetary object within a `16000` unit search
radius for the nearest valid option (`isValidClosestCloner()` excludes
city-banned players and faction-locked/Jedi-only facilities), separately
resolves the player's `ghost->getCloningFacility()` bound facility (only
offered if it's on the *same zone* -- an off-planet bind shows as
"off-planet (unavailable)" rather than being silently dropped from the
list), and appends Force Shrine / Jedi Enclave entries gated on
`force_title_jedi_rank_01` / FRS light-or-dark novice ranks respectively
(the latter additionally requires `FrsManager::isFrsEnabled()`, so
Jedi Enclave cloning as an option can be globally toggled off per
server). **Death in a space zone redirects the whole cloning flow back
to the player's ground `getSpaceLaunchZone()`/`getSpaceLaunchLocation()`**
-- there is no space-based cloning facility; dying in space always
resolves through your ground clone options.

**Arriving at the cloner always applies a partial wound/shock penalty
unless you cloned at your specifically pre-designated (bound)
facility.** `sendPlayerToCloner()`
(`PlayerManagerImplementation.cpp:1739-1908`): after the zone switch,
if `preDesignatedFacility == nullptr || preDesignatedFacility != cloner`
(i.e., you cloned at the nearest/a special facility rather than your
bound one), the player takes a flat `100` wounds to Health, Action, and
Mind (`addWounds(..., false)` -- `notifyClient=false`... actually
`doShockWounds=false` per the 4th param, since shock is handled
separately right after) plus `100` shock wounds directly via
`addShockWounds(100, true)`. Cloning at your bound facility skips this
penalty entirely -- **binding at a cloner is a real, mechanically
meaningful choice**, not just a spawn-point preference: it's the
difference between reviving healthy-ish and reviving badly wounded.

**Faction status can auto-downgrade on clone depending on the
covert/overt config toggle, and this is one of only a few places that
branches on `Core3.PlayerManager` config vs. the covert/overt system
flag documented in section 49's config coverage.** If
`ConfigManager::useCovertOvertSystem()` is on, an `OVERT`-status
non-Jedi player cloning somewhere other than their own faction's
dedicated facility gets flipped to `COVERT`; if that system is off, the
equivalent rule instead sets `ONLEAVE` status for non-Jedi-master
players. Either branch is skipped entirely for players cloning at their
own faction's dedicated Imperial/Rebel facility -- cloning "at home" 
never triggers a faction-status change.

**Item condition decay on death is real, config-driven only for the
"wipe food/drink filling" side effect, and insurance halves the decay
rate rather than preventing it -- and consumes the insurance in the
process.** Decay only fires for `typeofdeath == 0` (a plain PvE/normal
death; other death-type codes skip the decay report entirely -- worth
tracing further if a custom death-type is ever added, since decay
isn't automatically applied to every death path). For each item
returned by `getInsurableItems()`: insured items
(`OptionBitmask::INSURED` set) take `1%` of `getMaxCondition()` as
condition damage and then have the `INSURED` bit stripped --
**insurance is single-use per death, not a standing protection** --
while uninsured items take `5%` instead and keep whatever bitmask they
had. A SUI "DECAY REPORT" itemizes every affected item's resulting
condition percentage. Separately, `Core3.PlayerManager.
WipeFillingOnClone` (default `false`) can wipe food/drink filling to
zero on clone, an opt-in hunger-reset penalty most default configs
don't enable.

**Insurance eligibility itself is a specific, narrow item-type filter,
not "everything you're wearing."** `getInsurableItems()`
(`PlayerManagerImplementation.cpp:4331-4365`) walks every top-level
slotted container except datapad/bank/default-weapon (recursing into
each via `addInsurableItemsRecursive()`), and only actually queues an
item if it `isArmorObject() || isWearableObject()` **and** passes
`isInsurable()` **and** doesn't have an anti-decay kit applied, isn't a
Jedi robe, and isn't a Union ring (`item->hasAntiDecayKit() ||
isJediRobe() || isUnionRing() || !isInsurable()` are all hard excludes,
`:4351`). Notably weapons in the default weapon slot and anything in
the bank/datapad are structurally exempt from decay by virtue of never
being scanned at all -- there's no separate "protect my weapon" flag to
manage, the slot itself is safe. The `onlyInsurable` parameter flips the
function between "give me currently-uninsured-and-eligible items" (used
by whatever UI lets a player pay to insure gear) and "give me everything
insurable regardless of current insured state" (used by the decay pass,
since decayed items need to be found whether insured or not).

**Jedi characters additionally take a direct experience penalty on
clone, independent of the item-decay system entirely.** If
`ghost->getJediState() >= 2`, the player loses `5%` of their
`jedi_general` XP cap (`awardExperience(player, "jedi_general",
negativeAmount, true)`), floored at a hardcoded `-10000000` total
negative XP so repeated deaths can't XP-bomb a Jedi into an
arbitrarily deep negative hole. This is a distinct, Jedi-specific death
penalty layered on top of the universal wound/decay penalties everyone
takes.

**A `PLAYERCLONED` observer event fires at the end of the flow, making
this hookable without touching the cloning code itself**
(`player->notifyObservers(ObserverEventType::PLAYERCLONED, player, 0)`,
`:1888`) -- the same `Observable`/`Observer` system documented in
section 47. Recovery from the incapacitated/dead state is handled by a
short (`3` second) `PlayerIncapacitationRecoverTask`, not inline in
this function.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any custom death-penalty or death-related
add-on should hook `ObserverEventType::PLAYERCLONED` rather than
patching `sendPlayerToCloner()` directly -- the event already fires at
exactly the right point with the player reference available. (2) the
single-use nature of the `INSURED` bit means any custom item-insurance
UI/mechanic must re-set the bit after each decay event if "always
insured" behavior is desired -- the engine's default behavior is
insure-once-consume-once, not a persistent flag. (3) `typeofdeath == 0`
gating the decay pass is a loose thread worth checking before adding
new death types -- a custom death path that doesn't route through
`typeofdeath == 0` will silently skip item decay and the Jedi XP
penalty both, which may or may not be the intended behavior. (4) the
bound-vs-nearest distinction is the main lever for "how bad does dying
feel" -- a custom QoL feature that always auto-selects the nearest
cloner would inadvertently make every death carry the wound/shock
penalty that binding is specifically meant to let players avoid.

---

## 54. Structure Maintenance, Decay & Condemnation

Traced through `StructureMaintenanceTask::run()`,
`StructureObjectImplementation::isDecayed()/getDecayPercentage()/
scheduleMaintenanceExpirationEvent()`, and `StructureManager`'s
condemn/pay/withdraw SUI flows. This extends section 37's housing-
decoration/permissions coverage with the actual upkeep economy that
determines whether a structure survives at all -- and it turns out
buildings and non-building structures (harvesters, factories, turrets)
are treated meaningfully differently at the point of destruction.

**Maintenance is a self-rescheduling `Task` (the same generic pattern
documented in section 48), and its very first move on firing is a
sanity re-check, not the decay logic itself.** `StructureMaintenanceTask
::run()` (`StructureMaintenanceTask.cpp:22-143`) is only meant to fire
once `getSurplusMaintenance()` has actually reached `<= 0` -- if it
somehow fires early with positive surplus still remaining (a scheduling
race), it just calls `scheduleMaintenanceExpirationEvent()` again and
returns, rather than assuming its own timing is correct. It also
defensively re-checks `isServerLoading()` (deferring a further second
if the zone server itself is still coming up) and requires a valid
`CreditObject` and non-empty owner name, immediately destroying the
structure with a logged reason if either is missing -- an orphaned
structure with no resolvable owner is treated as unconditionally
destroy-eligible, not something to leave dangling.

**Once truly out of maintenance, the task first tries an automatic
bank withdrawal covering a full week up front, and only starts the
decay clock if that fails.** The task computes `oneWeekMaintenance =
7*24*maintenanceRate - surplusMaintenance` (plus city property tax
folded in for buildings in a city region, plus whatever negative
surplus/"uncondemn cost" already exists), and if the owner's
`CreditObject` bank balance covers that amount, it silently withdraws
it via `strongRef->payMaintenance(oneWeekMaintenance, creditObj,
false)`, emails the owner a "withdrawn from bank" notice
(`sendMailMaintenanceWithdrawnFromBank`), and reschedules a week out --
**structures don't actually start decaying the instant maintenance
hits zero if the owner has sufficient bank funds; the engine
auto-drafts from the bank first.** This is gated by
`Core3.StructureMaintenanceTask.AllowBankPayments` (default `true`,
checked in `StructureManager::payMaintenance()`,
`:1376-1377`) -- an operator can disable bank auto-draft entirely,
forcing players to keep maintenance topped up manually or decay
immediately once the pool is empty.

**Decay itself runs on a real wall-clock daily cycle (with a
build-time debug override), and "decayed" is a binary state derived
from a condition-percentage calculation, not a separate flag.**
When the bank-draft fails or is disabled, the task reschedules itself
every `24*60*60` seconds (a `#if DEBUG_STRUCTURE_RAPID_DECAY` build flag
compresses this to `15` seconds for testing) as long as
`!strongRef->isDecayed()`, emailing a decay-warning notice each cycle
(`sendMailDecay()`, using a different message body for buildings --
"will be condemned" -- vs. non-buildings -- "will be destroyed").
`isDecayed()` is simply `getDecayPercentage() == 0`
(`StructureObjectImplementation.cpp:629-631`), and
`getDecayPercentage()` (`:633+`) computes `(maxCondition -
conditionDamage) * 100 / maxCondition`, rounded up and clamped to
[0,100] -- so "decayed" specifically means the structure's tracked
condition damage has already reached its max condition, a state that
must be driven up by some other mechanism (out-of-maintenance decay
presumably inflicts condition damage over time elsewhere in the
codebase, consistent with how insured/uninsured item decay in section
53 works via direct `inflictDamage()` calls against `getMaxCondition()`).

**Buildings get a condemnation grace period with a configurable
back-maintenance threshold before actual destruction; non-building
structures (harvesters, factories, turrets, etc.) do not -- they are
destroyed immediately on first reaching the decayed state.** Once
`isDecayed()` is true, the task branches on `strongRef->isBuildingObject
() && !shouldBuildingBeDestroyed(strongRef)`
(`:125`): if true, the building is merely **condemned** (a mail
notice, a sign-name update via `building->updateSignName(true)`, and
another daily reschedule -- the building keeps existing, just
inaccessible, until either paid off or the destroy threshold is
crossed), but if false (either it's not a `BuildingObject` at all, or
`shouldBuildingBeDestroyed()` says it's been decayed for too long), the
structure is destroyed outright via `destroyStructureWithReason()`.
`shouldBuildingBeDestroyed()` (`:268-283`) computes `maxBackMaintenance
= delayDestroyHours * maintenanceRate` (per-structure-type configurable
via `getDelayDestroyHours()`) and returns `true` (destroy) only once
`maxBackMaintenance + surplusMaintenance <= 0` -- i.e., the negative
maintenance balance has grown deep enough, scaled by how many hours of
grace the structure type is configured for. **The practical asymmetry:
a player house can sit condemned indefinitely (as long as its negative
balance doesn't exceed the delay-destroy threshold) and be recovered by
paying the uncondemn cost, but a harvester or factory has no such
grace -- it's gone the moment it decays.**

**Condemned buildings are recovered via a dedicated SUI flow that
computes the exact payoff cost from the negative maintenance balance,
not a flat fee.** `StructureManager::promptPayUncondemnMaintenance()`
(`StructureManager.cpp:1149-1198`) computes `uncondemnCost =
-structure->getSurplusMaintenance()` (i.e., exactly enough to bring the
pool back to zero) and shows one of two SUI messages depending on
whether the owner's bank balance covers it -- if it does, a confirm
dialog offers to auto-deduct and uncondemn; if not, the player is told
they lack sufficient funds and must add more before returning. This is
a separate, player-initiated recovery path distinct from the
automatic-bank-draft-on-maintenance-task-tick behavior described above
-- a condemned building specifically needs the owner to manually
uncondemn it even if they later have sufficient bank funds, rather than
being auto-recovered on the next maintenance tick.

**Destruction always exports a `TransactionLog` synchronously before
the structure object is actually torn down, and building destruction
explicitly destroys everything stored inside it.**
`destroyStructureWithReason()` (`StructureMaintenanceTask.cpp:145-160`)
wraps the destroy call in a `TrxCode::DESTROYSTRUCTURE` transaction log
entry with the human-readable reason attached and forces a synchronous
export (`trx.exportRelated()`) specifically because, per the code
comment, "the objects will be deleted before we can export them" --
this is a real ordering constraint, not stylistic: transaction logging
for a doomed object must happen *before* deletion, unlike most other
transaction logging in the codebase which can presumably happen
after-the-fact against a still-live object. The destroy email
(`sendMailDestroy()`) explicitly warns "All items in the building were
also destroyed" for building-type structures -- contents are not
auto-ejected or auto-mailed back to the owner on structure destruction,
they're simply gone along with the building. A
`#if DEBUG_STRUCTURE_TASK_NO_DESTROY` build flag exists to no-op the
actual destroy call for testing while still logging what *would* have
happened.

**Civic and zero-maintenance-rate structures are explicitly exempted
from the entire expiration system, with a self-checking error log if
that exemption looks suspicious.** `scheduleMaintenanceExpirationEvent()`
(`StructureObjectImplementation.cpp:363-373`) returns immediately if
`getMaintenanceRate() <= 0`, but first checks: if the structure has no
owner, that's expected and it silently returns; otherwise, if it's
*also* not in a city region and not a turret/minefield/scanner, it logs
an `error()` -- a maintenance-free, unowned-by-a-city, non-military
structure is flagged as a likely misconfiguration rather than silently
accepted. `updateStructureStatus()` similarly early-returns for
`isCivicStructure()` structures (city halls, etc.) with the same
not-in-a-city sanity check. This means player-placed turrets/minefields/
scanners (GCW base defenses, tying back to section 35's siege coverage)
are architecturally exempt from the normal maintenance-decay-condemn
cycle entirely, not merely configured with a very low decay rate.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any custom structure type should decide
early whether it wants building-style condemnation-with-grace-period
behavior or immediate-destroy-on-decay behavior -- that fork is purely
`isBuildingObject()`, so a custom non-`BuildingObject` structure that
still wants a grace period would need its own explicit handling, it
won't get one automatically. (2) `Core3.StructureMaintenanceTask.
AllowBankPayments` is the single global switch between "structures
mostly take care of themselves as long as the owner has bank credits"
and "owners must actively manage maintenance pools" -- worth checking
before assuming either behavior when reasoning about a live server's
actual structure-loss rate. (3) the synchronous-export-before-delete
pattern in `destroyStructureWithReason()` is the correct model to copy
for any other "this object is about to be deleted, not just modified"
logging need -- exporting after the fact would capture a
already-deleted object. (4) structure content is not preserved through
destruction -- any custom feature that destroys a structure
programmatically (rather than through this natural decay path) should
consider whether it needs to explicitly rescue/mail contents first,
since the engine's own destroy path does not.

---

## 55. SkillMod Aggregation Pipeline (`SkillModManager`)

Traced through `SkillModManager.h`/`.cpp`,
`server/zone/objects/creature/variables/SkillModList.h`, and
`CreatureObjectImplementation::addSkillMod()/getSkillMod()`. This is
the answer to "how does a number like `getSkillMod("healing_ability")`
actually get computed" -- a question that matters far beyond
healing, since nearly every profession/combat/crafting formula
documented elsewhere in this guide reads its inputs through
`getSkillMod()`. It's also directly relevant to this project's own
open backlog item (companion `grantSkill()` not calling
`addSkillMod()`), since this section explains exactly why that gap
means learned companion skills don't yet affect anything mechanically.

**Every stat bonus is stored twice: once bucketed by *source type*, and
once as a live cached total -- and the source-type bucketing is the
part that makes multi-source stacking correct instead of an
overwrite.** `SkillModList` (`SkillModList.h:35-37`) holds `VectorMap<uint32
sourceType, SkillModGroup>`, where each `SkillModGroup` is itself a
`VectorMap<String skillModName, int value>` -- so `"healing_ability"`
might simultaneously have an entry under `SKILLBOX` (from a learned
skill box), `WEARABLE` (worn gear), `BUFF` (a temporary buff), `CITY`,
`STRUCTURE`, and `DROID` all at once, each tracked completely
independently. `SkillModManager.h:43-58` enumerates the fixed source
types in three tiers -- `PERMANENTMOD` (`TEMPLATE`, `SKILLBOX`),
`BONUSMOD` (`WEARABLE`, `STRUCTURE`, `CITY`, `DROID`), and
`TEMPORARYMOD` (`BUFF`, `ABILITYBONUS`) -- and `getSkillMod()`
(`SkillModList.h:146-171`) sums across *every* source-type bucket that
has an entry for that mod name, applying each source type's own
min/max clamp (`SkillModManager::getMinSkill()/getMaxSkill()`)
independently before summing. **This is why removing one source
(unequip an item, lose a buff) never accidentally wipes bonuses from
an unrelated source** -- each bucket is edited in isolation via
`add()`'s per-bucket delta arithmetic (`SkillModList.h:78-94`).

**Nothing is derived lazily from `skillList`/worn-items/active-buffs at
read time -- `getSkillMod()` only ever reads the pre-computed
`skillModList` cache. Every system that grants a bonus is individually
responsible for calling `addSkillMod()`/`removeSkillMod()` to push the
change into that cache, and a "verify" reconciliation pass exists
*per source type* to self-heal drift.** `CreatureObjectImplementation
::addSkillMod()` (`CreatureObjectImplementation.cpp:1647-1683`) is the
one real mutator: it updates the type-bucketed `skillModList`, then
recomputes and compares the *visible* (permanent+bonus, not temp)
total via `getVisibleSkillMod()`, sending a delta packet only if that
visible total actually changed. `SkillModManager::verifyWearableSkillMods
()`/`verifySkillBoxSkillMods()`/`verifyBuffSkillMods()`/
`verifyStructureSkillMods()` (`SkillModManager.cpp:100+, 314+, 375+,
421+`) each independently recompute what the *entire* bucket for their
one source type *should* contain from ground truth (worn items'
`getWearableSkillMods()`, the real `skillList`'s per-skill
`getSkillModifiers()`, the active `BuffList`, or the parent
structure's `getTemplateSkillMods()`), then call the shared
`compareMods()` (`SkillModManager.cpp:450+`) to diff against what's
actually stored and force-correct any mismatch via paired
`removeSkillMod()`/`addSkillMod()` calls. **These four `verify*`
functions are the actual live application mechanism for their
respective source type** -- they're not just a debug/audit tool despite
the "verify" naming; they're called at the moments those sources
change (skill learned, item equipped, buff applied, structure entered)
to push the recomputed bucket into `skillModList`.

**This directly explains the open companion `grantSkill()` gap: a
learned skill only produces real stat bonuses if something calls
`verifySkillBoxSkillMods()` (or an equivalent direct `addSkillMod()`
call) against that creature afterward -- simply adding to a skill
list/ledger is not sufficient on its own.** For a real player,
`SkillManager`'s skill-grant path calls `verifySkillBoxSkillMods()`
as part of the normal learn flow, which is why granting a skill to a
player visibly changes their stats. A companion's own `grantSkill()`
(per this project's own NOTES.md/HANDOFF.md) writes to a separate
companion-specific skill ledger that was never wired into this
verify/compare pipeline -- so even a "learned" companion skill
produces zero `skillModList` entries and thus zero effect on any
`getSkillMod()`-driven formula anywhere in the engine (combat,
crafting, healing, taming, all of it), exactly matching this project's
own "learned, not yet applied to combat" self-diagnosis. **The correct
fix shape, confirmed by this trace, is not to reinvent a companion-
specific stat system: it's either (a) calling
`SkillModManager::instance()->verifySkillBoxSkillMods(companionCreature)`
after `grantSkill()`/`removeSkill()` if the companion's skill data
lives in the real `SkillList`, or (b) if it deliberately uses a
separate ledger, writing an analogous `verifyCompanionSkillMods()`-
style function that reads that ledger and calls `compareMods()` the
same way the four existing `verify*` functions do** -- the
`compareMods()` diff-and-correct machinery itself is source-agnostic
and would work unmodified for a fifth source type.

**Min/max clamps are per-source-type, not per-mod-name, and a
misconfigured clamp pair silently disables clamping entirely rather
than erroring.** `getMaxSkill()`/`getMinSkill()`
(`SkillModManager.h:86-92`) look up a flat ceiling/floor keyed only by
`modType` (e.g., all `WEARABLE` mods share one max, not a per-stat
max) -- every clamp check in `SkillModList` is explicitly gated
`if (maxSkill != 0 && minSkill != 0)`, so a source type whose defaults
were never configured (both left at `0`) applies **no clamp at all**
for that type, rather than defaulting to "no bonus allowed." This is a
real footgun for a hypothetical new source type: forgetting to call
`setDefaults()`-equivalent configuration for it doesn't fail loud, it
just silently makes that source type's contributions unbounded.

**A separate, unrelated `disabledWearableSkillMods` blocklist can
suppress specific mod names from ever being read off worn items,
independent of the item's own data.** `isWearableModDisabled()`
(`SkillModManager.h:94-96`) checks a `SortedVector<String>` set during
`verifyWearableSkillMods()`'s scan (`SkillModManager.cpp:142-144`) --
a mod name on this list is skipped entirely for every wearable, a
blunt global kill-switch presumably used to retire an exploited or
deprecated stat without having to touch every item template that
grants it.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) `getSkillMod()`/`getSkillModOfType()` are
always safe, cheap, lock-protected reads (`skillModMutex`) -- any
formula needing a stat should read through these, never try to
recompute a bonus from raw skill/item/buff data directly, since
`skillModList` is the actual single source of truth every other system
already trusts. (2) any new bonus-granting mechanic (a custom item, a
new buff type, a companion stat system) must explicitly call
`addSkillMod()`/`removeSkillMod()` with an appropriate source-type
constant -- there is no automatic derivation, ever, for any source.
(3) reuse an existing source-type constant (`WEARABLE`, `BUFF`, etc.)
only if the new mechanic is genuinely "more of the same kind of
thing" and fine sharing that type's clamp settings; otherwise a truly
new source type needs its own `SkillModManager::setDefaults()` min/max
entry or it will be unclamped. (4) the `verify*`-then-`compareMods()`
pattern (recompute expected state from ground truth, diff against
cached state, patch only what's wrong) is a clean, reusable
reconciliation idiom worth copying verbatim for the companion
skill-mod gap specifically, rather than inventing a new mechanism.

---

## 56. PvP Formal Duel System

Traced through `DuelCommand.h` and
`CombatManager::requestDuel()/requestEndDuel()/declineDuel()/
freeDuelList()/areInDuel()`. Worth flagging up front: a same-named-
sounding helper, `QueueCommand::checkForArenaDuel()` (used throughout
the healing commands documented in section 51), is **not this system
at all** -- it checks `FrsManager::isPlayerFightingInArena()`, the
separate Force-Rank-System Jedi arena, not a real player-to-player
`/duel`. The two are easy to conflate by name; they share no code path.

**There is no dedicated "duel state" field anywhere -- a duel's entire
existence is derived from whether two players' per-player duel lists
mutually contain each other, and "accepting" a duel is nothing more
than issuing the same challenge command back.** Each `PlayerObject`
(ghost) carries its own duel list (`addToDuelList()`/
`removeFromDuelList()`/`requestedDuelTo()`/`isDuelListEmpty()`) of
players it has challenged. `CombatManager::requestDuel()`
(`CombatManager.cpp:3223-3286`) always adds the target to the
requester's own list first; it then checks whether the *target* had
already, separately, added the requester to *their* list
(`targetGhost->requestedDuelTo(player)`) -- if so, the duel is
instantly live (both sides get `ObjectFlag::ATTACKABLE|AGGRESSIVE`
PvP-status packets and matching pet status updates), if not, both
players just get a "challenged"/"was challenged" message and nothing
else happens yet. **A second player typing `/duel` back at the first
is literally the "accept" action** -- there's no separate accept
command or button; `areInDuel()` (`:3472-3482`) itself is just `ghost1
->requestedDuelTo(player2) && ghost2->requestedDuelTo(player1)`, a
live AND-check over both lists with no cached boolean anywhere.

**A duel challenge is scoped, range-limited, and area-restricted at
request time, but the duel's live/active checks don't re-verify any of
that afterward.** `DuelCommand.h:36-52` gates the request itself on: a
25-unit range check, and any currently-active `ActiveArea` on the
requester flagged `isNoDuelArea()` (a designated "no dueling" zone,
e.g. cities/starports) outright blocking the challenge. Notably these
checks only run at the moment of *requesting* -- once a duel is live,
nothing in `areInDuel()`/`requestEndDuel()` re-checks range or
no-duel-area status, so two dueling players who walk far apart or into
a no-duel zone mid-fight remain "in a duel" (still mutually
attackable) until one side explicitly ends it. `DuelCommand.h` also
independently checks `ghost->isIgnoring(creature->getFirstName())`
before allowing a challenge -- an ignored player cannot duel-challenge
you, layering the ignore-list system (chat-focused per section 45)
into PvP request gating too.

**Ending a duel is symmetric-cleanup, not just a flag flip: both
sides' pets get their PvP status reverted too, and pet cleanup is
deliberately deferred through the generic task-executor rather than
done inline.** `requestEndDuel()` (`:3288-3361`) only actually tears
anything down if the duel was mutual (`targetGhost->requestedDuelTo
(player)` still true) -- ending a one-sided pending challenge is just
list removal with no PvP-status reversal needed, since one-sided
challenges never grant `ATTACKABLE|AGGRESSIVE` in the first place.
For a genuinely mutual/live duel, both players' active pets get
`removeDefender()` calls against the opposing player, and each pet's
own defender-list mutation specifically against the *other* side is
wrapped in `Core::getTaskManager()->executeTask([...] { Locker
locker(pet); pet->removeDefender(target); }, ...)` (the same generic
task-execution idiom documented in section 48) rather than done inline
under the already-held locks -- presumably because a pet needs its own
separate lock that the enclosing function isn't already holding, so
deferring avoids a lock-ordering conflict rather than for scheduling
reasons.

**A duel challenge that's never accepted or declined doesn't
auto-expire on its own -- it persists on the requester's duel list
indefinitely until something else clears it, and there's a dedicated
bulk-cleanup entry point for exactly that.**
`CombatManager::freeDuelList()` (`:3363-3445`) iterates a player's
entire duel list and cleanly un-challenges/un-duels every entry
(presumably called on logout/zone-out/death, though this trace didn't
confirm every call site) -- it's written defensively, wrapping each
iteration in a `try`/`catch(ObjectNotDeployedException&)` so a target
that's already left the world mid-iteration doesn't abort the whole
cleanup, just gets force-removed from the list instead.
`declineDuel()` (`:3447-3470`) is the explicit rejection path -- it
only does anything if the *target* is the one who challenged (checks
`targetGhost->requestedDuelTo(player)`, the reverse direction from
`requestDuel()`'s own-list check), removing just that one-directional
entry with no PvP-status side effects, since a declined (never-mutual)
challenge never applied any.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't confuse `checkForArenaDuel()` (FRS
Jedi arena) with the real duel system documented here -- they're
unrelated despite the similar name, and a search for "duel" in this
codebase will surface both. (2) the mutual-list-membership model means
any custom PvP-adjacent feature checking "are these two players
currently dueling" should call `CombatManager::areInDuel()` rather than
looking for a status flag on the creature object -- there isn't one.
(3) since live duel state isn't re-validated against range/location
after the fact, a custom feature that cares about "duels should end if
players separate" would need to add that itself (e.g., a periodic
distance check triggering `requestEndDuel()`) -- the engine doesn't do
this today. (4) the pet-`removeDefender()`-via-deferred-task pattern
around dueling pets is the correct model to follow for any other
"clean up a pet's combat state as a side effect of the owner's PvP
state changing" feature -- consistent with how companion combat-state
cleanup should likely also be deferred through the task manager rather
than done inline, per the locking lessons already learned repeatedly
in this project's own companion-crash fixes.

---

## 57. Bio-Engineer DNA Sampling / Creature Creation

Traced through `CreatureManagerImplementation::sample()`,
`SampleDnaTask.h`, and `DnaManager::generateSample()/
generationalSample()/generateXp()`. This is the Bio-Engineer
profession's front end: sampling DNA off a live wild creature to
eventually craft a custom, spawnable pet -- a fully separate creation
path from Beast Mastery taming (section 52), which captures an
existing creature rather than manufacturing a new one.

**Sampling gates on a `hasDNA()`/`canCollectDna()`/
`hasSkillToSampleMe()` triple check before even starting, then runs as
a three-phase, self-rescheduling `Task` (the same generic shape as
`TameCreatureTask` in section 52) with a full 10-second "SAMPLING"
hold, not just a fixed cooldown.** `CreatureManagerImplementation::
sample()` (`CreatureManagerImplementation.cpp:1239-1270`) blocks
mounted players, players already mid-sample (`"sampledna"` named
`PendingTask`, the same reusable-cooldown idiom from sections 51/52),
and creatures the caller lacks skill to sample. `SampleDnaTask`
(`SampleDnaTask.h`) then runs `BEGIN` -> `SAMPLING` (ticks once per
second for a fixed `waitCount == 9`, i.e. roughly 10 seconds total) ->
`END`. During `BEGIN`, the creature is temporarily defanged for the
duration of the sample: `prepareCreatureForSampling()` sets the
creature's faction to the sampling player's own faction and clears its
`PvpStatusBitmask` entirely, restored via `resetCreatureStatus()`
whichever way the task ends -- **a creature literally cannot be
legally attacked by anyone while being sampled**, not just by the
sampler.

**Outcome resolution is a five-branch result table driven by two
independent random rolls (a base roll plus a luck-scaled roll) compared
against skill-derived thresholds, and the *same* successful-sample
event can still simultaneously aggro the creature or outright kill
it.** At `END` (`SampleDnaTask.h:90-199`): `sampleRoll = random(100) +
random(luck + force_luck)`, and `rollMod` is a skill-vs-creature-level
differential formula (`((skillMod - creatureLevel) / creatureLevel) +
(skillMod - creatureLevel)`, halved) -- the code's own inline comments
show the author explicitly reasoning through edge cases (a master
biologist against a CL70 creature needs a **worse** roll than against
a CL2 one, since the formula's sign flips on skill-vs-level parity).
The five outcomes: (1) critical failure (`sampleRoll < 5`, always
possible regardless of skill) -- no sample, aggro; (2) ordinary
failure -- no sample, no aggro; (3) success-with-aggro; (4)
success-but-the-creature-dies (once `getDnaSampleCount()` exceeds a
skill-scaled `maxSamples = ceil(skillMod / 25)` ceiling -- "the shock is
too much," per the code's own comment); (5) clean success, no side
effect. **A creature has a hard per-creature sample budget tied to the
sampler's skill, not an unlimited resource** -- pushing past it doesn't
just fail, it kills the source creature outright
(`killCreature()`, a literal `9999999` damage inflict across all three
primary HAM pools).

**A successful sample produces a quality-tiered crafting resource
routed through the real `CraftingManager`, not a special bio-engineer-
only item type -- DNA sampling is a resource-gathering profession
feeding the ordinary crafting pipeline (section 20), not a standalone
creature-spawning shortcut.** `award()` (`SampleDnaTask.h:215-260`)
computes a `qualityRoll` (another luck-scaled random roll plus
`rollMod`) mapped into a `low`/`mid`/`high` quality band whose exact
numeric tiers themselves shift with skill (a master's "low" roll still
outperforms a novice's "high" roll -- the whole 3-band range slides
upward as `skillMod` crosses 15/30/45/60/75 thresholds), then calls
`DnaManager::generateSample(creature, player, quality)`
(`DnaManager.cpp:338+`), which checks inventory space and routes
through `zoneServer->getCraftingManager()` to produce the actual
resource item. XP is awarded separately under the
`"bio_engineer_dna_harvesting"` type via a dedicated quartic-in-level
formula (`DnaManager::generateXp()`, `:152-159`) rather than reusing
any generic level-scaled XP helper seen elsewhere in this guide.

**The DNA sample item is explicitly a crafting *ingredient*, not the
finished pet -- actual creature creation is a separate downstream step
consuming a `PetDeed`.** `DnaManager::generationalSample(PetDeed*
deed, CreatureObject* player, int quality)` (`DnaManager.cpp:168+`)
is a distinct method from `generateSample()`, taking an existing
`PetDeed` as input rather than producing a raw resource -- confirming
the full chain is: sample a live creature (this section) -> get a
quality-graded DNA resource -> feed that resource into a crafting
schematic/station (the ordinary crafting-manager pipeline) to produce
or upgrade a `PetDeed` -> deed becomes a spawnable custom creature
pet, structurally similar to how the vehicle/droid deed-to-object flow
works (sections 43/33). This section did not trace the schematic/
crafting-station side of that chain in detail, only confirmed the
hand-off point exists and is real.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) DNA sampling and Beast Mastery taming
(section 52) are two entirely separate pet-acquisition paths sharing
only the surface-level "three-phase self-rescheduling `Task`" idiom --
don't conflate them when reasoning about "how do players get pets" in
this codebase. (2) the per-creature sample budget tied to skill
(`maxSamples = ceil(skillMod/25)`) and its lethal overflow consequence
is a real, deliberate resource-scarcity design, not a bug -- any
custom feature interacting with `getDnaSampleCount()`/`DnaState` should
preserve that scarcity rather than trivially resetting it. (3) quality
generation here follows the same "roll + luck, banded into tiers that
shift with skill" shape used elsewhere in this guide's crafting
coverage (section 20) -- worth treating as the canonical quality-roll
pattern for any new skill-gated random-outcome mechanic. (4) the
"neutralize the creature's faction/PvP flags for the duration of a
timed interaction, restore afterward" pattern
(`prepareCreatureForSampling()`/`resetCreatureStatus()`) mirrors
`TameCreatureTask`'s identical technique in section 52 -- a reusable
idiom for any future timed, interruptible interaction with a live
NPC that shouldn't be attackable mid-interaction.

---

## 58. Generic NPC Conversation/Dialogue Framework

Traced through `ConversationManager.h`,
`ConversationObserverImplementation.cpp`,
`ConversationTemplate.h`/`ConversationScreen.h`. This is the framework
underneath every simple "click an NPC, pick a dialogue option" flow in
the game -- distinct from the Lua *screenplay* system (section 3),
which drives scripted quest events, and distinct from the trainer/
skill-teaching SUI flows documented in this project's own companion
work. This system is specifically the branching-dialogue-tree engine,
and it's directly relevant to this project since the companion
trainer's own `trainer_conv.lua`/`trainerData.lua` (confirmed
"100% generic/data-driven" per this project's own prior research pass)
is built on exactly this framework -- this section is the missing
"why" behind that finding.

**One `ConversationObserver` instance is shared across every NPC using
the same conversation template -- conversations are not per-NPC
objects, they're a single stateless dispatcher keyed by template CRC,
built directly on the `Observable`/`Observer` system from section
47.** `ConversationManager::getConversationObserver()`
(`ConversationManager.h:22-45`) lazily creates-or-reuses one
`ConversationObserver` per `conversationTemplateCRC` in a `HashTable`
-- an NPC "having a conversation" is really just that NPC's
`Observable` having this shared observer registered for the relevant
conversation event types (`CONVERSE`, `STARTCONVERSATION`,
`SELECTCONVERSATION`, `STOPCONVERSATION`, plus `POSITIONCHANGED`,
which the observer explicitly filters for in its very first check,
`ConversationObserverImplementation.cpp:20-22`). All actual
conversation *state* lives on the player's side instead, in a
`ConversationSession` attached via the generic `SessionFacadeType::
CONVERSATION` session-facade slot (the same session-facade mechanism
used for trading/crafting/other stateful player interactions
elsewhere in the engine) -- the shared observer is pure dispatch
logic with no per-conversation mutable state of its own.

**Conversation content is 100% Lua-authored data -- screens and their
branching options -- loaded through `readObject(LuaObject*)`, and once
loaded a screen is permanently read-only, forcing any dynamic/
programmatic modification through an explicit clone.**
`ConversationScreen::readObject()` (`ConversationScreen.h:240-278`)
parses a screen's `id`, `leftDialog` (an STF string-table key, the
same localization mechanism used throughout this guide),
optional `animation`/`playerAnimation`, a `stopConversation` flag, and
an `options` table of `[displayText, linkedScreenID]` pairs -- then
sets `readOnly = true` (`:277`), after which every mutator on the
class (`addOption()`, `setDialogText()`, etc.) throws if called
(`:120-121` etc.). **Branching is just each option's `linkedScreenID`
string** -- `getNextConversationScreen()`
(`ConversationObserverImplementation.cpp:180-206`) resolves the next
screen purely by looking up `lastScreen->getOptionLink(selectedOption)`
against the template's screen map, with no other state machine
logic involved. A screen with `stopConversation = true` ends the
session the moment it's shown, regardless of whether it has any
options.

**C++ "screen handlers" can intercept a specific screen ID to inject
dynamic content (real player state, computed text, conditional
branching) without touching the Lua-authored static screen -- and the
clone-then-modify requirement above is exactly why this needs a
loop-until-unmodified pattern rather than a single dispatch call.**
`runScreenHandlers()` (`ConversationObserverImplementation.cpp:208-235`)
checks a `screenHandlers` map keyed by screen ID; if a handler exists
for the screen about to be shown, it's called with
`conversationScreen->cloneScreen()` (never the read-only original) and
may either return a modified screen directly, or signal "redirect to a
different screen ID entirely" by returning `nullptr` plus a
`getNextScreenId()` value, looping until some screen is finally
returned unmodified. This is the mechanism a conversation needs if it
wants to, say, show different dialogue text depending on the player's
faction or quest state -- the Lua data defines the *shape* of the
conversation tree, the C++ handler supplies *dynamic content* at
specific nodes within it.

**Player movement during a conversation is actively policed via the
same `POSITIONCHANGED` observer registration, auto-canceling the
session if the player walks out of range -- this is opt-in per
conversation, registered only once a conversation actually starts, not
a permanent listener.** `createPositionObserver()`
(`ConversationObserverImplementation.cpp:150-152`) registers the
shared observer for `POSITIONCHANGED` on the *player* (not the NPC)
only inside the `STARTCONVERSATION` handler, and
`cancelConversationSession()` explicitly `dropObserver()`s it again on
end -- so a player not currently in any conversation incurs zero
position-observer overhead. The `POSITIONCHANGED` handler
(`:62-87`) checks `sessionNpc->checkInConversationRange()` and force-
cancels via `StopNpcConversation` if the player has wandered out of
it, with a special-cased space-ship variant
(`SpaceCommTimerTask`/`"SpaceCommTimer"` named `PendingTask`) that
delays cancellation instead of doing it immediately, presumably to
tolerate ship-to-ship range fluctuation during space comms without
constantly interrupting the conversation.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) this is the correct framework for any new
branching, multi-step NPC dialogue that doesn't need full screenplay-
level scripting (section 3) -- author the tree as Lua data
(`id`/`leftDialog`/`options` per screen), and only reach for a C++
screen handler if a specific node needs truly dynamic content. (2) a
conversation template is looked up and shared by CRC
(`CreatureTemplateManager::getConversationTemplate()`), so two NPCs
(or, relevantly, a companion and its trainer) can point at the exact
same conversation data without duplicating anything -- confirming why
this project's own `trainer_conv.lua` needed zero companion-specific
code to work correctly for companion trainer NPCs. (3) any screen
meant to be dynamically modified at runtime must go through
`cloneScreen()` first -- attempting to mutate a screen fetched
directly from the template will throw, by design, since the template's
own copy must stay stable for every other NPC/player sharing it. (4)
the position-observer auto-cancel pattern (register on start, drop on
end, gate off the frequently-firing `POSITIONCHANGED` event to only
the active conversation window) is a clean model for any other
"only care about this frequent event while a specific interaction is
live" feature -- avoids paying a permanent per-tick cost for state
that's usually inactive.

---

## 59. Structure Lot / Placement Validation

Traced through `StructureManager::placeStructureFromDeed()`,
`PlanetManagerImplementation::isBuildingPermittedAt()`, and
`PlayerObjectImplementation::getLotsRemaining()`. This is the gate a
structure deed has to clear before it becomes a real, live
`StructureObject` -- and it turns out to be a long, strictly-ordered
chain of independent checks, each with its own player-facing error
message, rather than one monolithic validation function.

**Lot capacity is a live-recomputed sum over currently-owned
structures, not a decremented counter -- there's no separate "lots
used" field to drift out of sync.** `PlayerObjectImplementation::
getLotsRemaining()` (`PlayerObjectImplementation.cpp:3142-3158`)
starts from a flat `maximumLots` (a `byte` field, default `10`, set at
character creation -- `PlayerObject.idl:113,387`) and subtracts
`getLotSize()` for every structure in the player's `ownedStructures`
list, resolved fresh from the object manager each call. **This means
lot capacity self-corrects automatically if a structure is destroyed
through any path** (natural decay per section 54, GM command, a future
custom feature) -- there's nothing to separately reconcile, unlike a
counter-based scheme where destroying a structure without also
decrementing a counter would leak lot capacity permanently.
`hasLotsRemaining(lots)` (`PlayerObject.idl:546-548`) is just
`lots <= getLotsRemaining()`, checked once late in the placement chain
(`StructureManager.cpp:452-459`) against the specific deed's own
`getLotSize()` -- different structure types cost different lot
amounts, not a flat per-structure charge.

**Placement validation runs a long, strictly front-loaded chain of
independent checks -- faction/deed compatibility, zone allow-list,
no-build zones, footprint collision, city rank/zoning, then finally
lots and ability -- and each failure returns immediately with its own
distinct player-facing message, so a placement attempt fails on
whichever check is hit first, not a combined report.**
`placeStructureFromDeed()` (`StructureManager.cpp:270-476`) checks, in
order: (1) not already mid-placement
(`SessionFacadeType::PLACESTRUCTURE`); (2) faction-restricted deeds
(base deeds) require the placer be actively declared to a matching
faction, not neutral/on-leave (ties into section 35's GCW base
coverage); (3) `serverTemplate->isAllowedZone()` -- some structure
templates are hard-restricted to specific planets/zones; (4)
`PlanetManager::isBuildingPermittedAt()` (broken out further below);
(5) the target point isn't inside a `isClientRegion()` city (a
special/reserved region type that blocks building outright); (6) a
footprint-overlap check against every scene object within 128 units
using axis-aligned `BoundaryRectangle` corner-containment tests in
both directions (does the new footprint contain any existing
footprint's corner, or vice versa -- **it's a coarse rectangle
intersection test, not true polygon collision**, so oddly-shaped or
rotated footprints are approximated as boxes); (7) city rank
requirement (`getCityRankRequired()`) and, only if inside a city,
zoning rights (`hasZoningRights()`), rank threshold, civic-structure-
requires-mayor, and unique-structure-per-city dedup; and only *after*
all of that, (8) deed possession re-verification (guards against the
deed being traded away mid-placement-UI-flow) and (9) the lots/ability
checks described above. **The ordering itself is meaningful** -- a
player who lacks lots but also picked an invalid spot will see the
placement-location error, never the lot error, since lots are checked
dead last.

**Terrain/environment legality is delegated to a separate
`PlanetManager` function covering zone boundaries, no-build areas
(both region-based and per-object exclusion radii), water, and
proximity to points of interest -- structure placement doesn't
duplicate any of this logic itself.**
`isBuildingPermittedAt()` (`PlanetManagerImplementation.cpp:1356-1388`)
checks, in order: the target point is within the zone's own
boundaries at all; no `ActiveArea` flagged `isNoBuildZone()` covers the
point; `isInObjectsNoBuildZone()` (a per-object exclusion radius --
e.g., certain POIs or lairs project their own no-build bubble
independent of any drawn region); `isInWater()`; and finally
`isInRangeWithPoi(x, y, 150)` -- a flat 150-unit minimum distance from
any point of interest, regardless of that POI's own type or size. This
function is reused by the *camping* system too
(`isCampingPermittedAt()` sits immediately below it in the same file,
sharing several of the same checks) -- structure and camp placement
share a common "is this spot legal terrain" foundation even though
they're otherwise unrelated systems.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any custom structure-placement feature
(a programmatic "spawn this building here" tool, a custom deed type)
should call the existing `isBuildingPermittedAt()` /footprint-overlap
logic rather than reimplementing terrain/collision checks -- this is
genuinely the single source of truth other systems (camping) already
reuse. (2) the footprint check's box-approximation means an oddly-
shaped structure's true collision boundary is not exactly what gets
validated -- worth knowing if a custom structure template has a very
non-rectangular footprint and placement behaves surprisingly. (3) lot
capacity being a live recompute (not a stored counter) means a custom
feature that transfers structure ownership between players, or grants
a temporary structure, doesn't need to separately manage a lot-count
field anywhere -- `getLotsRemaining()` will simply reflect reality the
next time it's called. (4) the strict, early-exit check ordering means
error messages shown to a player don't necessarily reflect *every*
reason a placement would fail, only the first one hit -- useful to
know when debugging a "why won't this deed place" report, since the
visible error may not be the only problem.

---

## 60. Camp / Tent Deployment System

Traced through `CampKitMenuComponent.cpp`,
`StructureManager::placeCamp()`, and `CampSiteActiveArea.idl`. This is
the vanilla handheld-camp-kit placement flow -- worth flagging
immediately since this project's own codebase also has a
similarly-named but **entirely separate, companion-specific** file,
`server/zone/managers/companion/CampDeploymentManager.h`, which is
explicitly documented in its own header comment as "spec 4E" of this
project's companion system, modeled on but distinct from the real
system documented here (it sources its tent from a companion's private
inventory instead of a player-carried `CampKit`, gated on companion
Ranger/Scout skill rather than the owner's `"camp"` skill mod). This
section covers only the real, general-engine system.

**A camp is a real `StructureObject` with a real medical rating,
mechanically indistinguishable from a hospital for the purposes of
section 51's wound-healing location gate -- but it's placed through a
carried consumable item, not a deed, and has an unusually long list of
placement-time environment checks layered on top of the generic
structure-placement validation from section 59.**
`CampKitMenuComponent::handleObjectMenuSelect()`
(`CampKitMenuComponent.cpp:31-317`) gates deployment on: `"camp"`
skill mod meeting the specific camp template's required level; not in
combat; not inside a cell (must be placed outdoors); actually carrying
the kit (`isASubChildOf(player)`); standing and not mounted; not inside
a city region at all (**camps are unconditionally banned in cities**,
stricter than the general "needs zoning rights" rule from section 59);
not swimming/in water; not already owning another camp structure
anywhere (`isCampStructure()` scan over the player's
`ownedStructures`); and not already standing inside someone else's
active camp (`getCurrentCamp()`, the same accessor referenced in
section 51's medical-rating check). Camps additionally self-exclude
