based on *other* nearby camps/lairs/buildings within a
template-defined radius (own `getNoBuildRadius() + campRadius`) --
including a specific check that walks `OBJECTDESTRUCTION`/
`CREATUREDESPAWNED` observers on nearby objects looking for one typed
`ObserverType::LAIR` (the observer-typing mechanism from section 47),
specifically to detect and reject placement too close to an NPC lair
even though a lair isn't itself a `StructureObject`.

**Placement delegates terrain legality to `isCampingPermittedAt()`, a
close sibling of section 59's `isBuildingPermittedAt()` living in the
same `PlanetManager` file, deliberately more permissive about city
no-build zones specifically** (per the code's own comment: "Allows
building in city no-build zone but not within city limits which are
checked above" -- the city-membership check above is the real gate;
the no-build-zone flag alone doesn't block camps the way it blocks
permanent structures). Once legal, `StructureManager::placeCamp()`
constructs the actual `StructureObject`, and the handler then
independently constructs and wires up a `CampSiteActiveArea`
(`object/camp_area.iff`) -- a *separate* object from the structure
itself, flagged `ActiveArea::NOBUILDZONEAREA` (so a camp automatically
projects its own no-build bubble the instant it exists, feeding back
into the very radius check other players' camp placements will hit)
and explicitly wired via `setCamp()`/`setOwner()`/`setTerminal()` to
know its parent structure, owning player, and an in-camp `Terminal`
child object located by scanning the structure's `getChildObjects()`
for the first `isTerminal()` match. **If no terminal child is found on
the newly spawned structure, the whole camp is torn back down
immediately** (`campObject->destroyObjectFromWorld/
destroyObjectFromDatabase`) -- the terminal is treated as a hard
structural requirement of a valid camp, not optional dressing.

**A sufficiently-skilled faction camp registers itself on the
planetary map with a faction-colored icon, gated by a specific named
skill-mod threshold constant, not just "any faction camp."** If
`skillRequired >= MAP_REGISTER_MOD` and the camp's faction isn't
neutral, the terminal inherits the placer's faction/status and the
whole camp gets `setPlanetMapCategory()` + `registerObjectWithPlanetaryMap()`
under an `"imperial"`/`"rebel"` category -- meaning only *advanced*
faction camps (built by a sufficiently-trained camper) show up as
faction-colored map blips to other players; a low-skill camp exists
and functions but stays off the planetary map. A successful deployment
fires `ObserverEventType::DEPLOYEDCAMP` (the observer system from
section 47 again) with the new `CampSiteActiveArea` as the event
subject, and consumes one use from the camp kit item
(`decreaseUseCount()`) rather than destroying it outright -- a single
camp kit is evidently a multi-use consumable, not a single-shot deed.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't confuse the real engine camp system
documented here with this project's own `CampDeploymentManager` --
they're related by concept and file-header-documented lineage but are
structurally separate code paths with separate gating rules (skill
source, item source, and target actor all differ). (2) the
lair-detection-via-observer-type-scan technique
(`ObserverType::LAIR` on `OBJECTDESTRUCTION`/`CREATUREDESPAWNED`
observers) is a reusable pattern for any future feature that needs to
detect "is there an NPC lair near this point" without lairs being a
distinct queryable object type of their own -- lairs are identified
structurally, by what kind of observer they've registered, not by a
dedicated flag or class check. (3) a camp providing hospital-equivalent
medical rating (section 51) plus the not-a-structure-you-need-a-deed-
for placement model makes it a natural template to study for any
custom "temporary, player-deployed, self-service" structure feature --
the whole flow (kit item -> environment checks -> structure + linked
active-area pair -> terminal-as-hard-requirement) is a clean,
self-contained example to copy from. (4) the `MAP_REGISTER_MOD`-gated
planetary-map registration is a good precedent for any custom feature
that should only surface on the map for suitably-skilled/high-tier
placements rather than unconditionally for every instance.

---

## 61. Group Loot Distribution / Master Looter Rules

Traced through `GroupObject.idl`'s loot-rule fields,
`GroupLootTask.h`, and `GroupManager::createLottery()/doRandomLoot()`.
This extends section 13's group-fundamentals coverage with the actual
loot-split mechanics -- credits and items are handled completely
separately, and each of the four loot rules has genuinely different
code, not just a different permission check on one shared path.

**A group has exactly one active loot rule at a time
(`FREEFORALL`/`MASTERLOOTER`/`LOTTERY`/`RANDOM`, `GroupManager.h:65-68`,
default `FREEFORALL`), stored directly on the `GroupObject`
(`lootRule`/`masterLooterID` fields, `GroupObject.idl:37-51`), and
looting a corpse always runs as a short-lived `Task` triggered per
loot attempt, not a persistent per-corpse state machine.**
`GroupLootTask::run()` (`GroupLootTask.h:32-124`) branches on
`group->getLootRule()` and either returns early (permission denied),
falls through to the shared "let this player open the corpse"
tail logic, or -- for `LOTTERY`/`RANDOM` -- hands off entirely to a
`GroupManager` function and returns immediately, since those two modes
resolve item ownership as a side effect rather than opening a
container for one specific player.

**Cash credits are always split evenly among in-range group members
regardless of loot rule -- `splitCredits()` runs identically for
`FREEFORALL`/`MASTERLOOTER`'s "let this one player open it" path as it
does for `LOTTERY`/`RANDOM`'s item-distribution paths -- only
*items* are gated by the loot rule, credits never are.**
`splitCredits()` (`GroupLootTask.h:126-224`) collects every group
member currently within `128` units of the corpse
(`membersInRange()`'s identical range constant is reused independently
in `createLottery()`/`doRandomLoot()` too -- a member outside 128
units from the kill simply isn't eligible for either credits or
items, full stop), applies a `force_luck` skill-mod bonus to the total
pool (`+luck/20` of the base amount) before splitting, divides evenly
with the remainder (`lootCredits % payees.size()`) distributed as
single extra credits to a randomly-ordered subset of payees rather
than dumped entirely on one player, and finally **shuffles which
specific payee receives which specific payout amount** via repeated
`System::random()` draws against a shrinking pool -- a cosmetic
touch, but a deliberate one: eligible members can receive slightly
different amounts (base vs. base+1) and *which* member gets the "+1"
values is randomized each time, not always the same person or always
the looter.

**`LOTTERY` mode locks the entire corpse behind a real session object
and an explicit `ContainerPermissions` deny-rule on every item inside
it, specifically to prevent theft while group members are still
being asked to roll -- reusing the same permissions ACL system
documented for housing in section 37.**
`GroupManager::createLottery()` (`GroupManager.cpp:748-799`) creates a
`LootLotterySession` (attached via `SessionFacadeType::LOOTLOTTERY`,
the same session-facade pattern noted in section 58's conversation
coverage) and, before anything else, iterates every item in the
corpse's inventory setting `denyPermission("player",
ContainerPermissions::OPEN)` and `MOVECONTAINER)` -- **no group
member, including the eventual winner, can open or move any loot item
until the lottery actually resolves**, a hard lock rather than a
soft "please don't loot yet" convention. Only in-range members get
added as eligible lottery participants (`addEligiblePlayer()`); an
out-of-range member is explicitly told why via a "too far away for
lottery" message rather than silently excluded. If a lottery is
already in progress on a corpse when another member tries to loot, 
`GroupLootTask` detects the still-active `LOOTLOTTERY` session and
just tells them to keep waiting (`:60-70`) rather than starting a
second, conflicting lottery.

**`RANDOM` mode is the only rule that never asks players to do
anything -- it deterministically (from the players' perspective,
though internally random) assigns every single item on the corpse to
a randomly chosen in-range member, one item at a time, immediately.**
`GroupManager::doRandomLoot()` (`GroupManager.cpp:801-846+`) walks the
corpse's inventory back-to-front, and for each item **checks
`getOwnerID() != 0` on that item's own container permissions and skips
it if already owned** (`:842-844`) -- a defensive check against
double-processing or a partially-completed prior pass, consistent with
this codebase's general "verify before mutate" caution seen elsewhere
(section 39's anti-exploit coverage, section 55's `compareMods()`).
Eligible recipients are the same in-range-member scan as everywhere
else in this file; this section's trace didn't follow the exact
per-item winner-selection call past its start, but the structure
(iterate items, pick a random eligible candidate per item,
transfer ownership) is unambiguous from the surrounding code.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the `128`-unit in-range requirement is
the single load-bearing distance constant for *all* group loot
eligibility (credits and items alike, across all four rules) -- a
custom loot-adjacent feature should reuse this exact radius rather
than picking an arbitrary new one, for consistency with player
expectations already set by the base game. (2) `MASTERLOOTER` is
implemented as nothing more than a permission gate
(`checkMasterLooter()`) wrapped around the same generic "open this
corpse to this player" tail every other rule eventually reaches for a
single-player loot -- it's the simplest of the four rules
mechanically, despite being the one most associated with loot
"drama" in player culture. (3) any custom mechanic that wants to lock
an item against being taken prematurely (not just loot -- any
timed/contested item-claim feature) should reuse the
`ContainerPermissions` deny-`OPEN`/`MOVECONTAINER` pattern from
`createLottery()` rather than inventing a new gate -- it's already the
established idiom for "this item exists and is visible, but nobody
may take it yet." (4) credits and items are fully decoupled in this
system -- a custom loot-rule variant only needs to override the item-
distribution logic; `splitCredits()` can be called unmodified
regardless of what new item-distribution behavior is added.

---

## 62. NPC Lair Spawning System

Traced through `LairObserverImplementation.cpp` (the dominant, richest
file in this area). This is entirely distinct from section 40's
resource-node spawning (simplex-noise density maps) -- a lair is a
real, destructible `TangibleObject`/`LairObject` with its own HP
("condition") pool, and creature spawning is driven **by damage dealt
to the lair**, not by any timer. The system is a second major example,
alongside sections 47/58/60's observer-based designs, of this
codebase's preference for event-driven world logic over polling loops.

**A lair's entire spawning behavior is orchestrated through one shared
`LairObserver` instance registered on the lair's `Observable`,
reacting to combat and lifecycle events rather than ticking on its
own schedule -- the same Observer/Observable foundation as sections
47/58/60, applied here to full NPC-spawn logistics.**
`LairObserverImplementation::notifyObserverEvent()`
(`LairObserverImplementation.cpp:28-211`) switches on:
`DAMAGERECEIVED` (checks for new spawn waves, boss-mob eligibility, and
self-healing, each deferred into a short-delay scheduled task on the
**zone's own named task queue** -- `zone->getZoneName()` used directly
as the custom queue name, the same named-custom-queue mechanism from
section 48), `OBJECTDESTRUCTION` (disseminates XP via
`DisseminateExperienceTask`, clears the threat map, plays a heavy-
damage effect, and fully destroys the lair object), `OBJECTREMOVEDFROM
ZONE` (despawns every creature the lair ever spawned),
`CREATUREDESPAWNED` (schedules an individual mobile respawn),
`NOPLAYERSINRANGE` (a farming/"milking" detector, below), and
`AIMESSAGE` (simple broadcast fan-out to every currently-spawned
creature). **Nothing in this file runs on a periodic tick of its own
-- every action traces back to some upstream event notification.**

**Spawn waves are gated on the lair's *condition-damage* crossing
fixed thresholds, not elapsed time, and are capped at three total
waves per lair lifetime (before any "repopulation").**
`checkForNewSpawns()` (`LairObserverImplementation.cpp:381-537`) uses
an internal `spawnNumber` counter (0/1/2/3): wave 0 fires immediately
on lair creation, wave 1 requires `conditionDamage > 0` (i.e., the lair
has taken *any* damage at all), wave 2 requires damage past *half* the
lair's max condition, and beyond wave 2 no further ordinary waves
fire -- **attacking a lair is what makes it spawn more defenders, up to
a hard limit**, not random chance or a repeating timer. Spawn *count*
per wave is difficulty-scaled (`Math::min(difficultyLevel,
spawnLimit/3)` for creature-type lairs, a random half-to-full range
for NPC-type lairs) and mobile *choice* per spawn is a weighted random
pick from the lair template's mobile list, batched into a
name->count map before scheduling individual `SpawnLairMobileTask`s
(staggered ~200ms apart for the fast initial wave, randomized between
`SPAWN_TIME_MIN`/`MAX` seconds for later waves).

**A creature-type lair (as opposed to an NPC-type lair) can
additionally spawn a one-time boss mobile once the lair's remaining
condition drops below a difficulty-scaled threshold, and boss spawns
trigger an unconditional (not 50/50-rolled) full-group aggro.**
`checkForBossSpawn()` (`:539-588`) is capped at one boss per lair
lifetime (`bossesSpawned > 0`, or `> 1` if the lair has been
repopulated once), picks randomly among the template's weighted
`bossMobiles` map, and immediately follows up with a `LairAggroTask`
constructed with `allAttack=true` -- contrasted with
`doAggro()`'s (`:267-296`) normal per-spawn **coin-flip** (each
regular spawned creature independently rolls `random(100) < 50` to
decide whether it joins the fight at all when `allAttack` is false).

**Damaged lairs can self-heal by tasking a randomly-chosen living
spawned creature to go heal it -- healing is delegated to an NPC
"caretaker" via the AI blackboard/movement-state system, not a direct
structure-heal call.** `checkForHeal()` (`:304-373`) picks a random
live, non-pet spawned creature that resolves to a real `AiAgent`
(retrying up to 5 times if the random pick doesn't cooperate), then
`writeBlackboard("healTarget", lair)` and
`setMovementState(AiAgent::LAIR_HEALING)` -- the actual healing
*behavior* presumably lives in the AI behavior-tree system (referenced
but not traced further in this pass), reusing the generic
blackboard-driven AI-task-assignment pattern rather than a
lair-specific heal function.

**Individual dead/despawned mobiles auto-respawn on a random timer
tied to the lair, indefinitely, unless the lair has been flagged as
belonging to a "destroy mission."** `checkRespawn()` (`:590-640`)
schedules a fresh `SpawnLairMobileTask` on a
`random(RESPAWN_TIME_MIN..MAX)` delay for any despawned mobile, except
when `isDestroyMissionLairObserver()` is true, in which case respawn
is skipped entirely -- **a lair generated as the target of a "destroy
the lair" mission doesn't replenish itself**, presumably so the
mission's kill-count target stays achievable rather than being an
infinite-respawn treadmill.

**A dedicated "milking" farming detector deliberately repopulates
(partially heals and resets) a lair that's mostly-dead but still
significantly damaged once no players remain nearby -- explicitly
allowing repeat-farming of the same lair location rather than
requiring it fully die and despawn/respawn elsewhere.** The
`NOPLAYERSINRANGE` handler (`:162-176`) bails out early if the lair's
`getConditionDamage()` is still under half its max condition -- i.e.
**it only proceeds once the lair is more than half damaged**, so a
barely-scratched lair doesn't get force-repopulated just because
players wandered off. Past that threshold, if enough living creatures
still remain, it schedules a `LairRepopulateTask`. `repopulateLair()` (`:832-857`)
heals the lair to `75%` of its max condition, resets `spawnNumber` back
to `0` (re-enabling the full three-wave spawn sequence from scratch),
and flags `setLairRepopulated(true)` -- which itself **doubles the
ordinary spawn limit and permits one additional boss spawn** per the
earlier `spawnLimit *= 2` / `bossesSpawned > 1` checks. This is a
real, deliberate "reward repeat engagement with the same lair instead
of only ever spawning a fresh one" design, not incidental behavior.

**A small chance exists for any non-baby creature spawn on a
creature-type lair to become a flagged "scout," with a custom
nameplate suffix and tracked ID, capped at one scout per lair at a
time.** `spawnLairMobile()` (`:642-830`) rolls
`SCOUT_SPAWN_CHANCE` only when `scoutCreatureId == 0` (no existing
scout) and the lair is creature-type; a chosen scout gets
`ObjectFlag::SCOUT`, a re-run `setAITemplate()` (presumably swapping in
scout-specific AI behavior, not traced further here), and a
`" (scout)"` nameplate suffix. Separately, a lair also implements a
lightweight "baby follows an adult" social mechanic -- once more than
one creature is spawned, a newly spawned baby is flagged
`ESCORT|FOLLOW` and set to follow the first-spawned (presumably adult)
creature in formation, with a randomized left/right formation offset.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) lairs are damage-reactive, not
time-reactive -- any custom "wild spawn point" feature modeled on this
system should drive its escalation off `DAMAGERECEIVED` observer
events and condition thresholds, not a periodic task, to match this
codebase's established idiom. (2) the `spawnLimit *= 2` /
`bossesSpawned > 1` repopulation-doubling is the concrete mechanism
behind farmable "milking" lairs -- any balance work on lair difficulty
needs to account for the repopulated state being a meaningfully
different (harder, more rewarding) lair than its fresh-spawn state.
(3) `isDestroyMissionLairObserver()` is the correct flag to check (or
set, for a custom mission type) if a new mission wants a lair that
doesn't infinitely respawn its defenders -- reuse this rather than
inventing a new respawn-suppression mechanism. (4) the scout/escort
mechanics are cosmetic/social-AI flourishes layered on top of the core
spawn logic via `ObjectFlag` bits and blackboard writes, not separate
systems -- a good model for adding similar lightweight "flavor" AI
behavior to any custom spawn type without touching the core spawn-wave
logic at all.

## 63. Combat Damage-Over-Time (DoT) Internals

Traced through `CombatManager::applyDots()/applyWeaponDots()` and
`DamageOverTimeList.cpp`. This extends section 10's combat basics with
the specific mechanics of bleed/poison/disease/fire (and force-choke)
-- a distinct system from the per-hit damage resolution documented
there, running as its own ticking subsystem layered on top of a
creature's normal HAM pools.

**There are two structurally independent ways a hit can apply a DoT --
attack-defined DoTs from the special-attack's own data, and
weapon-innate DoTs from the weapon item itself -- and only one of them
currently has a real resist stat wired up, per an explicit code
comment acknowledging the gap.** `applyDots()`
(`CombatManager.cpp:1711-1763`) iterates `CreatureAttackData::
getDotEffects()` (a list attached to the *attack/command* being used,
so specific special attacks can carry their own DoT payloads), each
independently rolling `System::random(100) > effect.getDotChance()`
to decide whether it lands, summing skill-mod-based resist across
whatever `getDefenderStateDefenseModifiers()` the effect specifies.
`applyWeaponDots()` (`:1765-1816`) instead reads DoTs baked into the
*weapon item itself* (`weapon->getNumberOfDots()`/`getDotType(i)`/
etc.), covering the four classic types (poison/disease/fire/bleed) --
but the code's own comment is explicit: *"SOE strings only provide
this ONE specific type of mod (`combat_bleeding_defense`) and there's
no evidence (yet) of other 3 WEAPON dot versions also being
resistable"* -- so weapon-sourced poison/disease/fire currently apply
with **zero** resist mod applied (the `resist` variable stays `0` for
those three cases, only bleed's is actually populated), a
faithfully-preserved asymmetry from the original game rather than an
oversight in this port.

**Weapon DoTs are a limited, consumable resource per weapon
(`getDotUses()`), and a charge is only spent on a successful,
unresisted application -- a resisted roll costs nothing.** The final
gate in `applyWeaponDots()`'s loop
(`weapon->getDotPotency(i) * (1.f - resist/100.f) > System::random(100)
&& defender->addDotState(...) > 0`) only decrements
`setDotUses(getDotUses(i) - 1, i)` if both the potency roll succeeds
*and* `addDotState()` itself returns a positive value (meaning the DoT
actually landed inside `DamageOverTimeList`, not resisted by its own
independent roll there too -- there are effectively two chained
resist rolls for weapon DoTs, one in `CombatManager` and one inside
`addDot()` itself). **Certain AI agents are categorically DoT-immune**
via a `ObjectFlag::NODOT` creature-bitmask check that both
`applyDots()` and `applyWeaponDots()` check identically up front --
presumably used on bosses/raid-tier mobs to prevent DoT-kiting
strategies from trivializing a fight.

**All of a creature's active DoTs live in one `DamageOverTimeList`,
keyed by a composite `(dotType, pool, objectID)` hash, and ticking is
driven by one shared `nextTick` timestamp checked externally, not by
one scheduled `Task` per DoT.** `addDot()`
(`DamageOverTimeList.cpp:114-223`) computes its own independent
land/resist roll (`potency > 0 && random(100) >= clamp(potency *
80/(100+defense), 5, 95)` -- a floor of 5% and ceiling of 95% land
chance baked directly into the formula, so nothing is ever
unconditionally-lands or unconditionally-resisted) before even
constructing the DoT. `activateDots()` (`:15-85`), the actual tick
function, is called by some external caller (not traced further in
this pass, but structurally this is the same "something else drives
this on its own schedule" pattern as section 48's task system) and
iterates every stored DoT checking `dot->nextTickPast()`
individually, applying damage via `dot->applyDot(victim)` only for
those actually due -- the list-level `nextTick` field is a single
aggregate "when do I next need to be checked at all" hint, not a
per-DoT scheduled callback, keeping the tick-check itself cheap even
with many simultaneous DoTs. Expired DoTs are pruned inline during the
same pass, and `CreatureState` bits (`BLEEDING`/`POISONED`/
`DISEASED`/`ONFIRE`) are cleared automatically the instant a DoT of
that type is no longer present in the list -- state and DoT-list
membership are kept in lockstep rather than tracked as two separate
things that could drift.

**Reapplying a DoT of the same type doesn't stack additively -- it's a
strength comparison that either replaces the existing DoT's damage
value while preserving its tick timing, or is silently discarded in
favor of the stronger existing one.** `addDot()`'s merge logic
(`:176-200`) walks any existing entry under the same composite key: if
the existing DoT has already expired, the new one simply replaces it;
if the existing DoT is still active and the *new* DoT's strength is
`>=` the old one's, the new DoT takes over but **inherits the old
DoT's `nextTick` value** (`setNextTick(dot.getNextTick())`) rather than
resetting the tick timer -- so refreshing a DoT with a stronger hit
doesn't grant a free extra tick's worth of delay; if the new DoT is
*weaker* than the still-active existing one, it's dropped entirely and
the existing (stronger) DoT is left untouched. Disease is further
special-cased to a synthetic fixed `objectID`
(`Long::hashCode(CreatureState::DISEASED)`) specifically so **only one
disease DoT can ever be active regardless of source** -- multiple
disease sources collapse onto the same composite key and fight over
the strength-comparison rule above rather than stacking as separate
entries the way multiple bleed/poison/fire sources from different
weapons/attacks legitimately can.

**Curing/healing a DoT is a partial-reduction mechanic, not a binary
cure-or-not, and duration can independently shrink via a
per-DoT-type dissipation skill mod capped at 90%.** `healState()`
(`:248-307`) applies a float `reduction` value against every active
DoT instance of the matching type via `dot->reduceTick(reduction)`,
consuming as much of the cure's "juice" as needed across potentially
multiple stacked instances (poison/fire/bleed can have several
simultaneous instances from different sources, per the no-stacking
rule only applying *within* the same composite key) -- a cure that
doesn't have enough reduction to fully clear every instance leaves the
DoT active but weakened, rather than an all-or-nothing cure roll.
Separately, `addDot()` applies `dissipation_poison`/`_disease`/`_fire`/
`_bleeding` skill mods to shrink the DoT's initial *duration* (not its
damage), explicitly capped at a `90%` maximum reduction
(`:157-162`) -- so a sufficiently high dissipation stat can make a DoT
expire almost immediately, but never guarantees zero duration.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) a custom DoT-inflicting item/attack should
go through `CreatureObject::addDotState()` (which just calls
`DamageOverTimeList::addDot()`) rather than manipulating HAM pools
directly on a timer -- this gets the resist roll, duration-dissipation,
same-type strength-comparison, and state-bit bookkeeping for free.
(2) if a new DoT-like mechanic wants true unconditional stacking
(multiple simultaneous instances from the same source), it needs a
distinct `objectID` per instance in the composite key -- the existing
disease-style "force to one shared key" trick is the model to copy if
the opposite (hard single-instance) behavior is instead wanted. (3)
`ObjectFlag::NODOT` is the correct, already-established flag to set on
any custom boss/raid-tier AI template that should be immune to DoT
strategies, rather than special-casing that creature in combat code.
(4) the weapon-DoT resist gap (only bleed has a real resist mod wired
up) is a genuine, source-comment-acknowledged asymmetry -- worth
knowing before assuming poison/disease/fire resistance stats on a
custom item or armor actually do anything against weapon-sourced DoTs
specifically (they do work against attack-defined DoTs via
`applyDots()`'s generic `getDefenderStateDefenseModifiers()` list,
just not against the weapon-innate path).

## 64. Travel / Shuttle Ticket System

Traced through `TravelTerminalImplementation.cpp`,
`PurchaseTicketCommand.h`, and `TicketCollectorImplementation.cpp`.
Two distinct terminal types split this system across purchase and
boarding: a `TravelTerminal` sells tickets, a separate
`TicketCollector` object is what a player actually interacts with to
board the shuttle and travel, and the two are not the same object even
though they're often placed together at a starport.

**Ticket *purchase* UI is entirely client-driven -- the server's only
role at the terminal is telling the client which travel point to open
its native purchase interface for; the real purchase logic runs
later, from a slash command, not from the terminal interaction
itself.** `TravelTerminalImplementation::handleObjectMenuSelect()`
(`TravelTerminalImplementation.cpp:13-29`) does nothing but resolve
the terminal's associated `PlanetTravelPoint` and send an
`EnterTicketPurchaseModeMessage` -- a client-opcode message that tells
the game client to switch into its own built-in ticket-purchase mode,
not a server-driven SUI dialog like nearly everything else in this
guide's coverage of terminals. The client then presumably issues the
real purchase as a `PurchaseTicketCommand` slash command once the
player picks departure/arrival points in that native UI.

**Fare calculation, city travel tax, and payment all happen inside one
long command handler, with a real bank-then-cash payment-splitting
rule and independent ban checks on both the departure and destination
city.** `PurchaseTicketCommand::doQueueCommand()`
(`PurchaseTicketCommand.h:20-318`) requires standing within `8`
units of a real `TRAVELTERMINAL`-type object, checks the player isn't
banned from the *departure* city (`isBanned()`) and separately that
the resolved arrival shuttle's own city hasn't banned them either
(`:56-59`, `:139-143`) -- **a ticket purchase can fail specifically
because of the destination city's ban list**, not just wherever the
player is currently standing. Fare is `pmDeparture->getTravelFare
(departurePlanet, arrivalPlanet)` plus a departure city's
`getTravelTax()` (skipped for `isClientRegion()` -- a special/reserved
region type, the same flag seen gating structure placement in section
59) -- doubled for a round trip. Payment always drains the bank first,
only touching cash for whatever the bank can't cover
(`:220-263`), logged as two separately-committed but
`groupWith()`-linked `TransactionLog` entries when split across both
sources (the same transaction-audit system from section 39). **Travel
legality itself is asymmetric and independently checked per
direction** -- `isTravelToLocationPermitted()` is checked once for the
outbound leg and, only for round trips, checked *again* in the reverse
direction, meaning a one-way-only route can still sell a single ticket
even if the return leg would be blocked.

**A one-time "New Player Travel Coupon" item can substitute for cash
on a one-way ticket specifically, offered via an explicit SUI choice
rather than auto-applied.** If a matching item CRC
(`new_player_travel_coupon.iff`) is found in inventory and the ticket
isn't a round trip, the command stops short of charging anything and
instead opens a `SuiMessageBox` (`SuiWindowType::TRAVEL_TICKET_
SELECTION`) letting the player explicitly choose "use coupon" vs. "pay
credits normally" (`:172-213`) -- the coupon is never silently
consumed even when present and cheaper, keeping the choice in the
player's hands. **This entire code path is skipped for round-trip
purchases** -- the coupon mechanic only ever applies to single tickets.

**A successful purchase creates real, transferable ticket item(s) via
the departure/arrival `PlanetManager`s' own `createTicket()` factory,
checked against inventory volume *before* any credits are spent** --
`spaceNeeded = (roundTrip ? 2 : 1) + inventorySize` is validated
against `getContainerVolumeLimit()` up front (`:159-168`), so a
purchase can't leave a player having paid but unable to receive the
physical ticket item. If the post-payment `transferObject()` call
still somehow fails, the already-created ticket is explicitly
`destroyObjectFromDatabase()`-cleaned rather than left orphaned
(`:279-296`) -- consistent with this codebase's broader "don't leave
half-completed state behind on a failure path" discipline seen
elsewhere (structure destruction in section 54, camp placement
rollback in section 60).

**Boarding the shuttle at a `TicketCollector` dispatches through a raw
opcode constant via `executeObjectControllerAction()`, not a normal
`QueueCommand`/slash-command -- the same low-level action-dispatch
mechanism documented in section 25's network/packet-layer coverage.**
`TicketCollectorImplementation::handleObjectMenuSelect()`
(`TicketCollectorImplementation.cpp:41-72`) for the standard "board"
radial option (`selectedID == 20`) does nothing but call
`player->executeObjectControllerAction(0x5DCD41A2)` -- a literal
hashed opcode identifying the client's own "boardShuttle" action,
resolved and handled entirely inside the object-controller action
pipeline rather than this file. This section did not trace that action
handler itself, only confirmed the entry point. Separately, a
`TicketCollector` can moonlight as a quest trigger point completely
unrelated to travel -- a specific Force-sensitive village quest step
("Obtain Satellite Data") adds its own radial option gated on
`JediManager`'s progression mode and the player's active quest-bit
state, dispatching into a Lua screenplay function
(`DirectorManager`/`FsCrafting4.obtainSatelliteData`, the Lua bridge
from section 29) directly from C++ -- a concrete example of a single
object class serving two functionally unrelated purposes (travel
boarding and an unrelated quest interaction) gated by different radial
option IDs on the same object.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't assume every terminal interaction in
this codebase drives a server-authored SUI -- `TravelTerminal` is a
real counterexample where the entire purchase form lives in the
client's own built-in UI, with the server only supplying the relevant
travel-point context via a client-opcode message. (2) fare/tax/coupon
logic all lives in one command handler rather than being split across
smaller helper functions -- any custom modification to fares (a new
discount type, a loyalty program, etc.) needs to be inserted carefully
into this existing flow rather than assumed to live in some separate
pricing service. (3) the destination-city ban check is easy to miss
when reasoning about "can this player travel here" -- both ends of the
route are independently checked, not just the player's current
location. (4) `executeObjectControllerAction()` with a raw opcode
constant is this codebase's escape hatch for triggering client-side
built-in behaviors (like boarding a shuttle) that don't have a
corresponding server-side `QueueCommand` -- worth recognizing this
pattern if a future trace runs into an unfamiliar hex constant passed
to that function elsewhere in the codebase.

## 65. Structure Power System (Harvesters/Factories)

Traced through `StructureObject.idl`'s power fields,
`InstallationObjectImplementation.cpp`,
`InsertPowerSuiCallback.h`, and
`ResourceManagerImplementation::getAvailablePowerFromPlayer()/
removePowerFromPlayer()`. This is a third, independent upkeep resource
alongside credits-based maintenance (section 54) -- but only for
`InstallationObject`s (harvesters, factories), not ordinary housing --
and unlike maintenance, running out of power just pauses work rather
than triggering decay/condemnation/destruction.

**Power is fueled by literally consuming harvested energy-type
resources from a player's inventory, weighted by that specific
resource's Potential Energy (PE) stat -- a higher-quality energy
resource is worth more power per unit consumed, directly tying
resource quality (sections 5/40) into structure upkeep economics.**
`ResourceManagerImplementation::getAvailablePowerFromPlayer()`
(`ResourceManagerImplementation.cpp:299-324`) scans a player's
inventory for `ResourceContainer`s whose resource spawn `isEnergy()`,
computing `power += quantity * max(1.0, PE/500.0)` per stack -- so two
otherwise-identical energy resource stacks of the same quantity can
fuel meaningfully different amounts of power depending on the specific
spawn's rolled PE quality. `InsertPowerSuiCallback::run()`
(`InsertPowerSuiCallback.h:23-69`) is the deposit flow: validates the
requested amount against what the player's inventory can actually
supply, calls `installation->addPower(energy)` and
`removePowerFromPlayer()` (which spends down the *actual* resource
stacks, oldest-container-first per its loop direction, not just an
abstract number) as a matched pair, and reports the installation's new
`getSurplusPower()` back to the player.

**Power and maintenance are checked and consumed completely
independently during a harvester/factory's elapsed-time extraction
catch-up, and either one running out independently truncates how much
of that elapsed time actually counted as "working."** The shared
elapsed-time-processing function in
`InstallationObjectImplementation.cpp` (around `:280-328`) computes
`payAmount = (elapsedTime/3600) * maintenanceRate`; if that exceeds
`surplusMaintenance`, it recomputes a shorter `workTimePermitted` from
however much maintenance was actually available and sets
`shutdownWork = true`. **Then, entirely separately**, it computes
`energyAmount = (elapsedTime/3600) * basePowerRate` (using the
*already-possibly-truncated* elapsedTime from the maintenance check)
and repeats the identical pattern against `surplusPower` -- so a
harvester with plenty of power but no maintenance, or plenty of
maintenance but no power, is throttled to whichever resource actually
ran out first, and a `getBasePowerRate() == 0` structure (most
non-installation structures, and some installation types) skips the
power check entirely via that guard. This is the same core mechanic as
section 40's offline-extraction-catchup formula, just with two
independent resource ceilings feeding into it instead of one.

**A structure whose base power rate is zero is architecturally exempt
from power tracking altogether -- power isn't a universal structure
concept the way maintenance is, it's opt-in per structure type via
`getBasePowerRate()`.** Ordinary housing, guild halls, and most
civic structures never check `surplusPower` at all (`basePowerRate !=
0` gates the entire block); only installations that actually do
resource-extraction or crafting work (harvesters, factories) have a
nonzero base power rate and therefore participate in this system.
Operators are proactively warned when an installation is running dry:
`InstallationObjectImplementation.cpp:92-98` broadcasts a
`"power_deposit_incomplete"` chat message to all operators the moment
`surplusPower <= 0` on a power-consuming installation, mirroring an
identical maintenance-exhausted broadcast right below it
(`:100-106`, `"harvester_no_maint_4"`) -- both warnings exist
side-by-side as the same kind of proactive operator notification, even
though the two resources have very different downstream consequences
(power exhaustion pauses work; maintenance exhaustion, per section 54,
eventually decays and destroys the structure entirely).

**Practical takeaways:** (1) power exhaustion is a soft, recoverable
"stop working until refueled" state, structurally distinct from
maintenance exhaustion's hard "decay, then condemn, then destroy"
consequence chain (section 54) -- a custom feature reasoning about
"why did this harvester stop producing" needs to check both resources
separately, since only one of the two failure modes threatens the
structure's actual existence. (2) any custom power-consuming structure
type just needs a nonzero `getBasePowerRate()` to opt into this entire
system automatically -- the elapsed-time truncation, operator warning
broadcast, and deposit UI all already generically handle any
installation with a nonzero rate, no new plumbing required. (3) the
PE-weighted power-value formula is a concrete, reusable example of
"a raw resource's rolled stat quality feeding directly into gameplay
value," worth reusing verbatim if a custom mechanic wants resource
quality to matter for something other than crafting (section 20) or
raw extraction (section 40). (4) `removePowerFromPlayer()` walks and
mutates a player's actual resource-container stacks, not an abstract
currency -- a custom "auto-refuel my harvester" convenience feature
would need to call this exact function (or replicate its stack-
draining logic precisely) rather than just decrementing a number, to
keep the player's inventory state consistent with what was actually
"spent."

---

## 66. Static/Dynamic NPC Spawn System (World Population)

Traced through `SpawnObserver.idl`,
`DynamicSpawnObserverImplementation.cpp`, and `SpawnAreaMap.h`. This
is the open-world wildlife/herd population layer, structurally
distinct from the damage-reactive lair system in section 62 even
though the two share a common ancestor class.

**`LairObserver` (section 62) and `DynamicSpawnObserver` are sibling
subclasses of one shared `SpawnObserver` base, not independent
systems that happen to look similar.** `SpawnObserver.idl:17-39`
defines the common fields both actually use --
`lairTemplate`/`spawnedCreatures`/`difficulty`/`babiesSpawned`/`size`
-- as an `abstract` `Observer` subclass with no default spawn behavior
of its own; each concrete subclass supplies its own
`notifyObserverEvent()` implementing genuinely different lifecycle
rules on top of that shared bookkeeping. This is the same
Observer/Observable foundation used throughout this guide (section
47), applied here to two different flavors of "thing that spawns and
manages a group of creatures."

**Where a lair's spawn waves are gated by combat damage, a dynamic
spawn point's population is gated by a hard per-creature respawn
count -- once every creature has individually respawned three times,
the entire spawn point self-destructs.**
`DynamicSpawnObserverImplementation::notifyObserverEvent()`
(`DynamicSpawnObserverImplementation.cpp:11-77`) reacts to
`CREATUREDESPAWNED`: if the despawning agent's
`getRespawnCounter() > 2` (i.e., this is its fourth life), it's
permanently removed from `spawnedCreatures` rather than respawned
again, and **only once every tracked creature has been removed this
way** does the whole spawn point schedule its own destruction via
`DespawnDynamicSpawnTask` (a 60-second delayed cleanup). Any creature
still under its 3-respawn budget instead gets a fresh
`RespawnCreatureTask` scheduled on a level-scaled delay (`(60 +
level*2)` seconds) -- respawn timing scales up for tougher
creatures, unlike lairs where individual respawn timing
(section 62) is a flat random range regardless of creature level.

**Dynamic spawns natively support herding creatures via a dedicated
`CreatureHerdObserver`, coordinating group movement formation for an
entire pack rather than each creature acting independently -- a
capability the lair system doesn't have.**
`spawnInitialMobiles()` (`:79-209`) picks a random weighted mix of
mobile templates (the same weighted-random pattern used by lairs in
section 62), and for any spawned creature whose template
`isHerd()`, the *first* one spawned becomes the herd leader hosting a
new `CreatureHerdObserver` (registered via `ObserverEventType::HERD`
on itself); every subsequent herd-eligible creature registers onto
that *same* observer instance and gets `ObjectFlag::HERD`,
`FOLLOWING` movement state pointed at the leader, and (per the code's
own comment) dynamically-computed formation positioning handled
inside `CreatureHerdObserver` itself rather than a fixed offset
computed once at spawn time. This is a materially richer social-AI
capability than the lair system's simpler baby-follows-first-adult
mechanic (section 62) -- herding is explicitly a "many followers, one
shared coordinator observer" design, not pairwise following.

**A dynamic spawn point is anchored to a `SceneObject` (a
"building" parameter, likely a lightweight invisible marker object
rather than a real structure) instead of a destructible `TangibleObject`
lair -- there's no condition/HP pool, no maintenance, nothing to
attack; the only way this spawn point ends is by every creature
naturally exhausting its respawn budget or the anchor object itself
leaving the zone.** `OBJECTREMOVEDFROMZONE` triggers an immediate
`despawnSpawns()` (the same cleanup call lairs use on the equivalent
event), but there's no `OBJECTDESTRUCTION`/`DAMAGERECEIVED` handling
at all in this class -- consistent with dynamic spawns representing
ambient, non-combat-triggered wildlife (herds of grazing/roaming
creatures) rather than a defended camp a player is meant to assault.

**World-level spawn eligibility is governed by a separate
region-based registry, `SpawnAreaMap`, holding both positive spawn
regions and an explicit negative "no spawn" list -- this is the layer
that decides *where in the world* lairs/dynamic spawns are allowed to
exist at all, upstream of either observer's own runtime behavior.**
`SpawnAreaMap` (`SpawnAreaMap.h:14-53`) is a per-zone
`SynchronizedVectorMap<uint32, SpawnArea*>` keyed by a spawn hash, plus
a separate `noSpawnAreas` vector -- `addSpawnArea()`/
`addNoSpawnArea()` are the only mutators, and the class explicitly
allows duplicate inserts (`setAllowDuplicateInsertPlan()`), implying
multiple distinct spawn definitions can legitimately share the same
region. This is purely a registry/lookup structure; this section's
trace didn't follow how initial world population actually consumes it
to place lairs/dynamic spawn points at zone load, only confirmed the
registry itself and its role as the upstream "is spawning even
allowed here" gate that both spawn systems' initial placement must
consult.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) `SpawnObserver` is the correct base class
to extend for any genuinely new "manages a group of spawned NPCs"
feature -- it already provides the shared bookkeeping
(`spawnedCreatures`/`difficulty`/`babiesSpawned`) that both existing
subclasses build on, rather than starting from scratch. (2) the
respawn-counter-then-permanent-despawn lifecycle
(`getRespawnCounter() > 2`) is specifically a *dynamic-spawn* pattern,
not shared with lairs -- a lair respawns its mobiles indefinitely
(section 62) unless flagged as a destroy-mission lair, while a dynamic
spawn point has a hard, self-limiting lifetime baked in from the
start. Don't assume these two systems share expiration semantics. (3)
`CreatureHerdObserver` is the reusable component for any future
"group of NPCs should move and position together" feature -- it's
already decoupled from the dynamic-spawn-specific spawning logic that
creates it, registered as a standard observer on each herd member. (4)
`SpawnAreaMap`'s duplicate-allowing, region-plus-exclusion-list design
is a reasonable model for any custom "where is X allowed to happen in
the world" gate that needs both inclusion and exclusion zones checked
together, rather than a single boolean region flag.

---

## 67. Force Rank System (FRS) Council Arena

Traced through `FrsManagerImplementation.cpp`'s arena-challenge
functions and `handleDarkCouncilDeath()`. This is the real system
behind `checkForArenaDuel()`/`isPlayerFightingInArena()`, referenced
but explicitly flagged as *unrelated to the real PvP duel system* back
in section 51 (healing restrictions) and section 56 (the formal duel
system) -- this section is the actual explanation of what that arena
is. It extends the FRS overview already in section 9's Jedi/Force
coverage with the specific rank-challenge/promotion mechanics.

**FRS ranks are earned through real, lethal PvP combat inside a
dedicated arena cell -- winning a challenge against the current
rank-holder swaps their positions outright (promote the winner,
demote the loser), and the fight must end in an actual deathblow, not
just incapacitation, or the outcome doesn't resolve.**
`handleDarkCouncilDeath()` (`FrsManagerImplementation.cpp:3399-3465+`,
with an implied light-side mirror by naming convention) is invoked on
a real creature-death event, matches the killer/victim pair against
the live `ArenaChallengeData` list resolving which side was the
original challenger, and only proceeds if that specific challenge
`!isChallengeCompleted()` yet -- **any kill happening to coincide with
an active challenge, if the two combatants aren't the actual
registered challenger/accepter pair, is ignored by this function
entirely**, it's not simply "any arena kill resolves the nearest open
challenge." An accompanying player-facing message
(`"arena_incap_opponent"`) explicitly warns that incapacitating (not
killing) your opponent requires both players to remain in the arena
until the match fully resolves, warning that leaving prematurely can
forfeit the challenge -- **the system anticipates and explicitly
messages around the incapacitate-without-deathblow edge case** rather
than leaving players confused about why nothing happened.

**Challenging requires meeting a specific rank gate and an explicitly
open arena status window -- arenas aren't always available, and a
player can't challenge arbitrarily far above their current rank.**
`canPlayerIssueArenaChallenge()` (`FrsManagerImplementation.cpp:4041-
4053`) requires `rank > 0 && rank < 11` (an 11-tier rank ladder, floor
and ceiling both excluded from challenging further), `getArenaStatus()
== ARENA_OPEN` (a global open/closed toggle,
`FrsManager.idl:54-55` -- `ARENA_CLOSED` presumably blocks all new
challenges server-wide, e.g. during maintenance or a scheduled
non-arena window), `isEligibleForPromotion(player, rank+1)` (the
challenger must qualify for the *next* rank specifically, not any
arbitrary higher one), and `playerAbleToChallenge()`. The mirror
function, `canPlayerAcceptArenaChallenge()` (`:4027-4039`), requires
`rank > 1` (a rank-1 player apparently can't be challenged at all --
possibly the entry tier), at least one open challenge actually
targeting that rank (`getTotalOpenArenaChallenges(playerRank) > 0`),
and that the accepter hasn't already accepted a different pending
challenge. **Winning promotes the challenger to the loser's rank and
demotes the loser** (`:3461-3464`, only in the `challengerWon`
branch) -- when the *defender* (current rank-holder) wins instead, no
promotion/demotion happens at all, ranks simply stay as they were,
consistent with the mail text quoted directly in the source: the
defender "will remain at their station," while a losing challenger
merely "will live in shame for their defeat" without any rank penalty
mentioned.

**A winning fight still awards real PvP experience through the
ordinary PvP XP formula, but a forfeit explicitly skips XP entirely --
FRS arena kills aren't a separate, disconnected reward system, they
route through the same combat-XP pipeline as any other PvP kill.**
`calculatePvpExperienceChange()` is called for both the killer and
victim (asymmetric args -- the victim's call passes an extra flag
distinguishing it as the losing side's XP calculation) and applied via
`adjustFrsExperience()`, but only `if (!forfeit)` -- so a challenge
resolved by forfeit (presumably one side disconnecting or leaving) still
processes the rank promotion/demotion outcome but grants no XP to
either side. `removePersonalEnemyFlag()` is called on both
participants afterward, clearing whatever combat-flagged-enemy state
the fight itself set up, and PvP status is explicitly re-synced
between the two (`sendPvpStatusTo()` both directions) once the match
concludes -- since they were flagged attackable against each other
specifically for this match, that flag needs explicit unwinding once
it's over, the same category of "temporarily neutralize/re-flag PvP
status for a scoped interaction" pattern seen in section 56's duel
system and section 52/57's taming/DNA-sampling creature-neutralization
techniques.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) `checkForArenaDuel()` (section 51) and
this system are now both fully traced and confirmed genuinely
unrelated to the real formal duel system (section 56) -- three
separate "two players fighting under special rules" concepts exist in
this codebase (formal duels, FRS arena challenges, and ordinary open
PvP), each with its own state tracking and none sharing code with the
others. (2) FRS promotion is a real zero-sum swap, not a point-
accumulation ladder -- a custom feature touching Jedi progression
needs to account for the fact that someone is always demoted when
someone else is promoted via this path, there's no "everyone can rank
up simultaneously" mode. (3) the challenger/accepter-pair matching
logic in `handleDarkCouncilDeath()` is a good model for any future
"two specific players are in a scoped 1v1, only their mutual kill
counts" feature -- it explicitly guards against an unrelated
third-party kill in the same arena resolving someone else's pending
challenge. (4) `ARENA_OPEN`/`ARENA_CLOSED` is the correct global gate
to check before assuming FRS challenges are even possible at a given
moment -- unlike the formal duel system (always available) or ordinary
PvP, FRS arena access can be server-side toggled closed entirely.

---

## 68. Group/Combat XP Distribution Formula

Traced through `PlayerManagerImplementation::disseminateExperience()`
(`PlayerManagerImplementation.cpp:1937-2210+`). This extends section
13's group fundamentals and is a deliberate structural contrast to
section 61's loot distribution: **loot splits evenly across in-range
group members regardless of contribution; XP is strictly
damage-proportional per attacker, with grouping only adding a flat
multiplier on top** -- the two systems solve "how do we divide the
spoils of a kill" in genuinely opposite ways.

**Every attacker who dealt any damage to the kill -- grouped or not,
even from a completely different group -- gets XP proportional to
their own share of total damage dealt, read directly off a per-kill
`ThreatMap`.** For each `ThreatMapEntry` (`:2149-2180`), and for each
weapon/XP-type tracked within that entry separately (a `ThreatMap`
entry breaks damage down by `xpType`, so a player who used two
different weapon types during the fight gets XP split correctly across
both skill lines): `xpAmount = baseXp * (damage / totalDamage)`, capped
per-type at `playerLevel * 300`, with `winningFaction`-matching GCW
bonus and (only if the attacker is currently grouped)
`groupExpMultiplier` applied afterward. **Grouping never redistributes
anyone else's earned share -- it purely scales up what each individual
attacker already earned from their own damage contribution.** This
directly falsifies the common assumption (carried over from loot
mechanics) that group XP is "pooled and split" -- it isn't; each
attacker's XP is computed entirely independently from every other
attacker's, using only their own damage numbers.

**A group leader earns a separate, additional "squad" XP bonus scaled
by both the fight's combat XP and the group's size -- a real
leadership incentive layered on top of ordinary XP, not just
cosmetic.** `squadXp = (combatXp * 0.1) + (combatXp * 0.1 *
groupSize)` (`:2189-2190`) is computed per-attacker and awarded
separately to `group->getLeader()` (not the attacker themselves,
unless they happen to be the leader) -- so a group leader earns bonus
XP off of *every* member's individual kills, scaling with how many
people are in the group, entirely independent of whether the leader
personally participated in that specific kill at all.

**Jedi XP is deliberately discounted and excluded from the general
combat-XP pool, and DoT-sourced damage is excluded from weapon-specific
XP while still counting toward the combat-XP total.**
`xpType != "jedi_general"` gates whether damage counts toward
`combatXp` at all (`:2168-2172`) -- Jedi XP is earned at a flat `20%`
rate and never feeds the shared `combat_general`/squad-leader-bonus
pool the way ordinary weapon-type XP does. Separately, `xpType ==
"dotDMG"` skips the per-type `awardExperience()` call entirely
(`:2174-2176`) -- DoT damage still contributed to `combatXp` upstream,
just doesn't get credited to any specific weapon skill line, since
there's no single weapon that "caused" a bleed/poison/fire tick the
way a direct hit has an obvious attributable weapon.

**Creature-handler pets earn XP through a completely separate,
flat (non-damage-proportional) formula, divided across the owner's
total active creature-pet count -- and this branch shares the exact
same `isPet()`/`PetControlDevice`-cast pattern already identified as
this project's own root-cause family for the TEF and friendly-fire
bugs.** The pet-attacker branch (`:2038-2115`) computes
`xpAmount = levelRatio * 500` (clamped to `1` if the target is more
than double the pet's level, otherwise capped at `attackerLevel * 50`
and divided by `totalPets` -- the code's own `// TODO: Find a more
correct CH xp formula` comment flags this formula as provisional, not
finalized), gated on `pcd->getPetType() == PetManager::CREATUREPET`
(`:2052-2057`) -- **the identical cast-to-`PetControlDevice`-and-check-
type pattern that this project already found and fixed for TEF
flagging (`CombatManager.cpp`) and friendly-fire (`AiAgentImplementation
.cpp`/`CreatureObjectImplementation.cpp`)**. A companion dealing damage
during a kill would fail this cast exactly like those two previously-
fixed cases, meaning **a companion's damage contribution likely
currently earns its owner zero XP credit through this specific pet-XP
branch** -- though critically, if the owner *also* personally dealt
damage in the same fight, the owner still earns their own full,
correctly-computed XP share through the ordinary `isPlayerCreature()`
branch for their own contribution; only a companion's own separate
damage-share specifically would be silently dropped, the same
"pet-family bug, but bounded to just this one branch" scope already
established for the previously-fixed issues.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any custom XP-related feature should
reuse the `ThreatMap`-share formula (`baseXp * damage/totalDamage`,
level-capped, group-multiplied) rather than assuming an even split --
this is the load-bearing mental model correction versus the loot
system documented in section 61. (2) the squad-leader bonus is a real,
separate incentive worth knowing about when reasoning about "who
benefits from being group leader" -- it's not just an organizational
role, it has a direct passive-XP payoff scaling with group size. (3)
**this section surfaces a new, not-yet-fixed candidate instance of the
isPet()/PetControlDevice-cast bug family** in the creature-handler
pet-XP branch specifically -- flagged here and cross-referenced into
HANDOFF.md's backlog for whichever chat next does companion combat/XP
work, following the exact same fix shape already proven for the TEF
and friendly-fire fixes (extend the `isPet()`/cast check with
`isCompanionObject()` + `getLinkedCreature()` fallback at this one
call site). (4) the DoT-damage-counts-for-combatXp-but-not-weapon-XP
split is worth remembering for any custom DoT-dealing item/ability --
it will contribute to the attacker's overall combat XP total and squad
bonus, but never to a specific weapon skill line's XP.

## 69. Crafting Experimentation / Quality-Roll Formulas

Traced through `CraftingManagerImplementation::
calculateExperimentationSuccess()/calculateExperimentationFailureRate()`,
`SharedLabratory::calculateAssemblySuccess()/
calculateExperimentationValueModifier()`, and `ResourceLabratory::
experimentRow()`. This extends sections 20/42's crafting/manufacturing
coverage with the actual "roll a nine-tier outcome, then nudge a
crafted item's stats toward their resource-determined ceiling" formula
chain underneath the classic SWG crafting experimentation UI.

**Crafting is split into a `SharedLabratory` abstraction with
per-category subclasses (`ResourceLabratory`, `GeneticLabratory`,
`DroidLabratory`), each schematic declaring which lab handles it --
assembly and experimentation share the same overall formula shape but
are computed and applied through genuinely different code paths, not
one shared "craft" function.** `CraftingManagerImplementation::
initialize()` (`CraftingManagerImplementation.cpp:11-15`) builds a
`labs` map keyed by `DraftSchematicObjectTemplate`'s lab-type constant
(`RESOURCE_LAB`/`GENETIC_LAB`/etc.), and both
`calculateAssemblySuccess()` and `experimentRow()` simply look up the
schematic's own declared lab and delegate to it -- meaning a custom
schematic category with genuinely different crafting rules (the
project already has precedent for this with genetic/droid labs) is
architecturally supported by adding a new `SharedLabratory` subclass,
not by branching inside a shared function.

**Both assembly and experimentation rolls follow the identical
nine-tier outcome formula shape -- a skill-scaled roll compared
against fixed thresholds, with city specialization, Force bonuses, a
food buff, and tool effectiveness all independently stacking into the
same roll.** `calculateExperimentationSuccess()`
(`CraftingManagerImplementation.cpp:63-132`, `SharedLabratory::
calculateAssemblySuccess()` mirrors it almost line-for-line at
`SharedLabratory.cpp:143+`): `experimentingPoints = (skillMod +
force_experimentation) / 10`, a `failMitigate` term derived from the
*other* (assembly) skill mod clamped to `[0,5]`, a `toolModifier =
1 + effectiveness/100` further boosted by an active food buff
(`FOOD_EXPERIMENT_BONUS`/`FOOD_CRAFT_BONUS` respectively -- the code
comments name the specific consumables, "Bespin Port" for
experimentation and "Pyollian Cake" for assembly, real in-universe
flavor items), and a base `luckRoll = random(100) + cityBonus`
(`private_spec_experimentation`/`private_spec_assembly` -- the same
`SkillModManager::CITY`-tagged bonus mechanic from section 34's city
specialization coverage) that can early-return `AMAZINGSUCCESS`
outright if it clears a bonus-adjusted `95` threshold, or spiral
further negative via a second random draw if it falls under a
mirrored low threshold (the `CRITICALFAILURE` branch is explicitly
commented out in the experimentation path -- `//if(luckRoll < 5)
return CRITICALFAILURE;` -- meaning critical failure is reachable via
the low-roll cascade but not as its own explicit early-return branch
today). The final `experimentRoll = toolModifier * (luckRoll +
experimentingPoints*4)` is compared against seven descending
thresholds (`70/60/50/40/30/20`) producing
`GREATSUCCESS`/`GOODSUCCESS`/`MODERATESUCCESS`/`SUCCESS`/
`MARGINALSUCCESS`/`OK`/`BARELYSUCCESSFUL` -- a nine-outcome tier
(including the two extremes) from one continuous roll, not nine
separate probability checks.

**Each outcome tier maps to a fixed percentage-point modifier applied
directly to a crafted item's stat rows, with failures actually
*subtracting* from quality rather than merely granting zero --
experimentation is a real risk/reward mechanic, not a
capped-at-zero-downside one.**
`calculateExperimentationValueModifier()`
(`SharedLabratory.cpp:21-51+`) maps outcome tier to a flat modifier:
`AMAZINGSUCCESS` = `+0.08`, descending through the tiers to
`MARGINALSUCCESS` = `0.00`, then genuinely negative for the bottom
tiers -- `OK` = `-0.04`, `BARELYSUCCESSFUL` = `-0.07`,
`CRITICALFAILURE` = `-0.08` -- so experimenting isn't a one-way
ratchet toward better stats; a bad roll on a subsequent experimentation
pass can measurably *undo* quality already achieved on that same
attribute row. `ResourceLabratory::experimentRow()`
(`ResourceLabratory.cpp:120-158`) applies that modifier to **every
attribute sharing the same "experimented group"** as the row being
worked on (a "row" in the crafting UI is really a named group of
attributes that move together, e.g. all the stats that share one
resource-quality lever), clamping the result to `[0, maxPercentage]`
per attribute -- `maxPercentage` itself is resource-quality-derived
(tying back to sections 5/40's resource-attribute coverage), so the
experimentation roll only ever moves a stat *toward* the ceiling the
chosen ingredients already set, never past it.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) a custom crafting category should extend
`SharedLabratory` and override `experimentRow()`/
`calculateAssemblySuccess()` rather than trying to special-case
existing lab logic -- the architecture already expects and supports
category-specific crafting rules via this exact extension point. (2)
the nine-tier outcome-to-percentage-modifier table
(`calculateExperimentationValueModifier()`) is the single place that
defines "how much does each success tier actually move the needle" --
any crafting-balance tuning work should start there rather than
touching the roll-threshold formula itself. (3) experimentation
genuinely risks quality loss on a bad roll, not just "no gain" -- a
custom crafting UI/assistant feature should account for and clearly
communicate this downside risk to players rather than assuming
experimentation is safe to always attempt. (4) resource quality
(`maxPercentage`) is the hard ceiling experimentation rolls can never
exceed regardless of skill -- any custom "guaranteed max quality"
crafting shortcut item/ability would need to either bypass this
clamp explicitly or accept that it's fundamentally bounded by
whatever resources were used, consistent with this codebase's
resource-quality-matters design philosophy seen throughout sections
5, 20, 40, and 65.

## 70. Skill Training / Trainer NPC System

Traced through `SkillManager::canLearnSkill()/awardSkill()/
surrenderSkill()/fulfillsSkillPrerequisites()`
(`SkillManager.cpp:329-1030+`). This is the missing piece behind
section 55's SkillMod pipeline coverage -- the actual moment a
learned skill's bonuses get pushed into `skillModList` -- and, notably,
this file already contains a real, deployed companion-system patch
worth knowing about directly.

**Learning a skill costs two independent currencies simultaneously --
a shared "skill points" pool and skill-type-specific experience --
and both are withdrawn together as one transaction, not two separate
purchase steps.** `canLearnSkill()` (`SkillManager.cpp:929-971`)
gates on: not already having the skill, `fulfillsSkillPrerequisites()`
passing, sufficient `ghost->getExperience(skill->getXpType())` against
`skill->getXpCost()` (skipped if `noXpRequired`), and sufficient
`ghost->getSkillPoints()` against `skill->getSkillPointsRequired()`.
`awardSkill()` (`:329-450+`) is the actual grant: it recursively
awards any missing required skills first (if `awardRequiredSkills` is
set), re-validates via `canLearnSkill()`, then withdraws both
currencies as a single `TrxCode::SKILLTRAININGSYSTEM`-logged
transaction (skill points via `ghost->addSkillPoints(-cost)`,
experience via a grouped, separately-logged `TrxCode::EXPERIENCE`
transaction) before actually granting anything.

**This is the exact call site that pushes a learned skill's bonuses
into `skillModList` -- confirming and sharpening section 55's finding
about the companion `grantSkill()`/`addSkillMod()` gap with the
precise one-line-per-modifier pattern to replicate.**
`awardSkill()` (`:384-391`) loops the skill's own
`getSkillModifiers()` and calls `creature->addSkillMod
(SkillModManager::SKILLBOX, modName, modValue, notifyClient)` **directly
inline**, per modifier -- not through a separate reconciliation pass.
This means the real mechanism a companion's own skill-grant path is
missing isn't necessarily a call to `verifySkillBoxSkillMods()`
(section 55's more general-purpose suggestion) but potentially just
this exact loop, copied verbatim: for each modifier the granted skill
provides, call `addSkillMod(SkillModManager::SKILLBOX, key, value,
notifyClient)`. The same grant call also adds abilities
(`addAbilities()`), grants any `getSchematicsGranted()` draft schematic
groups via `SchematicMap`, recalculates XP caps
(`updateXpLimits()`) and Force power max
(`ghost->recalculateForcePower()`), and -- for any skill whose name
contains `"master"` -- looks up and awards a matching `Badge` (the
badge system from section 22), including a hardcoded special-case
alias (`crafting_shipwright_master` maps to the `crafting_shipwright`
badge specifically, a naming mismatch the code works around directly
rather than fixing at the data level).

**This exact function already contains a real, live companion-system
patch -- not something for a future chat to add, it's already
deployed.** `canLearnSkill()`/`awardSkill()` both special-case
`skillName.beginsWith("companion_master_")`
(`:958-963`, `:366-373`) to skip the skill-points cost entirely
(XP cost is *not* exempted, only skill points), with an inline
comment explicitly citing `docs/companion_system/NOTES.md`, "Skill
point isolation / companion_master player profession." **This is the
real player's own skill-point economy being protected from the
companion-training UI** -- learning companion-master tiers must not
compete with or drain the player's own real skill-point budget, so
this project already patched the shared, general-engine
`SkillManager` function to carve out that exemption rather than
building a fully separate companion skill-training path. Worth
knowing this patch exists here specifically if a future trace of
`SkillManager.cpp` seems to behave unexpectedly for
`companion_master_*` skill names -- it's intentional and documented.

**Surrendering (forgetting) a skill is gated by a dependency check in
the *opposite* direction from learning, and certain skill categories
can't be surrendered through this generic path at all.**
`surrenderSkill()` (`:591-650+`) first checks whether *any* currently-
held skill lists the skill-to-be-surrendered as one of its own
prerequisites (`checkSkill->isRequiredSkillOf(skill)`) -- you can't
drop a skill that something else you still have depends on, the
inverse direction of `fulfillsSkillPrerequisites()`'s forward check
used when learning. `force_`-prefixed (Jedi) skills route through a
separate `JediManager::canSurrenderSkill()` gate entirely, and
`pilot_`-prefixed (military rank) skills are blocked from manual
surrender outright unless `allowPilot` is explicitly passed --
instead redirecting the player to a **faction recruiter NPC** via a
`SuiMessageBox` with a "Get Waypoint" option and faction-specific
flavor text (Corellia for Rebel, Naboo for Imperial, Tatooine for
neutral pilots) -- military/pilot rank surrender is intentionally
routed through an in-world NPC interaction rather than a bare command,
presumably to keep it a deliberate, narratively-grounded choice rather
than a casual one-click undo.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) `awardSkill()`'s `addSkillMod
(SkillModManager::SKILLBOX, ...)` loop is the precise, minimal fix
target for the companion `grantSkill()`/stat-application gap flagged
in sections 55 and 68's HANDOFF.md backlog entries -- this section
confirms the exact call shape to replicate rather than needing to
build a general reconciliation pass. (2) the existing
`companion_master_`-prefix skill-point exemption already live in this
shared function is a real precedent for "carve out a narrow,
name-prefix-gated exemption in shared engine code rather than forking
it" -- worth following the same pattern for any future companion-
specific tweak to core skill-learning behavior, rather than
duplicating `SkillManager` logic elsewhere. (3) skill learning/
surrendering both independently validate prerequisites in their
respective directions -- a custom skill tree addition needs to
correctly declare `getSkillsRequired()` for this bidirectional
validation to behave correctly, in both learn-order and
surrender-order. (4) if a custom feature ever needs to route a
player through an NPC conversation as part of a restricted action
(mirroring the pilot-surrender recruiter flow), the `SuiMessageBox`-
with-waypoint-button pattern here is a clean, reusable template for
"you can't do this directly, go talk to someone" UX.

## 71. Group Invite / Kick / Disband / Leadership Mechanics

`GroupManager.cpp` (`server/zone/managers/group/`) implements group
membership as a genuinely two-phase invite-then-accept flow, not a
single atomic action. `inviteToGroup()` (line 41+) doesn't add anyone
to a group directly -- it just stamps a `groupInviterID` field on the
*target* creature (a plain object-ID field, not a session object or
pending-request list) and sends the client-side invite prompt. The
actual join only happens later when `joinGroup()` is separately called
(from the client's accept action), which reads that same
`groupInviterID` back off the target. This two-step shape has a real
edge case handled explicitly: if the group's leader changed between
the invite being sent and the invitee accepting, `joinGroup()` detects
the mismatch and silently fails the join with a "leader has abdicated
to X" message rather than blindly joining the invitee under whatever
leader is now in charge. If the inviter isn't in a group at all yet,
accepting instead calls `createGroup()`, forming a brand-new group
rather than erroring.

Invites are leader-only (with one exception: an owner can always invite
their own pet, regardless of who leads the group), gated by a hard
20-member cap (`group->getGroupSize() >= 20`) and the
`Core3.PlayerManager.GalaxyWideGrouping` config toggle, which affects
whether the invite prompt shows the target's display name or a raw
object ID depending on cross-galaxy visibility rules. Pets get a small
but deliberate extra: when an owner invites their own pet, the actual
join is deferred through a randomized 250-500ms scheduled task
(`Core::getTaskManager()->scheduleTask(..., "PetJoinGroupLambda", ...)`)
rather than joining synchronously -- a small stagger to avoid races
when multiple pets join in the same tick.

**Leaving, kicking, and disbanding all funnel through the same
"a group of one isn't a group" rule.** `leaveGroup()` (line 379+) and
`kickFromGroup()` (line 480+) both check the resulting group size after
removing the member: if it would drop below 2, the *entire* group is
disbanded via `group->disband()` rather than leaving a lone member
sitting in a one-person "group." `kickFromGroup()` is leader-only;
`leaveGroup()` is self-service. Both also explicitly tear down the
departing member's group-chat-room membership
(`groupChat->removePlayer()` + `sendDestroyTo()` on both the group chat
room and its parent room) rather than relying on the chat system to
notice the roster change on its own. `disbandGroup()` (line 435+) is
leader-only and has one extra piece of cleanup neither leave nor kick
needs: it explicitly closes three specific Group Loot SUI window types
(`GROUP_LOOT_RULE`, `GROUP_LOOT_CHANGED`, `GROUP_LOOT_PICK_LOOTER`, see
section 61) for every player member before disbanding, so nobody is
left staring at a loot-rule popup for a group that no longer exists.

`leaveGroup()`'s implementation is also a clean, concrete example of
this codebase's defensive locking idiom under exception safety: it
takes the group lock, does its work inside a `try` block, and the
`catch (...)` handler re-acquires the creature's own lock
(`creature->wlock()`) before re-throwing -- guaranteeing the caller
always gets back a creature in the same lock state it was passed in,
even if something inside the try block throws partway through. The
same shape (lock, try, restore-lock-on-catch-then-rethrow) recurs
throughout the manager layer wherever a function's contract promises a
specific pre/post lock state.

`makeLeader()` (line 558+) is comparatively simple: it validates the
new leader is actually a current member and that the caller is still
the group's actual current leader (guards against a stale/racing
leadership-transfer request), locks the new leader, and calls
`group->makeLeader(newLeader)` -- no group-chat or SUI cleanup needed
since membership itself doesn't change, only who holds the leader
flag. `joinGroupEntertainingSession()` (line 582) is unrelated to
membership -- it's a small helper that lets a currently-performing
entertainer's music/dance session follow them into whatever
`EntertainingSession` context applies, called when relevant rather
than being part of the invite/join/leave flow itself.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) `groupInviterID` is the correct model for
any future two-phase "invite must be separately accepted" feature --
a plain ID field on the target plus a leader-mismatch re-check at
accept time, not a pending-request collection that needs its own
cleanup. (2) the "auto-disband below 2 members" rule means any code
that reasons about "the group" after a leave/kick must not assume the
group object is still valid -- always re-check `group->getGroupSize()`
or re-fetch after either operation. (3) the lock/try/restore-on-catch
idiom in `leaveGroup()` is the reusable template for any manager
function whose contract requires guaranteeing a caller's object is
left in a known lock state regardless of whether an exception occurs
mid-operation. (4) pets already have a proven, working group-membership
path (`inviteToGroup()`'s pet branch + the randomized join-delay task)
-- a companion-in-group feature could very plausibly reuse this exact
mechanism rather than building new group-membership code, since
companions and pets already share several other abstractions
(`linkedCreature`, see section 43).

---

## 72. Entertainer Performance Formulas (extends section 23)

The real performance loop lives in
`objects/player/sessions/EntertainingSessionImplementation.cpp`
(backed by `EntertainingSession.idl`), driven by a 10-second self-
rescheduling tick (`startTickTask()`/`EntertainingSessionTask`,
lines 230-238) -- the same named-recurring-Task idiom documented in
section 48. Each tick runs, in order: `doEntertainerPatronEffects()`
(wound/shock healing), `awardEntertainerExperience()`, then
`doPerformanceAction()` (action-point drain).

**Wound/battle-fatigue healing is a real skill-scaled formula, not a
flat tick.** `doEntertainerPatronEffects()` (lines 33-126) pulls the
relevant skill mod (`healing_dance_wound`/`healing_dance_shock` for
dance, `healing_music_wound`/`healing_music_shock` for music) plus two
optional bonuses -- a building perk (`private_med_battle_fatigue`) and
a same-faction building perk (`private_faction_mind_heal`), both only
if the entertainer is OVERT and registered in a qualifying building.
The actual heal amounts read from a per-performance datatable row
(`datatables/performance/performance.iff`, exposed via
`Performance::getHealMindWound()`/`getHealShockWound()`):
`woundHeal = ceil(healMindWound * (woundHealingSkill/100))`,
`shockHeal = ceil(healShockWound * ((skillHeal+buildingHeal)/100))` --
and critically, **both are then multiplied by `(flourishCount+1)`**,
so performing flourishes doesn't just add buff strength (below), it
directly multiplies wound-healing throughput for that tick, applied to
both the entertainer and every patron in `PerformanceManager::HEAL_RANGE`.

**There is no numeric "mood" system affecting buff magnitude.** The
`sendEntertainmentUpdate()` mood mechanic (line ~808) is purely
cosmetic -- it drives the chat mood animation
(`ChatManagerImplementation::getMoodAnimation()`) and
`setMoodString()`, nothing else. Instrument choice similarly only
gates which songs/animations are available, not buff strength -- a
full codebase search found no instrument-quality-affects-buff logic
anywhere. This is worth documenting explicitly since it contradicts a
plausible assumption (that better instruments or a matching "mood"
would produce stronger buffs) -- in this codebase they don't.

**Buff strength/duration accrue per-patron, per-tick and per-flourish,
then crystallize into a real `PerformanceBuff` object once thresholds
are met.** `increaseEntertainerBuff(patron)` runs every tick (and
again on every flourish via `addEntertainerFlourishBuff()`) for any
patron who is either grouped with the entertainer or has explicitly
targeted them via `/setPerformanceBuffTarget`. Duration growth is
`2.0 * buffAcceleration` minutes per call, where
`buffAcceleration = 1 + (accelerate_entertainer_buff skill mod / 100)`,
capped at ~120 minutes total. Strength growth per call is literally
the performance's own `getHealShockWound()` datatable value, capped at
the entertainer's `healing_dance_mind`/`healing_music_mind` skill mod
(itself capped at 125%) plus an optional `private_faction_buff_mind`
building bonus -- strength gained beyond that cap doesn't convert to
extra healing XP either. The buff only actually applies once a patron
has accumulated **at least 10 seconds of buff duration and 60
continuous seconds of watching/listening**, at which point
`activateEntertainerBuff()` instantiates a real
`objects/creature/buffs/PerformanceBuff` (`performance_enhance_music_
focus`/`_willpower` for music, `performance_enhance_dance_mind` for
dance), sized by `buffStrength/100` and lasting `buffDuration*60`
