seconds -- and only *replaces* an existing buff if the new one is
strictly stronger, never downgrades a patron's current buff.

**XP is a multiplicative-bonus formula, not additive.**
`awardEntertainerExperience()`: `xpAmount = flourishXp +
performance->getBaseXp()`, then multiplied by
`totalBonus = 1 + groupMod + audienceMod + applauseMod`, where
`groupMod = 0.05` per other entertaining group member within 40m,
`audienceMod = min(bandAudienceSize, 50) / 50.0`, and
`applauseMod = applauseCount / 100.0` -- so a well-grouped, well-
attended, well-applauded performance can multiply base XP well beyond
1x, not just add flat bonuses per source. Flourishes themselves
(`doFlourish()`) drain action points scaled by Quickness and are capped
at 5 per performance loop, each adding `getFlourishXpMod()` toward
`flourishXp` up to a duration-derived cap.

**Group "band" mechanics are ID-equality checks, not a dedicated join
API.** There's no literal `joinGroupEntertainingSession()` function --
group participation for buff/XP-sharing purposes is determined purely
by `CreatureObject::getGroupID()` matching between performers, checked
inline wherever group bonuses apply. `joinBand()` does exist for a
narrower purpose: when a musician joins an already-performing grouped
band, it forces their song selection to match whatever the group is
currently playing (via `PerformanceManager::getMatchingPerformanceIndex()`),
stopping them if no match is found. `getBandAudienceSize()` sums
`getAudienceSize()` (real patron counts) across every grouped,
actively-performing member, which is what feeds the `audienceMod` term
in the XP formula above.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the flourish-multiplies-heal-output
mechanic means flourish spam is a legitimate, real DPS-equivalent
throughput lever for a dedicated healer-entertainer build, not just
flavor. (2) any new "performance buff" content (a custom song/dance,
or a companion performing) should read real values from a
`performance.iff` datatable row via the existing `Performance` class
rather than hand-rolling healing numbers, to stay consistent with the
skill-mod-capped formula already in place. (3) since mood/instrument
quality provably don't affect buff magnitude in this codebase, any
future feature description or UI shouldn't imply they do. (4) the
group-bonus system being pure `getGroupID()` equality (not a
dedicated "band" membership list) means any companion-as-entertainer
feature would need the companion to actually share the owner's real
group ID to participate in group XP/audience bonuses -- consistent
with section 71's finding that pets/companions already support real
group membership.

---

## 73. Overt/Covert Faction Status System

The whole subsystem is gated by one master config switch,
`ConfigManager::useCovertOvertSystem()` (`Core3.GCWManager.
useCovertOvertSystem`, default off) -- when off, the server falls back
to simpler legacy PvP logic, and roughly 35 call sites across the
codebase branch on it. The status itself is a plain `int` field on
`TangibleObject` (not `CreatureObject`), `FactionStatus.h` defining
just three real values: `ONLEAVE=0`, `COVERT=1`, `OVERT=2`. There is
**no distinct "Special Forces" enum value** -- that's purely client-
facing flavor text for `OVERT`, confirmed by the exact strings sent on
status change and terminal-access messages.

**Changing status is asymmetric by design.** Going ONLEAVE/OVERT ->
COVERT is a 30-second field SUI confirmation
(`PlayerObjectImplementation::doFieldFactionChange()`). Going -> OVERT
in the field takes a full 5 minutes and is explicitly blocked if
you're already OVERT or have a change already pending -- and going
OVERT -> COVERT specifically **cannot** be done in the field at all
("Go talk to a faction recruiter"), only via a dedicated recruiter NPC
screenplay. A separate, faster COVERT -> OVERT path exists via
`DeclareOvertCommand`: no timer at all, but only usable within 50m of
a friendly player-placed GCW base. Declaring OVERT (either path)
applies a real cooldown (`declare_overt_cooldown`, default 300s,
overridable per-zone via `GCWManagerImplementation::getOvertCooldown()`)
before it can be changed again.

**What each status actually gates.** With the system on,
`CreatureObjectImplementation::isAttackableBy()` requires OVERT-vs-OVERT
(or a TEF'd COVERT player) for opposing-faction PvP attackability -- a
plain COVERT player with no active TEF cannot be freely attacked. The
same exemption applies against hostile faction NPCs. GCW base terminals
can be restricted to OVERT-only ("Special Forces personnel only");
PvE-flagged bases require at least COVERT. Base *vulnerability*
(section 35) is gated on the building's own OVERT flag, not directly
the attacker's status. COVERT players get a 40% random detection roll
from scanner/contraband checks that OVERT players don't. Bounty hunting
(section 44) bypasses covert protection entirely -- a player with an
active bounty mission against them is attackable regardless of faction
status.

**Interaction with duels and TEF.** Formal duel participants
(section 56) are unconditionally exempt from GCW-TEF generation and
`isAttackableBy` short-circuits to `true` for them regardless of
faction status -- duels operate as a wholly separate attackability
channel layered on top. Attacking an opposing-faction target outside a
duel while COVERT-or-higher sets `ObjectFlag::TEF`, cleared once all
active TEF sources (GCW/bounty-hunter/crackdown/PvP-area) have expired.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any feature checking "can these two
characters fight" needs to account for faction status, TEF state, *and*
duel-list membership as three independently-gating layers, not one
check. (2) the asymmetric timer design (fast/no-timer to declare
OVERT near a base, slow/recruiter-gated to go OVERT->COVERT in general)
is a deliberate anti-abuse shape worth preserving if this ever gets
touched -- it prevents using OVERT status as a consequence-free
toggle. (3) `useCovertOvertSystem()` being off by default on a fresh
config matters for any feature relying on faction-status gating --
verify it's actually enabled on this server before assuming these
restrictions are live.

---

## 74. Bazaar / Commodities Cross-Vendor Search (extends section 24)

A search request lands in `AuctionManagerImplementation::getData()`,
which resolves scope via a `locationType` switch --
`LT_MARKET`/`LT_REGION`/`LT_PLANET`. **There is no true galaxy-wide
scope**, only vendor/region/planet, contrary to what "commodities
exchange" might imply. The request is offloaded 100ms later onto an
`AuctionSearchTask` rather than answered synchronously on the network
thread.

**There is no persisted search index.** `AuctionsMap` holds a live tree
(planet -> region -> vendor OID -> a real `SortedVector<AuctionItem*>`
per vendor). A search collapses the relevant branch of that tree into a
flat list of terminal item-lists and then does a genuine nested loop
over every terminal and every item in scope, applying filters
(category bitmask, min/max price with optional vendor entrance-fee
inclusion, case-insensitive substring name match) as it goes, capped at
100 results. This is a full live scan every time, not a cached/indexed
lookup -- consistent with this codebase's general pattern (seen
elsewhere too) of recomputing from live state rather than maintaining
a separate synced index.

**Remote purchase is a two-step, mail-mediated process, not instant
teleport-to-inventory.** Instant buy resolves the vendor object, moves
credits via a `TransactionLog`-audited `TrxCode::INSTANTBUY` (same
audited-transfer substrate as every other credit movement in this
codebase, section 39), and mails both buyer and seller a waypoint
pointing at the vendor's actual world location -- but the item itself
stays owned by the vendor entry. Physical retrieval only happens when
the buyer later visits that specific vendor/bazaar terminal in person
(an 8m range check, plus a city-region match for bazaar terminals) and
explicitly retrieves it, itself a second `TransactionLog`-audited
transfer.

**Fees are real and layered.** Listing costs a flat `SALESFEE=20`
credits (5x for featured/premium), discounted by Merchant skill mods
down to 60% at max rank. City sales tax (cross-referencing the city
government treasury system, section 77) is applied twice -- once
baked into the listed price at listing time, and deducted again from
the seller's proceeds at sale time, routed into the selling city's
treasury. Vendor listings expire after 30 days, bazaar/commodity
listings after 7.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "search all vendors" is always scoped
(vendor/region/planet), never truly galaxy-wide -- don't describe a
feature as searching "the whole galaxy" without checking which scope
constant is actually being requested. (2) the mail-plus-physical-
retrieval purchase model means a remote buy is never instantaneous
item delivery -- any UI/feature describing "buy" should reflect that
the item still has to be picked up. (3) both the sale and the retrieval
legs reuse the same `TransactionLog` substrate documented in section 39,
reinforcing that this is the correct pattern for any new credit/item
movement feature.

---

## 75. NPC AI Behavior Tree / Aggro / Patrol Deep Dive (extends section 28)

`AiAgentImplementation::runBehaviorTree()` is the real per-agent tick
entry point: it early-outs on disabled/dead/no-players-in-range (unless
following/retreating/load-testing), then calls the root behavior node's
`doAction()`. Re-tick interval is dynamic, not fixed: `PATROLLING`/
`RESTING` tick every 1000ms, `WATCHING` every 700ms, and everything
else -- combat, following, fleeing -- ticks at the fastest rate,
400ms, via constants on `AiAgent.idl`.

**The decision tree is real, authored Lua data (a Selector), not
hardcoded C++ branching.** `rootDefault` (`default.lua`) checks, in
priority order: HEAL -> call-for-help -> target/equip/attack (combat)
-> AWARE (detection) -> crackdown-scan -> chat-reaction -> IDLE
(patrol/rest/wander). **Pets run a genuinely different, shorter tree**
(`rootPet`, `pet.lua`): HEAL -> target/attack -> HARVEST -> AWARE ->
IDLE -- same engine, same node types, different authored data,
selected per-agent via `setAITemplate()`.

**Aggro detection** scans nearby players via a `LookForPlayer`
decorator (rejecting dead/feigning/invisible/cross-cell-without-LOS
targets), gated by `getAggroRadius()` (from the creature's template,
falling back to a `DEFAULTAGGRORADIUS=24` constant, capped at 96 by an
`aggroMod`), a stealth/camouflage check, an aggro-delay timer, and
faction/PvP aggression rules (`isAggressiveTo()`). **Pets skip
independent aggro-radius detection entirely** -- their `awarePet`/
`targetPet` branches key off explicit pet commands
(ATTACK/GUARD/PATROL/STAY) and owner proximity instead of the
creature aggro-radius path, a structurally different (not just
data-different) detection model.

**Movement states** form a 17-value enum (`OBLIVIOUS`, `WATCHING`,
`STALKING`, `FOLLOWING`, `PATROLLING`, `FLEEING`, `LEASHING`,
`EVADING`, `PATHING_HOME`, `FOLLOW_FORMATION`, `MOVING_TO_HEAL`,
`NOTIFY_ALLY`, `CRACKDOWN_SCANNING`, `HARVESTING`, `RESTING`,
`CONVERSING`, `LAIR_HEALING`), transitioned both from Lua leaf nodes
and from a large per-state C++ switch inside `setDestination()`.
**Patrol points are randomly generated, not per-spawn authored** --
`generatePatrol()` either queries the navmesh
(`PathFinderManager::getSpawnPointInArea`) or, off-navmesh, picks a
random offset within a configurable distance of the agent's home
location.

**Leashing (giving up combat/returning home)** has two independent
triggers: a distance-from-home threshold check that force-peaces and
resets the agent, and a separate out-of-sight mechanic specific to
`FOLLOWING` -- losing line-of-sight beyond 75 units accumulates an
out-of-sight counter that, past 30 ticks, has a 40% per-tick chance to
force a leash; entering a player's private structure also
unconditionally force-leashes.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any companion-AI tuning work should know
pets structurally bypass the aggro-radius/`LookForPlayer` detection
path used by wild creatures -- companion aggression, if any, would need
its own explicit trigger rather than inheriting creature-style
autonomous target acquisition. (2) the dynamic tick-interval-by-state
mechanic (400/700/1000ms) means a companion's responsiveness in combat
vs. idle is already differentiated by the engine itself, not something
that needs separate tuning. (3) several creature-only behaviors (the
out-of-sight leash, private-structure leash) are explicitly
`!agent->isPet()`-guarded -- yet another site in the same `isPet()`
family already documented as unreliable for companions (sections 52,
55, 68) -- worth checking if a future companion feature ever wants
these leash behaviors to actually apply.

---

## 76. Food/Drink Consumable Buff System

Consumption is dispatched through a radial-menu handler,
`ConsumableImplementation::handleObjectMenuSelect()` (menu ID 20),
not a dedicated eat/drink command -- `EatCommand` itself is just a
locomotion-state gate with no buff logic. Buff magnitude is
**quality-scaled at craft time, then applied as a flat value at
consumption**: `updateCraftingValues()` interpolates nutrition/filling/
duration between the schematic's template min/max using the exact same
percentage-interpolation formula as the crafting experimentation system
(section 69) -- the resolved value is written directly into the buff,
there's no separate consumption-time datatable lookup for magnitude.
Foraged (non-crafted) food skips this interpolation and uses raw
template values instead.

**There is no `BuffType::DRINK`** -- food and drink both use
`BuffType::FOOD`, and the buff itself is a plain instance of the
generic `Buff` base class (section 31), not a subclass. Duration is
crafting-scaled too (from the "flavor" attribute), with a flat +10%
bonus for Twi'lek characters specifically.

**Stacking has a genuinely two-layered rule that's easy to get
wrong.** At the point of consumption, re-eating an item that would
produce the *same* buff (matching `buffCRC`, a hash of the item's own
buff name) while that buff is still active is normally blocked
("You are already under the influence of that food...") -- except for
plain attribute-effect, non-foraged food, which is explicitly allowed
to be re-consumed. And once two same-named buffs *do* coexist,
`BuffList::addBuff`'s normal same-CRC replacement logic is itself
bypassed for `FOOD`-type attribute buffs, meaning duplicates can
genuinely stack as separate list entries rather than refreshing/
replacing one another -- a deliberate carve-out, not an oversight.
Different-named food and drink items apply fully independently
regardless, since they use different `buffCRC` values.

**Filling/satiation is a separate resource from buff slots.**
`PlayerObject` tracks `foodFilling`/`drinkFilling` against separate max
values, decaying over time; consumption is rejected outright if the
item's `filling` value would exceed remaining headroom, independent of
whether the buff itself would be allowed to apply.

**No interaction with entertainer buffs.** Performance buffs
(section 72) use their own `BuffType::PERFORMANCE` and unrelated name
hashes, so they occupy independent `buffList` entries alongside food/
drink buffs with no special-cased conflict found anywhere.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any new consumable content should define
magnitude via the schematic's crafting-attribute min/max range (reusing
`updateCraftingValues()`), not a flat hardcoded buff value, to stay
consistent with how every existing food/drink item works. (2) the
same-CRC-bypass-for-FOOD-attribute-buffs stacking exception is a real,
deliberate behavior worth testing explicitly if a new consumable type
is ever added, since it's easy to assume standard same-key-replaces
buff semantics apply uniformly and they don't. (3) filling/satiation
and buff-slot eligibility are two independently-enforced gates -- a
consumable can fail for either reason, and error handling for a new
feature should distinguish them.

---

## 77. Player City Government Deep Dive (extends section 17)

City mayoral government is a **fully separate election mechanic from
guild leadership** (section 41's simple stored-leader-OID model).
Running requires the `social_politician_novice` skill and citizenship;
`registerForMayoralRace()` blocks duplicates, non-citizens, existing
mayors elsewhere, and enforces a 24-hour re-registration cooldown.
Voting happens at a dedicated `terminal_city_vote` object.
`updateCityVoting()` runs on a real weekly cycle (config-driven,
default `CityUpdateInterval` = 10080 minutes), tallying votes,
awarding 300 political XP per vote *received* (not cast), and handing
the city (including any active city-specialization cooldown, section
34) to the highest-vote-count candidate, incumbent winning ties.
Registration locks after the second of three voting cycles.

**City rank is a real 6-tier ladder** (`CLIENT` -> `OUTPOST` ->
`VILLAGE` -> `TOWNSHIP` -> `CITY` -> `METROPOLIS`) gated purely on
citizen-count thresholds (`{2,4,6,8,10}` by default), checked every
update cycle -- a city that falls below its current rank's threshold
automatically contracts, and each rank also expands the city's
physical radius (150m up to 450m). New cities get a grace period
(1440 min) to hit the first threshold or their city hall is destroyed
outright; established cities get a longer grace period (4320 min)
before forced contraction to `OUTPOST`.

**Taxes are genuinely five separate types feeding one shared
treasury**: income (collected from citizens via a scheduled mail
task), property (skimmed as a percentage of each structure's own
maintenance payment at payment time, tying directly into section 54's
maintenance system), sales (skimmed from bazaar/vendor transactions,
section 74), travel (added to shuttle ticket price, section 64), and
garage (surcharges vehicle repair cost). All five ultimately fund
`cityTreasury`, which is drained weekly for civic-structure
maintenance, mission terminal upkeep, and -- confirming the section 34
cross-reference directly -- the active city specialization's own
recurring cost; if the treasury can't cover it, the specialization is
force-reset and its skill mods stripped, exactly as section 34
describes from the other direction.

**Zoning is binary access control, not sub-zone typing.** A mayor can
toggle `zoningEnabled` and grant/revoke per-player zoning rights; when
enabled, structure placement validation (section 59) explicitly checks
those rights before allowing a build. There's no residential/
commercial/no-build sub-zone classification anywhere in the code --
zoning here means only "can this specific player build in this city at
all."

**Structure registration to a city is automatic and geographic, not a
manual opt-in command.** Any structure/citizen whose coordinates fall
within a city region's radius is auto-enrolled on region entry --
civic and commercial structures are tracked separately, and a
residence owner is automatically registered as a citizen if not
already one. There's no explicit "register my house with the city"
action to remember or document as a separate step.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the property-tax-as-percentage-of-
maintenance mechanism means any change to structure maintenance
math (section 54) has a knock-on effect on city treasury income --
the two systems are coupled, not independent. (2) zoning in this
codebase should never be described to a user as supporting different
zone *types* (residential/commercial/etc.) -- it's purely a build/
no-build permission per player. (3) since structure/citizen
registration is fully automatic on geographic entry, any companion-
adjacent housing feature doesn't need to worry about a separate
city-registration step -- it already happens for free via the region's
`notifyEnter()`.

---

## 78. Loot Table Roll Mechanics Deep Dive (extends section 15)

Loot assignment is per-`CreatureTemplate`, sourced from the mobile's
own Lua file (a `lootGroups` field), not hardcoded in C++ -- fully
data-driven, same authoring model as everything else in this engine's
content layer. The actual roll is a **three-tier weighted-random
cascade**: (1) each `LootGroupCollectionEntry` independently rolls
against its own `lootChance` (out of a 10,000,000-unit scale, default
scaling with creature level) to decide if that loot "slot" produces
anything at all; (2) if it procs, a second roll picks among that
entry's weighted `LootGroups` references using classic cumulative-sum
selection; (3) the winning group name is resolved through a
`LootGroupTemplate`, which can itself reference further sub-groups
recursively (up to a 32-deep guard) before finally resolving to an
actual item template, using the identical cumulative-weight-bucket
selection formula at every level.

**Boss/named/elite loot is not a separate subsystem** -- there is no
dedicated "boss loot table" class. Elite creature templates are simply
separate `CreatureTemplate` entries that reference different,
higher-value loot-group files a normal spawn of the same base creature
never references. "Guaranteed" drops are achieved the same way any
other outcome is made certain in a weighted system: setting a single
entry's weight to the full 10,000,000-unit range (100% of the roll),
not a special deterministic code path. A full-codebase grep for
"treasure map" or similar found no such mechanic anywhere -- there is
no quest-loot/treasure-map system distinct from ordinary weighted
drops.

**Item stat rolling on a dropped item reuses the crafting-quality
system wholesale, not a separate loot-specific formula.**
`LootValues` directly subclasses `CraftingValues` (the same class
crafting experimentation, section 69, is built on), and loot item
generation calls the identical `updateCraftingValues()`/quality-
interpolation API real crafted items use, after first rolling an
"exceptional tier" (base/yellow/exceptional/legendary) via its own
config-driven chance table. Concretely: a dropped item's final stats
come from the exact same value-distribution machinery as a player-
crafted item, just fed a different quality-tier roll as input.

**Placement is synchronous at death, not deferred.** Loot generation
and insertion into the corpse's inventory happens directly inside the
creature-destruction call chain, under a real container lock, before
the corpse-despawn timer is even scheduled -- there's no queued/
deferred loot-generation step to account for.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any new "special" or "boss-only" loot for
a custom creature should be implemented the same way the existing
elite mobs do it -- a dedicated loot-group Lua file referenced only
from that creature's template -- rather than inventing a parallel
mechanism. (2) a literal 100%-weight single entry is the established,
idiomatic way to express "this always drops X" in this codebase.
(3) since dropped-item quality reuses the crafting quality-roll
pipeline exactly, any future change to that pipeline (e.g. for a
companion-crafting feature) would also silently affect loot item
quality -- the two are the same code, not parallel implementations
that happen to look similar.

---

## 79. Combat Action / Command Queue Internals (extends section 10)

There is a genuine per-creature FIFO-ish structure behind every combat
action, `CommandQueue`, not a synchronous-only execute-on-press model.
Enqueueing (`enqueueCommand`) is capped at 15 pending actions for
players and only 5 for AI agents. Dequeue/selection
(`getNextAction()`) prioritizes `IMMEDIATE` over `FRONT` over the
oldest queued `NORMAL`-priority action -- so a genuinely urgent action
(an interrupt-style ability, or an AI's own reaction) can jump ahead of
whatever a player already queued up. Dispatch happens through a
self-rescheduling `CommandQueueTask`, the same named-recurring-Task
idiom documented across this codebase (section 48).

**Cooldowns are timestamp comparisons, not per-ability scheduled
Tasks.** Each `QueueCommand` checks a `CooldownTimerMap` entry keyed by
a name derived from the command itself (`"command_" + name` by
default) against the current time -- no dedicated Task object exists
per ability, cooldown enforcement is pure timestamp bookkeeping,
consistent with how cooldowns are implemented elsewhere in this engine
(the healing-profession cooldowns in section 51 use the same shape).

**HAM cost validation is check-then-deduct, fully atomic, not
partial.** Force cost is checked and deducted first (aborting cleanly
if insufficient); Health/Action/Mind costs are then computed from the
weapon's base cost times per-command multipliers, and validated
against current HAM pools *before* any deduction happens -- if any
single pool would go negative, the entire attempt fails with no
partial deduction and (at this specific check) no player-facing error
message at all, that message is generated one layer up by the calling
command's own failure-code handling.

**Weapon speed and per-ability cooldown are two independent, stacked
gates, not the same mechanic.** `calculateWeaponAttackSpeed()`
computes a genuine haste formula (base speed reduced by a speed mod, a
skill-derived speed ratio, and the `combat_haste` skill mod, floored at
a minimum), and that duration becomes the delay before the creature's
*next* normal-priority queued action can run -- entirely separate from
any given ability's own explicit cooldown timer. A fast weapon with a
slow-cooldown special attack is still gated by both independently.

**Basic and special attacks share one execution function.** Both route
through the same `CombatQueueCommand::doCombatAction()` ->
`CombatManager::doCombatAction()` path -- differentiation (damage
range, DoT/state effects like knockdown or stun, area/cone shape) is
entirely data-driven from each command's own Lua-defined template
fields, not a structurally separate code path per attack type. This
mirrors the same "one shared mechanism, data-driven behavior
differences" shape already documented for buffs (section 31) and
NPC dialogue (section 58).

**AI agents use the identical queue and combat-resolution path as
players**, with narrow, explicit branches: HAM cost checking is
unconditionally skipped for AI attackers (an early-return, not a
zero-cost calculation), the post-action delay uses a fixed 2-second
value rather than the weapon-speed formula, and the AI queue cap is 5
instead of 15. Everything else -- prioritization, cooldown checking,
the actual damage-resolution function -- is shared code, not a
parallel AI-specific implementation.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any companion combat-ability feature
should go through the same `CommandQueue`/`CombatQueueCommand` path
real creature and player attacks use, rather than a bespoke execution
path, to automatically inherit correct cooldown/priority/queueing
behavior. (2) the AI-skips-HAM-cost branch is worth knowing explicitly
if a companion is ever meant to have a real resource cost for its
abilities -- today it wouldn't, by default, since companions are
AiAgents and would hit the same unconditional skip. (3) the "same
function, data-driven differences" pattern for basic vs. special
attacks means a new custom attack type is authored as Lua command
data, not new C++ combat-resolution code.

---

## 80. Waypoint / Datapad / Quest Journal System

Waypoints are **not** stored in the datapad container -- they live in
a dedicated `WaypointList` field directly on `PlayerObject` (the
"ghost"), a delta-synced map keyed by object ID with helper lookups by
name, special type, or world position. No server-side capacity limit
exists anywhere in the C++ code (`addWaypoint` only dedupes by ID/name/
special-type) -- any cap a player experiences is purely a historical
client-side UI limit, not enforced by this server.

**Mission waypoints are a special case that bypasses `WaypointList`
entirely.** A `MissionObject` creates and owns its own waypoint
directly (`createWaypoint()`), naming it after the mission title and
pushing live position updates to the owning player (and, if grouped,
propagating the nearest-mission waypoint to the whole group). Because
this waypoint rides along with the mission ticket object itself rather
than being inserted into the player's `WaypointList`, destroying the
mission (completion or abandonment) cascades to destroy the waypoint
automatically as a side effect of object destruction -- not a separate
explicit cleanup step.

**Quest journal state is completely independent of waypoints.**
Screenplay quest progress (section 3) is tracked via two bit-array
fields on `PlayerObject`, `activeQuests`/`completedQuests`, with simple
set/check-bit accessors -- there's no structural link between a quest
bit being set and a waypoint existing. Screenplay Lua scripts must
explicitly call `addWaypoint` when a given step actually warrants one,
meaning **not every quest step gets a waypoint** by default -- that's
an authoring choice per script, not automatic.

**Manual waypoints exist via a `/waypoint` command**, creating the same
underlying `WaypointObject` type mission/quest waypoints use, defaulted
to a generic name. The data model has **no explicit player-created vs.
system-created flag** -- the only differentiator is `specialTypeID`
(zero for a plain manual waypoint, nonzero for system categories like
FIND or QUESTTASK) plus whatever custom name was given.

**Client updates ride the existing delta-message protocol**, not a
standalone waypoint packet type -- `WaypointList` changes go out via
the generic `PlayerObject` delta message (add/remove/update subtypes),
while mission-ticket waypoints instead ride the `MissionObject`'s own
separate delta baseline, consistent with them being structurally
owned by the mission rather than the player's waypoint list.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) since there's no server-side waypoint cap,
a future feature that programmatically creates many waypoints (e.g. a
companion marking points of interest) wouldn't be blocked by the
engine itself -- only by client-side display limits. (2) any new
quest-like feature wanting "waypoint on active step" behavior needs to
explicitly call `addWaypoint` per step, it won't happen automatically
just from setting an active-quest bit. (3) the mission-waypoint's
automatic-destruction-via-object-cascade pattern (rather than an
explicit cleanup call) is a reusable idiom worth remembering for any
future feature where a temporary UI element should be tied to a
parent object's lifetime instead of manually tracked.

---

## 81. Jedi Force Powers / Lightsaber Crafting Deep Dive (extends section 9a)

`JediManager.cpp` itself is a thin Lua-dispatch bridge with no combat/
crafting logic -- section 9a's village-Jedi coverage already accounts
for everything real in that file. The genuinely new material is
lightsaber crafting and how Force powers execute as attacks.

**Lightsaber crafting reuses the standard crafting/experimentation
pipeline wholesale -- there is no separate lightsaber crafting
system.** Crystal stat generation overrides the same
`updateCraftingValues()` hook every crafting component uses (section
20/69), branching entirely on the schematic's `color` experimental
attribute: color 31 is a real "Force crystal" that rolls actual combat
stats (damage, attack speed, HAM sacrifice costs, wound chance, Force
cost) from a level-scaled curve; colors 0-11 are purely cosmetic
blade-color crystals with no stat roll at all. Assembly/experimentation
itself has zero lightsaber-specific branching in
`ManufactureSchematicImplementation`/`CraftingSessionImplementation` --
it's identical to crafting any other weapon.

**What's actually unique to lightsabers is post-craft crystal
assembly**, via a dedicated `saber_inv` container component on the
finished hilt. Crystals must be individually "tuned" (bound to a
player, costing real Force Power scaled by crystal quality) before
insertion; the container enforces exactly one cosmetic blade-color
crystal but allows multiple stat-affecting Force crystals up to volume
capacity, additively stacking their stats onto the parent weapon on
insertion and removing them on extraction. Crystal swapping is blocked
while the saber is equipped. Force-rank gating (`force_title_jedi_
rank_01` and up) applies at crystal-tuning/use time, not at crafting
time -- an untuned or insufficiently-ranked player can craft a saber
but only sees "UNTUNED" rather than real stats.

**Force powers as attacks go through the exact same combat pipeline
documented in section 79, not a separate system.** The
`ForcePowersQueueCommand` base class extends `CombatQueueCommand`
directly and calls the identical `CombatManager::doCombatAction()`
entry point melee/ranged attacks use -- individual powers just add
state checks (e.g. armor-type gates) on top. The one genuinely new
mechanic here is FRS-modified Force cost: `getFrsModifiedForceCost()`
adjusts a power's Force cost using `force_manipulation_light/dark`
skill mods combined with the player's actual FRS council rank
(section 67) -- a direct, previously-undocumented link between the
Force Rank System and ordinary Force-power combat economics.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any custom lightsaber-adjacent content
(a new crystal type, a companion wielding a saber) should hook into
the existing `saber_inv` container/crystal-tuning mechanism rather
than inventing new stat-application logic -- it's a clean, self-
contained, already-proven system. (2) Force powers needing custom
combat behavior belong as `ForcePowersQueueCommand` subclasses, fully
consistent with section 79's "basic and special attacks share one
execution function, differentiated by data" finding. (3) the FRS-rank-
affects-Force-cost link is a concrete, previously-missing piece
connecting sections 9a, 67, and 79 -- worth remembering if a future
balance question ever comes up about why two players with identical
skill training pay different Force costs for the same power.

---

## 82. Survey Tool / Harvester Concentration & Tier Mechanics (extends section 40)

The survey tool displays the **literal, unfuzzed simplex-noise value**
from section 40's resource-location system -- `SpawnDensityMap::
getDensityAt()` computes `SimplexNoise::noise(x*modifier, y*modifier,
seed*modifier)` (clamped to zero, scaled by the resource's density
cap) and that exact float is what gets sent to the client as the
displayed concentration percentage, sampled across a grid of points
around the survey location. There is no server-side randomization
layered on top of what the player sees -- the survey reading is
genuinely accurate to the underlying density field, not an
approximation.

**There is no separate "probe" tool for inorganic resources** -- a
single `SurveyTool` class covers every resource category (solar,
chemical, flora, gas, geothermal, mineral, water, wind, fusion,
inorganic) differentiated only by a `type` field on the tool template,
matched against the target resource's own survey-type tag at survey
time. The classic memory of a distinct probe-vs-survey tool split
doesn't apply to this codebase.

**Harvester tiers are crafted values, not a fixed installation-type
table.** Base `extractionRate`/`hopperSizeMax` fields exist on
`InstallationObject` but get overwritten at crafting time from the
placing deed's own experimental attribute rolls (`extractrate`/
`hoppersize`), meaning a harvester's real capacity depends on both its
deed schematic's tier-specific min/max ranges (personal harvesters
roll a much lower range than heavy harvesters) *and* the crafting
quality roll used to place it (section 69) -- two harvesters built from
the same deed schematic can have meaningfully different real-world
capacity depending on how well the deed itself was crafted.

**Concentration directly and simply multiplies extraction rate**: a
harvester's actual per-tick yield is `craftedExtractionRate *
spawnDensity`, where `spawnDensity` is captured once at activation
from the exact same density-field lookup the survey tool uses at that
harvester's specific tile. There is no cap on simultaneous harvesters
beyond the generic structure-lot allowance (10 lots by default) --
nothing specifically limits harvester count or spacing within a
resource concentration zone.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) since survey readings are unfuzzed, any
feature or guide describing "resource scouting" can treat the
displayed percentage as ground truth, not an estimate. (2) a
harvester's real yield depends on two independently-rollable quality
sources (the deed's crafting roll and the resource's live
concentration at placement time) -- a "why is my harvester
underperforming" investigation needs to check both. (3) the total-
lot-cap-only limit means there's no dedicated anti-harvester-spam
mechanic tied to resource zones specifically -- if that's ever wanted,
it would need new code, not a config toggle.

---

## 83. Weather / Environment System

Weather is real server-side simulation, not client-only dressing --
one `WeatherManager` instance runs per planetary zone (only for zones
with weather explicitly enabled in their Lua config; Tatooine,
Corellia, Dantooine, Dathomir, Endor, Lok, Naboo, Rori, Talus, and
Yavin4 all have it). Pattern generation is procedural: a weighted
random weather-tier roll (CLEAR through EXTREMESTORM) spawns a
Simplex-noise-based `WeatherMap` that varies intensity spatially across
the zone and ramps up/down over the pattern's duration, self-
rescheduling via a `WeatherChangeEvent` task once the current pattern
expires -- the same named-recurring-task idiom seen throughout this
codebase (section 48).

**Weather is confirmed cosmetic with exactly one real gameplay
exception.** A targeted codebase-wide check found weather state
referenced in only three files total, none touching combat accuracy,
aggro/detection radius (section 75), or resource spawning (section
40) -- those systems are entirely unaffected by current weather. The
sole exception: Tatooine and Lok can be flagged for damaging
sandstorms, and an `EXTREMESTORM` pattern on those planets applies
real periodic damage (blinding the player for 60 seconds, HAM wound
damage reduced by armor coverage on specific gear slots, a small
knockdown/dismount chance) -- with no shelter exemption for being
indoors, mounted, or camped.

**Delivery is per-player, not zone-broadcast.** Each player independently
polls their own position against the zone's weather map on a
3-second cooldown as part of their normal tick/heartbeat, and only
receives an update packet if their local weather value actually
changed -- meaning two players on the same planet can genuinely be
experiencing different weather simultaneously if the noise field
differs enough between their positions.

**Space has a structurally distinct, mechanically real equivalent.**
Nebula zones generate periodic lightning strikes that raycast against
nearby ships and apply real shield damage -- unlike planetary weather,
this is unambiguously gameplay-mechanical for every ship caught in a
nebula, not a rare exception.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't describe planetary weather as
affecting combat, stealth, or detection in this codebase -- it
provably doesn't, aside from the two-planet sandstorm-damage
exception. (2) the per-player independent weather-polling design means
weather can't be used as a reliable "everyone on this planet is
experiencing X right now" signal for a new feature -- it's local, not
global. (3) nebula lightning is the correct model to imitate if a
future feature wants an environmental hazard with real mechanical
teeth, rather than planetary weather's mostly-cosmetic pattern.

---

## 84. HAM Stat Pool Allocation (Character Creation & Growth)

Starting HAM pools are fully deterministic from profession and race,
**not** a client-supplied point allocation -- the character-creation
packet handler never parses any per-attribute distribution from the
client, only race/profession/name/appearance. `PlayerCreationManager`
sets base/current/max HAM directly from the chosen profession's data
table, then additively layers the race's own flat per-attribute
modifier table on top -- both fully data-driven from
`attribute_limits.iff`/`racial_mods.iff`/profession datatables, no
player choice involved at the moment of creation.

**A genuine point-allocation mechanic does exist, but it's narrowly
scoped to the tutorial.** A stat-migration session lets a player
redistribute a fixed total point pool (exactly matching the species'
`getTotalAttributeLimit()`) across the 9 HAM attributes within
species-specific min/max caps -- but this is gated to only work while
the character is physically in the tutorial zone, or for privileged
staff accounts. This is not a general-purpose respec system.

**Skill training never touches HAM pool size.** A targeted search of
the skill-award code path found zero HAM-mutating calls -- skill boxes
grant SkillMods (section 55), abilities, and XP-type unlocks
exclusively, never base/max HAM changes. Post-creation, a player's
HAM pool is fixed except for the tutorial-only respec above and
transient runtime reconciliation (`fixHAM()`, recomputing max HAM from
base plus active buff modifiers minus encumbrance -- never touching
base HAM itself, only what buffs/encumbrance currently add or
subtract).

**There is no level-up or milestone stat-growth system at all.** The
`level` field on a creature is a combat-difficulty value used for
group-difficulty calculations and NPC scaling, not a player XP-level,
and has zero connection to HAM. This is fully consistent with SWG's
skill-based (not level-based) character progression design -- there's
no hidden "gain stat points at level N" mechanic anywhere in the
player-management code.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any feature wanting to grant a companion
or player extra HAM should model it as a buff/skill-mod-style modifier
(reconciled through `fixHAM()`) rather than trying to mutate base HAM
directly, since that's not how any existing system in this codebase
does it. (2) if a future feature wants a general (non-tutorial) respec
option, the tutorial's `MigrateStatsSession` is the correct existing
mechanism to extend/relax the gating on, rather than building a new
one. (3) race and profession are the only two inputs to starting HAM
-- nothing else in the character-creation flow affects it.

---

## 85. Squad / Ops Group Mechanics -- Confirmed Absent (extends section 71)

No structure larger than the single 20-member `GroupObject` documented
in section 71 exists anywhere in this codebase -- no "ops group,"
"raid group," or multi-group linkage of any kind, for chat, loot, or
coordination purposes. This is a clean, thoroughly-checked negative
result, the same category of finding as sections 22 (Collections) and
46 (Instances).

What *does* exist under superficially similar names is unrelated to
player grouping: a `SquadObserver` system manages formations of **AI
NPC troopers** for GCW base-defense/siege events (tracked via its own
`ObserverEventType::SQUAD`, operating on `AiAgent` objects, not
players), a parallel `SQUADRON` observer type does the same for space
NPC wingmen, and an `outdoors_squadleader_novice` skill grants a
combat-XP bonus that operates entirely within one existing
`GroupObject` -- none of these create or reference any container
bigger than a single 20-member group. "Squad"/"raid" also appear
purely as quest/mission flavor text in several screenplay names, with
no gameplay mechanic behind the word.

There is also no content-level assumption of multi-group encounters --
no creature template or spawn definition anywhere carries a minimum-
group-size field or an explicit multi-group HP/damage-scaling
annotation, distinct from (and additional to) section 46's finding
that true per-group *instancing* is absent.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) if a future feature request asks for
"raid" or "ops group" functionality, be upfront that this is entirely
new engine work -- there's no partial scaffolding to extend, unlike
some other "confirmed absent" findings in this guide that at least
have adjacent machinery. (2) the `SquadObserver` NPC-formation system,
while unrelated to player grouping, could plausibly be studied as a
reference for "multiple AI agents coordinating as one unit" if a
future companion-squad-of-companions feature is ever considered.

---

## 86. Chat Moderation / Profanity Filter / Mute System (extends sections 19, 38, 45)

**The profanity filter is real but deliberately narrow in scope --
it validates names and short fixed strings, never free-text chat or
mail.** `NameManager::isProfane()` runs input against a large regex
list loaded from Lua config, and is called for character/creature
names, guild/city/vendor/chatroom/ship names, chat room titles/paths,
structure names, vendor barker phrases, and the short text argument of
a handful of combat "shout" commands (warcry, intimidate, retreat,
etc.). It is confirmed **never** called against ordinary spatial/tell/
group/guild/planet/auction chat messages or mail bodies -- free-text
communication in this codebase has zero automated content filtering;
moderation of message content relies entirely on manual GM
intervention (section 38).

**Spam/flood prevention is confirmed entirely absent** -- no rate-
limiting, message-counter, or flood-detection logic exists anywhere
in the chat pipeline.

**The `/report` command is a confirmed inert stub** -- it validates
locomotion state and returns success, with no logging, database
write, or notification of any kind. The codebase's real player-support
channel is a separate, unrelated CS ticket system
(`CsCreateTicketCommand`/`CsGetTicketsCommand`), not `/report`.

**Muting is a real, enforced, per-character chat flag, structurally
distinct from account bans.** A `mutedReason`/`isMuted()` flag on
`PlayerObject` is checked before every chat channel send (room,
social, spatial, tell, group, guild, planet, auction -- mail is
notably **not** gated by it), set/cleared by GM freeze/unfreeze
commands. This operates entirely independently of the account-level
ban flag, which blocks login rather than chat -- a muted player can
still log in and play, just not communicate through gated channels.

**`NameManager` is a general name-validation utility, not a
chat-specific filter class** -- the same filter this project's own
companion custom-naming feature already calls is exactly the
`isProfane()` function described above, confirming the companion
naming feature correctly reuses the real engine filter rather than
needing (or having) a bespoke one.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any future feature wanting real chat
content moderation (profanity-filtering actual messages, not just
names) would be new work -- the existing filter structurally can't be
pointed at message bodies without new call sites. (2) `/report` looking
functional but doing nothing is worth knowing before assuming any
past in-game player report was ever actually recorded anywhere. (3) a
muted player's mail still works -- worth remembering if mute is ever
used as an enforcement tool and someone asks "can they still reach me
another way."

---

## 87. Character Deletion & Server Transfer System

Character deletion has **no cooldown, no server-side confirmation
step, and no restriction checks** (no guild-leadership check, no
vendor-item check, no pending-mail check) -- the login server trusts
the client's delete request outright once ownership is verified,
relying entirely on client-side UI confirmation.

**Deletion is a genuine two-stage soft delete, not instant
destruction.** The character row is synchronously moved from the live
`characters` table to a `deleted_characters` table at request time,
but the actual in-game object (inventory, structures, everything in
the ODB) isn't touched yet. A separate periodic purge task (default
10-minute interval, batches of up to 250) does the real destructive
work later -- disconnecting any still-connected client, destroying the
object from the world, and purging it from the database -- and only
*then* frees the character's name for reuse and removes it from the
in-memory name-uniqueness map. Practical effect: a deleted character's
name stays reserved for up to the purge interval after deletion, not
released instantly.

**Cross-galaxy or server-to-server character transfer is confirmed
completely absent** -- no transfer/migrate mechanic exists anywhere in
the codebase, including in the external realm-hosting API layer that
already exists for other cross-process concerns (name lookups,
deletion-purge batching). This joins sections 22/46/85 as another
clean, thoroughly-checked negative finding.

**Character slots per galaxy are capped at a configurable default of
10**, enforced server-side at creation time (hard rejection, not just
a client-side UI hint, though a client-facing hint does exist too) --
distinct from a separate, unrelated concurrent-online-characters-per-
account cap.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any feature that assumes a deleted
character's data is immediately gone should account for the up-to-
10-minute soft-delete window -- the object technically still exists
in the database briefly after a delete request succeeds. (2) if a
future feature ever wants "undo character deletion," the soft-delete
window is exactly the mechanism to hook, though it's short by default.
(3) since transfer is fully absent, any user-facing promise of moving
a character between galaxies/servers would need to be built from
scratch, not configured.

---

## 88. Crafting Station vs. Handheld Tool Differences (extends sections 20, 42, 69)

**A crafting station's real value is gating, not a stat bonus.** Its
`effectiveness` value is stored but never actually read by the
assembly-success or quality formulas -- those only read the handheld
tool's own effectiveness. What a station actually provides is
structural: it's the sole gate on whether experimentation (and factory
crate production) is even reachable at all -- without a station
present, crafting silently skips straight to "assemble without
experimenting," regardless of how good the handheld tool is. A station
also raises the maximum schematic complexity a player can even
attempt, overriding the handheld tool's own (lower) complexity
ceiling.

**Stations are profession-locked, sharing the same type enum as
handheld tools** (clothing/food/generic/Jedi/space/structure/weapon),
with one deliberate cross-exception: a weapon station also accepts
Jedi (lightsaber) tools, tying back into section 81's lightsaber-
crafting coverage. There is no generic "any station works" fallback.

**Handheld tools have no tier system that closes the gap with a
station.** Each profession has exactly one tool template with a fixed
complexity ceiling (20 for most professions, 15 for generic) -- there's
no "novice vs. advanced handheld tool" progression, and no handheld
tool, however good, ever unlocks experimentation. The only real
handheld variance is a small set of Jedi reward tools granting
guaranteed-critical-roll counters, a special-reward mechanic entirely
separate from any general tiering.

**Public and private stations differ in real, not just
permission-based, ways.** Private (player-crafted/placed) stations
have a meaningfully higher complexity ceiling than public stations of
the same type, and public stations skip creating an ingredient-hopper
child object that private ones get -- access control itself comes from
ordinary building entry permissions, not from anything crafting-code-
specific.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "can I craft this without a station, just
slower" is not accurate for this codebase -- above the handheld
complexity ceiling, or for anything needing experimentation/factory
runs, a station isn't optional, it's a hard gate. (2) any new crafting-
adjacent feature (e.g. a companion crafting station bonus) should model
station value as unlocking capability, not as a stat multiplier, to
match how every real station in this codebase actually works. (3) the
weapon-station-accepts-Jedi-tools exception is a small but real detail
worth remembering if lightsaber crafting is ever extended.

---

## 89. Ship Component Installation & Weapon Energy Management (extends section 26)

Component installation has a real, enforced slot-type validation layer
-- each ship chassis slot carries a compatibility tag, and each
component's own data carries a matching tag; installation is rejected
outright on any mismatch (a weapon genuinely cannot go in an engine
slot), alongside separate certification and total-mass-budget checks.
Ammo/missile installation has its own parallel type-matching check
(launcher type vs. ammo type/class).

**Weapon firing has a real, depletable, regenerating energy cost --
not just a refire cooldown.** Each shot checks the ship's current
capacitor energy against a per-shot cost (itself a crafted/rolled
attribute, adjusted by component energy efficiency); insufficient
capacitor charge silently drops the shot. Capacitor energy regenerates
over time toward a max value, and that regeneration itself competes
for reactor throughput -- meaning sustained rapid fire can genuinely
outpace regeneration and leave a ship temporarily unable to fire
regardless of cooldown state.

**There is a real, per-tick reactor power budget, and installing too
much power-hungry gear has a genuine runtime consequence.** Every
recovery tick, the reactor's total generation is distributed across
all installed components in iteration order; components later in that
order can receive only a fractional share ("brownout," reducing their
effective output) or, if the budget is fully exhausted, get flagged
disabled-for-lack-of-power entirely. This isn't caught at install
time -- an over-ambitious loadout installs successfully and only
reveals the problem at runtime.

**Component condition is a real, functionally-meaningful stat**, not
cosmetic -- each installed component tracks its own hitpoints
independent of the ship chassis, and that condition ratio directly
scales the component's effective output (a half-damaged shield
generator provides roughly half the shielding, not full shielding
until sudden failure). A component flagged disabled or demolished
contributes zero regardless of nominal stats.

**Ship components are crafted items, not fixed-stat loot**, using the
identical `updateCraftingValues()`/experimentation pipeline documented
in sections 45/69 -- every component class (weapons, capacitors,
reactors, shields, etc.) pulls its real stats from post-quality-roll
crafting attributes, the same mechanism as any other crafted item in
the game.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) a ship loadout can pass installation
checks and still underperform badly at runtime due to reactor
starvation -- any diagnostic feature or guide should check the power
budget, not just slot occupancy. (2) component condition degrading
output gradually (not a hard on/off) means combat repair timing
matters continuously, not just at zero. (3) since ship components use
the same crafting pipeline as everything else, any future
companion-crewed-ship feature would automatically inherit correct
component behavior by reusing existing component classes rather than
reimplementing stats.

---

## 90. Structure Maintenance Automation -- Maintenance Droid (extends section 54)

There is no player-facing "recurring auto-pay" toggle beyond the
last-resort bank auto-draft already documented in section 54 --
`Core3.StructureMaintenanceTask.AllowBankPayments` only affects an
informational warning message in the *manual* pay-maintenance command
handler, it has zero effect on the automatic weekly-draft task itself,
which always attempts the bank draft unconditionally once surplus
maintenance hits zero.

**A genuine maintenance-automation object does exist: a droid-mounted
maintenance module.** A crafted maintenance module can be installed on
a pet droid, letting a player assign several structures (up to a
rating-gated maximum) to it via a radial menu and SUI flow. Running it
is explicitly manual and session-based, not passive background
automation -- the player initiates a "maintenance run," the droid
"travels" for a duration scaled by what it needs to service, and
credits are deducted directly from the player's cash-plus-bank total.
Critically, **this droid does not collect harvester hopper proceeds**
to fund itself -- there is no auto-collect-and-pay mechanic anywhere in
the codebase, funding is always drawn from the player's existing
liquid credits.

**Manual payment is a straightforward radial-menu-to-SUI flow**
(cash-only, no bank option in the manual path), with a parallel,
separate SUI specifically for paying off a condemned structure's
uncondemn cost.

**Notification is real but reactive, not proactive** -- the system
mails the player when maintenance is auto-drafted from the bank, when
daily decay actually begins, when a structure becomes condemned, and
on final destruction. There is no "your maintenance is getting low"
warning before the surplus actually reaches zero.

**Vendors have a completely separate, smaller upkeep pool from the
structure they're placed in** -- a flat hourly maintenance drain
(reduced by Merchant skill mods), with its own condition-damage/
"on strike"/escalating-warning-then-deletion mail sequence, funded only
by manual cash-then-bank player payment. There's no automatic bank
draft for vendor upkeep the way structures get one.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) if a future feature wants genuine
hands-off maintenance automation (auto-collect-and-pay), that's new
work -- the existing maintenance droid is a manual convenience tool,
not passive automation, despite being droid-themed. (2) vendor upkeep
and structure maintenance are two entirely independent credit drains
with different funding rules -- a player can have a healthy structure
and a striking vendor (or vice versa) with no connection between the
two. (3) the total absence of harvester-proceeds-funds-maintenance
automation is worth knowing if a future companion feature is ever
imagined as "a companion that manages my harvester income" -- that
would be new integration work, not a hookup to something that already
exists.

---

## 91. COD Mail -- Confirmed Absent -- & Secure Trade Edge Cases (extends section 39)

**Cash-on-delivery item mail does not exist in this codebase at all.**
The mail message object carries only sender/subject/body/timestamp/
status and optional waypoint data -- there is no item reference, no
credit amount field, and no escrow/payment-gate concept anywhere in
its structure. Every real mail-with-a-waypoint case already documented
elsewhere (auction/bazaar sale notifications, section 74) is purely
informational, sent alongside a separate real item/credit transfer
that happens through ordinary trade or vendor mechanics -- the mail
itself never carries the item or payment. Player-to-player item-for-
credits exchange in this codebase happens exclusively through the
secure trade window or vendor/bazaar sales, both already documented
(sections 39, 74); there is no third, mail-based path, joining the
several other "confirmed absent" findings in this guide.

**Secure trade is safe against disconnects, with one minor UX gap, not
a duplication risk.** No item ever leaves an inventory until both
parties' independent verification flags are true, checked inside one
crossed-lock block -- a mid-trade disconnect cannot produce a partial
transfer. The gap that does exist: a hard disconnect only cleanly
tears down the disconnecting player's own trade session; the
counterpart's session isn't proactively notified or aborted and sits
stale until that player next interacts with the trade UI. This is a
UX rough edge (a confusing stuck trade window), not a security or
duplication issue.

**Proximity is checked only at verification time, not continuously.**
A distance threshold is enforced specifically when either party clicks
Verify, not at trade-window opening and not on an ongoing basis --
parties can walk apart mid-negotiation freely; the trade simply fails
at the next verify attempt rather than auto-cancelling the moment
they separate.

**One structurally interesting detail**: the client-visible "Accept"
button's underlying flag is never actually read by the server-side
transfer logic -- only the separate "verified" flag (set by a
different action) gates the real item/credit exchange. The UI's
accept/verify distinction doesn't fully match what the server actually
checks, though this doesn't create any actual safety gap since the
verify flag alone is sufficient and correctly cross-locked.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't build or describe any feature
assuming COD mail exists -- any "mail someone an item with payment
required" request needs to be built from scratch using the trade or
vendor substrate, not extended from mail. (2) the stale-trade-session-
on-disconnect gap is a minor, known rough edge worth fixing someday
but isn't a security issue -- no funds or items are ever at risk from
it. (3) proximity being checked only at verify time (not continuously)
means a trade UI could stay open indefinitely even after both parties
have wandered far apart, which is expected/correct behavior for this
codebase, not a bug to "fix" if ever encountered.

---

## 92. Static World Content Loading -- Terrain / POI / Dungeons (extends sections 4, 12)

Terrain itself is loaded from real, unmodified client `.trn` files at
`PlanetManager` construction time -- this codebase contains a genuine
from-scratch reimplementation of the client's procedural terrain
layer-graph format (affectors, filters, boundaries), evaluating the
same layer graph server-side rather than reading a precomputed height
grid. A legacy custom heightmap format also exists in the source tree
but is confirmed dead code -- its load call is commented out and
unreachable.

**Points of interest are a separate, narrower thing than they might
sound.** A real client-authored POI datatable is loaded once
server-wide, but it's consulted only for proximity/no-build checks --
it does not spawn anything. Actual "POI as spawnable content" (a
building that despawns when unpopulated) is a wholly different
mechanism, already covered under section 4's `PoiBuilding` class.

**Static dungeons/caves/bunkers split cleanly into two independent
layers, matching section 4's existing structure.** Geometry (cell
layout, fixed building placement) comes from a real client World
Snapshot format (`.ws` files, genuinely distinct from the mustela/ODB
live-persistence format covered in section 11 -- these are unrelated
despite superficially similar naming), recursively instantiated into
real scene objects with fixed object IDs at load time. Population
(the actual mobs/loot/terminals inside that static geometry) is
separately authored as Lua screenplay content that looks up the
snapshot-created objects by their fixed IDs and spawns content at
hardcoded coordinates within them -- geometry and population are
authored and loaded through completely different pipelines that only
meet at the fixed-object-ID handshake.

**Regions are a separate abstraction from all of the above, already
section 12's territory** -- they govern spawn-density/city/PvP
subdivision only. Terrain, world-snapshot buildings, and the POI table
are all zone-wide data that never reference region objects, confirming
this new material extends sections 4/12 rather than needing its own
region-adjacent section.

**Nearly everything here loads synchronously at server boot**, not
lazily on player entry -- terrain, regions, the POI table, and all
world-snapshot geometry finish loading before the zone server
considers itself started, as does every screenplay-authored static
population. The one genuinely lazy, runtime-triggered layer is the
dynamic creature population (LairObserver/DynamicSpawnObserver,
section 66) sitting on top of this static foundation -- confirming
that distinction is real and deliberate, not just a naming coincidence.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any feature wanting to add new static
world content (a new dungeon, a new POI) needs to touch two genuinely
separate authoring pipelines (snapshot geometry plus screenplay
population), not one unified system. (2) server boot time scales with
total static content across all loaded zones, since virtually all of
it is synchronous startup work -- worth knowing if boot time is ever a
concern for a content-heavy addition. (3) "mustela"/"snapshot" sound
similar but are unrelated systems (live DB persistence vs. static
world-authoring format) -- worth being precise about which one a
future conversation means.

---

## 93. Emote / Social Action System

Emotes are dispatched through exactly two generic commands, not one
registered command per emote. A gating-only command exists purely so
client-issued `/wave`, `/bow`, etc. pass the normal locomotion/state
checks every queue command gets; the actual execution command takes a
target ID and an integer emote ID chosen client-side -- the specific
emote (which animation, which text) is never a server-parsed string
argument, it's an opaque ID the client already resolved.

**Server-side validation of the emote ID is looser than it might seem.**
A real datatable maps emote IDs to names, but the execution path
doesn't actually validate the incoming ID against it before
broadcasting -- an invalid or out-of-range ID still gets relayed to
nearby clients as a real emote packet, with the datatable lookup only
consulted downstream for a narrow secondary purpose (gating the
entertainer applause-count increment for the small set of IDs that map
to applause/cheer/clap). This means the emote system trusts the client
further than most other systems in this codebase, which more
typically re-validate client-supplied choices server-side.

**Locomotion/state gating reuses the same shared, data-driven
mechanism every queue command uses** -- a per-command state bitmask and
invalid-locomotion list loaded from the command datatable, not
emote-specific hardcoded logic. This is the same gating substrate
documented for combat commands in section 79.

**Targeted emotes resolve their target for secondary NPC-reaction
purposes only (pets react, monsters may sit, ordinary NPCs may trigger
a scripted reaction) -- there's no authoritative server-side check
that the claimed target is actually valid or in range for the
player-visible broadcast itself, that part just relays what the
client sent.**

**Animation delivery uses a dedicated packet type distinct from spatial
chat**, though it reuses the same proximity/ignore-list broadcast
infrastructure (iterating nearby players, respecting each recipient's
ignore list) that spatial chat uses.

**There is no cooldown or anti-spam specifically on ordinary social
emotes** -- consistent with section 86's finding that chat generally
has no flood protection -- only the account-level mute flag and
per-recipient ignore-list filtering apply. The one actual emote-
adjacent cooldown in the codebase belongs to a specific holo-emote
generator item, unrelated to standard social emotes.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the emote system trusting client-supplied
IDs without server validation is worth knowing if any future feature
ever wants to gate specific emotes behind an unlock/skill requirement
-- that enforcement doesn't exist today and would need new server-side
validation, not just a datatable entry. (2) since animation delivery
already reuses the chat proximity/ignore-list broadcast pattern, any
new "broadcast a visible action to nearby players" feature (e.g. a
companion performing an idle animation) has a ready-made, proven
delivery mechanism to reuse rather than inventing a new one.

---

## 94. Pet / Vehicle / Vendor Store-Summon Persistence (extends sections 11, 27)

**Storing a real pet or vehicle never actually removes it from server
memory or the database's live object graph -- it only removes it from
the physical world.** Both store paths despawn the object from the
zone/quadtree and reparent it into the owning control device's
container tree, but the object itself remains a fully live, referenced
`ManagedObject` in server RAM the entire time it's "stored." No real
persistence call happens at store or summon time -- the container-
transfer machinery that runs during both does call a method named
`updateToDatabase()`, but per this guide's existing section 11 finding,
that method has a confirmed-empty body in every class; it's the
already-documented vestigial no-op, not the real persistence primitive.

**Summoning reads directly from whatever's already in server memory,
never fresh from the database** -- there's no explicit reload-from-DB
step, because the object's reference chain never actually went cold in
the first place.

**This is the same "native setter never calls the real persistence
primitive" gap pattern already found and fixed for this project's own
companion system, confirmed present in the real, non-companion pet
system too.** The real `PetControlDevice`'s vitality setter mutates the
field directly with no dirty-mark call, and `CreatureObject`'s HAM
setter is likewise a plain native mutator with no persistence call --
structurally identical to the exact gap this project already found and
patched for `CompanionObject`. One narrow, accidental partial
mitigation exists for real pets that companions didn't have: a
different, non-native vitality-*penalty*-tier setter happens to be a
plain idlc-generated method (rather than hand-written native code),
which incidentally dirty-marks the object whenever a penalty tier
actually changes -- but this doesn't cover ordinary vitality drift
within a band, or HAM changes at all, so it's a partial accident, not
a deliberate safety net.

**Vendors aren't store/summon objects at all** -- a player-placed
vendor is a continuously-spawned NPC, not something with a stored
state to compare. Its sale bookkeeping (`AuctionItem` field mutations
during a purchase) relies on the same passive dirty-flag/CRC-sweep
mechanism documented in section 27, with no explicit persistence call
found in the purchase path either. There is no vendor-equivalent of a
"control device" pattern at all.

**Practical takeaways -- and one worth flagging back to this project's
own backlog:** (1) this finding directly validates that this project's
own persistence-gap fix (documented elsewhere in this repo's HANDOFF/
NOTES files) was addressing a real, systemic engine pattern, not a
companion-specific oversight -- the same class of bug exists in the
shipped, real pet system too, just less consequential in practice
since a genuinely idle stored pet has little state left to lose beyond
vitality. (2) if this server's real pet system is ever found to lose
vitality/HAM state across a restart, this is the exact, now fully-
traced root cause -- worth remembering rather than re-diagnosing from
scratch. (3) any future new store/summon-capable object type in this
codebase should NOT assume the container-transfer machinery's
`updateToDatabase()` call provides real persistence -- it doesn't, for
anyone, and this has now been confirmed twice (once for companions,
once for real pets/vehicles).

---

## 95. Doctor Profession Buffs & Poison/Disease-as-Weapon (extends sections 51, 63, 69)

**Doctor "enhance" buffs are a real, skill-scaled HAM stat buff
system, structurally similar to but distinct from wound/shock healing
(section 51).** A crafted enhancement item buffs one of the six
primary attributes (or a resistance/"protection" variant), with
magnitude driven by the item's own crafted effectiveness, a battle-
fatigue ratio (for non-protection buffs only), the healer's medical-
rating bonus stack (the same city/droid/structure-sourced bonus
already documented in section 51, including the OVERT-plus-faction-
building perk), and a treatment skill mod -- the resulting object is a
plain generic `Buff` (section 31), gated on non-city medical rating
being present and blocked while either party is in active combat.

**Poison/disease canisters are crafted items using the completely
standard crafting/experimentation pipeline** -- no special-cased
crafting logic exists for them at all, same mechanism as section 69.
What's fixed at the template level (not player-choosable at craft
time) is which HAM pool the effect drains and whether it's poison or
disease.

**Application is a genuine ranged/thrown attack, not a melee-weapon
modifier**, with its own Mind cost and cooldown, routing directly into
the exact same DoT-list mechanism documented in section 63.

**Doctor-applied poison/disease is resistible, and this is a real,
confirmed divergence from the weapon-innate DoT path already
documented in section 63.** Section 63 found weapon-innate poison/
disease DoTs apply with zero resist value baked in. Doctor-crafted
canisters, by contrast, pass a real, dedicated resistance skill mod
into the identical underlying land-roll formula -- meaning the exact
same DoT type (poison, disease) is resistible or unresistable purely
based on *which delivery path* applied it, not the DoT type itself.
This is a subtle, easy-to-misremember distinction worth stating
explicitly.

**Curing is partial-reduction, not a binary cure**, reusing section
63's own DoT-healing mechanism, gated by the same shared PvP/faction
healing-eligibility check documented in section 51, with its own
independent cooldown separate from the wound/shock-healing pools.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "is this poison resistible" cannot be
answered generically for this codebase -- it depends entirely on
whether it came from a weapon's innate DoT or a Doctor-applied
canister, two structurally different application paths for the
identical DoT type. (2) Doctor enhance buffs and food/drink buffs
(section 76) and entertainer buffs (section 72) are three independently-
typed buff sources that can all stack simultaneously on the same
target with no cross-interaction, consistent with this codebase's
general pattern of buff types being isolated by `buffCRC`/`BuffType`.
(3) any new "combat support consumable" content should follow the
`DotPackCommand`/ranged-throw-with-Mind-cost shape already proven here
rather than trying to bolt DoT application onto melee weapons directly.

---

## 96. Server Console / Remote Admin Tooling (extends section 38)

Distinct from in-game GM commands (section 38), the server process
itself exposes a real, fairly extensive console command set (roughly
28 named commands) read from stdin on a dedicated reader thread and
dispatched on the main server thread -- covering save (with multiple
format flags), shutdown/exit, connection-cap adjustment, broadcast,
PvP-mode toggling, screenplay/manager hot-reload, config dumping, and
diagnostic commands (queue/quadtree/octree logging, CRC lookup, log
level).

**Graceful shutdown and an immediate exit are two genuinely different
paths, not the same command with a flag.** The graceful shutdown path
schedules a countdown that broadcasts warnings to all connected
players every 60 seconds before actually disconnecting anyone, while
an immediate exit broadcasts a single "shutting down now" message with
no countdown at all. Both eventually funnel into the same real
graceful-shutdown sequence documented in section 27 (waiting for
in-progress saves, disconnecting players, stopping pathfinding
services, then a real full backup save) -- a hard crash bypasses this
entire sequence, including the player warnings, confirming that a
crash and a console-initiated shutdown are meaningfully different
events for connected players even though both end the server process.

**There is no general live config-reload command** -- only a single
named-manager hot-reload path exists at the console, plus direct
runtime mutation of specific values (like PvP mode) coded as their own
dedicated commands. Most configuration genuinely requires a full
restart to take effect, consistent with section 49's existing
hot-reload findings, which already noted this is per-system rather
than universal.

**A genuine remote-admin channel exists, separate from console/SSH
access** -- an optional, separately-buildable REST API exposes
token-authenticated HTTPS endpoints that can invoke any console
command remotely, read/write live config values, and read server
statistics, all without needing terminal access to the machine
running the server.

**Broadcast/announcement at the console level uses the identical
underlying broadcast function GM in-game commands use** -- the only
difference is the access-control layer (console/REST access instead
of an in-game ability check), not a separate messaging mechanism.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any future live-ops tooling (a dashboard,
an automated alerting system) should target the REST API rather than
trying to interact with the console's stdin directly -- it's the
already-built, network-accessible surface for exactly that purpose.
(2) the crash-bypasses-player-warnings distinction matters for
understanding player-reported "the server just vanished with no
warning" reports -- that's consistent with an actual crash, not a
normal admin-initiated shutdown, which always warns first. (3) since
most config changes need a restart, any troubleshooting checklist
should not assume a config edit takes effect immediately just because
the server is still running.

---

## 97. GCW Crackdown System (extends sections 73, 75)

**Crackdown is not a city-triggered or city-wide mechanic at all --
it's the opposite.** It's a per-planet, per-player wild NPC contraband-
scan encounter that explicitly excludes any player standing inside a
city region. A recurring, randomized-interval task periodically rolls
eligible outdoor players (on planets configured for it) for a scan
chance, skipping anyone indoors, in a city, mounted-but-parented,
on cooldown, dead, incapacitated, in combat, or privileged.

**A scan is a real, stateful NPC encounter, not an instant flag
check.** On success, the scanning NPC enters the `CRACKDOWN_SCANNING`
movement state referenced in section 75's AI tree, follows/confronts
the player, and runs a multi-stage sequence checking faction rank and
status. Same-faction players caught with contraband get a real choice
(pay a credit fine or take a faction-standing penalty for refusing/
ignoring). Opposite-faction players who are detected trigger
reinforcements (an NPC shuttle dropping additional hostiles) and
immediate combat -- this is a genuinely different, more consequential
outcome than the same-faction contraband case, not just a bigger fine.

**The "crackdown TEF" is the mechanical payoff of a hostile
detection**, distinct from the ordinary GCW/duel TEFs documented in
section 73. It's set specifically toward the detecting faction and,
critically, when checked by NPC attackability logic it **bypasses the
normal overt/covert faction-status gate entirely** -- any NPC of the
scanning faction can legally attack the flagged player regardless of
their actual overt/covert status for the TEF's duration. This is a
meaningfully different mechanism from ordinary PvP TEF, which only
affects player-vs-player attackability; crackdown TEF affects
player-vs-NPC attackability.

**Cooldowns exist on both sides** -- a per-player scan cooldown
(measured in days, long enough that a given player won't be
repeatedly re-scanned) and a shorter per-scanner reuse cooldown,
independent of the TEF's own much shorter duration (minutes).

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "crackdown" and "city militia" (section
98) sound like they might be related city-security concepts but are
completely unconnected systems -- one is a city permission tier, the
other is an open-world random NPC encounter that specifically avoids
cities. (2) the crackdown-TEF-bypasses-overt/covert-gating mechanic is
a real, structurally distinct attackability channel worth remembering
