alongside section 73's duel-exemption and ordinary-TEF findings --
there are now three separate ways a player's normal faction-status
protection can be bypassed, each with different triggers and scope.
(3) since crackdown explicitly skips city regions, any GCW-flavor
companion feature themed around "law enforcement encounters" would
need to be built as new content -- there's no existing city-integrated
version of this mechanic to extend.

---

## 98. City Militia System (extends section 77)

Militia is a thinner mechanic than the name suggests: **it is a player
permission tier, not a spawned NPC defense force.** Membership is
simply an object-ID list stored directly on the city region, and the
mayor is always implicitly a militia member regardless of that list.

**Recruitment is mayor-appointment-only, with real guardrails.** Only
the mayor (or an admin) can open the militia management dialog, gated
by a dedicated ability distinct from general mayoral power. A prompted
target must already be a citizen of the city and the mayor must be
standing near the city terminal to add someone; removal has no such
proximity requirement. Losing citizenship automatically strips militia
status as a side effect, not a separately-tracked revocation.

**What militia status actually grants is a bundle of real permissions,
not combat NPCs:** the ability to ban/pardon non-citizen visitors from
city services, the same zoning-rights grant/revoke power documented in
section 77 that's otherwise mayor-exclusive, a visible name-tag suffix
in citizen listings, and -- the closest thing to a "defense" role --
a real combat skill-mod bonus (`private_defense`) from the active city
specialization (section 34), but only active while the player is a
recognized militia member. There's no NPC guard spawning, no automatic
combat intervention, and no cap on militia size at any city rank.

**It's fully independent of faction status.** Nothing in the militia
code path checks overt/covert status (section 73) or faction rank
(section 100) -- militia is purely a citizenship-plus-mayor-appointment
permission, unconnected to a player's GCW standing.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't describe city militia as "city
guards" or defenders in the NPC-combatant sense -- it's a player
permission/authority tier with one passive combat skill-mod perk, not
an automated defense system. (2) the zoning-rights overlap with mayoral
power (section 77) means militia members are effectively junior
co-administrators for build permissions specifically, worth remembering
if a future feature wants to distinguish "who can authorize building
here" from "who holds real city political power." (3) the always-
implicit-mayor-membership detail matters for any code that iterates
militia lists expecting completeness -- checking the raw list alone
will silently miss the mayor.

---

## 99. Vehicle / Mount Terrain Restrictions & Speed Tiers (extends section 43)

**Indoor vehicle summoning is a real, enforced server-side check, not
a client-only restriction** -- any player whose current parent is a
cell object (meaning they're inside any building, cantina, or house
interior) is unconditionally blocked from summoning a vehicle, checked
independently at both the initial summon-request stage and again at
actual spawn time. Vehicles are also blocked from spawning in any
non-ground zone (space, instances). City-level restrictions exist only
for the *repair* flow (a city can ban garage access), not for ordinary
summon/dismiss.

**Speed really does differ meaningfully by vehicle type**, sourced
from the same shared creature-template speed field every `CreatureObject`
uses (vehicles are `CreatureObject` subclasses, not a separate
movement-stat system) -- a landspeeder, swoop, and speederbike each
carry genuinely distinct run-speed values from their own template, and
mounting swaps the rider's effective speed cap to the vehicle's own
value, confirmed by the same code path that validates a player isn't
speed-hacking.

**There is no real terrain-cost differentiation between mounted and
on-foot movement** -- both use the identical position-update code
path, differentiated only by which speed cap applies, not by any
slope/obstacle-aware terrain model. In fact, the one collision check
that could have differentiated vehicle movement from walking is
confirmed present in source but entirely commented out, meaning
neither mounted nor on-foot movement currently gets server-side
slope/obstacle collision enforcement at all.

**There is no vehicle certification or skill-gating system** analogous
to weapon certification (section 36) -- any player can mount any
vehicle they own immediately, with only a narrow Jedi-specific
skill-mod affecting acceleration/turn responsiveness, not eligibility.

**A following pet or companion has no catch-up mechanic when its
owner mounts a faster vehicle.** Real pets are explicitly exempted
from the out-of-sight leash-teleport mechanic non-pet followers get
(section 75), meaning a pet left behind by a mounted owner simply
falls behind via normal pathing with no compensating speed boost or
teleport-to-owner behavior.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the indoor-summon block being genuinely
server-enforced (not just a client UI restriction) means any future
feature assuming "vehicles can't be indoors" can rely on that as an
actual engine guarantee, not just convention. (2) the total absence of
vehicle certification gating means a future "advanced vehicle" feature
would need entirely new gating logic -- there's no existing
skill-requirement scaffolding to extend the way there is for weapons.
(3) a companion riding along with a mounted owner would visibly and
permanently fall behind with current engine behavior -- any future
companion-follows-mounted-owner feature would need genuinely new
catch-up logic, since neither the pet-follow system nor the vehicle
system provides one today.

---

## 100. GCW Military Rank System & Faction Recruiter NPC (extends sections 73, 77)

**A real, distinct military rank ladder exists, entirely separate from
FRS Force rank (section 67) and city mayoral rank (section 77).**
Rank is stored directly on the creature object and progresses through
a real, data-driven ladder (title names live in a binary datatable,
not source) with per-rank point costs and point-transfer ratios --
this is a third, independent rank/progression track alongside the two
already documented elsewhere in this guide.

**Progression is standing-based, not time or kill-count based
directly.** Faction standing (a capped point pool) accrues from NPC
kills and PvP kills (with a real, meaningful positive/negative split
for PvP specifically), and can even be voluntarily transferred between
players at a rank-gated ratio -- a mechanic with no clear parallel
elsewhere in this guide. Actual rank-up isn't automatic once enough
standing accrues -- it requires visiting the faction recruiter NPC and
explicitly completing a promotion conversation, which spends the
required standing at that moment.

**Rank unlocks real mechanical gates, not just cosmetic titles.**
Higher ranks are required for GCW base HQ terminal access and
privileged-structure reporting (layering on top of, not replacing,
section 73's overt-only terminal gating), and rank increases a
player's detection chance/recognition behavior during crackdown scans
(section 97) -- including automatic same-faction recognition and
distinct "caught by the enemy" dialogue at high enough rank. Titles and
salute animations exist too, but they sit on top of these functional
gates rather than being the only effect.

**The faction recruiter NPC is a genuine multi-function hub**, not
just the OVERT/COVERT-transition gatekeeper already noted in section
73 -- the same NPC/screenplay also handles initial faction selection
for a neutral new character, the rank-promotion ceremony itself,
functions as a faction-points vendor (weapons, armor, uniforms,
furniture, GCW base deeds, hirelings, schematics), offers a
credits-for-standing "bribe" path, and displays overall GCW score.

**There is no rank decay mechanic** -- unlike structure decay (section
54) or pet vitality decay (section 52), faction standing and rank are
fully monotonic outside of explicit events (spending it, losing it in
PvP, or a full reset on voluntary resignation via the recruiter, or GM
override).

**Practical takeaways:** (1) this codebase now has three fully
independent player rank/progression tracks (Force rank, city mayoral
rank, GCW military rank) that are easy to conflate in conversation --
worth being precise about which one is meant. (2) the recruiter NPC
being a genuine multi-function hub (not just a status-toggle NPC) is
worth remembering if a future feature ever wants to add a new
faction-related interaction -- it's the established, idiomatic place
to hang it. (3) the point-transfer-between-players mechanic (delegate
faction points) is a rare example in this codebase of a direct
player-to-player progression transfer -- worth studying as a reference
if a similar mechanic is ever wanted elsewhere.

---

## 101. Bounty Mission Posting Mechanics -- Confirmed Automatic, Not Player-Initiated (extends section 44)

**There is no player-facing "post a bounty on another player" feature,
and no GM tool for it either -- posting is fully automatic, triggered
by a Jedi skill milestone.** A player becomes a live bounty target the
moment they're awarded a specific mid-tier Jedi rank skill, with the
bounty entry refreshed automatically on every subsequent login for as
long as they still hold that skill. There is no NPC "most-wanted"
equivalent of this player-bounty object -- generic (non-player) bounty
targets shown at terminals are procedurally generated per-terminal
instead, an entirely separate code path.

**Because posting is automatic and skill-triggered, the griefing
concerns one might expect from a player-initiated bounty system don't
apply -- there's no posting fee, no faction-status requirement, and no
way for one player to target another directly.** Eligibility gating
instead covers online status, a cap on simultaneously active hunters
per target, a minimum time buffer since the target's last relevant
kill, a visibility threshold (the target must be suficiently
"visible," not stealthed/hidden), and same-account exclusion.

**The reward is never escrowed from any player -- it's minted by the
mission system itself at payout time**, computed from the target's own
Jedi skill investment and FRS rank rather than drawn from any
"poster's" funds (there is no poster). Payout routes through the same
shared mission-completion path every mission type uses, fully wrapped
in the `TransactionLog` audit substrate documented in section 39.

**Discovery requires the bounty hunter profession specifically**
(a dedicated skill gate) and happens through genuine terminal-side
randomization that can optionally anonymize a live player's identity
behind a generic faction-aligned label rather than exposing their real
name at the terminal.

**Expiration ties to the same skill milestone that created the
bounty** -- losing the qualifying Jedi skill (or the character being
destroyed) removes the bounty entry and auto-fails every currently-
assigned hunter, with nothing to refund since nothing was ever
escrowed.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) if a future feature request asks for
"let players put a bounty on each other," be clear this is entirely
new work -- the existing bounty system's posting side is a one-way,
automatic, skill-triggered mechanic with no player-initiation path to
extend. (2) the visibility-threshold eligibility check is worth
remembering if a future stealth/companion-concealment feature is ever
built -- it already interacts with an existing "can this player be
bounty-targeted" gate. (3) since reward is minted, not escrowed, this
system has no analog to the COD-mail-escrow question raised (and
answered negatively) in section 91 -- there was never an escrow model
to begin with here either.

---

## 102. Structure Condition Repair -- Confirmed Tied to Maintenance, No Repair Kits Exist (extends section 54)

**There is no consumable structure repair kit, no repair command, and
no repair SUI anywhere in this codebase.** A structure or installation's
condition damage is not an independent, repairable stat at all -- it's
a directly computed reflection of the maintenance deficit, recalculated
from scratch on every scheduled maintenance status update. Paying
maintenance (section 54) is the *only* way condition damage changes;
there is no separate "wear and tear" damage source, and no way to
actively repair a structure the way a weapon, armor, vehicle, or ship
component can be repaired.

**This is confirmed structurally distinct from every other repair
mechanism in this codebase** -- the generic consumable repair-tool
system used for weapons/armor/clothing has no game-object-type mask
covering structures at all, meaning it's not just unused for
structures, it's structurally incapable of ever targeting one. Ship
component repair (section 89) and vehicle garage repair (section 43)
are likewise completely separate, unrelated item/service paths that
never touch a structure's condition value.

**GCW siege damage (section 35's 8-stage vulnerability/destruction
state machine) does not use the structure condition stat at all.** No
siege-related code was found writing to condition damage anywhere in
the GCW base siege task chain -- destruction progresses purely through
that stage machine, entirely independent of the maintenance-driven
condition value documented here. A base's displayed turret "health" in
its control terminal does read the condition stat, but nothing in the
siege system actually damages it.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "repair my structure" is not a real
in-game action in this codebase -- any feature or guide describing
structure upkeep should say "pay maintenance," never "repair," since
those are the same lever, not two separate systems. (2) since GCW
siege damage and maintenance-driven condition are fully independent,
a base can simultaneously show healthy condition (well-maintained) and
be deep into siege vulnerability stages, or vice versa -- don't assume
one implies anything about the other. (3) if a future feature wants a
genuine structure repair mechanic distinct from maintenance payment,
that's entirely new engine work -- there's no partial scaffolding
(unlike some other systems in this guide) to extend.

---

## 103. Structure / Harvester Placement Spacing -- Confirmed Footprint-Only, No Minimum Distance (extends section 59)

**There is no minimum-distance-between-structures requirement anywhere
in this codebase, separate from simple footprint-rectangle overlap.**
Two structures -- including two harvesters on the same resource
concentration spot -- can be legally placed edge-to-edge with
effectively zero gap between them. The placement-check function that
handles this actually shrinks both the new and existing footprint
rectangles by a small floating-point tolerance before testing overlap,
which exists purely to permit exact edge-touching cleanly, not to
create any spacing buffer -- if anything it makes adjacency slightly
*more* permissive than a naive check would.

**Harvester-spam on a single resource location is therefore limited
only by the generic structure-lot cap (section 82), not by any
physical spacing rule specific to harvesters or to resource-extraction
structures generally.** A codebase-wide check found harvester
placement routes through the exact same generic deed-placement
function every other structure type uses, with zero harvester-specific
branching.

**A genuinely separate point-radius mechanism does exist, but it
doesn't apply to ordinary structure-to-structure spacing** -- certain
specific object templates (cloners, some decorations, other flagged
world objects) carry their own no-build radius enforced via real
Euclidean distance, and a separate, unconditional 150-meter no-build
buffer exists around any point-of-interest entry from section 92's
static-content table. Neither of these is a general structure-spacing
rule; they're narrow, template-specific or POI-specific exclusion
zones.

**City zoning (section 77) adds no spacing or adjacency rule either**
-- its placement-time checks are purely permission and per-city
structure-count-cap gates, layered on top of the same footprint check,
with no positional component.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) if a future balance concern is ever
raised about harvester density on rich resource spots, the lot cap
(section 82) is the only existing lever to adjust -- there's no
spacing mechanism to tighten instead. (2) don't assume any new
structure type automatically gets spacing protection from its
neighbors beyond simple footprint overlap -- if genuine minimum
spacing is ever wanted for a new structure type, it would need new,
dedicated distance-check logic, following the no-build-radius
mechanism's Euclidean-distance shape as the closest existing template
to build from.

---

## 104. New Player Tutorial System

**The tutorial is a real, dedicated server zone every new character
passes through, not just a client-side flag or a state on a normal
starting planet.** Choosing to take the tutorial at character creation
spawns a private, per-player instanced building (a multi-room hall)
inside a zone literally named for the tutorial, with each room
implemented as a separate cell. Players who opt to skip the tutorial
still pass through the same zone, just dropped into one shared,
static building near the exit point rather than getting their own
private instance -- the tutorial zone is universal infrastructure, the
walkthrough content is what's actually optional.

**The walkthrough itself is genuine Lua screenplay content layered on
top of C++ instancing/positioning logic**, covering movement/camera
basics, inventory and toolbar familiarization, banking and bazaar
introduction, cloning/insurance lore, a real scripted combat encounter
against a self-detonating tutorial-specific enemy, a profession
trainer re-teaching the player's chosen starting skill, and finally a
mission-giver gating access to the real city-selection travel
terminal that ends the tutorial. This is authored content, not a
generic onboarding checklist -- each room is a distinct, purpose-built
scripted scene.

**The stat-migration/respec screen documented in section 84 is not
part of this scripted room sequence** -- it's a separately-reachable
client-driven session, usable at any point while the player is in the
tutorial zone rather than being tied to a specific tutorial room or
step.

**Skipping is decided once, at character creation, not via an in-game
choice later** -- a client-sent flag on the create-character request,
combined with a server config toggle for whether the tutorial is even
offered at all, determines which of the two zone-entry paths a new
character takes. There's no "opt out mid-tutorial" command; the
decision is made before the character exists.

**Leaving the tutorial is a deliberate command-triggered zone
transition, not a shuttle ride or automatic timeout** -- selecting a
starting city at the room-11 terminal switches the player's zone to
their real starting planet and explicitly destroys the private
tutorial-building instance behind them (only for players who had one;
skippers share a persistent building with nothing to destroy).

**Starting gear uses the exact same underlying grant function as the
non-tutorial path** -- there's no tutorial-exclusive gear table, only
a presentation difference (items appear in an in-scene container the
player interacts with, rather than landing directly in inventory).

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any future onboarding-related feature
(e.g. introducing a companion to a brand-new player) has a real,
purpose-built content pipeline to extend -- the tutorial screenplay,
not a separate onboarding system that would need to be invented.
(2) since skip-vs-full-tutorial is decided once at creation with no
later opt-in, a feature wanting to reach *all* new players regardless
of that choice needs to trigger from something both paths share (zone
entry into "tutorial," or the eventual city-arrival transition) rather
than from inside the scripted room sequence itself, which skippers
never see. (3) the stat-migration session being independently reachable
throughout the tutorial zone (not gated to one room) confirms it's
designed as a standing utility available during onboarding generally,
not a single scripted step.

---

## 105. Combat Defenses: Dodge / Parry / Block / Counterattack (extends sections 10, 79)

**Defense resolution is two sequential rolls, not independent
per-type checks.** A hit/miss roll happens first (accuracy vs. a
capped defense total, run through a diminishing-returns curve). Only
if that roll is a hit does a second, entirely separate evasion contest
even get attempted -- and critically, **the defender's own equipped
weapon type determines which single secondary defense (dodge, block,
or counterattack) is even reachable for that hit**, not player choice
or random selection among all three. A one-handed melee or pistol
wielder can only ever dodge; a two-handed melee or carbine wielder can
only ever counter; a polearm or rifle wielder can only ever block;
unarmed defenders roll randomly among the three. This means a
character's weapon choice silently determines their entire defensive
identity, not just their offense.

**Both primary and secondary defense values are hard-capped at 125**
before additional group/food/PvP bonuses stack on top uncapped --
meaning defense investment has real diminishing returns built in at
the base-skill-mod level, but stacking bonuses from other sources can
still meaningfully push past that cap. No defense outcome is ever
guaranteed regardless of build, since the secondary evasion check is
itself an opposed roll against a live attacker value, not a static
threshold.

**There is no equippable melee/ranged shield item in this codebase**
-- the only "shield" mechanics that exist are the unrelated Jedi Force
shield buff (a flat damage-mitigation percentage) and ship shields
(sections 26/89), both structurally unconnected to personal combat
defense resolution.

**Counterattack has a genuine offensive payoff, not just damage
negation.** Dodge fully negates incoming damage, block halves it, but
counterattack does both *and* immediately forces the defender to
execute a real attack back against the original attacker -- a true
free counter-swing dispatched through the normal attack-command
system, not a cosmetic flourish.

**Posture/locomotion genuinely affects both defense rolls** -- a
defender's current stance (standing, moving, crouching, prone) feeds a
real modifier into both the primary and secondary defense totals via a
datatable lookup. There is no cover or line-of-sight mechanic
affecting defense at all.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) weapon-type-determines-defense-type is a
significant, easy-to-miss balance fact -- any future combat content or
guide should be precise about which weapon categories map to which
defense, since it's not player-selectable. (2) the hard 125 cap on
base defense mods is the correct reference point for evaluating
whether a new defensive skill mod or item bonus is meaningfully
additive or redundant. (3) counterattack's forced free-swing makes it
mechanically the strongest of the three secondary defenses --
worth remembering if a future feature ever needs to reason about
relative weapon-category defensive value.

---

## 106. Encumbrance System (extends sections 76, 84)

**Encumbrance is driven entirely by equipped armor's own stats, not
by carried inventory weight at all** -- a genuinely different model
than "weight-based encumbrance" might suggest. Every armor piece
carries three crafted, quality-scaled encumbrance values (health/
action/mind), and equipping or unequipping that single piece is the
only thing that changes a character's encumbrance -- items sitting in
a backpack or a companion's inventory bag contribute nothing
regardless of how much is carried.

**The HAM penalty is a direct, uncapped 1:1 max-pool subtraction, not
a tiered threshold system.** Each encumbrance value is subtracted
straight from the corresponding pair of max-HAM attributes the moment
armor is equipped, with current HAM simultaneously reduced by the same
amount so the pool doesn't momentarily overflow. This is also enforced
proactively -- equipping a piece that would reduce a max stat below
its current base value is blocked outright with a specific error
identifying which stat failed, rather than being allowed and then
silently corrected.

**The stat updates live and is fully client-visible**, broadcast the
instant a piece is equipped or removed rather than on any periodic
recalculation tick -- though the periodic HAM-reconciliation pass
documented in section 84 does also fold encumbrance back into its
max-HAM formula as a matter of course.

**Encumbrance affects nothing beyond max HAM** -- no movement speed,
accuracy, or action-cost penalty was found anywhere tied to it, a
narrower scope than the mechanic's name might suggest.

**The only mitigation is a Slicing mini-game applied per armor piece**
-- there is no general "encumbrance reduction" skill or exempt
container type. A successful slice permanently and partially reduces
that specific piece's encumbrance contribution, an outcome gated by
the wielder's Slicing skill, not the armor-wearer's own skills.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) since encumbrance is armor-stat-driven,
not weight-based, any feature reasoning about "is this character
overloaded" should look at equipped armor pieces specifically, not
total inventory contents. (2) the equip-time-blocking behavior means
encumbrance failures are caught before they happen, not corrected
after -- a future companion auto-equip feature (section on companion
auto-equip elsewhere in this repo's own history) should be aware this
exact check already exists and would apply identically if companions
ever route through the same equip-validation path. (3) encumbrance
reduction is exclusively a Slicing-profession service on existing
armor, not a stat any wearer can self-improve through their own skill
choices.

---

## 107. GCW Score / Planetary Faction Control (extends section 100)

**GCW score is not a personal or per-kill stat at all -- it's a
live, per-planet aggregate of standing player-placed faction bases,
recomputed from scratch on an hourly cycle, not accumulated or
persisted.** Each active PvP-flagged faction base on a planet
contributes a fixed point value (looked up per base template) to its
owning faction's running total for that specific planet; there is no
individual-player leaderboard or ranking anywhere in this system --
the only real "score" is which faction currently controls more base
value on a given planet, and it's explicitly marked non-persistent,
existing only as a live recomputed snapshot.

**There is no decay curve** -- destroying a base simply removes its
contribution the next time the hourly recompute runs; the score isn't
gradually eroding on its own between recomputes.

**The winning faction's advantage is real and mechanical, not
cosmetic.** Whichever faction currently holds the higher score on a
planet gets a meaningful vendor price discount advantage over the
losing faction (a real percentage split, not symmetric), a flat GCW
experience bonus, and an increased crackdown-scan difficulty scaling
applied against the *losing* faction specifically -- directly tying
this system into section 97's crackdown mechanic as an actual
consequence, not just flavor.

**Display is minimal** -- the faction recruiter's conversation screen
shows the current planet's two faction totals, and a privileged-only
console-style command exists for staff to inspect the same numbers
plus base counts. There's no public galaxy-wide dashboard.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "GCW score," faction standing (used for
military rank, section 100), and city government (section 77) are
three entirely separate numbers that happen to live in the same
broad GCW thematic space -- worth being precise about which one a
future conversation or feature means. (2) since winning-faction status
feeds real crackdown-difficulty and economic bonuses, a base-heavy
faction presence on a given planet has knock-on effects well beyond
that planet's own base-siege gameplay. (3) the fully-recomputed,
non-persisted nature of this stat means there's no historical record
to query -- a "which faction controlled this planet last month"
feature would need new tracking, since the engine itself only ever
knows the current live state.

---

## 108. GCW Base Turret Combat AI (extends sections 35, 97)

**A turret is structurally not an AI agent at all** -- unlike every
creature/NPC documented in sections 66/75, it has no behavior tree, no
patrol/aggro-radius system, nothing in common with the
`AiAgentImplementation` combat-decision machinery. Its targeting and
firing logic instead lives in a dedicated data component driven by a
self-rescheduling fire task, a structurally simpler, purpose-built
mechanism appropriate for a stationary defender rather than a reused
general creature-AI system.

**Targeting is a genuinely separate, simpler check than the
aggro-radius/perception system documented in section 75** -- candidates
come from nearby-object scanning rather than a perception sweep,
filtered by attackability, range, line-of-sight, and (in automatic
mode) active threat/aggression state, with random selection among
valid targets rather than nearest-target or threat-based prioritization.
One special-cased template type "sticks" to its last target across
ticks rather than re-rolling every cycle.

**There is no ammo consumption of any kind** -- once a target is
acquired and in range, a turret fires on a pure cooldown/cadence timer
with no resource depletion, structurally unrelated to the real,
depletable ship-weapon capacitor economy documented in section 89
despite both being "weapon energy" in a loose sense. A separate,
unrelated minefield-donation mechanic lets players contribute mine
objects to a turret's container, but that's a distinct feature from
the turret's primary weapon capability.

**Player-piloted control is real and routes through the same shared
combat command infrastructure documented in section 79** -- taking
manual control via the terminal SUI still ultimately fires through the
identical `CombatQueueCommand`/`doCombatAction` pipeline every other
attack in the game uses, just dispatched server-side by the turret's
own fire task once a player has selected a target through the control
UI, rather than the player personally queuing each shot client-side.

**Turret power is entirely independent of the structure power system**
documented in sections 41/65 -- no power-reserve check exists anywhere
in the turret code; a turret can only be disabled by taking enough
condition damage to be destroyed, never by running out of energy.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) turrets being a data-component-plus-task
pattern rather than a true AI agent is worth remembering if a future
feature ever wants "smarter" turret behavior -- that would mean
extending the fire-task/targeting logic directly, not hooking into the
AI behavior-tree system documented in sections 66/75, since turrets
never touch that machinery at all. (2) reusing the exact same combat
command pipeline for player-piloted turret fire as for personal
attacks means any future combat-command change (e.g. a new damage
formula) automatically applies correctly to turret fire too, with no
separate turret-specific combat code to keep in sync. (3) turret power
being fully decoupled from the structure power system means a
future "power-starve the base's defenses" siege mechanic doesn't
already exist and would need genuinely new logic to connect the two
systems.

---

## 109. Schematic Acquisition: Reverse Engineering & Loot Schematics (extends sections 20, 69)

**The normal trainer path grants schematics as a direct side effect of
learning a skill box, with no separate acquisition step** -- awarding
a skill automatically expands that skill's associated schematic groups
into concrete entries on the player's known-schematics list, the exact
same moment the skill's stat modifiers are applied (section 55/70).

**Three genuinely separate, additional acquisition paths exist beyond
the trainer default**, each tracked with its own source-type tag on
the player's schematic list (mission-reward, loot, and quest-reward
are distinct categories, not merged into one undifferentiated pool --
letting the engine cleanly reclaim a schematic if its granting
mission/item is later removed):

**Reverse engineering is real but narrower than a generic
"deconstruct any item" mechanic** -- it's implemented specifically
around ship components and schematic fragment items, not arbitrary
crafted gear. A dedicated analysis tool either statistically improves
an existing ship component's stats by combining matching components
(not schematic-granting at all), or, when fed the right combination of
collected fragment items, assembles and grants a genuinely new
schematic once every required fragment piece has been gathered.

**Loot schematics are a real, standalone lootable item type** -- a
distinct tangible object that, when used via its own radial option
(gated by a required skill check), grants a specific target schematic
directly onto the player's list and is consumed in the process. These
genuinely drop from loot tables (including named dungeon-specific loot
folders) the same way any other lootable item does, and being ordinary
tangible objects, they're independently tradeable/vendor-sellable
before use -- a schematic can pass through several players' hands
before anyone actually learns it.

**Mission and faction-vendor paths round out acquisition** -- certain
crafting delivery missions grant a schematic as a reward on
completion, an XP-purchase mechanic lets a player spend experience
points directly for a specific schematic, and the faction recruiter
vendor (section 100) sells faction-point-gated exclusive schematics
not obtainable through ordinary skill training at all.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "how does a player get a new recipe"
has at least five distinct real answers in this codebase (trainer
skill-grant, ship-component RE, loot schematic item, mission reward,
faction vendor) -- any crafting-adjacent feature description should be
precise about which path it means. (2) loot schematics being tradeable
items is a real economic lever already built into the game -- a rare
schematic can function as a genuine tradeable commodity, not just a
personal unlock. (3) the reverse-engineering system's narrow scope
(ship components/fragments only) means it's not a template to point to
for a hypothetical "reverse-engineer any crafted item" feature request
-- that would be new work, not an extension of existing RE code.

---

## 110. Faction Perk (`private_*`) Skill Mod Catalog (reference, cross-cutting)

This section consolidates a mechanism referenced piecemeal across many
earlier sections (51, 60, 72, 77, 95, 98) into one reference: the
`private_*`-prefixed skill mod family, granted through location/
context rather than trained skills.

**Two structurally independent grant paths produce mods with the same
naming convention.** City specialization (section 34) applies its
active specialization's skill-mod table to any unbanned creature
physically inside city bounds via the `CITY`-tagged aggregation
bucket, live on region enter/exit -- one specific mod in that table
(`private_defense`) carries an additional eligibility check requiring
militia membership (section 98) on top of simple city presence.
Separately, buildings (faction HQs, hospitals, cantinas, and by
extension camps, section 60) apply their own template-defined skill
mods via the `STRUCTURE`-tagged bucket on building enter/exit. Both
paths ultimately write into the same aggregation pipeline documented
in section 55, and because they're tagged by different source types,
**they stack rather than override each other** -- a player can hold a
city-granted and a building-granted `private_*` mod of the same name
simultaneously, added together, not one replacing the other.

**A third, narrower tier exists for OVERT-plus-same-faction bonuses**
(`private_faction_medical_rating`, `private_faction_mind_heal`,
`private_faction_buff_mind`), checked live at the point of use rather
than aggregated ahead of time -- requiring the player be OVERT,
same-faction as the building, and currently registered within it.
Notably, every shipped faction-HQ template currently has these
specific values commented out in its data -- the gating code is real
and live, but no current content actually populates this bonus tier,
making it dormant despite being fully implemented.

**"Private" is mostly a naming/visibility convention, not a mechanical
restriction** -- for the large majority of `private_*` mods (combat
state modifiers, accuracy/damage scalers, CC duration scalers, and
more), the prefix simply marks a server-internal modifier that isn't
surfaced in client UI, unrelated to faction or location at all. Only
the specific medical/entertainer faction-bonus tier described above
carries genuine access-restriction semantics tied to the word
"private."

**Nearly everything in this family is a live, per-use lookup, not a
persistent buff** -- the CITY/STRUCTURE aggregation itself is
synchronized immediately on entering/leaving the relevant region or
building, with nothing surviving departure. The one real exception is
the entertainer performance buff (section 72), which crystallizes a
`private_faction_buff_mind`-capped value into a genuine timed buff
object at the moment it activates -- but that's the derived buff
persisting, not the underlying mod itself.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any future "where does my HAM/medical/
combat bonus actually come from" investigation should check both CITY
and STRUCTURE tagged sources, since they're independent and additive,
not alternatives. (2) the dormant faction-bonus tier (commented out in
every current template) is worth knowing before assuming any live
server actually grants OVERT-plus-faction-building medical/
entertainer bonuses today -- the code path exists but isn't currently
reachable through any shipped content. (3) since most `private_*` mods
are purely an internal/external-visibility naming convention, don't
assume the word "private" implies a faction or location restriction
without checking the specific mod.

---

## 111. Guild Hall / Guild Structures -- Confirmed Not a Distinct Object Type (extends section 41)

**There is no dedicated guild-hall structure class at all.** "Guild
hall" status is a purely derived, on-the-fly condition -- any ordinary
player-owned building becomes a guild hall the instant a Guild
Terminal object is placed somewhere inside it, and stops being one the
moment that terminal is removed. There's no persisted flag; the check
simply scans the building's contents each time it's asked.

**Ownership remains genuinely individual, never guild-wide** -- a
guild hall is still owned by a single player under the hood, with
guild-wide access granted entirely through the same permission-list
ACL mechanism documented in sections 37/39, extended to support a
guild's own object ID as a valid list entry alongside individual
player IDs. "Transferring" a guild hall to a new owner (e.g. when the
original owner has been offline long enough) is implemented as an
ordinary player-to-player structure transfer, not a guild-specific
operation.

**The "treasury" is a shared withdrawal privilege on an individually-
owned maintenance pool, not a separate guild bank account.** Any
player can pay into a structure's maintenance regardless of guild
membership (same as any ordinary structure, section 54), but only
guild halls specifically expose a withdraw-back-out option, gated to
anyone holding admin-level permission on that structure (whether
granted individually or via the guild's own ID on the ACL) -- letting
withdrawn maintenance surplus become that player's personal cash. This
creates the appearance of a shared guild fund without there actually
being one.

**There is no sanctuary, no-PvP, or GCW-specific property tied to
guild-hall status** -- a guild hall follows exactly the same PvP and
city rules as any other structure of its type; nothing about the
guild-hall designation itself changes combat legality.

**The guild permission bitmask (section 41) has no structure-related
bit at all** -- guild-role permissions (mail, sponsor, kick, war,
disband, etc.) and structure access permissions are two fully separate
systems that only meet at the ACL entry allowing a guild ID to be
listed on a structure's permission lists.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "guild hall" should be described as a
derived label on an ordinary building, not a distinct feature -- any
future guild-structure feature request should be scoped as "extend the
Guild Terminal + ACL pattern," not "build a new guild-hall object
type." (2) the individually-owned-but-shared-withdrawal treasury model
is a real, working pattern worth reusing if a future feature ever
wants a similar "shared pool, individually owned" resource. (3) since
guild-hall status can silently appear or disappear based on whether a
Guild Terminal happens to still be present, any code checking
`isGuildHall()` should treat it as a live, re-derived fact each time,
never a value safe to cache.

---

## 112. Combat State Effects: Stun / Knockdown / Blind / Dizzy / Intimidate & Incapacitation (extends sections 31, 63, 79)

**State effects use the same generic bit-flag/buff-wrapper system
documented in section 31, applied through a genuinely different
pipeline than DoTs (section 63) despite both being combat attack
modifiers.** Each state is a real bit in a creature's state bitmask,
toggled by a dedicated setter that also drives client-visible effects
and system messages, with most states wrapped in a timed buff object
whose activation/deactivation simply flips that bit. Knockdown is the
one exception, applied as a direct posture change rather than a
state-buff, and gated by its own dedicated cooldown rather than a
resistible roll.

**Application runs through a virtual, per-attack-command override
function, distinct from the shared `CombatQueueCommand`/
`doCombatAction()` path documented in section 79 for basic damage
resolution** -- meaning state-effect application is itself a
data-driven, per-command customization point, consistent with this
codebase's general "one shared execution path, data-driven behavior
differences" pattern seen elsewhere (buffs, dialogue, basic-vs-special
attacks).

**Resistance is a genuinely different formula from DoT resistance
(section 63), not the same mechanism reapplied.** A state application
runs its own hit-or-miss probability roll (accuracy plus a bonus,
against a defender's own state-defense skill mods scaled and combined
with level), with a Jedi-specific second resistance roll layered on
top for Force-trained characters. Critically, even a fully successful
resist roll only ever *shortens* the resulting duration through a
separate formula, never fully prevents the state below a fixed
minimum floor -- meaning a state effect can never be reduced to
literally zero duration by pure defense investment, only minimized.

**Reapplication refreshes rather than stacks** -- attempting to apply
an already-active state effect extends/resets its timer rather than
increasing its magnitude or stacking multiple simultaneous instances,
consistent with how ordinary buffs are generally handled elsewhere in
this codebase. Knockdown instead uses a hard cooldown window that
suppresses being knocked down again at all while active, a diminishing-
returns immunity shape rather than a refresh.

**Incapacitation is a real, distinct three-strike mechanic, not merely
"stun taken to zero HAM."** Reaching zero on a HAM pool doesn't kill a
player outright -- it triggers a countable incapacitation event within
a rolling time window; only the third such event within that window
results in actual death, with the first two instead putting the player
into a genuinely separate incapacitated posture that recovers on its
own timer. This gives PvP combat a real "downed but not dead" phase
distinct from every other state effect in this system.

**None of the crowd-control states have an active cure** -- unlike
poison/disease (section 95), which has dedicated cure commands, stun/
dizzy/blind/intimidate/knockdown all resolve purely on their own timer
with no player-facing ability to actively remove them early. Only
incapacitation has its own dedicated recovery task, and that's still
timer-based, not player-cured.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the duration-only-shrinks-never-zeroes
resist model means state-effect-heavy content should always factor in
some minimum uptime regardless of target build, rather than assuming
maxed resistance can neutralize crowd control entirely. (2) the
complete absence of an active cure for crowd-control states (as
opposed to poison/disease's real cure mechanic) is a real, deliberate
asymmetry worth remembering when comparing "how do I counter X"
questions across different combat-debuff categories in this codebase.
(3) the three-strike incapacitation window is the correct mental model
for any PvP-related feature reasoning about "is this player actually
dead yet" -- a single zero-HAM event is not death, and code checking
for player death should distinguish incapacitation from an actual
kill.

---

## 113. Skill Point Budget & Profession Point Economy (extends sections 55, 70)

**The classic 250-point skill cap is a config-driven value set once at
character creation, not a hardcoded engine constant** -- it's read
from a Lua config script and stamped onto the new character's skill-
point field at that moment, meaning it could in principle be changed
per-deployment by editing config, though no in-game mechanism (GM
grant, veteran reward) was found that raises an individual character's
cap after creation. Somewhat surprisingly, the same 250 value is
independently hardcoded a second time inside the skill manager itself,
used only as an internal integrity-check reference rather than the
actual source of truth -- a minor duplication worth knowing about if
the cap is ever changed, since both places would need updating.

**Point cost is per-skill-box, datatable-defined, and genuinely
enforced before every grant** -- `canLearnSkill()` (section 70) checks
available points against the box's own cost before allowing the
award, with one real, deliberate carve-out: this project's own
companion-master skill line is exempted from the point cost entirely
(though not the XP cost), a pre-existing patch already documented
elsewhere in this guide's companion-adjacent findings.

**Surrendering a skill unconditionally refunds its full point cost**,
but only after confirming no currently-held skill still depends on it
as a prerequisite -- dependents must be surrendered first, enforced by
a live scan of the character's current skill list rather than a
precomputed dependency graph. Jedi and pilot skills carry additional,
separate surrender restrictions layered on top of the basic dependency
check.

**There is a real self-healing integrity check on every single grant
and surrender** -- both operations end by recomputing total spent
points from the actual live skill list and force-correcting the
stored point total if it's drifted, logging an error when it does.
This is a genuine defensive pattern worth remembering: the system
doesn't fully trust its own running point total, it re-derives and
corrects it after every mutation.

**Multi-profession budgeting is entirely player-driven, with zero
system-level guidance or restriction** -- nothing in the skill-award
code steers a character toward "reasonable" profession combinations;
the only constraints on what's learnable are ordinary prerequisite/
species/Jedi-state gates, unrelated to point budgeting itself. A
separate badge/title reward exists specifically for fully mastering a
profession tree (any skill box with "master" in its name triggers a
badge award), layered on top of the skill grant itself as a
recognition mechanic, not a mechanical gate.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the point-cost check happening inside
`canLearnSkill()` (already load-bearing for section 70's core grant
path) means any future skill-economy tweak (a new point-cost curve, a
raised cap) has exactly one real enforcement point to modify, plus the
duplicated 250 constant to keep in sync. (2) the self-correcting
integrity check is a good defensive pattern to imitate for any future
resource-budget system in this codebase, not just skill points. (3)
since multi-profession support is purely player-driven with no system
nudging, a future "recommended build" or "respec helper" feature would
be entirely new UX, not an extension of anything that already exists.

---

## 114. Damage Type / Armor Resistance System (extends section 10)

**There are nine real damage types, but only five ever appear as a
weapon's actual base damage type.** Kinetic, energy, blast, stun, and
lightsaber are the damage types weapons are actually assigned; heat,
cold, acid, and electricity exist purely as elemental resistance/
vulnerability categories (relevant to armor stats and certain state/
DoT effects) rather than as base weapon output -- Force attacks are
the one path that can freely assign any of the nine types regardless
of weapon.

**Armor mitigation is a flat, sequential, multiplicative percentage
reduction with no diminishing-returns curve baked into the formula
itself** -- Force armor/shield, personal shield generators, and worn
armor each apply their own flat percentage cut in sequence, one after
another, rather than one combined formula. Weapon armor-piercing
modifies damage *before* any of these resist multipliers apply, using
an exponential formula based on the gap between piercing rating and
armor rating -- meaning a sufficiently high piercing rating can make
even strong armor resistance largely irrelevant, and conversely
under-penetrating a well-armored target compounds against you
exponentially, not linearly.

**Resistance values are genuinely per-damage-type and independently
crafted/quality-scaled**, not a single overall "armor rating" -- each
armor piece stores separate values for every one of the nine damage
types, sourced from the same crafting-experimentation pipeline
documented in section 69, meaning two otherwise-identical armor
pieces can have meaningfully different real-world effectiveness
depending on how they were crafted and against what specific damage
type they're facing.

**Damage type is fixed per weapon at creation, never selectable via
ammunition or power-pack choice** -- weapon powerup components (the
crafted enhancement items covered elsewhere) only ever scale numeric
stats like damage range, speed, and accuracy; none of them alter a
weapon's fundamental damage type. This contradicts a plausible
assumption that different ammo could change a weapon's damage
category -- in this codebase it can't.

**There is no explicit resistance ceiling enforced in code** -- the
mitigation formula itself has no hard cap preventing resistance from
exceeding 100%, relying entirely on crafted-value ranges in content
data to keep it sane rather than a code-level safety clamp. Separately,
an armor "vulnerability" flag against a specific damage type skips
resistance entirely rather than amplifying damage -- a vulnerable
piece takes full raw damage, not bonus damage. Wound chance (section
51) is rolled independently of armor resistance, using the weapon's
own wound-ratio stat against post-mitigation damage -- meaning armor
reduces how much HAM damage lands, but never affects the separate
chance of that hit causing a wound.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the no-hard-cap-in-code detail is worth
flagging if a future crafted-item or buff feature could theoretically
push a resistance value very high -- nothing in the engine itself
would catch an over-100% resistance value, only careful content
authoring does. (2) the exponential armor-piercing formula means
"armor rating vs. piercing rating" is a much sharper, more decisive
relationship than a flat percentage difference would suggest --
relevant for balancing any new weapon or armor content. (3) since
elemental damage types (heat/cold/acid/electricity) never appear as
base weapon damage, any new "elemental weapon" content would need to
route through the Force-attack-style flexible damage-type assignment
mechanism rather than the normal fixed-per-weapon-template model.

---

## 115. Weapon Range Mechanics (extends sections 10, 105)

**Range accuracy is a continuous, three-point piecewise-linear
interpolation curve per weapon, not a discrete band system** (no
literal "point-blank/short/medium/long" tiers exist in code) --
each weapon defines its own point-blank, ideal, and maximum range
values paired with an accuracy modifier at each point, and actual
accuracy at any given distance is linearly interpolated between
whichever two points bracket the current range, recalculated fresh at
every single attack resolution using live world positions, not cached
from when the attack was queued.

**"Minimum range" is real but implemented as a soft accuracy penalty,
not a hard rejected-shot cutoff.** Rifles and heavy weapons in
particular carry a sharply negative accuracy value at their
point-blank range point, meaning firing a rifle at extreme close range
is a real, meaningful accuracy penalty (not a flat miss), rising
toward a much better accuracy value at the weapon's ideal range and
falling off again toward maximum range. Pistols and carbines, by
contrast, have comparatively mild or nonexistent close-range
penalties, making them the better choice at short range by design.

**Beyond a weapon's maximum range, accuracy simply flattens at its
worst value rather than the attack becoming impossible** -- a queued
attack still executes, just at that floor accuracy, unless a separate,
earlier range-gate check (used only to validate whether an attack
command can even be issued in the first place) already rejected it for
being too far away entirely.

**Melee weapons run through the exact same interpolation function as
ranged weapons, just with all three range points collapsed to an
identical value** -- there's no structurally separate melee-range
code path, the shared formula simply degenerates to a flat constant
when point-blank, ideal, and maximum range are all equal, which is how
every melee weapon template is authored.

**Range can be genuinely extended by crafted weapon powerup
components**, which directly shift a weapon's ideal/maximum range
control points (and related accuracy values) rather than adding a
separate additive range bonus on top -- there is no general
creature skill mod that extends weapon range; only crafted
attachments do.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "minimum range" being a real, weapon-
category-dependent accuracy penalty (not a hard cutoff) means a
kiting-vs-rifle-user tactical dynamic is a genuine, intentional
mechanic in this codebase, not folklore. (2) since range powerups
shift the actual interpolation control points rather than adding a
flat bonus, their effect is most pronounced for weapons whose base
curve has a steep accuracy slope near the ideal range -- worth
knowing when evaluating whether a given powerup is actually impactful
for a specific weapon. (3) the live, per-shot recalculation (not
cached at queue time) means a target moving during an attacker's
queued action genuinely changes that attack's accuracy outcome, not
just its ability to connect at all.

---

## 116. Solo / Non-Grouped Corpse Looting Permissions (extends sections 15, 39, 61, 68, 78)

**Loot rights for an ungrouped kill go entirely to whichever single
player (or their group, if grouped) dealt the single highest
cumulative loot-eligible damage -- not the killing blow, not "first to
tag," and not proportionally shared the way group XP is (section
68).** This is a genuinely different reward-division philosophy than
XP distribution: XP splits by damage proportion among every
contributor, while solo/mixed-party loot rights go entirely to one
winner determined by a damage-total comparison, with everyone else
getting zero container access regardless of how much they
contributed, unless their own total happens to exceed the winner's.

**There is no time-limited "tap" window that opens looting to everyone
after some delay** -- ownership is fixed for the corpse's entire
lifetime (until it despawns) to whichever single winner the damage
comparison produced at the moment of death; it never becomes open
access later.

**Loot ownership is implemented as an ordinary container-permission
ACL entry, the exact same mechanism documented in section 39**, not a
bespoke loot-specific system -- the corpse's inventory container gets
its owner field stamped with either the winning player's ID or their
group's ID, and the loot command itself checks that field the same way
any other container-permission check in this codebase works.

**Player corpses cannot be looted at all, structurally, regardless of
PvP kill legality.** The loot command explicitly only operates against
creature/NPC targets; a player's own inventory container is
permanently self-owned from the moment their character object is
created and this ownership is never reassigned to a PvP killer, no
matter how the death occurred or how the attackability rules (section
73) were satisfied. Killing another player never grants any container
access to their belongings in this codebase.

**Permission never "opens up" over time -- the corpse is simply
deleted once its despawn timer (already documented in section 78,
shortened once the rightful owner finishes looting) elapses.** There's
no expanding-access mechanic to account for; access is binary and
permanent until the object itself ceases to exist.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) loot rights and XP rights use genuinely
different division philosophies for the same kill event -- worth being
precise about which one a future balance or fairness question is
actually asking about. (2) the winner-take-all model means an
ungrouped "kill steal" (a second player finishing off a creature
someone else nearly killed) can legitimately flip loot ownership
entirely if their damage total happens to exceed the original
attacker's -- a real, intentional incentive against casual non-grouped
cooperative killing that a future social feature might want to be
aware of. (3) player corpses being structurally unlootable means any
future "loot a defeated player" feature request is unambiguously new
work, not a permission tweak on an existing mechanism.

---

## 117. GCW Base Placement / Deed System (extends sections 35, 59, 97, 100)

**A GCW base is placed via an ordinary purchased/tradeable structure
deed, not a crafted item and not gated by military rank at all** --
unlike some other faction-adjacent systems in this guide, placing a
base requires no minimum rank (section 100's rank ladder only becomes
relevant *after* placement, gating admin-terminal access on an
already-built base, not the placement action itself). The only
faction requirement is the same generic faction-match check any
faction-flagged deed enforces: the placing player must share the
deed's faction and not be neutral or on-leave.

**Placement is capped by three independent, stacking limits beyond
the standard structure placement chain**: a hard planet-wide cap on
total active bases, a separate hard per-player cap on how many bases
one player can own simultaneously, and a same-faction base-density
check preventing too many bases from clustering near each other
(with an explicit allowance for one intentional "base complex" of a
few co-located bases). All three layer on top of, rather than replace,
the same generic structure-placement validation chain documented in
section 59 -- including its city-region exclusion, meaning bases
cannot be placed inside city boundaries at all.

**A real five-tier deed ladder exists**, each tier with a PvP-flagged
variant, giving a genuine small-outpost-to-full-base progression
similar in spirit to (but structurally unrelated to) the city rank
ladder documented in section 77 -- tier stat differences live in
client-side template data rather than server C++ logic.

**Initial vulnerability/HP is fixed per deed tier, not dynamically
scaled by anything at placement time** -- there's no member-count or
guild-size-based scaling of a base's starting durability; a given deed
tier always produces the same starting stats regardless of who places
it or how large their faction group is.

**Any individual player holding a valid deed can place a base
independently** -- ownership and placement rights are per-player, not
gated by guild leadership or faction military rank, meaning base
proliferation is limited entirely by the placement caps described
above rather than by any organizational-authority requirement.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the total absence of a rank requirement
to place (contrasted with rank mattering for later administration) is
a subtle but real distinction worth getting right if a future feature
or explanation touches GCW base mechanics. (2) the three independent
placement caps (planet-wide, per-player, density) are the actual
levers available if base proliferation is ever a balance concern --
there's no single unified "base limit" setting, all three would need
consideration. (3) since base stats come from fixed per-tier templates
rather than dynamic scaling, a "stronger base for a bigger guild"
feature would be new work, not a config tweak on existing scaling
logic that doesn't currently exist.

---

## 118. Player Command Macro System -- Confirmed Client-Side Only

**The classic SWG saved multi-command macro feature (binding a
sequence of slash-commands to one hotbar slot) has zero server-side
representation in this codebase.** An exhaustive search found no
macro class, no macro-related field on the player object, no macro
persistence of any kind, and no macro-aware dispatch path anywhere in
the server source -- this is architecturally consistent with how the
original game worked: the client expands a saved macro into its
individual commands locally and sends each one to the server exactly
as if it had been typed manually, one at a time.

**Because the server never receives any signal that a command
originated from a macro, every macro-issued command is, from the
server's perspective, indistinguishable from a directly-typed command**
-- it goes through the identical command-dispatch and queue pipeline
documented in sections 6/79 with no special-casing whatsoever. There
is consequently no macro-specific command count limit, no
macro-specific disallowed-command blocklist, and no macro-aware
anti-automation detection -- any throttling that exists (ordinary
per-command cooldowns) applies equally regardless of whether a human
typed the command or a client-side macro expanded it.

**A genuinely unrelated feature uses similar-sounding vocabulary and
is worth explicitly distinguishing.** This project's own companion
system has a real, server-side "macro list" of granted companion
ability commands (registering real `command_table.iff` rows onto an
owner's hotbar as skills are learned) -- a completely different
mechanism serving a different purpose, but described in its own source
comments using language that could easily be mistaken for the classic
player-macro feature covered here. They are unrelated: one is a
client-only convenience feature the server has no model of at all, the
other is a real server-side command-grant system for companion
abilities.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) if a future feature ever wants to detect
or restrict macro-driven play (e.g. for anti-bot purposes), that
would require an entirely new client-cooperation or heuristic-
detection mechanism -- there is no existing server-side hook to build
on, since the server fundamentally cannot tell a macro-issued command
from a manually-typed one. (2) don't confuse this guide's "macro"
(the classic player convenience feature, confirmed absent server-side)
with this project's own companion ability-macro-granting system --
they share a name by coincidence, not by mechanism.

---

## 119. Vehicle Deed Acquisition (extends sections 43, 109)

**Most real vehicle deeds are crafted output, going through the exact
same crafting/experimentation pipeline as any other manufactured item**
(sections 20/69) -- ordinary draft schematics exist for the common
civilian speeder/swoop/jetpack lineup, requiring no dedicated
"vehicle engineer" profession beyond the general assembly skill any
crafter can hold, confirming vehicles aren't a mechanically separate
crafting category despite being a visually distinct item class.

**There is no direct credit-purchase vendor path for vehicle deeds**
-- unlike some other item categories in this game, no Starport or
vendor NPC sells a vehicle deed outright for credits. The one real
non-crafted acquisition path is a limited-use rental coupon granted
through the new-player introductory content, producing a speederbike
capped at a small fixed number of uses before it's permanently
consumed -- a starter freebie, not a genuine alternative acquisition
channel for ongoing vehicle ownership.

**Claiming and mounting a vehicle deed requires no certification or
skill check whatsoever** -- consistent with section 99's finding that
there's no vehicle certification system analogous to weapon
certification (section 36), the deed-claim process only validates
ownership, location, and combat/parent-state gates, never a skill
requirement.

**A loot-schematic acquisition path exists for vehicles too, but it's
narrow and confirmed non-random** -- exactly one vehicle schematic in
the entire codebase is obtainable this way, and even that one is a
guaranteed reward for completing a specific dungeon instance rather
than a random creature drop; ordinary mob and mission loot tables were
confirmed to never drop vehicle deeds or vehicle schematics generally.
This is a meaningfully narrower use of the loot-schematic mechanism
(section 109) than crafting schematics generally enjoy.

**There is no insurance or reclaim mechanic for a lost/destroyed
vehicle** -- vehicles aren't normally destructible in ordinary play,
and the only self-consuming vehicle in the codebase is the starter
rental speederbike, which expires on a simple use-counter rather than
any damage or loss event.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "how do I get a new vehicle type" almost
always means "craft it," not "buy it" or "loot it" in this codebase --
any future vehicle content should default to the crafting-schematic
model unless there's a specific reason to deviate, matching the
established pattern. (2) the single guaranteed-dungeon-reward vehicle
schematic is a useful, already-proven template if a future feature
ever wants a similarly exclusive, non-craftable vehicle reward. (3)
since vehicle claiming has zero certification gating, a future
"advanced vehicle requires training" feature would need genuinely new
gating logic, mirroring section 99's identical finding for actually
riding a vehicle.

---

## 120. Storage Crates & House Cell Connectivity (extends sections 12, 37)

**"Storage crate" is not a distinct object class -- it's an ordinary
generic container object, the same single container class used for
backpacks, crafting hoppers, and every other container in the game**,
distinguished only by its template's configured volume and container
type. There's no dedicated storage-crate capacity or permission model
separate from what any other container already has.

**House room/cell layout is fixed per building template at
construction time, with no player-driven ability to add or remove
rooms afterward** -- the total cell count comes directly from the
building's own client-side layout data, cells are created once as a
flat list when the structure is placed, and no code path exists
anywhere to remove a cell later. Room-to-room connectivity itself is
purely client-side visual geometry -- the server only tracks which
cells exist as a flat list, not any kind of navigable room graph.

**A real house-wide item count cap exists, independent of any
per-cell volume limit** -- civic structures get one flat ceiling,
while ordinary player housing scales with the number of lots the
structure occupies, capped at an absolute maximum regardless of size.
This is enforced by walking up to the structure's root and counting
every player-placed item across all cells combined, layered on top of
(not instead of) each individual cell's own volume-limit check from
section 37.

**True nested storage (a crate placed inside another crate) is
structurally blocked, not just discouraged** -- the container-
insertion validation explicitly rejects placing one general container
type inside another, and separately rejects any loose (non-slotted)
container object being placed into a target container that has no
defined slot arrangement, which describes every ordinary storage
crate. The practical effect is a hard, enforced two-level maximum
nesting depth: a house cell can hold storage crates, and those crates
can hold ordinary items, but crates cannot hold further crates.

**Nesting doesn't multiply available capacity, but the interplay is
asymmetric and worth knowing precisely.** A crate placed inside a cell
consumes exactly one slot of that cell's own volume at the moment it's
inserted; the cell's volume tracking is not continuously re-validated
against everything later placed inside that already-nested crate. The
house-wide item-count cap, by contrast, does count recursively through
nested contents. So a cell's own volume limit and the house-wide count
cap behave differently with respect to nested crates -- one is
effectively a one-time slot cost, the other tracks true recursive
contents.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the crate-cannot-contain-crate rule is a
hard engine constraint, not a UI suggestion -- any future storage-
related feature should assume a strict two-level depth ceiling rather
than trying to build deeper nesting. (2) the house-wide item-count cap
being count-based (not volume-based) and applying across every cell
combined is worth remembering for any feature that reasons about "how
much can this house hold" -- the real limiting factor for a large,
many-cell house is often the flat item-count ceiling, not any
individual room's volume. (3) since storage crates are just ordinary
containers with no special capacity model, any future "expanded
storage" item (a bigger crate, a special deep-storage container) is
purely a matter of authoring a template with a larger
`containerVolumeLimit`, not new container-class code.

---

## 121. Jedi Holocron Item Mechanic (extends sections 9a, 58, 81)

**A holocron is a real tangible item, but what using one actually does
depends entirely on which Force-sensitive progression mode the server
is configured for** -- the item itself is a thin dispatcher that hands
off to whichever progression script is currently active, meaning
"what does a holocron do" has no single universal answer in this
codebase.

**Under hologrind progression, the holocron is purely informational,
not a progression trigger at all.** Consuming it just surfaces hints
about which hidden professions still need mastering; actual
Force-sensitive unlock happens automatically once enough
randomly-assigned hidden professions have been mastered, detected via
a badge-award observer rather than anything holocron-related.

**Under village progression -- the mode this guide's other Jedi
sections focus on -- the holocron is a Force-power replenishment
consumable usable only by characters who are already Jedi, not a
progression-starting item at all.** The actual eligibility trigger for
starting the village questline is a separate, automatic check run at
login, unrelated to holding or using a holocron. This is a genuinely
counterintuitive finding worth stating plainly: despite the strong
classic-SWG association between "finding a holocron" and "becoming
Force-sensitive," in this codebase's default (village) progression
mode, using a holocron neither starts nor advances that journey --
it's a mid-progression utility item for existing Jedi.

**Holocrons are real, rare loot drops, but from a narrow, specific
creature pool, not a universal kill-chance.** Only a handful of
Force-sensitive-flavored NPCs (certain Dantooine "Kun" creatures and
dark Jedi thug templates) carry a holocron entry in their loot tables
at a modest relative weight -- ordinary creatures never drop one
regardless of level or type.

**Reuse is gated by a straightforward 24-hour per-character cooldown**
on the village-mode Force-replenishment use case -- there's no
evidence of any lockout preventing a character from acquiring multiple
holocrons or restarting Force-sensitive progression after abandoning
it; the only real restriction found is this reuse-throttling cooldown.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any player-facing explanation of "how do I
become a Jedi" must be precise about which progression mode a given
server runs, since the holocron's role is completely different (and in
village mode, essentially irrelevant to starting the journey) between
modes. (2) the badge-award-observer trigger for hologrind completion is
a clean, already-proven pattern worth remembering if a future feature
ever wants "complete N of a hidden set of objectives" logic elsewhere
in this codebase. (3) since holocrons only drop from a narrow,
specific creature pool, any future "increase holocron drop rate"
request would mean editing a small number of specific loot-group
files, not a global drop-table change.

---

## 122. Vendor Barker / Advertisement System (extends sections 24, 74, 86)

**Barking is a real, active proximity broadcast, not a static label
shown only on direct interaction.** A player-placed vendor with
barking enabled genuinely announces its configured phrase as a real
spatial-chat bubble message to any player who walks within a real,
fairly short range, complete with a chosen mood and a brief
accompanying animation before the vendor NPC turns back to its
resting orientation -- this is an active broadcast event triggered by
player proximity, not a passive tooltip a player has to seek out.

**Setup goes through a real multi-step SUI wizard**, letting the owner
choose between a set of canned category phrases or a fully custom
message (capped at a modest character limit), plus a mood and
animation to accompany it -- and the custom-message path is
confirmed to route through the same profanity filter already
documented in section 86, one of the small set of real call sites for
that filter.

**A parallel, structurally distinct mechanism exists for droid
merchant vendors specifically** -- rather than the proximity-triggered
event used by player-placed vendors, a droid merchant runs its own
simple self-rescheduling announcement loop on a hardcoded interval,
broadcasting to whoever happens to be in range each time it fires,
regardless of whether anyone new has entered proximity since the last
announcement.

**Unlike ordinary player chat (section 86, confirmed to have zero
flood protection), vendor barking has real, deliberate spam
prevention** -- both the player-vendor and droid-merchant barking
paths enforce their own cooldown between announcements, and the
player-vendor path additionally avoids re-barking at the same nearby
player repeatedly while they remain in range, a level of self-
throttling this codebase's regular chat system conspicuously lacks.

**Barker phrases and vendor names are not searchable through the
bazaar cross-vendor search system (section 74)** -- that search
indexes item listings exclusively; there's no way to discover a vendor
by its advertisement text or display name through the commodities
search terminals. Barking is purely a textual/audio-flavor proximity
mechanic, with no tie to vendor appearance customization or a
nameplate/sign object of any kind.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) vendor barking having real spam
prevention while general chat has none is a useful, concrete example
of this codebase's inconsistent-by-design approach to different
communication channels -- worth remembering rather than assuming
"chat" is a single uniform system. (2) since barker text isn't
searchable, a player-run shop's real discoverability still depends
entirely on the bazaar item-listing search (section 74), not clever
advertising -- a future feature wanting "discover shops by theme/
advertisement" would need genuinely new search infrastructure. (3) the
droid-merchant barker's simpler always-fire-on-timer design (vs. the
player vendor's proximity-triggered, per-target-throttled model) is
worth knowing if a future feature ever wants an NPC that announces
itself periodically without needing the more complex player-vendor
mechanism.

---

## 123. Personal Shield Generator (PSG) Mechanics (extends section 114)

**A PSG is a fully crafted item, going through the identical armor-
crafting pipeline as any other piece of armor** (sections 20/69) --
there's no separate "shield engineering" profession or special
crafting path; it's authored and experimented on exactly like any
other armor schematic, with the same quality-scaled attribute rolls.

**Despite the "shield" name evoking a depletable energy pool (the way
ship shields work, section 89), a PSG's protection is actually a flat
per-hit percentage damage reduction with no depletable resource at
all** -- a structurally simpler mechanic than ship shielding, closer
in spirit to ordinary worn armor than to any recharging-pool concept.
What genuinely does deplete is the PSG item's own durability: each hit
it mitigates inflicts real condition damage on the PSG itself
proportional to the damage absorbed, meaning a PSG degrades and can
eventually break from sustained use, conceptually different from a
rechargeable shield running dry.

**A PSG occupies a dedicated equipment slot (the utility belt), not a
separate deployable or activatable device** -- it's simply worn
alongside other gear rather than being toggled on/off or requiring
activation.

**Resistance is genuinely per-damage-type, following the exact same
nine-type profile structure as worn armor (section 114), and the
default/common PSG variant has a real, meaningful weakness profile**
-- it's explicitly configured with zero or near-zero protection
against kinetic, blast, and acid damage specifically, while offering
solid protection against energy, electricity, stun, heat, cold, and
lightsaber damage. This is a deliberate trade-off, not an oversight:
a PSG-wearing character is genuinely more exposed to certain damage
categories than others, a real tactical consideration for both attacker
and defender.

**There is no profession or skill gate on equipping a PSG** -- any
character can wear and benefit from one immediately once crafted or
acquired, with no certification requirement analogous to weapon
certification (section 36).

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "shield" terminology across this codebase
means genuinely different things depending on context -- ship shields
(section 89) are a real depletable/regenerating resource, while
personal shield generators are a flat percentage armor-style
mitigation with item-durability decay instead. Don't conflate the two
when discussing "shields" generically. (2) the default PSG's real
vulnerability to kinetic/blast/acid damage is a concrete, exploitable
weakness worth knowing for any combat-balance discussion -- a
