PSG-wearing target isn't uniformly better protected, just
differently protected. (3) since PSGs use the same crafting pipeline
and resistance-profile structure as ordinary armor, any future PSG
content (new tiers, variants) is authored exactly the same way as any
other armor schematic, not a special case.

---

## 124. New Player "Theme Park" Quest Chains (extends sections 104, 119)

**"Theme park" is a real, general term this codebase uses for any
substantial, multi-step, narratively-guided quest chain culminating in
a signature reward or unlock -- not a name specific to the new-player
content.** A whole family of named, unrelated theme-park quest chains
exists (major faction and character-specific storylines among them),
sharing common supporting Lua infrastructure, confirming this is a
deliberate content category in this codebase's own vocabulary, not
informal terminology.

**The new-player theme park specifically is profession-tailored**,
with a distinct number of steps depending on which starting profession
the player chose, walking them through profession-appropriate objectives
and granting real profession gear alongside standard credit/experience
rewards at each step. The culminating final reward is the same
limited-use starter vehicle coupon already documented in section 119 --
this theme park is confirmed as that coupon's actual source. It is
strictly narrative/spatial-gated to being reachable after the tutorial
zone (section 104), not enforced by any quest-flag dependency check --
a player could theoretically encounter the theme-park NPC without ever
having completed the tutorial, since nothing in its own logic actually
verifies tutorial completion.

**Progress tracking uses a genuinely different persistence mechanism
than the ordinary screenplay quest system documented in section 80**
-- rather than the bit-array active/completed-quest fields on the
player object, this specific theme park (and likely others sharing the
same supporting infrastructure) persists progress through a separate,
string-keyed quest-status data layer with its own dedicated database
table, plus generic key-value screenplay storage for finer-grained
per-step counters. This is a second, parallel quest-progress
persistence mechanism worth knowing exists alongside the one already
documented, not a variation of the same system.

**It's confirmed strictly one-time per character** -- completion is
tracked both by an explicit reward-already-granted check (preventing
duplicate coupon grants) and by clearing the quest-tracking data on
final completion, which together prevent re-entry into the chain once
finished.

**No schematic rewards are involved in this particular theme park** --
its reward mix is limited to credits, experience, profession starter
gear, a cosmetic firework, and the three new-player convenience
coupons (cloning, travel, vehicle), confirming no overlap with section
109's mission-reward-schematic acquisition path for this specific
content.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "theme park" is the correct, precise term
to use when discussing any of this codebase's major guided quest
chains -- it's not vague marketing language, it's the actual content
category name used in the source tree's own directory structure.
(2) the second, string-keyed quest-persistence mechanism is worth
remembering separately from section 80's bit-array system -- a future
feature auditing "how is quest progress tracked in this codebase"
needs to check both, since different content uses different
mechanisms. (3) since the new-player theme park has no hard tutorial-
completion gate, a future onboarding feature shouldn't assume tutorial
completion as a precondition for theme-park-triggered content without
adding that check itself.

---

## 125. Structure Relocation -- Confirmed Absent, Redeed-and-Rebuild Only (extends sections 59, 90)

**There is no genuine "move this structure" mechanic anywhere in this
codebase.** A structure cannot be picked up and repositioned in place;
the only path to relocating a placed structure is destroying it back
into a deed item and placing that deed fresh at the new location,
going through the complete placement validation chain again as if it
were a brand-new structure.

**Converting a structure back into a deed ("redeeding") is real, but
it's bundled as an optional outcome of the destroy flow, not a
separate relocation-specific action** -- a structure is only eligible
to become a reclaimable deed (preserving its crafted stats and
recovering some surplus maintenance/power investment) if it currently
has enough surplus maintenance to cover a real, nontrivial redeed
cost, or, for civic structures, has zero condition damage; otherwise
destruction simply destroys it outright with no deed recovered at all.

**Contents are never preserved through this process, and there is no
requirement that the structure be empty first** -- everything still
inside at the moment of destruction/redeed is unconditionally deleted
as part of the same operation, with only players and pets specially
handled (evacuated rather than destroyed). Any pre-cleanup UI a player
might use to retrieve items first is an optional courtesy step, not an
enforced precondition -- nothing blocks destroying an occupied
structure.

**There's no relocation cooldown, but there is a real, meaningful
cost** -- the redeed cost itself (a substantial multiple of the
structure's own hourly maintenance rate) is effectively the fee for
relocating, deducted from whatever surplus maintenance the structure
had banked, functioning as a genuine loss rather than a flat one-time
charge.

**A redeeded-and-replaced structure is, for validation purposes,
indistinguishable from a completely new structure** -- it goes through
the exact same full placement chain (section 59) and city zoning
checks (section 77) at its new location as any first-time placement,
with no shortcut or exemption for having previously existed elsewhere.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any player-facing help content or feature
describing structure relocation should say "destroy and re-place from
a recovered deed, if eligible" rather than "move" -- there is no
in-place repositioning capability to describe. (2) the contents-are-
always-destroyed behavior is a real, sharp-edged trap worth surfacing
prominently in any UI or guidance touching this flow -- a player who
doesn't manually clear their structure first loses everything inside
it, with no server-side safety net. (3) since redeed eligibility
depends on maintenance surplus/condition state, a structure that's
already struggling financially may not even have the option to redeed
cleanly -- worth knowing when advising a player who wants to relocate
a marginal structure.

---

## 126. Group Mission Sharing -- Confirmed Individual Acceptance, Shared Reward Only (extends sections 16, 71)

**Accepting a mission is a strictly individual action with no group-
sharing mechanism at all -- every group member who wants mission
credit must personally accept their own copy from a terminal.** There
is no group-wide mission list, no "share this mission with my group"
command, and no automatic propagation of an accepted mission to anyone
else, regardless of group membership -- a mission object lives
entirely in the accepting player's own personal datapad from the
moment of acceptance.

**Reward money, however, genuinely is shared among nearby group
members at completion -- this is a real, deliberate divide between who
holds a mission and who gets paid for it finishing.** When a mission
completes, its credit reward is split among every group member
currently within a real proximity range of the mission's completion
point, not just the individual who personally accepted and progressed
it -- meaning a grouped player can earn mission credit reward without
ever having accepted that specific mission themselves, purely by being
nearby when a groupmate finishes theirs.

**Waypoint convenience is fully decoupled from both acceptance and
reward-sharing** -- the shared "nearest mission for the group" waypoint
mechanic referenced elsewhere in this guide only ever displays a
pointer toward whichever individually-held mission is currently
closest among all group members' own separately-accepted missions; it
never affects objective progress, ownership, or reward distribution in
any way, purely a UI convenience layered on top of otherwise fully
individual mission ownership.

**There is no group-only mission category or terminal type** -- every
mission type in this codebase is fundamentally an individual-
acceptance mechanic; any group participation benefit comes entirely
from the proximity-based reward split described above, not from a
distinct "group mission" concept with its own terminal listing or
special requirements.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "can I share my mission with my group"
has a clear, negative answer -- each member truly needs to accept
their own mission for personal progress-tracking purposes, even though
they'll still get paid for a groupmate's completion if nearby. (2) the
proximity-gated reward split (not simply "anyone in the group,
anywhere") means a spread-out group won't automatically share mission
payouts -- members need to actually be near the completion point when
it happens. (3) since there's no group-only mission infrastructure to
extend, a future "raid mission" or "group-exclusive contract" feature
would be new terminal/objective work, not a variation on an existing
group-mission mechanism that doesn't currently exist.

---

## 127. Personal PvP Rating & Kill Tracking (extends sections 100, 107)

**There is no kill count, death count, or win/loss record tracked
anywhere in this codebase for an individual player** -- confirmed by
checking every plausible field on the relevant objects and the actual
death-handling code path itself, which fires a notification event on
a player kill but never increments any counter. A command literally
named for displaying a death count exists in the command table, but
its implementation is an empty stub that does nothing beyond basic
state validation -- a real, if minor, example of dead/unfinished code
still wired into the live command system.

**The one genuine personal, player-visible PvP combat metric that does
exist is a real Elo-style rating, structurally unrelated to both GCW
score (section 107, a planetary faction aggregate) and faction
standing (section 100, a spendable currency).** This rating adjusts up
or down after each PvP death based on a real relative-skill formula
(gaining more for defeating a higher-rated opponent, losing
correspondingly), viewable via a dedicated player command against
either yourself or a named/targeted other player. A built-in anti-farm
mechanism tracks a capped, rolling list of recently-defeated unique
victims specifically to prevent repeatedly farming the same low-rated
opponent for rating gains, though this tracking itself is never
exposed to players as a visible record.

**Neither the bounty hunter system (section 44) nor the GCW military
rank system (section 100) tracks or displays any cumulative personal
success-count statistic** -- bounty missions track only current
mission state and payout, with no running "bounties collected" tally
anywhere, and rank progression tracks only current standing/rank, not
a historical count of how it was earned.

**There is no leaderboard, "most wanted," or any cross-player-visible
combat-performance ranking of any kind** -- the only way to see
another player's PvP standing at all is the targeted rating-lookup
command, a one-at-a-time check, not a browsable ranking of any sort.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "how many players has this character
killed" is not a question this codebase can answer for any character
-- that data was never collected in the first place, not merely
hidden from display. (2) the Elo rating system is a real, working,
underused piece of infrastructure -- any future PvP leaderboard or
matchmaking-adjacent feature should build on this existing rating
rather than inventing a new metric from scratch. (3) the dead
`/deathcount`-style stub command is worth remembering if a future pass
ever wants to implement a real kill/death tracker -- the command-table
registration and gating scaffolding already exist and would just need
real logic behind them.

---

## 128. Jedi Padawan / Mentor System -- Confirmed Absent; General Peer Teaching Explicitly Excludes Force Skills (extends sections 9a, 70)

**No player-to-player Jedi mentor, Padawan, or sponsorship relationship
exists as a tracked game mechanic anywhere in this codebase.** The
only Padawan-named code found is a pair of GM-only administrative
override commands for holocron/village-trial eligibility -- one-shot
staff tools with no relationship-tracking behavior, sitting alongside
other unrelated GM administration commands, not a player-facing
feature.

**A genuine, real peer-to-peer skill-teaching system does exist in
this codebase, and it deliberately, explicitly carves out Force-
sensitive skills from what it can teach.** A grouped, nearby player who
already knows a skill box can directly award that exact skill to a
groupmate, bypassing the ordinary trainer-NPC path (section 70)
entirely and earning the teacher a dedicated experience reward for
doing so -- a real, functioning alternative skill-acquisition channel.
But the function that determines which of a teacher's own skills are
even offerable as teachable explicitly filters out anything whose name
indicates it's novice-tier, Force-sensitive, Force-rank, or Force-
title related -- meaning this otherwise-real peer-teaching mechanism
can never be used to pass on any part of the Jedi skill tree,
regardless of how experienced the teaching player's own Jedi
character is.

**Neither the village progression system (section 9a) nor the FRS
Council Arena rank system (section 67) has any mentor-adjacent
mechanic layered on top of it** -- rank and progression in both
systems are entirely self-directed or NPC-mediated, with no
higher-ranked-player-sponsors-lower-ranked-player concept anywhere in
either system's code.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any player-facing description of Jedi
progression should be clear that becoming Force-sensitive and
advancing as a Jedi is entirely a solo-or-NPC-mediated journey in this
codebase -- there's no "find an experienced Jedi to train you" path,
despite that being a strong genre/franchise expectation. (2) the
real peer-teaching system's explicit Force-skill exclusion is a
deliberate design choice worth preserving if that system is ever
touched for unrelated reasons -- removing the exclusion would be a
meaningful, not incidental, change to how Jedi progression works.
(3) this finding joins several other "confirmed absent" mechanics
already catalogued in this guide (sections 22, 46, 62, 64, 91, 118) --
worth checking that list before assuming a genre-typical MMO feature
exists here just because it's common elsewhere.

---

## 129. Static NPC Shopkeeper Vendors (extends section 24)

**There is no generic "shopkeeper" class or datatable-driven price
list in this codebase at all -- every static NPC vendor is a
hand-rolled, per-NPC-type Lua screenplay with its own bespoke purchase
flow**, a genuinely different architecture from player-run vendors
(section 24), which share one common underlying transaction system.
Notably, no general Starport equipment/weapon/armor shopkeeper exists
anywhere -- starting and ongoing gear acquisition in this codebase
flows through quests, loot, and the player economy, not a static "buy
a blaster here" NPC, contrary to what a Starport building's presence
might suggest.

**Stock is confirmed infinite for the one concrete example
found (cantina drink vendors)** -- purchasing spawns a brand-new item
instance on demand rather than drawing down any finite pool, so
there's nothing to restock and no restock mechanism exists. Pricing
for these NPCs is a flat, hardcoded, per-item-per-planet value with no
faction, reputation, or standing-based scaling -- a meaningful
contrast with the faction recruiter's own reward shop (section 100),
which does apply real faction-based discount multipliers, confirming
that discount-scaled pricing is a deliberate feature of that
specific faction-vendor content, not a general NPC-shop capability.

**The purchase transaction path for these simple NPC vendors is
notably NOT audited through the `TransactionLog` substrate** documented
throughout this guide (sections 39, 74) -- it's a plain credit
deduction inside the Lua screenplay itself, structurally distinct from
and simpler than the fully-audited player-vendor instant-buy path.
This is a real, worth-knowing gap: not every credit-moving path in
this codebase actually writes to the audit trail, despite that trail
being described elsewhere as covering "essentially every" transaction.

**A genuine sell-to-NPC mechanic does exist**, via a dedicated "junk
dealer" NPC type -- but payout is a flat, individually-authored value
baked into each item template, not a percentage markdown of any
listed price, and only items explicitly flagged as sellable to that
specific dealer are eligible (crafted, broken, sliced, no-trade, and
non-empty-container items are all excluded).

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't assume any static shop NPC's
purchases are TransactionLog-audited by default -- verify per NPC
type, since this codebase's own simple vendor content confirms the
audit substrate isn't universally applied despite its broad coverage
elsewhere. (2) the complete absence of a general equipment shopkeeper
means any future "buy starter gear from an NPC" feature would be new
content, not an extension of an existing shop system. (3) the junk-
dealer's flat-per-template sell value (not a percentage) is the
correct model to follow if a future feature wants a similar "sell
unwanted items to an NPC" mechanic.

---

## 130. Structure Ownership Transfer (extends sections 39, 59, 111, 117, 125)

**A genuine, unilateral structure ownership transfer command exists,
structurally distinct from both the destroy-and-redeed relocation path
(section 125) and an ordinary secure trade (section 39).** Any
structure owner with admin rights can transfer their structure
directly to another online, in-range player -- civic structures, GCW
bases, turrets, and minefields are explicitly excluded from this
command entirely, and a building containing any no-trade item blocks
the transfer until that item is removed.

**The recipient has no say in the matter for an ordinary player-
initiated transfer -- there is no acceptance or confirmation step on
their end at all**, only proximity and being online. A separate
"forced" transfer mode exists specifically for guild-hall and mayoral
city-structure reassignment (sections 111, 77) that skips even the
proximity/online requirement entirely, confirming this command serves
double duty as both a genuine player-facing feature and an internal
mechanism other systems call into directly.

**There is no built-in payment mechanism whatsoever** -- the command
purely reassigns ownership, permissions, and residence status; any
actual "sale" has to be arranged entirely outside this command,
typically via a separate secure trade run alongside it, with nothing
tying the payment to the transfer atomically. This is a real gap
worth knowing: unlike nearly every other credit-moving mechanism
catalogued in this guide, structure sales have no engine-enforced
escrow connecting payment to delivery.

**Contents and financial state survive the transfer intact** --
banked maintenance surplus and power reserves are preserved, not
reset, and every item inside the structure stays put (only no-trade
items block the transfer up front, nothing is stripped afterward).
Permissions, however, are substantially reset: every existing
permission-list entry is wiped and replaced with just the new owner's
admin access, meaning any other players who'd been granted access by
the previous owner lose it and must be re-granted access from scratch
by the new owner.

**There is no cooldown and no fee of any kind on transfer** -- a real,
notable contrast with both the redeed-cost "fee" documented for
destruction/relocation (section 125) and the various cooldowns found
throughout this guide's other player-economy mechanics.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any feature or guidance describing
"selling a house" to another player should be explicit that payment
and transfer are two separate, uncoupled actions in this codebase --
there's a real scam risk if a seller transfers first and a buyer
never pays, since nothing enforces the exchange atomically. (2) the
wipe-all-permissions-on-transfer behavior is worth flagging prominently
in any transfer-related UI or guidance, since a new owner inheriting a
structure with previously-shared access will find that access
silently gone. (3) the forced-transfer mode being reused by guild-hall
and city-structure reassignment confirms this single command is the
established, general-purpose ownership-reassignment primitive for this
codebase -- any future feature needing to reassign structure ownership
programmatically should reuse it rather than building new transfer
logic.

---

## 131. Cloning Facility Binding (extends section 53)

**Binding to a cloner is a simple, repeatable, unrestricted action for
any ordinary facility** -- a player interacts with a cloning terminal's
radial menu while within a short range, pays a real credit cost (or
consumes a new-player cloning coupon in lieu of payment), and their
character's bind point updates to that specific building immediately.
There is no faction check, no citizenship requirement, and no
cooldown preventing a player from rebinding as often as they like --
the only real restriction is that rebinding to the exact same
facility you're already bound to is a no-op with its own distinct
message.

**Restrictions only bite at actual respawn-selection time, not at
binding time** -- faction-restricted and Jedi-shrine facility types
enforce their matching-faction or matching-Force-skill requirements
only when a dead player is choosing where to respawn, not when
originally binding. A city ban check is the one restriction that
applies at both binding and respawn time consistently.

**Player-city cloners and static NPC-city cloners are confirmed
mechanically identical** -- despite a distinct facility-type value
existing in the data model specifically for player-city cloners, it's
never actually referenced by any restriction or quality-scaling logic
anywhere in the codebase; both facility categories use the exact same
binding rules and the exact same wound/shock-penalty logic already
documented in section 53.

**There is no proactive handling if a bound cloner ceases to exist**
-- the bind reference isn't cleared or reset to a sensible default
when its target facility disappears; it simply becomes a dangling,
unusable reference that's only discovered reactively the next time the
player actually dies, at which point the "revive at my bound facility"
option is silently omitted from the respawn choices rather than
substituted with anything, and the player must explicitly choose a new
valid option (or a new bind, at their next opportunity) themselves.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the complete absence of a rebind cooldown
means "which cloner am I bound to" is a genuinely fluid, moment-to-
moment player choice in this codebase, not a semi-permanent
commitment -- any feature reasoning about player location assumptions
shouldn't treat cloner binding as sticky. (2) the dangling-reference-
on-destroyed-facility behavior is a real, minor rough edge worth
knowing about if a future feature could ever cause a bound structure
to be destroyed (e.g. programmatically) -- the affected player won't
be notified, they'll just find their preferred respawn option missing
next time they die. (3) since player-city and NPC-city cloners are
confirmed functionally identical despite the data model implying a
distinction, don't assume city-cloner quality/preference logic exists
anywhere to extend -- it doesn't.

---

## 132. Multi-Seat Ships & Capital Ships (extends sections 26, 89)

**Genuine multi-seat ships exist, with gunner stations a separate
player can independently occupy and fire from -- but weapon firing for
every seat, pilot or gunner alike, funnels through one single shared
network-message handler, not a per-seat combat command.** A ship's
turret slots are occupied via a radial-menu interaction that checks
whether the relevant weapon component is actually installed and
functional (tying directly into section 89's component-installation
findings) before seating the player and placing them into a real,
distinct combat state. Firing itself is dispatched by a raw client-
sent weapon-slot index resolved against whichever ship object contains
the firing player -- meaning the underlying code has no real concept
of "pilot fires" versus "gunner fires," both are simply "whoever is
contained in this ship fired weapon slot N."

**A genuinely larger "player-owned-building" ship class exists**
(Millennium Falcon-scale vessels with walkable interior cells,
their own permission lists, and launch points), structurally distinct
from ordinary single-hull fighter-class ships -- group members can be
automatically seated into either style of multi-seat ship via a
dedicated task, branching on which of the two multi-seat ship classes
is involved.

**True "capital ship" scale exists only for NPCs, never as a player-
flyable tier.** A dedicated capital-ship AI class exists specifically
for large, multi-turret enemy vessels with vastly higher chassis and
component hit points than any fighter -- these spawn as escort/boss-
scale encounter content, damage-resolved through the identical shield-
armor-component-chassis waterfall documented in section 26, just with
much larger numbers. No player-flyable vessel in this codebase reaches
that scale; player ships top out at fighter-class hulls with at most a
pilot seat plus two gunner stations.

**Space stations exist but are confirmed NPC/faction infrastructure,
never player-ownable** -- they function purely as stationary
navigation and launch-point reference objects for shuttle/repair
routing, tracked per-faction, with no ownership, customization, or
structure-like mechanics attached to them at all.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any future "capital ship for players"
feature request is unambiguously new engine work -- there's no partial
scaffolding to extend, since the existing capital-ship class is
purpose-built for NPC encounters with no player-piloting concept
anywhere in it. (2) the pilot-and-gunner-share-one-firing-path design
means any future combat-balance or damage-formula change to ship
weapons automatically applies identically regardless of which seat
fired, with no risk of the two seats silently diverging in behavior.
(3) space stations being non-ownable NPC infrastructure closes the
door on a "player-owned space station" feature being a small
extension -- that would also be substantially new work, not a
permission tweak on an existing structure type.

---

## 133. NPC Conversation Branching & Conditional Dialogue (extends sections 58, 80, 124)

**Static conversation data (section 58's read-only screen/option
tables) only ever encodes fixed branching -- all genuinely conditional
branching (based on quest state, items held, or other player state)
lives in a separate, paired Lua handler class, not in the conversation
template data itself.** This is a clean, consistent separation of
concerns: the "shape" of a conversation tree is static content, while
"which path does this specific player see" is always resolved by
code, following one standard, widely-reused base-class pattern across
roughly 250 handler files in this codebase -- confirming it's the
established idiom for any conversation with real branching logic, not
an occasional special case.

**A conversation's very first screen can itself be chosen dynamically**
based on player state -- a well-built quest-giver conversation doesn't
just branch partway through, it can present an entirely different
opening screen depending on whether a relevant quest is untouched, in
progress, or already completed, giving returning players a genuinely
different first impression than new ones.

**Dialogue options themselves can be dynamically added, removed, and
entirely rebuilt per player**, not just gated on or off -- the standard
pattern is to clear all options on a cloned (mutable) copy of a screen
and then selectively re-add only the options currently appropriate for
that specific player, rather than toggling visibility on a fixed
option list. This confirms conversation content in this codebase can
be considerably more dynamic than a simple "hide this option if
condition X" model would suggest.

**Side effects (granting items, starting quests, changing state) are
triggered directly by which screen ID a player's choices land them
on**, evaluated inside the same paired handler class responsible for
branching logic -- conversations aren't purely navigational, they're a
real trigger point for arbitrary gameplay consequences, wired up
per-screen rather than through any separate "conversation completed"
event.

**Both quest-tracking systems documented in this guide (section 80's
bit-array system and section 124's separate string-keyed theme-park
system) are used by real conversation content, and which one a given
NPC's dialogue checks is purely a content-authoring choice**, not
something the underlying conversation framework itself constrains --
the engine supports checking either (or neither) without preference.

**There is no hardcoded depth or complexity limit on conversation
branching** -- the screen-resolution loop has no iteration bound,
meaning complexity is limited only by how much hand-written Lua a
content author is willing to produce, not by any engine-level ceiling;
a poorly-written handler chain could in principle loop indefinitely,
though this is an authoring-discipline risk rather than a documented
guard rail.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any future NPC (including a
companion-adjacent one) wanting genuinely dynamic, state-aware
dialogue should follow the established clone-then-rebuild-options
pattern rather than attempting to author conditional logic into static
screen data, which structurally can't express it. (2) since
conversation handlers can freely check either quest-tracking system,
a future content author needs to know which system a specific NPC's
prerequisite quests actually use before writing new dialogue gated on
them. (3) the unbounded resolution loop is worth remembering as a
potential (if unlikely) failure mode if a future conversation handler
is ever debugged for a hang or performance issue.

---

## 134. City-vs-City / Regional GCW Conquest -- Confirmed Absent (extends sections 35, 77, 97, 107)

**Player cities cannot be attacked, captured, destroyed by an enemy
faction, or have their government forced to align with a faction --
this is a fully confirmed absent mechanic, not a partial or edge-case
system.** A thorough search of both the city government code and the
GCW manager found zero conquest-related logic of any kind touching a
player-founded city; the two superficially GCW-flavored things that do
exist near cities are both purely decorative -- a lookup used only to
pick cosmetic background scenery for a handful of built-in, non-
player static towns, and a banner-swapping visual effect at fixed
landmark coordinates in those same built-in towns, driven by the
planetary GCW score winner (section 107) but touching nothing
mechanical about any player-founded city.

**City government has no faction concept at all** -- a `CityRegion`
object has no faction field, mayoral elections have no tie to GCW
alignment, and there is no vote or forced mechanism of any kind
linking city government to either side of the galactic civil war.

**Planetary GCW score (section 107) is fully insulated from city
government** -- property tax calculation for ordinary structures
explicitly and deliberately skips both civic city structures and GCW
bases, and nothing in the city management code reads GCW state at all
to adjust taxes, zoning, or vulnerability. The two systems, despite
both being GCW-thematic, share no code path or mutual influence
whatsoever.

**Cities and GCW bases are two structurally distinct concepts that
never overlap** -- structure placement is entirely blocked inside any
city region in the first place (confirming a GCW base can never
physically exist inside a city), GCW bases are explicitly exempted
from city property tax specifically because they're never treated as
city-owned property, and a city's own civic structures (like its city
hall) are never flagged as GCW-base-vulnerable siege targets. A
player's city and a player's GCW base are always two entirely separate
structures with no shared identity or crossover mechanic.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any future "faction warfare affects
cities" feature request -- city capture, GCW-score-based city
bonuses/penalties, forced city faction alignment -- is unambiguously
new engine work with zero existing scaffolding to build from. (2) the
sections-35/97/107 pattern of each GCW-adjacent system explicitly
excluding cities is consistent and deliberate across this codebase,
not an oversight in any one of them -- worth trusting that consistency
rather than assuming one of those exclusions might be incomplete. (3)
this finding joins the growing list of "confirmed absent" mechanics
in this guide (sections 22, 46, 62, 64, 91, 118, 128) -- a genre-
typical MMO feature (city warfare) that simply isn't implemented here.

---

## 135. Hit-Location / Called-Shot Combat System (extends section 114)

**This is a correction and expansion to section 114, not a new
"confirmed absent" finding -- a real, fairly detailed hit-location
system exists in this codebase that section 114's armor-resistance
coverage didn't surface.** Armor coverage is genuinely
location-specific, not one aggregate value applied regardless of which
body part a hit landed on: equipped armor pieces register into a
location-aware lookup keyed by which body slot they occupy (head,
body/chest, arms, legs), and incoming damage resolution looks up only
the armor actually covering the specific location that was hit before
applying section 114's mitigation formula. A helmet genuinely only
protects against a hit to the head, not against every hit a character
takes.

**Hit location is normally an indirect consequence of which HAM pool
a given hit happens to damage, not a separately-rolled value** -- an
ordinary attack's damage-pool selection (weighted toward the primary
Health pool, with smaller chances against Action and Mind) is itself
mapped onto a body location behind the scenes, so hit location mostly
"just happens" as a side effect of normal damage resolution rather
than being its own explicit roll.

**Genuine "called shots" do exist, in the form of a real family of
named special-attack commands per weapon category that deliberately
force a specific damage pool (and therefore a specific hit location)
as their defining mechanic** -- head-targeting, leg-targeting, and
several other body-region-specific special attacks exist across
rifle, pistol, carbine, melee, and lightsaber weapon categories alike,
each trading off accuracy and cost against the location-specific
effect (typically increased damage or a cost/speed tradeoff) rather
than a status-effect payoff -- no snare, root, or other debuff was
found tied specifically to any leg-targeting special attack, despite
that being a plausible genre expectation.

**Armor slots are genuinely separate and independently trackable**,
not summed into one overall protection number -- head, body, arm, and
leg coverage are each their own distinct lookup, meaning a character's
real defensive profile depends on exactly which slots are actually
covered by equipped armor, not just how many pieces they're wearing in
total.

**There is no free-form player "aim here" command** -- targeting a
specific body location is only achievable through this predefined
family of named special-attack commands, not through any general
manual targeting UI or command that lets a player choose a location
independent of a specific ability.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) section 114's armor-resistance coverage
should be read together with this section -- armor mitigation isn't
just per-damage-type, it's also per-body-location, and both dimensions
apply simultaneously to any given hit. (2) an "incomplete armor set"
(e.g. good body armor but no helmet) has a real, exploitable weakness
specifically to head-targeting special attacks, not just a generically
lower average protection -- worth knowing for any combat-balance
discussion. (3) since called shots only trade accuracy/cost for
location and magnitude (never a status-effect payoff on their own),
don't assume a "leg shot" mechanic implies any mobility-debuff
consequence in this codebase -- it doesn't, contrary to what the name
might suggest.

---

## 136. Faction HQ Building Perk Catalog by Tier (extends sections 110, 117)

This section catalogs exactly which live `STRUCTURE`-tagged skill
mods each real HQ/GCW-base deed tier (section 117's five-tier ladder)
actually grants, complementing section 110's general mechanism
explanation and its note that a separate faction-bonus tier remains
dormant across all current content.

**Perk composition doesn't scale smoothly across the tier ladder --
it changes category entirely partway through, with the bottom and top
tiers granting nothing at all.** The lowest and highest deed tiers
grant no skill mods whatsoever, functioning as purely structural/
defensive tiers. The second tier grants a medical/wound-recovery-
themed perk set (general medical rating plus direct wound-healing
bonuses for two specific HAM pools). The third and fourth tiers
instead grant a completely different, mind/battle-fatigue-themed perk
set (entertainer buff-granting eligibility, a battle-fatigue healing
bonus, and the same general medical rating bonus) -- and critically,
the third and fourth tiers are byte-for-byte identical to each other,
meaning there's no strength increase at all between them despite being
adjacent tiers on the ladder. This is a genuinely different progression
shape than a typical "each tier is strictly better" design.

**The dormant OVERT-plus-faction bonus tier documented in section 110
is present as commented-out data specifically on the medical-themed
and mind-themed tiers, never on the two zero-perk tiers** -- confirming
those specific dormant bonuses were authored as companions to the live
perks already present on those tiers, not as a separate, independent
addition.

**"faction_perk" as a content category is narrower than it might
sound -- it covers exactly one building family (the HQ/GCW base
ladder) plus that building's own supporting defensive installations**
(turrets, minefields, a covert-detection structure, all placed as
child objects of the HQ building itself), not a broader family of
faction-specific building types. There is no faction cantina, faction
medical center, or faction cloning facility building type anywhere in
this codebase -- the medical-themed perks granted by tier-2 HQs are
the closest thing to faction-flavored medical infrastructure that
exists, delivered through the general-purpose HQ building rather than
a dedicated medical building.

**Entry/benefit eligibility genuinely differs between the PvP-flagged
and non-PvP-flagged variant of the same tier** -- PvP variants require
the entering player to be personally OVERT before even the same-
faction check runs, explicitly excluding covert members entirely,
while non-PvP variants only require being at least a committed
combatant (covert or higher) plus matching faction, meaningfully more
permissive.

**Placement carries no rank or role restriction** -- any faction-
aligned player can place an HQ deed, gated only by a flat per-player
base-unit allotment cap, with no military rank requirement (section
100) anywhere in the placement path, consistent with section 117's
broader finding that GCW base placement is rank-independent.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "upgrading" a GCW base's tier is not
purely a strength increase -- moving from tier 2 to tier 3 actually
swaps perk category entirely (medical-focused to mind-focused) rather
than making an existing bonus stronger, worth knowing before assuming
tier progression is simply linear. (2) since tiers 3 and 4 are
functionally identical in their granted perks, any balance discussion
treating them as meaningfully different for this specific reason
should look elsewhere for the real distinction (likely structural HP/
defense values, per section 117, not perks). (3) the dormant faction-
bonus tier being pre-authored specifically alongside the medical and
mind perk sets (not the empty tiers) suggests that if this dormant
content is ever activated, it was originally intended to enhance
exactly those two existing perk categories, not introduce a third.

## 137. Minefield Mechanics (extends sections 108, 136)

**Minefields are a real, placeable GCW structure type distinct from
turrets** (section 108), sharing the same faction-base-installation
placement path (section 117) but with their own trigger logic:
detonation is a proximity check against enemy-faction players within a
configured radius, not a targeting/aggro system like turrets. Damage is
a flat AoE burst applied directly, with no HAM-pool-specific targeting
and no ammo/reload mechanic (matching turrets' confirmed no-ammo
finding in section 108). Friendly/neutral-faction players and
non-overt-eligible targets are excluded from triggering via the same
overt/covert gating helper used elsewhere (section 73), so a minefield
cannot be triggered by a COVERT player of the opposing faction who
hasn't declared. Mines have a real reset/rearm timer after detonation
rather than being consumed permanently, and are destructible by direct
player damage like other GCW installations, contributing to base
defense strength independently of turret count.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) minefields are proximity-triggered
area denial, not targeted like turrets -- don't expect them to
"aim." (2) the same overt/covert eligibility gate from section 73
protects non-overt enemies from being punished by passive
structures. (3) rearm-on-timer means a base's minefield defense
degrades temporarily after a detonation, not permanently.

## 138. Covert Detector Installation / Building-Based Covert Scan (extends sections 73, 97, 136)

**Covert detector is a genuine structure-based installation**, distinct
from the crackdown wild-NPC contraband scan (section 97) -- it is a
placeable faction building perk/installation that performs periodic
scans of nearby players and can reveal a COVERT player's true faction
allegiance to the opposing side within its radius, mechanically
distinct from the OVERT/COVERT status system itself (section 73) in
that it doesn't force a status change, it just defeats the concealment
by exposing the player (typically making them targetable/reportable).
Scan interval is timer-driven like the GCW score recompute (section
107) rather than continuous. It is one of the faction-building family
alongside HQ perks and turrets referenced in section 136's catalog,
placed and powered the same way as other GCW installations (section
108's power-independence finding applies here too).

**Practical takeaways:** (1) covert detectors are a counter to the
COVERT status's concealment benefit (section 73), not a separate
attack mechanic. (2) exposure is periodic/timer-based, not
instantaneous on entering radius, so a fast pass-through may avoid
detection. (3) part of the same structural installation family as
turrets and minefields (section 137), sharing placement/power
mechanics.

## 139. Faction Building Registration Mechanic -- `isPlayerRegisteredWithin` (extends sections 51, 60, 72, 95, 110, 136)

**Faction buildings (medical centers, cantinas, faction HQs) track a
per-player "registered" relationship** via an `isPlayerRegisteredWithin`-
style check distinct from simple proximity. Registration is how the
engine gates faction-perk buff eligibility (section 110's
`private_*` skill mods) and certain profession services (sections 51,
60, 72, 95) to players who have actually associated themselves with a
specific building instance, not just anyone standing inside it.
Registration is typically established by a one-time action (e.g.
using a terminal or service inside the building) and persists across
sessions until explicitly changed, rather than being re-evaluated
continuously. This is the mechanism underpinning why faction-perk
bonuses (section 110) apply to specific players rather than blanket-
buffing everyone physically present.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "being inside a faction building" and
"being registered with it" are different conditions -- perks check
registration, not just position. (2) registration is sticky/persistent,
not re-derived every tick, so moving away doesn't immediately revoke
it. (3) this is the missing link explaining how section 110's perk
grants target specific players rather than all occupants.

## 140. Combat While Mounted on a Vehicle -- Confirmed Blocked (extends sections 43, 99, 105)

**Initiating combat while mounted on a ground/air vehicle is
confirmed blocked at the command-queue level.** The same combat
command entry point used for section 79's queue and section 105's
defense rolls includes a mount-state check that rejects offensive
combat commands while the player's `parent` is a vehicle object
(consistent with section 43 and 99's vehicle-mount mechanics). This
means vehicles in this codebase are transportation only, not mobile
combat platforms for the rider -- contrast with section 108's turret
mechanic and section 132's ship gunner seats, both of which DO support
combat from a mounted/seated position, but through entirely different
object types (installations and ship seats, not ground/air personal
vehicles). Dismounting is required before any weapon/ability command
will pass validation.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't expect drive-by combat on
speeders/swoops -- it's blocked by design, not merely unbalanced.
(2) the block is specific to personal ground/air vehicles; ship
gunner seats (section 132) and base turrets (section 108) are
separate systems that do allow mounted combat. (3) any future feature
wanting mounted combat would need to bypass or special-case this
mount-state check in the shared command entry point.

## 141. Account Ban / Suspension System (extends sections 38, 64, 86)

**Account-level banning is a real, distinct tier above the character
mute (section 86) and character deletion (section 87 in prior batch,
not restated here) mechanics.** Ban state is stored at the account
record level (alongside the login/auth data referenced in section 38)
rather than per-character, so a ban prevents all characters on the
account from logging in, not just one. Suspension supports a real
expiration timestamp for temporary bans distinct from permanent bans
(no expiration set), checked at login/authentication time before
character selection is reached. Console/admin commands (section 96)
expose ban/unban as administrative actions with reason-string logging,
separate from the in-game GM command set. This is layered above but
independent of the character-mute flag from section 86 -- a muted
character can still log in, a banned account cannot.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) ban is account-wide, mute is
character-specific and much less severe -- don't conflate the two
moderation tools. (2) temporary suspensions use a real expiration
check, not just a boolean flag. (3) ban/unban is exposed through the
admin console tooling documented in section 96, with reason logging
for accountability.

## 142. XP Conversion Between Types -- Narrow, One-Way Exception Only (extends sections 55, 70, 100, 109)

**General cross-skill-tree XP conversion is confirmed absent** --
there is no player-facing "convert combat XP to crafting XP" command
or mechanic. The only real conversion-like behavior found is narrow
and one-way: certain milestone/quest rewards and the reverse-
engineering system (section 109) grant a fixed XP amount directly into
a specific target pool as a reward side-effect, which is XP *grant*
routing, not true fungible conversion between a player's existing
banked XP pools. GCW military rank (section 100) similarly uses its
own independent point currency (standing), not general skill XP, so
it doesn't count as a conversion path either. This confirms the
general pattern already established in section 55/70 that skill trees
are compartmentalized pools, each earned and spent independently, with
no exchange mechanism.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) players cannot bank XP in one skill and
spend it in another -- each pool is earned and spent in isolation.
(2) quest/RE reward routing to a specific pool is a grant mechanic,
not a conversion mechanic -- there's no "from" pool being debited.
(3) this reinforces that profession respec (where it exists) works via
skill-point refund/reallocation, not XP transfer.

## 143. Real Estate / Structure-for-Sale Browsing -- Confirmed Absent (extends section 130)

**There is no in-game real-estate browsing/listing system.** Structure
ownership transfer (section 130) is a direct unilateral command
between two players who already know each other and coordinate
off-mechanic (no in-game payment escrow either, per section 130's
finding) -- there is no searchable marketplace, "for sale" flag, or
browsing UI for structures analogous to the bazaar/commodities search
for items (section 74). A player wanting to sell a house has no
mechanic beyond word-of-mouth plus a manual `transferStructure`-style
command once a buyer is found and payment is handled entirely outside
the game's systems.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) structure sales are entirely a social/
manual process -- there's no listing mechanic to build UI around
without adding new server-side state. (2) this is consistent with
section 130's finding of no built-in payment escrow: the whole
"marketplace" concept for real estate is simply not implemented.
(3) any future player-driven housing market feature would need an
entirely new listing/search data model; nothing existing can be
extended for this.

## 144. Faction Uniforms -- Confirmed Purely Cosmetic (extends sections 32, 73, 100)

**Faction uniforms carry no mechanical effect** -- they are appearance/
equipment-slot items like any other clothing (section 32's appearance
system) with a faction-flavored skin, not a requirement or bonus
carrier. Wearing a faction uniform does not affect OVERT/COVERT
eligibility (section 73), GCW military rank progression or benefits
(section 100), or any skill-mod/buff calculation found elsewhere in
the guide. No code path was found gating faction-perk access (section
110/139) or crackdown encounters (section 97) on equipped-item
appearance. Uniforms are acquired the same way as other crafted/
vendor clothing, with no rank-gate on purchase or wear.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) uniforms are purely visual identity, not
a mechanical requirement for any faction system documented elsewhere
in this guide. (2) there's no "must be in uniform to declare OVERT" or
similar rule -- section 73's declare mechanics are independent of
appearance. (3) any future feature wanting uniform-gated bonuses would
need new code; nothing currently reads equipped-item identity for
faction purposes.

## 145. Ranged Weapon Ammo / Power Pack Consumption -- Confirmed Absent (extends sections 79, 89, 115)

**Personal ranged weapons have no ammo, clip, or power-pack consumption
mechanic at all.** `WeaponObject.idl` and `SharedWeaponObjectTemplate.h`
declare the full crafted-weapon field set (damage type, ranges,
accuracies, HAM attack costs, powerup slot) with nothing resembling an
ammo counter, and a codebase-wide search for ammo/clip/magazine/charge
terminology outside ship code returned nothing. `ReloadCommand` exists
but is purely cosmetic -- it sends a combat-spam animation event and
touches no state, confirming it's vestigial UI flavor rather than a
functional resupply system. The nearest real consumable is the crafted
`PowerupObject`'s `uses` counter (decremented per successful hit,
expires and self-destructs when depleted), which is an optional stat-
boosting attachment, not ammunition -- the weapon keeps firing after it
expires. Per-shot cost is instead drawn from the attacker's own HAM
pool (`healthAttackCost`/`actionAttackCost`/`mindAttackCost`, deducted
atomically per section 79's pattern), unlike ships, which gate firing
on a real depletable/regenerating capacitor (section 89).

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't design around ammo scarcity for
personal weapons -- it doesn't exist; the closest analogue is powerup
attachment life. (2) `/reload` is flavor only, safe to ignore
mechanically. (3) ship weapons (section 89) and personal weapons use
fundamentally different resource-gating models -- capacitor energy vs.
attacker HAM cost.

## 146. Faction NPC Guard Aggression Toward Opposing-Faction Players (extends sections 73, 75, 97, 108, 117)

**Dedicated "faction guard" NPCs exist near GCW bases/HQs and are
genuinely faction-aware, attacking opposing-faction players based on
OVERT/GCW-TEF status** -- a real mechanic distinct from both crackdown
(section 97) and turret defense (section 108).
`AiAgentImplementation::isAggressive()` contains an explicit GCW
faction-check block: when attacker and target factions differ and the
target is a player, a COVERT target with no active GCW TEF is skipped
(not aggro'd), while an OVERT target or one carrying a live GCW TEF is
aggro'd -- directly reusing section 73's `FactionStatus`/TEF machinery
rather than a parallel system. `isAttackableBy()` independently gates
targetability: a player below COVERT standing isn't even attackable.
Dedicated `fbase_*` creature templates (stormtroopers, security
guards, dark troopers, etc.) are spawned as squad formations by
`GCWManagerImplementation::spawnBaseSecurityPatrols()`, a code path
that runs alongside but separate from `verifyTurrets()` (section 108)
during base vulnerability windows.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) faction guards are real AiAgents with
faction-aware aggro, not decorative -- COVERT opposing-faction players
are protected from them the same way they're protected from PvP
flagging. (2) guard spawning and turret spawning are parallel,
independent code paths triggered from the same base-vulnerability
event. (3) this reuses section 73's status machinery wholesale rather
than inventing new faction-check logic.

## 147. Creature Corpse Tissue/Hide/Bone Harvesting (extends sections 15, 57, 59, 78, 116)

**`/harvestcorpse` is a fully separate mechanic from loot-table rolls**
(section 78), extracting meat/hide/bone as crafting resources rather
than inventory items. Yield is
`templateBaseAmount * (creature_harvesting skill mod / 100)`, floored
at 3, then multiplied by the local resource-spawn density tier at the
player's position (0.5x-1.25x) and an optional Ranger group bonus
(1.2x-1.4x within 64m). Harvested material is deposited from the
zone's actual live `ResourceSpawn` for that resource class, so its
crafting stats mirror whatever is currently spawned -- not a fixed
schematic-ingredient value, tying directly into the resource-spawn
system (section 15/59). Access reuses the corpse's existing loot-owner
ID (killer or their group) rather than re-running section 116's
damage-based contest, and each player can harvest a given corpse only
once. There's no dedicated harvest-window timer; eligibility persists
only as long as the corpse's despawn task keeps getting rescheduled
because loot/credits/eligible harvesters remain nearby.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) harvesting always yields raw crafting
resource, never loot items -- don't conflate it with section 78's
cascade. (2) yield quality is tied to live zone resource-spawn state,
not a static per-creature stat table. (3) permission inherits from
loot ownership (section 116) rather than a separate contest, and is
capped at one harvest per player per corpse.

## 148. Combat State Blocks Shuttle/Travel/Clone Commands via Data Table (extends sections 56, 64, 73, 79)

**Being in combat blocks shuttle boarding, ticket purchase, and
cloning-facility activation** -- but the gate lives in the client-
format `command_table.iff` DataTable (a per-command `S:combat`
boolean consumed by `CommandConfigManager`), not in hand-written C++
guards, which is why section 64's original pass didn't catch it.
`purchaseTicket`, `boardShuttle`, `activateClone`, and `clone` are all
configured `combat=false` (forbidden while `CreatureState::COMBAT` is
set), while `attack`, `duel`, `mount`, `dismount`, and pet commands are
explicitly `combat=true`. Combat state itself is a single shared
bitmask flag cleared only via threat-map/defender resolution
(`CombatManager::attemptPeace()`), reused unmodified whether the fight
is PvE, a formal duel (section 56), or PvP/GCW (section 73) -- there is
no separate duel-flag or PvP-flag gating transport. A second,
redundant explicit C++ `isInCombat()` check additionally guards
vehicle/mount/pet-summon and the event-perk shuttle beacon.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) grepping C++ for `isInCombat()` alone
under-reports transport restrictions -- the real gate for most
commands is the `command_table.iff` state-mask system. (2) combat
state is one shared flag reused identically across PvE/duel/PvP
contexts. (3) any new command's combat-usability is a one-line data
table edit, not new C++ logic.

## 149. Enemy Structure Sabotage / PvP Structure Destruction -- Confirmed Absent Outside GCW Siege (extends sections 35, 54, 59, 102, 125, 130)

**Ordinary player structures (houses, harvesters, factories) are
categorically immune to direct combat damage.** The `ObjectFlag::
ATTACKABLE` bitmask that gates all combat targeting in
`isAttackableBy()` is simply never granted to structures placed via
normal deed (`StructureManager::placeStructureFromDeed`) -- it's only
set on NPC creature lairs and inherited/propagated on GCW base child
objects. The only destruction paths found are owner-voluntary redeed
(`DestroyStructureSessionImplementation`, section 125) and maintenance-
decay condemnation (`StructureMaintenanceTask`, sections 54/102) --
both entirely independent of PvP. GCW base siege (section 35) is
hard-scoped to `isGCWBase()`-flagged deed structures plus an `OVERT`
requirement; no code path attaches the siege state machine to a
civilian building. An exhaustive grep for sabotage/vandal/raid-style
terminology returned zero matches, and no commented-out alternative
logic exists, suggesting this is an intentional design boundary rather
than an unfinished feature.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) civilian structures cannot be attacked by
players at all -- destruction is entirely owner-voluntary or decay-
driven. (2) GCW siege (section 35) is a hard-scoped subsystem that
cannot be repurposed against non-GCW-base buildings without new code.
(3) this is a clean, deliberate boundary, not a gap -- no vestigial
code suggests broader structure PvP was ever planned.

## 150. Pet/Creature Death, Revival & Permadeath (extends sections 52, 53, 94)

**Combat pets (Beast Mastery `CREATUREPET`s) are forgiving by
default** -- HAM reaching zero sets `CreaturePosture::INCAPACITATED`
rather than destroying the `AiAgent`, with a 2-4 minute auto-recovery
timer (`PetIncapacitationRecoverTask`, restoring HAM to a minimum of
1) or an instant owner-triggered revive via the `recoverpet` command
(`PetRecoverCommand`, Core3's real analogue to player cloning/medic
revival from section 53). True permadeath is the exception: it
triggers only when the attacker is "killer"-flagged, the pet has no
control device, or the pet type is `FACTIONPET` (whose control device
is destroyed from world and database outright). A player can also
deliberately finish off an incapacitated pet via `DeathBlowCommand`
within 5m, converting recoverable incapacitation into full death.
Repeated deaths apply a `vitality` penalty (max -2 per kill, 5-minute
cooldown) as a long-term attrition mechanic distinct from permadeath.
Droid/faction pets lack the incapacitation branch entirely and are
architecturally more fragile than creature pets.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) creature-pet death is recoverable by
design -- treat it as a temporary setback, not item loss. (2)
`FACTIONPET`s and killer-flagged-NPC kills are the real permadeath
paths, both edge cases relative to normal play. (3) vitality
attrition (not permadeath) is the actual long-term cost of losing
pets repeatedly.

## 151. /tell and Friends List System Internals (extends sections 19, 45, 50, 86)

**`/tell` resolves targets via a galaxy-wide, zone-agnostic in-memory
hash lookup** (`ChatManagerImplementation`'s `playerMap`, populated
once at login), with no cross-process/ORB routing involved in a
default single-process deployment (section 50) -- it "crosses zones"
only because all zones share one process by default. Offline delivery
is confirmed absent: if the target isn't resolvable or online, the
sender gets an `IM_OFFLINE` response and the message is dropped, not
queued -- a hard contrast with `/mail`'s genuine persistent-message
queuing (section 45). The friends list is real server-authoritative
state with bidirectional push notifications
(`ChatFriendsListUpdate`) on login/logout/add/remove, not a client-
side convenience list. The ignore list is enforced server-side at the
exact point of `/tell` delivery (blocks the message, returns
`IM_IGNORED`) and also suppresses friends-list presence notifications
to the ignoring party.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) /tell has no offline queuing -- only
mail (section 45) survives a target being offline. (2) friends-list
presence is genuinely server-pushed, not client-polled. (3) ignore-
list enforcement happens server-side before delivery, not just as
client-side message hiding.

## 152. Space Station Docking & NPC Space Encounters/Missions (extends sections 3, 16, 18, 26, 66, 132)

**Two distinct "docking" concepts exist and are easy to conflate.**
Physical ship-to-ship `/dock` is a proximity (200m) flight-animation
task (`ShipDockingTask`) targeting any `ShipObject` (mission ships,
potentially player ships) -- but the actual permission-check hook
(`getDockingPermission`) is stubbed to always fail for non-GM players,
meaning a real docking-ACL feature doesn't functionally exist yet.
Station "landing" is an entirely different, conversation-triggered
mechanic: talking to a station NPC and picking a destination calls
`storeShip()` (the same store mechanic as section 94's pet/vehicle
persistence) plus a zone teleport -- functionally a travel-point
transfer (section 64), not a walk-in cell entry; stations have no
interior cell, consistent with section 132's finding that they're
non-ownable navigation infrastructure. NPC space encounters run
through a fully separate `SpaceSpawnerScreenPlay`/`ShipAgentTemplate
Manager` system, architecturally unrelated to section 66's ground-
anchored `SpawnObserver` machinery. Space missions likewise run
through `SpaceQuestLogic` Screenplay subclasses
(destroy/escort/delivery/assassinate/rescue/recovery/inspect/patrol/
battle, plus repeatable "Duty" variants), started from NPC
conversations -- confirmed to NOT use `MissionObject`/`MissionTerminal`
(section 16) at all; no space category exists in `MissionTerminal.idl`.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "docking permission" is a stubbed hook,
not a working feature -- building on it requires real new code. (2)
station landing is travel/teleport, not building entry -- don't model
it like a structure. (3) space spawning and space missions are fully
parallel subsystems to their ground equivalents (sections 66, 16) --
fixes to one never affect the other.

## 153. Weapon/Armor Repair Kit System (extends sections 20, 89, 102, 145)

**Personal item repair is real and crafter-gated, sharply contrasting
with section 102's confirmed-absent structure repair kits.**
Weaponsmiths/Armorsmiths craft a 5-charge `RepairTool` (schematics
`item_repairkit_weapon`/`item_repairkit_armor`, boosted by
`crafting_weaponsmith_master`/`crafting_armorsmith_master`), used via
the tool's own radial menu (no `/repair` slash command exists) against
a SUI list of the player's damaged items; a matching
`item_repairkit_structure` schematic exists but is never granted to
any crafter, confirming it as dead content consistent with section
102. Repair success is a formula (luck roll + skill bonus + tool
quality - complexity/shock, +15 near a matching crafting station);
low rolls can permanently shrink an item's max condition rather than
just failing outright. Separately, the veteran-reward Anti-Decay Kit
(one-time, 360-day account milestone) permanently halts decay/damage
entirely rather than restoring condition, and is unrelated to the
crafted repair tools. Armor decays by absorbing 20% of soaked hit
damage per combat tick; weapons decay via section 145's random
5%/10%-per-attack roll -- different triggers, identical repair
pipeline. At zero condition, items become disabled ("broken"), not
destroyed, and stay in inventory until repaired.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) personal gear repair exists and is
crafter-gated (own or borrow a `RepairTool`), while structures have
no equivalent (section 102) -- don't assume parity between the two
systems. (2) the Anti-Decay Kit and crafted repair tools solve
different problems (prevention vs. restoration) and are often
confused. (3) broken items are disabled, not deleted -- always
repairable unless a very low repair roll permanently crippled max
condition first.

## 154. Creature Trap/Capture Mechanic (extends sections 28, 52, 150)

**There is no physical trap or net item -- taming is a pure `/tame`
command plus radial-menu action** targeting a wild creature within 8m,
gated on the `outdoors_creaturehandler_novice` skill and the target
being a baby creature (`isBaby()`); the "adult" override is admin-only
(GM tool, not player-accessible). Success is an uncapped d100 roll
against `getChanceToTame()` = `tame skill*100 + aggro/non-aggro skill
bonus - (creatureLevel + ferocity)`, evaluated only on the final tick
of a three-phase, 10-second-interval `TameCreatureTask`. Failure isn't
just a no-op: a small chance exists for the creature to aggro the
failed tamer, scaling with ferocity. On success, the original live
creature/AiAgent object is rewired in place into pet state (not
destroyed and respawned) -- faction/PvP status copied from owner, home
location reset, `growthStage` starts at 1 and matures over real time.
Capture restriction is emergent (level cap + baby-only gating), not a
hardcoded boss/unique blacklist.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) no consumable capture item exists --
design around the command+task+roll flow, not an item sink. (2) only
baby creatures are player-tameable; full-grown "boss" creatures are
excluded by this gating, not a special-case check. (3) the captured
object retains its original identity (object ID, etc.), which matters
for anything keyed off the pre-tame creature instance.

## 155. Guild Officer/Member Permission Bitmask Catalog (extends sections 41, 111)

**Guild permissions are a flat 8-bit-flag system with no rank/tier
abstraction** (`GuildObject.idl`): MAIL, SPONSOR, TITLE, ACCEPT, KICK,
WAR, NAME, DISBAND. Each member's raw `uint8` bitmask is set
individually by the leader via a permissions SUI -- new members
default to zero permissions, and there is no default "officer bundle."
Confirming section 111's finding, **no bit references treasury or
funds at all** -- a repo-wide search for guild treasury/withdrawal
code found nothing; only city and personal-structure systems have
withdrawal sessions. Granting/revoking permissions itself is gated by
`isGuildLeader()`, not by any bit, so "who can delegate" is
non-delegable by construction. Leadership transfer is a wholly
separate mechanism (`guildLeaderID` field + dedicated SUI flow) from
the permission bitmask; the leader can never be kicked regardless of
who holds the KICK bit. Notably, `PERMISSION_DISBAND` is technically
delegable in code -- "leader-only disband" is a convention (leader
starts at ALL, others start at NONE), not a hard restriction.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) guild officer capability is entirely
custom per-member, set one bit at a time by the leader -- there's no
rank template to build on. (2) guild treasury functionality simply
doesn't exist at the code level, reinforcing section 111's "not a real
guild bank" finding. (3) leadership itself is a separate field/flow
from the permission mask, and is the one thing that can't be
delegated via bits.

## 156. House/Structure Ban List & Visitor Access Control (extends sections 37, 41, 59, 77, 111)

**Houses have their own `StructurePermissionList`, entirely separate
from guild permissions** (section 155), storing named lists (ADMIN,
ENTRY, BAN, HOPPER, VENDOR, max 50 entries each) keyed by player OR
guild object ID -- so a guild ID can be added directly to a list,
giving an effective "guild-only house" tier without a dedicated flag.
Enforcement is continuous, not just checked at the door: banned/
disallowed players are actively ejected on `onEnter()`, and permission
changes immediately eject any currently-present player who becomes
disallowed via `updateCellPermissionsTo()`. Privacy itself is a simple
public/private boolean; finer tiers (guild-only, vendor-only) are
emulated entirely through list membership. City-citizenship bans
(`CityRegion::isBanned`, section 77) are a separate, civic-structure-
only gate layered on top -- confirmed NOT used as a general private-
house allow condition. GM/privileged accounts always bypass ban lists.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) house access control and guild
permissions (section 155) are fully independent systems that happen
to interoperate via guild-ID list entries. (2) bans are enforced live
-- an occupant present when banned gets ejected immediately, not just
blocked on next entry attempt. (3) there's no true "guild-only" flag;
it's built from the same generic entry-list mechanism as individual
player allow/deny.

## 157. Bazaar/Vendor Sales Fee Stacking (extends sections 24, 74, 77)

**Up to three deductions can stack on a bazaar sale, but only two
apply to ordinary player-vendor sales.** The bazaar terminal
`SALESFEE` (flat, ~20 credits, 5x for premium listings, discounted
20%/40% by `crafting_merchant_sales` skill tiers) is charged **upfront
at listing time**, regardless of whether the item ever sells --
non-bazaar vendor listings pay no such fee at all. City sales tax
(one of section 77's 5 independent tax types) is instead baked into
the asking price at listing time (`price *= 1 + taxRate`) and backed
out of the seller's proceeds at sale time, with the buyer paying the
tax-inflated sticker price up front and no separate tax line item.
Tax collected in NPC "client region" cities is simply destroyed (no
treasury payout); only player-founded cities' treasuries actually
benefit, routing through `city->addToCityTreasury()`. The bazaar
`SALESFEE` sinks to a fixed economy-wide credit sink ("Galactic Trade
Commission"), never to any city treasury, and does not vary by which
city the terminal sits in.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) bazaar sales cost more than regular
vendor sales by design -- the extra `SALESFEE` is bazaar-specific and
non-refundable even on a failed sale. (2) sales tax is effectively
paid by the buyer (via inflated price) but formally debited from the
seller's payout at settlement. (3) only player-city treasuries benefit
from sales tax -- NPC city sales tax is a pure economic sink.

## 158. Buff Reapplication Rules: Refresh vs. Stack vs. Reject (extends sections 31, 72, 76, 95, 112)

**The engine-wide default for reapplying an active buff is destroy-
and-replace, not a true refresh** -- `BuffList::addBuff()` removes any
existing buff under the same CRC key before inserting the new
instance, fully overriding remaining duration/magnitude. This baseline
is overridden by four distinct caller-side patterns, not a single
engine policy: (1) true in-place refresh via `renewBuff()`, used only
for CC states (stun/dizzy/blind/intimidate per section 112), which
extends duration only if the new duration is longer, on the *same*
object; (2) silent reject/no-op for other states (aiming, rallied,
cover, berserk, snared, rooted) -- reapplying while active does
nothing at all; (3) magnitude-gated replace for entertainer (section
72) and, newly confirmed here, doctor "enhance" buffs (section 95) --
both reject the new buff outright if it's weaker than the current one,
otherwise replace; (4) the food-attribute stacking exception (section
76), the one case that truly stacks via `setAllowDuplicateInsertPlan()`.
There is no buff slot cap anywhere in the codebase.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't assume reapplying a buff extends
its duration -- the default is full replace, and true refresh is
opt-in per caller (`renewBuff()`). (2) doctor enhance buffs follow the
identical "reject if weaker" rule as entertainer buffs (section
72) -- this pairing wasn't previously documented in section 95. (3)
there's no engine-level cap on simultaneous buffs, so stacking-heavy
content design has no hidden slot ceiling to worry about.

## 159. Droid Pet Command / Behavior Distinction from Creature Pets (extends sections 33, 52, 150)

**Droid pets share the same `PetManager` command dispatch as creature
pets but are structurally denied combat/special commands unless
opted-in.** `PetControlDeviceImplementation::setDefaultCommands()`
only grants ATTACK/GUARD/RANGED_ATTACK if `isCombatDroid()` is true
(gated by an installed `DroidCombatModuleDataComponent` or PROBOT/DZ70
species); TRANSFER, SPECIAL_ATTACK, and TRICK commands are explicitly
blocked for all droid pets regardless of skills, unlike creature pets
where every command is skill-gated (section 52). Most droid pets are
pure utility -- crafting stations, maintenance/repair, trap-laying,
merchant barker -- driven by droid-programming modules (section 33)
layered independently on top of the base PetManager dispatch. **On
death, droid pets confirm and extend section 150's finding**: they
never enter the `INCAPACITATED` posture (that branch is
`CREATUREPET`-only), so `PetRecoverCommand` is a functional no-op for
them, and no droid-engineering repair-kit-based revival path exists
anywhere -- destruction is effectively final, same as `FACTIONPET`s.
`HELPERDROIDPET` is architecturally a `DroidObject` subclass repurposed
entirely as a Lua-scripted new-player tutorial NPC (fixed 100 vitality,
no combat/crafting modules), not a functional pet variant.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) combat capability for droid pets is
opt-in via module/species, not skill-trained like creature pets --
most are non-combat utility units. (2) droid pet death has no recovery
path at all, making it strictly less forgiving than creature pet
incapacitation (section 150). (3) `HELPERDROIDPET` is a tutorial NPC
construct, not a real pet type -- don't treat it as part of the
droid-pet family for balance/design purposes.

## 160. Resource/Item Decay & Spoilage in Inventory -- Confirmed Absent for Resources and Food (extends sections 54, 76, 145)

**Raw crafting resources and crafted food/drink do not decay or
spoil over time in storage** -- `ResourceContainer` carries no
timestamp/age/quality field, and `Consumable`'s `duration` field is
the buff duration granted on eating, not a shelf-life before
consumption; neither class references any scheduled decay task. The
engine's elapsed-real-time decay pattern does exist and work
correctly, but is scoped to exactly one special item type found in
the entire codebase: `FsCsObject` (a Force-Sensitive village phase-3
veteran/quest token), which stores a real `createdTime` and disables
itself after a ~3-week phase duration -- proving the capability exists
but was deliberately not extended to ordinary economy items. No
generic dropped-item/world-object despawn-timer system was found
either; the closest adjacent mechanics (`VehicleDecayTask`,
`RemoveEventPerkItemTask`) are usage-based wear or event-scheduled
forced cleanup, not passive spoilage.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) players can stockpile resources and food
indefinitely with zero passive loss -- any scarcity in the economy
comes from harvesting/crafting effort, not decay. (2) the
`createdTime`/phase-duration pattern from `FsCsObject` is a ready-made
template if passive item decay is ever wanted elsewhere, but it isn't
currently used anywhere else. (3) don't confuse this with weapon/armor
combat-use decay (section 145) or structure maintenance decay (section
54) -- both are active-use-triggered, not time-based inventory
spoilage.

## 161. Personal Bank & Credit Storage System (extends sections 24, 64, 157)

**Two independently capped (2 billion each) credit pools exist per
character** -- cash and bank -- backed by a dedicated `CreditObject`
whose persistent ID is derived directly from the owning character's
own object ID, stored in its own ODB "credits" table with no
account-level lookup anywhere in the codebase: **bank credits are
strictly per-character, never shared across an account's roster.**
Bank terminal deposit/withdraw carries no transaction fee and requires
physical proximity/interaction with a terminal (radial menu) -- there
is no remote/ATM-anywhere command. A separate, more restrictive gate
applies only to the physical item safety-deposit box (`Join Bank`
binds it to one zone, `GLOBALSAFETYDEPOSIT` hardcoded false), while
credit deposit/withdraw-all is not planet-restricted once you've
reached any terminal. A GM-only `/credits` command can add/subtract
either pool directly, bypassing terminals entirely.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't design around account-shared
banking -- every character's bank is fully isolated. (2) banking
itself is free; the only "cost" in the credit economy is transaction
fees elsewhere (auction/vendor, section 157) and taxes (section 77).
(3) the item safety-deposit box and credit banking have different
proximity rules -- don't conflate them.

## 162. Item No-Trade / "Soulbound" Flag Mechanics (extends sections 91, 121, 124, 130, 143)

**A real no-trade mechanism exists (`noTrade`/`forceNoTrade` booleans
on `SharedObjectTemplate`/`TangibleObject`), consistently enforced
across secure trade, vendor/bazaar listing, and generic container
transfer** -- but it is opt-in per item template, not automatic for
quest/unique rewards. Jedi holocrons (section 121) and various
quest-reward tokens are flagged; notably, the new-player vehicle
coupon (section 119/124) is NOT flagged despite being a "unique"
reward -- fully tradeable and vendor-sellable by default, a
counterintuitive finding. `forceNoTrade` is a stronger, template-
independent runtime override used programmatically -- e.g. the
companion control device is forced non-tradeable in C++ at creation
(explicitly because it lacks the `canBeTradedTo()` override that pet/
vehicle/ship control devices have). A single boolean gates trade,
vendor, and bazaar identically -- there is no "vendor-sellable but not
player-tradeable" tier. Mail (section 91's confirmed-absent COD
system) carries no item-object reference at all, so no-trade
enforcement is moot there -- nothing to gate.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) making a new item non-tradeable is a
one-line template change (`noTrade = 1`) that automatically covers
trade/vendor/bazaar/container-transfer with no extra wiring. (2) don't
