assume unique/quest rewards are bound by default -- verify per item;
the vehicle coupon is a live counterexample. (3) there's no partial-
restriction tier (sellable-but-not-giftable) -- that would require new
logic if wanted.

## 163. Structure Paint/Coloring Customization -- Confirmed Absent (extends sections 32, 37)

**No house/structure recolor mechanic exists in this codebase** --
exhaustive search of `BuildingObject`/`StructureObject` and their
menu components found no color/hue/dye field or paint-can item
targeting structures. The engine's only consumable "paint" mechanic
is `ShipPaintKit` (two-use primary/secondary ship recolor). The
closest analog, item dye for armor/goggles, is entirely item-scoped
(reusing the same `SuiColorBox` + `AssetCustomizationManagerTemplate`
machinery that backs Image Designer, section 32) and skillMod-gated
rather than consumable -- it is never wired up to the building shell
itself, only to worn items, droids, vehicles, and ships. Section 37's
housing customization coverage is confirmed to be about furniture
placement/ACL, not exterior/interior recoloring.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) house paint is a real gap, not
overlooked documentation -- there is no scaffolding to extend, unlike
some other "confirmed absent" findings. (2) the generic customization-
variable/palette engine (shared by Image Designer, item dye, and ship
paint) is the right template to reuse if this feature is ever built,
since it's item-agnostic infrastructure. (3) don't conflate ship
paint kits (real, consumable, 2 uses) with a general structure-paint
system (doesn't exist).

## 164. Vendor NPC Appearance / "Mannequin" Feature -- Confirmed Server-Randomized Only (extends sections 24, 32, 122)

**Vendor NPC appearance is customized once, server-side, at creation
via random rolls -- not a player-facing merchandising feature.**
`VendorManager::randomizeVendorLooks()` picks clothing from a fixed
Lua `Outfits` table, hair, facial features, and height, reusing the
same `CreatureObject` customization-variable/equip machinery as
character appearance (section 32) -- there is no vendor-specific
appearance subsystem. Critically, **there is no "display slot" where
an item actually for sale is shown worn/held by the vendor** -- the
randomized outfit is entirely disconnected from the vendor's real
`AuctionItem` sale inventory. This is purely cosmetic with zero
coupling to the barker/advertisement system (section 122) or sales-
commission code.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "dress your vendor with what you're
selling" is a plausible-sounding feature that simply doesn't exist --
confirmed absent, not just undocumented. (2) vendor look randomization
happens once at spawn and is never re-rolled or player-editable. (3)
any merchandising-display feature would need new code connecting
`AuctionItem` sale data to the vendor's equip slots -- nothing
existing bridges them.

## 165. Auction Bid War / Proxy Bidding Mechanics (extends sections 24, 157)

**Bidding is a full eBay-style proxy-bid system with no fixed minimum
increment** -- a new bid need only exceed the current price by any
positive amount, and a stored proxy max auto-raises the current
bidder's price when a later bidder's proxy is still lower, without a
new player action. Funds are escrowed immediately at bid time (not at
auction close), and an outbid player is automatically refunded plus
notified via both system message and mail. Bid retraction/cancellation
is confirmed absent -- no client packet or code path exists for it.
Auction expiration is fixed-schedule with **no anti-snipe extension**
-- bidding in the final seconds never pushes back the end time.
Cross-referencing section 157's flagged bugfix comment: the actual
bug fixed was narrowly scoped to `expireAuction()`'s seller-payout
step (item transfer and both-party mail notification already worked;
only the seller's bank credit was missing), mirroring
`doInstantBuy()`'s already-correct payout block -- buyer-side escrow/
refund logic was never broken.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) proxy bidding means the "current price"
a bidder sees can already reflect an unseen competing max -- design
UI/expectations around eBay-style behavior, not flat English-auction
increments. (2) no bid retraction exists -- a bid is permanently
committed once placed (aside from being outbid). (3) no anti-snipe
mechanic means last-second bid wars are possible and unmitigated by
design.

## 166. City Specialization Bonus Catalog (extends sections 9, 77, 100, 107)

**Eight specializations are defined, but two have zero code consumers
-- effectively no-op bonuses despite being fully selectable.** Sample
Rich (survey/harvest bonus), Manufacturing Center (factory assembly
quality), Medical Center (heal-power bonus), Research Center
(crafting experimentation bonus), Improved Job Market (+15% mission
rewards), and Stronghold (defense bonus, but confirmed to only benefit
sworn militia members per section 98, not all citizens) all have real
skill-mod consumers found in code. Clone Lab and Entertainment
District are defined in the same Lua table with identical structure
but have **no consumer anywhere in the codebase** -- selecting them
produces no mechanical effect. Selection requires the mayor to
personally hold a `city_spec_*` Politician-tree ability, city rank
≥ 3 (Township), and is subject to a 1-week cooldown; the listed "cost"
is not a purchase price but a recurring per-cycle treasury drain that
silently revokes the spec if the treasury can't cover it. Spec bonuses
apply geofenced to physical presence (any unbanned creature benefits,
not just citizens) and are tagged as an independent `SkillModManager::
CITY` category that stacks additively with GCW planetary-control
bonuses (section 107), which use an entirely separate faction-standing
mechanism.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't assume all 8 specializations do
something -- Clone Lab and Entertainment District are confirmed inert
in current code. (2) specialization bonuses benefit any unbanned
visitor physically present, not just city citizens -- a meaningful
distinction from citizen-only benefits elsewhere. (3) the "cost" is
ongoing upkeep, not a one-time purchase -- a cash-poor city can lose
its specialization involuntarily.

## 167. Jedi Visibility / Force-Sensitivity Unlock Mechanic (extends sections 67, 81, 121)

**Force-sensitivity unlock under village progression (this codebase's
active/default mode) is a deterministic multi-category badge
threshold, not XP-based and not a random per-action roll like classic
SWG's village mechanic.** A player must simultaneously hold badges
meeting minimums across five categories (exploration_jedi ≥3,
exploration_dangerous ≥2, exploration_easy ≥5, master ≥1, content ≥5),
checked on login and reactively on every badge award. Once satisfied,
the unlock fires immediately and deterministically -- the only
randomness remaining is cosmetic delay timing for the subsequent NPC
encounters, not whether the unlock happens at all. The first tangible
step is a scripted "Old Man" encounter granting a Force Crystal item,
followed by a Sith Shadow ambush and a multi-stage chain culminating
in the Dathomir Force-sensitive village and a `FS_VILLAGE_ELDER`
quest; only after that does the actual `force_title_jedi_novice`
starting skill box get auto-awarded on next login. Confirmed live and
default (`jediProgressionType = VILLAGEJEDIPROGRESSION`), not
vestigial -- alternate Hologrind/Custom Jedi manager modes exist in
code but aren't the operative default.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) Jedi unlock is a deliberate cross-
profession/cross-activity milestone gate, not luck-based like classic
SWG -- a broadly-accomplished character will always eventually
unlock, a narrowly-focused one never will regardless of playtime. (2)
the holocron (section 121) genuinely plays no role in the unlock
itself -- it only matters after a character is already Jedi. (3) the
badge-threshold check runs reactively on every badge award, so unlock
can trigger mid-session without a login event.

## 168. Death Penalty / XP Loss on Player Death (extends sections 53, 106)

**XP loss on death is Jedi-only** -- `sendPlayerToCloner()` deducts
5% of the `jedi_general` XP cap (clamped at a 10-million floor) only
if `jediState >= 2`; a repo-wide check of every `awardExperience()`
call site confirms zero XP penalty of any kind for non-Jedi
characters, regardless of profession. The flat 100/100/100 HAM +
100 shock "death wound" penalty (applied only when NOT cloning at
your bound facility) uses the exact same `addWounds()` API as ordinary
combat wounds -- it is a larger dose of the identical mechanic, not a
separate "battle fatigue"/"clone sickness" wound category; no such
named mechanic exists anywhere in the codebase. There is no death-
streak or diminishing-returns penalty for repeated deaths -- the
incapacitation counter is unconditionally reset to zero on every
death, so dying twice in a minute costs exactly the same as dying
twice a week apart. No post-respawn stat debuff/clone-sickness buff
is applied on revival; the recovery task only restores state (posture,
floor HAM at 1, clear cloning flag) with no buff/skillmod side effect.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) death is essentially penalty-free for
non-Jedi beyond the standard, fully-healable wound pool -- there's no
hidden XP or stat cost to worry about balancing around for most
professions. (2) Jedi XP loss is the one real stake-raising mechanic
tied to death, reinforcing why Jedi play is treated as higher-risk in
this codebase's design. (3) anyone wanting a repeat-death penalty or
clone-sickness debuff would be building entirely new state -- nothing
existing tracks death frequency or applies post-revival penalties.

## 169. Species/Race Mechanical Differences (extends sections 84, 99, 113)

**Species is a real, non-cosmetic gameplay input across four
independent systems.** Starting HAM: `addRacialMods()` adds a per-
species, per-attribute modifier on top of whatever the profession
template set (confirming and detailing section 84's "fully
deterministic from profession+race" finding -- the mechanism is
additive layering, not a lookup table swap). XP gain rate: a
previously-undocumented `getSpeciesXpModifier()` applies a per-species,
per-XP-type percentage bonus inside the main `awardExperience()` path
-- a genuine, always-on progression-speed difference by species. Innate
abilities: four hardcoded species-gated combat commands exist
(Wookiee Roar, Zabrak Equilibrium/Vitalize, Trandoshan Regeneration),
each guarded by a direct species-enum check in C++, plus a generic
`getSpeciesRequired()` skill-prerequisite gate usable for any future
species-locked skill. Imperial faction-vendor pricing: alien species
pay a real per-species multiplier penalty on Imperial-aligned goods
(Wookiee/Mon Calamari 3x, Twi'lek 1.5x, Human 1x) -- lore-consistent
discrimination baked into `GCWManagerImplementation::getGCWDiscount()`.
Confirmed absent: no species branching for movement speed or jump
height in C++ (any such variance would have to live in absent-from-
repo template data), and no species-gated profession or equipment
restrictions anywhere.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) species affects starting stats, XP gain
rate, a handful of innate abilities, and Imperial shop pricing -- treat
it as a real balance lever, not flavor. (2) no profession or equipment
is species-locked; only specific consumables and the four innate
commands use hard species checks. (3) the `getSpeciesRequired()`
skill-prerequisite pattern is the ready-made hook for any new species-
exclusive skill.

## 170. Character Title & Surname System (extends sections 22, 41, 77, 86, 100)

**Renaming is a GM-only support action, not a player-facing service or
purchasable token** -- `/setFirstName`/`/setLastName` are gated behind
a `godOnly` staff skill; there is no veteran-reward or cash-shop rename
mechanic. There is exactly one true unified "title" field on
`PlayerObject` (the skill/profession title, set via
`/setCurrentSkillTitle`, gated to titles the player has actually
earned) -- guild title (section 41), GCW military rank (section 100),
and mayoral rank (section 77) are all structurally separate fields
sent to the client independently; the **client**, not the server,
composes/prioritizes what's displayed on screen. A `SetLoginTitleCommand`
exists but is a confirmed inert stub. Titles are purely cosmetic --
`setTitle()` has zero downstream mechanical read sites beyond display
packets, though the underlying rank *tiers* some titles represent
(GCW rank specifically) do gate real mechanics (section 100), just not
via the title string itself. The profanity filter (section 86)
confirmed to cover both name segments on every rename via the same
`NameManager::isProfane()` path.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't build a player rename feature by
extending `/setFirstName` -- it's staff tooling with no cost/cooldown
model suited for player use. (2) there's no single server-side
"display title" string -- guild/GCW/mayor titles are independent
fields the client stitches together, important for anyone building
new UI that shows player names. (3) title text itself carries zero
mechanics; don't confuse a cosmetic title with the rank tier it
represents.

## 171. Group Finder / LFG System -- Confirmed Passive Self-Tagging Only, No Matchmaking (extends sections 19, 71, 151)

**An LFG flag exists and is queryable, but there is no active
matchmaking, group listing, or auto-group feature.** `/lfg` toggles a
single bitmask bit on `PlayerObject`, auto-cleared the moment the
player joins any group. The only server-side "finder" tool is
`RequestCharacterMatchCommand` (backing `/who`/Character Match), a
proximity-limited (nearby objects only, capped at 32 results) player
*search* filterable by roleplayer/newbie-helper/LFG/faction/species/
profession bits -- not a listing of groups or missions seeking members.
Two client-referenced "matchmaking profile" commands
(`SetMatchMakingCharacterIdCommand`/`SetMatchMakingPersonalIdCommand`)
are confirmed pure no-op stubs, suggesting the original SWG
matchmaking-profile concept was never implemented server-side. No
auto-group or recommended-group logic exists for missions or
instances anywhere in the codebase.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "LFG" in this codebase means a self-set
visibility flag surfaced through `/who` search, not a queue or
matchmaker -- set expectations accordingly. (2) the matchmaking-ID
commands look like they should do something but are dead code --
don't build on them. (3) any real group-finder feature (cross-zone
group listing, mission-based auto-group) would be new server logic;
`PlayerBitmasks`/`RequestCharacterMatchCommand` is the natural
extension point.

## 172. GCW Score & Faction Standing Decay -- Confirmed Absent (extends sections 100, 107)

**Both GCW planetary score and personal faction standing are
decay-free by design.** The hourly GCW score recompute (section 107)
is a pure full-rebuild snapshot -- `setRebelScore()`/`setImperialScore()`
plain setters, not `+=`/decay against the prior value -- discarding and
recalculating totals from currently-existing bases every cycle with no
memory of past values. Personal faction standing
(`FactionStandingList`) is mutated only through explicit `+=`/`-=` calls
tied to real gameplay events (kills, PvP, recruiter bribes, delegate
transfers) -- never from a scheduled task, login handler, or timer.
There is no "use it or lose it" mechanic for GCW bases either: a
base's score contribution is a fixed template lookup unaffected by
age, activity, or defense state; bases leave the score roll only via
explicit destruction, not gradual erosion. This confirms and extends
section 100's "no rank decay" finding across every adjacent GCW-scoring
system.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) an idle player's standing and an idle
faction's planetary score both simply hold steady indefinitely --
inactivity has zero mechanical effect on either number. (2) any
activity-decay or "use it or lose it" feature for score/standing/base
upkeep would be genuinely new logic, not an extension of a partial
existing mechanic. (3) don't confuse this with structure *condition*
decay from missed maintenance (section 54) -- a different stat on a
different object entirely.

## 173. Vehicle/Ship Vanity Naming (extends sections 18, 43, 86, 119)

**Only ships are vanity-nameable -- ground vehicles have no equivalent
feature at all.** Ship renaming is a real, free, unlimited player
mechanic via the ship-deed radial menu (`SET_NAME` -> `SuiInputBox` ->
`NameShipSuiCallback` -> `setShipName()`), filtered by the same
`NameManager::isProfane()`/reserved-name checks documented in section
86, plus a rule rejecting names that look like serial numbers (runs of
more than 3 consecutive digits). `VehicleControlDeviceImplementation`
(ground speeders/swoops) has no radial option, SUI, or command hook
for renaming whatsoever -- confirmed absent, not just undocumented. A
generic `/setname` command exists but is a `godOnly` staff tool with no
ownership check, not a player feature. `ShipObject` does carry a
`uniqueID` field distinct from `shipName`, but it's an ephemeral
16-bit space-zone radar/targeting slot index, not a player-visible
registration/plate system -- no such registration concept exists for
ships or vehicles.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) ship naming is real and free; ground
vehicle naming is a genuine gap -- copying the ship radial-menu/SUI
flow is the template if it's ever added. (2) don't confuse
`ShipObject.uniqueID` with a registration plate -- it's internal
bookkeeping, invisible to players as an identifier. (3) `/setname` is
staff-only tooling, not a rename mechanic to build player features on.

## 174. Duel Rematch/Cooldown & Record Tracking (extends sections 56, 127)

**No duel-request cooldown exists at all** -- challenges are gated
only by range, an already-in-duel check, and a duplicate-pending-
request guard, none of which is time-based; nothing stops immediate
re-challenges after a duel ends. Critically, **duel kills DO feed the
Elo-style `pvpRating` from section 127 exactly like any open-world PvP
kill** -- the "in a duel" check only affects broadcast message text and
explicitly exempts duel kills from GCW faction-point awards, but never
gates the rating-update path. No per-player duel win/loss counter
exists anywhere in the codebase -- consistent with section 127's
finding that only the Elo rating (not a raw counter) tracks PvP
outcomes. A duel can end via mutual death, explicit `/endDuel`, a
one-sided cancel of a pending challenge, or bulk cleanup on death/
logout (the closest thing to a "disconnect forfeit," but pure list
cleanup with no scored outcome) -- there is no draw/tie state.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any anti-spam/rematch-cooldown feature
would be entirely new work -- nothing to extend today. (2) don't
assume duels are isolated from ranking systems -- they affect
`pvpRating` identically to open-world PvP; only GCW standing is
duel-exempt. (3) a duel win/loss leaderboard would need new persistent
state; the Elo rating-update call site is the natural hook point.

## 175. GCW Faction Recruiter Bribe Mechanic (extends sections 73, 100)

**Bribing is a flat credits-to-faction-standing converter, not an
instant rank-up** -- two hardcoded tiers (20,000 credits -> 250
standing, or 100,000 credits -> 1,250 standing) simply add to the
standing pool that a separate, normal promotion conversation later
spends on rank; the player must still complete that conversation
manually. No scaling formula ties cost to current rank. There is no
explicit cooldown or per-day limit -- the only constraint is a live
cap check (`max(1000, rankCost*20)`) re-evaluated on every attempt, so
a player can bribe repeatedly back-to-back until standing would
exceed the current rank's cap. Bribing is double-gated: it requires
both the Smuggler `combat_smuggler_underworld_04` skill AND OVERT
faction status (section 73) -- the parallel COVERT conversation
branch never even offers the bribe option, and it's framed narratively
as an under-the-table Smuggler-only deal.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) bribing accelerates standing
accumulation, not rank itself -- don't conflate the two when modeling
GCW progression speed. (2) it's a Smuggler-specific, OVERT-only
mechanic, not available to the general faction-aligned population.
(3) the effective "cooldown" is really a soft cap tied to the current
rank's point ceiling, not a timer -- spending standing on a promotion
reopens bribing headroom immediately.

## 176. Crafted-Item Salvage / Resource Reclamation -- Confirmed Absent (extends sections 20, 129)

**Destroying, junking, recycling, or reverse-engineering a crafted
item never returns constituent crafting resources.** `DestroyCommand`
is a literal no-op; the real destroy path only ever calls
`destroyObjectFromWorld/Database`, with its sole special-case payout
being unwrapping an installed Anti-Decay Kit (the ADK item itself, not
resources). `RecycleTool` exists but explicitly rejects anything that
isn't a raw resource container -- it converts resource-to-resource,
never touches crafted items. `ComponentAnalysisTool` (reverse
engineering, section 109) consumes source components to produce
another item/schematic, never raw resources. Most tellingly, crafted
items can't even reach the junk dealer's flat-credit payout (section
129) -- its eligibility filter explicitly excludes anything with a
non-empty `getCraftersName()`, meaning player-manufactured items yield
literally nothing on disposal: no credits, no resources.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) a "salvage into resources" feature would
be entirely new content -- there is no partial mechanic to extend.
(2) crafted-item disposal is currently a pure sink with zero return in
any form, a genuine economic dead-end worth knowing about. (3) if
built, `RecycleTool`'s insert-item/get-resource-back UX pattern and
`ComponentAnalysisTool`'s quality-scaled-yield pattern are the two
closest structural templates to adapt.

## 177. Veteran Reward System Catalog (extends sections 145, 162)

**A real, live veteran-reward ladder exists, gated by DB account-
creation age, not real subscription time.** Twelve fixed day-
thresholds (90 through 1080) each carry a Lua-defined reward pool,
with a new milestone auto-generated every 360 days indefinitely once
the fixed list is exhausted. Notably corrects prior sections: the
Anti-Decay Kit (section 145/153) is specifically the 360-day reward,
and the Sorosuub space yacht deed (section 162) is specifically the
180-day reward, both `oneTime=true`. Account age is measured from the
emulator's own `accounts.created` DB timestamp (optionally reset to
first-connection time via config) -- on a private server this is
trivially adjustable, unlike a real subscription-linked system.
Claiming is player-initiated (`/claimVeteranReward` -> SUI list ->
confirm), not automatic or NPC-mediated. Critically, the "claimed"
record is stored **per account**, not per-character or per-item --
destroying a granted one-time item does not reopen it for reclaiming;
only a GM `/clearVeteranReward` command can reset a milestone.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't assume veteran rewards track real
paid subscription time -- it's DB row age, spoofable on private
servers. (2) losing a one-time veteran item is permanent for normal
players -- there's no self-service recovery path. (3) the reward pool
is entirely Lua-data-driven (`player_manager.lua`), easy to retune
without a C++ rebuild.

## 178. OVERT/COVERT Resignation Mechanic (extends sections 73, 100, 175)

**Resigning via the faction recruiter is a full faction reset --
`Faction`, `FactionRank`, and `FactionStatus` all zeroed -- but costs
zero banked faction-standing points**, a genuinely different action
from the simple in-place status downgrades ("go on leave," "go
covert"), which only touch `FactionStatus` and leave faction
membership/rank intact. Two parallel conversation flows exist with
different timers depending on `useCovertOvertSystem()` config: 15
minutes under the modern covert/overt system, 5 minutes under a
legacy path -- both cancelable while pending. Re-declaring OVERT after
resignation requires rejoining a faction from scratch, then going
through the normal COVERT->OVERT declaration path and its standard
300-second cooldown -- there's no resignation-specific extra penalty
timer beyond that. Resignation is player-initiated and self-cancelable
only; the sole way to force a faction reset on someone else is a GM
`/setfaction` override (distinct from the automatic OVERT-to-COVERT
demotion that happens when an OVERT player clones at a neutral
facility, which only changes status, not faction/rank).

**Practical takeaways:** (1) resignation is destructive to rank and
faction membership but standing-preserving -- a meaningfully different
cost profile from simple status changes. (2) the resignation timer
length depends on server config (`useCovertOvertSystem()`) -- always
verify which system is active before quoting 5 vs. 15 minutes. (3) no
player can be forced to resign; only a GM command can replicate that
outcome on someone else's behalf.

## 179. Faction Standing Delegate/Transfer & "Cries of Alderaan" (CoA) Bonus (extends sections 100, 172, 175)

**Both mechanics are live, functional, and confirmed active mutators
of faction standing beyond section 172's baseline finding.**
`/delegatefactionpoints` lets an OVERT/"declared" player transfer
standing to a same-faction target, but with a built-in tax: the cost
ratio (`getRankDelegateRatioFrom/To`) usually charges the sender more
points than the receiver gets. Abuse resistance is purely economic --
a mandatory 200-point floor on the sender and the receiver's normal
rank-cap ceiling -- there is no cooldown/rate-limit of any kind on
delegation. "CoA" is Cries of Alderaan, a multi-episode GCW theme-park
quest chain whose weekly-recomputed "winning faction" (based on quest-
completion scores, not GCW base score from section 107) grants a flat
+10% bonus to any standing gain for members of the winning side,
applied automatically inside `increaseFactionStanding()` itself.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) delegation is real and abusable only by
its economic tax, not by any rate limit -- a determined player could
funnel standing to an alt with zero cooldown friction. (2) the CoA
bonus is a hidden, automatic +10% multiplier that silently affects any
standing-gain calculation for the currently-winning faction -- easy to
miss when reasoning about "why does this player's standing gain not
match the expected formula." (3) CoA's winning-faction determination
is a completely separate scoring system from section 107's GCW base
score -- don't conflate quest-chain scoring with base-ownership
scoring.

## 180. Vehicle/Droid Custom Color Dye System (extends sections 32, 163, 169)

**Vehicle and droid recoloring share one engine (`*CustomKitObject
MenuComponent` -> `Custom{Vehicle,Droid}SuiCallback` -> `SuiColorBox`
-> `ColorWithKitSuiCallback`) but differ in one key respect: droid
recoloring is skill-gated, vehicle recoloring is not.** Both are
finite-charge consumable kits (crafted items with a `useCount`,
destroyed at zero), unlike armor/item dye (section 163), which is
unlimited/skillMod-gated rather than consumable. For vehicles, the
color-range cap defaults to an effectively-unrestricted 500; for
droids, the applying player's own `droid_customization` skill mod
(granted only by Droid Engineer crafting boxes, 32-64 range) sets a
real palette-size ceiling -- though even a zero-skill player is
floored to 32, giving baseline access without the profession. Both
draw their actual color palette from the same per-appearance-template
`AssetCustomizationManagerTemplate` infrastructure used by item dye
and Image Designer (section 32), not a separate shared palette.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't assume vehicle and droid recolor
work identically -- droids have a real profession-influenced palette
cap, vehicles don't. (2) both consume a crafted kit charge, unlike
unlimited armor dye -- a meaningful cost difference worth remembering
when comparing customization systems. (3) the palette-source
infrastructure is fully shared across Image Designer, item dye, and
vehicle/droid recolor -- one engine, several consumption models
layered on top.

## 181. Lightsaber Crystal Color Mechanic (extends sections 81, 89, 145)

**Blade color is entirely a function of which crystal is socketed in
the special `saber_inv` container -- there is no independent player
color-picker UI.** A freshly-crafted hilt defaults to `bladeColor = 31`
(colorless); inserting a color crystal sets both `bladeColor` and a
customization variable to that crystal's color, and removing it
reverts to colorless. All 12 base colors (red, dark red, light/dark
green, blue, dark blue, yellow, dark yellow, light/dark purple,
orange, brown) come from a single loot template rolled uniformly at
random (0-11) -- **no engineered rarity tiers exist for specific
hues**, contrary to classic-SWG lore expectations about "rare" colors.
A separate, harder-hitting "Force crystal" variant (Krayt Dragon
Pearl) is hard-pinned to colorless and functions purely as a stat
upgrade, not a color source. Legacy unique-named color string IDs
(12-30, e.g. "Kenobi's Legacy") exist in the string table but have no
reachable loot/craft path in current code -- vestigial content. Color
is fully swappable post-craft (pull crystal, insert a different one)
and carries zero light/dark alignment gating in code.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) blade color is socket-state, not a saved
player preference -- track it via crystal presence, not a separate
field. (2) all 12 standard colors are equally common by design in
current code -- any "rare color" expectation from classic SWG lore
doesn't hold here. (3) the unique legacy color names are dead content
-- don't assume they're obtainable through any current drop table.

## 182. Recall / Instant-Travel-Home Item -- Confirmed Absent (extends sections 64, 131, 148)

**No player-facing recall/hometown teleport command or consumable
item exists anywhere in the codebase.** The only teleport-family
commands (`/teleport`, `/teleportTarget`, `/teleportTo`) are
GM/staff-only, admin-ability-gated, and operate on arbitrary
coordinates or target players -- none reference a stored "home"
location. No `ConsumableTeleport`-style item class exists in loot,
veteran rewards, or crafted schematics. The only mechanisms that get a
player somewhere are the fully passive/paid alternatives already
documented: cloner rebinding (section 131, respawn-point only, not an
active teleport) and paid shuttle travel between fixed terminals
(section 64). No structure-specific "teleport to my house" convenience
command exists either.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) this is a genuine, clean gap -- not a
documentation oversight -- confirmed via command-table, source, and
script-wide search. (2) building this feature would require entirely
new scaffolding: a stored home-coordinate field, a new command/item
class, and likely a combat-state gate mirroring section 148's shuttle-
travel restriction pattern. (3) don't confuse this with cloner binding
(section 131) -- that only determines respawn location on death, it
has no active-use component at all.

## 183. GM Invisibility / Teleport-to-Player Admin Tools (extends sections 13, 96, 152)

**GM invisibility is a real client-side hide mechanism, distinct from
both PvP-invulnerability and raw damage immunity.** `/invulnerable
invis` toggles `TangibleObject::setInvisible()`, which suppresses
transform-update broadcasts on zone re-insertion -- genuinely
unseen-while-moving, not just a cosmetic flag. Called without a
sub-argument, the same command instead toggles PvP-attackability
(`ObjectFlag::PLAYER` bitmask) -- a separate effect entirely. True
damage immunity is a third, separate flag (`isInvulnerable()`) not
exposed by any admin command found. All three teleport commands
(`/teleport`, `/teleportTo`, `/teleportTarget`) skip normal zone-
transition validation (travel tickets, faction locks) via the same
permissive `hasGodMode()`-bypass pattern already flagged in section
152's docking-permission stub -- confirming this is a repeated design
pattern across the codebase, not an isolated shortcut. `hasGodMode()`
additionally doubles as a stealth-from-tracking flag: `VisibilityManager`
skips GMs both when computing their own visibility accrual and others'
detection of them, an easily-missed side effect. Admin commands are
auto-logged whenever tagged `characterAbility='admin'` in the command
table -- confirmed for all teleport/invisibility commands -- except
`/setGodMode`, which self-logs via a manual call instead of the
central gate.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) invisibility, PvP-invulnerability, and
damage-invulnerability are three genuinely separate flags -- don't
assume one implies another when reasoning about GM state. (2) the
`hasGodMode()`-bypass-permission-stub pattern recurs across systems
(docking, teleport) -- worth checking for elsewhere if auditing
permission gates. (3) `/setGodMode` is the one admin command that
doesn't rely on the central audit-logging gate -- worth double-
checking any new admin command actually sets `characterAbility='admin'`
if audit logging is expected.

## 184. Structure Maintenance Grace Period & Eviction Sequencing (extends sections 54, 77, 102)

**The full unpaid-maintenance timeline has two windows: an unbounded
daily-decay/condemnation state, capped by a hard-coded 30-day
(720-hour) back-maintenance threshold before final destruction.**
The engine first attempts an automatic weekly bank auto-draft
(config-toggleable); only on failure does daily decay begin, sending
a warning mail each cycle until the structure is fully decayed, at
which point buildings are condemned (not destroyed) while non-
buildings (harvesters, factories, turrets) are destroyed immediately
with **zero grace period** -- a sharp asymmetry. A condemned building
can be recovered at any time before the 30-day cutoff via a manual,
player-initiated "uncondemn" SUI that pays off the exact negative
balance -- condemnation is explicitly not the point of no return.
Four distinct mail notifications fire at each stage (auto-draft
success, daily decay warning, condemnation, final destruction) -- no
separate login popup exists. City property tax delinquency is
confirmed to have **no separate eviction path** -- unpaid tax is
mathematically folded directly into the structure's own maintenance
draw as a surcharge, accelerating that structure's decay clock rather
than triggering any city-side seizure mechanic.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the 30-day destruction threshold is a
single hard-coded constant with no per-structure-type override --
changing it requires a source edit, not a config change. (2) harvesters/
factories/turrets get no condemnation grace at all, unlike player
housing -- a meaningful asymmetry worth remembering when reasoning
about structure loss. (3) there's no such thing as "city tax eviction"
as a distinct mechanic -- it's entirely subsumed into ordinary
maintenance decay, so don't design around a separate tax-delinquency
consequence.

## 185. No-PvP/No-Combat Safe Zone System -- Real but Currently Unused by World Content (extends sections 56, 92, 97, 108)

**A fully functional no-combat/no-duel zone mechanism exists in the
engine (`ActiveArea`'s `NOCOMBATAREA`/`NODUELAREA` bitmask flags), but
no current planet region data actually uses it** -- confirming and
extending section 56's finding that sibling PvP-related area flags
"ship unused." `NOCOMBATAREA` is checked deep in the core
attackability pipeline (`isAttackableBy()`) on both the attacker and
defender side, for both PvE and PvP alike -- it's a hard kill-switch
on new attacks, not a duel/PvP-specific restriction like the narrower
`NODUELAREA` (which only gates the `/duel` challenge command itself).
Critically, the flag only blocks the *next* attack attempt -- it does
NOT forcibly end an in-progress fight or eject combatants on
area-entry; an already-active fight only halts on the next attack
attempt after the flag takes effect. This is a genuinely different
mechanism from faction-neutral city safety (overt/covert + TEF logic,
sections 49/97) and from the Force-sensitive village's bespoke
combat-eviction override (`FsVillageAreaImplementation`, which
actively teleports combat-flagged players back outside its boundary on
entry) -- three separate answers to "why can't I fight here."

**Practical takeaways:** (1) adding a safe zone to a starport/cantina/
hospital is a one-line Lua region-table addition (`setNoCombatArea`/
`setNoDuelArea`) -- zero C++ work needed, the plumbing already exists
and works. (2) don't confuse this with faction-neutral city safety --
that's an entirely different overt/covert-based mechanism. (3) the
generic flag doesn't force-eject or force-peace on entry; only the
Force-village's bespoke subclass does that -- model any "actively
eject combatants" requirement on `FsVillageAreaImplementation
::notifyEnter()`, not the generic flag.

## 186. Player Container Lock/Combination System -- Confirmed Absent (extends sections 24, 120, 156)

**No per-container combination/password mechanic exists for player
storage** -- confirmed via exhaustive search of `ContainerPermissions`
and `Container.idl`. `ContainerPermissions` is purely a coarse group-
bitmask ACL (owner/admin/named lists) sharing the exact same
infrastructure as the house ban/entry list system (section 156), not
a secret-code system. `Container` does carry a `locked` boolean, but
it's exclusively a **static world loot-crate slicing gimmick**
(Smuggler skill minigame), randomly assigned only to
`STATICLOOTCONTAINER`-type objects at load -- and its enforcement in
`canAddObject()` is dead/commented-out code, meaning even that flag
doesn't actually block insertion. No storage crate, radial menu, or
command exists to set a lock on ordinary player containers. Vendor
stockrooms and bank storage reuse the identical group-ACL mechanism
(via `MOVEVENDOR` permission and proximity checks respectively) rather
than any distinct locking system.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) house-level access control (section 156)
is the only real "lock" concept in this codebase -- there's no
finer-grained per-container secret. (2) the `locked` field on
`Container` is a loot-crate-only mechanic with dead enforcement code
-- don't build on it for player storage. (3) a genuine player-set
combination-lock feature would be entirely new work with no partial
scaffolding to extend.

## 187. Ground Escort Missions -- Real via Screenplay System, Confirmed Dead in MissionObject/MissionTerminal (extends sections 3, 16, 152)

**`MissionTypes::ESCORT`/`ESCORT2ME`/`ESCORTTOCREATOR` CRCs exist and
stringify correctly but are never used to generate a live ground
mission** -- confirming section 16's list is functionally complete
despite the raw enum values existing. A genuine, live ground escort
mechanic DOES exist, but entirely through the Screenplay/quest system
(`quest_tasks/escort.lua`, a reusable `Task` subclass), architecturally
parallel to space's `SpaceEscortScreenplay` split from `MissionObject`
documented in section 152 -- the same "ground missions and space
missions both bypass MissionObject for escort-type content" pattern.
The escort NPC is flagged `AI_ESCORT + AI_FOLLOW + AI_NOAIAGGRO`
(won't initiate its own combat), success is purely location-based (an
`ENTEREDAREA` observer on a destination active-area), and -- notably
-- the reusable base module has **no built-in death-tracking/failure
logic at all**; any "escort dies = quest fails" behavior must be
layered on by the specific subclassing quest chain. Confirmed live in
the Force-Sensitive village quest chain and several theme-park/tutorial
quests.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) ground escort is real but lives entirely
outside the mission-terminal system -- extend `Escort:new{...}`, don't
try to wire it through `MissionObject`. (2) don't assume escort NPC
death auto-fails a quest -- the base module doesn't track it; verify
per-quest-chain. (3) this is the third confirmed case (after space
missions in section 152) of a content category having dead enum
values in the terminal-based system while a real implementation lives
in the parallel Screenplay system.

## 188. AFK Status -- Confirmed Purely Player-Toggled, No Auto-Detection or Idle-Kick (extends sections 79, 171)

**The AFK bit is self-toggled only (`/afk` command) -- there is no
server-side inactivity detection feeding it, and no idle-kick/auto-
logout timer exists for a genuinely inactive-but-connected player.**
This is a real, separate finding from linkdead handling (section 189),
which is triggered purely by actual network disconnection, not input
inactivity -- a player who stops providing input while still connected
is never flagged or logged out by anything in this codebase. AFK does
carry real mechanical teeth, but only restrictive ones aimed at the
AFK player themselves: `CombatManager::startCombat()` blocks an AFK
attacker from initiating combat, queuing combat commands returns a
general error, and DNA sampling (section 33/57) is blocked. Nothing
exempts an AFK player from being attacked, auto-removes them from a
group, or changes their PvP exposure -- AFK only restricts what the
AFK player can *do*, never what can be done *to* them. Combat does not
automatically clear the AFK flag either.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't design around server-detected
idleness -- it doesn't exist; AFK is purely a self-reported status
flag, like an away message. (2) AFK players remain fully vulnerable to
attack and combat targeting -- it provides zero defensive benefit.
(3) any genuine idle-kick feature would need entirely new
input-recency tracking; nothing currently monitors last-action
timestamps.

## 189. Linkdead (LD) Disconnect Grace Period & Reconnection (extends sections 5, 30, 171, 188)

**Disconnection triggers a real "linkdead" limbo state, not instant
removal from the world** -- the character lingers in-zone, fully
combat-vulnerable (killable and lootable by enemies), for up to a
configurable grace period (`Core3.PlayerObject.LinkDeadDelay`, default
3 minutes), or near-instantly if it was a safe/voluntary logout.
Reconnecting within the window seamlessly resumes the exact same live
object -- position, HAM, buffs, target, and group membership are all
preserved, with no forced return to character-select. If the grace
period expires without reconnection, a full forced-logout cleanup
fires: missions deactivated, vehicles/pets stored, ejected from
buildings, removed from any group, duel list cleared, chat rooms left,
and the body destroyed from the zone -- but notably **no explicit XP
or credit penalty is applied** for a lapsed linkdead timeout. One
targeted anti-abuse gate exists: a same-account character cannot
beneficially heal a linkdead character unless a specific config flag
is enabled (anti-multibox-heal protection) -- but this only restricts
being helped, not being attacked.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) linkdead is a real vulnerability window,
not a safety net -- a disconnected player can be killed and looted for
up to 3 minutes by default. (2) reconnection is seamless and stateful
-- no data loss or position reset for a timely reconnect. (3) letting
the timer expire is a clean, penalty-free logout from a mechanics
standpoint, aside from whatever happened to the character while
vulnerable during the grace window.

## 190. Doctor/Medic Group & Area-of-Effect Healing (extends sections 27, 51, 95)

**Group/AOE healing is real but implemented as a crafted-item
property, not a distinct ability or command** -- `HealDamageCommand::
handleArea()` fires automatically whenever the equipped stim pack has
its `isArea()` experimental attribute set (a crafter's choice at craft
time, not a player command choice), healing every nearby *healable*
target within the item's radius -- with no group-membership
requirement at all, benefiting any non-hostile nearby character,
grouped or not. Scaling is full-strength-per-target (the identical
single-target formula applied independently to each recipient) with
zero diminishing returns, and cost is charged exactly once for the
whole AOE action (one Mind-cost deduction, one item-charge
consumption, one cooldown) regardless of how many targets are healed
-- making AOE stims strictly more resource-efficient than repeated
single-target casts with no built-in balancing penalty. Confirmed
structurally separate from entertainer group healing (section 72,
purely tick-based dance/music mechanic) and from Jedi Force heal
commands (`HealAllOther/Self` -- despite the naming, these are Jedi
abilities, not Doctor/medic ones) -- all three healing sources stack
independently with zero cross-interaction.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "group heal" for Doctors is really "AOE
heal item" -- there's no group-restricted targeting, any nearby ally
benefits. (2) AOE stims are a pure efficiency win with no
per-target cost scaling -- worth knowing for any balance discussion.
(3) don't confuse `HealAllOther/SelfCommand` naming with Doctor
group healing -- those are unrelated Jedi Force abilities.

## 191. Force-Sensitive Jedi Robe Crafting -- Confirmed Not Player-Craftable, Real Stat Bonuses (extends sections 20, 32, 81, 144, 167)

**Jedi robes bypass the crafting system entirely -- they are code/
screenplay-granted rewards, not Tailor schematics** -- confirmed
absent from the entire `draft_schematic` tree; robes are instead
directly instantiated and given to the player on becoming Force-
sensitive (Jedi trials completion) and swapped automatically on every
FRS rank-up (section 67). Wear restriction reuses the generic weapon-
style `certificationsRequired`/`hasSkill()` cert-gate (the same
mechanism documented for weapon certifications, not a bespoke species/
Force-sensitivity flag) -- since only actual Jedi hold the required
`force_rank_*`/`force_title_jedi_rank_*` skill boxes, this structurally
restricts equip to Force-sensitive characters. Unlike faction uniforms
(section 144, confirmed purely cosmetic), Jedi robes carry **real
mechanical stat bonuses** -- flat `+jedi_force_power_max`/
`+jedi_force_power_regen` skill mods that directly feed the Force-
power-cost math from section 81. Robe appearance is also explicitly
FRS-rank-gated -- a 5-tier visual ladder (`s01` novice through `s05`
master) swapped server-side on each promotion, per section 67's rank
system. Robes are hard-flagged no-trade and hard-excluded from item
insurance.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't look for a Jedi-robe crafting
recipe -- there isn't one; robes are pure reward/promotion content.
(2) unlike faction uniforms, robes are a real Force-pool stat item --
losing one has actual mechanical consequences for a Jedi, not just
cosmetics. (3) the cert-gate pattern reused here is the same one
backing weapon certifications -- a useful template for any future
skill-gated wearable.

## 192. Structure No-Build Zones Around Static POIs (extends sections 59, 77, 92, 103, 117)

**A real, three-layer no-build system stacks on top of section 103's
ordinary structure-to-structure footprint check, uniformly across all
structure types.** Named `ActiveArea` regions can carry a
`NOBUILDZONEAREA` flag (e.g. a dedicated no-build rectangle drawn
around Theed independent of and larger than the city's own boundary);
individual object templates can carry a per-instance `noBuildRadius`
exclusion bubble (used by lairs, shuttle beacons, event-perk deeds);
and a flat, hardcoded 150-unit minimum-distance check applies against
every entry in the client-exported POI datatable, regardless of POI
type or size. All three checks live inside one shared gate
(`isBuildingPermittedAt()`), reused verbatim for camp placement
(section 60) and NPC spawn validation (section 66) -- one unified
"is this terrain legal" function serving multiple systems. Structure
type is irrelevant to any of these checks -- a GCW base gets no special
exemption or extra restriction near a starport relative to an ordinary
house. City founding has its own separate, larger-radius exclusion
check (1024-unit against other player cities, `radius*2` against
existing NPC/static cities) evaluated independently of ordinary
structure placement.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) three independent no-build mechanisms
stack -- don't assume a single flag governs POI exclusion. (2) the
checks are structure-type-agnostic, unlike some other placement rules
in this guide -- no GCW-base-specific carve-out exists. (3) city
founding uses a completely separate, larger-radius distance rule from
ordinary structure placement -- don't conflate the two when reasoning
about why a placement was rejected.

## 193. World Dynamic/Random Events System (extends sections 3, 66, 92, 177)

**Only one true holiday event exists (Life Day), and no rampage/
faction-raid mechanic exists at all -- both confirmed via exhaustive
grep.** Life Day is a `ScreenPlay`-framework event gated by an internal
Lua date-window check (`os.date` against a hardcoded Dec 1-31 range)
rather than a real recurring scheduler -- it only actually activates if
the server happens to (re)start during its window or is manually
force-started, since `DirectorManager::startGlobalScreenPlays()` only
runs its registration pass once at zone-server boot. Several other
one-shot narrative "event" screenplays exist in the same directory
(Bestine Election, Cries of Alderaan -- section 179's CoA source,
Secrets of the Syren) but these are permanent quest-chain content that
stays active once registered, not recurring random triggers. A
rancor/AT-ST/creature-rampage-attacks-a-town mechanic, or any faction-
raid-on-a-city system, is confirmed completely absent -- zero real
hits for "rampage" anywhere in the C++, Lua, or SQL trees. None of the
found event screenplays touch GCW score (section 107) or city
government (section 77) APIs.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't expect a cron-like world-event
scheduler -- what exists is boot-time registration plus internal
date-gating, a fragile trigger model worth knowing if events seem to
"not fire." (2) rampages/faction raids are a genuine gap, not an
oversight -- building one would be new content using the generic
`ScreenPlay`/`DirectorManager` framework as a base. (3) none of the
existing event content integrates with GCW or city systems -- any
"event affects GCW score" feature would be new wiring.

## 194. Jedi-Specific Bounty Hunting Content (extends sections 20, 44, 73, 97, 101)

**Player bounty targets are exclusively and unconditionally Jedi --
confirmed airtight across every code path.** The only mechanism that
populates the player bounty list is holding the
`force_title_jedi_rank_02` skill, checked at grant time, re-verified
on every login, and removed when the skill/character is lost -- there
is no PvP-kill, crime, or GM-triggered path that ever adds a non-Jedi
player. Dark-side/Force-flavored NPC bounty targets do exist (Dark
Adept, Nightsister, feral Force wielder, etc.) but as ordinary entries
mixed into the standard high-level NPC bounty pool, not a
mechanically distinct category -- they use the identical flat
level-based reward formula as any other NPC bounty, no Force-specific
bonus. Jedi *player* bounty rewards, by contrast, use a genuinely
different formula scaling with spent Jedi skill points and FRS rank
(section 67), confirming section 101's finding about automatic,
milestone-triggered posting. Bounty-hunter TEF (`hasBhTef()`) is
confirmed as a distinct, third attackability-bypass channel alongside
duel-exemption (section 56) and crackdown TEF (section 97) -- it lets
a bounty hunter attack a COVERT Jedi target that would otherwise be
protected, entirely independent of GCW mechanics.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any design assuming non-Jedi players can
become bounty targets is wrong -- this is a Jedi-exclusive mechanic by
hard-coded design, not a policy choice that happens to favor Jedi.
(2) Force-flavored NPC bounty targets exist as flavor content only --
there's no differentiated reward/difficulty system to extend without
new code. (3) bounty TEF is a complete third bypass channel worth
remembering alongside duel and crackdown TEFs when reasoning about
"why was this COVERT player attackable."

## 195. Dual Wielding -- Confirmed Absent by Design (extends sections 10, 81, 105, 115)

**`CreatureObject` has exactly one weapon reference field -- there is
no off-hand slot, no dual-wield skill mod, and no code path that ever
reads a second weapon for extra attacks or damage.** Equipping a
second one-handed weapon is not blocked outright, but the equip
command (`TransferItemWeaponCommand`) automatically evicts the
previously-equipped weapon back to inventory first -- it's always a
swap, never a simultaneous hold, cosmetic or otherwise. No skill mods,
certifications, or command definitions anywhere in the skill tree
reference dual wielding, off-hand attacks, or two-weapon fighting.
Lightsaber/Jedi melee (section 81) reuses the identical single-weapon
combat command pattern as every other melee weapon -- there is no
saberstaff/dual-blade mechanic despite that being a plausible Jedi
fantasy feature.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) dual wielding is a clean, confirmed
absence -- not a bug or oversight, a deliberate one-weapon design
baked into the core `CreatureObject` field structure. (2) equipping a
second weapon silently swaps rather than blocking, which could
surprise a player expecting to hold two weapons. (3) any dual-wield or
saberstaff feature would require adding a genuine second weapon slot
to `CreatureObject` and threading it through `CombatManager` --
substantial new work, not a toggle.

## 196. Vehicle/Pet/Ship Control Device Loss & Replacement -- No Reissue Mechanic, But Devices Are Also Nearly Indestructible (extends sections 53, 94, 119, 131, 150)

**A stored control device (pet/vehicle/ship deed) is structurally
immune to the ordinary loss vectors that affect other items -- but if
it IS ever lost via one of two narrow edge-case paths, there is no
reissue mechanic whatsoever.** The player `/destroy` command hard-
rejects any object sitting in a datapad slot before it ever reaches
deletion logic, and combat destruction is moot since a stored device
isn't present in the zone quadtree at all. Datapad storage is
confirmed *stronger* protection than item insurance (section 53) --
insurance-eligible-item scanning explicitly skips the datapad
container entirely, and control devices are `IntangibleObject`s
anyway, structurally ineligible for insurance regardless of location.
The only two confirmed genuine permanent-loss paths are narrow,
purpose-built edge cases: a rental starter speederbike self-destructs
on use-counter exhaustion, and `FACTIONPET`-type combat pets have
their control device destroyed outright on death (section 150). No
GM or player-facing "reissue lost deed" command or ticketing flow
exists anywhere in the codebase.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) losing a stored vehicle/pet/ship deed is
essentially impossible in normal play -- the datapad slot itself is
the real protection mechanism, stronger than insurance. (2) the two
narrow paths where loss IS possible (rental speederbike expiry,
FACTIONPET death) are confirmed permanent with zero recovery option.
(3) a "lost deed insurance/reissue" feature would be entirely new
engine work -- there's no ticket queue or reclaim table to extend.

## 197. Structure/House Insurance Against Destruction -- Confirmed Absent (extends sections 35, 53, 125, 184)

**No insurance mechanic exists for structures at all -- deeds,
contents, or partial credit refund on destruction are all
unrecoverable through any documented path.** The entire item-insurance
subsystem (section 53) is hard-scoped to `isArmorObject() ||
isWearableObject()`, categorically excluding structure deeds/control
devices regardless of who's carrying them or where. Every destruction
path -- maintenance decay (section 184), city eviction, GCW base siege
(section 35), city hall dissolution -- funnels into one shared
`DestroyStructureTask` that unconditionally destroys the structure
from world and database with **no code that salvages, refunds, or
mails back cell contents** to the owner. The only recoverable outcome
at all is the player-*voluntary* redeed flow (section 125), which
returns the bare deed with leftover maintenance/power credited -- but
never contents, and only for structures flagged redeedable; this is a
deliberate demolition action, not insurance against involuntary loss.
GCW base destruction's "refund" message is confirmed to be a
base-placement-slot allowance credit, not a financial or item
refund -- easily mistaken for real insurance given the terminology.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) structure loss is always total and final
except for the narrow voluntary-redeed path -- there's no safety net
against maintenance-decay destruction or siege loss. (2) don't confuse
GCW base "refund" messaging with actual insurance -- it only restores
your base-placement allowance, not the base's value. (3) any future
structure-insurance feature would need entirely new logic layered onto
`DestroyStructureTask` -- no partial mechanism exists to build from.

## 198. Faction Vendor Exclusive Item Catalog by Rank (extends sections 100, 169, 175)

**The faction recruiter's vendor sells six item categories, but rank
gates purchases only indirectly -- through the standing-cap ceiling,
not an explicit rank check in the purchase code.** Weapons/armor,
uniforms, furniture, GCW installations (HQ deed tiers, turret/
minefield/covert-detector deeds -- section 117/136/137/138), NPC
hireling control devices (SpecForce/Stormtrooper pets), and one
Cries-of-Alderaan-gated schematic are all confirmed recruiter-
exclusive, with no loot/crafting/ordinary-vendor path found for any of
them. Purchase eligibility is gated purely on banked faction standing
exceeding item cost plus a 200-point floor -- since standing itself is
capped by rank (`getFactionPointsCap`, section 175), expensive items
become emergently unreachable at low rank without ever being coded as
rank-gated. Pricing multipliers come from GCW winner/loser status,
species racial penalty (confirming section 169's Imperial-alien
pricing finding), and Smuggler skill discount -- rank is never a
pricing multiplier. Vendor purchasing itself works identically under
both COVERT and OVERT status, unlike the bribe sub-feature (section
175), which is OVERT-exclusive.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "minimum rank to buy X" is a myth for
this vendor -- it's really "minimum standing," which correlates with
rank but isn't literally checked. (2) don't confuse vendor access
(available to COVERT and OVERT alike) with the bribe feature
(OVERT-only) -- easy to conflate given they're the same NPC
conversation. (3) HQ deeds, faction installations, and hireling pets
are genuinely recruiter-exclusive content with zero alternate
acquisition path.

## 199. Combat Target Selection/Cycling -- Client-Driven Selection, Server-Validated Execution (extends sections 10, 75, 79, 105)

**Target selection itself is essentially trusted client input with
minimal server validation, while target legality is enforced
separately and later, at attack-execution time.** The persisted
`CreatureObject::targetID` field (drives the UI target window/health
bar) is set directly from a raw client packet with only an
existence check -- no range, line-of-sight, or attackable validation
happens at selection time. Critically, actual attack commands carry
their own independently-parsed target ID per queued command, entirely
bypassing the persisted `targetID` -- so legality checks (line-of-
sight, range, attackable state, per sections 79/105) happen at attack
execution, not at target selection, and cycling your visible "current
target" doesn't retroactively affect already-queued attacks. NPC/AI
targeting is confirmed to use a completely different, server-
authoritative mechanism entirely -- `ThreatMap`-based highest-attacker
selection (section 75's aggro/threat system) -- with no shared code
path or "target manager" class between player and AI targeting. No
"auto-target nearest enemy" convenience logic exists for players
anywhere.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) target selection and target validation
are two separate systems at two separate times -- don't assume
selecting a target implies it's legal to attack. (2) the UI target
window and the actual attack-command target are distinct values that
can diverge -- useful when debugging "why did my attack go to a
different target than what's highlighted." (3) player and AI
targeting share zero code -- any targeting bugfix/feature needs to be
applied to both systems independently if it should affect both.

## 200. Factory Mass-Production Batch Size & Run Limits (extends sections 17, 42, 88)

**A hard, server-enforced cap of 1000 units exists per manufacture-
schematic run, immune to client packet manipulation.** Any requested
batch count is clamped server-side regardless of what the client
sends, and the schematic's own remaining-count field is a real,
persistent counter decremented once per unit produced -- reaching zero
destroys the schematic and auto-stops the factory. Production speed is
purely complexity-based (`complexity * 8` seconds per unit), with no
separate factory-tier speed stat -- since achievable complexity is
itself capped by the crafting tool/station used (section 88's ceiling
findings), per-unit speed is indirectly bounded by the same tool-tier
hierarchy already documented. Pausing a factory run is fully safe:
stopping and restarting resets only the on-screen session display
counter, while the actual schematic remaining-uses counter (the real
progress toward the cap) is untouched by stop/start cycles. No
factory-count limit per player/structure was found anywhere -- any
effective cap on simultaneous factories comes from the general
structure/lot placement system, not factory-specific code.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) 1000 is a hard, unbypassable ceiling per
run -- useful for any economic-balance modeling of maximum production
throughput. (2) complexity is the only lever affecting production
speed -- installation/factory tier is irrelevant, contrary to what
might be assumed. (3) pausing a factory is genuinely safe and
progress-preserving -- don't warn players against stopping a run
mid-way.

## 201. Structure Entrance/Access Fee (Toll) Mechanic (extends sections 122, 156, 161)

**A real, fully-wired player toll feature exists on `BuildingObject`,
gated by a specific crafting skill and restricted to public
structures only.** The owner sets a fee amount and a duration (15
minutes to 48 hours) via a two-step SUI flow, but only if they hold
`crafting_artisan_business_01` AND are on the structure's admin list
-- and only on structures that are NOT flagged private (section 156's
public/private boolean). A visitor without an unexpired paid-access
window is prompted to pay and ejected until they do; paying grants a
timed pass (not permanent, not per-visit within the window) tracked
in a runtime `paidAccessList`, with periodic sweeping to eject anyone
whose window lapses while still inside. Collection is fully automatic
-- the fee routes directly into the owner's bank via `addBankCredits()`
inside the payment handler itself, with no manual pickup step, plus a
small merchant-XP bonus per paid entry. A 10-minute cooldown gates how
often the owner can change the fee/duration.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) this is effectively a shop/merchant-house
toll feature, not a general anti-freeloader house lock -- it requires
a specific business skill and only works on public structures. (2)
payment buys a time-boxed pass, not permanent access -- visitors get
re-billed after the window expires even mid-visit. (3) fee collection
is synchronous and automatic straight into the owner's bank (section
161) -- no separate collection command or in-world credit drop exists.

## 202. Space Asteroid Mining -- Confirmed Absent (extends sections 15, 18, 26, 59, 92, 152)

**No space-zone resource harvesting mechanic exists at all.**
`AsteroidObject` is a pure collision/flight-obstacle class for ship
physics and targeting, structurally unrelated to the ground
`ResourceSpawn`/`ResourceContainer` hierarchy -- it implements exactly
one method and carries no resource-type, harvest, or extraction
fields whatsoever. All 68 asteroid Lua templates are static-geometry
content (section 92's static-world pipeline) with zero resource
metadata. No survey device, mining tool, or command targets asteroids
at all. The only "mining" content that exists is purely narrative/
combat-flavored -- a Tatooine/Dantooine story arc with themed NPC
guard ships and matching loot tables, representing combat risk around
a mining *theme*, not risk while performing an actual extraction
mechanic, since no such mechanic exists to put at risk.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) space resource gathering is a genuine,
clean gap with zero partial scaffolding -- building it would require
entirely new IDL classes, not an extension of the ground harvester
stack (section 15/59). (2) don't confuse the "mining" story content
(guard ships, themed loot) with an actual mining mechanic -- it's
flavor text and enemy naming only. (3) asteroids exist purely as flight
hazards/collision geometry in the space-combat system (section 26).

## 203. GM Player Confinement -- No True "Jail," But a Real Freeze/Mute Lock Exists (extends sections 13, 86, 96, 141, 183)

**A dedicated `/jail`-style command (teleport-to-cell + confinement)
is confirmed completely absent, but `/freezePlayer`/`/unfreezePlayer`
provides a genuinely different and arguably more useful lockdown
tool: movement-lock-without-relocation.** Freezing zeroes the target's
movement speed directly (independent of client input), mutes chat
(reusing section 86's mute mechanism), and sets a `FROZEN` creature
state that gates command execution through the same per-command
state-mask system documented in section 148 -- any command not
explicitly flagged frozen-safe is blocked outright, not just movement
commands. This is the functional opposite of the teleport tools from
section 183: freezing never relocates the target at all, while
`/teleportTo` relocates with zero behavioral enforcement -- the
codebase has one tool for each half of "jail" but never combines them.
Release requires an explicit `/unfreezePlayer` call clearing both a
1-hour buff timer AND a redundant raw state-bit set directly by the
freeze command -- making the lock practically indefinite until a GM
manually intervenes, not reliably self-expiring.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't look for a jail-cell command --
none exists; `/freezePlayer` is the real confinement tool and it
works in place, not via relocation. (2) freezing is a genuine,
engine-enforced lock (speed=0 + command-mask block + mute), not just
a cosmetic flag -- more restrictive than it might sound. (3) a true
"send to a jail cell and hold" feature would need to compose
`/freezePlayer` with a teleport, since neither alone provides both
relocation and lock.

## 204. Image Designer -- Self-Service and Profession-Service Share One Code Path (extends sections 32, 180)

**Any player holding `social_entertainer_novice` can fully self-
customize via `/imagedesign` -- there is no separate mirror/item
mechanism, and no second player is structurally required.**
Self-service is simply the degenerate case where designer and target
are the same character, running through the identical
`ImageDesignSession`/negotiation flow as servicing another player;
the only real differences are that cross-player service additionally
requires being in the same group, and payment (computed as `max
(requiredPayment, offeredPayment)`) nets to zero when payer and payee
are the same account. Skill-gating is confirmed binary per-attribute,
not a graduated quality scaler like droid recoloring's skill-based
palette range (section 180) -- each customization attribute either
fully unlocks (skill mod meets the IFF-defined threshold) or silently
no-ops entirely; there is no "better designer produces finer detail"
mechanic in the live code path, despite dead/commented-out code
suggesting a tiered skill-level system was once planned. Self-service
XP is confirmed halved relative to servicing another player.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) Image Designer doesn't actually require
finding another player -- any suitably-skilled character can self-
serve, contrary to what the "profession service" framing might
suggest. (2) skill gating is pass/fail per attribute, not graduated --
unlike droid dye's real skill-scaled range (section 180), there's no
partial-quality outcome here. (3) self-service intentionally earns
half XP, a real design lever discouraging pure self-service farming
without blocking it outright.

## 205. Weapon/Armor Condition Directly Reduces Combat Stats Before Reaching Zero (extends sections 93, 114, 145, 153)

**Contrary to a "no effect until broken" assumption, weapon damage and
attack speed are actively reduced by condition damage well before an
item becomes disabled.** The reduction curve is graduated: no penalty
below 75% wear, then linear scaling up to a 50% penalty cap at full
wear ("broken"). Damage output, attack speed (which gets *slower*, not
faster, as condition worsens), and every armor mitigation type
(kinetic/energy/blast/stun/etc., section 114) all use this identical
formula. Weapon accuracy stats are confirmed condition-independent --
only damage and speed are affected on the offensive side. Critically,
"broken"/disabled does NOT stop a weapon from attacking -- it simply
locks the penalty at the 50% cap and additionally zeroes the weapon's
armor-piercing value for that attack, correcting section 153's
"disabled" framing: a broken weapon keeps functioning at reduced
effectiveness, it doesn't go inert. Broken armor suffers an additional
penalty beyond the mitigation curve -- it loses its armor rating
entirely against piercing attacks and becomes flagged vulnerable to
all damage types.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) condition matters continuously, not just
at the zero-threshold -- weapon/armor maintenance has real, ongoing
combat impact starting well before an item is "broken." (2) a broken
weapon still swings, just capped at the worst-case 50% penalty and
stripped of armor-piercing -- don't model it as non-functional. (3)
broken armor is doubly punished: mitigation percentage AND full
armor-rating loss against piercing, plus universal vulnerability --
worth flagging as a meaningfully worse state than "just less
effective."

## 206. Harvester Hopper Capacity Mechanics (extends sections 15, 40, 59, 65, 82)

**Hopper capacity is a crafted, experimentation-rolled stat baked
permanently onto the deed at crafting time, not a fixed per-tier
constant or a later-upgradable value.** Different harvester deed
schematics define their own capacity experimentation ranges (e.g.
25,000-50,000 for one ore-harvester tier), so final capacity depends
on both deed tier and the crafter's own quality roll -- and once
placed, there is no in-game command or upgrade path that changes it
again. A full hopper is a hard extraction ceiling, not overflow --
production throttles to exactly the remaining space and then the
harvester auto-deactivates entirely, which as a side effect also
halts power draw (section 65) since power consumption is gated on
active state, not a direct capacity-to-power rule. No yield is ever
wasted; unattended-past-capacity time simply costs uptime, not
resources. Collection always requires physical presence within a
hardcoded 20-meter range plus either ownership or explicit `"HOPPER"`
structure-permission-list access (section 156's permission-list
infrastructure) -- there is no remote or offline collection mechanism
anywhere in the codebase.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) capacity planning happens entirely before
deployment -- there's no later upgrade lever, so choosing deed tier
and crafting quality matters more than any in-game adjustment. (2) a
full hopper costs uptime, not yield -- nothing is lost to overflow,
just production time until manually collected. (3) remote/offline
collection is a genuine gap -- any AFK-friendly harvesting feature
would need new client/server messaging since both collection paths
hardcode a 20m proximity check.

## 207. Bounty Hunter Target Tracking Mechanic (extends sections 20, 44, 101, 194)

**Tracking is implemented via physical droid items (seeker droid,
Arakyd orbital probe droid, bio-signature transmitter), not a datapad
UI feature, and is confirmed to have zero target-side detection or
countermeasures.** Mission-level gating gives access to FIND/probe
abilities at level 2, TRACK specifically at level 3+. Success chance,
search speed, and total re-track count all scale with dedicated
Bounty Hunter Investigation skill mods (`droid_find_chance/speed`,
`droid_track_chance/speed`, `droid_tracks`) offset against the
target's level, clamped 5-95%. Precision differs meaningfully by
method: the seeker droid reports direction and distance, while the
Arakyd probe only reveals the target's zone/planet -- a coarser
result. Tracking is confirmed pulse-based, not continuous real-time --
each successful use starts a periodic re-report loop (roughly 75-225+
seconds between pulses depending on skill) that exhausts after the
skill-determined `droid_tracks` count, at which point the trail is
lost and must be re-initiated. Since section 194 confirmed all player
bounty targets are exclusively Jedi, this tracking system in practice
only ever operates against Force-sensitive targets.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) there is no way for a tracked player to
know they're being hunted or take evasive action -- confirmed absent,
a meaningful one-sidedness worth knowing about bounty gameplay
balance. (2) higher-tier BH skill investment directly improves hit
chance, speed, AND total re-track budget simultaneously -- a
compounding investment payoff, not diminishing returns. (3) this
system is exclusively exercised against Jedi targets in practice
(section 194), even though the code itself doesn't hard-restrict
target type.

## 208. Multi-Component/Sub-Schematic Assembly Crafting (extends sections 20, 69, 89, 109)

**Crafting schematics genuinely distinguish raw resources from
crafted sub-components at the code level, and a sub-component's own
rolled quality measurably propagates into the parent item's final
stats.** `ResourceSlot` (raw resource) and `ComponentSlot` (crafted
item, matched by item-template inheritance, not schematic reference)
are separate classes with entirely separate handling code. When a
crafted component is consumed, the object is cloned with its
already-baked-in post-quality-roll attribute values intact, and those
values feed into the parent's stat calculation via one of five
combine modes (linear, percentage, bitset, override, or limited) --
so a higher-quality sub-component genuinely improves the assembled
item's stats, except under the one override mode where the parent
schematic's own value wins regardless. Nesting depth is confirmed
unlimited by design, not merely untested -- there is no recursive
resolution function at all, since each tier is a fully separate,
sequential player crafting session producing a concrete finished
item that the next tier references by template path. A concrete
3-level droid chassis-and-frame chain confirms this works in live
content today, not just in theory.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) sub-component quality is a real,
combinable input to final item stats -- crafting a superior sub-
assembly is a genuine strategy, not wasted effort, except under
override-mode slots. (2) there's no depth limit or recursion guard to
worry about -- arbitrarily deep crafting chains are safe by
construction. (3) distinguishing a resource slot from a component
slot in a new schematic is a one-field change (`ingredientSlotType`),
making multi-tier crafting chains straightforward to design.

## 209. Custom Chat Room / Channel System (extends sections 19, 45, 86, 151)

**A fully-implemented, player-createable custom chat room system
exists (`ChatRoom` class, type `CUSTOM`), distinct from and layered
alongside group/guild/tell chat.** Players are capped at 3 owned
rooms, 25-character names, and 5 levels of nested path depth; the
creator automatically becomes owner and moderator, with full
invite/kick/ban/promote-moderator tooling and a public/private +
moderated (speak-restricted) flag set. Built-in default rooms exist
too and are structurally identical `ChatRoom` instances -- a galaxy-
wide `Chat` room, `Auction`, one `Planet` room per zone, plus
`group`/`guild`/`system` rooms -- but these are recreated fresh at
every server boot rather than database-persisted, while custom rooms
survive restarts as real ODB objects (`chatrooms.db`). Persistence is
metadata-only in both cases, though -- actual chat messages in ANY
room type are never logged to disk, fire-and-forget just like group/
tell chat (section 151); only mail is durably stored. Room name
validation runs through the same `NameManager::isProfane()` path
documented in section 86, confirming that section's "chatroom names"
reference.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) custom chat rooms are real, complete
functionality, not a stub -- full moderation tooling exists if a
feature needs to expose it. (2) the 3-room-per-player cap and 5-level
nesting cap are hard, code-enforced limits worth knowing before
assuming unlimited room creation. (3) no chat message is ever
persisted regardless of room type -- don't expect message history/
logs to exist anywhere for auditing or moderation review.

## 210. Individual Jedi Force Power Mechanics (extends sections 67, 81, 112, 121)

**A substantial roster of individual Force power commands exists
(Choke, Knockdown tiers, Throw, Intimidate, Lightning, Weaken,
Feedback, Armor, Shield, Absorb, Protection, Speed/Run, cure/resist
variants, Meditate, Drain/Transfer/Channel Force), but two classic
SWG powers are confirmed completely absent: Force Sense and Force
Warning.** All offensive powers route through a shared
`ForcePowersQueueCommand` base that checks and debits the Force pool
per use, with per-power costs set individually in Lua (ranging from
28 to 400+ Force), and FRS rank (section 67) modifies cost via
`frsLight/DarkForceCostModifier` multipliers applied on top of the
`force_manipulation_light/dark` skill mod -- confirming and detailing
section 81's cost-modification finding. **There is no distinct
per-power cooldown system** -- pacing between Force power uses reuses
the exact same weapon-speed-style command-duration gate as melee
combat (haste-modified), not a bespoke Force cooldown timer. CC
application (knockdown, stun, intimidate) reuses the identical
`StateEffect` pipeline consumed by ordinary weapon attacks (section
112) -- Force Choke is the one outlier, implemented as a pure HAM
damage-over-time effect rather than a state effect. No dedicated
Force-power unlock "tree" exists in this repo -- skill-box-to-command
mapping lives in external client data, and FRS rank only modifies
cost/damage on top of whatever skill box already grants access.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "Push"/"Pull" map to `ForceKnockdown1-3`/
`ForceThrow1-2` in code, not literally named powers -- and there is no
TK/object-manipulation power at all. (2) Force Sense/Warning are
confirmed absent -- don't assume parity with live SWG's full power
roster. (3) Force power pacing is governed by the same haste-modified
speed gate as melee, not a unique cooldown mechanic -- useful when
reasoning about DPS/action-economy calculations involving Jedi.
