## 211. Item Stacking Mechanics -- Confirmed Special-Cased to Two Object Types Only (extends sections 15, 20, 42, 120)

**Ordinary tangible items (weapons, armor, clothing, food) do not
stack at all -- true stacking is confirmed limited to exactly two
object types: raw resources and pre-extraction crafted-item crates.**
`ResourceContainer` stacks via a single global cap
(`MAXSIZE = 100000`), with combine/split commands available, though
notably `combine()` performs no server-side check that two containers
actually hold the same resource spawn -- that safeguard currently
relies entirely on client-side drag-drop behavior, a real (if minor)
integrity gap worth flagging for anyone investigating dupe/exploit
vectors. `FactoryCrate` (section 200's manufacturing output) stacks
identical manufacturing-run copies up to a per-crate cap (default
100, schematic-derived), matched strictly by serial number -- meaning
only items from the exact same crafting run (identical rolled stats)
share a crate, not merely the same template. Critically, **extraction
from a crate permanently un-stacks a crafted item** -- once in
ordinary inventory, even byte-for-byte identical crafted items never
re-merge, because regular `TangibleObject` has no stacking logic
whatsoever.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't assume "same template" implies
stackable -- outside resources and unextracted crafted crates,
nothing merges, regardless of how identical two items appear. (2) the
missing resource-identity check in `combine()` is a genuine server-
side gap relying on client trust -- worth flagging alongside other
anti-exploit findings (section 39). (3) crafted items are only ever
stacked transiently, inside their origin crate -- inventory
management UX for crafted goods should never assume post-extraction
merging is possible.

## 212. Movement Speed-Hack Validation (extends sections 26, 28, 39, 99)

**Ground and mounted movement is genuinely validated against the
player's actual stat-derived speed, with violations silently
corrected rather than punished -- but space flight validation is
confirmed dramatically weaker.** Every position update is checked via
`checkPlayerSpeedTest()`, which correctly sources the "allowed" speed
from vehicle or mount stats when applicable (not just base character
speed), applies a 5-10% grace multiplier plus a 1-second minimum
check interval and a buff-transition grace window to avoid lag-
related false positives, and exempts privileged/GM accounts entirely.
On violation, the response is a silent server-side position snap-back
to the last validated location (invisible-to-the-cheater correction)
plus a log-only warning message -- **there is no automated kick, ban,
or escalation of any kind** tied to repeated violations; a human must
review logs to act on persistent offenders. Space flight movement, by
contrast, uses a dramatically looser tolerance -- 10x actual max ship
speed (or a 200-unit floor) before even triggering a silent resync,
with no logging at all -- making moderate space speed-hacking
functionally undetectable by comparison to ground movement.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) ground/mounted speed-hacking is
meaningfully checked and self-correcting, but generates no automatic
consequence beyond a log line -- any real anti-cheat enforcement
program would need to be built around log monitoring, not
server-side auto-action. (2) space flight is a genuine soft spot in
anti-cheat coverage -- 10x tolerance is far looser than ground's 5-10%
grace band. (3) the correction mechanism (silent snap-back) means
speed-hacking mostly just wastes the cheater's effort rather than
exposing an exploitable gap -- but it also means it's invisible unless
someone reads the error logs.

## 213. Vehicle/Pet/Ship Datapad Capacity Limits (extends sections 43, 132, 150, 196)

**Each control-device type has its own independent hard cap, all
config-driven from one Lua table, with wildly different default
values and only one type having any augmentation path at all.**
Default caps: 2 creature pets, 3 faction/hireling pets, 5 droids, 3
vehicles, 3 ships (with an additional sub-cap of exactly 1 player-
owned-building-interior ship regardless of total ship count, per
section 132). Only creature pets have an increase path -- a genuine
skill-mod bonus (`stored_pets`) gated behind the Creature Handler
novice skill box, explicitly excluded from being grantable by
wearables. Vehicles, droids, ships, and faction pets have zero
capacity-increase mechanism anywhere in the codebase -- no veteran
reward, crafted upgrade, or skill mod touches any of those four
caps. Hitting a cap produces a hard rejection with a system message
at both deed-claim time and control-device gift/trade time -- there
is no "replace an existing one" prompt; the player must manually
store or destroy something first and retry.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the vehicle cap (3) is tied for tightest
alongside creature pets (2), and unlike pets has no augmentation path
whatsoever -- a meaningful asymmetry worth knowing. (2) any "increase
garage capacity" feature has a ready-made template to copy: the
`stored_pets` skill-mod pattern, currently unique to creature pets.
(3) cap violations are hard rejections, never soft prompts -- any UX
wanting a "swap this old vehicle for the new one" flow would be new
work layered on top of the existing reject-only behavior.

## 214. NPC Vendor Restocking -- Confirmed Universally Infinite, No Exceptions Found (extends sections 108, 129)

**Section 129's "infinite stock, spawns fresh instance per purchase"
finding is confirmed to be a universal, exception-free rule across
every static NPC vendor and NPC-shop-adjacent mechanic in the
codebase** -- cantina bartenders, the faction recruiter reward shop
(section 100/198), and the junk dealer's sell-path (section 129) all
share this pattern with zero counter-examples found. No per-item or
per-vendor purchase cooldown exists anywhere -- the only timer/
timestamp pattern found near vendor NPCs is an unrelated 30-second
"rumor" chat-listening Easter egg on bartenders, easy to mistake for
a purchase throttle if skimming the same file. No genuinely finite/
depleting stock with a restock timer exists anywhere, and no dynamic
supply/demand pricing exists either -- all vendor prices are
hardcoded flat integers, identical for every purchase regardless of
prior sales volume.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) this closes out section 129's finding
with high confidence -- infinite stock is a codebase-wide design
constant, not a per-vendor quirk. (2) don't confuse the bartender's
rumor-listening timer with a purchase cooldown if reading
`bartenders.lua` -- they share the same timestamp-gating pattern but
serve unrelated purposes. (3) a genuinely limited-quantity quest
vendor would be entirely new content -- there's no existing
quantity-tracking scaffolding anywhere to extend.

## 215. Profession Change / Respec -- Confirmed Absent as a Discrete Mechanic, and Effectively Moot (extends sections 84, 92, 113)

**No player-facing "change profession" feature exists, and the reason
is structural: `starterProfession` is write-once at character
creation and is never consulted by the skill-grant gate afterward.**
`canLearnSkill()` has zero references to the starting-profession
field -- gating is limited entirely to prerequisites, species, Jedi
state, and the section 113 point budget. The only two respec-adjacent
tools in the codebase touch completely disjoint data: the tutorial-
only HAM stat-migration respec (section 84) never touches skills, and
the GM-only `ResetJediCommand` (staff `godOnly` skill required) only
strips Jedi skills without granting a new starting template -- neither
is a genuine profession swap, and no combined mechanic exists. Because
any character can freely train any non-Jedi, non-species-gated skill
box for points via ordinary surrender-and-retrain (section 113),
"profession" is effectively cosmetic/historical after character
creation -- making a dedicated respec feature functionally redundant
with a mechanic that already exists.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't build toward a "profession change"
command -- the underlying skill system already makes it unnecessary;
any character can walk from one tree to another via ordinary surrender/
retrain. (2) the tutorial HAM respec and GM Jedi-reset are the only
two respec tools that exist, and they don't compose into a real
profession swap. (3) a "respec helper" UI (bulk surrender + bulk
grant) would be new work with no existing single entry point to
build from, but the underlying capability (train anything, surrender
anything) is already fully present.

## 216. Guild/Faction Shared Crafting Station Access (extends sections 20, 41, 88, 111, 134, 156)

**Crafting stations perform zero access checks of their own --
station usability is gated entirely by the surrounding building's
ACL, one layer up, reusing the exact same `StructurePermissionList`
mechanism documented in section 156.** If a player can enter the
room, they can use any station inside; the station code itself only
checks proximity (7m) and station-type compatibility. This means a
guild CAN effectively share a private crafting station -- not via any
guild-hall-specific mechanism (section 111 already confirmed no such
distinct object type exists), but simply by the structure owner
adding the guild's object ID to the building's ENTRY or ADMIN list,
the same generic ACL pattern used for house access (section 156) --
guild role permissions (section 134's bitmask) never intersect
structure ACLs at all except through this indirect guild-ID-as-list-
entry path. The ingredient hopper radial is gated more strictly --
ADMIN list only, not the broader HOPPER list -- an inconsistency worth
flagging. **No faction-specific shared crafting station exists at
all** -- faction HQ buildings (section 115/136) have zero
crafting-station child objects; faction membership alone never grants
station access, only guild ID via the building ACL does. Station
access and the private-vs-public complexity ceiling (section 88) are
confirmed fully independent mechanisms -- one is a building-entry ACL
check, the other a static per-template integer, with no coupling
between them.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "shared guild crafting station" is
achievable today purely through ordinary house-ACL management --
no special guild-hall feature needs to exist or be built. (2) faction
membership grants nothing craft-related -- only guild ID via the
generic ACL mechanism does; don't assume faction HQs double as
shared workshops. (3) the ingredient hopper's stricter ADMIN-only
gate (vs. general station use's building-entry gate) is worth
double-checking if building a permission-editing UI around crafting
stations -- the two aren't consistently scoped.

## 217. Guild War Declaration & Resolution (extends sections 41, 73, 134)

**Guild war is a real, two-step opt-in mechanism that grants a
persistent, cost-free, timer-free mutual-PvP-consent flag between two
guilds' rosters, fully bypassing normal faction/Overt-Covert
attackability gating.** A `PERMISSION_WAR`-holding officer declares
war via a terminal SUI, moving the target guild to a one-sided
`WAR_OUT`/`WAR_IN` state; only when the target's own war-permission
officer reciprocates does it become `WAR_MUTUAL` -- the sole state
that actually opens PvP between members. Ending a war is a two-step
downgrade, not instant peace -- toggling from mutual reverts to a
one-sided declaration that either side must then separately cancel.
Once mutual, `isInWaringGuild()` is checked as an independent,
superseding branch in both the aggression and attackability pipelines
-- ahead of the same-faction and Overt/Covert gating -- meaning
warring guildmates can fight even if both are neutral, same-faction,
or never declared Overt. No cost, cooldown, or duration exists
anywhere in the code; it's a permanent flag until manually toggled
off. Critically, grouping still overrides guild war -- the same-group
early-return in `isAttackableBy()` runs before the guild-war check,
so warring guildmates who party together remain protected from each
other.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) guild war is a standing, mutual-consent
PvP flag between rosters, architecturally independent from GCW/Overt-
Covert (section 73) -- don't conflate the two attackability systems.
(2) ending a war takes two separate actions from two separate
officers, mirroring the two-step declaration -- there's no "instant
peace" button. (3) grouping is a universal PvP-suppression override
that applies even to warring guildmates, worth remembering when
reasoning about "why can't these two warring players fight."

## 218. Personal Inventory Slot Cap (extends sections 15, 106, 120)

**Personal inventory is capped at a hard 80-item slot count
(`containerVolumeLimit`), pure item-count arithmetic with zero
weight-based mechanic** -- confirming and extending section 106's
finding that encumbrance comes solely from equipped armor stats, never
from carried-item mass. A full inventory hard-rejects any add/loot/
craft/pickup attempt with a specific error message, checked
proactively before most gain-item actions (looting, crafting,
fishing, farming, factory-hopper collection, event perks all pre-
check `isContainerFullRecursive()` before even allowing the attempt)
-- nothing partially completes or silently drops. The base 80-slot
cap has zero increase path -- no skill, veteran reward, or item raises
it directly. The only capacity-expansion mechanism is equipping a
separate wearable backpack, itself an independently-capped 50-slot
container nested under the player, not a modification of the base
inventory's limit.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) inventory management is purely slot-
count-based -- there's no weight mechanic to reason about for carried
items, unlike some other games. (2) a backpack is the only capacity
lever in this codebase -- 80 base + 50 backpack = 130 effective slots
maximum, with no other multiplier anywhere. (3) full-inventory checks
happen proactively across many systems (not just on pickup) -- worth
remembering when debugging "why did this action fail silently," since
the failure is actually a pre-check rejection with a specific error
message.

## 219. GCW Base Siege Outcome -- Player Bases Destroyed, Static POI Bases Can Flip Faction (extends sections 35, 107, 113, 117)

**Siege outcome genuinely differs by base type -- player-placed
deed bases are destroyed outright with no capture, while a small,
fixed set of world-authored static POI bases DO support a real
faction-occupation flip.** For `PLAYERFACTIONBASE` (the type a player
actually deeds and defends), siege completion unconditionally
destroys the structure and refunds the *losing* owner's base-unit
placement allowance (section 117) -- the winning attacker gets nothing
but the base's removal from the GCW score pool (section 107) on the
next hourly recompute; there is no ownership-transfer field anywhere
on `BuildingObject` for this base type. For `STATICFACTIONBASE` --
a handful of named world POIs like Rori/Talus/Corellia encampments,
not player property -- siege completion instead calls a Lua
`flipBase()` handler that respawns the opposing faction's NPC garrison
and re-tags the building's faction, a genuine capture/occupation
mechanic. This fully confirms and refines section 113's "city-vs-city
GCW conquest absent" finding: it's specifically true for player
bases and cities, but not for this small set of static POIs. Siege
rewards for players are limited to per-hacking-stage slicing XP; no
loot or standing payout is wired to the final destruction event
itself.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't design around player-base capture
-- it's confirmed structurally absent; only destruction and a
placement-slot refund exist. (2) the static-POI faction-flip mechanic
is architecturally separate and tiny in scope (a handful of named
locations) -- don't generalize it to all GCW content. (3) siege
rewards are XP-only, paid incrementally during the hack, not a lump
sum on final base destruction.

## 220. Crafting Session Staging -- Single Continuous Session, Not a Classic Two-Stage Prototype/Create Flow (extends sections 20, 42, 69, 88, 109, 200, 208)

**Crafting in this codebase is architecturally a single continuous
session with one terminal action, not classic SWG's separable
"craft a prototype, decide later whether to finalize" two-command
flow.** `CraftingSessionImplementation` creates both a working
manufacture schematic and a placeholder prototype object shell up
front, then drives ingredient selection, initial assembly, and
experimentation (section 69's formula) all within one session ending
in exactly one of two terminal calls -- `createPrototype()` (single
item, real or "practice") or `createManufactureSchematic()` (factory-
ready blueprint, section 200). The real commit point for resources is
not the final creation call -- it's leaving the ingredient/resource
screen (`nextCraftingStage()`'s first call), which flags the
schematic `assembled`; canceling before that point fully returns
resources, canceling any time after does not. "Practice" mode
(`createItem=false`) is the closest analog to a disposable prototype
-- it still consumes resources (already locked at assembly) but
discards the finished item afterward in exchange for bonus XP, rather
than genuinely letting a player preview before committing resources.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any crafting-assistant tooling should
treat "leaving the ingredient screen" as the actual resource point-of-
no-return, not the final create-item click -- a meaningfully earlier
commit point than the classic-SWG mental model suggests. (2) practice
mode isn't a true no-cost preview -- resources are already spent by
the time it's selectable. (3) single-item crafting and factory-
schematic crafting share one identical session up until the very last
action -- there's no separate "decide to mass-produce" staging step
either.

## 221. Bounty Mission Cancellation & Auto-Expiration (extends sections 16, 44, 101, 194, 207)

**Bounty mission abandonment uses the fully generic mission-abort
pipeline shared with every other mission type (section 16), with
exactly one bounty-specific gate and one bounty-specific consequence.**
Aborting is blocked outright if the hunter recently fought the target
(`hasBhTef()`) -- "cannot abort this soon after combat." Voluntary
cancellation and involuntary mission-timer expiration (bounty missions
have their own configurable expiration timer, distinct from the
generic 48-hour mission duration) converge on the identical cleanup
path and carry the identical consequence: a default 24-hour, per-
target re-accept cooldown recorded on the specific bounty -- but this
penalty applies **only to player-target bounties** (confirming and
narrowing section 194's Jedi-only-target finding); NPC-target bounty
abandonment has no cooldown consequence at all, since the underlying
tracking record never applies to NPC target IDs. Critically,
abandoning or failing a bounty never ends it for other hunters -- only
the abandoning hunter's own claim is removed from the target's
hunter-ID list; the bounty itself stays live and hunt-able by anyone
else (or by the same hunter again after the cooldown lapses).

**Practical takeaways:** (1) there's no reputation/faction-standing
penalty for quitting a bounty -- the only cost is a per-target
re-accept cooldown, and only for player targets. (2) one hunter
abandoning never denies the bounty to others -- it stays open, so
"camping" a bounty by repeatedly accepting-and-abandoning to block
other hunters doesn't work. (3) voluntary cancellation and timeout
expiration are functionally identical in consequence -- there's no
advantage to manually aborting versus simply letting a bounty time
out.

## 222. Weapon-Category Special-Attack Catalog (extends sections 6, 11, 36, 39, 63, 79, 135)

**A large roster of weapon-category-specific special attacks exists
(melee 1h/2h, polearm, unarmed, pistol, rifle, carbine, heavy weapon,
thrown, plus separate lightsaber-specific variants), but differentiation
is entirely Lua data on top of structurally identical C++ command
shells -- not distinct combat-resolution code per category.** Category
gating happens via a runtime weapon-bitmask AND check inside the
shared `CombatQueueCommand::doCombatAction()`, comparing each
command's Lua-configured `weaponType` against the equipped weapon's
own type bitmask -- `ThrowGrenadeCommand` is a notable exception,
defaulting to `ANYWEAPON` and therefore usable regardless of currently
-equipped weapon. Three genuinely independent gates control whether a
player can use a given special: skill training (does a trained skill
box list the command), weapon-type match (bitmask check at cast
time), and certification (section 11/36, damage-only -- lacking
certification never blocks the command from firing, it only caps
damage and suppresses weapon DoTs). Contrary to section 79's
theoretical "stacked independent cooldown gates" framing, in practice
**no per-command cooldown exists on the standard weapon-category
special-attack roster at all** -- cooldown fields are set only on
GM/admin commands in the sampled Lua files; ordinary specials are
paced purely by the shared weapon-speed queue delay. Category-unique
mechanics do exist beyond called shots (section 135): pistol
`BleedingShotCommand` applies a genuine bleed DoT, and heavy-weapon-
exclusive cone attacks (acid/lightning/flame) provide true AoE not
found in any other category.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) adding a new weapon-category special is
a thin C++ shell plus a Lua data file -- no combat-resolution changes
needed, confirming this is a highly extensible pattern. (2) don't
assume every special attack has an independent cooldown distinct from
weapon speed -- verify per-command; the vanilla roster doesn't use
this theoretically-supported mechanism. (3) skill training, weapon-
type match, and certification are three separately-timed, separately
-enforced gates -- a "I have the skill but can't use it" bug report
needs triage against all three independently.

## 223. Movement Speed-Boost Consumables (extends sections 51, 76, 190, 210, 212)

**A genuine crafted-consumable movement-speed buff exists -- two
Chef-crafted food items wire directly into the Scout "Burst Run"
ability, bypassing its normal skill gate entirely.** Eating either
item triggers the identical function the real Burst Run command
calls, applying a substantial (~82%) speed and acceleration multiplier
for 30 seconds at a food-quality-scaled HAM cost and cooldown --
meaning any player, not just Scouts, can access this speed boost via
crafted food, a genuinely surprising cross-profession interaction.
This is Chef-crafted (food), not a Doctor stim -- confirming HAM-pool
stims (section 51/190) are scoped only to the standard nine HAM
attributes and never touch movement speed. It explicitly cannot
combine with Jedi Force Speed (section 210), mount/vehicle riding, or
other exclusive-movement buffs -- these are hard-blocked at activation
or mount time via named-buff exclusion checks, not merely diminishing
-returns-stacked. No numeric engine-enforced speed ceiling exists
anywhere -- safety relies entirely on these mutual-exclusion checks
plus the speed-hack validator (section 212), which recomputes rather
than caps the allowed threshold.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) movement speed buffs live in the food/
Chef system, not the medical stim system -- an easy category mistake
when reasoning about consumable buffs. (2) burst-run-via-food
democratizes a Scout-exclusive ability to any profession -- worth
knowing for balance discussions. (3) there's no hard speed cap in the
engine -- any new speed-granting content must implement its own
mutual-exclusion logic rather than relying on an existing ceiling.

## 224. Harvester Tier Upgrade -- Confirmed Absent, Extends to All Installation Stats and Subtypes (extends sections 82, 104, 125, 200, 206)

**No in-place upgrade mechanic exists for a placed harvester, and
this absence generalizes to every harvester stat and every
installation subtype (factories, generators), not just hopper
capacity (section 206).** Extraction rate, hopper size, and power
draw are all baked in exactly once -- at deed-crafting time via
experimentation, then copied to the live installation once at
placement -- with zero setter, command, or component anywhere that
touches them again afterward. Redeed-and-replace (section 125) is
genuinely the only route to a better harvester on the same spot, and
it comes with a harsh precondition: destruction is explicitly blocked
while the hopper holds resources, and the only way to clear it is a
discard command that destroys the contents outright rather than
banking or transferring them -- meaning upgrading a harvester requires
sacrificing whatever unharvested resources remain inside first. This
pattern is confirmed uniform across all three installation subtypes
(harvester, factory, generator) -- identical "empty/deactivate then
redeed" gating, no exceptions found.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) upgrading requires total loss of hopper
contents before redeed is even possible -- factor this into any
player-facing guidance about harvester management. (2) this is a
codebase-wide installation design pattern, not harvester-specific --
factories and generators behave identically. (3) any future in-place
upgrade feature would need genuinely new setter/command
infrastructure across all three installation types -- there's no
partial mechanism anywhere to extend.

## 225. Group Leadership Auto-Transfer on Leader Departure (extends sections 47, 71, 189)

**Group leadership is not a stored attribute -- it's derived live as
`groupMembers[0]`, so removing the current leader implicitly promotes
whoever is next in the internal member-list order, with zero explicit
election logic.** `GroupObjectImplementation::getLeader()`
(GroupObject.idl:146-154) simply returns
`groupMembers.getSafe(0)`. When the leader leaves,
`GroupObjectImplementation::removeMember()`
(GroupObjectImplementation.cpp:182-261) removes that entry from the
`DeltaVector`-backed `groupMembers` list, which shifts subsequent
members down -- whoever was at index 1 becomes the new leader purely
as a side effect of the shift, not through any seniority, random, or
scoring logic. This is architecturally distinct from the explicit
`/makeleader` command path (`makeLeader()`,
GroupObjectImplementation.cpp:319-387), which deliberately swaps a
target into index 0 and broadcasts a `"group:new_leader"` system
message to the group -- the implicit departure-triggered transfer
sends **no such notification**; members simply discover the new
leader live. If the leader's departure drops the group below 2
members, `GroupManager::leaveGroup()`/`kickFromGroup()`
(GroupManager.cpp:379-433, 480-556) disbands the group outright
(calling `disband()`, GroupObjectImplementation.cpp:389-431) instead
of leaving a 1-person "leader." Critically, voluntary `/leavegroup`
and forced logout/linkdead-timeout departure use the **identical**
code path -- both funnel through `GroupManager::leaveGroup()`
(LeaveGroupCommand.h:34 and PlayerObjectImplementation.cpp:455-459
respectively) -- so there is no special-cased behavior for a
disconnecting leader. The linkdead grace period documented in section
189 only delays *when* the removal fires relative to disconnect; once
it fires, the leadership shift is synchronous and immediate, with no
separate grace period for reassigning leadership itself. A leader who
reconnects after LD-triggered removal simply rejoins as a regular
member, not as leader.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any group-leadership feature work should
treat "leader" as a derived property of list position, not a settable
field -- there's no `leaderId` to hook. (2) implicit transfers (via
departure) are silent; only the explicit `/makeleader` command
notifies the group, which could surprise players expecting a
handoff message. (3) a leader's disconnect and voluntary leave behave
identically, so testing one covers the other.

## 226. Guild Sponsorship/Recruitment Flow Deep Dive (extends sections 41, 134)

**Guild recruitment is a mandatory two-officer-role, two-step
sponsor-then-accept handshake with no player-initiated "apply to
join" path and no direct-invite alternative.** A member holding
`PERMISSION_SPONSOR` targets a nearby (within 32m), unguilded,
online player via `sponsorPlayer()`
(GuildManagerImplementation.cpp:1428-1492), which sends the target a
confirmation SUI box; acceptance
(`acceptSponsorshipRequest()`, :1494-1535) adds them to a distinct
`sponsoredPlayers` pool (`SortedVector<uint64>`, GuildObject.idl:31,
161) -- **not** `guildMembers` -- and cancels any pending sponsorship
from another guild, since a player can only be sponsored by one guild
at a time. A second officer holding `PERMISSION_ACCEPT` must then
finalize via `acceptSponsoredPlayer()` (:1608-1671), which calls
`guild->addMember()`. Grepping the guild sources for "invite" returns
zero matches -- sponsorship is the *only* recruitment mechanic,
deliberately splitting "who can bring in candidates" from "who can
finalize membership." New members always start at
`PERMISSION_NONE` (`GuildMemberInfo::GuildMemberInfo()`,
GuildMemberInfo.cpp:11-16) regardless of entry path -- there is no
probation flag, timer, or auto-assigned starter title; rank/title is
set manually by an officer afterward. Guild capacity checks count
`getTotalMembers() + getSponsoredPlayerCount()` together
(:1441-1444), so a guild can hit its member cap purely from unresolved
pending sponsorships. No re-join cooldown exists after leaving a
guild: `leaveGuild()` (:2085-2132) writes no timestamp/lockout field,
so a departed player can be re-sponsored into a different guild
immediately.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) sponsorship and acceptance can be held
by different officers, letting a guild delegate recruiting without
granting full admission authority. (2) the `sponsoredPlayers` vs
`guildMembers` split means capacity planning must account for
pending sponsorships, not just actual headcount. (3) there's no
cooldown or probation to build around -- a player can leave one guild
and be fully sponsored+accepted into another within moments.

## 227. Faction Initial Join Process -- Becoming COVERT for the First Time (extends sections 73, 100, 178)

**Joining a GCW faction is conversation-only via a Faction Recruiter
NPC, always starts a player at COVERT status (never OVERT or
ONLEAVE), and gates entry purely on accumulated faction standing (≥200),
with no level/skill/quest requirement.** There is no slash command or
standalone quest object to join -- the entire flow lives in
`recruiterConvoHandler.lua`/`rebel_recruiter_conv.lua` Lua
screenplays, with two parallel variants selected by
`ConfigManager::useCovertOvertSystem()` (default `false`): a legacy
path (`greet_neutral_start` -> `join_military` -> `accept_join`) and a
covert/overt-system path (`greet_neutral_start2` -> `join_military2`
-> `accept_join2`). Both ultimately call `setFaction(...)` +
`setFactionStatus(1)` -- and `FactionStatus::COVERT == 1`
(FactionStatus.h:13-15) -- so **every new recruit joins COVERT**,
confirmed at recruiterConvoHandler.lua:35-37 and :125-146. There is no
option to declare OVERT at the moment of joining; that requires the
separate `/declareovert` command afterward (DeclareOvertCommand.h:16-74,
covered in section 178), which itself requires standing within 50m of
a friendly GCW base HQ. The only join prerequisite is
`recruiterScreenplay.minimumFactionStanding = 200`
(recruiterScreenplay.lua:8), checked both client-side (offering the
join option) and server-side at `accept_join2`
(recruiterConvoHandler.lua:129-139) to prevent bypass -- standing is
earned pre-join by turning in GCW theme-park items to a recruiter
(e.g. FactionRecruiterContainerComponent.cpp:83-121 awards +500 on a
disk hand-in). No character level, profession, or quest chain gates
entry. Faction is a single mutable scalar field
(`creature->getFaction()`), so membership is always exclusive --
a player can never sit in both factions' pools simultaneously, and
switching sides requires resigning first (section 178) before a new
join can occur.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "joining" and "going overt" are two
fully separate steps/commands, gated by different preconditions (200
standing vs. proximity to a friendly HQ) -- don't conflate them. (2)
the join gate is a pure standing threshold with no level/skill/quest
requirement, so a fresh level-1 character can theoretically join as
soon as they accumulate 200 standing points. (3) both the legacy and
covert/overt configs converge on the same COVERT starting status,
so this behavior is config-independent.

## 228. City Mayor Election Voting Mechanics Deep Dive (extends sections 54, 77)

**Mayoral elections are simple-plurality with an incumbent tiebreak
and incumbent-default-on-no-challengers -- a city can never lose its
mayor purely from voter apathy or an uncontested race.** Voting is
gated only on `city->isCitizen()`
(CityManagerImplementation.cpp:2135-2138, 2181-2184) with **no
minimum citizenship duration** tracked anywhere -- any current citizen
may vote, and may change their vote at any time (votes simply
overwrite the prior entry in `mayoralVotes`, CityRegion.idl:681-693).
Candidacy is self-nomination only (`registerForMayoralRace()`,
:2207-2264) -- no petition/signature system -- gated on citizenship,
not already being a candidate, not already mayor of a *different*
city, the `social_politician_novice` skill, and a 24-hour
re-registration cooldown; registration freezes entirely once
`city->isVotingLocked()` is true. Election timing is Lua-tunable
(`city_manager.lua:57-64`): a ~21-day term
(`CityVotingCycles = 3` x `CityUpdateInterval` = 7 days), with the
ballot locking for the final ~7-day cycle
(`CityVotingCyclesUntilLocked = 2`). Tabulation
(`updateCityVoting()`, CityManagerImplementation.cpp:1118-1255) is
pure plurality: highest vote count wins, **ties break in favor of the
incumbent** (line 1167), and each valid candidate earns 300 political
XP per vote received regardless of outcome. `topCandidate` is
pre-seeded to the current mayor's ID before the vote loop runs
(line 1125), so an empty candidate list or zero votes cast leaves the
incumbent in place automatically -- there is no code path that leaves
a city mayor-less. On an actual change of mayor, civic structures and
the city-specialization cooldown transfer to the winner
(lines 1186-1207).

**Practical takeaways:** (1) there's no anti-fraud citizenship-age
check on voting eligibility -- a player who joins a city moments
before an election can vote immediately. (2) the incumbent has a
structural advantage twice over: tiebreak priority and automatic
retention when unopposed. (3) all timing constants live in
`city_manager.lua`, so election cadence is tunable without touching
C++.

## 229. Pet Growth Stage (growthStage) Progression Mechanics (extends sections 52, 150, 154)

**Pet growth is real-time-gated (12 hours per stage, 108 hours total
to full maturity) but evaluated lazily on pet-call rather than via a
background tick, and growth genuinely scales combat power, not just
appearance.** `PetControlDeviceImplementation::growPet()`
(PetControlDeviceImplementation.cpp:625-711) computes elapsed stages
from real-clock delta since `lastGrowth`
(`timeDelta / 43200` seconds = 12h/stage), but is only invoked
opportunistically -- on `callObject()` (pet summon, :194), first spawn
from a crafted deed (PetDeedImplementation.cpp:581), bio-engineer "fix
stats" SUI callbacks, or admin/GM override
(`TameCreatureTask.h:164`, forces instant stage 10). A pet left in
storage past maturity simply "catches up" fully the next time it's
summoned. `growthStage` starts at 1 and clamps at 10 (fully grown,
:629, 658-659). Crucially, growth is **not cosmetic-only**: inside
`growPet()`, `newLevel = (adultLevel/10.0) * newStage` feeds
`CreatureImplementation::setPetLevel()`
(CreatureImplementation.cpp:443-504), which rescales weapon
min/max damage and all 9 HAM pools in lockstep with height/size
(:665, :699-701) -- an immature pet is measurably weaker in combat,
not just smaller. Growth interacts with mount-training: if further
growth would push the pet out of `CANBEMOUNTTRAINED` eligibility and
it's already trained as a mount, growth auto-arrests
(`arrestGrowth()`, :713-764) or the owner is prompted via a
`MOUNT_GROWTH_ARREST` SUI box to lock growth early. No feeding/care
command or XP-like player interaction drives growth -- it is purely
elapsed real time. The separate `isBaby()` flag (governing wild
NPC baby-creature taming difficulty, distinct from `growthStage`) is
explicitly cleared at tame/deed-spawn time and should not be
conflated with growth progression.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) growth catches up lazily on next summon,
so there's no background job to account for when reasoning about pet
state. (2) growth stage is a genuine combat-power lever (level, HAM,
weapon damage all scale with it), useful context for any
pet-balance work. (3) players who want a permanently mount-eligible
pet must deliberately arrest growth early via the SUI prompt before
it outgrows the mount-size window.

## 230. Camp/Tent Passive Healing Formula & Duration Deep Dive (extends sections 27, 36, 51, 54, 72, 76)

**A deployed camp does not push heal packets -- it grants a
`STRUCTURE`-sourced skill mod that feeds into the same universal
2-second player regen tick used everywhere else, and mind-wound
healing is effectively broken (wrong skill-mod name wired in every
camp template).** On `notifyEnter()`
(CampSiteActiveAreaImplementation.cpp:65-108), the camp calls
`addTemplateSkillMods(player)`, applying per-tier values from its
`.lua` template (e.g. `scout_camp_s0.lua` vs. `s5.lua`):
`private_medical_rating` 60->100, `private_med_wound_health` 20->100,
`private_med_wound_action` 20->100. These mods are consumed by
`CreatureObjectImplementation::activatePassiveWoundRegeneration()`
(CreatureObjectImplementation.cpp:3235-3274), which every 2-second
`PlayerRecoveryEvent` tick accumulates
`healthWoundHeal += mod * 0.2` and fires `healWound()` on HEALTH +
STRENGTH + CONSTITUTION together once the accumulator hits 100
(mirrored for ACTION/QUICKNESS/STAMINA via
`private_med_wound_action`). **No camp template grants
`private_med_wound_mind`** -- all camps instead grant an unrelated
`private_buff_mind` mod -- so despite `CampStructureTemplate` parsing
a `mindWoundRegenRate` field, camps provide **zero** passive
mind-wound healing in practice, a genuine bug/gap. This is wound
healing (raises the HAM ceiling), not raw HAM-damage regen, which is
unaffected by any camp mod. Benefit radius is 12-20m depending on
tier, stripped instantly on leaving the `ActiveArea`. It stacks freely
with doctor wound-pack heals (section 51) and entertainer/food buffs
(section 72, 76) since those use separate direct `healWound()` calls
on the same finite pool -- and a camp's `private_medical_rating`
conveniently satisfies the non-CITY location gate `HealWoundCommand`
requires, making camps a natural doctor+passive-heal combo spot.
Camps are fully exempt from the section 54 maintenance/power/decay
pipeline (`baseMaintenanceRate = 0`); instead two hardcoded timers
govern lifespan -- a 55-minute despawn
(`CampSiteActiveArea::DESPAWNTIME`) and a 1-minute owner-absence
abandon timer that any combat event triggers immediately and
synchronously (`notifyCombatEvent()`, :152-166) -- so engaging in
combat instantly abandons your own camp.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) camp healing is entirely reusable skill-mod
plumbing (grant a `private_med_wound_*`-named `STRUCTURE` mod on
enter/exit), not a bespoke tick loop -- follow this pattern for any
new deployable-heal feature. (2) mind-wound healing from camps is
broken in the live codebase (wrong mod name) -- worth flagging if
full-HAM camp healing is an assumed baseline feature. (3) combat
instantly abandons a camp via the owner-absence path, which is a
sharp, easy-to-miss edge case for anyone testing camp durability in a
fight.

## 231. Power Generator Installation Mechanics Deep Dive (extends sections 41, 65, 82, 206, 224)

**Generators (solar, fusion, wind, photo_bio) reuse the harvester
extraction/hopper machinery wholesale to produce an "energy" resource
commodity, but are architecturally decoupled from other structures'
power reserves -- there is no shared city/lot power grid, and solar
output is not affected by weather or time of day.** All four
generator deed types (`generator_{solar,fusion,wind,photo_bio}_deed.lua`)
extend `GeneratorObject` (GeneratorObject.idl:10), itself an
`InstallationObject`, and use the identical
`extractionRate * spawnDensity` per-tick harvest formula
(InstallationObjectImplementation.cpp:392, 733-740) that ore
harvesters use, accumulating into their own `resourceHopper`.
`StructureManager.cpp:1033` explicitly excludes generators
(`!structure->isGeneratorObject()`) from the surplus-power logic
harvesters/factories use for *consuming* power -- generators only
*produce*. A player must manually collect the harvested energy
resource and deposit it into a specific target structure via
`InsertPowerSuiCallback::run()`
(InsertPowerSuiCallback.h:23-69), which calls
`installation->addPower(energy)` on that one structure -- there is no
automatic grid; each harvester/factory maintains its own independent
power reserve requiring individual manual refueling. Extraction rate
depends only on a static Simplex-noise-style `SpawnDensityMap` lookup
(ResourceSpawnImplementation.cpp:191-201) with no time-of-day or
weather input -- consistent with section 60's finding that weather is
referenced in only three files codebase-wide, none touching resource
spawning -- so solar generators genuinely produce the same output
"at night" as during the day. Like harvesters, extraction rate and
hopper size are one-time experimentation-rolled stats baked in at
deed-crafting time (e.g. solar `extractrate` 6-15,
generator_solar_deed.lua:55-57) with zero runtime upgrade path,
extending section 224's "no in-place upgrade, ever" finding to
generators explicitly.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't design around a "power grid" --
every structure's power reserve is independently, manually fed via
SUI deposit from a player carrying harvested energy. (2) solar
generators are solar in name/flavor only -- there's no
weather/day-night hook to exploit or account for. (3) generator
extraction rate/hopper size follow the exact same immutable-after-crafting
pattern as harvesters (section 224) -- redeed-and-replace is the only
upgrade path.

## 232. Weapon/Armor Repair Resource Cost -- Confirmed Zero Beyond Tool Charge (extends section 153)

**Repairing a weapon or armor piece via RepairTool costs exactly one
of the tool's 5 built-in charges and nothing else -- no crafting
resources, no credits, confirming and closing out section 153's
description as complete.** The entire flow lives in
`TangibleObjectImplementation::repair()`
(TangibleObjectImplementation.cpp:1334-1444): validate item/tool,
compute `repairChance` from a luck roll + skill/skillmod bonus + tool
quality + station bonus − shock wounds − complexity, call
`repairAttempt(repairChance)`, then
`repairTool->decreaseUseCount(1, true)` (line 1441) -- that's the only
consumption call in the function. `decreaseUseCount()`
(:949-959) only decrements the tool's own `useCount` and destroys the
tool object at 0 -- it is the tool's own charge pool being spent, not
a separate resource stack. The condition-restore logic in
`WeaponObjectImplementation::repairAttempt()`
(WeaponObjectImplementation.cpp:712-734) and
`WearableObjectImplementation::repairAttempt()`
(WearableObjectImplementation.cpp:231-253) only call
`setMaxCondition()`/`setConditionDamage()` -- neither touches
resources, inventory, or credits. The nearby-crafting-station check
(`getNearbyCraftingStation()`, line 1420-1422) is the *only* station
interaction in the whole path -- a pure proximity check adding +15 to
the roll, never triggering resource withdrawal or any station-side
effect, and it is optional, not required, to repair. No
`subtractCredits`/bank-credit call exists anywhere in the repair path
or in `RepairToolSuiCallback::run()` (RepairToolSuiCallback.h:20-48).

**Practical takeaways:** (1) repair is exactly "spend 1 tool charge,
roll dice" -- confirmed with zero hidden resource-consumption step,
closing the open question from section 153. (2) the crafting-station
proximity bonus (+15) is purely a success-roll modifier, not a
resource or cost gate -- repair works fine without a station nearby.
(3) repair outcome quality (fail/imperfect/slight/perfect, 65-95% of
max condition) is a pure function of the roll and never varies
resource cost, since there is none.

## 233. Force Rank System (FRS) Light/Dark Council Mechanics -- Real, Faction-Locked, and Mechanically Significant (extends sections 43, 58, 67, 194, 210)

**"Dark Jedi" and "Light Jedi" are not player-chosen roleplay labels
-- they are a real, persistently tracked backend mechanic (the Force
Rank System, distinct from the FRS *arena* already covered in
sections 43/67) with a discrete Light-vs-Dark council choice tied
1:1 to GCW faction, exclusive skills, exclusive cloning facilities,
and PvP rank-progress rules.** `PlayerObject.idl:115` declares
`protected int jediState;` (0 = non-Jedi, 4 = "Light FRS", 8 = "Dark
FRS"), and a separate `FrsData` struct
(`objects/player/variables/FrsData.h:12-75`, held on the player via
`PlayerObject.idl:131`) persists `councilType` (1=Light, 2=Dark,
`FrsManager.idl:29-30`) and a 0-11 `rank`. Council membership is
granted as real skills (`force_rank_light_novice` /
`force_rank_dark_novice`, `FrsManagerImplementation.cpp:447-521`) and
is **hard-gated by GCW faction**: Light requires
`Factions::FACTIONREBEL`, Dark requires `FACTIONIMPERIAL`
(:488-490) -- so alignment cannot be chosen independently of faction,
unlike a free-form morality slider. Rank advances via a vote/
challenge/arena-PvP system (`VoteStatusTask.h:31-61`,
`FrsManagerImplementation.cpp:1082-1091`) with an explicit
same-council exclusion: "No credit if [attacker and victim] are in
the same council" (:1083-1090) -- only killing the *opposite*
alignment's Jedi progresses rank.

**Confirmed mechanical effects, not merely cosmetic:** (1) Force
regen skill mods differ by side -- Light uses
`force_control_light`/`force_manipulation_light`, Dark uses
`force_power_dark`/`force_manipulation_dark`
(`PlayerObjectImplementation.cpp:2510-2520`, :3752-3757). (2)
Exclusive cloning facilities: `LIGHT_JEDI_ONLY`/`DARK_JEDI_ONLY`
cloner types check the respective council-novice skill
(`PlayerManagerImplementation.cpp:1700-1701`,
`MapLocationEntry.cpp:148-150`). (3) GCW contraband scanning has
dedicated dark-Jedi detection logic
(`ContrabandScanSessionImplementation::isDarkJedi()`, :411-413; scan
dialogue branches on novice/light/dark state at :703-704, 723). (4)
Server-verified title/rank display via `ShowCouncilRankCommand.h`,
`EnclaveCouncilRankSuiCallback.h`, and a GM override command
(`GmJediStateCommand.h`) -- not player-typed text. This system
remains entirely separate from section 194's bounty-hunter target
selection, which targets any Jedi regardless of council/alignment.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) treat FRS council alignment as a real,
faction-locked backend field (`jediState`/`FrsData.councilType`), not
a cosmetic title -- any "Dark Jedi" content should hook these fields
directly. (2) alignment is binary and faction-derived, not an
accumulated morality score -- a player cannot be "partially dark."
(3) same-council PvP kills grant zero FRS rank credit, a deliberate
anti-farming rule worth knowing before designing any rank-based
reward.

## 234. Player-Run Tournament/Event Support -- Confirmed Absent as a Discrete System, Built on Unused PVPAREA Primitive (extends sections 32, 43, 67, 164, 185, 196, 217)

**No bracket/tournament/multi-match event system, spectator mode, or
event-running admin commands exist anywhere in the codebase -- all
PvP structure is limited to 1v1 duels, guild wars, and the FRS
arena.** A repo-wide search for tournament/bracket/multi-match classes
returns nothing but unrelated string hits (e.g. quest item names).
There is no `TournamentManager`, no round/seeding/winner-tracking
object, and no ODB table for anything beyond pairwise state.
"Spectator" returns zero genuine hits -- no code path distinguishes
participant from observer damage/collision, so there is no
built-in safe-observation mechanic. No GM/admin commands exist for
teleport-all-to-arena, forced dueling, or prize distribution.

**However, the engine does have the raw primitive an open-invite
arena would need, and it mirrors the already-documented
`NOCOMBATAREA` flag's unused status (sections 164/185): `ActiveArea`
defines `PVPAREA = 0x001000`
(ActiveArea.idl:44, getters/setters :210-212, Lua hooks in
`LuaActiveArea.h:43-44`/`LuaActiveArea.cpp:153-162`).
`PlayerObjectImplementation::isInPvpArea()` (:3765-3786) checks it,
and `CreatureObjectImplementation.cpp:3776` permits combat between
two players **regardless of faction/overt status** when both stand
in a `PVPAREA` -- the direct inverse of the no-combat flag, i.e. a
real "forced PvP, ignore faction gating" primitive. Like
`NOCOMBATAREA`, `setPvpArea` is never called from any shipped `.lua`
world content (`grep -r setPvpArea bin/` returns nothing) -- it is
dead/unused infrastructure, present only as an engine hook a server
team would have to wire up themselves.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) building tournament support means
writing new code from scratch: a match/bracket manager, a
`TournamentArea` built on the existing unused `PVPAREA` flag for the
fighting pit, a separate no-damage `ActiveArea` for spectators, and
new signup/seeding/payout commands. (2) `PVPAREA` is the natural
foundation for the fighting pit specifically because it already
overrides faction-based combat gating at the C++ level -- no combat
manager changes needed, only Lua wiring. (3) today, player-run
tournaments rely entirely on the vanilla `/duel` command plus
external, out-of-game bracket tracking and honor-system spectating.

## 235. Cybernetic Limbs/Prosthetic Augmentations -- Confirmed Not Implemented as a Gameplay Mechanic (extends sections 61, 93, 148)

**Cybernetic/prosthetic augmentation does not exist as a distinct
equipment system -- the only codebase reference is a single
non-equippable quest trophy item, and no species-equip-restriction
infrastructure exists at all (so a live-SWG-style "Wookiees can't use
cybernetics" rule isn't modeled and couldn't be toggled on today).**
A repo-wide search for "cybernetic"/"prosthetic"/"bionic"/"cyborg"
turns up exactly one gameplay object:
`mellichae_cybernetic_arm`
(loot/items/mellichae_cybernetic_arm.lua:1-12), tied to the
Force-sensitive village "Mellichae" quest chain outro
(loot/groups/mellichae_outro.lua, weight 3,000,000/10,000,000 in
loot table 101) and flavored as "a Broken Cyborg Arm." Critically,
it's built as a plain `SharedTangibleObjectTemplate` with
`slotDescriptorFilename = ""`
(object/tangible/item/quest/force_sensitive/objects.lua:811-868) --
meaning **it cannot be equipped to any body slot at all**; it is a
narrative trophy, not gear. All remaining hits are flavor-text NPC
dialogue (`doc/ConversationEditor/stringfiles.js`) about an Imperial
"cybernetic pilot" story arc with no backing object/stat code.

Every wearable/armor item in the codebase shares one generic stat
model regardless of hypothetical cybernetic status --
`ArmorObjectTemplate.h:14-216` (encumbrance fields, per-damage-type
resist floats, `SuitLocations` hit-zone bitmask) and
`WearableObject.idl:16-112` (socket-based skill mods, shared by all
clothing/armor) -- there is no subclass, flag, or field anywhere
distinguishing a cybernetic slot type or granting it unique,
non-wearable-equivalent bonuses. A search for
`speciesRestrict`/`raceRestrict`/species-gated-equip logic across
`src/` returns nothing relevant to wearables (the only "species
restrict" hits are unrelated pet-food-consumption checks) --
confirming section 148's species differences are limited to innate
stat modifiers, never equipment eligibility. The one existing
cybernetic item is a fixed loot-table drop with no crafting
schematic or vendor SKU anywhere in the schematics tree.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) cybernetics are absent as gameplay --
building them means creating a new wearable subclass/slot type from
scratch, not extending existing scaffolding. (2) there is zero
species-based equip-restriction engine support for *any* wearable
today, so a Wookiee-cybernetics-style lore restriction would need
entirely new gating code, not a config flip. (3) the sole existing
"cybernetic" object is a non-equippable quest trophy -- don't mistake
it for a precedent of a working augmentation system.

## 236. Abandoned Structure Cleanup -- Fully Automatic Self-Destruct Chain, No DB Safety Net, No Bulk GM Tool (extends sections 30, 184)

**A condemned structure destroys itself entirely automatically once
the 30-day threshold passes -- no GM action or player zone-in
required -- but there is no independent database-level cleanup job
acting as a safety net, and destruction discards contents
irreversibly.** `StructureMaintenanceTask::run()`
(StructureMaintenanceTask.cpp:22-143) is the sole driver, rescheduling
itself daily (`decayCycleSeconds = 24*60*60`, line 108). Non-building
structures (harvesters, lairs) are destroyed immediately once
`isDecayed()` (lines 122-140); buildings instead become
**condemned** (`sendMailCondemned`, line 129) and are re-checked
daily via `shouldBuildingBeDestroyed()` (lines 268-283) against the
hard-coded `getDelayDestroyHours()` = 30*24 hours
(StructureObjectImplementation.cpp:808-810). Past that point,
`destroyStructureWithReason` -> `StructureManager::destroyStructure()`
(StructureManager.cpp:648-653) spawns a `DestroyStructureTask` fully
automatically. No cron-style script, orphan-row purge, or
inactive-account sweep exists anywhere in `sql/` or the engine --
abandonment is detected *exclusively* through this in-world daily
task chain, meaning a broken/missed reschedule (e.g. extended server
downtime) has no fallback cleanup path. The `destroystructure`
command (DestroystructureCommand.h:15-118) is a **single-target,
interactive, player-self-service command** (requires ownership unless
`ghost->isStaff()` bypasses it) -- not a bulk sweep tool; no
purpose-built bulk-clear-abandoned-structures command exists anywhere
in the codebase. Both the auto-decay and manual-destroy paths
recursively call `destroyObjectFromDatabase(true)` on every
slotted/contained/child object (SceneObjectImplementation.cpp:314-348)
-- items are simply deleted with **no mail-back or COD mechanism**;
only the voluntary `redeedStructure()` path (StructureManager.cpp:
795-834+) checks inventory space before returning the deed, and that
safeguard does not apply to decay-driven or GM-forced destruction.
Occupants are teleported out (optionally killed if `killOccupants`)
before deletion (DestroyStructureTask.h:80-102).

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the 30-day condemned-to-destroyed window
is a real, self-scheduling daily chain with zero external-intervention
requirement -- and zero DB-level fallback if that chain ever breaks.
(2) CS/GM staff have no bulk cleanup tool, only the same single-target
command players use, elevated via `isStaff()`. (3) decay-destruction
item loss is total and irreversible -- CS cannot "recover" stored
items from an auto-decayed structure the way a voluntary redeed
protects against loss.

## 237. NPC Kill Effects on Faction Standing -- Real for Faction-Tagged NPCs, Absent for Truly Faction-less Wildlife, No Generic Reputation System Exists (extends sections 73, 106, 125, 158)

**Killing an NPC affects GCW faction standing if and only if that
NPC's template carries a non-empty `faction` string -- many NPCs that
look like "regular" mobs (Tusken Raiders, bandits, thugs, pirates,
CorSec, etc.) are actually faction-tagged and do move standing, while
genuinely neutral wildlife (e.g. bantha) does not, and no generic
reputation/infamy system exists anywhere beyond GCW standing and the
separate Elo PvP rating.** `CreatureManagerImplementation::
notifyDestruction()` (CreatureManagerImplementation.cpp:572-671) is
the single generic death handler for every `AiAgent`; the
faction-standing branch fires at line 664 --
`if (!destructedObject->getFactionString().isEmpty() &&
!destructedObject->isEventMob())` -- calling
`FactionManager::awardFactionStanding()` (:667-670), which itself
calls `increaseFactionStanding`/`decreaseFactionStanding` for every
ally/enemy of that faction (FactionManager.cpp:91-152). Verified via
templates: `bantha.lua:4` sets `faction = ""` (no effect);
`tusken_raider.lua:4` sets `faction = "tusken_raider"` (real effect).
A search of the player-object sources for
`reputation|infamy|notoriety` returns zero matches -- the only other
persistent per-player combat stat is the structurally separate Elo
PvP rating (section 106).

**Faction guard kills (section 125) grant standing via the same
generic path but a distinct, level-scaled formula, and never touch
GCW score.** `fbase_stormtrooper.lua:6` sets `faction = "imperial"`;
killing one routes through `awardFactionStanding()`
(`gain = level * adjustFactor`, `lose = gain*2`,
FactionManager.cpp:105-106) -- a genuinely different code path and
formula from killing an actual enemy-faction player, which instead
uses `awardPvpFactionPoints()` (FactionManager.cpp:238-257, flat
±30/±45 regardless of level). No `gcwScore`/`GCWManager` call exists
anywhere in `notifyDestruction()`. Beyond this, a real, separate
"social faction" reputation web covers ~50 non-GCW factions (tusken
raider, bandit, thug, corsec, hutt, nightsister, jabba, etc., each
with its own ally/enemy list) defined in
`managers/faction_manager.lua:12-82`, sharing the same
`factionStandingList`/`isPvpFaction()` machinery
(FactionStandingList.h:104-106), capped at ±1000/-5000 for non-GCW
factions versus rank-capped for Rebel/Imperial.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) "non-faction NPC" must be read literally
-- check the template's `faction` field, not the NPC's visual/flavor
category, before assuming a kill is standing-neutral. (2) faction
guard kills are a real, level-scaled GCW-standing income source
distinct from player PvP kills, but never move GCW score itself. (3)
there is no reputation/infamy stat beyond GCW standing and Elo PvP
rating -- don't assume or design around one existing.

## 238. Structure/City Zoning Restrictions -- No District System Exists; City Specialization and GCW Bases Are Fully Orthogonal to Placement Legality (extends sections 35, 54, 77, 82, 96, 145, 166, 171)

**No residential/commercial (or any sub-city) zoned-district system
exists anywhere in the codebase -- structure placement checks are
entirely template- and citywide, never positional-within-a-city --
and GCW bases are not code-level barred from player cities, contrary
to what section 117's phrasing might imply.**
`SharedStructureObjectTemplate.h:57-119` exposes only planet-level
`allowedZones`, a flat `cityRankRequired`, and boolean
`isCivicStructure()`/`isCommercialStructure()` flags -- nothing keyed
to sub-city location. `StructureManager::placeStructureFromDeed`
(StructureManager.cpp:401-431) checks only: city rank threshold,
civic-structure-requires-mayor, unique-per-city dedup, and the single
citywide `zoningEnabled`/`hasZoningRights()` toggle
(CityRegion.idl:81,433-435, default true). A grep for
`district`/`RESIDENTIAL`/`COMMERCIAL_ZONE` across `objects/region`
returns zero hits. City specialization (sections 145/166) applies
purely as geofenced `SkillModManager::CITY` skill mods
(`applySpecializationModifiers()`, CityRegionImplementation.cpp:
872-923) -- nothing in `StructureManager.cpp` or
`PlanetManagerImplementation::isBuildingPermittedAt`
(:1356-1388) references it, confirming zero placement-restriction
interaction. The generic per-player lot cap is a flat `maximumLots`
(default 10, PlayerObject.idl:113,387), not split by structure
category; the only category-like cap is `isUniqueStructure()` +
`hasUniqueStructure(uint32 crc)` (CityRegionImplementation.cpp:736),
limiting *civic* buildings (city hall, bank, cantina, cloning
facility, garage, garden, hospital, shuttleport, theater) to one
instance per template CRC per city, mayor-placed only -- "guild hall"
is not a distinct structure class at all, just a Guild Terminal in an
ordinary building, inheriting the owner's generic lot cap. Finally,
`city->isClientRegion()` in `placeStructureFromDeed` (line 339) gates
only *static/NPC* cities (Theed, Coronet) -- player cities face the
same generic zoning-rights check every structure type does; GCW-base
placement gating lives entirely in
`PlaceGCWBaseComponent::placeStructure`
(PlaceGCWBaseComponent.cpp:18-57) and
`GCWManagerImplementation::canPlaceMoreBases`/`hasTooManyBasesNearby`/
`isPlanetCapped` (:486-603,1360), neither of which references
`CityRegion` or player-city membership -- so a base can legally be
placed inside a player city's boundary if zoning allows it; exclusion
is a social/default-setting effect, not a hardcoded rule.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) no zoned-district feature exists to
extend -- building one is wholly new work. (2) city rank +
`isCivicStructure`/`isUniqueStructure` are the only "one per city"
mechanism, and apply solely to mayor-placed civic amenities, never to
houses/vendors/guild halls. (3) correct any assumption that GCW bases
are code-barred from player cities -- verify against
`PlaceGCWBaseComponent.cpp`'s actual checks, which don't reference
`CityRegion` at all.

## 239. Heroic Instance Loot Lockout & Reset Timers -- Confirmed Absent, Consistent with Section 22's "No Instancing" Finding (extends sections 22, 55, 62, 85)

**No lockout system, per-character/account/group cooldown, or
instance-reset mechanic exists for heroic/boss encounters -- because
no instancing substrate exists at all in this codebase, a finding
independently re-confirmed here and fully consistent with section
22.** A repo-wide grep for `lockout`/`Lockout`/`LOCKOUT` across `src/`
and `bin/scripts/` returns zero gameplay hits (only unrelated matches
in the external Berkeley DB library and archived SQL files). A second
sweep for `InstanceManager`, `HeroicManager`, `isInstance()`,
`InstanceType`, `createInstance`, `cloneZone`, `privateZone`,
`instancedZone` returns zero files. There is also no multi-group
"ops/raid" container a lockout could be scoped to (section 85
independently confirms no structure larger than the single 20-member
`GroupObject` exists; `SquadObserver`/`SQUADRON` operate on `AiAgent`
NPCs, not players, and carry no loot/lockout semantics). Loot
generation is entirely per-`CreatureTemplate`/per-death: a weighted
`LootGroupCollectionEntry` -> `LootGroups` -> `LootGroupTemplate`
cascade rolls fresh and synchronously at the moment of death, with
"boss/named/elite" loot simply being a `CreatureTemplate` pointed at
richer loot-group files -- no dedicated boss-loot subsystem, no
per-kill flag, no counter that could throttle a repeat kill. Since
drops are computed independently on every death with zero persisted
per-player/per-account state consulted, repeat kills of the same
boss-tier mob yield full, unthrottled loot every time. "Dungeon"
content is built entirely on the standard shared-world lair/spawn-group
system, verified directly in
`LairObserverImplementation.cpp:590-636`: `checkRespawn()` schedules a
`SpawnLairMobileTask` after a randomized delay between
`RESPAWN_TIME_MIN` (120s) and `RESPAWN_TIME_MAX` (240s)
(LairObserver.idl:26-27) -- a shared, world-persistent respawn timer
on the lair itself, re-fightable by any player/group once it
respawns, not a per-player completion cooldown. There is no
"in-progress vs. cleared" instance state at all, because there is no
instance object.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) confirmed absent, not merely
undocumented -- no lockout, no instance manager, no cloned-zone
substrate, no ops/raid-group container anywhere in the codebase. (2)
the only "reset timer" that exists is the lair's own 120-240s
world-shared respawn window, which gates when the mob exists, not who
may loot it. (3) building daily/weekly lockouts or true per-group
instancing would be entirely new engine work -- there is no partial
scaffolding (persisted completion flags, instance-ID tracking) to
extend.

## 240. Personal Crafting Tool Quality/Speed Stats -- Real Effectiveness Multiplier via `usemodifier`, No Speed Stat, No Condition-Based Decay (extends sections 45, 65, 220)

**A personal crafting tool's own rolled `usemodifier` stat feeds
directly into the experimentation/assembly success formula as a
scalar multiplier -- but crafting *time* depends solely on schematic
complexity, never on tool stats, and tool condition/wear has zero
effect on crafting effectiveness (a clean contrast with weapon/armor
condition decay, section 205).** `CraftingTool.idl:33-39` defines
seven `toolType` values (CLOTHING/FOOD/GENERIC/JEDI/SPACE/STRUCTURE/
WEAPON); each type's Lua template sets a `complexityLevel` (15 for
GENERIC, 20 for WEAPON/JEDI/STRUCTURE/FOOD/CLOTHING/SPACE,
`.../crafting/station/{generic,weapon,jedi,structure}_tool.lua:73-74`)
that caps which schematics `CraftingSessionImplementation::
selectDraftSchematic()`/`filterSchematicList()` (.cpp:129,137) even
lists -- tool tier mainly gates *access*, not raw power. The actual
success-roll modifier is a single rolled attribute:
`CraftingToolImplementation::updateCraftingValues()`
(CraftingToolImplementation.cpp:129-132) sets
`effectiveness = values->getCurrentValue("usemodifier")`, passed
unmodified into `calculateAssemblySuccess(...,
craftingTool->getEffectiveness())`
(CraftingSessionImplementation.cpp:765); both
`CraftingManagerImplementation::calculateExperimentationSuccess()`
(.cpp:63-132) and `SharedLabratory::calculateAssemblySuccess()`
(SharedLabratory.cpp:143,161) compute
`toolModifier = 1.0f + (effectiveness/100.0f)`, multiplying the
entire experiment roll. A small set of Jedi reward tools additionally
carry `forceCriticalExperiment`/`forceCriticalAssembly` counters that
force an outright `AMAZINGSUCCESS`
(CraftingSessionImplementation.cpp:767-769, 1098-1104). No tool speed
stat exists anywhere: `startCreationTasks(manufactureSchematic->
getComplexity() * 2, ...)` (.cpp:1390,1394) is the only duration
call site, and it never references `craftingTool->getEffectiveness()`
or any tool field -- tool quality affects only the success-tier roll,
never how long crafting takes. Crafting tools are themselves real
crafted items with resource-rolled stats, not fixed vendor items:
`item_weapon_tool.lua:44-80` (and matching generic/structure/etc.
schematics) is a real `DraftSchematic` with metal/mineral/chemical
ingredients, and the target templates declare
`experimentalProperties = {..., "CD"}` with
`experimentalMin/Max = {..., -15, 15}` on the same `usemodifier`
group -- the identical experimentation pipeline documented in
section 45, feeding directly back into finding #2's effectiveness
stat (starter tools from character creation are spawned directly from
the `.iff` template, bypassing crafting, but instantiate the same
rollable template). No call to the `getConditionReduction()`
mechanism weapons/armor use for combat decay appears anywhere in
`CraftingManagerImplementation.cpp`, `SharedLabratory.cpp`, or
`CraftingSessionImplementation.cpp` -- tool condition/wear is
confirmed to never degrade crafting effectiveness.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) treat tool quality purely as a
success-tier multiplier (`1 + effectiveness/100`), never as a
time-saver. (2) "better tool tier" mainly buys schematic-category
access (complexity ceiling/enabled tabs), not raw power -- a maxed
generic tool still caps at complexity 15. (3) tool stats are worth
min-maxing at crafting time since `usemodifier` rolls -15..+15 exactly
like any other crafted item, but tool condition/repair state can be
safely ignored in any effectiveness calculation.

## 241. Player-Built Droid Component Upgrade/Swap -- Confirmed Fused-at-Unpack, Same Immutable Pattern as Harvesters (extends sections 8, 138, 187, 208, 224)

**A built droid pet is effectively a fused object once "readied" from
its deed -- its live module set is a one-time load snapshot with zero
player-facing add/remove/swap path, matching the exact
bake-in-once-then-immutable pattern already confirmed for harvesters
(section 224).** Droid Engineering's multi-component assembly wipes
and fully rebuilds the deed's `modules` HashTable on every
crafting-session callback
(`DroidDeedImplementation::updateCraftingValues`,
DroidDeedImplementation.cpp:198-298, `modules.removeAll()` at
213/53) -- but this only happens *during the deed's own
crafting/experimentation session*. On "Ready Droid Unit"
(`DroidDeedImplementation::handleObjectMenuSelect`, :406-463), the
module set transfers **once** into the live `DroidObject`'s hidden
`crafted_components` satchel (line 448), the deed's table is cleared
(459), and `droid->initDroidModules()` populates the in-memory
`modules` vector (DroidObjectImplementation.cpp:217-242).
`initDroidModules()` itself is confirmed to run at only three fixed
points -- object load, pet-store recall, and deed-unpack -- with zero
command, radial, or crafting-session code calling it again afterward,
and no `addModule`/`removeModule`/`swapModule` function exists
anywhere on `DroidObject`. The only in-game satchel view is a
GM/privileged-only **read-only** "View Components" radial
(TangibleObjectMenuComponent.cpp:65-76, 136-159). No "reprogram"/
"reconfigure" stat command exists (`CustomizeDroidCommand.h` only
gates cosmetic paint UI, section 159). A genuinely distinct
"reprogram" mechanic *does* exist but is architecturally unrelated --
`DroidCommandProgrammingCallback` (packet 0x435) lets players
add/remove `DroidProgrammingChip` command modules into a
`PetControlDevice` datapad for **space-ship droid-brain command
behaviors**, a different object type, different container, and
different capability (ability grants, not combat/utility stat
contribution) than ground `DroidComponent` modules.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the only "upgrade" route for a ground
droid pet is redeed/rebuild via Droid Engineering crafting (destroy
pet, re-experiment a new deed) -- identical to the harvester pattern.
(2) don't confuse the real, working chip-swap mechanic
(`DroidCommandProgrammingCallback`) with ground droid stat modules --
it only manages space-combat command chips, a separate subsystem.
(3) any new "swap droid module" feature needs genuinely new
infrastructure (a live container-change hook plus a re-call to
`initDroidModules()`) -- there's no partial mechanism to extend.

## 242. Structure Permission Tiers -- Six Named Lists (Not a Bitmask), ADMIN List Functions as Real Multi-Person Co-Ownership (extends sections 134, 155, 156)

**Structure access is not binary ban/allow -- it's six fixed named
lists (ADMIN/ENTRY/HOPPER/BAN/VENDOR/QUEST), but access rights are
hardcoded per list rather than a composable bitmask like guild
permissions, and there is no intermediate "friend" tier with
container-but-not-furniture rights.** `StructurePermissionList`
(StructurePermissionList.h:16-37) stores an `idPermissionLists` map
of list-name -> `SortedVector<uint64>`, capped at 50 entries per
list, accepting both player and guild IDs. `ENTRY`/`VENDOR` only
grant walk-in rights (`isOnEntryList()`,
StructureObjectImplementation.cpp:829-848); real container
manipulation requires `isOwnerOf() || isOnAdminList()`
(`StructureContainerComponent::checkContainerPermission()`,
:12-46, line 29), with `VENDOR`-list members getting only
`MOVEVENDOR` rights on vendor objects specifically. Furniture
move/rotate is dedicated-command-gated and **always** requires
ADMIN (`RotateFurnitureCommand.h:171,190-202`) -- a plain
ENTRY/HOPPER member is explicitly refused ("You must be an admin to
manipulate objects"). `HOPPER` is narrower still, scoped only to
harvester/factory deposit-withdraw rights
(`isOnHopperList()`, :867-884). So access is effectively
three-valued in practice: banned, entry-only (walk in, view open
containers), or ADMIN (full interior control). Critically, **ADMIN
membership already functions as real multi-person co-ownership**:
`PlayerManagerImplementation::getInRangeStructureWithAdminRights()`
(:3750-3782) checks `isOnAdminList()`, not `isOwnerOf()`, and gates
`PaymaintenanceCommand`, `DestroystructureCommand`,
`NameStructureCommand`, `StructurestatusCommand`, and
`PermissionListModifyCommand` itself -- any ADMIN-list member can pay
maintenance, redeed/destroy, rename, and manage ban/entry lists, not
just the literal owner. Only `TransferstructureCommand.h:34,47`
re-checks true ownership before allowing an ownership transfer,
confirming day-to-day management is co-ownable but transfer itself
is not. Guild IDs work directly as list entries on all 6 lists,
so "whole guild gets ADMIN/ENTRY" needs no per-member setup. Contrast
with guild permissions (section 134): those are a true combinable
bitmask (`PERMISSION_MAIL=0x01` through `DISBAND=0x80`, 8
independent composable rights) -- structure lists are simple
set-membership on hardcoded-meaning lists, not composable.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) there's no out-of-the-box "friend" tier
with container-only rights -- adding one would require a new named
list plus new checks threaded through both
`StructureContainerComponent::checkContainerPermission` and the
furniture-move commands. (2) ADMIN-list membership is a real,
already-working co-owner mechanism today (maintenance, destroy,
rename, ban-list edits) -- only ownership transfer stays
single-owner. (3) guild IDs populate any of the 6 lists directly,
making guild-wide structure access trivial to set up without
per-member entries.

## 243. Mounted Player as Combat Target -- Identical Hit/Damage Math, Mount-Specific Dismount-on-Posture-Effect, Independently Killable Mount (extends sections 84, 91, 140)

**Being mounted changes nothing about a player's chance to be hit,
dodge, parry, or block, or how much damage they take -- combat math
is identical whether the target is mounted or on foot -- but
knockdown/posture-break/dizzy effects convert into a forced,
damage-free dismount rather than being applied or blocked outright,
and the mount itself is an independently killable target whose death
also force-dismounts the rider.**
`CombatManager::getDefenderSecondaryDefenseModifier()`
(CombatManager.cpp:2056-2075) and the hit-chance pipeline
(:2030-2054, 2081+) contain zero `isRidingMount()` checks -- the only
object-type short-circuit is `isVehicleObject()` (zeroing the
*vehicle's own* secondary defense, not a rider's, since a mounted
player remains a plain `CreatureObject`). Damage calculation
(:2460-2492, 2656-2682) branches only on `isAiAgent()`/
`isVehicleObject()`, never mount state. However,
`CombatQueueCommand::applyEffect()` (CombatQueueCommand.h:647-658,
673-684, 704-715) special-cases KNOCKDOWN/POSTUREUP/POSTUREDOWN: if
`defender->isRidingMount()`, it resets the mount-dismount cooldown
and calls `defender->dismount()` **before** applying the posture
change -- knockdown isn't blocked, it's converted into a forced
dismount plus posture change. A parallel path,
`DizzyFallDownEvent::run()` (DizzyFallDownEvent.h:35-39),
independently dismounts a dizzied rider 200ms after the fall-down
animation fires. There is no dismount trigger from ordinary damage
or hits -- only these specific posture-effect paths, plus mount
death. `dismount()` (CreatureObjectImplementation.cpp:2639-2641) only
repositions the rider via `DismountCommand` with **no fall damage
applied** in any traced path. Mounted players also lose
`canFeignDeath()` (returns false while `isRidingMount()`,
:2671-2673), removing that evasion tool. The mount creature itself is
a normal, independently attackable/killable `AiAgent`; its death
routes through `PetManagerImplementation::notifyDestruction()`
(PetManagerImplementation.cpp:505-517), which explicitly checks
`isMount() && hasRidingCreature()` and force-dismounts the rider via
the same safe-reposition path -- no fall damage there either.
Personal (non-creature) `VehicleObject` destruction/ejection was not
located in this pass and needs separate verification.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) mount status is purely offensive-side
(section 140 blocks attacking) -- as a target, a mounted player is
mechanically identical to one on foot for hit/dodge/damage purposes.
(2) knockdown-family effects never fail to apply to a mounted
player; they're rerouted into a safe forced dismount instead,
meaning "immunity while mounted" is not a real defensive strategy.
(3) the mount is a legitimate separate kill target, and killing it is
actually a *safe* way to dismount a rider (no fall damage) --
relevant for any combat-balance work involving mounted PvP.

## 244. Entertainer Flourish Mechanic -- Real Server-Tracked Multiplier on Buff Accrual and Wound-Heal Throughput, No Combo/Streak System (extends sections 48, 72)

**Flourish is a genuine server-aware mechanic, not client-only
animation flavor: each successful flourish fires an extra
buff-accrual pulse and multiplies wound/shock healing throughput by
`(flourishCount+1)`, but there is no combo/streak/variety-reward
system -- spamming one flourish index is mechanically identical to
alternating them.** `FlourishCommand::doQueueCommand`
(FlourishCommand.h:18-57) calls
`session->doFlourish(index, true)`;
`EntertainingSessionImplementation::doFlourish`
(EntertainingSessionImplementation.cpp:629-692) drains
Quickness-scaled action points, broadcasts the animation packet,
increments a server-side `flourishCount`, and fires an
`ObserverEventType::FLOURISH` event exposed to Lua screenplays. Each
successful flourish (capped at `flourishCount < 5` per tick, line
674) calls `addEntertainerFlourishBuff()` (:614-627), running the
same `increaseEntertainerBuff()` function the normal 10-second tick
uses -- flourishing is a genuine *extra* buff-accrual pulse, not
decoration. Separately, `doEntertainerPatronEffects()` multiplies
wound/shock healing by `(flourishCount+1)` for both the entertainer
(:85) and every patron in range (:103) -- a direct throughput lever.
No streak/combo/no-repeat tracking exists anywhere:
`EntertainingSession.idl` only has `flourishXp`, `oldFlourishXp`,
`healingXp`, `flourishCount`, `applauseCount` -- no `lastFlourish`
field, and `doFlourish()` never inspects which flourish index was
previously used. The only caps are quantity-based: the per-tick
`flourishCount < 5` limit, and a separate, stricter per-tick XP cap
(`flourishCap = 10/loopDuration` -- 1 for dance/10s loops, 2 for
music/5s loops, :679-684). Flourish usage does raise XP gain, but via
this same quantity mechanism: each counted flourish adds
`getFlourishXpMod()` to `flourishXp`, folded into
`awardEntertainerExperience()`'s total (:1059-1069); unused flourish
XP decays rather than banking (`oldFlourishXp`, :1015-1025), and both
`flourishCount`/`flourishXp` reset every tick.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) flourish is a legitimate mechanical
lever (heal-throughput multiplier + extra buff pulse + XP), worth
treating as a real system, not cosmetic. (2) there is no
"watch the audience for cues" combo mechanic in this codebase --
don't design around one existing; alternating vs. repeating flourish
indices is mechanically irrelevant. (3) the only real limits are the
flat per-tick count cap (5) and a stricter, separate per-tick XP cap
(1 dance / 2 music) -- any companion-entertainer feature should reuse
