`doFlourish()`'s existing pattern rather than inventing streak logic.

## 245. Per-Player NPC Quest/Conversation State Persistence -- Fully Player-Owned, NPCs Are Stateless Dispatchers (extends sections 34, 57, 112)

**All quest and conversation state lives on the player's own objects,
never on the NPC -- meaning two different players can be at
completely different steps of the same quest with the same static
NPC instance with zero interference -- and only explicit
state-mutating calls are durable across logout; the "current
conversation screen" itself is not checkpointed.** Two separate
persistence layers exist, both anchored to the player: (1) generic
dialogue-tree state via a `ConversationSession` Facade attached to
the player's own `CreatureObject`
(`conversingPlayer->addActiveSession(SessionFacadeType::CONVERSATION,
new ConversationSession(conversingNPC))`,
ConversationObserverImplementation.cpp:146-148), holding
`lastConversationScreen`; (2) screenplay/quest-step tracking via a
`ScreenPlayObserver` registered on the player's `SceneObject`
(`DirectorManager::createObserver(..., pPlayer)`, confirmed in
multiple Jedi-trials/quest-task scripts). Durable completion flags
live in `PlayerObject.idl`'s `activeQuests`/`completedQuests`
`DeltaBitArray` fields (lines 283-286), and named key/value quest
data goes through `DirectorManager::setQuestStatus`/`getQuestStatus`
into a global `questStatuses` table persisted to `questdata.db`
(DirectorManager.cpp:186-255) -- per-player scoping here is a
**script convention** (keys conventionally prefixed
`<playerObjectID>:<questName>:<field>`), not engine-enforced, so a
key missing the player-ID prefix is genuinely global/shared (a real
collision risk for careless script authors). Because
`ConversationObserverImplementation` is a single stateless handler
shared by the NPC and derives all state fresh from
`player->getActiveSession(...)` for whichever player triggered the
event, two players talking to the same NPC instance simultaneously
have fully independent screen pointers with no cross-contamination.
Nothing is keyed by NPC object ID -- only by quest/screenplay name
and player ID. On logout, durable state (quest bits,
`setQuestStatus` calls) is committed immediately via the ORB's normal
dirty-object pipeline the moment the mutating Lua call executes, but
the ephemeral `ConversationSession` screen pointer has no logout-save
hook and is simply lost/reset.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) NPCs are pure stateless dispatchers --
any custom screenplay must register observers on the player object,
not the NPC, to get this per-player isolation for free. (2) verify
any new script uses the `<playerObjectID>:<questName>:<field>` key
convention -- omitting the player-ID prefix creates a genuinely
global/shared quest-state key, a real footgun. (3) only explicit
quest-flag/journal calls are durable across logout; mid-dialogue
screen position is not preserved.

## 246. Structure Interior/Exterior Customization Limits -- Windows/Doors/Walls Confirmed Fixed and Immutable, a Genuine Gap Like Structure Paint (extends sections 12, 35, 37, 142, 163)

**No command, SUI, or GM tool exists anywhere to change a structure's
windows, doors, walls, or overall layout post-placement -- this is a
confirmed, genuine gap with zero scaffolding, directly analogous to
the already-documented structure-paint absence (section 142).**
`SuiWindowType.h:99-116` enumerates every `STRUCTURE_*` SUI type
(STATUS, DESTROY_CODE/CONFIRM, MANAGE_MAINTENANCE, ADD_ENERGY,
CREATE/NAME/DESTROY_VENDOR, VENDOR_STATUS/REGISTER/PAY/WITHDRAW,
UNCONDEMN_CONFIRM, SET_ACCESS_FEE/DURATION, CONSENT_PAY_ACCESS_FEE,
SELECT_SIGN, ASSIGN_DROID) -- none touch windows, doors, or walls;
the closest is `SELECT_SIGN`, which only picks a vendor sign graphic.
Each structure template maps 1:1 to a single fixed, hardcoded
`SharedStructureObjectTemplate` string resolved from the deed
(`StructureManager::placeStructureFromDeed()`, :277,309) -- there is
no array/index of alternate floor plans, and `PlaceStructureCommand.h`
only accepts deed ID, x, y, and a 4-way rotation angle (0/90/180/270,
:22-134) as placement-time variability. Interior door/portal geometry
is parsed once from client-authored static `.iff`/CELL data
(`CellProperty::loadVersion4/5()`/`CellPortal::readObject()`,
CellProperty.cpp:5-134) with zero server-side mutation path found
anywhere in `objects/building` or `objects/structure`. Housing
decoration (section 37, confirmed re-checked here) is exclusively
furniture placement/ACL through the generic `ContainerPermissions`
bitmask -- it governs who may place/move objects inside a cell, not
the shell itself. No admin/GM-only structural-appearance tool exists
either: the only appearance-editing commands found
(`EditAppearanceCommand.h`, `SetPlayerAppearanceCommand.h`) are
scoped exclusively to character customization, and
`BuildingObjectImplementation.cpp` contains no
`setAppearance`/`appearanceTemplate`-swap method for staff or anyone
else.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) structure customization stops hard at
furniture placement -- shell geometry (windows, doors, walls, floor
plan) is immutable client-baked data with zero server exposure,
confirmed absent like structure paint (section 142). (2) building
this feature requires genuinely new C++: a new `STRUCTURE_*` SUI
type plumbed through `StructureTerminalMenuComponent`, plus making
template resolution deed/instance-configurable instead of a single
hardcoded string. (3) even GM/staff tooling has no structural
appearance override today -- this isn't a player-only restriction,
it's a total gap.

## 247. Space Escort/Convoy Missions -- Real, Live, and Architecturally Distinct from Ground's Dead Escort Mechanic (extends sections 131, 152, 187)

**Unlike the ground escort mission mechanic confirmed dead in section
187, space has a fully live, functional escort/convoy-defense
mission archetype with genuine "protect me" NPC ship AI -- built as
its own class hierarchy entirely separate from the ground `escort.lua`
Task module, and like all space missions, routed through the
Screenplay system rather than `MissionObject`/`MissionTerminal`
(consistent with section 152's finding).** `SpaceEscortScreenplay`
(SpaceEscortScreenplay.lua:1-1013) is a full `SpaceQuestLogic`
subclass with its own state machine: rendezvous waypoint setup,
escort-ship spawn, randomized multi-leg patrol routing, periodic
distance policing with escalating warnings, and scripted hostile
attack waves. A repeatable "Duty" variant,
`SpaceDutyEscortScreenplay`, subclasses it directly. The escort ship
itself is genuine protect-target AI, not a scripted cutscene prop:
`spawnEscortShip()` (:296-399) instantiates a `ShipAiAgent`, flags it
`setFixedPatrol()` + `setEscort()`, sets a per-quest
`setEscortSpeed()` (real C++ fields on `ShipAiAgent.idl:90,239,
892-898`), faction-allies it to the player, and locks it to the
mission owner -- it flies a randomized waypoint sequence and the
quest fails via a `SHIPDESTROYED` observer if it dies. This is fully
live content, not dead code: `CorsecSquadronScreenplay.lua` alone
defines at least 8 distinct escort instances with real ship types,
real waypoint coordinates, and scripted attack waves, each registered
via `registerScreenPlay(name, true)` (the `true` flag marking it a
real selectable quest entry, contrasted with the base class's own
`registerScreenPlay(..., false)`), reachable from live NPC
conversation handlers. Other confirmed-live space mission types found
alongside it in the same squadron files: assassinate, duty-destroy
(boss ship + multi-wave), plus patrol, delivery, inspect, rescue,
recovery, and battle screenplays, all following the same
real-data-instantiation pattern. None of these route through
`MissionObject`/`MissionTerminal` -- no space category exists in
`MissionTerminal.idl` at all; the Screenplay/`SpaceQuestLogic` system
is the sole pipeline for space mission content, started from NPC
conversations.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) space escort content is real and
playable today -- don't assume it shares ground escort's dead-code
status just because the mission archetype name matches. (2) the
escort ship carries genuine defend-or-fail AI semantics
(`setEscort`, faction-allied, death triggers quest failure via
observer), a solid reference implementation for any "protect an
NPC" ground feature that might be built later. (3) extending space
mission content means following the `SpaceQuestLogic` subclass +
squadron-file instantiation + conversation-handler wiring pattern --
never attempt to route new space missions through `MissionObject`,
which has no space category at all.

## 248. Bazaar/Vendor Search Filter and Sort Mechanics -- Live Unindexed Linear Scan, Name/Category/Price Only, No Stat Search, Hardcoded 100-Result Page Cap (extends sections 50, 136, 157)

**Bazaar/vendor search is a genuine live, uncached linear scan over
the `AuctionsMap` tree (not a precomputed index), filterable only by
name substring/category/price -- crafted-item stat/attribute search
is confirmed absent entirely -- with a hardcoded (not
config-driven) 100-result page cap and no server-side sort-by-price
or sort-by-name option.** Filtering happens in
`AuctionManagerImplementation::fillAuctionQueryHeadersResponseMessage()`
(AuctionManagerImplementation.cpp:1580-1698), driven by
`searchType, itemCategory, filterText, minPrice, maxPrice,
includeEntranceFee, offset` parameters: category via
`checkItemCategory()` matching `getItemType()`/
`getCratedItemType()`; price via straight `minPrice`/`maxPrice`
comparison (optionally inflated by vendor `accessFee`); name via
case-insensitive substring match against `getItemName()`. The
`AuctionItem.idl` schema (lines 15-91) stores only `itemType, price,
itemName, itemDescription, ownerID/Name, status` -- no crafted-item
stat/attribute fields anywhere, confirming stat-range search (e.g.
"kinetic resist > X") is not a server-side capability at all.
Pagination is real and offset-based: the scan loop bounds itself at
`displaying < (offset + 100)` (lines 1609, 1624), a hardcoded literal
`100` (not a named/config constant) baked into three call sites; when
the cap is hit, a `continues` flag is set in
`AuctionQueryHeadersResponseMessage` (lines 1768-1772, 142-152)
telling the client to re-request with an advanced offset -- genuine
server-side pagination, not a full client-side dump. Notably,
`ST_PLAYER_BIDS`/`ST_PLAYER_STOCKROOM` branches (lines 1711-1721)
have no `offset`/`displaying` gating of their own -- they only stop
once the outer loop's shared 100-item budget across the whole pass is
exhausted. There is no persisted search index -- `AuctionsMap` is a
live tree of `planet -> region -> vendor OID ->
SortedVector<AuctionItem*>`, and every search genuinely re-scans it.
Result ordering comes from `AuctionItem::compareTo()` (:95-110),
sorting purely by `auctionedItemObjectID` descending (newer items
first) -- there is no server-exposed sort-by-price or sort-by-name
parameter; any different ordering the client shows is UI-layer only.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't design around a stat-search
feature ("find armor with X resist") -- it would require adding new
fields to `AuctionItem.idl` and new filter logic from scratch, there
is no partial scaffolding. (2) the 100-result cap is three hardcoded
literals (`AuctionManagerImplementation.cpp:1609,1624,1768`), not a
tunable config value -- any cap change needs a source edit at all
three sites consistently. (3) apparent price/name sorting in the
client UI is purely cosmetic re-sorting of an already-fixed,
object-ID-ordered server response -- the server never sorts by
those fields.

## 249. Vehicle Collision/Ramming Damage -- Confirmed Absent, `CollisionManager` Is a Movement Validator Only (extends sections 78, 140)

**No mechanic exists anywhere for a moving vehicle to deal collision
damage to a player or another vehicle -- `CollisionManager` is purely
a navmesh/anti-noclip position validator, and its one live hook into
movement is currently disabled code.** `CollisionManager.cpp`
contains only line-of-sight raycasting
(`checkLineOfSightInBuilding`), navmesh/portal intersection queries
(`getCollisionAppearance`), and `checkMovementCollision` -- a
proposed-move validator that never calls `inflictDamage` or touches
any HAM pool. Critically, the sole call site of
`checkMovementCollision`, in `DataTransform.h:337-341`, is **entirely
commented out** -- even the anti-noclip check for mounted/vehicle
movement is currently dead code. `VehicleObjectImplementation::
inflictDamage` (:257-262) is a pass-through to the standard
`TangibleObjectImplementation::inflictDamage`, existing only so
vehicles can *receive* weapon damage as a combat target -- it has no
role in a vehicle *dealing* damage via movement. A codebase-wide
search for ramming/collision-damage/crash/run-over terminology
returns zero relevant hits. Since no such mechanic exists as a
separate code path, the question of whether it's exempt from section
140's mounted-offensive-command block is moot -- there's nothing to
be exempt.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) ground/air vehicles are transportation
objects only -- movement never damages nearby creatures or vehicles,
confirmed absent rather than an unnoticed stub. (2) the
`CollisionManager` name is misleading for combat purposes; it's a
geometry/anti-noclip validator, and its live movement-validation hook
is presently disabled entirely. (3) building a ramming mechanic would
be genuinely new work with no partial infrastructure to extend --
there's no anti-griefing scaffolding (cooldowns, city no-ram zones)
to build on either, since there's no base mechanic to protect
against.

## 250. Crafting Resource Quality -> Final Item Stat Mapping -- Schematic-Defined Weighted Formula, Confirmed Hard Ceiling on Quality (extends sections 45, 208, 240)

**Resource stats never redefine an item's min/max stat range (that's
fixed per-schematic) -- they only set a percentage ceiling within
that range, computed via a two-level weighted average that skill and
experimentation can approach but never exceed.** Each `DraftSchematic`
declares its own resource-stat-to-output-attribute weighting via
`experimentalGroups`/`experimentalProperties`/`experimentalWeights`,
parsed into `ResourceWeight` objects
(SharedTangibleObjectTemplate.cpp:391-459). The engine's fixed raw
stat vocabulary (`CR`/`CD`/`DR`/`HR`/`FL`/`MA`/`PE`/`OQ`/`SR`/`UT`,
etc., CraftingManager.idl:26-35) is universal, but which codes feed
which output attribute -- and at what weight -- is authored
per-schematic, not globally fixed. Combination across multiple
ingredient slots is a genuine **quantity-weighted average**:
`SharedLabratory::getWeightedValue()` (SharedLabratory.cpp:73-142)
computes `weightedAverage += stat * quantity` per slot, normalized by
total quantity -- so ingredient ratios genuinely matter, not just
which resources are selected. `ResourceLabratory::
setInitialCraftingValues()` (:61-99) then sums these per-stat
weighted values using the schematic's own normalized group
percentages. This weighted sum derives a `maxPercentage`
(ResourceLabratory.cpp:93-96) that acts as a hard clamp:
`AttributesMap::setCurrentPercentage()` clamps against it
(AtributesMapImplementation.cpp:241-266), and experimentation gains
in `ResourceLabratory::experimentRow()` are explicitly capped at
`maxPercent` (:138-147) -- skill/experimentation success only moves
the current percentage toward this resource-set ceiling, confirmed
to never push past it. The final numeric value is
`min + percentage*(max-min)` (CraftingValues::recalculateValues(),
CraftingValues.cpp:63-109), where min/max are the schematic's own
fixed bounds.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) poor resources hard-cap final item
quality regardless of crafter skill -- there is no skill-based
compensation path past the resource-derived ceiling. (2) ingredient
quantity ratios matter, not just resource selection -- using more of
a high-stat resource shifts the quantity-weighted average measurably.
(3) to find which resource stats matter for a given item, inspect
that specific schematic's `experimentalGroups`/`experimentalWeights`
fields -- there is no universal fixed OQ/DR/etc. mapping shared
across all schematics.

## 251. Player Vendor vs. Bazaar Terminal -- Distinct Placeables Sharing One Backend, Capacity and Fees Differ by Ownership Not Object Type (extends sections 50, 101, 136, 157, 248)

**A player Vendor and a Bazaar Terminal are structurally distinct
placeable object types that share one transaction/search backend
(`AuctionManagerImplementation`) -- selling works identically whether
the owner is online or offline, and the real differentiator is
ownership, not object type.** `isVendor()`
(TangibleObjectImplementation.cpp:1621-1629) checks for a
`VendorDataComponent`; Bazaar/kiosk terminals instead derive from
`Terminal` (Terminal.idl:11,48-55) with `isVendorTerminal()`/
`isBazaarTerminal()` flags -- both share `AuctionTerminalDataComponent`
as a base, and `VendorDataComponent::getOwnershipRightsOf()`
(:122-132) treats `ownerId == 0` as "belongs to no one (bazaar)."
Inventory capacity on your own vendor scales with the
`vendor_item_limit` skill mod; listing on a vendor/terminal you don't
own (including any bazaar) hard-caps at a flat `MAXSALES = 25`
(AuctionManager.idl:37, enforced :864,873), with a universal price
ceiling `MAXVENDORPRICE = 99,999,999` applying to both. Owner presence
is irrelevant to selling: the only `isOnline()` check in the entire
sale path (:780) merely decides whether to send an underbid
notification message -- `doInstantBuy()`/`checkSaleItem()`/
`addSaleItem()` have no owner-presence guard anywhere, distinct from
static NPC shopkeepers (which spawn infinite fresh stock rather than
drawing from a real listed inventory). Fee stacking differs sharply:
a plain (non-bazaar) vendor listing pays **zero listing fee**, only
city sales tax if physically sited in a taxed city; a bazaar/
commodity listing additionally pays a flat `SALESFEE = 20` credits
(discounted by `crafting_merchant_sales` skill) charged **upfront
regardless of sale outcome**, sinking to a fixed Galactic Trade
Commission rather than any city treasury. Tax rate is always
determined by the listing vendor's own city, never the buyer's
browsing location.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't expect divergent sale logic
between vendor types -- both funnel through the same
`AuctionManagerImplementation`/`AuctionsMap` backend. (2) capacity is
an ownership distinction (your vendor scales with skill training;
any vendor you don't own hard-caps at 25), not an object-type one.
(3) vendors sell around the clock with the owner fully offline --
there is no online gate anywhere in the purchase path.

## 252. Lightsaber Combat Forms/Stances -- Confirmed Absent, Lightsabers Use the Identical Generic Special-Attack System (extends sections 58, 81, 201, 210, 222)

**Live SWG's Form I-VII lightsaber stance system is confirmed absent
from Core3 -- lightsaber combat is mechanically a labeled subset of
the same generic melee special-attack roster every other weapon
category uses, differentiated purely by Lua data and animation
strings, not dedicated resolution code.** A codebase-wide search for
`SaberForm`/`LightsaberForm`/`CombatForm`/`stance` tied to Jedi combat
returns zero matches -- no command toggles a fighting style, no
per-form stat table, no form-level progression exists anywhere.
`JediCombatQueueCommand` (JediCombatQueueCommand.h:13-24) is a
two-line subclass of the same `CombatQueueCommand` base every weapon
category uses, only setting `visMod = 25` and
`isJediCombatCommand() = true`. All 38 individual `Saber*` attack
commands (SaberSlash1/2, Saber1hCombo/Flurry/HeadHit/Hit,
Saber2hBodyHit/Frenzy/Hit/Phantom/Sweep, SaberPolearm variants,
SaberThrow, etc.) call the identical `doCombatAction()` entry point
as any other melee special -- exactly mirroring section 222's finding
that special attacks differ only via Lua data on structurally
identical C++ shells. Force powers route through the same
`ForcePowersQueueCommand -> CombatManager::doCombatAction()` pipeline
melee/ranged attacks use, with no aggressive/defensive stance toggle
found and no deflect/reflect-blaster-bolt mechanic anywhere. The only
genuinely dedicated Jedi-weapon logic found: `isJediWeapon()` exempts
Jedi from the standard can't-melee-while-kneeling restriction
(CombatQueueCommand.h:220); wielding/attacking with a Jedi weapon
adds +25 to Force-sensitive visibility used by Bounty Hunter tracking
(CombatManager.cpp:95-97,105-107); the universal `NOJEDIARMOR` gate
applies uniformly to Force-power and Saber commands alike (blocking
the command outright rather than degrading a stance); and the
`saber_inv` crystal-tuning container additively stacks stat bonuses
at crafting time (section 81) -- a gear-customization system, not a
runtime combat stance. Weapon-type detection confirms lightsabers
aren't even a distinct weapon category:
`isJediOneHandedWeapon()`/etc. (WeaponObject.idl:531-544) check
template inheritance while still reporting the base
`ONEHANDMELEEWEAPON`/`TWOHANDMELEEWEAPON`/`POLEARM` gameObjectType.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't assume parity with live SWG's saber
form system -- it doesn't exist here. (2) treat lightsaber attacks as
just another named branch of the generic special-attack catalog
(section 201/222), not a separate mechanical system. (3) any "add
lightsaber forms" feature requires entirely new state-machine
infrastructure -- there's no partial mechanism (a stance flag, a
form-selection command) to extend.

## 253. Cash-On-Delivery (COD) Mail -- Confirmed Absent as a Payment-Gated Mechanism, Independently Re-Verified (extends section 68, corrects reference to section 91)

**Core3's mail system has no item-attachment or payment-gating
capability at all -- COD mail as a "pay to receive an attached item"
mechanism does not exist, confirmed by direct inspection of the mail
object's full field set, not merely by re-citing prior documentation.**
`PersistentMessage.idl:16-40` defines the mail object's complete
fields: `senderName`, `subject`, `body`, `timeStamp`, `status`,
`receiverObjectID`, `stringIdParameters`, `waypointParameters` --
there is no item reference, no credit-amount field, no paid/COD flag,
and no escrow container anywhere.
`PersistentMessageImplementation.cpp:13-35` implements only mail
identity/routing methods, no payment or item-transfer logic; all
three `sendMail` overloads in `ChatManagerImplementation.cpp:
1783-1963` construct `PersistentMessage` objects from text/waypoint
fields only. Because the underlying mechanism doesn't exist, every
sub-question about it is moot: there is no accept-and-pay transaction
to block on insufficient funds (no `SuiCallback` or command anywhere
checks bank+inventory credits against a mail item price), no
expiration/return-to-sender logic (mail carries only NEW/READ/UNREAD
status and a timestamp, with no item-linked auto-delete), no price
cap (no COD price field exists to cap), and no preview-before-paying
gate (nothing to preview against). The closest real analogue is
auction/bazaar sale notification mail, which carries only a
`waypointParameters` pointer to a vendor location -- purely
informational, sent alongside a transaction already completed through
separate vendor mechanics, not carried by the mail itself. All real
player-to-player item-for-credit transfers happen via the secure
trade window or vendor/bazaar sales (sections 68, 248), never through
mail.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) do not design or describe any feature
assuming COD mail exists in this codebase -- it is a from-scratch
build requirement, not an extension point. (2) building COD-like
functionality would need new `PersistentMessage` fields (item
reference, credit amount, paid flag) plus entirely new fund-check/
expiry/price-validation server logic -- none of it currently exists
to extend. (3) mail today is purely a text/waypoint notification
system; conflating it with the separate, fully-functional secure
trade and vendor/bazaar transaction systems is a common but
incorrect assumption.

## 254. GCW Base Component Health/Upgrade Mechanics -- Turret Stats Are Static Template Values (Not Even Crafting-Rolled), No Post-Placement Upgrade Path Anywhere (extends sections 87, 96, 219, 224, 231)

**GCW base components are not merely as immutable as harvesters --
turrets are *more* rigid: their stats skip even the one-time
crafting-experimentation roll harvesters and generators get, coming
straight from static templates with zero per-instance variance, and
no post-placement upgrade setter exists anywhere in the turret,
generator, or HQ-building object hierarchy.**
`TurretObjectImplementation::loadTemplateData()`
(TurretObjectImplementation.cpp:40-66) sets `armorRating` and all
nine damage-type resists directly from a
`SharedInstallationObjectTemplate` -- a static, client-authored
template read once via `getIntField`/`getFloatField` calls, with no
experimentation roll and no per-instance variance whatsoever (unlike
harvester `extractrate`, which is at least crafting-rolled once).
Turret weapon output is likewise a fixed template CRC, not a
manufactured item. A codebase-wide search for any setter
(`setArmorRating`/`setKinetic`/`setChanceHit`/etc.) on `TurretObject`
finds calls only inside `loadTemplateData()` -- zero calls from
commands, GM tools, `GCWManager`, or any runtime path; turret max HP
follows the same load-once-from-template pattern as any generic
`TangibleObject`. Generators used in GCW bases instead follow the
already-documented harvester crafting-roll-then-frozen pattern
(section 231) -- one-time experimentation-rolled extraction rate,
never touched again. The HQ/base "tier" itself is a fixed deed
selection, not an upgrade path: a real five-tier deed ladder exists
(section 117), but tier stat differences live in client template
data, and initial HP/vulnerability is fixed per deed tier with no
member-count or guild-size-based scaling found anywhere. No
"control tower"/"shield generator" object classes exist as separate
upgradable entities -- base defense bookkeeping lives entirely in
`DestructibleBuildingDataComponent`, which only tracks turret/
minefield/scanner object-ID slots and an 8-stage hack-state integer.
A search for `upgradeBase`/`upgradeTier` finds only the generic
redeed-for-refund flow, identical to harvesters/factories/generators
-- no in-place tier-upgrade command exists.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) this is a genuine confirmation, not an
exception, of section 224's codebase-wide immutable-after-placement
pattern -- redeed-and-replace is the only route to a "better" base
or component. (2) turrets are actually the most rigid installation
type found so far -- not even a one-time crafting roll applies to
them, unlike harvesters/generators. (3) any future in-place base
upgrade feature (tier 1->2 without redeed) requires entirely new
setter/command infrastructure across `TurretObject`, `GeneratorObject`,
and the HQ `BuildingObject` -- no partial plumbing exists today.

## 255. Drink and Spice Consumable Categories -- Real Sub-Categories with Independent Buff Slots and a Genuine Spice Addiction Mechanic (extends sections 53, 137, 223)

**Drink and Spice are not "just food with different flavor text" --
both are mechanically real sub-categories of the same
`Consumable`/`Food` hierarchy with their own buff-slot tracking, and
Spice carries a genuine addiction/withdrawal debuff loop entirely
absent from ordinary food.** `Consumable.idl` defines
`consumableType` constants `FOOD = 0x01`/`DRINK = 0x10` and an
`effectType` enum including `EFFECT_SPICE = 0x05`; `Drink.idl` is a
thin subclass setting `consumableType = DRINK`, while spice items are
ordinary `Consumable`/food objects flagged `effectType = EFFECT_SPICE`
-- `isSpice() = isSpiceEffect() && isFood()` confirms spice is
mechanically classified as a food-type item with a special effect
flag, not a separate object class. Buffs from all three categories
occupy **independent slots and stack simultaneously**: food/drink
buffs are both built as `new Buff(player, buffName.hashCode(),
newDuration, BuffType::FOOD)` (ConsumableImplementation.cpp:191,199)
but keyed by per-item `buffName` CRC in `BuffList`, so different
items produce different, co-existing buffs; food and drink also track
fully independent "fullness" pools (`getFoodFilling()` vs.
`getDrinkFilling()`) rather than competing for one stomach capacity.
Spice uses its own `BuffType::SPICE` via a distinct `SpiceBuff`
object, tracked separately in `BuffList::spiceActive` -- a player can
be under food, drink, and spice buffs simultaneously. Spice alone
carries a real downside: `SpiceBuffImplementation::deactivate()`
(:13-32) fires a 120-second `SpiceDownerBuff` on expiry that inverts
the positive attribute mods into penalties, triggers a
`heavy_cough_vomit` animation immediately and every 15 seconds --
mitigable only (never eliminated) by a special Chef dessert buff
carrying `BuffCRC.FOOD_REDUCE_SPICE_DOWNTIME`. Both drink and spice
are crafted by the same Chef profession via distinct skill lines
(`food_assembly`/`food_experimentation` for drinks,
`spice_assembly`/`spice_experimentation` for spice) -- no separate
Bartender or "stim" profession exists in this codebase; `pharmaceutical`/
`StimPack` items are unrelated Doctor healing items.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) food, drink, and spice buffs stack
freely and simultaneously -- section 137's same-CRC refresh rule only
blocks re-stacking the *identical* item, not cross-category stacking.
(2) spice is the only consumable category with a live-game-authentic
addiction mechanic (forced-vomit animation + inverted-stat comedown
debuff), never fully removable, only mitigated by a specific dessert
item. (3) all three categories are Chef sub-specializations -- there
is no Bartender profession to build around if one were assumed to
exist.

## 256. Squad/Group Passive PvP Combat Bonuses -- Real but Leader-Skill-Gated Defense Buff, Zero Group-Size or Formation/Positioning Effect on Combat Math (extends sections 44, 62, 68, 85)

**Grouping alone grants no accuracy/damage/crit bonus and group size
never enters `CombatManager`'s formulas anywhere -- but a real passive
defense bonus does exist, conditionally, gated entirely on the
group's leader having trained further Squad Leader skill boxes.**
`GroupObjectImplementation::addMember()` (:129-162, trigger :157-159)
automatically calls `addGroupModifiers(newMember)` whenever a player
joins **if** `hasSquadLeader()` is true (:433-441, checking only that
the leader holds the base `outdoors_squadleader_novice` skill).
`addGroupModifiers()` (:474-504) silently attaches a
`SquadLeaderBuff` granting `private_group_ranged_defense`/
`private_group_melee_defense` (defense/avoidance only, not accuracy
or damage) plus movement mods, with values **copied unscaled directly
from the leader's own skill-mod totals** (:497-500) -- meaning the
bonus is real and automatically applied on join, but its actual
magnitude is zero unless the leader has trained additional Squad
Leader skill boxes granting those mods to themselves; there is no
multiplication by group size anywhere in this path. A full-directory
grep of `CombatManager` confirms zero references to `getGroupSize()`/
`groupSize`/`isGrouped()` -- no "safety in numbers" damage reduction
or coordinated-group bonus exists in the hit/damage/defense pipeline
at all; the only size-scaled mechanic anywhere is the *XP* payout to
squad leaders (`squadXp = combatXp*0.1 + combatXp*0.1*groupSize`,
section 68), not a combat stat. Formation/positioning is purely
cosmetic and, notably, applies only to companion pets/droids via
`FormationManager` (line/wedge/box spatial arrangement) -- never to
player groups; the Squad Leader command gate
(`isValidGroupAbilityTarget()`) requires same-zone/same-building
proximity for ability targeting, not a positional/facing bonus, and
no flanking mechanic exists anywhere in `CombatManager`. Consistent
with section 85, no multi-group "ops"/"raid" container exists beyond
a single 20-member `GroupObject` for combat purposes.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the only real passive combat perk from
grouping is defense-only and entirely dependent on the leader's own
Squad Leader skill training -- a group led by a non-Squad-Leader
gets zero passive combat bonus. (2) group size affects nothing in
`CombatManager` directly -- the only size-scaled mechanic anywhere is
the squad leader's XP payout, a reward mechanism, not a combat stat.
(3) formation/positioning bonuses don't exist for player groups at
all in this codebase -- `FormationManager` is companion-pet-only, so
any "flanking bonus" or "shield wall" feature would be entirely new
work.

## 257. Post-Creation Appearance Customization Scope -- Self-Service Image Designer Reaches Every Slider Except Species/Gender, No GM-Only Re-Roll Tool Exists (extends sections 7, 183, 204)

**Every true customization variable (body/face sliders, height/scale,
hair, colors) can be changed post-creation via the self-service Image
Designer path, but species and gender are architecturally outside its
reach entirely -- they determine which object template the creature
was instantiated from, not a customization variable -- and no
separate GM-only appearance re-roll command exists anywhere.** The
only command that mutates appearance is `ImagedesignCommand.h:30-33`,
gated on the `social_entertainer_novice` skill with no
`AdminLevel`/`godLevel` check anywhere in it or in
`ImageDesignManager.cpp`/`ImageDesignSessionImplementation.cpp` -- a
codebase-wide search of all 857 creature-command files for any
admin-only appearance mutation path found nothing. All writes trace
to `ImageDesignManager::updateCustomization()`
(ImageDesignManager.cpp:26-121), reachable only through a negotiated
`ImageDesignSession`. Character creation
(`PlayerCreationManager.cpp:381`) instantiates the `CreatureObject`
from a `serverObjectCRC` tied to the chosen species/gender file, and
`ImageDesignManager::loadCustomizationData()` (:349-357) keys all
customization data per that same species-gender template CRC --
`ImageDesignManager` only ever calls `setCustomizationVariable()`,
`setHeight()`, or hair-slot object swap functions, never
`setSpecies`/`setGender` or a template swap; those setters exist only
in `PlayerCreationManager.cpp` at creation time. Self-service (skill
`social_entertainer_novice`, designer==target per section 183) can
therefore reach every slider except species/gender. Cooldown/cost is
session-internal, not a distinct self-service mechanic: the only
timers are a 4-minute stat-migration anti-bypass floor and a 2-minute
accept-timeout, identical whether self-servicing or servicing
another player; payment nets to zero for self-service since payer and
payee are the same account, and the only self-service-specific
penalty is halved XP reward. Hairstyle changes go through a genuinely
separate mechanism -- object creation/re-slotting into the `"hair"`
container slot, not variable mutation -- and no hair-growth-over-time
simulation exists anywhere (a repo-wide search for growth-related
hair terms returned zero matches).

**Practical takeaways:** (1) GMs have no bespoke appearance-reset
tool -- they'd use the same `/imagedesign` self-service flow players
do, or direct database/ODB manipulation. (2) species and gender are
permanently locked post-creation for everyone, self-service included
-- any "species change" feature needs entirely new
object-template-swap infrastructure. (3) hair state only changes via
explicit Image Designer action; there's no passive regrowth system to
account for in any character-appearance tooling.

## 258. Weapon Hit-Chance Formula -- Single Canonical Function for All Weapon Types, 75% Base at Parity, Called Shots Add Accuracy Rather Than Subtracting It (extends sections 84, 94, 105, 114, 135, 178)

**There is exactly one hit-resolution entry point for every weapon
type and even Force attacks -- melee, ranged, unarmed, and
turret/installation combat all branch through the same function
rather than using separate formulas -- and called-shot commands
(head/leg/body) grant an accuracy bonus rather than imposing a
penalty, trading it for speed/resource cost instead.**
`CombatManager::getHitChance()` (CombatManager.cpp:2081-2245) is the
sole canonical entry point, reached from both the creature-vs-creature
call site (:456) and the tangible-attacker-vs-creature call site
(:622, covering turrets/installations); melee vs. ranged vs. unarmed
vs. Force attacks are internal branches (keyed on
`data.isForceAttack()` and `weapon->isMeleeWeapon()`/
`getAttackType()`), not separate formulas, and all feed the same
`hitChanceEquation()` helper (:2247-2269). For a normal attack,
`accuracyTotal = accuracySkill + accuracyWeapon + accuracyPosture +
accuracyBonus` (:2144) and `defenseTotal = defenseSkill +
defensePosture` (:2145): `accuracySkill` sums weapon accuracy skill
mods with a hardcoded **-15 unskilled penalty** fallback if raw total
is 0; `accuracyWeapon` is the range-band piecewise-linear
interpolation (section 94); `accuracyPosture` is a locomotion/posture
lookup; `accuracyBonus` folds in the attacking command's own accuracy
bonus. `defenseSkill` (`getDefenderDefenseModifier()`, :2020-2054)
hard-caps the defender's level+weapon-defense-mod total at **125**
before uncapped group/dodge bonuses stack on top. No cover/line-of-sight
term exists anywhere in this function, confirming section 105's
finding. `hitChanceEquation()` computes `roll = (accuracy -
defense)/50` and applies a diminishing-returns 3-step curve starting
at 75, stepping by 25 -- **at exact accuracy/defense parity, hit
chance is 75%, not 50%** -- then hard-clamps to [0,100], the true
floor/ceiling regardless of stat differences. Called-shot Lua
definitions carry **positive** `accuracyBonus` values --
`headShot1/2/3` +5 (1.5x damage, 1.5x speed cost, 0.5x health cost),
`legShot1` +25 (2x speed cost, 2.25x health cost), `bodyShot1` +50
(2x damage) -- confirming and refining section 135: the tradeoff for
called shots is speed/resource cost and forced damage-pool targeting,
not an accuracy penalty.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) treat `getHitChance()`/
`hitChanceEquation()` as the single source of truth for any
combat-balance work -- there is no separate ranged-vs-melee formula
to reconcile. (2) base hit chance at equal accuracy/defense is 75%,
not the 50% one might assume, and defense skill mods themselves cap
at 125 before uncapped bonus layers apply. (3) don't design called
shots as accuracy-penalized -- in this codebase they're
accuracy-*positive*, balanced instead by speed and health-pool cost.

## 259. GCW Base Resource/Supply Dependency -- Confirmed Absent, Vulnerability Is Purely Timer/Attacker-Action Driven, Fully Decoupled from Maintenance or Power (extends sections 41, 87, 96, 254)

**No GCW-specific "supply line" mechanic exists -- base
vulnerability/hackability is a pure siege-clock plus attacker-action
state machine, completely decoupled from maintenance pool, power
status, or any external resource dependency, and destroying nearby
harvesters/resource infrastructure has zero effect on base
defenses.** A full-text search of the entire `managers/gcw/` tree for
harvester/resource/commodity/resupply/supply terminology returns zero
matches -- no commodity must be delivered to a GCW base to keep it
functional. `GCWManagerImplementation::isBaseVulnerable()`
(:1240-1248) checks only the `DestructibleBuildingDataComponent`
state enum (INVULNERABLE through REBOOTSEQUENCE, states 0-8) and the
building's OVERT PvP flag -- no reference to maintenance pool,
condition damage, or power anywhere in the function or its callers.
The vulnerability schedule is purely `vulnerabilityFrequency`/
`vulnerabilityDuration` timers; the 8-stage hack-state progression
advances via attacker actions (slicing terminals, DNA sampling, a
power-regulator toggle-puzzle SUI minigame) during that timer
window -- `isPowerOverloaded()` (:1330-1338) just checks
`state == OVERLOADED`, set after a player completes the hacking
minigame, unrelated to the structure's actual generator/power
reserve. `TurretObjectImplementation.cpp` has no
`isPowered`/`hasPower`/maintenance-gating logic on its combat/firing
path -- only a cosmetic condition-damage display value. `TurretObject`
and the base's `GeneratorObject` are ordinary `InstallationObject`
subclasses paying upkeep via the identical generic
`updateMaintenance()`/`surplusMaintenance`/`setConditionDamage()`
pipeline every harvester/factory uses (section 41/65) -- confirmed as
the exact same system, with the GCW manager's "power" references
(power-regulator SUI, switch states/rules) belonging entirely to the
attacker-facing hacking minigame, not the structure's real generator
power.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) there is no exploit or mechanic where
cutting off a base's external resource supply weakens its defenses --
confirmed absent by exhaustive grep of the `gcw/` manager tree. (2)
the only way a GCW base becomes non-functional is the same generic
path any structure follows: maintenance depletion causing condition
damage, or outright destruction/redeed -- zero GCW-specific resource
layer exists on top. (3) base vulnerability is entirely siege-clock
and attacker-action driven -- don't design around a resource-denial
strategy against GCW bases, since the code has no hook for it.

## 260. Character Slot Caps and Server Transfer -- Two Independent Per-Galaxy Caps, No Character Transfer System Exists at All (extends section 64)

**The "characters per account" question splits into two genuinely
independent, per-galaxy caps -- a creation cap and a much lower
concurrent-online cap -- and there is no character-transfer/migration
system in the codebase at all, making the "does transfer check
destination capacity" question moot.** The creation cap,
`Core3.PlayerCreationManager.MaxCharactersPerGalaxy` (default 10), is
enforced server-side in `PlayerCreationManager::createCharacter()`
(:321-328), comparing `client->getCharacterCount(galaxyID)` and
hard-rejecting with an `ErrorMessage` before any character object is
built; a client-facing UI hint reads the same value but is
cosmetic/secondary to the authoritative server check. A separate,
much lower concurrent-online cap, `onlineCharactersPerAccount`
(Lua-driven, default **2** per `player_manager.lua:47`), is enforced
in `PlayerManagerImplementation::increaseOnlineCharCountIfPossible`
(:6231-6263) and surfaced via a distinct system message at
character-select time -- an apparently vestigial, unenforced
login-server field `maxOnlineCharacters` (default 1) also exists but
shows no actual enforcement anywhere in the login-server code.
Critically, **both caps are per-galaxy, not account-wide**:
`ZoneClientSessionImplementation::getCharacterCount(int galaxyId)`
(:344-358) only counts characters matching the given galaxy ID, and
`AccountImplementation`'s character-list/ban bookkeeping is keyed by
`galaxyID` throughout -- an account is not globally limited to 10
characters total, and can hold characters on multiple galaxies
simultaneously (an account is never bound to one galaxy). There is no
character transfer/migration system anywhere in the codebase --
confirmed both by the existing guide's section 64 finding and
independently by grepping transfer/migrate terminology across the
entire login-server tree, returning zero matches -- so there is no
destination-slot-availability check to document because there is no
transfer mechanic to check it within.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the "10 characters" limit is per-galaxy,
not account-wide -- a single account can have up to 10 characters on
each galaxy it plays, and multi-galaxy accounts are already the
codebase's native model. (2) being logged in simultaneously is
governed by a separate, much stricter cap (default 2) enforced at
character-select, distinct from the creation cap. (3) any "transfer a
character to another server" feature would be entirely new work --
there is no existing transfer code path to extend or check capacity
against.

## 261. Crafting Schematic Trading/Loss -- Skill-Box Schematics Are Non-Tradeable List Membership, Restored Automatically on Relearning, Loot Schematics Are the Only Genuinely Tradeable Form (extends sections 45, 88)

**Skill-box-granted draft schematics cannot be traded, sold, or
dropped -- they are boolean-style list membership on
`PlayerObject::schematicList`, tied 1:1 to holding the granting skill
box, automatically removed on surrender and automatically restored on
relearning with no persistent record in between -- while loot/
mission/quest schematics remain genuinely tradeable physical items
until "learned," after which they convert into the same
non-tradeable list form.** `PlayerObject.idl:155` declares
`SchematicList schematicList` -- a `DeltaVector` of `DraftSchematic`
references, not a container; `SchematicMap` loads **one shared
singleton `DraftSchematic` instance per recipe globally**, and
`addSchematics()`/`removeSchematics()` just add/remove that same
shared reference to/from each player's list -- there is no per-player
physical object to move, drop, or trade. `SkillManager::awardSkill()`
(:407-409) calls `addSchematics()` the instant a skill box is
learned; `surrenderSkill()`/`surrenderAllSkills()` (:706-708, 828-830)
call the mirror `removeSchematics()` the instant the box is dropped.
Because grant/removal is purely derived from the skill's own
`getSchematicsGranted()` list looked up live against the shared
`SchematicMap`, relearning the identical skill box later -- on the
same or a different character -- runs the identical `addSchematics()`
path and grants back the identical schematic set, with no separate
"unlock flag" persisted outside current skill possession. Reward-sourced
schematics (mission/loot/quest) are tracked in a genuinely separate
`rewardedSchematics` map (`SchematicList.h:22,25,52-56`) supporting
finite use-counts: `CraftingSessionImplementation.cpp:970` calls
`decreaseSchematicUseCount()` after each assembly, which only acts if
the schematic is present in `rewardedSchematics` -- for a plain
skill-box schematic (never added to that map) this is a no-op,
meaning unlimited uses forever, while reward-sourced schematics can
exhaust and auto-remove via `removeSchematics()`. The physical loot
schematic item itself (`LootSchematicMenuComponent.cpp:43-95`, an
ordinary `TangibleObject`/`LootSchematicTemplate`) is the only
genuinely tradeable/vendor-sellable form -- using its "Learn
Schematic" radial option (`addRewardedSchematic()`, :82) converts it
into the same list-membership grant described above and consumes the
physical item via `decreaseUseCount()`.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) skill-box schematics cannot be traded
under any circumstances -- design any "schematic gifting" feature
around the loot/reward schematic path exclusively, since that's the
only tradeable form. (2) dropping a profession/skill box immediately
removes its schematics with zero grace period, but relearning
restores the exact same set automatically -- no "I forgot this
recipe forever" risk exists for skill-granted schematics. (3) loot
schematics are physical tradeable items only *before* being learned;
post-learn they behave identically to skill-box schematics except for
carrying a finite, trackable use-count via `rewardedSchematics`.

## 262. Named/Elite/Boss NPC Difficulty Scaling -- No Engine-Level Eliteness System, Every Stat Is Hand-Authored Per Template (extends sections 38, 42, 55, 62, 66)

**There is no `Difficulty`/`Eliteness` enum or automatic stat
multiplier anywhere in `CreatureTemplate` -- "elite," "boss," and
named lore NPCs are each fully independent hand-tuned templates using
the exact same spawn plumbing as ordinary mobs, with only loot *roll
chance* (not loot content) scaling automatically by level.**
`CreatureTemplate.h:23-121` has no difficulty tier field; the only
bitmask flags (`STALKER`/`BABY`/`KILLER`/`HEALER`/`PACK`/`HERD`/
`SCOUT`/`NODOT`) are cosmetic/behavioral, not power tiers. Comparing
an "elite" variant against its non-elite counterpart shows the
"elite" prefix is purely a display-name string plus manually larger
numeric fields (level, `baseHAM`, `damageMax`) -- no shared engine
multiplier is applied. Named lore NPCs (e.g. a named Imperial
captain) use `customName`, a field that exists on every
`CreatureTemplate`, registered via the identical
`CreatureTemplates:addCreatureTemplate()` call every generic mob uses
and spawned through the same `CreatureManagerImplementation::
spawnCreature()` path (section 62/66) -- there is no separate "named
NPC" spawn subsystem; quest/screenplay `npcTemplate` lists mix named
and completely generic mob template names interchangeably. Loot
richness has exactly one automatic lever:
`lootChance = 2000000 + (level * 20000)` (`LootGroupCollectionEntry.h:
38-42`), reading the creature's own manually-set `level` field --
higher-level creatures get proportionally better roll odds for a
*given* loot-group entry, but the actual list of loot groups
assigned to a creature is 100% hand-authored per template (a captain
variant might have an extra loot group a base trooper lacks, entirely
by manual template authoring, not an engine rule). No engine-level
bonus-ability mechanism exists for elite/boss NPCs either -- elite
and non-elite variants draw from identical attack-skill pools, with
only baked-in numeric stats differing. The one real engine "boss"
mechanism found is lair-specific rather than template-driven:
`LairObserverImplementation::checkForBossSpawn()` (:539-588) selects
from a lair template's `bossMobiles` map and forces full-group aggro
-- an aggro-behavior trigger, not a stat/ability boost; the boss
mobile itself remains just another hand-tuned `CreatureTemplate`.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) there is no shared scaling formula to
extend -- creating a tougher variant of an existing mob means
manually copying and rescaling the Lua template (level, damage, HAM,
resists, loot groups) exactly as shipped content already does. (2)
named lore NPCs are mechanically ordinary creatures with a
`customName` field -- no dedicated named-NPC infrastructure exists to
build on. (3) loot generosity has one small automatic lever (roll
chance scales with `level`), but which loot groups exist at all is
always a manual per-creature authoring decision -- plan any
"richer loot for tougher mobs" feature as an authoring convention,
not an engine hook.

## 263. Bulk/Multi-Structure Management Tools -- Confirmed Absent, Every Structure Managed Individually via Its Own Session (extends sections 30, 67, 163)

**No aggregate structure dashboard, bulk maintenance-pay command, or
bulk redeed tool exists anywhere -- even the maintenance-droid
"auto-pay" convenience is per-droid, manually configured per
structure, and capped, not a true account-wide automation -- and the
destroy/redeed command explicitly blocks running a second concurrent
session, confirming one-at-a-time management is a deliberate design,
not an oversight.** `PlayerObjectImplementation` maintains a raw
`ownedStructures` ID list, but it's only ever consulted internally --
for lot-cap arithmetic (`getLotsRemaining()`, :3142-3158) and mass
destruction on character deletion (:3053-3101) -- never surfaced to
the player as a status dashboard; the only status-reporting command,
`/structurestatus` (StructurestatusCommand.h:21-56), operates
exclusively on the single structure the player is inside or has
targeted. The maintenance droid
(`DroidMaintenanceModuleDataComponent.cpp/.h`) requires structures to
be individually assigned one at a time via each structure's own
radial menu, holds a hard cap of 3/6/9/10 structures depending on
`moduleRating`, and running a maintenance session is a manual,
player-initiated `SuiTransferBox` loop where the player picks each
structure and pay-amount individually before executing
`payStructures()` -- a semi-bulk convenience (one run settles several
pre-assigned structures) but neither automatic/passive nor
account-wide. `DestroystructureCommand.h:23-53` operates on a single
targeted structure only and explicitly rejects a second concurrent
destroy attempt ("You already have an outstanding destroy command for
another structure..."), enforced via a single-slot session type -- a
deliberate one-at-a-time restriction. No command grep for
`payAllMaintenance`/`redeedAll`/`bulkPay`/`listStructures` returns any
hits anywhere in the codebase. There is also no separate hard
account-wide structure-count cap beyond the existing per-character
`maximumLots` budget (default 10, `PlayerObject.idl:113,387`) -- all
structure types except vendors (tracked separately via
`ownedVendors`) draw from the same flat lot pool.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any "manage all my structures" feature
is entirely new work -- there's no aggregate query or bulk-session
infrastructure to extend, and the single-slot destroy-session design
would need reworking to support concurrent operations. (2) the
maintenance droid is the closest existing bulk tool, but setup
(per-structure assignment) and the pay-amount step remain manual per
structure even within one droid session. (3) the only real structure
ceiling today is the per-character `maximumLots` (default 10) -- no
separate account-wide cap exists to reconcile against.

## 264. Combat XP and Level Difference -- Confirmed No Grey-Mob Scaling, XP Is Pure Damage-Share of a Fixed Template Value with Only a Killer-Side Cap (extends sections 44, 68, 92)

**Core3 has no "grey mob"/de-leveling XP suppression for combat kills
-- a max-level character and a low-level character receive identical
damage-share-proportional XP for killing the same trivial creature;
the only level-related term is a cap tied to the killer's own combat
level, which can only raise the achievable ceiling for stronger
players, never reduce XP for killing weak targets.** `AiAgent::
getBaseXp()` returns a fixed `CreatureTemplate::baseXp` value loaded
once from the Lua mob template at parse time -- never referencing the
attacking player's level or skills. In
`PlayerManagerImplementation::disseminateExperience()` (:1937-2229),
each attacker's XP share is `xpAmount = baseXp * (damage/totalDamage)`
(:2153-2156), pure damage-proportional distribution of the fixed base
value (matching the group/threat model in sections 44/68). The only
level-related factor is a cap, not a scaling curve:
`xpAmount = min(xpAmount, playerLevel * 300)` (:2159), where
`playerLevel` is the killer's own weapon-skill-derived combat level
-- this only ever *reduces* XP if the raw damage-share would exceed
the killer's own cap, and never references the creature's level at
all; a max-level character's cap (25 x 300 = 7500) sits far above
what any trivial mob's tiny `baseXp` could produce, so the cap never
actually engages for weak-mob kills. Other multipliers (species XP
modifier, food/buff bonus, group bonus, GCW faction bonus, global
config multiplier) are all non-level-relative. Notably, the separate
Creature Handler pet-XP path (same function, :2098-2115) *does* use a
`levelRatio = creatureLevel/attackerLevel` check that zeroes XP below
a 0.5 ratio (flagged in-source as a `TODO: find a more correct CH xp
formula`) -- but this is a distinct `creaturehandler` xpType branch,
never applied to ordinary `combat_general`/weapon-type combat XP.
Crafting and entertainer XP are similarly confirmed level-independent,
deriving flat amounts from session mechanics (quality rolls,
performance duration) with no target-vs-actor level comparison
anywhere.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't assume any level-scaling protection
against XP farming trivial mobs -- none exists for ordinary combat
XP; a max-level character farming weak creatures gets full
damage-share XP just like a low-level character would. (2) the only
level-linked term is a killer-side ceiling
(`playerLevel * 300`) that can only help stronger characters, never
penalize kills against weak targets. (3) a level-ratio downscale
pattern already exists in the codebase (Creature Handler pet XP) and
could be ported to combat XP if grey-mob scaling were ever desired --
but it is not currently applied there.

## 265. Bio-Engineer DNA Sample Stat Inheritance -- Donor-Specific Snapshot, Not a Fixed Species Template, Quality-Scaled Through the Same Crafting Pipeline (extends sections 33, 45, 126, 229, 250)

**A DNA sample is not a fixed species/template roll -- it's a
donor-specific snapshot of that individual creature's live HAM/level/
resists/damage at sample time, converted through quality-scaled
formulas, meaning a boss/unique individual yields a measurably better
sample than a generic mob of the same species.**
`DnaManager::generateSample()` (DnaManager.cpp:338-473) reads live
values directly off the specific `Creature*` instance being sampled
-- `getMaxHAM()`, `getEffectiveResist()`/`getArmor()`,
`getChanceHit()`, `getDamageMin/Max()`, `getLevel()` -- converting
them via `Genetics::hamToValue`/`resistanceToValue`/etc. into the
`DnaComponent` fields; the `source` field also stores the donor's
unique name if it has one, explicitly flagged in-source as "Check
Here for unique npcs." Sample quality (VLQ-VHQ, a 1-7 scale rolled
in `SampleDnaTask::award()` from `dna_harvesting` skill mod + luck)
directly scales the resulting creature's stats exactly like resource
quality scales item stats (section 250) -- each `Genetics::*ToValue()`
call feeds quality into `randomizeValue()`, narrowing/raising the
random band around the donor-derived base. Creature assembly combines
**five** DNA samples (physique/prowess/mental/psychological/aggression
slots) via weighted formulas in `GeneticLabratory::
setInitialCraftingValues()` (:187-543), then applies a crafting
success modifier (`calculateAssemblyValueModifier()`, returning 1.05
on `AMAZINGSUCCESS`) that can lift the final creature's cap above the
raw weighted-average of the donor samples -- a genuine "exceed the
template" mechanic through ordinary crafting-success rolls, not a
separate rare/mutation system. `GeneticLabratory` derives from the
same `SharedLabratory` base as ordinary item crafting
(`ResourceLabratory`), reusing `CraftingValues` and the standard
assembly/experimentation success formulas -- the DNA-specific
behavior lives entirely in overridden `setInitialCraftingValues()`
and `experimentRow()`, which treat the five samples as component-slot
ingredients whose stats set experimentation caps, mirroring how
resource quality caps item stats.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) sampling a unique/named individual (vs.
a generic species mob) yields a measurably better DNA sample because
live stats, not base template stats, are captured. (2) higher
`dna_harvesting` skill produces both a better sample quality roll and
(via the shared crafting pipeline) a better finished creature. (3) no
single donor fully determines the outcome -- the final creature blends
five weighted DNA components, but an Amazing Success assembly roll can
push results up to 5% above the raw weighted average of all five
donors.

## 266. Ground Vehicle Fuel/Energy Consumption -- Confirmed Absent, Zero Per-Use Operating Cost, Only Passive Condition Decay (extends sections 18, 74, 78, 98, 210, 231)

**Ground vehicles have zero per-use operating cost -- no fuel,
energy, or charge field exists anywhere on `VehicleObject`/
`VehicleDeed`, and summoning/dismounting/driving never deducts any
resource; the only recurring cost is passive time-based condition
decay repaired with flat credits, not a fuel mechanic.**
`VehicleObject.idl:18-34` declares only `vehicleType`, `paintCount`,
`rentalVehicle`, `rentalUses` -- no fuel/energy member exists;
`getEnergy()` (:285-288) is confirmed to be an armor-effectiveness
resistance stat (`armor_eff_energy`, resistance to the "energy"
damage type), entirely unrelated to a consumable resource. A
codebase-wide search for fuel-related terminology returns only
unrelated crafting-resource-taxonomy hits
(`degraded_fuel_petrochem_solid`, a `RecycleTool` resource entry, not
a vehicle field). The generator-refuel pattern documented for
structures (sections 210/231) and ship capacitor/power research
(section 74) have zero counterpart anywhere in
`VehicleObjectImplementation.cpp`/`VehicleControlDeviceImplementation.cpp`
-- confirmed exclusively structure/ship concepts. Summon/dismiss from
the datapad
(`VehicleControlDeviceImplementation::generateObject()`, :22-118) is
gated only by not-dead/not-indoors/not-in-combat checks, a max-2
spawned-vehicles limit, and a 15-second `call_mount` delay outside
cities/camps -- no credit, fuel, or resource subtraction occurs
anywhere in the summon/store path. The only depleting counter found
is `rentalUses`, a time/use-limited rental-lease expiration counter
unrelated to fuel and never touched by non-rental vehicles.
`VehicleDecayTask::run()` periodically inflicts condition damage
(default every 600 seconds while spawned) independent of distance
traveled or actions taken -- a passive timer, not usage-based fuel
burn -- repaired via `RepairVehicleSuiCallback` for a flat credit cost
(`calculateRepairCost()`, paid via `subtractBankCredits()`) plus
optional city garage tax, never a consumable resource.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't design around a vehicle
fuel/energy system -- it's confirmed entirely absent, and the closest
analog (structure generators, ship capacitors) is architecturally
walled off from ground vehicles. (2) the only real recurring vehicle
cost is passive condition decay on a fixed timer, functionally a
maintenance tax paid in flat credits. (3) rental vehicles use a
separate use-count lease mechanic (`rentalUses`) that's easy to
mistake for fuel but is purely a rental-expiration counter.

## 267. Player Corpse Persistence -- No Despawn Timer, Bodies Are Permanently the Player's Own, PvP Corpse-Looting Structurally Absent (extends sections 29, 53, 95, 116)

**A killed player's body is not a separate corpse object at all --
it's the persistent `CreatureObject` character record itself, so
there is no despawn timer, no PvP corpse-looting is structurally
possible, and unlooted items are never lost, only condition-decayed
on clone.** `PlayerManagerImplementation::killPlayer()` (:1315-1573)
just sets posture to DEAD and calls `sendActivateCloneRequest()` --
it never calls anything like `scheduleDespawn()`; the body remains
exactly where the player died indefinitely until they select a
cloning facility, with no forced-clone timer if they never choose or
disconnect. This contrasts sharply with NPC/creature corpses, which
do have a real hardcoded despawn timer
(`CreatureManagerImplementation::notifyDestruction()`, :707-726: 10
seconds if empty of loot, 300 seconds/5 minutes if lootable) -- but
this applies only to `AiAgent` targets, never `CreatureObject`
players. Player corpses are structurally unlootable by other players,
confirmed by two independent code paths:
`LootCommand::doQueueCommand()` explicitly rejects any target that
isn't `isAiAgent()`, and `LootPlayerCorpseCommand.h`/
`SearchCorpseCommand.h`/`CorpseCommand.h` are all empty stubs with no
container-transfer logic whatsoever -- confirming and independently
re-verifying section 116's finding that killing another player never
grants any container access to their belongings. There is no timer
difference between PvP and PvE deaths, but a real decay-rule
difference exists by death type and insurance: inside
`sendPlayerToCloner()` (:1836-1878), the decay report only fires for
standard kills (`typeofdeath==0`, excluding coup-de-grace finishes) --
insured items take 1% max-condition damage and lose their single-use
`INSURED` bit, uninsured items take 5%, but **no item is ever
destroyed** by this process, only condition-decayed. Since the
player's own inventory is never opened to looters and nothing is
destroyed, there is no auto-return/mailbox fallback needed or found
-- unlooted items simply stay in the dead player's inventory and
travel with the character through cloning.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) there is no "corpse looting window" to
model for players in this codebase -- PvP corpse-looting simply
isn't implemented at the command level. (2) the only real despawn
timer in the corpse system (10s/300s) governs NPC kills exclusively,
never player deaths. (3) item risk on player death is entirely a
condition-decay mechanic (1% insured / 5% uninsured on standard
kills only), never a loss/destruction mechanic -- any "corpse
camping" feature request would require genuinely new systems, not a
config change.

## 268. Guild Bank/Treasury -- Confirmed Absent as a Distinct Mechanic, "Treasury" UI Strings Are Cosmetic Labels on Ordinary Structure Maintenance Surplus (extends sections 90, 111, 134, 140, 155, 156, 242)

**`GuildObject` has zero credit balance field of its own -- guilds
have no financial state whatsoever, and the "guild treasury" players
see in-game is entirely the generic per-structure maintenance-surplus
withdrawal mechanic (section 242's ADMIN-list access), relabeled with
guild-hall-specific UI strings, not a distinct guild-owned economic
system.** `GuildObject.idl`'s full field set (lines 24-444) is
entirely social/administrative -- `guildMembers`, `sponsoredPlayers`,
`waringGuilds`, election state, the permission bitmask -- with no
`credits`/`bank`/`funds` field anywhere; a repo-wide grep for guild
bank/treasury terminology returns zero matches, and the 8-bit
permission bitmask (section 134/155) has no funds-related bit,
consistent with there being no treasury object to gate access to in
the first place. What actually exists is `StructureManager::
promptWithdrawMaintenance`/`withdrawMaintenance`
(StructureManager.cpp:1229-1256, 1389-1409+), a "withdraw from
treasury" SUI flow gated by `structure->isGuildHall() &&
structure->isOnAdminList(creature)` -- the identical generic
per-structure ADMIN-list ACL any structure uses (section 242),
merely extended so a guild's object ID can be listed on that ACL.
Client strings like `@player_structure:withdraw_admin_only` are
cosmetic labels on the structure's own `getSurplusMaintenance()`
pool -- money any player contributed to that structure's upkeep,
regardless of guild membership -- not a guild-specific storage
container. Consistent with section 111's finding that "guild hall" is
not a distinct structure class at all (just any ordinary
player-owned structure with a Guild Terminal placed inside it, still
individually owned under the hood), the apparent "shared guild fund"
is entirely an emergent artifact of (a) any player being able to pay
maintenance into that structure and (b) ADMIN-list withdrawal being
restricted to structures flagged `isGuildHall()`.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) guilds have no financial state of their
own to query or modify -- `GuildObject` is purely social/
administrative. (2) the only "treasury" in the codebase is a
structure's maintenance-surplus pool, gated by the same generic
per-structure ADMIN list every structure uses, not any guild
permission bit. (3) building a real guild bank feature requires net-new
state on `GuildObject` (a credits field, deposit/withdraw natives, a
new permission bit) -- none of that scaffolding exists today; treat
"guild treasury" in player-facing strings as a naming choice on top
of ordinary structure mechanics, not evidence of a distinct system.

## 269. Emote System Scope -- Fixed Client-Resolved Catalog of Hundreds, No Freeform Text Emote, Two Confirmed Mechanical Side Effects (extends sections 70, 93)

**Emotes are dispatched through exactly two generic queue commands
handling an opaque client-resolved emote ID, not one command per
emote and not a freeform `/emote text` broadcast -- there is no
`/socialType`-style custom text composer anywhere in the codebase --
and while the catalog runs to several hundred entries with
essentially no server-side ID validation, only two systems attach any
mechanical consequence to specific emote IDs.** `SocialCommand.h:
16-25` is a pure locomotion/state gate for client-issued emote
commands (`/wave`, `/bow`, etc.) and does no text parsing at all; the
real execution path, `SocialInternalCommand.h:22-133`, parses only
`targetID` + integer `emoteID`, handing off to
`ChatManagerImplementation::handleSocialInternalMessage()`
(:796-902), which further reads `targetID emoteID anim text` where
`anim`/`text` are just 0/1 flags packed into the outgoing `Emote`
packet -- there is no server-parsed arbitrary string anywhere in this
path; the specific animation/text is an opaque client-resolved ID,
never player-typed text. A dedicated search for a classic-SWG-style
`/socialType text` freeform composer found nothing -- spatial chat
(say/shout, free text with no animation) and the emote catalog are
architecturally disjoint systems. `CreatureEmote.h` (explicitly
commented "Partial list," named IDs running to 366+) implies the real
datatable backing it has on the order of several hundred rows (the
reaction-manager Lua alone lists ~90 named emotes for its "insulting"
subset), and server-side validation of the incoming `emoteID` against
that datatable is essentially absent before broadcasting -- meaning
the entire standard catalog is equally accessible to any player with
no species/profession gate. The one exception is the separate
Holo-Emote system (`HoloEmoteCommand.h:165-191`), a distinct 16-item
catalog gated by owning a purchased holoemote generator, a charge
count, and a 30-second cooldown -- the only emote-adjacent cooldown
found anywhere. Two confirmed mechanical side effects exist beyond
pure cosmetics: `PetEmoteCommand.h:51-61` maps specific emote IDs to
real pet obedience/behavior state changes (praise, shame, alert,
follow-order with an obedience-chance roll), and
`ReactionManagerImplementation.cpp:260-370` implements an Imperial
guard "insult" mechanic where directing certain emotes at Imperial
NPCs triggers credit fines, faction-standing loss, and knockdowns via
a SUI fine-payment dialog.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the emote catalog is large but trusts
the client entirely -- any feature wanting to gate/unlock specific
emotes needs genuinely new server-side validation logic, since none
currently exists. (2) no freeform `/me`-text emote exists or is
plumbed anywhere; adding one would require a new command plus new
packet/broadcast logic, though it could reuse the proven
proximity/ignore-list broadcast machinery both spatial chat and
`Emote` already share. (3) only two hardcoded ID-lookup systems
attach mechanical consequences to emotes today (pet obedience,
Imperial-guard insult fines) -- there is no general "emote-as-trigger"
framework to extend for new content.

## 270. Player City Disincorporation -- Citizen-Count-Driven, Not Mayor-Inactivity-Driven, Ordinary Structures Survive Unharmed, City Hall Destruction Is the Actual Code-Level Trigger (extends sections 54, 77, 163, 207, 238)

**Disincorporation is triggered purely by citizen count falling below
a threshold, never by mayor inactivity -- ordinary player houses
survive city loss completely unharmed and merely stop being "in a
city," while civic/decoration structures beyond the contracted rank's
support are actively destroyed with mail warnings, and destroying the
city hall (for any reason) is the actual code-level event that
finalizes disincorporation.** City rank/citizen-count is re-evaluated
every update cycle in `CityManagerImplementation::processCityUpdate()`
(:737-812): if citizens fall below the current rank's threshold,
`contractCity()` runs; if citizens also fall below the rank-1
(OUTPOST) threshold (default 2, from `CitizensPerRank = {2,4,6,8,10}`
in `city_manager.lua:76`), the city is forced back to OUTPOST and
flagged for reassessment. No separate "mayor abandons city" trigger
exists anywhere in the city-management code -- mayor turnover is
handled entirely by the weekly election (section 207), a distinct
mechanism from disincorporation. `CityRegionImplementation::
destroyAllStructuresForRank()` (:749-796) explicitly **skips** any
structure where `!isCivicStructure()` -- only civic/decoration
structures requiring a rank the shrunken city no longer supports are
force-destroyed with warning mail; ordinary houses are never touched.
Because city membership is geographic and `SceneObject::cityRegion`
is a transient cached pointer resolved by region containment, once
the city region is destroyed, ordinary structures simply fall outside
any `CityRegion` and become effectively wilderness structures for
zoning/tax purposes -- not force-condemned, suffering no direct
destruction, just losing city tax/zoning association since there's no
longer a city to receive it. Two genuinely distinct grace periods
exist, separate from the maintenance/eviction grace period (section
163): `NewCityGracePeriod = 1440` minutes (24h) for a brand-new city
to reach minimum population, and `OldCityGracePeriod = 4320` minutes
(72h) for an established city that regresses below the minimum before
forced contraction, both enforced via `scheduleCitizenAssessment()`
with mayor warning/outcome mail at each step. Civic structures get
distinct, special-cased handling: destroying the city hall
specifically is itself the finalizing trigger --
`CityHallZoneComponent::destroyObjectFromWorld()` detects city-hall
destruction and calls `CityManager::destroyCity()` directly,
regardless of cause (assessment failure, redeed, GM action) -- with
no equivalent hook existing for ordinary player houses.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) disincorporation risk is purely a
population-tracking concern, not a mayor-engagement one -- a city
with an inactive but present-enough citizenry never disincorporates.
(2) player structures are safe from any disincorporation cascade --
only civic amenities beyond the new rank's support get destroyed,
with warning mail first. (3) city hall destruction (via any cause) is
the actual programmatic trigger for full disincorporation -- a useful
hook to know if building any city-lifecycle tooling.

## 271. Ranged Weapon Scope/Attachment System -- Confirmed Absent as a Post-Craft Mechanic, "Scope"/"Barrel" Are Pre-Crafting Ingredient Names Only, Genuine Gap vs. the Lightsaber Crystal Socket (extends sections 11, 181, 224, 240, 250)

**There is no scope/attachment slot system for ranged weapons
analogous to the lightsaber crystal socket -- "scope" and "barrel"
exist only as pre-crafting `Component`-class ingredients consumed
once during the parent weapon's crafting session, with zero
post-craft swap/upgrade path, confirming this is a genuine
implementation gap rather than an undocumented feature.**
`SceneObjectType.h:138-140` defines only `CLOTHINGATTACHMENT` and
`ARMORATTACHMENT` as attachment game-object types, plus an unrelated
`SHIPATTACHMENT` for space-ship components -- no `WEAPONATTACHMENT`
constant exists anywhere, and `Attachment.idl:26-27` hard-codes only
`CLOTHINGTYPE`/`ARMORTYPE`. A grep of `WeaponObjectImplementation.cpp`
for slotted-object usage shows exactly two slot names in use:
`"saber_inv"` (the lightsaber crystal container, section 181) and
`"default_weapon"` (the equipped-weapon slot) -- no scope/barrel/stock
slot container exists on `WeaponObject` at all. Weapon scopes and
barrels do exist as item-template categories, but as independent
craftable `Component`-class objects with their own experimentation
stats, consumed as raw ingredients rather than equipped: a pistol
schematic's `ingredientTitleNames` lists `"scope"` and a
weapon-specific barrel entry pointing at a `Component`-class resource
template, feeding the standard experimentation/assembly formula once
during the parent weapon's crafting, then ceasing to exist as a
separate object -- matching the immutable-after-crafting pattern
already confirmed for droid modules and crafting tools (sections
224/240). A dungeon-drop special-ingredient barrel functions exactly
like a superior ore/chemical substitute in the normal
resource-quality-inheritance pipeline (section 250), not an
attachable post-craft object. There is no swap/upgrade command, no
"scope slot" radial menu, and unlike `saber_inv`, no extraction/
reinsertion path for weapon components after the target weapon has
been produced.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) treat "weapon scope/barrel" purely as
crafting-ingredient vocabulary -- do not confuse it with the
lightsaber crystal socket system, the only genuine post-craft-swappable
weapon customization in the codebase. (2) building a real
scope/attachment-slot system requires new scaffolding from scratch: a
`WEAPONATTACHMENT` game-object type, a dedicated slotted container on
`WeaponObject` mirroring `saber_inv`, and insert/remove command
support. (3) the existing `Attachment` class (armor/clothing only)
is a plausible extension precedent to model such a system on, since it
already implements a generic reusable socketed-bonus-item pattern.

## 272. Jedi Padawan-to-Knight Trial Requirements -- Solo Screenplay-Driven Grind, No Mentor Mechanic, Gated by Skill-Point Build Completion Rather Than Level or Time (extends sections 100, 107, 146, 194, 213, 233)

**Progression from Padawan to Jedi Knight is entirely solo and
screenplay/NPC-driven with zero player-to-player mentorship
mechanic, gated by finishing two full Force discipline skill trees
(206+ cumulative Jedi skill points) rather than character level or
elapsed playtime, and the Knight Trials' Light/Dark Council choice is
the actual mechanical unlock point for FRS council rank tracking
(section 233), not an earlier milestone.** Padawan Trials
(`padawan_trials.lua`, driven by `trialData.lua:8-141`) require
completing all of 16 defined quests: one randomly selected first
(excluding the lightsaber trial), then further random selections from
`TRIAL_TALK`/`TRIAL_KILL`/`TRIAL_HUNT` types until 7 are done, at
which point the `TRIAL_LIGHTSABER` (craft a training saber, tune a
crystal) is forced as the final trial; a 3-strikes failure system
resets ALL padawan trial progress on a third failure. Knight Trials
(`knight_trials.lua`, `trialData.lua:143-235`) are 14 sequential
(not random) mostly kill-quota trials, with trial #8 forcing an
irrevocable, faction-gated Light/Dark Council choice (Imperials can't
choose Light, Rebels can't choose Dark) that determines trials 9-11's
enemy-faction targets. No mentor/sponsor mechanic exists anywhere --
both trial types compute eligibility and completion purely from the
player's own skill/screenplay state, consistent with and
independently reconfirming section 107's "Confirmed Absent" finding
for player-to-player Jedi mentorship. Eligibility gating goes well
beyond raw Force-sensitivity unlock (section 146): Padawan Trials
require 6 of the Force-sensitive discipline branches already learned
(`learnedBranches >= 6`); Knight Trials require **at least 2 fully-maxed
`force_discipline_*` skill trees and a cumulative total of ≥206 Jedi
skill points** spent -- a skill-point/build-completion gate, not a
level or playtime requirement. On completion, Padawan Trials award
`force_title_jedi_rank_02`, set `jediState=2`, and grant a Padawan
robe; Knight Trials award `force_title_jedi_rank_03`, set
`jediState` to 4 (Light) or 8 (Dark), call `setFrsCouncil()`/
`setFrsRank(0)` (the actual FRS eligibility unlock point, cross-referencing
section 233's council mechanics), force the player's faction to
Rebel/Imperial with Overt status, and grant a council-specific Knight
robe with a waypoint to the appropriate Jedi Enclave.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) Jedi progression is a solo grind with
zero mentorship infrastructure to build on -- any "Jedi mentor"
feature would be entirely new work. (2) the real gate before Knight
Trials is a skill-point/build-completion threshold (206+ points, 2
