maxed discipline trees), not character level -- a fast-leveled but
build-incomplete Jedi cannot rush Knight Trials. (3) FRS council
tracking (section 233) doesn't begin until Knight Trials completion,
not at Force-sensitivity unlock or Padawan promotion -- useful to
know when reasoning about when a Jedi character first becomes
FRS-eligible.

## 273. Crafting Station Public/Private Access -- Purely a Naming Convention, Governed Entirely by the Containing Structure's ENTRY List (extends sections 65, 242)

**"Public" crafting stations are not a real access-control mechanism
-- they're an item-naming convention that only affects whether an
ingredient hopper spawns, and station use is gated purely by the
containing structure's ENTRY list, with no station-specific
permission layer at all.** `RequestCraftingSessionCommand::
doQueueCommand()` performs zero building/ACL checks when starting a
crafting session -- it only verifies the station's parent is a cell
or the player is outdoors, and range (7m). The only actual permission
gate in the whole chain is one layer up:
`BuildingObjectImplementation`'s walk-in check
(`isOwnerOf` -> true, `isOnBanList` -> false, else
`isPrivateStructure() && !isOnEntryList(player)` -> false) -- the
identical ENTRY-list mechanism documented in section 242. Once a
player has physically entered the cell, no station-specific re-check
occurs. `CraftingStation.idl` stores only `type`/`effectiveness`/
`complexityLevel` -- no public/private boolean flag exists on the
object at all; `CraftingStationImplementation::
handleObjectMenuSelect()` merely checks whether the object's name
string contains "public" to decide whether to lazily spawn an
ingredient hopper -- a cosmetic naming check with zero bearing on who
can *use* the station. City/starport "public" stations use identical
access logic to private house stations -- the difference is entirely
data (public templates set a lower `complexityLevel`, e.g. 25 vs. 100
for private), not code; both extend the same `CraftingStation` class
with no separate "PublicCraftingStation" subclass. Draft schematics
for player-craftable public stations exist, meaning a player could
place a "public"-named station inside a private house, and it would
still only be reachable by whoever passes that house's ENTRY check --
"public" naming does not make a station world-accessible. The one
exception is the ingredient-hopper radial menu, which requires the
stricter ADMIN list rather than ENTRY -- an inconsistency worth
flagging for anyone reasoning about "who can fully use a station."

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't build a permission UI around
station-level access control -- there's no station-specific ACL to
intercept; all gating happens one layer up in the containing
structure's permission lists. (2) a "public" station is only truly
public if placed inside a structure with open/citizen-wide ENTRY
access (e.g. a city crafting district) -- placing one in a private
house doesn't make it accessible to outsiders. (3) hopper access is
gated stricter (ADMIN) than session-start access (ENTRY), a subtle
two-tier inconsistency to account for in any station-access tooling.

## 274. Entertainer Buff Duration Cap and Diminishing Returns -- Hard 2h10s Accrual Ceiling, No Anti-Shopping Cooldown, No Classic DR Curve (extends sections 48, 72, 137, 158, 244)

**Entertainer buffs have a hard duration ceiling on the pre-buff
accrual counter (~2 hours 10 seconds), but once applied the buff runs
on a single fixed-expiry timer with zero decay, buff-shopping between
entertainers is governed by the same ordinary same-CRC "reject-if-weaker"
replace rule documented in section 137 with no cooldown, and no
classic diminishing-returns curve exists anywhere in this system.**
`EntertainingSessionImplementation::addEntertainerBuffDuration()`
accumulates `2.0 * buffAcceleration` minutes per 10-second tick/flourish
into a per-patron counter, hard-capped at 120 minutes + 10 seconds --
that counter becomes the actual `PerformanceBuff` duration once
`activateEntertainerBuff()` fires. Once instantiated, the buff runs
on a single one-shot `BuffDurationEvent` timer that simply deletes the
buff at expiry -- no re-check, no decay, no renewal (`checkRenew()`
is false for this buff type, unlike some CC states). Switching
performers is governed by ordinary magnitude-gated replace: the new
buff is discarded outright if weaker than the existing one
(`oldBuff->getBuffStrength() > buffStrength`), otherwise
`BuffList::addBuff` destroys and replaces it -- **there is no
cooldown/timer preventing immediate re-application from a different
entertainer**, identical to the doctor-enhance-buff pattern (section
158). Two gates exist before any buff is even *offered* -- a 10-second
minimum accrued-duration floor and a 60-continuous-second minimum
watch/listen requirement -- but these are one-time thresholds to earn
a buff, not anti-shopping cooldowns. No scaling-down of buff magnitude
exists for repeated applications from different sources, and no
engine-wide buff-slot cap exists anywhere (independently re-confirmed
here); the only magnitude limiter is a flat skill-mod-based strength
ceiling (125% cap) on a single entertainer's own output, not
cross-entertainer stacking. While watching, buff strength/duration
counters only ever accumulate toward the caps above -- nothing
decrements them mid-performance, and once applied, the resulting
buff's strength is fixed for its full duration with no decay-while-active
logic anywhere.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) repeated re-buffing is bounded only by
the ~130-minute accrual cap and the 125% strength cap, plus the
standard reject-weaker/destroy-and-replace same-CRC rule -- no
diminishing-returns curve exists to model. (2) "buff shopping" between
entertainers works exactly like any other same-CRC refresh: instant
replace if strictly stronger, silent no-op otherwise, with zero
cooldown penalty. (3) any future anti-abuse or DR mechanic would need
entirely new infrastructure (a cooldown field, an application-count
tracker, or a magnitude-decay function) -- none of that scaffolding
exists in `EntertainingSessionImplementation` or `PerformanceBuff`
today.

## 275. Space Real Estate / Player-Owned Space Structures -- Confirmed Absent, All Space Content Is Ship-Centric, `PobShipObject` Is the Closest (Incomplete) Substitute (extends sections 111, 131, 152)

**There is no player-placeable structure in space zones anywhere in
the codebase -- every ownable space object traces back to
`ShipObject`/`ShipAiAgent`, and `SpaceStationObject` is confirmed
NPC-only infrastructure with zero ownership/permission/customization
scaffolding to extend.** A repo-wide search for space-zone structure
placement, lot systems, or deeds found nothing tying
`StructureObject`/lot-placement machinery to any space object type.
`SpaceStationObject.idl` extends `ShipAiAgent` (the NPC/AI ship
base, not a player-container base), and its implementation only
defines an out-of-range navigation constant -- it has no permission
list, no ownership field, no interior cells, and no customization
hooks, confirmed as a pure navigation/launch-point reference object.
This is distinct from the docking-permission stub (section 131/152),
which is a ship-to-ship proximity feature, not station ownership.
`PobShipObject` (Player-Owned-Building ship, the Millennium
Falcon-scale hull) is the closest thing to a "mobile base," providing
walkable interior cells, a `ShipPermissionList` with ADMIN-list
checks, a 100-item player-storage cap, and multiple launch points --
but a targeted search found **no** tie between `PobShipObject` and
crafting-station or vendor placement anywhere in the source tree, so
it functions as a mobile container/hangout with access control, never
a crafting hub, guild hall, or vendor platform -- it doesn't carry
the guild/city functions ground structures do. This is a clean,
verifiable absence, not a stubbed/partial feature: every relevant
object type traces to `ShipObject`/`ShipAiAgent`, with no
space-specific subclass of `StructureObject` or any lot/deed system
reachable from a space zone.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) a "player space station" feature would
be wholly new engine work -- `SpaceStationObject` has zero
ownership/permission/customization scaffolding to extend; it's purely
an AI-agent navigation marker. (2) `PobShipObject` is the nearest
available substitute for space housing but explicitly lacks
crafting-station/vendor/guild-function integration -- don't assume
parity with ground houses when reasoning about space real estate
features. (3) space-zone player content is 100% ship-centric with no
lot/deed/structure-placement pathway into space zones at all.

## 276. GCW Faction Standing Cap -- Three-Tier Structure by Faction Type/Relationship, No Diminishing Returns, Rank and Standing Share One Points Pool (extends sections 79, 100, 175, 179)

**Faction standing has no single flat cap -- it's a three-tier
structure gated by faction type and relationship to the player's own
declared faction, gains never taper as the cap approaches (flat-add-then-clamp,
not a smoothing curve), and rank/standing share the identical points
pool rather than being separate resources.**
`PlayerObjectImplementation::increaseFactionStanding()` applies one of
three clamps: non-GCW factions cap at a flat **5000**; the player's
own declared GCW faction (rebel/imperial) caps at a rank-scaled value
= `max(1000, getRankCost(rank) * 20)` -- genuinely rising as the
player's current rank rises, not fixed; and a GCW faction that isn't
the player's own (enemy-faction standing) caps at a flat **1000**.
Gains are computed at full nominal value every time, then hard-clamped
once via `Math::min` -- there is no scaling-down as standing approaches
the cap; a kill/quest/bribe grants its full amount right up to the
last point, with overflow simply truncated, and once at the cap the
client switches to a distinct "max faction" message rather than
showing a reduced gain. `FactionStandingList` stores `rebelPoints`/
`imperialPoints` as the *only* backing values for GCW standing --
`factionRank` is stored merely as a string title, not a points total,
confirming rank promotion spends directly from this same standing
pool (via the recruiter conversation) rather than feeding a separate
rank-XP ladder. Both the delegate/transfer mechanic (section 179) and
the Cries of Alderaan bonus respect the cap with double enforcement:
`DelegateFactionPointsCommand` pre-checks the target's resulting
total against their cap and rejects the transfer outright before even
calling the standard clamped `increaseFactionStanding()`; the CoA
bonus likewise applies its +10% and then re-clamps against the
recipient's own rank cap -- there is no known path to push a
recipient's standing above their rank's ceiling through either
mechanic.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) quote the correct tier when discussing
"max standing" -- 5000 for regular/non-GCW factions, a rank-scaled
value for the player's own GCW faction, 1000 for enemy-faction
standing -- there is no single universal number. (2) model standing
gain as flat-add-then-clamp, never a smoothing/taper curve as the cap
nears. (3) don't design around a separate "rank currency" resource --
`rebelPoints`/`imperialPoints` are simultaneously the standing pool
and the rank-progression currency in one field.

## 277. Root/Snare Crowd-Control -- A Real Status-Effect Category Exists in the Engine but Is Almost Entirely Unused, PvE-Only, No Trap-Disarm Counter-Play (extends sections 91, 114, 116, 117, 189, 210)

**A genuine root/snare status-effect category (`IMMOBILIZED`/
`FROZEN`) exists in the engine, mechanically wired into movement code,
but is almost entirely dormant in live gameplay -- the sole exception
is a PvE-only Scout throwable trap, and neither weapon special
attacks nor Force powers apply any root/snare effect anywhere.**
`CreatureState.h:31-36` defines `IMMOBILIZED=0x10000` and
`FROZEN=0x20000` as distinct bits from `STUNNED`/`BLINDED`/`DIZZY`/
`INTIMIDATED`, exposed via `isSnared()`/`isImmobilized()` (both test
`IMMOBILIZED`) and `isRooted()`/`isFrozen()` (both test `FROZEN`).
These are real movement-only debuffs, not incapacitation:
`AiAgentImplementation.cpp` halves NPC speed on `IMMOBILIZED` and
drops speed to near-zero on `FROZEN`; player movement packets are
blocked server-side while `isFrozen()`.
`CreatureObjectImplementation.cpp` provides `setSnaredState()`/
`setRootedState()` wrapping a `StateBuff` with proper fly-text --
but critically, `setSnaredState()` is confirmed dead code, never
invoked anywhere in the codebase, and `setRootedState()` is invoked
exactly once, by the GM-only moderation command `FreezePlayerCommand`
(freeze+mute a player, section 203), not any player combat ability. A
genuine deployable Scout trap system does exist, distinct from
minefields (section 116): `/throwTrap`, gated by
`outdoors_scout_novice` + a `trapping` skill mod, applies a
`TrapBuff` -- one crafted variant, the "Adhesive Mesh" trap, sets
`FROZEN` for a real 10-second root. However this is explicitly
**PvE-only**: the command hard-blocks pets and requires the target be
`isCreature() && isMonster()`, re-checked again at throw-resolution
time -- it cannot target players under any circumstance. Weapon
special attacks (section 114/201/222) and Force powers (section 210)
were confirmed via targeted search to apply zero root/snare effects
anywhere -- the called-shot leg-targeting family only forces a
damage-pool/hit-location outcome, never a movement debuff. No
trap-disarm/detection mechanic exists anywhere, unlike the covert
detector system for minefields (section 117) -- a placed Scout trap
simply expires on its own timer or use-count with no counter-play for
the target.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) root/snare is real, mechanically wired
infrastructure (`IMMOBILIZED`/`FROZEN` genuinely slow/halt movement)
that's almost entirely unused by shipped content -- a strong
extension point if PvP CC content were ever desired. (2) the one live
root effect (Scout's Adhesive Mesh trap) is hard-locked to PvE
targets by an explicit `isMonster()` check -- there is no player-usable
root/snare anywhere in PvP today. (3) `setSnaredState()` is genuinely
dead code worth knowing about if reviving/wiring a snare mechanic --
the plumbing exists but nothing calls it.

## 278. Structure Furniture Lighting -- A Server-Tracked Burnout Timer Only, No Illumination/Visibility Mechanic, No Toggle Command, No Weather Interaction (extends sections 12, 37, 60, 246)

**Lit furniture (lamps, etc.) has real server-tracked state, but it
governs only a burnout/decay countdown, not illumination -- there is
no light intensity/radius field, no on/off toggle command, no
stealth/visibility hook, and no interaction with the day-night/weather
system anywhere in the codebase.** A real `LightObject` class
(extending `FurnitureObject`) tracks `lifespan`/`burntOut`/
`lifespanSeconds` per object, populated from crafting experimentation
attributes -- but no radius, intensity, or "illumination" field
exists anywhere, and the base `FurnitureObject` class itself has zero
extra members beyond this. "On" and "off" lamp states are **separate
crafted item templates**, not a runtime toggle -- e.g. a desk lamp
has one draft schematic targeting an unlit template and another
targeting a lit template, entirely distinct crafted objects.
Server-side, a `LightObserver` watches for the object being placed in
a cell and tracks lifespan; once the lifespan expires, the object
auto-destroys itself and spawns a replacement using the
unlit/extinguished appearance template, setting `burntOut=true` --
there is no `ExtinguishCommand`/`RelightCommand`/toggle radial found
anywhere, and a targeted search for toggle-related terminology across
the repo returns zero server code matches. No detection/stealth/
visibility hook of any kind exists -- the light object's attribute
list only ever writes a cosmetic lifespan tooltip string; nothing
touches `CreatureObject` stats, stealth/concealment mods, or any
detection/combat calculation. The weather/day-night system (section
60) is entirely disconnected from structures -- a grep of the weather
manager directory for interior/cell/indoor terminology returns zero
matches, consistent with section 246's finding that structure
interiors are fixed client-baked geometry with no server lighting
state tied to exterior time-of-day.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) placing/crafting a "lit" lamp only buys
a countdown timer server-side -- when it expires, the object
auto-replaces itself with the unlit template; this is a decay/consumable
mechanic, not an illumination system. (2) there is no in-game verb to
manually turn a lamp on/off -- "on" and "off" are simply separate
factory-crafted item variants players must craft/place separately.
(3) do not expect any tie between interior lighting and stealth/
detection/combat, or between weather/day-night cycle and structure
interiors -- both couplings are confirmed absent.

## 279. Direct Player-to-Player Item Transfer Outside Secure Trade -- `GiveItemCommand` Provides an Unconfirmed, Zero-Consent Direct Transfer, Correcting the "Secure Trade Is the Only Mechanism" Assumption (extends sections 68, 175, 253)

**Secure trade is NOT the only player-to-player item-transfer
mechanism -- `GiveItemCommand` provides a direct, single-action
transfer straight into a target player's inventory with no
confirmation dialog and no recipient-side consent check at all,
correcting an assumption implicit in earlier sections that trade or
mail exhausted the transfer options.** `GiveItemCommand.h`'s general
case (when the drop target is any `CreatureObject` that isn't a
vendor/pet/droid-module target) directly calls
`targetObject->transferObject(giveObject, -1, true)` once
`canAddObject()` succeeds -- no SUI, no trade-window state machine
like `SecureTradeCommand`, firing instantly as an `'immediate'`
command with a `'required'` target type. Permission checks in this
path only ever cover the *giver* -- `checkContainerPermission(creature,
MOVEOUT)` on the source container and `checkContainerPermission(creature,
MOVECONTAINER)` on the item itself, both validating the giver's own
ownership -- while `canAddObject()` on the recipient's side only
validates container-type/volume/no-trade-lineage rules, **never**
checking the recipient's own OPEN/MOVEIN container permissions. This
confirms a genuine, functioning `/give`-equivalent distinct from
ground-drop (visible/interceptible by anyone nearby) or shared-container
placement (gated by that structure's own permission groups) -- it
delivers straight into a chosen player's inventory via a single
client action (the "Give" drag/radial). The companion-as-mule
workaround this raises is confirmed foreclosed:
`CompanionObjectImplementation::isAuthorizedActor()` gates every
companion interaction to the linked owner or a privileged GM, and no
`transferCompanion`/reassign-owner method exists anywhere in the
companion object tree -- every "transfer" reference concerns moving
items into/out of a companion's own inventory bag, never reassigning
the companion itself to a different player, so loading a companion
with gear and handing off the companion is not a viable indirect
gifting path.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) sections 68/253 should be understood as
incomplete on this point -- secure trade is not the sole item-transfer
mechanism; `GiveItemCommand` bypasses it entirely with zero recipient
consent. (2) this `giveItem` path is arguably a larger scam/griefing
surface than mail (which is confirmed item-incapable per section 253)
precisely because it requires no recipient acknowledgment -- worth
flagging for any anti-exploit/anti-scam review. (3) the companion
system remains a dead end for indirect item-gifting -- ownership
binding via `isAuthorizedActor()`/`getLinkedCreature()` is hard-coded
and non-transferable.

## 280. Non-Grouped Kill-Credit Sharing -- Shared Per-Creature ThreatMap Grants XP to Every Damaging Attacker Regardless of Group, Loot Goes Winner-Take-All by Damage Contribution (extends sections 37, 44, 55, 61, 68)

**The `ThreatMap` used for XP distribution is a single shared map per
creature covering every attacker regardless of group membership, so
non-grouped players genuinely "assist-farm" off each other's kills
with full damage-proportional XP for both parties -- but loot is
winner-take-all by aggregate damage contribution, enforced by a real
container-permission gate, not a first-come/loot-ninja free-for-all,
and there is no minimum-contribution threshold for either.**
`ThreatMap` is a single `VectorMap<TangibleObject*, ThreatMapEntry>`
owned by the creature itself, keyed by individual attacker with zero
per-group partitioning anywhere in the class -- damage is recorded
per-attacker for every damage event regardless of group.
`PlayerManagerImplementation::disseminateExperience()` loops over
every entry in the map with no group filter, awarding
`xpAmount = baseXp * damage/totalDamage` per damage-type bucket to
each individual attacker -- group membership only multiplies the
result by a group bonus and adds separate squad-leader XP, it never
gates eligibility; the only eligibility filter found is a
proximity/zone check (must share the destructed object's zone, within
80 units). Confirmed directly: two solo, non-grouped players who both
damage the same creature **both** receive damage-proportional XP.
Loot rights instead go to `getHighestDamageGroupLeader()`, which
scans the whole threat map, aggregates damage per group (or per lone
individual), and returns whoever/whichever group holds the single
highest aggregate (excluding DoT damage) -- for two non-grouped
players this reduces to a simple higher-total-damage-wins comparison,
not first-hit tagging and not final-blow. This is enforced by a real
permission gate, not merely a convention:
`ContainerImplementation::canAddObject()` checks the corpse's stamped
`lootOwnerID` against the looting player's own object ID and returns
`NOLOOTPERMISSION` on mismatch -- a lower-damage non-grouped player
genuinely cannot open/loot the corpse. However, there is no minimum-damage
threshold anywhere in this path -- even one point of damage earns a
threat-map entry, an XP share, and (if it happens to be the highest)
full loot rights.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) non-grouped players can freely
assist-farm XP off each other's kills with no group requirement --
every attacker on the shared threat map gets damage-proportional XP.
(2) loot is winner-take-all by total damage contribution, hard-enforced
by a container-permission check -- a low-damage participant earns XP
but cannot loot even a creature they helped kill. (3) there is no
anti-kill-steal threshold for either XP or loot -- one point of damage
is sufficient to be XP-eligible, and being the single top damage
dealer (even marginally) is sufficient to win loot outright.

## 281. Structure Lot Allocation -- Per-Player Recomputed Budget, Not a Finite City-Wide Pool, No Cooldown, No Leasing (extends sections 35, 54, 77, 260, 270)

**A "lot" is a per-player, live-recomputed budget (default 10), not a
finite pool a city can run out of -- destroying or redeeding a
structure frees both lot capacity and physical placement space
instantly with zero cooldown, and no lot-rental/leasing mechanic
exists anywhere as an alternative to outright deed ownership.**
`PlayerObjectImplementation::getLotsRemaining()` starts from a flat
`maximumLots` field (default 10, set at character creation) and
subtracts `getLotSize()` for every structure currently in that
player's `ownedStructures` list, resolved fresh on every call -- there
is no separate "lots used" counter and no city-side
`totalLots`/`lotsAvailable` field anywhere in the city management
code; lot capacity is purely an individual player attribute, not a
shared civic resource other citizens compete over. Because this is a
live recompute rather than a decremented counter, once a structure
leaves `ownedStructures` via destruction or redeed, the player's lot
capacity self-corrects on the very next call with nothing to
reconcile -- and the physical placement footprint-overlap check
scans live scene objects, so once a structure is actually removed
from the world (immediate, not deferred), the ground it occupied is
immediately eligible for a new placement by any player, with no
grace-period field anywhere. A targeted search for lease/leasing/
rental terminology across the structure and lot code returns nothing
relevant -- the only "rental" concept in the codebase is an unrelated
vehicle-rental NPC service; the only recurring-payment mechanic tied
to structures is maintenance-upkeep/property tax on an *owned*
structure, never a payment for temporary lot occupancy. `maximumLots`
itself is adjustable only via a GM-only `/adjustLotCount` command.
City rank does not affect a player's personal lot capacity at all --
it instead gates which *structure types* (civic/rank-required
buildings) may be placed within that city and caps civic-amenity
counts scaled by rank, an entirely separate mechanism from personal
lot budgets.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) lots are a per-player recomputed budget,
not a finite city-wide resource -- there's nothing for a city to "run
out of" at the civic level. (2) structure destruction/redeed frees
both lot capacity and physical space instantly with no cooldown to
model. (3) no leasing/rental system exists for lots -- the only
ownership path is deed-purchase-then-own, and city rank affects civic
structure eligibility, never personal lot allowance.

## 282. Combat Critical Hit Mechanic -- Confirmed Absent, No Crit-Chance RNG Layer Anywhere, Damage Variance Is Entirely Weapon Roll Plus Fixed Multipliers (extends sections 201, 222, 258)

**Core3 combat has no random critical-hit system at all -- after a
successful hit (per section 258's formula), damage variance comes
entirely from a single weapon min/max roll plus a short list of
deterministic, fixed multipliers, with zero "crit chance" skillmod or
probability roll anywhere in the pipeline.**
`CombatManager::calculateDamage()` (all three overloads) is the full
post-hit pipeline: it sets damage to the weapon/attack's minimum, adds
exactly one `System::random(diff)` call (the weapon/attack max-min
spread), then applies only deterministic multipliers -- additive
skill-mod bonuses via `applyDamageModifiers()`, a flat 1.5x
player-vs-NPC multiplier, a flat 1.25x melee multiplier, a flat 1.5x
knocked-down/prone bonus, toughness/Force-defense mitigation, and a
flat 0.25x PvP reduction. There is exactly one random roll per damage
calculation across all three overloads -- the min/max weapon-damage
roll itself, never a second "did it crit" roll.
`applyDamageModifiers()` enumerates every skill mod consulted for
damage (`private_melee_damage_bonus`, `private_ranged_damage_bonus`,
`private_damage_bonus`, `private_damage_multiplier` -- itself a flat
multiply, not a chance-based roll -- `private_damage_divisor` and its
variants, `private_damage_susceptibility`); none of them, nor any
other skill mod in the codebase, reference "crit" -- a full-text
case-insensitive search for "crit" returns zero hits in
`CombatManager.cpp/.h`, `CreatureAttackData.h/.cpp`, or any skill-mod
table (the only "crit" string matches anywhere are unrelated: an
incapacitation message key and crafting's `AMAZINGSUCCESS`
terminology, a wholly separate mechanic). Called shots use the fixed
`damageMultiplier` field documented in sections 201/222/258 (headShot
1.5x, bodyShot 2x, etc.) -- a plain float set once per Lua command
definition, never touched by `System::random()` anywhere in
`CreatureAttackData.cpp` or the `calculateDamage` call sites.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) do not design around a "crit chance"
stat/skillmod -- it has no runtime representation anywhere in this
codebase; the closest analog to burst damage is the called-shot fixed
multiplier or Force-power min/max variance. (2) damage variance for
balance purposes reduces to: weapon min/max spread + additive
skillmods + a short list of hardcoded flat multipliers -- fully
deterministic given the single roll. (3) a "crit" feature would need
genuinely new code in `applyDamageModifiers()`/`calculateDamage()`;
nothing in the existing pipeline can be reinterpreted as one.

## 283. Vendor/NPC Purchase Haggling -- Confirmed Absent, All Prices Are Fixed "Buy It Now," Auction Bidding Is the Only Price Flexibility and Only Allows Bidding Up (extends sections 101, 108, 136, 144, 157, 214, 251)

**No haggling/negotiation mechanic exists anywhere for buying from
NPC or player vendors -- all purchases are pay-the-listed-price, the
only "merchant discount" skills reduce seller-side costs never
buyer-side prices, and the sole price-flexibility mechanism (auction
bidding, section 144) is structurally one-directional, rejecting any
bid below the seller's floor.** A codebase-wide search for haggle/
negotiate/barter terminology returns zero gameplay-relevant hits --
flavor dialogue in a junk-dealer NPC's conversation script even
states explicitly in-universe "No barter. Ya deal or not deal."
`crafting_merchant_sales_01/02/03` and `crafting_merchant_master`,
the only "merchant discount" skills found, reduce bazaar listing fees
and player-vendor maintenance rate -- both seller-side costs
documented in section 157, never touching what a buyer pays.
`AuctionManagerImplementation::doInstantBuy()` charges exactly the
seller's listed price plus any baked-in city sales tax, with zero
buyer input into the amount; the only price flexibility anywhere is
the seller-initiated bid-war mechanic (section 144), but
`checkBidAuction()` explicitly rejects any bid below the listed
price -- a buyer can only offer at or above the seller's floor, never
negotiate below it, meaning the mechanism cannot function as
buyer-favorable haggling under any circumstance. Consistent with
section 214's independent finding that all vendor prices are
hardcoded flat integers with no dynamic supply/demand pricing, and
confirmed here that NPC shopkeepers use the identical
`AuctionManager`/vendor-terminal backend as player vendors -- there is
no separate "shopkeeper" class, so NPC and player-vendor purchases
share identical fixed-price mechanics with zero exceptions found.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) confirmed absent, with in-game flavor
text even acknowledging it diegetically -- there is no haggle/
negotiate/barter mechanic to model or account for anywhere. (2) the
`crafting_merchant_*` skill line is entirely seller-side (listing fee
and maintenance-rate reduction); don't confuse it with a buyer
discount. (3) building a genuine haggling feature requires wholly new
scaffolding -- no existing hook (skill mod, dialogue branch, or
price-modifier field) exists anywhere to extend for buyer-initiated
discounts.

## 284. Guild Inactive-Member Auto-Removal -- Confirmed Absent, the Periodic Guild Update Task Only Prunes Deleted Characters, Never Inactive Ones (extends sections 47, 90, 226, 268)

**Guilds have zero automatic inactivity-purge mechanic -- membership
persists indefinitely absent manual action (kick, self-leave,
disband, or character deletion), and the recurring hourly-to-weekly
`GuildObject` update task is a data-integrity sweep for
no-longer-existing character IDs, not an engagement/activity
mechanic.** `GuildMemberInfo`'s complete field set is `playerID`,
`guildTitle`, `permissions`, and a deprecated allegiance field -- no
`lastLogin`/`lastOnline`/`lastActivity` timestamp exists anywhere in
the guild data model, confirmed via full binary/JSON serialization
inspection. `GuildManagerImplementation::processGuildUpdate()`,
scheduled on a randomized 1-hour-to-1-week cadence, performs exactly
one membership check: `existsPlayerCreatureOID(memberID)` -- a lookup
against the player-name registry that only confirms whether the
character object ID still exists in the database (i.e., the character
was permanently deleted or transferred away), never whether the
player has logged in recently or is currently online. This is
character-existence garbage collection, structurally analogous in
*scheduling pattern* to `StructureMaintenanceTask` (a recurring
task) but functionally unrelated to activity -- it never inspects
login time, online status, or session history in any way. A
secondary consequence: if member count drops below the guild's
required minimum after this prune, the guild auto-disbands -- but
this is triggered exclusively by deleted characters, never inactive
ones. No guild dues/membership-fee mechanic exists either (a search
for dues/upkeep/fee/lastLogin terminology in the guild code returns
nothing) -- guild-hall structures have their own separate
maintenance-payment system (a structure-object property, per section
90), but non-payment affects the structure only (condemnation), never
touching the guild's member roster.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) guild membership in this codebase is
permanent absent explicit action -- there is no AFK-kick or
inactivity-purge system to account for in any guild feature. (2) the
recurring `processGuildUpdate` task is a data-integrity sweep (dead
OIDs, sponsorship cleanup, election processing), not an engagement
mechanic -- don't confuse the two when reasoning about guild
lifecycle. (3) implementing an inactivity purge would require adding
a genuinely new field to `GuildMemberInfo` and a new check in
`processGuildUpdate` (or a dedicated task) -- none of that scaffolding
exists today.

## 285. Parallel Crafting Sessions -- Single-Session-Per-Player for Interactive Crafting (Silent Replace, Not a Hard Block), Factory Mass-Production Runs Fully Decoupled (extends sections 45, 179, 200, 220)

**A player can never have two interactive hand-crafting sessions open
at once -- starting a second silently cancels the first rather than
blocking the request -- but factory mass-production is architecturally
independent of the interactive `CraftingSession` machinery entirely,
meaning a crafter can run an unattended factory and simultaneously
open a normal personal-station crafting session with zero conflict.**
`CraftingSession` is stored via the generic single-slot session
facade (`SessionFacadeType::CRAFTING`), and `CreatureObject` exposes a
single active-session-per-type lookup -- there is no vector/list of
concurrent sessions anywhere in the searched tree, so a given creature
can hold at most one `CraftingSession` reference regardless of how
many crafting tools/stations exist nearby.
`RequestCraftingSessionCommand.h` confirms the enforcement mechanism:
any existing session is locked and unconditionally `cancelSession()`'d
before a brand-new session object is constructed for the request --
there is no "you already have a session open" rejection message
anywhere; the player is never blocked, the old session is simply torn
down (invoking whatever resource-return logic applies, consistent
with section 220's finding that leaving the ingredient screen is the
real commit point -- pre-assembly cancellation returns resources,
post-assembly cancellation does not). Factory mass-production
(`FactoryObject`, section 179/200's 1000-unit cap) runs entirely
decoupled from this machinery: it's an `InstallationObject` subclass
whose `handleOperateToggle()`/`startFactory()` schedules a
self-contained background task running on the installation's own
timer, with zero references to `getActiveSession`, `SessionFacadeType`,
or `CraftingSession` found anywhere in the factory implementation file
-- only display metadata ties a run to its initiating player, never
session state. Practically, a crafter toggles a factory on, then can
immediately walk to a personal station and open a normal interactive
session -- the factory's background task keeps running unattended,
gated only by container/hopper/complexity mechanics, never by the
player's own session slot.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) interactive (hand) crafting is strictly
single-session-per-player, enforced by simple replace-on-new-request
logic rather than a hard reject -- any tooling built against this
must warn users before re-initiating a session, since the old one is
silently destroyed. (2) factory mass-production is a fully independent
background installation-task loop -- there's no coupling to the
interactive crafting session slot at all. (3) "parallel crafting" is
real but asymmetric: unlimited concurrent background factory runs are
possible (bounded only by lot/structure placement), while interactive
crafting remains strictly single-session.

## 286. Creature Mount Auto-Follow -- Real AI-Driven Follow Behavior While Unridden, Hard-Blocked Command Input and Position-Overwritten Movement While Ridden, No Auto-Restore on Dismount (extends sections 28, 78, 243)

**Summoned pets default to genuine AI-pathed follow-owner behavior,
but mounting a creature hard-blocks all pet-command inputs and
overwrites its position every tick with the rider's client-controlled
transform rather than formally pausing the AI tree -- and dismounting
never automatically re-issues a follow command, so whatever state
existed before mounting simply persists.** On pet summon,
`PetControlDeviceImplementation::spawnObject()` sets
`pet->setFollowObject(player)` and the last command to FOLLOW by
default, driven by genuine behavior-tree leaf actions that resolve a
follow target and steer the `AiAgent` toward it each tick via the
normal AI pathing system -- players can also re-issue an explicit
follow command to reset the target. When mounted, every pet-command
handler that would change AI behavior state
(`PetFollowCommand`/`PetAttackCommand`/`PetGuardCommand`/`PetPatrolCommand`/
etc., a dozen-plus command files) begins with an identical
`if (pet->hasRidingCreature()) return GENERALERROR;` check --
confirming command-driven AI control is hard-disabled while a rider
occupies the creature. Movement while ridden and movement while
following use genuinely different code paths: ridden transform
packets are mirrored directly from the rider's client input onto the
mount object every tick (`updateVehiclePosition()`, invoked whenever
the moving object's parent is a mount/vehicle), with no
`CollisionManager` pathfinding or `setNextPosition`/patrol queue
involved at all -- a direct positional mirror, not AI computation --
while an unridden following pet moves via genuine behavior-tree-issued
`setNextPosition()` calls, real AI-computed pathing steps. The
behavior tree itself is never torn down on mount (`runBehaviorTree()`
has no mounted-state gating, which is why the mount remains an
independently attackable target per section 243), but since commands
are blocked and position is overwritten every tick, no new follow/
patrol/guard state can be set while mounted -- the AI is effectively
starved of input rather than formally paused. Critically, dismount
commands only clear the mounted-state flags and reposition the
player; they never call `setFollowObject()` or re-issue a FOLLOW
command -- whatever follow target existed before mounting (or none,
if it was a vehicle) simply resumes/persists on the next AI tick with
no dedicated "restore follow on dismount" logic anywhere.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) summoned pets follow via real AI pathing,
not a scripted trigger -- useful precedent for any new pet-behavior
feature. (2) mounting doesn't pause the AI tree formally, it starves
it of command input and overwrites position every tick -- a subtle
distinction worth knowing if debugging mount-related pet state. (3)
there is no auto-restore-follow-on-dismount logic anywhere -- a
pre-mount follow target (or lack thereof) simply carries over
unchanged after dismounting.

## 287. Structure Nameplate/Signage -- A Real, Always-Present, Player-Examinable In-World Sign Exists for Ordinary Player Houses and Guild Halls, Not Just Vendors (extends sections 104, 152, 246)

**Contrary to section 246's narrower "vendor-only sign" framing,
ordinary player houses and guild halls ship with a default,
skill-free "house address" sign that is a real in-world object other
players can examine -- `/namestructure` is a dual-effect command that
updates both the internal management label and the physical sign's
displayed text simultaneously, and the vendor-gated `shop_sign` set
is a sibling option alongside this default sign, not a replacement
for it.** `NameStructureCommand.h` implements `/namestructure`,
requiring structure ownership, rejecting GCW HQs/turrets/minefields,
profanity-filtering the input, then calling
`structure->setCustomObjectName(name, true)` -- available on any
player-owned `BuildingObject` (house or guild hall) via a
management radial, not restricted to vendor-flagged structures.
`BuildingObject`'s override of this setter updates both `customName`
(the internal/management label used in `/structurestatus` and
tooltips) **and** `signName`, then calls native `updateSignName()`,
which pushes the new text onto the actual world `SignObject` --
these are not coincidentally shared concepts; the sign's displayed
text is literally driven by the structure's custom name field, with a
"Condemned" override automatically substituted if the structure is
condemned. That sign is a genuinely always-present, player-examinable
object: it exposes a "Read Sign" radial menu option any nearby player
can select, opening a message box displaying the current name.
Critically, every player-house and guild-hall template's child-object
list spawns a default `house_address` sign with **no required
skill** -- confirming this is baseline, universal structure content,
not a premium feature. Separate `shop_sign_s01-s04` entries are also
listed on the same templates, gated behind
`crafting_merchant_management_01-04` skill requirements -- this is
what section 246's "vendor-only sign" finding actually referred to,
but it's a sibling option the owner can swap to via a "Change Sign"
radial, not the exclusive signage mechanism for the structure.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) ordinary player structures have a real,
visible in-world nameplate system, not merely a management-UI label
-- section 246's narrower framing should be understood as specifically
about the vendor `shop_sign` set, not signage in general. (2)
`/namestructure` is genuinely dual-effect: it simultaneously updates
the management name and the physical sign text other players can walk
up and read. (3) condemned structures automatically override sign
text with a "Condemned" indicator, confirming the sign is live-rendered
world state, not a static cached label.

## 288. Jedi-vs-Jedi Lightsaber Dueling -- Confirmed Mechanically Identical to Any Other Profession's Duel, Zero Special-Cased Rules Outside the Fully Independent FRS Arena (extends sections 32, 43, 67, 127, 153, 252)

**Ordinary `/duel` between two Jedi carries zero special-cased logic
-- the request gating, damage pipeline, and end-of-duel flow are
identical to any other profession's duel, the FRS arena remains fully
independent with no shared code path beyond a single healing-restriction
guard, and there is no Jedi-specific duel achievement/tracking
distinct from ordinary duel record tracking.** `DuelCommand.h`'s
request gating (player-creature check, 25-unit range, no-duel-area
block, duplicate-challenge guard, ignore-list check) and
`CombatManager`'s duel functions (`requestDuel`/`requestEndDuel`/
`declineDuel`/`areInDuel`/`freeDuelList`) contain zero profession or
Force-sensitivity checks anywhere. Damage during a duel flows through
the same generic `CombatManager` pipeline as any other PvP fight --
the Jedi-specific mitigation code found nearby (Jedi toughness,
Force-armor/shield handling) is general Jedi-vs-anyone combat math
that applies identically in open-world PvP, PvE, and duels alike, not
duel-conditional logic. Per section 153's independent confirmation,
there is no per-player duel win/loss counter of any kind (Jedi or
otherwise) -- only the Elo-style `pvpRating` updates identically for
duel and open-world kills, and Jedi-related badges/collections are
all tied to holocron acquisition, Padawan trials, bounty content, or
FRS rank, never to ordinary duel outcomes. The FRS arena shares no
code with the ordinary duel system beyond a single naming-adjacent
touchpoint: `QueueCommand::checkForArenaDuel()` calls
`FrsManager::isPlayerFightingInArena()`, but this is invoked
exclusively from a dozen-plus healing/support commands to block
third-party healing of arena combatants -- `DuelCommand.h`/
`EndDuelCommand.h`/`CombatManager`'s duel functions never call any
`FrsManager` API at all, confirming zero bridge between the two PvP
systems.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't build "duel armor interaction" or
"Jedi duel damage cap" features expecting existing hooks -- none
exist; any such rule would be genuinely new code inserted into
`DuelCommand.h`/`CombatManager`. (2) any Jedi-only duel leaderboard or
achievement would require entirely new persistent state -- nothing in
the existing rating-update path distinguishes duel participants by
Force-sensitivity. (3) treat "Jedi-vs-Jedi duel" as a purely cosmetic
label -- mechanically it is a standard duel between two players who
happen to carry lightsabers and Jedi skill mods, with the FRS arena
remaining the only genuinely separate structured-PvP system for
Jedi.

## 289. Bounty Payout Scaling and Target Combat Behavior -- Level-Scaled NPC Formula, Skill-Scaled Jedi Formula, Zero Special Combat Buffs for Any Target Type (extends sections 20, 80, 186, 194, 200, 262)

**Bounty payout genuinely scales -- NPC bounty targets pay
`level * (tier-dependent range)`, while player (Jedi) bounty payout
scales with spent Jedi skill points and FRS rank instead of level --
but neither target type receives any bounty-specific combat buff,
stat multiplier, or special AI: difficulty comes entirely from the
target's own pre-existing stats, consistent with section 262's
confirmed absence of an engine-level eliteness system.** For NPC
bounty targets, `MissionManagerImplementation::
randomizeGenericBountyMission()` reads the target's
`CreatureTemplate::getLevel()` and computes
`reward = creoLevel * (200 + random(200))` at investigation tier 1,
scaling up to `creoLevel * (300 + random(300))` at tier 3 -- a
direct, tunable multiplier of target level, not a flat fee; mission
difficulty display scales identically (`3 * creoLevel + 7`). For
player (Jedi) bounty targets, reward instead comes from
`PlayerObjectImplementation::calculateBhReward()`:
`spentJediSkillPoints * 1000`, plus `frsRank * 100000` if applicable,
floored at a 25,000/50,000 minimum -- entirely unrelated to
"level," confirming section 194's Jedi-only bounty targeting uses a
genuinely distinct reward formula from the NPC path. A hidden flat-rate
override also exists: `getRealBountyReward()` forces a hardcoded
50,000/25,000 credit payout during an active bounty-debuff window,
overriding whatever the normal formula produced -- applying only to
player/Jedi targets, never NPC bounty missions. Critically, player
bounty targets receive **zero** special combat AI/stat boost -- the
bounty objective only registers `PLAYERKILLED` observers on the live
player and flags PvP visibility; no buff, stat multiplier, or AI
override is applied anywhere, so the Jedi target's combat behavior is
identical to any other player of their build/skills, with the only
bounty-specific consequence being an XP penalty on death (a
reward-scaled penalty clamped between -50,000 and -500,000). NPC
bounty targets are likewise ordinary `CreatureTemplate` spawns via the
same generic AI-agent spawn path any static/dynamic NPC uses -- no
special ability grant or aggro-behavior injection is added by the
bounty system itself; a "hard" bounty NPC is simply a hand-authored
template with higher stats, fully consistent with section 262. The
tier system that does exist is gated by the Bounty Hunter
Investigation skill line (novice/inv_01/inv_03 -> mission level 1-3),
controlling which pooled target-template level-range list is used and
the reward multiplier, not a separate "contract rating" field.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) payout genuinely scales by target
level for NPC bounties and by Jedi skill investment for player
bounties -- these are two structurally distinct formulas, not one
unified system. (2) no bounty target of either type receives any
combat advantage from being a bounty target -- difficulty is entirely
inherited from the target's own pre-existing build/template. (3) a
hidden flat 25k/50k payout override exists during an active
bounty-debuff window for player targets specifically, worth knowing
when reasoning about actual observed payouts vs. the formula.

## 290. Vendor Sale Proceeds Among Structure Co-Owners -- Per-Item Individual Payout, No Revenue-Sharing/Split Mechanic, ADMIN Co-Ownership Never Touches Sale Credits (extends sections 136, 157, 242, 251)

**Whoever places an item for sale always receives that item's own
proceeds directly, regardless of who else holds ADMIN rights on the
containing structure -- there is no revenue pooling or split among
co-owners, and the ADMIN-list co-ownership documented in section 242
is entirely about structure management (maintenance, redeed, rename),
never consulted anywhere in the sale/payout code path.** Each
individual `AuctionItem` (sale listing) carries its own `ownerID`/
`ownerName` field, set to whichever player actually listed it via
`createVendorItem()`/`addSaleItem()`. At settlement,
`doInstantBuy()` looks up the seller by that item-level owner field
and pays credits directly to their bank account, deducting city sales
tax from that same individual seller -- the structure/vendor's own
single `VendorDataComponent::ownerId` field is never credited
directly; it functions only as a fallback identity for the vendor
object itself. Because ownership lives on the item, not the vendor,
two different players who each place their own items on the same
shared vendor each receive their own sale's credits individually --
nothing in the buy/sell code references the vendor's own `ownerId`
for payout routing. One wrinkle exists for non-primary-owner listings:
if the lister isn't the vendor's single designated `ownerId`, the item
is created with an `OFFERED` status and the vendor owner receives a
notification -- a consignment/offer-visibility mechanic, but the item
still records the actual lister as its owner, and if bought, the same
individual-payout path still pays that lister directly, not the
vendor's owner. No code anywhere divides an item's sale price among
multiple recipients, and no lookup of the structure's ADMIN
`SortedVector<uint64>` occurs during any auction/vendor payout path --
section 242's ADMIN co-ownership machinery (maintenance payment,
redeed/destroy, rename, ban/entry-list editing) is architecturally
disconnected from bank-credit flows entirely; the vendor object's own
`ownerId` field is additionally a single scalar, structurally
incapable of representing a shared list even if it were consulted.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't assume ADMIN-list co-owners share
in vendor sale revenue -- co-ownership grants management rights only,
never a cut of sale proceeds. (2) multiple sellers can safely share
one vendor structure -- each keeps their own item proceeds
individually with zero risk of funds funneling to a different
"structure owner." (3) the `OFFERED` consignment flag for non-primary-owner
listings affects visibility/notification only, never payout routing
-- the actual lister is always paid directly.

## 291. Melee/Ranged Hybrid Weapons -- Confirmed Absent for Players, a Real But NPC-Only Weapon-Pair-Swap Mechanism Exists as a Design Precedent (extends sections 94, 201, 222, 231, 252)

**Every player-usable weapon in the codebase is strictly one attack
type (melee XOR ranged XOR unarmed XOR thrown XOR Force) with zero
dual-mode/hybrid instances -- `attackType` is a single scalar field,
not a bitmask, architecturally incapable of representing both
simultaneously -- but a real, if NPC-exclusive, weapon-pair-swap
mechanism exists as a useful design precedent for anyone wanting to
build a hybrid weapon feature.** `WeaponObject`'s `attackType` field
is tested with strict equality against enum values
(`MELEEATTACK=0`, `RANGEDATTACK=1`, `FORCEATTACK=2`, plus
TRAPATTACK/GRENADEATTACK/HEAVY* variants) -- a given weapon instance
can report true for exactly one of `isMeleeWeapon()`/`isRangedWeapon()`
etc., never both, a hard architectural constraint rather than merely
a data convention. No "throw melee weapon at range" special attack
exists anywhere -- the only "throw" commands present are the
inherently-ranged grenade attack and an unrelated pet-fetch trick,
confirmed absent as a combat mechanic. However, a genuine
weapon-template-pair mechanism does exist for certain NPCs: identical
weapon models ship as two separate templates differing only in
`attackType` and range (e.g. a melee sword template and a sibling
`_ranged` template with `FORCEATTACK`/32-unit range), used exclusively
by dark-Jedi/force-sensitive mob weapon groups -- an AI behavior-tree
comparison of primary vs. secondary weapon ideal-range against current
combat distance dynamically swaps which physical `WeaponObject`
instance is equipped, creating the visual/behavioral appearance of a
hybrid weapon while each individual instance still strictly satisfies
the single-attackType rule. These `_ranged` templates are never
referenced in any loot table, schematic, or crafting recipe --
confirmed inaccessible to players entirely. This mechanism is distinct
from and unrelated to lightsaber forms (confirmed absent, section
252).

**Practical takeaways:** (1) do not attempt to flip `attackType` at
runtime on a single item to build a hybrid weapon -- follow the
established NPC pattern instead (a paired template + AI-driven
equip-swap), or undertake the larger refactor of turning `attackType`
into a capability set. (2) `isMeleeWeapon()`/`isRangedWeapon()`/etc.
are safe to treat as mutually exclusive everywhere in player-facing
combat code -- the only exception is the internal AI weapon-pair-swap
path, which is NPC-only and inaccessible to players. (3) the `_ranged`
sibling-template trick is the only precedent in-tree for range-profile
switching and is worth reusing as a design reference for any future
hybrid-weapon feature.

## 292. Overhead Title Display Priority -- One Manually-Selected Skill-Title Field, Guild/GCW/FRS Titles Are Separate Wire Fields the Client Composes, No Server-Side Priority Algorithm (extends sections 100, 149, 156, 233, 268)

**There is exactly one true server-side "title" field on
`PlayerObject`, manually selected by the player via a real working
command and restricted specifically to earned profession/skill
titles -- guild title, GCW military rank, and FRS rank are entirely
separate, independently-tracked fields sent to the client as their own
wire values, with no server-side "highest priority wins" algorithm
anywhere; the client is what visually composes them together.**
`PlayerObject::title` is populated only via `/setCurrentSkillTitle`
(`SetCurrentSkillTitleCommand.h`), which validates the player actually
holds the target skill, then commits via `setTitle()` -- itself
re-validating that the skill object has `isTitle()==true` before
accepting it, meaning `title` can only ever be set to an earned
skill/profession title, never a guild title, GCW rank name, or FRS
rank name, since none of those are "title" skill objects. A second
command, `SetLoginTitleCommand`, is confirmed dead code -- it
validates state but does nothing else, leaving `/setCurrentSkillTitle`
as the sole functioning entry point. The game displays multiple
independent strings simultaneously, not one merged slot: nearby-player
serialization sends the base display name, the guild name (from
`GuildObject::getGuildName()`, entirely independent of `title`), and
`ghost->getTitle()` (labeled in-source "Profession Title") as three
separate fields; GCW rank is a fourth, separately-tracked string sent
through its own channel. `SceneObjectImplementation::getDisplayedName()`
only ever returns the base custom/object name -- it never concatenates
title, guild, or rank, confirming the SWG client itself stitches guild
tag + profession title + GCW rank into the nametag/examine display,
not the server. Guild titles are stored per-member in a completely
disjoint code path (`GuildMemberInfo::guildTitle`), structurally
separate from `PlayerObject::title`.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) there is no priority-resolution algorithm
to model -- each title/rank track (skill title, guild title, GCW
rank, mayoral rank, FRS rank) is an independent field, and any
"which one wins" behavior a player observes is purely client-side
composition. (2) the only field a player actively chooses is
`PlayerObject::title`, gated strictly to skill-derived titles via
`/setCurrentSkillTitle` -- `SetLoginTitleCommand` is a red herring,
confirmed non-functional. (3) veteran-reward or FRS titles, if
implemented as `Skill` objects with `isTitle()==true`, would flow
through this same single field/command gate as any profession title
-- worth verifying per title type before assuming universal behavior.

## 293. Harvester Placement Optimization Tooling -- A Real Per-Survey Auto-Best-Spot Waypoint Already Exists, No Wide-Area Heatmap or Cross-Region Automation (extends sections 15, 59, 82)

**Contrary to an assumption of purely manual point-by-point surveying,
each survey action already performs a built-in local optimization --
scanning a grid of points and auto-placing a waypoint at the single
highest-density cell found -- but no wide-area heatmap, cross-region
scan, or placement-legality-aware recommender exists anywhere, so
finding a good *region* remains entirely manual even though finding
the best spot *within* one survey's footprint is already automated.**
`ResourceSpawner::sendSurvey()` loops an N x N grid of sample points
around the player, tracks the single highest-density point found, and
-- if that maximum meets a minimum threshold -- automatically
creates/updates a `WaypointObject` pinned at that best grid cell; each
survey action is therefore a mini auto-optimizer over its sampled
area, not a manual single-point ping as might be assumed. Grid size
(3-5 points) and scan radius (64-384 meters) both scale with the
player's `surveying` skill mod via tiered thresholds, with all sampled
points packed into a single response packet delivering the classic
in-client survey bar-graph in one shot -- covering a grid, not one
coordinate at a time. However, the grid loop is explicitly centered on
and bounded by the player's current position and tool range -- it
never samples beyond the immediate survey area, so there is no way to
view the underlying zone-wide density map as a map-wide visual or
heatmap. The one other player-facing tool that sounds related, the
Interplanetary Survey Droid, only emails the player a list of *which
resource types exist on a given planet* -- it contains zero
coordinates and zero density/percentage data, so it functions purely
as an existence-checker, not a location or hotspot finder, and should
not be conflated with density/concentration data in any documentation.
Separately, the sampling minigame's "rich node" bonus waypoint is a
randomly gambled location, not derived from real density data, and
should also not be confused with genuine concentration optimization.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) a "mark the best point in my current
survey" feature already exists for free -- it's not a gap to fill,
it's built into every survey action automatically. (2) what's
genuinely absent is wide-area automation: no heatmap/overlay, no
multi-region auto-scan, and critically no tool that cross-references
resource density against structure-placement legality (`isBuildingPermittedAt()`)
-- these two systems don't currently talk to each other anywhere. (3)
the Interplanetary Survey Droid should never be described as
providing density/hotspot data in user-facing material -- it's purely
a resource-existence report with zero coordinate information.

## 294. Group Loot Distribution Modes -- Exactly Four Modes, No Need/Greed/Pass System, RANDOM Rolls Independently Per Item (extends section 37)

**Group loot distribution supports exactly four modes -- FREEFORALL,
MASTERLOOTER, LOTTERY, RANDOM -- confirmed exhaustive by the
governing switch statement's own `default: return`, with no
WoW-style per-item Need/Greed/Pass player-choice mechanic anywhere in
the codebase; loot is always either one player unilaterally opening
the corpse or the engine assigning items automatically with zero
player input.** A `GroupObject` holds exactly one active loot rule at
a time (default FREEFORALL), changed via a leader-only SUI
dropdown/list-box selecting one of the four rule IDs, never a
per-item prompt. `GroupLootTask::run()` switches on the active rule:
FREEFORALL falls through with no gate at all; MASTERLOOTER performs a
single permission check restricting corpse-opening to the designated
master looter; LOTTERY hands off to a dedicated lottery-session
creation function; RANDOM hands off to a random-assignment function.
Nowhere in this switch, the group manager, or any SUI callback is
there a per-item player choice -- no need/greed/pass enum, no
roll-request packet, no per-player per-item vote -- confirmed via a
codebase-wide search returning zero relevant hits beyond unrelated
Lua dialogue. RANDOM mode genuinely rolls independently per item, not
once for the whole drop: the implementation loops every item on the
corpse and picks a fresh random winner from eligible candidates
inside the loop for each individual item, skipping already-claimed
items as a defensive re-entry guard. LOTTERY instead creates one
session-wide gate for the whole corpse (locking all items via
container-permission denial until resolution, adding in-range members
as eligible participants, opening a dedicated lottery-window SUI),
but the actual winner selection still resolves per item once the
lottery closes, not a single all-or-nothing roll assigning the entire
drop to one winner. Credits are always split evenly regardless of
which item-distribution mode is active, entirely independent of the
item-loot logic.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) there is no Need/Greed/Pass system in
this codebase -- building one would require a fifth custom loot-rule
value plus an entirely new SUI roll-request flow layered onto the
existing loot-task switch. (2) RANDOM mode's per-item independent
roll is the closest existing analog to a "roll" mechanic, but it's
engine-decided with zero player input, not player-initiated. (3)
LOTTERY is the only mode with real player-facing roll UI and an
item-lock mechanism, making it the natural extension point if a
Need/Greed/Pass feature were ever added; MASTERLOOTER remains
mechanically trivial, with all "drama" purely social rather than
code-enforced.

## 295. GCW Base Power-Regulator Hacking Minigame -- A Deterministic "Lights Out"-Style Linked-Switch Puzzle, Single-Use Per Vulnerability Window, No Fail Penalty (extends sections 87, 96, 233, 254, 259)

**The power-regulator hack is a deterministic "Lights Out"-style
linked-switch puzzle (not a timing or sequence-memory minigame),
restricted to Commando heavy-weapons specialists within close range,
fires exactly once per vulnerability window as the DNA-to-OVERLOADED
stage transition, and carries zero fail penalty -- attackers can
retry indefinitely with no alarm, defender notification, or
cooldown.** The SUI lists N switches (default 7, server-config-wide
via a Lua global, not scaled per base tier) whose state comes from
the base's data component; toggling any switch flips both that switch
**and** a second, randomly-assigned linked switch per a
pre-generated coupling-rules table -- the classic Lights Out
mechanic, requiring players to find the correct toggle sequence to
bring all switches to ON simultaneously. Initial scramble difficulty
comes from 5-9 random flips applied to an all-ON starting state, with
a fallback re-flip guarding against an accidental instant-solve; no
difficulty scaling was found tied to base tier, attacker count, or
time remaining in the vulnerability window anywhere in this code
path. Access is gated by several pre-checks: opposing faction,
non-neutral status, the prior DNA-sampling stage already completed,
not in combat, same room and within 15 meters, and specifically
requiring the Commando heavy-weapons speed skill -- only one
profession can even open the puzzle. On an incorrect toggle
combination, there is no fail outcome at all: the SUI simply re-sends
itself so the player keeps trying, with no alarm, no defender alert,
and no lockout/cooldown triggered by wrong toggles. The puzzle is a
single, one-shot stage transition within the broader 8-stage
hack-state progression (INVULNERABLE through REBOOTSEQUENCE) -- it's
only offered once the DNA-sampling stage is already complete, and a
fully-solved grid moves the base directly to OVERLOADED state,
awards Slicing XP, and re-randomizes the switches for the *next*
base/vulnerability window -- the state transition itself happens
exactly once per successful solve, not recurring within a single
window.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) this is solvable deterministically once
the switch-pairing rules are known or inferred -- optimal play isn't
about timing or luck, it's a logic puzzle. (2) it's single-use per
vulnerability cycle and profession-gated to Commando heavy-weapons
specialists specifically -- not a general-access minigame any
attacker can attempt. (3) there is zero risk/penalty for failed
attempts -- attackers can experiment freely as long as the
proximity/faction/skill/combat-state gates hold, with no defender-side
feedback of failed attempts at all.

## 296. Account-Wide vs. Per-Character Unlocks -- Badges Are Strictly Per-Character, Veteran Reward Eligibility Is Genuinely Account-Wide Per Galaxy, Collections Don't Exist (extends sections 19, 156, 260, 268)

**Progression is not uniformly per-character -- badges are strictly
scoped to the individual `PlayerObject` with zero account sharing, but
veteran reward *eligibility bookkeeping* is genuinely shared across
every character on an account within a given galaxy, meaning a second
character can be permanently locked out of an entire milestone's
reward pool even for non-one-time cosmetics once any character on the
account has claimed it.** Badges live directly on the per-character
`PlayerObject` ("ghost") as a bitmask plus counters; `Account.idl`
has no badge field anywhere, and every badge-award code path writes
exclusively to the individual character's own badge storage --
confirmed zero cross-character sharing. Collections are confirmed
absent from the codebase entirely (no `Collection`/`CollectionManager`
class exists anywhere), making the account-sharing question moot for
that system since it was never implemented. Veteran reward "claimed"
state, however, is stored on `Account::galaxyAccountInfo` -- one
instance per galaxy, not per character -- and every character on the
same account+galaxy points at and shares the identical
`GalaxyAccountInfo` object via a cached reference set at load time.
Milestone eligibility checking works per-milestone-per-account, not
per-reward-per-character: once *any* character on the account has
picked *any* reward for a given milestone, that milestone is
permanently consumed for the entire account -- even for rewards
explicitly flagged as not one-time in the reward catalog -- with an
in-source comment confirming this is deliberate, "to prevent claiming
while multi-logged." Only a GM-only reset command can clear a
consumed milestone. Reward items themselves are never auto-granted to
alt characters -- each character must individually run the claim
command and receive the physical item in its own inventory; only the
"has this milestone been used" flag is shared. Because this claim
record lives on the account/galaxy object rather than the deletable
character object, it also survives character deletion -- deleting the
character that originally claimed a milestone does not reset or
delete the account's claimed-milestone record.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't assume uniform per-character
scoping across all progression systems -- badges are per-character,
but veteran-reward milestone eligibility is genuinely account-wide
per galaxy, a meaningful and easy-to-miss distinction. (2) the
practical effect is a soft cap of one veteran-reward pick per
milestone per account per galaxy, not one per reward-type per
character -- alts can be locked out of entire milestone pools. (3)
this account-wide claim record outlives the character that earned it,
surviving character deletion since it's stored on the account/galaxy
object rather than the character object itself.

## 297. Stealth/Camouflage Detection Mechanics -- A Real Scout-Only Anti-NPC-Aggro Roll, Zero PvP Stealth Counterpart, Structurally Unrelated to Covert GCW Status (extends sections 49, 84, 178)

**Core3 implements a genuine formula-driven camouflage/concealment
system, but it is scoped entirely to suppressing NPC aggro-tree
progression -- there is no player-vs-player invisibility, and it
shares no code or data with the covert GCW status flag (section 49)
despite the similar-sounding name.** `ConcealCommand::doQueueCommand`
(`ConcealCommand.h:99-229`) lets a Scout apply a zone-matched
Camouflage Kit to themselves or a nearby player (10m range, 32m
hostile-NPC exclusion zone), granting a `ConcealBuff` carrying the
`private_conceal` skill mod; a separate self-only `MaskscentCommand`
grants `mask_scent`, blocked while in combat. The actual detection
check lives in `AiAgentImplementation::isCamouflaged()`
(`AiAgentImplementation.cpp:3690-3844`, cached per-target in a
`camouflagedObjects` vector): base roll is `(100 + concealMod) -
creatureLevel`, modified by posture (prone +15) and movement
(running -10, walking -5), capped at 98%/95%, with instant auto-success
if the creature is non-aggressive or the player out-levels it by 10+.
Failure triggers `CamoTask`, which strips the buff and has a 50%
chance to aggro the NPC. Critically, the NPC behavior tree consumes
this via a `CheckIsCamouflaged` node gating the aggro/attack sequence
(`Checks.cpp:102-114`, wired into `default.lua`) -- and a
codebase-wide search confirms no "detection" skill mod or any
player-vs-player consumer of `isCamouflaged()` exists anywhere;
`checkHostileInRange`/`isCamouflaged` only ever evaluate `AiAgent`
(NPC) objects.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) camouflage/conceal is purely an
anti-creature-aggro tool themed around Scout wilderness survival --
it has zero effect on other players' ability to see, target, or
attack you, so it should never be documented or treated as a PvP
stealth mechanic. (2) it is architecturally unrelated to covert GCW
status (section 49) -- concealment is a rolled, range/posture/movement
-sensitive per-NPC check consumed by behavior trees, while covert is
a static `FactionStatus` visibility flag governing PvP attackability
with no roll involved. (3) breaking conditions are fully code-enforced
(combat state, movement, posture, proximity, cross-zone kit
mismatch), making this a clean, well-bounded system if ever extended.

## 298. NPC "Junk Dealer" Buyback -- A Narrow, Template-Flagged Sell-to-NPC Mechanic for Collectible Quest Items, Not a General Shopkeeper Buyback (extends sections 101, 108, 193, 262)

**A real player-to-NPC sell mechanic exists, but it is scoped to a
themed "Junk Dealer" screenplay system selling back a small set of
collectible/quest-flagged items at fixed template prices -- ordinary
vendor NPCs (barkers, restocking shops) have no buyback capability at
all, and a codebase-wide search for "buyback"/"sellback" outside the
junk-dealer scripts returns zero hits.** The entire mechanic is
Lua-driven (`screenplays/junk_dealer/junk_dealer.lua` and its
conversation handler), triggered only through dialogue with one of
~17 registered Junk Dealer NPC personas. Eligibility is gated by
`TangibleObject::getJunkDealerNeeded()` -- a per-template bitmask
matching the dealer's category -- combined with hard exclusions:
`getCraftersName() == ""` (must not be player-crafted), not broken,
not sliced, not no-trade, and an empty container. Price is a flat,
template-baked `getJunkValue()` integer (e.g. collectible rugs/gongs/
tables fixed at 1000 credits each) -- no condition-scaling, no
haggling, consistent with section 262's confirmed fixed-price NPC
model. Sold items are permanently destroyed
(`destroyObjectFromDatabase()`), not added to the NPC's resellable
stock, meaning this is structurally a credit sink for specific
collectible junk, not a general loot-liquidation system -- ordinary
weapons/armor/loot default to `junkValue = 0` and are simply never
listed as sellable.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) don't describe this as "you can sell
loot to any vendor" -- eligibility is a narrow per-template bitmask
match against one of ~17 specific NPCs, not a universal shopkeeper
feature. (2) sold items vanish from the economy entirely rather than
restocking the NPC's inventory, unlike the rotating-stock restocking
covered in sections 108/193. (3) building a general "sell any item to
any vendor" feature would require new eligibility/pricing logic --
the junk dealer's bitmask-gate pattern is the closest existing
scaffold to extend, but its destroy-on-sell behavior would need to
change for a true buyback loop.

## 299. Guild Leader Succession on Deletion/Abandonment -- Hard-Stored Leader Field (Unlike Derived Group Leadership), Lazy Detection, a Real 2-3 Week Leaderless Window Before Automatic Election (extends sections 16, 90, 134, 204, 225, 284)

**Unlike group leadership (sections 204/225, which is derived on-the-fly
as `groupMembers[0]`), guild leadership is a hard-stored
`guildLeaderID` field with zero special-case handling in the character
deletion pipeline itself -- detection and recovery are entirely lazy,
driven by the same weekly `processGuildUpdate` maintenance task that
prunes deleted members (section 284), producing a real, engine-mandated
window of up to roughly 2-3 weeks where a guild has no leader and no
one holds full permissions.** `DeleteCharactersTask::run()` and
`destroyPlayerCreatureFromDatabase()` contain no guild-related call at
all -- the dangling `guildLeaderID` is only caught inline during
`GuildManagerImplementation::processGuildUpdate()`, which checks
`existsPlayerCreatureOID()` for each member and immediately zeroes
`guildLeaderID` if it matches (a defensive same-check also exists in
`GuildObjectImplementation::removeMember()`). Recovery is a **two-cycle
forced election**, not instant promotion: the same maintenance pass
detects the null leader and sets `ElectionState = FIRST_WEEK`; the
following weekly tick advances to `SECOND_WEEK`; only the tick after
that runs `processGuildElection()` and calls `transferLeadership()`.
Since `GuildUpdateInterval` is 7 real days, the full pipeline spans
roughly 2-3 weeks. If no one voted, the winner defaults to
`getMemberWithHighestPermission()`, falling back to `getMember(0)`
(insertion order) if no one holds any permission bits -- meaning
succession can promote an arbitrary low-activity member rather than
an obvious second-in-command. A separate, instant voluntary path
(`/makeLeader` SUI, `transferLeadership()`) exists for a live leader
choosing their own successor.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) guilds are never *permanently*
leaderless, but there is a real multi-week window with `guildLeaderID
== 0` and no full-permission member -- worth knowing before assuming
guild-leader-dependent code always has a valid target. (2) this is a
notable, easy-to-miss gap: the only way to shorten that window is a
GM directly forcing `setGuildLeaderID`/`transferLeadership` -- there
is no player-triggerable emergency election. (3) automatic succession
is permission-based, not seniority-based -- it promotes whoever holds
the highest permission bitmask (section 134), or simply the earliest
remaining member if no one does.

## 300. Character Rename Mechanic -- A GM-Only Staff Tool Reusing the Character-Creation Name-Uniqueness Check, With Confirmed Stale-Reference Gaps in Friends Lists, Mail, and Structure Records (extends sections 87, 130, 134, 170, 232, 260)

**A first/last-name rename mechanic exists, but it is exclusively a
GM/CS staff tool (`/setFirstName`, `/setLastName`, gated behind the
`admin_player_management_02` staff skill) -- there is no player-facing
rename token, command, or purchase path, and `/setName` explicitly
refuses to touch player creatures.** The rename path reuses the exact
same `nameMap`/`NameManager::validateName()` uniqueness check used at
character creation (`PlayerManagerImplementation::checkPlayerName()`
vs. `setFirstName()`, both consulting the identical `CharacterNameMap`),
with a GM-only `--force` flag (adminLevel >= 15) able to skip filter
validation entirely. On success, the live object's display name,
chat-system registration, and the master name/OID index are all
updated correctly -- meaning `/tell`, guild rosters (OID-keyed, no
cached name), and group data (live object references, not cached
strings) all resolve the new name automatically with no cleanup
needed. However, several denormalized fields are confirmed to go
stale: friends lists only *remove* the renamed player under their old
name via `removeAllReverseFriends()` with no re-add under the new
name (anyone who had them friended must manually re-friend); mail
`senderName` (`PersistentMessage.idl`) is a permanent send-time
snapshot, so historical mail keeps the old name; and structure
`StructurePermissionList::ownerName` is a cached display field that
is never actually written by any `setOwner*` call (access control
itself stays safe since it's OID-based, but the display value is
effectively dead).

**Practical takeaways:** (1) treat character rename strictly as a
CS/support action, not a self-service feature -- there is no
in-game path for a player to rename themselves. (2) guild and group
systems are rename-safe by design (OID-keyed), a useful contrast with
the structure/mail cases. (3) support staff should expect two real
side effects after any GM-executed rename: silent friends-list
removal with no auto-re-add, and stale name display in old mail and
structure ownership records -- neither is a security issue, but both
are UX gaps worth flagging in any support documentation.

## 301. Structure Co-Owner (ADMIN List) Eviction -- A Live Permission Flip With No Data Migration, Peer-Evictable, Three Independently-Enforced Layers Protecting the True Owner (extends sections 135, 185, 242, 290)

**Removing a co-owner from a structure's ADMIN list is a live,
always-rechecked permission flag flip, not a data-migration event --
any current admin (not just the true owner) can evict any other
non-owner admin via the generic `permissionListModify` pipeline, and
the change takes effect immediately since every downstream check
(`isOnAdminList()`) re-reads the list fresh rather than caching it.**
`PermissionListModifyCommand::handleStructurePermissions` enforces
exactly two hard-coded protections: a player cannot remove themselves
from ADMIN, and the true owner can never be removed from ADMIN by
anyone -- beyond that, any admin can evict any other admin, a flatter
peer structure than might be assumed. Eviction does not touch the
former co-owner's placed items, hopper contents, or vendor objects --
it only flips the permission flag, so every subsequent live check
(`StructureContainerComponent::checkContainerPermission`,
`HarvesterObjectImplementation`'s hopper/activation gates,
`CreateVendorCommand`'s admin requirement) independently denies them
on their *next* attempt rather than retroactively. One sharper
