consequence: if the structure is private, losing ADMIN can trigger
immediate physical ejection via `updateCellPermissionsTo()` ->
`isAllowedEntry()` -> `ejectObject()`, since ADMIN membership implies
entry rights unless the player is separately on the ENTRY list. The
true owner field is protected at three independent layers: the
command layer's explicit guards, a second `CANTCHANGEOWNER` check
inside every `StructurePermissionList` grant/revoke/toggle mutation,
and the BAN-list layer refusing to ever ban the owner -- only an
explicit `/transferstructure` (owner-initiated) or a GM-driven
`StructureSetOwnerTask` can ever change the recorded owner.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) ADMIN eviction is peer-to-peer, not
owner-gated -- any co-owner can kick any other non-owner co-owner,
worth knowing when reasoning about trust among multiple ADMIN-listed
players. (2) evicted co-owners keep their placed items/vendor objects
untouched; they simply fail future access checks -- there's no
automatic cleanup or transfer of their structure-related assets. (3)
in a private structure, ADMIN eviction can mean instant ejection from
the building, not just loss of management rights -- a sharper
consequence than a public/vendor-only structure would produce.

## 302. Manual Resource Sampling -- No Daily or Session Quantity Cap Exists, Only a Flat 25-Second Cooldown and Ordinary HAM/Inventory Limits (extends sections 15, 59, 185, 197, 293)

**Confirmed absent: Core3 has no daily, per-character, or
session-based cap on manual resource sampling/foraging -- the only
throttles are a flat 25-second per-attempt cooldown
(`SurveySessionImplementation::rescheduleSample()`), the ordinary
Action-pool (HAM) cost per sample, and generic inventory/stack-size
limits, none of which reset on a day boundary or track a running
count.** `SurveySession.idl` declares no counter or timestamp field
capable of representing a daily allowance -- only session-scoped tool
and location state. `SampleTask::run()` simply re-invokes
`session->reSample()` on a fixed 25,000ms timer, identical to (not
layered beneath) the tool's own recharge behavior; the closest thing
to a throttle is the Action cost deducted per attempt
(`ResourceSpawner::sendSample`), which blocks further sampling only
until the pool naturally regenerates over minutes. The genuine
practical stopping points are `isContainerFullRecursive()` (inventory
space, per section 197) and `ResourceContainer::MAXSIZE` (100,000
per-stack cap) -- the same generic systems that gate every item
pickup in the game, not a sampling-specific mechanism. Global resource
depletion (`unitsInCirculation`, feeding section 15's spawn/respawn
curves) is tracked zone-wide, never decremented against any
per-player budget, and never blocks an individual character's further
sampling.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) a character with sufficient Action
regen, inventory space, and patience can sample the same node
indefinitely at roughly one attempt per 25 seconds -- there is no
anti-farming daily cap to design around or work within. (2) this
confirms manual sampling is architecturally distinct from the
automated harvester hopper cap (section 185), which does enforce a
hard capacity ceiling -- no equivalent exists for the manual
minigame. (3) if a future daily-cap feature were desired, it would
need entirely new state (a counter/timestamp) added to
`SurveySession` or the player object, since nothing resembling one
currently exists.

## 303. GCW Base Vulnerability Window Scheduling -- A Single Owner-Facing "Reset" Control With a 14-Day Cooldown, No Custom Time-of-Day Picker, No Bulk-Scheduling Tool (extends sections 10, 87, 96, 254, 259, 295)

**A GCW base owner cannot pick an arbitrary vulnerability window --
the only owner-facing control is a single HQ-terminal "Reset
Vulnerability" option that restarts the recurring cycle from "now,"
gated by a 14-day (Lua-config) per-base cooldown, with no way to
choose a specific clock time and no bulk/guild-wide scheduling tool
found anywhere in the code.** The schedule is auto-initialized at
placement (`GCWManagerImplementation::initializeBaseTimers`) as a
recurring cadence -- `vulnerabilityDuration` (3 hours by default) every
`vulnerabilityFrequency` (48 hours by default) -- stored as absolute
`Time` timestamps on `DestructibleBuildingDataComponent`, not a
daily clock-time range. The "Reset Vulnerability" menu option
(owner/GM only, hidden while the base is currently vulnerable) calls
`resetVulnerability()`, which re-anchors `nextVulnerableTime` to
`now + vulnerabilityFrequency` -- shifting the *phase* of the cycle,
never letting the owner set an explicit hour. It is hard-gated by
`hasResetTimerPast()` against a 14-day `resetTimer` config value, and
critically cannot be used while the base is already vulnerable --
meaning it can delay the *next* siege window but can never be used
reactively to cancel or dodge an imminent/in-progress one. Actual
vulnerability at attack-time is driven by two scheduled Tasks
(`StartVulnerabilityTask`/`EndVulnerabilityTask`) flipping a `state`
int, reconciled against wall-clock time on server restart via
`refreshExpiredVulnerability`. This is architecturally distinct from
the power-regulator hacking puzzle itself (section 295), which only
runs once the `state` gate here has already opened the base to
attack.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) there is no "set my hack window to a
specific time" feature -- owners only get a one-shot, heavily
cooldown-gated nudge to the existing recurring cycle. (2) the reset
tool is defensively useless against an active or imminent attack
since it's blocked while the base is already vulnerable -- it only
ever pushes the following cycle further out. (3) guild officers
managing multiple bases must reset each HQ terminal individually --
no multi-base scheduling API or command exists anywhere in this path.

## 304. Space Combat Reward/Loot Pipeline -- Reuses the Ground Loot-Roll Engine and XP Sink, But Bypasses MissionManager Entirely in Favor of a Ship-Destruction-Driven Reward Path With Static Per-Tier Templates (extends sections 44, 55, 74, 111, 226, 268)

**Space combat rewards are not mission-object-driven at all --
there is no space equivalent of `MissionManager`; rewards fire
directly off ship-destruction events through a parallel pipeline
(`ShipManager::notifyDestruction`, `ShipObjectImplementation::
awardLootItems`, `PlayerManagerImplementation::
disseminateSpaceExperience`) that reuses the ground engine's core
primitives (the same weighted `LootGroupMap`/`addLootGroupTemplate`
roll engine from section 55, the same underlying XP-award mechanism)
while diverging structurally everywhere else.** Reward configuration
lives on a per-ship-variant `ShipAgentTemplate` (`experience`,
`lootChance`, `lootTable`, `minCredits`/`maxCredits`,
`imperialFactionReward`/`rebelFactionReward`), with difficulty scaling
achieved through discrete static tier files (`_tier1` through `_tier5`)
rather than a runtime formula -- a structural contrast with the
dynamic bounty reward calculation in sections 268/289. Credits are
rolled once and paid only to the single highest-damage player ship;
item loot uses a dedicated `LootManagerImplementation::createLoot(...,
ShipAiAgent*)` overload that checks one named `lootTable` string
against a manual chance roll rather than the ground path's
multi-group `LootGroupCollection`, with item level hardcoded to 0
(no level-scaled item quality as ground loot has). XP instead runs
through a standalone `disseminateSpaceExperience()` function, entirely
separate from the ground group-XP formula (section 44) -- it splits
XP by threat-map damage-contribution across every in-range player
aboard every contributing ship, routes it into prestige pilot/faction
pools if the player has the relevant skill, and applies an "ace
badge" multiplier with no ground parallel. Faction standing rewards
come from static per-template fields, not a runtime formula tied to
target level.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) treat "space missions" (escort/patrol,
section 226) as scripted encounter dressing around a fundamentally
ship-kill-driven reward pipeline -- there's no posted-mission
object or reward structure to model the way ground bounties/missions
work. (2) loot tooling built for section 55's engine can extend to
ships since they share the same weighted-group roll code, but the
`ShipAiAgent` overload only supports one table + one chance check per
agent, a narrower interface than the ground multi-group path. (3)
credits and XP diverge sharply in distribution model -- credits go
to one winning pilot, while XP splits proportionally by damage across
every player on every contributing ship in range, a group-reward
asymmetry with no ground equivalent.

## 305. Alien Language / Comprehension System -- A Real Per-Species Skill and Wire-Level Language Tag Exist, But All Text-Garbling Is Deferred to the (Out-of-Tree) Client (extends sections 21, 34, 63, 148)

**Core3 implements the SWG language-tagging mechanic in full --
per-species `social_language_*_speak`/`_comprehend` skills, a
`languageID` field on `PlayerObject`, and a `languageID` byte on every
spatial chat packet -- but performs zero server-side text garbling;
the un-garbled real message is always delivered to every in-range
recipient, with the "you see gibberish" rendering left entirely to
the client.** Every species template grants Basic comprehension plus
its own native language pair at creation (e.g. Wookiee characters get
`social_language_wookiee_comprehend/speak`), while other alien
languages are purchasable skills (1000 credits each). A player's
currently-spoken language is tracked via `/setspokenlanguage`
(`SetSpokenLanguageCommand.h`) and set on `PlayerObject`.
`ChatManagerImplementation::broadcastChatMessage` builds a
`SpatialChat` packet containing the sender's raw, real `message` text
plus the numeric `languageID` tag, sent verbatim to every nearby
recipient regardless of their own skills -- confirmed via a
codebase-wide search for "garble"/"scramble" turning up only
unrelated droid/ship-scramble commands. The one legitimate server-side
consumer of these skills is Director/conversation-script gating (e.g.
one NPC's dialogue tree branches on `hasSkill("social_language_
moncalamari_speak")`), a narrow flavor-gate use, not a chat-wide
mechanic.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) do not expect or build server-authoritative
comprehension gating -- the `language_*` skill-mod strings are never
read anywhere in the C++ server, confirming this is a "tag-and-defer-
to-client" design, not a stub. (2) any server wanting enforced
comprehension (e.g. security/accessibility reasons) would need a new
check inside `broadcastChatMessage` comparing recipient skills against
the sender's `languageID` -- no such check exists today. (3) quest/
screenplay authors can reuse `hasSkill("social_language_<species>_speak")`
for flavor-gated NPC dialogue branches, following the one existing
precedent, without any engine changes.

## 306. Guild Emblem/Insignia Customization -- Confirmed Absent, Guild Identity Is Text-Only (Name/Abbreviation), No Image or Composited-Layer System Exists Anywhere (extends sections 16, 90, 134)

**Core3 has no guild emblem, insignia, or crest system of any kind --
`GuildObject.idl` carries no image, bitmap-index, or color/layer
field, the guild terminal's radial menu has no emblem-editor option,
and the Guild Information SUI displays plain text only.** A
codebase-wide case-insensitive search for "emblem" returns zero
matches anywhere in game code, scripts, or SQL; "crest"/"insignia"
only appear as unrelated flavor text. `GuildObject.idl` defines only
`guildName`/`guildAbbrev` (strings), membership/permission data
(section 134), and election state -- no bitmap or layer VectorMap of
any kind, unlike the genuine composited-appearance systems that do
exist elsewhere in the engine (Image Designer, section 7/183/236;
vehicle/droid dye system, section 159). The client baseline messages
for a `GuildObject` (`GuildObjectMessage3`/`6`) carry no image/CRC/
layer payload either, confirming the omission is symmetric across the
whole wire protocol, not just the UI layer. Guild identity everywhere
in the codebase -- structure/ship permission lists, player search
results, nametag suffixes -- is expressed purely as the short
`guildAbbrev` text string.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) do not point players or documentation at
a guild emblem editor -- unlike retail SWG's client (which does have
`.gob`/emblem shader support), Core3's server never populates or
transmits any such data, so the feature is entirely absent server-side
regardless of client capability. (2) guild halls/banners/structure
signs display only guild name/abbreviation text, never custom art. (3)
adding this feature would require genuinely new work -- a new
`GuildObject.idl` field, a new SUI callback, a new `GuildManager`
sender method, and new baseline message fields -- not a hidden toggle
to flip on.

## 307. Automatic "Master" Title/Badge Grant on Profession Completion -- "Master X" Is Just the Final Skill Box, the Only Automatic Side Effect Is a Private Badge, Title Selection Always Stays Manual (extends sections 19, 292, 296)

**Completing a full profession skill tree triggers no distinct
"tree completion" event -- the terminal "Master" box flows through
the exact same `SkillManager::awardSkill()` path as every other skill
box, and the only automatic side effect is a private badge award
gated by a bare substring check on the skill's own name (`skillName.
contains("master")`), never an automatic title change or server-wide
announcement.** `SkillManager::awardSkill()` performs the identical
skill-point withdrawal, `addSkill()`, skill-mod, and schematic-grant
sequence for every box in a tree; immediately afterward, if the just-
awarded skill's name contains "master," it looks up a matching
`BadgeList` entry (with one hardcoded shipwright-specific fallback)
and awards it via `PlayerManagerImplementation::awardBadge()`, which
sends a private `prose_grant` message and fires a `BADGEAWARDED`
observer event -- consumable by Lua screenplays, but never broadcast
zone-wide or server-wide. Crucially, `awardSkill()` never calls
`setTitle()` -- the title system (section 292) remains untouched by
mastering a profession; `PlayerObjectImplementation::setTitle()` is
called from exactly one place in the entire codebase, the manual
`/setCurrentSkillTitle` command. The `isTitle` flag that makes "Master
Rifleman" a selectable title is static data parsed straight from the
skill data table, not runtime-derived from "is this the last box in
the tree" -- confirming section 292's finding that title selection is
always a deliberate player action, with no exception for profession
mastery.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) authoring new "Master X" content only
requires setting `isTitle=1` on the final skill box plus, optionally,
a matching `BadgeList` entry keyed to the exact skill name -- no C++
completion-hook needs to be wired up. (2) players must always manually
run `/setCurrentSkillTitle` after mastering a profession; the engine
never auto-selects it, and there is no server-wide "X has mastered
Rifleman!" broadcast anywhere in the award path. (3) because the
badge check is a bare substring match, any skill whose internal name
happens to contain "master" (not just genuine tree finishers) would
trigger the same badge-lookup logic -- worth checking when auditing
for unintended badge grants.

## 308. Combat AOE/Splash Damage Mechanics -- Flat Radius-Gated Damage With No Distance Falloff, Grenades and Area Weapon Specials Share One Pipeline, Mines Are a Fully Separate System (extends sections 39, 84, 116, 201, 258)

**Core3 has no distance-based damage falloff anywhere in its AOE
code -- every target caught within a blast/cone radius rolls the
identical min-max damage formula as a single-target hit, with
proximity to the blast center affecting only whether a target is
included, never how much damage they take.** `CombatManager::
getAreaTargets` computes an effective range from the attack's
`areaRange`/`coneRange` config and walks the attacker's spatial index,
admitting each candidate purely via a boolean radius/cone-angle test
plus the standard `isAttackableBy()` faction/PvP/overt-covert check
(section 258) and a line-of-sight check -- there is no group-membership
exemption, so grouped-but-different-faction players remain vulnerable
to AOE friendly fire under the same rules as any single-target attack.
`calculateDamage()` never receives a distance argument, confirming
uniform full damage across the entire radius. Grenades
(`ThrowGrenadeCommand`) and weapon-based area/cone special attacks
share the identical `doCombatAction`/`getAreaTargets`/
`doTargetCombatAction` pipeline, configured via the same Lua command
fields (`areaAction`, `areaRange`, `coneAction`, `coneAngle`). Mines,
despite also being tagged `areaAction=true` in their Lua config, are
architecturally separate: `MinefieldAttackCommand` is a no-op stub,
with real detonation running through `MinefieldAttackTask::run()`,
which builds its own target list and calls a distinct damage-application
function, `CombatManager::doObjectDetonation()` -- never touching
`getAreaTargets`/`calculateDamage` at all.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) AOE balance/design work is purely a
range/inclusion tuning problem, since there is no falloff curve to
account for -- every target in radius takes full damage. (2)
friendly-fire safety in AOE relies entirely on the standard faction/
PvP attackability check, not group membership, so grouped players of
different factions can still hit each other with AOE. (3) mines are
not "just another area-action command" -- any fix or instrumentation
targeting mine damage must go through `MinefieldAttackTask`/
`doObjectDetonation`, a codepath completely separate from the shared
grenade/weapon-special AOE pipeline.

## 309. Vehicle Pilot License/Certification -- Ground Vehicles Are Fully Unrestricted, Space Ships Reuse Weapon-Certification Machinery But Gate Only at Launch, Uncertified Purchase Is Allowed at a Cost Penalty (extends sections 11, 18, 78, 111)

**Ground vehicles and mounts require no piloting skill of any kind --
`MountCommand` performs no certification check anywhere -- while
space ships genuinely reuse the exact same ability-list certification
mechanism as weapon certification (section 11), but the check fires
only once, at the moment of launch, with no continuous enforcement
afterward.** `MountCommand::doQueueCommand()`'s checks are limited to
cooldown, target validity, ownership, range/line-of-sight, and
vehicle state -- confirming section 78's terrain/speed-tier
restrictions are the only real gate on ground vehicle use. Space ship
certification is data-driven: each chassis carries a
`certificationRequired` ability string, checked by `ShipObjectImplementation::
canBePilotedBy()` via the identical `PlayerObject::hasAbility()`
list-membership check weapon certs use. This function is called from
exactly two places -- the `/launchIntoSpace` command (the actual
flight gate, returning `GENERALERROR` with "not certified" on
failure) and a Lua-exposed query for dialogue/quest scripts -- and is
never re-checked afterward, meaning a player placed in a capital
ship's pilot chair mid-flight (via a POB pilot-seat swap) is not
re-gated by certification. Certification itself is granted by Pilot
profession skill boxes, and critically does **not** block ship
*purchase* -- lacking certification only multiplies the dealer fee by
a 5x cost multiplier (`NO_CERT_COST_MULTI`), with the buy button
remaining fully functional either way.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any documentation claim of a ground
vehicle "driver's license" is false -- only terrain/speed-tier rules
(section 78) apply to speeders, swoops, and landspeeders. (2) space
piloting certification is enforced solely at the launch command, not
continuously -- a gunner/passenger seated via a pilot-chair swap on a
multi-crew ship bypasses the check entirely. (3) uncertified players
can always buy any ship deed at a 5x credit penalty -- the restriction
is purely "can you fly it," never "can you own it."

## 310. Harvester Hopper Auto-Withdraw/Auto-Sell -- Confirmed Absent, a Full Hopper Silently Deactivates the Harvester Rather Than Discarding or Auto-Transferring Resources (extends sections 15, 185, 203, 210)

**No auto-withdraw, auto-sell, or auto-transfer mechanism exists for
harvester hopper contents anywhere in the codebase -- manual
container-transfer withdrawal or the destructive
`HarvesterDiscardHopperCommand` are the only two ways to clear a
hopper, and a full hopper's only automatic behavior is deactivating
the harvester, never losing or redirecting resources.**
`InstallationObjectImplementation::updateHopper()` clamps each tick's
harvest amount to remaining hopper capacity -- excess resource simply
stays unharvested in the ground spawn rather than being wasted -- and
forces `setActive(false)` once the hopper reaches its cap, backed by
a dedicated client string, "Output hopper full. Shutting down." A
repo-wide search for auto-sell/auto-withdraw/auto-deposit patterns
tied to harvesters returns zero hits; the only other "hopper" auto-
behavior in the engine (factory manufacturing output) follows the
identical stop-not-discard pattern. `HarvesterDiscardHopperCommand`
is explicitly destructive -- it deletes hopper contents with no
credit or item granted -- distinct from the normal client UI path
where a player manually drags individual `ResourceContainer` stacks
out as ordinary inventory transfers. Hopper capacity itself is a
deed/tier property (section 203), not a runtime-configurable setting,
and no server-side Lua config toggle for automated hopper management
exists.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) a full hopper never loses material --
the practical cost of neglect is lost extraction *time* (the
harvester sits idle) rather than lost resources. (2)
`HarvesterDiscardHopperCommand` should be documented clearly as a
"delete, not sell" operation, since new players may reasonably expect
it to liquidate resources for credits. (3) reactivation after a
hopper-full shutdown is entirely manual with no auto-resume on space
freeing up -- harvester management is a genuine recurring chore with
no built-in mitigation, and any automation feature would need to be
built from scratch against `updateHopper()`'s shutdown branch.

## 311. Mail Item/Credit Attachments -- Confirmed Absent, `PersistentMessage` Is a Pure Text-Only Object With No Item or Credit Field, Architecturally Distinct From the COD Mailbox Path (extends sections 21, 140, 232)

**Regular player-to-player mail cannot carry item or credit
attachments at all -- `PersistentMessage`, the sole data structure
behind in-game mail, has no item reference, no credit field, and no
attachment container of any kind, on either the server object model
or the wire protocol in either direction.** `PersistentMessage.idl`
declares only sender/subject/body/timestamp/status plus optional
localized-text and waypoint chat parameters -- no `SceneObject*` and
no credit `long`. All three `ChatManagerImplementation::sendMail()`
overloads populate only text and chat-parameter fields; both the
client-to-server compose packet and the server-to-client delivery
packet likewise carry no OID or credit-amount field, confirming the
omission is symmetric across the entire protocol, not a one-sided
server gap. The only cap present is a 4000-character body-length
limit (`PM_MAXSIZE`); mailbox storage itself (a `SortedVector<uint64>`
of message IDs on `PlayerObject`) has no size cap on insert. System-
generated mail that references credits (e.g. city tax receipts)
interpolates the amount as plain text via a `StringIdChatParameter`
token, never as a real attachment -- the credits themselves move
separately through the bank ledger. This is architecturally distinct
from the structure/vendor COD mailbox mechanic (section 232), which
uses an entirely separate delivery path capable of carrying real
item/credit payloads.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the correct answer to "can I mail an item
to a friend" is no for ordinary mail -- direct trade, inventory
gifting, vendor purchase, or the COD mailbox (section 232) are the
only asset-transfer paths that exist. (2) building item/credit mail
attachments would require extending `PersistentMessage.idl` with a
container/credit field, extending both packet classes symmetrically,
and building a claim/retrieve flow with an inventory-full fallback --
none of which exists today as partial scaffolding. (3) mailbox storage
is genuinely unbounded (no stored-message count cap), so "mailbox
full" is not a real failure mode in this system, unlike inventory or
hopper capacity elsewhere in the engine.

## 312. Bounty Hunter Informant Conversation Gate -- A Mandatory Skill/Tier-Matched NPC Prerequisite for Tracker Access, No Paid Tips, NPC Targets Use a Simulated Moving Trail While Player Targets Are Always Live (extends sections 20, 80, 186, 200, 289)

**A dedicated informant NPC exists and is a mandatory conversation
gate the bounty hunter must clear before the tracking-droid/datapad
tracker (section 186) will function at all -- but it is a scripted,
skill-and-tier-matched trigger with zero credit cost and no
reputation gating, not a paid-tip or free-form clue system.** The
`informant_npc` template (three tiers matching bounty mission
difficulty) drives `InformantMissionScreenHandler`, which requires
the player hold `combat_bountyhunter_novice`, have an active bounty
mission, and match the informant's tier exactly to the mission's
level -- talking to a wrong-tier informant yields "find easier/harder"
flavor text with no progress. No `subtractCash`/payment call exists
anywhere in this flow. Until the informant conversation completes,
`BountyHunterDroid::findTarget()` and related tracker functions
explicitly refuse with "You must go speak with your informant before
you can track your target" -- confirming the informant is a hard
prerequisite gate, not an alternate lookup path. Target location
resolution then diverges sharply by target type: player bounty
targets always resolve via a genuine live `getWorldPosition()`/zone
lookup with zero staleness, while NPC bounty targets are driven by
`BountyHunterTargetTask`, a simulated "moving trail" that advances the
target's position toward a randomly-generated destination every 10
seconds (potentially routing through a starport and jumping planets
at higher mission levels), spawning the actual NPC only once the
hunter closes within 256 units.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the informant is a hard mission-flow
gate (skill + mission-level tier match), not a paid tip broker --
there is no credit-for-information mechanic anywhere in the bounty
system to conflate this with. (2) no cooling-trail/investigation
mechanic exists for player targets -- those are always resolved via
live position lookups, full stop. (3) NPC targets do have a genuine
"moving trail" analog worth knowing about when reasoning about
tracker behavior: a 10-second-tick simulated walk independent of and
downstream from the informant conversation, which only supplies the
mission's initial waypoint.

## 313. Force Rank System (FRS) Rank Decay/Demotion -- Genuinely Bidirectional via Four Independent Mechanisms, the Mechanical Opposite of Decay-Free GCW Rank (extends sections 43, 100, 151, 233)

**FRS rank is not a monotonically-increasing counter -- unlike GCW
rank/score (confirmed decay-free, sections 100/151), FRS rank can
decrease via at least four independent mechanisms, all funneling
through one `demotePlayer()` function that unconditionally drops rank
by one.** The core "decay" path is XP-debt driven: a **daily
maintenance tax task** runs against every council member (online or
not) at `baseMaintCost * rank`, so higher rank carries steeper daily
upkeep, banked as debt and applied on next login if not deducted
immediately -- a genuine structure-maintenance-style upkeep burden
(cross-ref section 30/67) rather than a simple timer. Two more XP-debt
triggers layer on top: a penalty for **missing promotion votes**
(`missedVotePenalty * rank^2`, a real participation/inactivity
penalty), and a **no-confidence challenge vote**, where a caller pays
credits to force a demotion, rate-limited to once per 7 days per
caller. Separately, the Dark Council supports direct **PvP-challenge
demotion**: a lower-ranked Dark Jedi who wins a formal duel against a
higher rank literally swaps ranks with them via simultaneous
`demotePlayer()`+`promotePlayer()` calls. Finally, a **mass rank wipe**
exists for unanswered arena challenges -- if a rank's answered-challenge
ratio stays below 50% across enough phases, every player holding that
rank is force-set to rank 0 simultaneously, a collective
responsiveness-driven demotion scoped (per the code read) to the Dark
Council.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) FRS rank can decrease via four
independent mechanisms -- daily tax, missed votes, lost arena
challenges, and manual no-confidence demotion -- so any tooling
assuming FRS rank is monotonic will be wrong. (2) high FRS rank is
inherently upkeep-gated via the daily maintenance tax, closer in
spirit to structure maintenance than to any other progression system
in the game. (3) do not conflate this with GCW rank/military standing
(sections 100/151) -- the two "rank" systems the game presents to
players behave oppositely at the code level: one immutable except by
explicit gameplay action, the other actively decaying by default.

## 314. Weapon/Armor Dye Customization -- Confirmed Absent, No Shared or Parallel Color-Layer Infrastructure Exists for Gear Despite a Working Vehicle/Droid Equivalent (extends sections 7, 142, 159)

**No weapon or armor recoloring mechanic exists anywhere in Core3 --
the vehicle/droid dye engine (section 159) is provably scoped
exclusively to those two object types, with zero equivalent
`*CustomKitObjectMenuComponent` class or SUI callback for weapons or
armor.** Every armor piece uses a generic `ArmorObjectMenuComponent`
with no color-kit hook, and every weapon/armor crafting schematic
ships with empty `customizationOptions`/`customizationStringNames`
tables -- a uniform pattern across the entire category, confirming no
schematic has ever populated a color/hue option. Several "dye"-named
assets do exist in the codebase but are dead or decorative rather
than functional: a static world-decoration "dye kit" prop with no
menu component at all, and orphaned chemistry-profession dye
components (`dye_clothing`/`dye_hair`) that are never consumed as an
ingredient by any other schematic anywhere in the tree -- vestigial
content, not a working post-craft recolor tool.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) do not conflate the vehicle/droid dye
engine (section 159) or structure paint (section 142) with gear --
they share no infrastructure whatsoever; weapons and armor are a
completely separate, undyed category. (2) building this feature would
require genuinely new work from scratch: a new menu-component class,
a paired SUI callback, and non-empty customization fields on every
armor/weapon schematic -- none of that scaffolding exists to extend.
(3) don't mistake a `grep -i dye` hit for evidence of a working
feature -- several dye-named items in the codebase are confirmed dead
or purely decorative.

## 315. Lightsaber Crystal Quality/Stat Tiers -- A Real Combat-Affecting System Separate From Color, Driven by a Per-Crystal-Type Static Table and a Loot-Level Roll, Not Resource Quality (extends sections 45, 58, 160, 229, 250)

**Lightsaber crystals split into two genuinely different kinds --
purely cosmetic color crystals with zero combat effect, and "Force
crystals" (`color == 31`) that carry a full stat block (damage, attack
speed, HAM sacrifice costs, wound chance, force cost) -- with stat
magnitude driven by a per-crystal-type static min/max table combined
with a loot-level-biased random roll, an entirely different mechanism
from section 250's resource-quality-based crafting formula.** Only
Force crystals apply any of the six combat-affecting setters at
socket-insertion time; cosmetic crystals only ever call
`setBladeColor()`. Stats come from a Lua-defined `jediCrystalStats`
table holding two entries -- a base "Force crystal" and the rarer
"Krayt Dragon Pearl" (a genuine loot-gated rarity tier with a strictly
better stat floor, dropped only from Krayt Dragons) -- with the actual
roll biased toward an `itemLevel` set automatically from the killing
NPC's combat level at loot-generation time, not from crafting
resource selection. A separate seven-tier "quality" label (POOR
through FLAWLESS) is purely a cosmetic display bucket derived from
`itemLevel`, also governing the Force-power cost to bind ("tune") the
crystal to its owner -- but the label itself doesn't independently
drive stats. No elemental/damage-type variation exists anywhere in
this system -- only magnitude and cost values change.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) crystal balance changes belong in the
`jediCrystalStats` Lua table, the single source of truth for min/max
ranges -- not in any schematic or resource-quality file. (2) a Force
crystal's effective roll is fixed at loot-generation time from the
dropping NPC's level, unlike ordinary crafted gear, which re-rolls
based on player-selected resources (section 250) -- crystals aren't
crafted-quality-dependent at all. (3) documentation should never
imply elemental crystal variants (fire/ice/etc.) -- Core3's crystal
system only varies magnitude, never damage type.

## 316. Bazaar/Vendor "Premium" Listing -- A Real 5x-Fee Cosmetic Flag With Zero Effect on Search Ranking, Filtering, or Placement (extends sections 136, 144, 227)

**Core3 does implement a "premium" listing option costing 5x the base
bazaar sale fee, but it has no effect whatsoever on search result
ordering, filtering, or placement -- confirming section 227's
unindexed linear scan and 100-result page cap apply identically to
premium and standard listings.** The premium flag is a bitmask value
set client-side at listing time, charged at `SALESFEE * 5` instead of
the base fee, and gate-checked only for credit sufficiency -- it
grants no extra listing duration and no priority queueing. Critically,
the entire query/filter/paginate routine that builds bazaar search
results never once calls the premium-check function or reads the flag
anywhere in its filtering logic; items are appended strictly in
vector-insertion order, identical for premium and free listings, and
capped by the same hardcoded 100-result window. The only place the
flag is ever read is the outbound packet builder, which forwards it
to the client purely so the UI can render a cosmetic premium
icon/highlight -- a vestige of live SWG's cosmetic premium-listing
flag, not a functional pay-to-rank feature in this engine.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) there is no paid-placement or boosted-
visibility mechanic in Core3's bazaar -- a premium listing can fall
past the 100-result cutoff exactly as easily as a free one. (2) the
5x fee buys nothing beyond a client-visible cosmetic flag; treat any
claim of "premium listings sell faster" as unsupported by the code.
(3) building a genuine featured-listing system would require adding a
secondary sort key to the query-building loop that prioritizes
premium items before applying the offset+100 cap -- no such logic
exists today.

## 317. Group/Raid Target Marker and Focus-Target Broadcast -- Confirmed Absent, Group Membership Carries Zero Shared-Targeting Data, `/assist` Is the Only Manual Approximation (extends sections 62, 178, 235)

**Core3 has no raid-marker icon system and no leader-driven
focus-target broadcast -- `GroupObject` carries no target field, no
target-ID list, and no method touching any member's targeting state,
confirming group membership is state-sharing for XP/loot/chat/
leadership only, never targeting.** Individual target state lives
entirely on each player's own `CreatureObject` as a private field,
broadcast only to that creature's own nearby observers via the
standard proximity-update system -- never routed through any
group-specific channel. The closest approximation is `/assist`, a
generic, group-membership-agnostic command that copies a chosen
player's current target onto the caller as a one-time snapshot and
queues an attack against it -- usable on any nearby player, not
specifically a group or raid leader, with no automatic propagation
and no persistent binding if the source player retargets afterward. A
broad search for marker/focus-target terminology (raid icons, kill
markers, focus-target fields) across the whole source tree returned
no hits beyond unrelated loot-item and screenplay function names.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) do not assume any shared-visibility
targeting exists at the group/raid level -- every player manages
their own target entirely independently, confirming and extending
section 235's finding that group membership has zero positional/
targeting side effects. (2) `/assist` is the only built-in
target-following tool, and it's a manual, one-shot, unrestricted
command -- not a raid-marker substitute. (3) adding raid-marker
functionality would require new `GroupObject.idl` state and a new
delta-broadcast method, since no existing plumbing can be repurposed
for group-scoped target sharing.

## 318. Space Station Ship Repair -- NPC-Conversation-Driven, Damage-Scaled Cost With a 6-Minute Per-Station Cooldown, Permanent Decay on Repeated Repair, No Fuel System Exists At All (extends sections 74, 111, 131, 132)

**Space station ship repair is a paid NPC-conversation flow (no
terminal, no automatic on-dock repair), with cost scaling to actual
accumulated damage and gated by a flat 6-minute per-station cooldown
-- and critically, each repair permanently shaves a fraction off the
repaired component's maximum stats unless the call explicitly
disables decay, meaning station repair is not a free reset over
repeated use.** The player need not be physically docked -- the
repair conversation is reachable via an extended 1000m
"space-station comm range," double the normal 500m limit. Repair cost
is `totalShipDamage * repairPercent * a flat multiplier`, with a flat
25/50/100-credit override for starter "basic"/"prototype" ships
regardless of actual damage. The 6-minute cooldown is tracked per
station (not per player), so any player who repairs there resets the
timer for everyone at that station. **No ship fuel/refueling system
exists anywhere in the codebase** -- a repo-wide search for fuel-related
fields on the ship object tree returns zero results, confirming ships
never consume or need to replenish a fuel resource. This is
architecturally distinct from ground vehicle repair (a garage-gated
SUI transaction with cost proportional to condition damage plus a
city garage tax and no permanent decay penalty).

**Practical takeaways:** (1) station repair is lossy over repeated
use -- permanent max-stat decay accumulates unless repaired via
decay-disabled GM tools, so "just repair at the station" is not a
zero-cost maintenance strategy for ship owners. (2) there is no
refuel mechanic to document or design around -- "ship fuel" is simply
not a system that exists in Core3. (3) the 6-minute cooldown is
per-station, not per-player -- a busy station can effectively block
repeat repairs for everyone until the timer clears.

## 319. Structure/Vendor Tip Jar -- Confirmed Absent as a Placed Object, `/tip` Is a Generic Peer-to-Peer Credit Command With No Entertainer, Vendor, or Structure Gating (extends sections 48, 101, 140, 244)

**No placeable "tip jar" container or vendor/structure-donation
feature exists -- what Core3 has instead is a generic `/tip`
chat command that transfers credits directly between any two
targetable players, with no special handling for entertainers, vendor
owners, or structures of any kind.** Two transfer modes exist: an
in-range (190m), online-only cash tip with no fee, and a bank/wire
tip usable on offline targets carrying a 5% surcharge (waived for
same-account transfers via a config flag), which mails both parties a
transfer receipt. Every credit movement is logged under a dedicated
transaction code for auditability. The only gating on `/tip` is
distance/online-state, a self-target block, and a positive-amount
check -- there is no check for the target performing, running a
vendor, or standing inside any structure, confirming this is purely a
peer-to-peer command with no object or location dependency. The only
"donate" mechanics found elsewhere in the codebase belong to the
unrelated GCW base-defense funding UI (turret/minefield donations),
not player tipping.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the correct answer for "how do players
tip entertainers/vendors" is `/tip <name> <amount> [bank]`, not any
placed object -- there is no tip-jar container to point players
toward. (2) tipping is entirely player-to-player and location-agnostic
-- owning a vendor or performing grants no special tip-receiving
mechanism. (3) the 5% bank-wire surcharge (waivable for same-account
transfers) is the only economic friction in the system; in-range cash
tips are fee-free.

## 320. Faction Guard NPC Patrol Routes -- No Guard-Specific Waypoint System Exists, Attackable Garrison NPCs Are Static Leashed Sentries While Hand-Authored Routes Are Reserved for Unarmed Ambient Civilians (extends sections 42, 52, 76, 125)

**Faction/GCW guard NPCs do not get a distinct, hand-authored
patrol-route system -- Core3 has three separate NPC-movement tiers,
and attackable garrison NPCs fall into the *least* mobile one (a
fixed static sentry that always leashes back to its exact spawn
point), not the hand-authored waypoint routes used by ordinary
townsfolk.** Generic wildlife/static spawns use a procedural
random-point wander (`GeneratePatrol`), picking random nearby points
near home with no authored route at all. GCW "crackdown" squad
mobiles (section 76) use this exact same generic random-wander node --
"patrolling" crackdown guards are not walking a placed route, they
wander randomly near their spawn, identically to ordinary animals.
Genuine hand-authored waypoint routes do exist, reading a literal
per-city coordinate table and walking a fixed sequence with
interrupt-then-resume behavior on combat -- but every city's patrol
list is populated exclusively with unarmed, non-attackable ambient
civilians (businessmen, commoners, nobles), never Imperial/Rebel
military templates. Attackable faction garrison NPCs are instead
flagged as static agents, which forces them to always path back to
their exact spawn coordinate rather than wander or patrol at all --
the fixed-sentry pattern, not a route.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) there is no "guard-specific" waypoint
patrol system to look for -- the hand-authored per-city patrol tables
are reserved for unarmed ambient civilians only. (2) attackable
faction/GCW garrison NPCs are static sentries pinned to their exact
spawn point, always leashing home rather than patrolling any route.
(3) GCW crackdown squads are the closest thing to a "patrolling
guard," but they use the same generic random-point wander as ordinary
wildlife -- no bespoke route data exists for them, and interrupt/
resume behavior on combat only meaningfully applies to the unarmed
civilian patrol system, not to any guard type.

## 321. Weapon/Armor "Set Bonus" Mechanic -- Confirmed Absent, No Set-Membership Field Exists on Any Item Class, Damage Mitigation Is Resolved Strictly Per Hit-Location Piece (extends sections 93, 148, 229)

**No set-bonus mechanic exists anywhere in Core3 -- armor and weapon
stats are purely additive per item, with no code path that detects
matching-set equipment and grants a bonus beyond each piece's own
stats.** Neither `ArmorObject.idl` nor `WeaponObject.idl` (nor their
common `TangibleObject` base) carries a set-ID, set-name, or any
set-membership field of any kind -- a codebase-wide search for set-bonus
terminology returns only an unrelated mission-reward-credits accessor
as a false positive. Damage mitigation is computed strictly per
hit-location piece via `CombatManager::getArmorReduction()`, which
resolves only the single armor piece covering the struck location
plus separate additive skill-mod reductions -- there is no aggregate
pass over all worn items to check set completion. No database schema
for item sets exists either, confirming the absence extends to the
persistence layer, not just runtime logic.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any "sets" referenced in loot tables or
schematic naming are purely cosmetic groupings with zero coded
mechanical synergy. (2) building set bonuses would require genuinely
new work -- a set-ID field on both item classes plus a new equipped-slot
scan (the engine already iterates worn items elsewhere for other
purposes, giving a natural integration point) -- none of that
scaffolding exists today. (3) because mitigation is resolved per
hit-location piece, mixing armor types/qualities across body slots is
fully supported with no hidden penalty or bonus either way.

## 322. Structure "For Rent"/Leasing -- Confirmed Absent, No Tenant Concept or Recurring Payment Exists, Only Permanent Ownership Transfer and Static Unpaid ADMIN Co-Ownership (extends sections 109, 122, 242, 301)

**Core3 has no mechanism for a structure owner to lease/rent their
structure to another player for periodic payment -- there is no
tenant concept, no temporary-access grant with an expiration, and no
recurring player-to-player payment tied to structure access anywhere
in the codebase.** `StructurePermissionList` carries no
expiration/duration/payment field of any kind -- ADMIN list grants
(section 301) are simple, indefinite, unpaid boolean toggles, entirely
distinct from a lease. The only "rental" concept anywhere in the
engine is an NPC vehicle rental coupon -- a single-player, use-count-limited
consumable with no second player involved and no periodic payment,
unrelated to structures entirely. The only "expiration" tied to a
structure is maintenance-fund depletion (the decay/condemnation
timer, sections 30/163), which is owner-funded upkeep, not tenant
rent paid to the owner. `/transferstructure` remains a one-shot,
irreversible ownership swap with no payment parameter and no return
path -- structurally incompatible with a recurring-rent model.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) do not conflate ADMIN co-ownership
(section 301) with leasing -- ADMIN is a static, unpaid, indefinite
toggle, while a lease implies a fee and a term, neither of which this
engine tracks. (2) building a landlord/tenant system would require
entirely new infrastructure: an expiration field on
`StructurePermissionList` and a scheduled task analogous to structure
maintenance for revoking access on a timer tied to payment -- nothing
exists to extend. (3) "rental" in the existing codebase refers
exclusively to single-player NPC vehicle coupons, an unrelated
mechanic that should never be cited as evidence for structure
leasing.

## 323. Vendor/Bazaar "Wanted List"/Shopping Alert -- Confirmed Absent, All Searches Are Synchronous One-Shot Queries With No Saved Criteria or New-Listing Notification Hook (extends sections 50, 227, 316)

**No wanted-list, watchlist, or shopping-alert mechanic exists --
every bazaar/vendor search in Core3 is a stateless, player-initiated
request that queries currently-listed items once and returns results;
nothing is persisted server-side to be re-evaluated against future
listings.** The search-type enum covers ten distinct query screens
(category, location, player sales/bids/stockroom, vendor
offers/selling/stockroom), and every one queries a live snapshot of
existing listings -- there is no watchlist/wanted search type and no
persisted-criteria table anywhere. Mail notifications only ever fire
from a transaction the player already initiated (bid outcome, instant
buy, sale completing/expiring, vendor maintenance) -- no code path
iterates over other players' stored search interests when a new item
is listed, because no such stored interest exists to iterate. The
vendor barker advertisement system (section 101) is a one-way,
radius-based broadcast of a vendor's own inventory, not a
personalized incoming-item alert, and should not be confused with
this confirmed-absent mechanic.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) there is no scaffolding to extend for a
"notify me when X is listed" feature -- it would require a new
per-player saved-criteria store and a listener hook on new-item
creation, built entirely from scratch. (2) the natural integration
point for such a feature would be the item-creation functions where
an `AuctionItem` first becomes visible, paired with the existing mail
API already used throughout the auction manager for transaction
notifications. (3) don't confuse this absence with the cross-vendor
bazaar search (section 50) or premium listings (section 316) -- both
of those operate only on the current snapshot at query time, never on
future listings.

## 324. Jedi Force Meditation / Passive Force-Point Regeneration -- Two Distinct Commands With Different Effects, `/forceMeditate` Genuinely Triples the Regen Tick, Force Power Is a Fully Separate Pool From Mind (extends sections 58, 61, 189)

**Force Power is a dedicated pool on `PlayerObject`, entirely separate
from the HAM triad, and Jedi have two distinct meditation commands
that are commonly conflated but do different things -- `/meditate`
(open to any profession) heals wounds/DoTs and never touches Force
power, while `/forceMeditate` (Jedi-only, requires no armor) genuinely
triples the passive Force regeneration tick from 5 to 15 per cycle.**
Both commands require the caller be out of combat and share the same
underlying posture/state setter, which sets sitting posture plus an
ALERT state bit -- meditation is architecturally just this
sit-and-flag state, making combat entry impossible while active per
normal state rules. The Force regen multiplier check is explicit and
narrow: only if a `"forcemeditate"` pending task exists does the
regen tick multiply by 3; plain `/meditate` never touches it. Base
Force regen itself is entirely Jedi-gated -- the governing skill mod
returns early (zero regen) for any non-Jedi character -- and is
further modified by light/dark-side control/manipulation skill mods
and faction perk multiplier/divisor mods, converting into a scheduling
interval for the next regen tick. A third related command,
`PowerBoostCommand`, explicitly requires plain meditation but rejects
the Force-meditate state, converting half of base Mind into a
temporary Force buff -- confirming it stacks only with `/meditate`,
never `/forceMeditate`.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) `/meditate` and `/forceMeditate` are
functionally unrelated beyond sharing a posture setter -- conflating
them is a common misreading, since only the latter affects Force
regeneration at all. (2) the regen multiplier is a clean 3x, applied
only while sitting, unarmored, and out of combat with the
Force-meditate task active -- any UI/tooling assuming a continuous or
skill-scaled meditation bonus would be inaccurate. (3) `PowerBoostCommand`
is a genuinely separate, mutually-exclusive-with-Force-meditate
mechanic worth distinguishing in any Force-power economy discussion.

## 325. Structure Crafting Station Concurrency -- No Occupancy Lock Exists, Stations Are Fully Shareable in Real Time, the Only Concurrency Constraint Is the Existing Single-Session-Per-Player Rule (extends sections 65, 252, 285)

**A placed public crafting station has zero occupancy state, lock, or
session tracking of its own -- any number of players can use the same
station to craft simultaneously, because the station is never the
thing that owns a session; it is only a passive lookup target
supplying a complexity cap and effectiveness multiplier, while all
mutable per-player state lives entirely on each player's own
`CreatureObject` and `CraftingTool`.** The station-lookup functions
used both when targeting a station directly and when auto-detecting
a nearby station perform zero availability/occupancy checks -- a
second, third, or Nth concurrent player calling either path receives
the identical station reference with no contention. Session
construction reads the station only for range validation and to copy
its read-only `complexityLevel`/`effectiveness` fields into the new
session at start time -- nothing is written back to the station
object, so concurrent users never mutate or contend for shared station
state. This confirms section 285's single-session-per-player rule is
the *only* concurrency constraint anywhere in the crafting pipeline,
scoped entirely to the player and their tool, never to the station.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) multiple players can freely share one
public Weaponsmith/Armorsmith station with fully independent,
simultaneous sessions -- matching live SWG's community-infrastructure
design, not a single-occupancy machine. (2) there is no separate
"station lock" layer to reason about beyond section 285's per-player
rule. (3) the only genuinely shared, lockable resource tied to a
station is its ingredient hopper container, guarded by ordinary
container permissions rather than any crafting-session-specific
mechanism.

## 326. Faction Disguise/Infiltration -- Confirmed Absent, NPC Aggro and Attackability Checks Never Inspect Equipped Items, Uniforms Carry No Faction Data on the Item Instance (extends sections 123, 125, 297)

**Wearing an opposing faction's uniform provides zero mechanical
disguise benefit -- the single choke point for NPC aggro decisions
reads only the wearer's own character-level faction/status fields,
never any equipped item, and wearable item classes (clothing, armor)
carry no faction field on the item instance at all for the engine to
read even if it wanted to.** Both the aggression check and the
attackability check independently gate on the same character-level
faction/GCW-status machinery already documented for faction NPC guard
aggression (section 125) -- at no point does either function consult
`getSlottedObject()` for faction purposes; the few slot lookups present
in that code serve unrelated combat/loot logic. This closes the last
plausible place a disguise check could have lived, and is consistent
with section 123's finding that uniforms are purely cosmetic, and
section 297's finding that the only real concealment system (Scout
camouflage) is an anti-creature-aggro roll entirely unrelated to
uniforms or faction identity. Any "infiltrator" NPC personas found in
quest content are static AI templates for narrative flavor, not a
player-usable disguise system.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) a player in full Imperial uniform
standing next to a Rebel guard is evaluated purely on their own
faction/status/TEF state -- appearance has zero bearing on any aggro
or attackability decision. (2) building a real disguise mechanic
would require genuinely new code: either an "apparent faction"
override consulted inside the aggro/attackability checks, or a
temporary buff analogous to the Scout conceal buff that guard AI
behavior trees check before aggroing -- nothing exists to repurpose.
(3) "infiltrator"-named NPC templates in screenplay content are
narrative-only and should not be cited as evidence of a player-facing
disguise system.

## 327. Structure Lot Merging -- Confirmed Absent, "Lots" Are an Abstract Per-Player Budget Number Rather Than Discrete World Objects, Larger Structures Simply Cost More Budget (extends sections 35, 171, 281)

**Core3 has no mechanism to merge adjacent lots into a larger buildable
footprint, because lots are not discrete world objects at all -- they
are an abstract integer cost debited from a per-player budget
(section 281), and a structure's footprint is a single fixed rectangle
baked into its own template.** No `Lot`/`Parcel` class exists anywhere
in the source tree, ruling out any merge operation since there is no
discrete object to merge. Lot cost (`lotSize`) is a static per-template
field loaded straight from the structure's IFF data, checked against
the player's recomputed remaining-lots budget at placement and
transfer time -- never tied to specific ground coordinates. Structure
footprint likewise comes from exactly one fixed rectangle per template,
computed purely from that structure's own geometry with no concept of
joining multiple footprint tiles. Concrete catalog data confirms the
pattern: small houses cost 1-2 lots, large houses and guild halls cost
5 lots each, harvesters/generators/turrets cost 1 lot -- larger
buildings simply carry a higher scalar cost on the same per-player
budget, never a literal merge of separate parcels. `lotSize` even
doubles as the storage-capacity multiplier for player items inside the
building, reinforcing it's purely a scalar cost/capacity value, not a
spatial unit.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) placing a guild hall or large house
doesn't require or consume adjacent lot parcels -- it deducts one
larger `lotSize` value from the same abstract per-player budget
documented in section 281. (2) larger footprints come entirely from a
structure's own dedicated footprint asset, never from unioning
neighboring deeds. (3) because lots aren't world objects, there's
nothing to "unmerge" either -- redeeding a structure simply returns its
`lotSize` to the owner's budget, consistent with section 260/281's
cooldown-free, leasing-free model.

## 328. Crafting Experimentation Critical Failure -- A Distinct Ninth Result Tier Exists in the Enum, But the Roll Branch That Produces It Is Commented Out, Leaving `BARELYSUCCESSFUL` as the Actual Floor (extends sections 45, 199, 215)

**`CRITICALFAILURE` is a genuine, distinct result tier defined
separately from the continuous quality spectrum -- but in the current
codebase, the roll logic that would return it is commented out in
both the assembly and experimentation success calculators, meaning
`BARELYSUCCESSFUL` is the actual reachable floor for ordinary rolls,
not critical failure.** Both roll functions contain an explicit,
disabled line (`//if(luckRoll < 5) return CRITICALFAILURE;`) that
falls through to the barely-successful branch instead. Where
`CRITICALFAILURE` is still reachable -- an anti-exploit sentinel
guarding against clients reporting impossible experimentation-point
usage, and a dead-but-still-wired assembly-stage branch -- the
consequence is a genuine destroy-and-lose outcome: the in-progress
prototype and every resource/component already transferred into it
are destroyed, and the player is reset to the resource-slotting
screen with a fresh empty prototype. By contrast, the
experimentation-stage handling for `CRITICALFAILURE` (also currently
unreachable via the live roll) only degrades stat percentages toward
a floor of zero -- for Bio-Engineer genetic crafting specifically, it
can additionally force an attribute to decrease instead of increase,
or degrade an unrelated attribute, but still never destroys the
prototype itself.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) treat the "critical failure" tier
documented in section 45's quality-roll formula as legacy/disabled
rather than a live gameplay outcome under current code -- the
reachable worst case is `BARELYSUCCESSFUL`. (2) item/resource
destruction as a failure consequence only exists at the assembly
stage's (currently dead) critical-failure branch -- experimentation-stage
failure of any tier only ever lowers stats, never destroys the item.
(3) tool quality/effectiveness (section 215) cannot change "critical
failure chance" under the current build, since that branch is
unreachable -- tool quality only shifts odds within the tiers that
are actually reachable.

## 329. Group Size Cap -- A Hard 20-Member Ceiling Enforced by Duplicated Manager-Layer Literals, Not a Structural Property of GroupObject, No Separate Raid/Ops-Group Container Exists (extends sections 44, 47, 62)

**Core3 hard-caps every group at 20 members, but the cap is a
duplicated literal checked in two separate manager functions, not a
property of `GroupObject`/`GroupList` itself -- and there is no
alternate "raid"/"ops group" container that raises or bypasses it,
confirming groups and any large-scale multi-group PvE content share
the same single 20-member primitive.** The cap is checked once at
invite time and again independently at accept time (closing the race
where a group fills between invite and join), but `GroupObject`'s own
member-add function performs no size check at all -- the invariant
only holds because every normal code path routes through the two
gated manager functions; any future direct member-add call would
silently bypass the cap. The `20` value is also treated as a design
constant elsewhere: the Squad Leader buff's regen modifier scales
against group size relative to this same ceiling, and group combat XP
distribution scales linearly per member up to it -- confirming 20 is
the canonical "full group" size baked into multiple formulas, not an
arbitrary invite gate.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) the cap is enforced by magic-number
literal in two places with no shared constant -- any future tuning
requires editing both, plus the Squad Leader modifier that implicitly
depends on the same value. (2) `GroupObject`/`GroupList` have no
self-enforced limit, so the 20-member invariant only holds as long as
all member-add paths route through the gated manager functions. (3)
there is no larger "raid"/"ops group" structure -- large-scale content
works around the 20-member ceiling via other mechanisms (shared
threat/kill-credit, per-creature loot rolls) rather than a bigger
group container.

## 330. Pet "Stable" Boarding -- Confirmed Absent, All Pet Storage Routes Through the Generic Control-Device Command With No Structure, Fee, or Capacity Distinct From the Existing Datapad Slot System (extends sections 18, 28, 71, 138)

**No dedicated pet stable/kennel/boarding structure or NPC exists
anywhere in Core3 -- pet storage and retrieval are handled entirely
through the generic pet control device command, with no location
requirement, no structure interaction, and no fee, confirming pets
diverge sharply from vehicles (which do use physical garage
structures, section 18).** Pet storage checks only combat/death state
and a flat 1-second cooldown before instantly destroying the pet from
the world (with a 60-second delay specifically for faction pets) --
there is no proximity check to any building or NPC anywhere in this
path. Capacity limits are the same generic per-account datapad slot
counts already covered in sections 71/192, extendable only via a
Beast Mastery skill mod, never by paying a stable-keeper NPC. The one
genuinely location-sensitive nuance is that calling a pet incurs a
15-second delay everywhere except inside a camp or a registered
player city, where it spawns almost instantly -- a city-wide
convenience, not a specific stable building's effect.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) document this as a confirmed absence --
live SWG's stable/boarding concept was never implemented in Core3; all
pet persistence funnels through the section 71 control-device
mechanic. (2) the only capacity and cost knobs available are datapad
slot caps and the relevant skill mod, never a per-building limit or
fee. (3) the 15-second call delay outside cities/camps is the nearest
thing to a location-based rule, worth treating as a footnote to
section 71 rather than a standalone stable mechanic.

## 331. Structure Ownership Transfer Tax -- Confirmed Entirely Free, No Credit Cost to Either Party and No City-Level Tax Triggered by the Transfer Itself (extends sections 109, 136, 163, 318)

**`/transferstructure` is a completely free operation with zero
credit cost to either the old or new owner, and there is no city-level
tax triggered by an ownership change -- confirming and extending
section 109's existing coverage of the transfer command.** The
transfer function performs only validation, proximity/online checks,
a lot-capacity gate on the recipient, and the actual ownership/
permission reassignment -- no credit-subtraction or bank-withdrawal
call exists anywhere in the path, and the transaction log records only
maintenance/power state snapshots for audit purposes, not a payment.
Guild hall "forced" transfers reuse the identical free code path with
no fee-charging branch for either use case. City property tax does
exist, but it's a continuous hourly maintenance surcharge computed
identically before and after any transfer -- never evaluated or
applied at the moment of ownership change itself, so a transfer
neither triggers nor avoids tax liability. This stands in clean
contrast to the bazaar/vendor sale path (section 136), which stacks
an upfront listing fee with baked-in city sales tax -- structure
transfer has no listing step and no analogous fee/tax deduction logic
anywhere in the command.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) treat `/transferstructure` as a pure
ownership/permission reassignment primitive -- any "sale" price must
be handled entirely out-of-band (e.g. a parallel secure trade), since
nothing in the engine atomically ties payment to the transfer. (2) the
vehicle garage-tax model (section 318) does not apply here at all --
structure transfer charges nothing to either party, unlike vehicle
retrieval's per-use fee. (3) city property tax is ownership-agnostic
and accrues identically regardless of who currently owns the
structure -- a new owner simply inherits the existing maintenance
surplus/deficit state as-is.

## 332. Special/Unique-Named Crafting Resources -- Confirmed Absent, Every Spawn Instance Uses the Identical Random-Roll Pipeline and Procedural Name Generator Regardless of Type or Rarity Perception (extends sections 15, 45, 229, 315)

**No special or uniquely-named "legendary" resource system exists --
every resource spawn instance, regardless of which spawning pool
creates it, runs through one identical generation function that rolls
stats via a uniform random range and assigns a procedurally generated
(not fixed/legendary) name, with the stat ceiling fixed per resource
*type* and identical across every spawn of that type.** Names come
from a combinatorial syllable-based generator picking from a handful
of category-specific name-data sets, stitching together a random
first/last name for every resource of a given category -- no
hardcoded unique names exist anywhere. Only two code paths ever bypass
the random roll, and neither represents a rarity upgrade: a
recycled-resource fallback that assigns a flat, deliberately
mediocre value to every attribute for the salvage/recycling tool, and
a GM-only manual-override console command for staff-created test
resources. This stands in clean contrast to section 315's lightsaber
crystal system, which deliberately tiers stat caps by item-template
rarity -- resources have no equivalent tiering; "getting lucky" only
ever means rolling near the top of a type's existing fixed window
(section 229), never encountering a spawn with a categorically higher
ceiling.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) any community-recalled "rare" resource
with unusually high stats is simply the tail end of the same random
roll against that type's config-defined maximum, or a GM-manually-created
test resource -- not an engine-level special-spawn feature. (2) the
recycled-resource flat-value fallback should not be conflated with a
"legendary" resource -- it exists purely to give salvage tools a
consistent, middling-quality input, not a bonus. (3) a fork wanting
true legendary resources would need a new resource-tree flag that
skips the random roll for a fixed high stat block and hardcoded name
-- no such branch exists today to extend.

## 333. Lightsaber "Throw" Special Attack -- A Real Named Attack That Reuses the Generic Ranged/Cone Combat Pipeline, No Weapon Detachment or Projectile Simulation Occurs At the Engine Level (extends sections 58, 201, 231, 291, 308)

**Lightsaber throw exists as three tiered named commands, but it is
mechanically nothing more than a themed ranged special attack (range
32) reusing the exact same generic combat-command pipeline documented
for every other weapon special attack -- the saber is never actually
detached from the character, spawned as a world projectile, or
animated returning to the hand at the engine level.** All three
commands are thin subclasses of the standard Jedi combat command base,
performing only generic state/armor checks before calling the same
`doCombatAction()` every other melee/ranged special attack uses --
there is no projectile spawn, no weapon-unequip, and no "return to
hand" logic anywhere in the server source. Behavior is entirely
data-driven from Lua tuning tables identical in structure to every
other combat command: increasing damage multipliers across the three
tiers, a knockdown effect added at tier two, and the third tier
explicitly reusing the generic cone-attack fields shared by roughly
thirty unrelated commands across every profession (rifle bursts,
pistol fan-shot, Force-lightning cones, and more).

**Practical takeaways:** (1) lightsaber throw belongs conceptually in
section 201's special-attack catalog rather than as its own distinct
subsystem -- it's a ranged-range, themed-animation variant of the same
generic pipeline, not a bespoke mechanic. (2) there is no simulated
"saber leaves the hand" state -- the weapon object never leaves the
held-item slot, so disarming, ground pickup, or a vulnerability window
during the throw are purely cosmetic/animation concepts, never modeled
server-side. (3) anyone debugging or extending this attack should look
at the generic cone/area combat-command pipeline (section 308) rather
than expecting bespoke SaberThrow-specific damage or targeting code --
none exists.

## 334. Droid-Operated Crafting and Vendor Automation -- A Real Crafting-Station Substitution Module Exists (With a Confirmed Power-Check Bypass), Merchant Module Is Advertisement-Only, No Autonomous Restocking Exists Anywhere (extends sections 8, 101, 138, 220)

**Droids gain two genuine dedicated modules beyond generic pet AI --
a crafting module that lets the droid stand in as a mobile crafting
station, and a merchant module that automates advertisement
broadcasting -- but neither lets a droid independently manufacture
items or restock a vendor; the "automation" is narrower than the name
implies.** The crafting module instantiates a real `CraftingStation`
object at default effectiveness when the droid is summoned, and a
dedicated lookup function lets a player substitute their own linked
droid for a stationary station when none is in range -- notably
**without requiring the droid to have power**, a confirmed
exploit-adjacent quirk explicitly referencing an original Mantis
bug-tracker ticket, contrasting with the harvest module's strict power
gating. This is purely a convenience substitution for the physical
proximity requirement -- the player still manually opens the crafting
UI, selects the schematic, and experiments; the droid's own module
handlers for skill mods and pet commands are confirmed no-ops,
contributing zero independent crafting logic. The merchant module is
purely a chat-broadcast automation -- a self-rescheduling task that
periodically announces a player-recorded message to nearby players --
and never touches a `VendorObject`, never lists, prices, or restocks
items. A repo-wide search confirms no autonomous vendor-restocking
mechanism exists anywhere tied to droids; restocking (section 108)
remains a manual player action.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) be precise about what "droid crafting
automation" means -- it only removes the proximity-to-a-station
requirement, never the manual crafting/experimentation loop itself.
(2) the merchant module is advertisement-only and should stay
cross-referenced to the human vendor barker system (section 101), not
conflated with true auto-vending. (3) the power-check bypass on the
crafting module is a notable, currently-exploitable quirk worth
flagging separately from the harvest module's stricter gating -- a
drained crafting droid still functions as a full station.

## 335. Ranged Weapon Special Ammo Effects -- Confirmed Absent, Damage Type and Armor-Piercing Are Fixed at Weapon-Template Load Time, the Only Post-Craft Attachment Is a Purely Numeric Stat Modifier (extends sections 93, 114, 124, 201)

**No ammo or power-pack item type changes a ranged weapon's damage
type, adds armor-piercing, or applies elemental combat effects --
damage type and armor-piercing are both set once from the weapon's
crafted template at load time and never reassigned by any consumable
or attachment afterward.** The only post-craft attachment that exists
is a single optional "powerup" slot, but its entire effect surface is
a fixed whitelist of purely numeric stats (accuracy, range, attack
speed, damage magnitude, various HAM costs) -- there is no damage-type
or armor-piercing branch anywhere in its implementation, and the
underlying template schema has no field to populate one even if
content wanted to. Every powerup content file in the game -- covering
ranged, melee, and thrown weapon variants -- draws exclusively from
this same numeric whitelist, confirmed via an exhaustive search
turning up zero elemental/damage-type terms anywhere in the powerup
script tree. This corroborates and extends section 114's finding that
damage type is fixed per weapon at creation and section 124's
confirmed absence of a personal-weapon ammo/clip system entirely --
the powerup slot is functionally closer to a permanent scope/barrel
modification than to ammunition of any kind.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) do not design content around "elemental
rounds" or "armor-piercing ammo" -- no code path exists for an
equippable item to alter a weapon's damage type or armor-piercing
post-creation. (2) the weapon powerup slot is the nearest real
analogue to "special ammo," but it's a numeric-only DPS/accuracy
modifier capped to a fixed attribute whitelist -- any true elemental-ammo
feature would require new engine fields, not just new content data.
(3) space combat's separate ammo/missile system is architecturally
unrelated and not a precedent to extend to personal ranged weapons
without substantial new engine work.

## 336. Guild Hall Shared Vendor Slots -- No Guild-Scaled Vendor Capacity Exists, Guild Halls Use the Identical Generic 50-Entry VENDOR Permission List as Any House, With One Reusable Guild-as-Single-Entry Trick Available to Any Structure (extends sections 90, 195, 242, 301)

**Guild halls have no guild-specific vendor-capacity system -- vendor
placement rights inside them are governed by the exact same generic
structure permission list documented for ordinary houses, capped at a
flat 50 entries regardless of guild size, with `CreateVendorCommand`
applying an identical admin-or-VENDOR-list check to guild halls and
private houses alike.** The permission-check function for every list
type checks the requesting player's own ID first, then falls back to
checking the player's *guild's* object ID -- a generic mechanism
usable on any structure, not something added specifically for guild
halls. This means a guild's entire membership can be granted blanket
vendor rights through a single permission-list entry (the guild's own
object ID), letting a guild hall's owner cover an unlimited-size
membership within the same 50-entry cap that would otherwise
constrain a non-guild owner sharing rights with individually-named
players. Guild hall ownership itself stays player-scoped rather than
entity-scoped -- the guild object is never set as a structure's
recorded owner, and guild hall transfer reuses the identical
player-to-player `TransferstructureCommand` path documented in
section 331. Per-player vendor-count limits (a skill-mod-driven cap)
remain entirely separate and unrelated to guild membership or rank.

**Practical takeaways:** (1) guild halls do not get a bigger or
guild-scaled vendor pool -- they use the identical 50-entry permission
list as any house. (2) the "shared vendor access for the whole guild"
feel comes entirely from the guild-as-single-entry permission trick,
which any structure owner (guild hall or private house) can use, not
a guild-hall-exclusive feature. (3) because guild membership is
resolved dynamically at permission-check time rather than baked into
the list, adding or removing a player from the guild automatically
grants or revokes their vendor rights with no separate structure-side
update needed.

# General Engine Architecture -- Foundational Reference (Sections 337-362)

The sections below shift focus from individual game *features* (the
bulk of this guide so far) to the underlying *engine architecture*
that every feature is built on top of: object model, codegen,
networking, persistence, locking, scripting, and the other load-bearing
systems a developer needs to understand before writing new code
efficiently. Researched via 26 parallel read-only passes over
`C:\Companion\Core3`, cross-referencing existing guide sections and
`docs/companion_system/NOTES.md`'s own hard-won, real bug-fix history
wherever relevant.

## 337. SceneObject Class Hierarchy -- The Root Object Model Every Game Type Descends From

Every placeable/world-referenceable object descends from **SceneObject**
(`server/zone/objects/scene/SceneObject.idl:76`), which forks into two
direct children: **TangibleObject** (`tangible/TangibleObject.idl:34`)
for physical, damageable objects, and **IntangibleObject**
(`intangible/IntangibleObject.idl:15`) for non-physical/logical objects
(waypoints, schematics, control devices, quest data). **CreatureObject**
(`creature/CreatureObject.idl:54`) is a further specialization of
TangibleObject, not a sibling branch -- every living/controllable actor
is tangible first. Other direct SceneObject children handle
structural/logical world entries with no HAM or damage state: `CellObject`,
`ActiveArea`, `ResourceSpawn`, `GuildObject`, `GroupObject`, `StaticObject`.

Each level adds a distinct capability layer. SceneObject provides world
identity/placement (zone reference, position, the container/slot
machinery, name/template, menu components) with no health or combat
state. TangibleObject adds condition/damage tracking, faction/PvP status,
threat/defender maps for combat targeting, and crafter/customization
data -- this is what "tangible" means: it can take damage and be
targeted. IntangibleObject stays deliberately sparse (`status`,
`datapadSize`, `itemIdentifier`) since it represents inventory-only
logical objects that never render as damageable world props.
CreatureObject adds the actor-specific state neither parent has: HAM
pools, posture/locomotion, movement stats, skill lists, command queue,
buffs/DoTs, group/guild references, equipped weapon, and control-device
linkage (pet/vehicle/companion ownership).

Real game types map onto this tree as: Building →
`BuildingObject extends StructureObject extends TangibleObject`; Vehicle
→ `VehicleObject extends CreatureObject`; Weapon →
`WeaponObject extends TangibleObject`; Resource spawn pool →
`ResourceSpawn extends SceneObject` (harvested item →
`ResourceContainer extends TangibleObject`); Waypoint →
`WaypointObject extends IntangibleObject`; NPC → `AiAgent extends
CreatureObject`; player data → `PlayerObject extends IntangibleObject`
(attached to the player's own CreatureObject); Mail → **not** in this
tree at all -- `PersistentMessage extends ManagedObject`, persisted but
never world-placed.

**Practical takeaway:** the real implementation logic for any `Foo`
class lives in a hand-written `FooImplementation.cpp` next to
`Foo.idl` -- never in the generated `src/autogen/.../Foo.h`/`.cpp`
pair (see section 338). When adding a new object type, find the
closest existing sibling in this tree first and extend from there
rather than starting at SceneObject.
