## 338. IDL -> C++ Codegen Pipeline -- How to Actually Add a New Field or Method

Source for nearly every persisted/networked class is a `Foo.idl` file
(field/method declarations) paired with a hand-written
`FooImplementation.cpp` (real logic). `idlc.jar`
(`utils/engine3/MMOEngine/lib/idlc.jar`, wired via
`cmake/Modules/FindEngine3.cmake:158` and invoked per-file from
`src/CMakeLists.txt:19-39`) generates one `.h` + one `.cpp` per `.idl`,
mirrored under `src/autogen/<same path>` -- e.g.
`autogen/server/zone/objects/area/areashapes/CircularAreaShape.{h,cpp}`.
**Never hand-edit anything under `src/autogen/` -- it's silently
regenerated/discarded whenever the source `.idl`'s mtime is newer.**

Annotation grammar seen across `.idl` files: `@read` (read-only
accessor), `@dirty` (marks a *method*, not a field -- despite the
name, this is a locking/dispatch annotation meaning "no pre-lock
requirement, establishes its own lock internally," confirmed by
grepping all 213 real usages; **it has nothing to do with
save-to-database dirty-tracking**, which is a separate runtime
mechanism, see section 341), `@preLocked` (caller must already hold the
object's lock -- generates a hard `assert(isLockedByCurrentThread())`,
see section 349), `@local` (C++-only, not exposed through the RPC/proxy
layer), `@dereferenced`, `@weakReference`, `@async`, and class-level
`@json`/`@lua`.

Each `.idl` class expands into up to five real C++ classes in the
generated pair: the **Stub** (the distributed-object proxy every
caller actually holds/passes around), the **Implementation** (real
fields + generated `readObject`/`writeObject` serialization -- this is
what the hand-written `FooImplementation.cpp` extends), the **Adapter**
(RPC dispatch glue, `invokeMethod()` switching on hashed method IDs),
the **Helper** (singleton factory registered with
`Core::getObjectBroker()`), and a **POD** DTO for `@json` partial
export. Stub methods check `_getImplementation()==NULL` and fall back
to RPC if the object isn't local -- this is the exact Stub/Servant/
Adapter machinery section 354's ORB-clustering research documents;
every `.idl`-generated class inherits it automatically via the base
`engine.core.ManagedObject.idl` (`@nativeStub native
DistributedObjectServant getServant()`), whether or not the current
deployment is actually multi-process.

**Practical recipe:** edit the `.idl` to add a field/accessor, or
declare a `native` method and write its body in the checked-in
`FooImplementation.cpp`. Rebuild with `ninja` for changes to an
*existing* `.idl`/`.cpp` (per-file dependency rule reruns
automatically on mtime change) -- but a **brand-new** `.idl` or `.cpp`
file requires a full `cmake` reconfigure first, since the file list is
captured via `file(GLOB_RECURSE)` only at configure time (this project
hit this exact bug live: two new `.idl` files were invisible to Ninja
until a reconfigure was run -- see section 355).

## 339. Command Dispatch End-to-End -- From Client Keypress to Server Effect

**Packet receipt:** `ObjectControllerMessageCallback::parse()`
(`packets/object/ObjectControllerMessageCallback.cpp:14-56`) is the
generic entry point for all game-action packets; it reads a sub-opcode
CRC and factory-dispatches to a concrete handler, e.g.
`CommandQueueEnqueueCallback` (`packets/object/
CommandQueueEnqueue.cpp:17-64`) for slash commands, which reads
`actionCRC` (the command name, already hashed client-side),
throttles at 5 commands/second, then calls
`player->enqueueCommand(actionCRC, ...)`.

**Name resolution:** commands are never string-matched in the hot
path -- `CommandList` is a `HashTable<uint32, QueueCommand*>` keyed by
`String::hashCode()`. Registration happens once at boot in
`ObjectControllerImplementation::loadCommands()`, two layers deep: (1)
C++ class registration via `CommandConfigManager::registerCommands()`
calling `commandFactory.registerCommand<T>(name)` for each
`QueueCommand` subclass, and (2) data-driven config via
`CommandConfigManager::loadCommandData()` reading
`datatables/command/command_tables_shared*.iff`, which for each row
calls `createCommand(name)` and fills in state mask, locomotion
restrictions, range, and cooldown from the table (optionally further
overridden by `scripts/commands/commands.lua`).

**Base contract:** `QueueCommand.h` declares one pure virtual --
`doQueueCommand(creature, target, arguments)`. Important: **the base
class does NOT automatically run state/locomotion/cooldown/range
checks before calling it** -- it only provides helper methods
(`checkStateMask()`, `checkInvalidLocomotions()`, `checkCooldown()`,
`checkDistance()`) that each subclass's `doQueueCommand()` must call
itself. What *is* centralized, in
`ObjectControllerImplementation::activateCommand()`, is skillMod
bonus application/removal, admin-permission gating, and command-group
mutual exclusion.

**Queueing:** `CommandQueue` is a per-creature FIFO
(`IMMEDIATE`/`FRONT`/`NORMAL` priorities, `WAITING -> RUNNING ->
DELAY` state machine) driven by a self-rescheduling
`CommandQueueTask` (default 50ms tick). This is why the class is
literally named "Queue"Command -- combat commands especially must
serialize behind attack-speed delays rather than firing instantly on
packet receipt.

**Result delivery -- three channels used together:** queue
ack/clear (`CommandQueueRemove` packet so the client UI knows the
action finished/failed), localized system messages on failure
(`@error_message:...`), and normal state/animation broadcast via the
delta-update system (section 350) -- combat commands additionally send
explicit `CombatAction`/`CombatSpam` packets for animation and damage
text (section 341).

## 340. Manager Singleton Wiring at Server Boot

Dozens of `Manager` classes (`SkillManager`, `PlayerManager`,
`CombatManager`, `FactionManager`, etc.) are wired via a classic
lazy-init static singleton, not a dependency-injection container:
`engine::util::Singleton<T>` (`MMOEngine/src/engine/util/
Singleton.h:54-76`) wraps a function-local static wrapper whose
`instance()` does a compare-and-set `new O()` on first call. Nothing
in the engine forces construction order beyond whichever code path
calls `::instance()` first.

Boot happens in layers regardless: `ZoneServerImplementation::
initialize()` (lines 151-236) pulls global singletons
(`ObjectManager`, `StringIdManager`, `CreatureTemplateManager`, ...),
eagerly `new`'s server-scoped managers with explicit constructor-arg
or setter wiring (`ChatManager`, `PlayerManager`, `CraftingManager`,
`LootManager(craftingManager, objectManager, ...)`, `ResourceManager`,
`CityManager`, `AuctionManager`, `MissionManager`, `PetManager`), then
spins up per-planet zones (each lazily constructing `PlanetManager`,
`CreatureManager`, `WeatherManager`, `GCWManager`) before a second
`startManagers()` pass builds `RadialManager`, `GuildManager`
(explicitly wired: `guildManager->setChatManager(chatManager)`),
`FactionManager`, and `DirectorManager`. A separate process-scoped
tier boots inside `ZoneProcessServerImplementation::initialize()`:
`VendorManager`, `SkillManager` (assigned to member `professionManager`),
`PlayerCreationManager`, `SuiManager`, `NameManager`, `HolocronManager`,
`ObjectController`, `FishingManager`, `GamblingManager`, `ForageManager`.

**Cross-manager references use no service locator.** Two mechanisms
coexist: direct injection for server-scoped managers wired explicitly
at boot (constructor args or setters), and pull-on-demand for
singleton managers, which hold **no cached pointers to each other** --
they reach peers at call time through the object graph, e.g.
`zone->getZoneServer()->getPlayerManager()`. `ZoneServer`/
`ZoneProcessServer` act as the de facto registry, reached via the
SceneObject -> Zone -> ZoneServer chain rather than injected.

**Practical takeaway for adding a new Manager:** inherit
`Singleton<YourManager>` for a global/lazy manager, or take a
`ZoneServer*`/`Zone*` reference in the constructor for a boot-eager
one; if boot-eager, add the `new YourManager(...)` call into
`ZoneServerImplementation::initialize()`,
`ZoneProcessServerImplementation::initialize()`, or
`GroundZoneImplementation::initializePrivateData/startManagers`
depending on scope, plus a getter on the relevant `.idl` if other code
needs it. Other managers then reach it via `YourManager::instance()`
or `zone->getZoneServer()->getYourManager()` -- never a stored pointer.

## 341. ODB Persistence -- The Real Mechanism Behind "Field Didn't Survive a Restart" Bugs

Storage is embedded **Berkeley DB 5.0.32** (`utils/engine3/MMOEngine/
external/db-5.0.32/`), opened via `DatabaseManager::openEnvironment()`
(`engine/db/DatabaseManager.cpp:107`) against a **relative** directory
name `"databases"` -- physically `MMOCoreORB/bin/databases/*.db` for a
normal launch, not an absolute/configured path.

**Correction worth flagging:** `@dirty` in `.idl` files is a
*locking* annotation on methods (see section 338), not a per-field
persistence opt-in -- there is no such field annotation anywhere in
this codebase. Persistence is structural: every field round-trips via
the generated `readObject`/`writeObject` pair regardless of
annotation, and the actual save gate is a **runtime** dirty flag
(`_setUpdated(true)`) that application code must call after a
mutation, not something IDL-declared.

**Save trigger:** a periodic sweep every `UPDATETODATABASETIME`
(default 300000ms/5min) collects only dirty-flagged objects; creation
and clean-shutdown paths funnel into the same collection.
`CommitMasterTransactionThread::commitData()` runs the actual BDB
`commitTransaction()` once per sweep.

**Crash protection is real and layered underneath the sweep, not a
substitute for it.** `openEnvironment()` enables `DB_INIT_LOG` +
`DB_INIT_TXN` (full transactional logging) and `DB_RECOVER` (default
on) -- every boot runs BDB's own log-replay crash recovery
automatically. Each committed local transaction calls `commitSync()`,
fsyncing the transaction log before returning (genuine per-commit
durability), and a forced checkpoint runs after every master-
transaction commit plus once at startup.

**Net conclusion, directly explaining this project's own recurring bug
class:** the WAL genuinely protects anything that was ever included in
a committed transaction -- BDB will not silently lose a committed
write on crash. The actual failure mode lives **upstream of BDB
entirely**: if application code never calls `_setUpdated(true)`/
`updateObjectToDatabase()` after a mutation (the "native setter never
marks dirty" gap this project has hit multiple times in the companion
system), that object is never even collected into a transaction, so
the WAL has nothing to protect. It's an application dirty-tracking
gap, not a storage-durability gap -- when a field doesn't survive a
restart, look for a missing `_setUpdated()` call, not a database
configuration problem.

## 342. Zone Spatial Indexing -- Finding Nearby Objects Efficiently

Ground zones index world objects in a real 2D **QuadTree**
(`server::zone::QuadTree`, `QuadTree.h/.cpp`), partitioned on X/Y only
(Z/height factors into distance formulas but not tree partitioning).
`GroundZoneImplementation` owns one instance sized to terrain bounds
(`-8192,-8192` to `8192,8192`). Every insertable object implements
`TreeEntry` (`SceneObject.idl`'s indexing interface), storing
`coordinates`, its current `TreeNode`, and a `CloseObjectsVector`
proximity cache. Note: `ActiveAreaQuadTree`/`ActiveAreaOctree` is a
*separate* tree used only for `ActiveArea` triggers (safe zones, POI
triggers) -- don't conflate it with the general-object tree.

**Updates are synchronous, on every move, not batched per-tick.**
`GroundZoneComponent::updateZone()` calls `zone->update(sceneObject)`
-> `quadTree->update(entry)` immediately after any position change,
then refreshes the object's own close-objects cache via
`zone->inRange(sceneObject, zone->getZoneObjectRange())`.

**Two query patterns exist.** A fresh tree query --
`Zone::getInRangeObjects(x, z, y, range, &objects, readLockZone)` --
recurses only into quadrant nodes overlapping the search circle, so
cost scales with **local density near the point**, not total zone
population. Most gameplay code instead prefers reading a cached
`sceneObject->getCloseObjects()` list (kept in sync as objects enter/
leave range) rather than re-querying -- e.g. AOE splash damage
(`CombatManager::getAreaTargets`) tries the cache first and only falls
back to a live query if it's null.

**Multiple range tiers layer on the same tree.** `CLOSEOBJECTRANGE =
192` is the baseline ground "client awareness" tier
(`ZoneServer.idl:129`); buildings widen it 4x. Individual features
(aggro range, weapon range, AOE radius, combat-spam range) issue their
own ad-hoc queries with feature-specific radii against the same
quadtree rather than each needing a separate index.

**Practical takeaway:** for "what's near this point," call
`Zone::getInRangeObjects(...)` (safe at any zone population); for
"what's near this specific object" at the standard 192m radius, read
`object->getCloseObjects()` instead of re-querying.

## 343. Object Template Pipeline -- Lua to Spawnable Object

A Lua template (e.g.
`scripts/object/tangible/deed/generator_deed/generator_solar_deed.lua`)
`:new{}`-extends a `shared_*` base file and is registered via
`ObjectTemplates:addTemplate(obj, "object/path/to.iff")` -- a virtual
identity path, CRC-hashed for lookup, that doesn't need to exist as a
real file unless a matching client asset is required (see below).

**Boot-time loading is real, not precompiled.**
`TemplateManager::loadLuaTemplates()` runs a genuine embedded Lua
interpreter over `scripts/object/main.lua`, which cascades through
`includeFile()` calls across thousands of real `.lua` files every
server boot. `ObjectTemplates:addTemplate` computes
`crc = crcString(file)` and calls the C++-bound `addTemplateCRC()` ->
`TemplateManager::addTemplate()`, which reads `templateType`,
instantiates the matching `SharedObjectTemplate` subclass via a
registered `templateFactory`, and stores it keyed by CRC.

**Field mapping and spawn resolution:**
`SharedObjectTemplate::readObject(LuaObject*)` iterates the Lua
table's string keys and dispatches each to a generated
`parseVariableData()` string-switch calling the matching C++ setter.
At spawn time, `ZoneServerImplementation::createObject` ->
`ObjectManager::createObject` -> `loadObjectFromTemplate` looks up the
template by the same CRC, reads `getGameObjectType()`, and uses a
*second* factory (`objectFactory`) to construct the actual runtime
`SceneObject` subclass, then copies template fields onto the live
instance via `loadTemplateData()`.

**Client `.iff` requirement is conditional, not universal.** If a Lua
template sets `clientTemplateFileName`, `addTemplate()` also opens
that binary `.iff` via the TRE-backed `DataArchiveStore` and merges
its fields in *before* Lua fields (Lua overrides) -- this is required
for anything reusing original SOE client assets (weapons, vehicles,
turrets). If `clientTemplateFileName` is left empty (common for
custom/new objects like companion scripts), the Lua table alone is the
source of truth -- no matching client `.iff` is needed, the same
model this project's own `.stf`-patch pipeline (section 351) already
relies on for text content.

**Practical recipe for a new spawnable type:** write/extend a Lua
template under `scripts/object/...`, register via
`ObjectTemplates:addTemplate`, pick an existing `templateType`/
`gameObjectType` pair (new ones require C++ factory registration), and
only worry about TRE assets if `clientTemplateFileName` or a
client-rendered appearance field is set.

## 344. SUI (Standard UI) System -- Generic Popup/Dialog Architecture

Real distinct window classes, all under `server/zone/objects/player/
sui/`: `SuiInputBox` (free-text entry), `SuiListBox` (scrollable
selectable rows via `addMenuItem(name, objectID)`), `SuiMessageBox`
(title+text+OK), `SuiTransferBox`/`SuiBankTransferBox` (dual-column
item/credit transfer), `SuiColorBox`, `SuiKeypadBox`,
`SuiSlotMachineBox`, `SuiFireworkDelayBox`, `SuiCharacterBuilderBox`,
and `SuiBoxPage` (a generic raw widget-tree page for more complex
custom layouts). A separate, purely server-side `SuiWindowType.h`
enum provides ~150 semantic window IDs used only for dedup/tracking
(`hasSuiBoxWindowType()`/`closeSuiWindowType()`) -- **this enum is not
synced to any client binary**, so new features can safely append their
own numeric block, as the companion system already did (1200-1210).

**Send/response lifecycle:** `SuiManager` helpers
(`sendMessageBox()`, `sendInputBox()`, `sendListBox()`, etc.) build the
concrete box, call its `generateMessage()` to produce a
`SuiCreatePageMessage`, and send it via `player->sendMessage(...)`.
The client responds with a `SuiEventNotificationCallback` (pageId,
eventIndex, argument list) that routes through
`SuiManager::handleSuiEventNotification()` to the box's registered
**`SuiCallback`** -- a hand-written C++ subclass (the pattern this
project's own `CompanionRenameSuiCallback.h` already follows) or a
`LambdaSuiCallback`/`LuaSuiCallback` for inline/script handlers.

**Disambiguation:** `PlayerObjectImplementation::getNewSuiBoxID()`
computes `boxID = (++suiBoxNextID << 16) + (uint16)type` -- a
per-player monotonic counter plus the window type, stored in a
`VectorMap<unsigned int, SuiBox>` on `PlayerObject` so multiple
simultaneous windows for the same player stay distinct. The box is
removed from the map *before* its callback runs (the callback can
re-add it to keep a multi-page flow open).

**Real, documented constraint (not a hard limit, a resolution gap):**
`SuiListBox.addMenuItem()` rows do **not** auto-resolve `"@table:key"`
STF references the way a window's own prompt title/text does -- see
section 351 for the full mechanism and the fix pattern this project
already applied. `forceCloseDistance` (default 32m) auto-closes a
window if the player wanders too far from the anchoring object.

## 345. Combat Pipeline End-to-End

**Entry:** `DefaultAttackCommand::doQueueCommand` delegates to
`CombatQueueCommand::doCombatAction`, which does pre-flight
range/LOS/kneel-prone/weapon-type checks and an early non-TEF
overt/covert field flip on illegal-target swings, then calls the real
entry point: `CombatManager::instance()->doCombatAction(attacker,
weapon, target, CreatureAttackData(...))`.

**Order of operations inside `CombatManager.cpp::doCombatAction()`:**
(1) `startCombat()` establishes combat state/aggro. (2)
`applySpecialAttackCost()` spends HAM/special-attack pool cost. (3)
Per defender (looped for AOE/cone via `getAreaTargets`):
`calculateDamage()` rolls raw weapon damage + modifiers **before** the
hit roll; `getHitChance()` resolves HIT/MISS/BLOCK/DODGE/COUNTER/
RICOCHET; a miss/block/dodge/counter branch zeroes or halves the
damage multiplier; `applyDamage()` runs armor/food mitigation per HAM
pool and calls `defender->inflictDamage()` for the actual subtraction;
`applyDots()`/`applyWeaponDots()` apply DoT effects only after real
damage landed on a still-living target. **No discrete critical-hit
roll exists anywhere in this pipeline** (confirmed, matches section
282) -- damage variance comes entirely from `calculateDamage()`'s
random range plus fixed multipliers.

**Broadcast is two separate, non-reused mechanisms:**
`broadcastCombatAction()` sends one `CombatAction` animation packet via
the standard in-range-subscriber broadcast; `finalCombatSpam()` ->
`broadcastCombatSpam()` separately scans close objects within
`COMBAT_SPAM_RANGE` and sends an **individual** `CombatSpam` message
(floating combat text, mitigation breakdown) to each nearby player.

**TEF is a late side effect, not a gate.** `checkForTefs()` runs only
if the hit didn't miss -- i.e. strictly *after* damage/DoTs are
already applied -- and only sets boolean out-params consumed back in
`doCombatAction` to stamp the actual TEF timestamp.

## 346. Skill / Ability / Command Relationship for a Real Player

`Skill::commands` (loaded from `skills.iff` column `COMMANDS`) is
populated into a global `abilityMap` at boot
(`SkillManager::loadClientData()`). When a player earns a skill box,
`SkillManager::awardSkill()` calls `creature->addSkill()` (the skill
*box* lives on `CreatureObject`) and separately `addAbilities(ghost,
skill->getAbilities(), ...)`, which pushes matching command-name
strings onto **`PlayerObject::abilityList`** (the "ghost" object) --
not onto `CreatureObject`. So `CreatureObject` holds the skill box,
`PlayerObject` holds the resulting ability strings (`hasAbility()`).

**Ability vs. raw command is the same unified gate, not two systems.**
Every `command_table.iff` row has a `characterAbility` column;
`ObjectControllerImplementation::activateCommand()` requires
`playerObject->hasAbility(characterAbility)` if that column is
non-empty. Commands like `/who` simply ship with an empty
`characterAbility`, so the identical check trivially passes.

**Client ability browser is independently derived, not
server-pushed.** The server only syncs the raw `abilityList` itself
(delta-serialized via `PlayerObjectMessage9`). The client has its own
baked-in copy of `command_table.iff` from TRE archives and derives
which abilities to show/allow by cross-referencing its own
`characterAbility`/`visible` columns against the synced ability
list -- both sides independently enforce the same contract from their
own data copies. A command with no row in the *client's*
`command_table.iff` is rejected locally before ever reaching the
server (confirmed empirically in this project's own companion
command-registration work).

**Concrete trace:** a combat skill box's `COMMANDS` field contains
`"bleedingShot"` -> loaded into `abilityMap` at boot -> `awardSkill()`
appends it to `ghost->abilityList`, delta-synced to client -> the real
`BleedingShotCommand` has a `command_table.iff` row with
`characterAbility = "bleedingShot"` and `visible` set -> client lights
up the ability on the hotbar; server re-validates via `hasAbility()`
on every activation regardless of what the client displays.

## 347. Observer/Event System -- Practical Hook-In Guide (extends section 23)

`ObserverEventType` (`templates/params/ObserverEventType.h:17-116`)
defines exactly 100 distinct event ordinals, from `POSITIONCHANGED`
through `HERD` -- representative examples beyond
DAMAGERECEIVED/STARTCOMBAT include `KILLEDCREATURE`, `PLAYERCLONED`,
`OBJECTINSERTED`/`CONTAINERCONTENTSCHANGED`,
`CRAFTINGEXPERIMENTATION`/`PROTOTYPECREATED`, `ZONESWITCHED`,
`BADGEAWARDED`, `FLOURISH`, `SHIPDISABLED`/`SHIPDESTROYED`, `SLICED`,
`LOGGEDIN`/`LOGGEDOUT`.

**Mechanics are synchronous and additive.** `ObserverEventMap` is a
`HashTable<uint32, SortedVector<ManagedReference<Observer*>>>`;
`notifyObservers()` calls each registered observer's callback inline,
on the notifying thread, with no queueing or deferral.
`registerObserver()` rejects only literal duplicate registrations, so
multiple unrelated observers coexist on the same event type on the
same object.

**Real architectural benefit, grep-confirmed via `STARTCOMBAT`:** five
unrelated subsystems independently register for the same event with
zero knowledge of each other -- fishing (cancels on combat), vehicle
and pet control devices (dismount/control-drop on combat), camp sites
(disables healing), and the companion system (threat response). One
`notifyObservers()` call fans out to all of them; none of
`CombatManager` or `CreatureObjectImplementation::setCombatState()`
know these listeners exist.

**The critical gotcha, hard-won via this project's own real SIGABRTs
(see also section 349):** an observer callback fires on whatever
thread was processing the *triggering* action, which holds the lock of
the actor that triggered the event -- never the lock of the object
being notified, if it's a different object. `CompanionThreatObserver`
originally called `@preLocked` companion methods directly with no lock
on the companion (a separate object reachable only via weak
reference), causing a real crash. The general rule: **an observer
callback never inherits any lock context from the object that
triggered notification -- assume nothing is locked except the
notifying `Observable` itself**, and defer any cross-object mutation
into a locked task (section 348).

## 348. Task Scheduling System -- Practical "How to Defer Work Safely" Guide (extends section 24)

Three real API patterns via `Core::getTaskManager()`
(`engine::core::TaskManager`/`TaskManagerImpl`): **one-shot
deferred-but-immediate** -- `executeTask(lambda, "name")`, wraps the
lambda in a `LambdaTask` and hands it straight to a worker thread (the
pattern this project's own `CompanionContainerComponent.cpp` uses
throughout); **delayed** -- `scheduleTask(lambda, "name", delayMs)`,
e.g. `CombatManager::forcePeace()` scheduling a defender-list cleanup
250ms out; **periodic/recurring** -- the dominant idiom is a real
`Task` subclass whose `run()` calls `reschedule(delayMs)` on itself at
the end (e.g. `RankMaintenanceTask`), not a `schedulePeriodic()` call
(which exists but is essentially unused in favor of manual
`reschedule()`).

**Why defer instead of running inline -- the general principle, drawn
from at least five real, separately-fixed SIGABRTs in this project's
own companion system:** a callback/hook fires on whatever thread
happened to be processing the *triggering* action, which only holds
the lock of the actor that triggered it -- not the lock of whatever
object new code needs to mutate. Autogen-generated `@preLocked`
setters hard-assert `isLockedByCurrentThread()` and SIGABRT if false.
Deferring via `executeTask()`/`scheduleTask()` lets the task body take
a *fresh* `Locker` on the real target(s) and, critically,
**re-validate state under that lock** (object still exists, still
parented as expected, not already mutated by a race) since time
elapsed between trigger and execution.

**Threading model is genuinely concurrent, not a single serialized
queue** -- multiple real worker threads across configurable
queue/thread-count pools, plus separate scheduler and IO-scheduler
pools. A task author must still take `Locker` on every object the task
body touches; the task system guarantees nothing about mutual
exclusion between tasks, only that the lambda runs off the triggering
thread.

**Documented gotchas:** always capture `Reference<>`/
`ManagedReference<>`, never a raw pointer, into the lambda (every real
example in this codebase does this) so the object can't be destroyed
between scheduling and execution; re-validate everything under lock at
the top of the task body; watch for signed/unsigned mismatches feeding
task logic (this project hit exactly this with a `containmentType`
sentinel, see section 353); and when the crashing call site is inside
an `.idl`'s inline `@dirty` body with no native `Implementation.cpp`
to add a `Locker` into, the fix is a new `@dirty native` "deferred"
wrapper method that itself does the `executeTask()`+`Locker` dance
before calling the original method.

## 349. Object Locking Model -- Practical Rules of Thumb

Every lockable object embeds a `Lockable` mutex wrapper (one mutex per
object, not a global lock table). `Locker` (`system/thread/Locker.h`)
is a scoped RAII guard: `Locker foo(objA)` locks `objA` (a no-op if
the current thread already holds it -- safe re-entry, not a true
recursive mutex); `Locker foo(objA, objB)` means "lock `objA`, given
`objB` is already locked by this thread" -- it asserts `objB` is
already held, then calls `objA->lock(objB)`, which does **not**
implement strict lock-ordering. Instead it's a try-and-backoff
protocol: `pthread_mutex_trylock` in a loop; on failure it releases
the already-held `objB`, optionally yields, reacquires `objB`, and
retries. **This breaks classic AB/BA deadlocks without requiring a
global "always lock A before B" convention**, because the primitive
itself gives up and retries rather than blocking indefinitely while
holding the other lock.

`isLockedByCurrentThread()` asserts (generated from `.idl`
`@preLocked` annotations, e.g. `CreatureObject.cpp:676`'s
`inflictDamage`) are plain `assert()` calls that are **not stripped in
this project's actual build configuration** -- every documented crash
in this codebase from this class of bug is a literal live `SIGABRT`,
so treat the assert as enforced in whatever build is deployed, not a
debug-only nicety.

**Two real worked examples from this project's own bug history:** an
auto-equip crash where `notifyObjectInserted()` fired on the
*inserting player's* thread (player locked, companion not) and then
mutated the companion directly -- lesson: a callback fires on whatever
thread triggered it, never assume that implies the object *you* need
is locked. A `CompanionThreatObserver` crash where an event registered
on the owner fired a callback mutating the companion (a separate,
only-weakly-referenced object) with just the owner locked -- lesson:
observer callbacks run under the event source's locking context, never
the notified object's.

**Lock order:** no global convention is enforced or documented;
call sites lock objects in the order naturally reached (e.g. player ->
device -> companion) and rely on the `Mutex::lock(cross)` retry/
backoff primitive (above) to make strict ordering unnecessary for
correctness. The one explicit house rule that recurs across every fix
in this project: defer cross-object mutation into a task lambda that
takes its own fresh `Locker`/`Locker(x, y)` pair rather than assuming
the calling context already holds what's needed.

## 350. Network Protocol -- Server-to-Client Packet Construction

`BaseMessage` (extends `BasePacket` -> `Message` -> `Packet`) has
**no reflection or auto-marshalling** -- every packet class hand-writes
its wire layout in its constructor by chaining `Packet`'s `insertByte`/
`insertShort`/`insertInt`/`insertLong`/`insertFloat`/`insertAscii`/
`insertUnicode`/`insertStream` calls. Field order in the constructor
*is* the wire format; getting it wrong desyncs or crashes the client
(this project hit exactly this class of bug once, see the
`WeaponRanges.h` crash investigation in `NOTES.md`). `BaseMessage`'s
own constructor first inserts a fixed SOE data-channel header before
subclass fields run.

**The packet type ID is `String::hashCode()` of the class name** -- the
identical CRC-variant algorithm this project's own
`docs/companion_system/tools/core3_hashcode.py` tool replicates for
TRE-record purposes. Practical pattern: `insertInt(String::hashCode(
"ClassName"))` right after the length/subtype short.

**Transport is a real session/connection abstraction over a
project-managed raw UDP socket, not a third-party networking
library.** `player->sendMessage(...)` forwards through
`ZoneClientSession` -> `BaseClient` (extends `DatagramServiceClient`)
-> the SOE-protocol reliability layer (sequencing, ack/resend,
compression/encryption flags) -> `DatagramServiceClient::send()`,
which owns a raw `UDPSocket*` and calls `socket->sendTo()`. Game code
never touches the socket directly.

**`DeltaMessage` is a distinct mechanism for incremental per-field
object-state updates**, not one-shot events -- it wraps a view onto an
object the client already has a baseline for, exposing
`addByteUpdate`/`addIntUpdate`/etc. keyed by a variable-group type
index, with concrete subclasses per object type/slot (e.g.
`CreatureObjectDeltaMessage3/4/6`, `PlayerObjectDeltaMessage3/6/8/9`).
Use a `BaseMessage` for a self-contained one-shot notification (combat
spam, a UI popup); use a `DeltaMessage` when updating fields of an
object the client already has baselined (HAM, posture, skill list, buff
icons) -- deltas are smaller and match the client's incremental-update
grammar. Delta messages route through the object's own `owner` client
reference and are silently dropped if `owner == nullptr` -- i.e. they
only work for player-owned objects, which is precisely why
non-player creatures (companions/pets) can't push delta-based state to
an observer's client.

## 351. STF Text Resolution -- The Client vs. Server Resolution Split

A literal string like `"@companion:skill_sheet_text"` is a `StringId`'s
full path: `"@" + table + ":" + key`, where `table` names an `.stf`
file under `string/en/` in the merged client data tree. Base-game
tables ship in Sony's original TRE archives; this project's own tables
(`companion.stf`, plus patched entries appended into stock files like
`exp_n.stf`/`skl_n.stf`) live as source under
`docs/companion_system/tools/patched/*.stf`, get regenerated by the
project's build tooling, and are packed into a patch TRE that merges
transparently alongside stock `.stf` files via the archive's
priority-based resolution.

`StringIdManager::populateDatabase()` walks every `.stf` under
`string/en/` across all loaded TRE archives (base-game and this
project's patch alike), hashes each `"@table:key"` path with
`String::hashCode()`, and stores it in a local database keyed purely
by that hash -- never by literal string compare. **Population only
runs on first boot or when explicitly forced** (a reload-strings
admin trigger or `-reloadstrings` flag) -- a rebuilt `.stf` will not
take effect on a running server without one of those triggers.

**The real, hard-won discovery: client and server resolve
`"@table:key"` differently depending on which UI field it lands in.**
A SUI window's own prompt title/text fields (`setPromptTitle()`/
`setPromptText()`) auto-resolve client-side when sent as a literal
`"@table:key"` string -- confirmed working. Individual `SuiListBox`
rows added via `addMenuItem()` do **not** auto-resolve client-side;
they render the literal unresolved text. This project hit this live
(a companion Skill Sheet showing raw `"@skl_n:..."` in list rows) and
fixed it the same way an existing, older codepath
(`StructureManager.cpp`) already had for a different feature:
pre-resolve server-side via
`StringIdManager::instance()->getStringId(key.hashCode()).toString()`
before handing text to the SUI.

**Practical rule:** default to pre-resolving server-side for anything
populated as repeated list/menu rows; only a window's own single
title/prompt fields are confirmed to auto-resolve client-side. There
is no documented flag distinguishing the two cases anywhere in engine
source -- it was discovered empirically, and the failure mode (silent
literal text, not a crash) makes it easy to miss without live-client
verification.

## 352. Lua Scripting Bridge -- Content vs. Logic Decision Guide (extends section 4)

Binding uses the classic `Luna<T>` template-based userdata pattern
(`MMOEngine/src/engine/lua/Luna.h`), not luabind/sol2 -- a real class
is wrapped in a thin `LuaXxx` adapter with a static `Register[]` table
of `{name, &Class::method}` pairs (e.g. `LuaCreatureObject.cpp:29-70`),
registered once per Lua state at boot (~35 such calls in
`DirectorManager::initializeLuaEngine()`). A separate flat mechanism,
`Lua::registerFunction()`, exposes plain global C-callbacks
(`createEvent`, `spawnMobile`, `getRandomNumber`, `registerScreenPlay`,
etc.). **Together these two lists are the entire surface Lua content
can touch** -- a C++ method not added to a `Register[]` table is
simply invisible to scripts, which is the real gate on "can this be
done in Lua."

**The content-vs-logic split is real, not just data vs. code by
convention.** `JediManager.cpp` (121 lines total) is a genuinely thin
dispatcher with zero unlock/gating logic in C++ -- every method just
calls into a named Lua "strategy" file selected at boot
(`loadConfiguration()` picks the file based on config). The real logic
-- genuine control flow, random rolls, conditional branching on quest
state and badge counts -- lives entirely in the Lua files
(`hologrind_jedi_manager.lua`, `village_jedi_manager.lua`). This
confirms Lua in this codebase isn't just template/content data; entire
pluggable progression strategies are selected by name and executed in
Lua with real branching logic.

**Practical decision rule:** if a new feature only needs primitives
already exposed via an existing `Luna<T>::Register[]` table or
`registerFunction()` global, and its logic is "react to triggers/
state, call existing engine operations," write it as a Lua screenplay/
manager-strategy file -- fast iteration, live-reloadable via the
`reloadscreenplays` admin command (`DirectorManager::
reloadScreenPlays()` just bumps an atomic version counter; each Lua
state lazily re-runs `loadScreenPlays()` when it notices its own
version is stale -- **no server restart needed**). If it needs a *new*
primitive not yet exposed (a new persisted field, new combat math, a
new observer type, or anything per-tick-across-many-objects
performance-critical), it must be C++ -- add the method, then add one
line to the relevant `Register[]` table so Lua can reach it. Lua alone
can never add capability, only orchestrate what C++ has already
exposed.

## 353. Container/Slot System -- Full Architecture Synthesis (extends section 65)

**`ContainerType`** (stored per-object as `containerType`,
`SceneObject.idl:1272-1279`) governs what an object's container will
accept, enforced entirely in `ContainerComponent::canAddObject()`:
`NONE` (nothing -- e.g. trap objects), `SLOTTED` (only real equip-slot
inserts -- e.g. ranged weapon attachment slots), `VOLUME` (only loose
tangible items -- backpacks, buildings), `INTANGIBLE` (only loose
intangible items -- the datapad), `GENERIC` (both, loose -- player root
inventory, vendors), `RIDABLE` (slots only, vehicle-specific -- rider
seats). `canAddObject()` also walks the full parent chain and rejects
if *any* ancestor is `NONE` -- you can't smuggle an item into a trap
sitting inside a bag.

**`containmentType`** is one signed int doing triple duty: `-1` means
"loose item in a VOLUME/INTANGIBLE/GENERIC container" (stored in the
`containerObjects` map); any value `>= 4` means "a real equip slot,"
with `arrangementGroup = containmentType - 4` indexing into the
*item's own* `getArrangementDescriptor(arrangementGroup)` slot-name
list, which are the actual keys into `slottedObjects` (a
`VectorMap<String, ManagedReference<SceneObject*>>` keyed by
descriptor **name**, not numeric index) -- so the transferred item
itself decides which named slots it fills.

**The component-swap pattern:** `ContainerComponent` defines the
contract as five virtual hooks (`canAddObject`, `transferObject`,
`removeObject`, `notifyObjectInserted`, `notifyObjectRemoved`) plus
`checkContainerPermission()`. Concrete objects don't subclass
`SceneObject` for custom behavior -- a Lua template sets a
`containerComponent = "SomeName"` string, resolved at load time
through `ComponentManager::getComponent<ContainerComponent*>(name)` to
a single **shared, stateless singleton** instance reused by every
object naming it. Three real, contrasting instances confirmed by
source: `PlayerContainerComponent` (the real validated "Wear"
pipeline -- race/faction/skill/encumbrance checks); `LootContainerComponent`
(built for a corpse -- unconditionally rejects every insert, and its
`MOVEOUT` permission only succeeds if `ContainerPermissions.ownerID` was
explicitly set); `CompanionContainerComponent` (subclasses
`PlayerContainerComponent`, not `ContainerComponent` directly, to
inherit the entire real equip pipeline "for free," then overrides only
what needs to branch on `containmentType` or re-target ownership at
`CompanionObject::isAuthorizedActor()`). This buys real value: a
designer retargets an object's entire container semantics by changing
one template string, no recompile, no new `SceneObject` subclass.

**Five hard-won lessons from this project's own real bugs, worth
internalizing before touching this system:** (1) `getContainmentType()`/
`setContainmentType()` are declared **unsigned**, but the `-1` "loose"
sentinel is signed -- comparing the unsigned getter directly against
`>= 4` is always true for a stored `-1` (reads back as `0xFFFFFFFF`),
silently misrouting loose inserts into the equip path; always cast to
signed before any `>=` comparison. (2) never reuse a corpse-only
(`LootContainerComponent`) template for a live, non-corpse container --
its permission model is fundamentally incompatible and fails silently
with a generic error. (3) destroying an object does not atomically-
and-verifiably vacate its parent's slot before immediate reuse --
`removeObject()` looks up the slot key from the *removed object's own
recorded `containmentType`*, and if that wasn't reliably what's
expected at destroy time, the slot never clears and the next
`transferObject()` into the same slot fails with an
indistinguishable generic error; explicitly call `removeObject()` and
check its return, or verify the slot is empty before attaching. (4)
`notifyObjectInserted()`/`notifyObjectRemoved()` fire with **no
locking guarantee** on the target -- any side-effecting override must
take its own `Locker` (deferred via a task, section 348) rather than
assume the caller holds one; this caused four separate real SIGABRTs
in this project alone. (5) `containerInheritPermissionsFromParent`
only affects permission *data* inheritance, not which component's
*methods* run -- the active component is fixed by the object's own
template field, a false assumption that let the corpse-only bug ship
unnoticed.

## 354. Multi-Process ORB Clustering -- Verified Against Current Source (extends section 26)

Re-checked against current source: all prior claims hold. New,
stronger evidence for "this deployment runs single-process by
design, not just single-process by default config": `src/
CMakeLists.txt:86` builds exactly **one** executable (`core3`; the
only other target, `odb3`, is dev-only ODB tooling, not a second
server role), `ServerCore.cpp:693-717` instantiates `LoginServer`,
`ZoneServer`, `PingServer`, and `StatusServer` all in-process inside
one `initialize()` call gated only by boolean config flags, and the
project's actual deployment script (`docker/run.sh`) launches a single
container exposing all four service ports from one process -- there is
no per-zone or per-service fan-out anywhere in the repo's deployment
scripts.

**The concrete `.idl` linkage for how any generated class gets ORB
transparency automatically:** `engine.orb.object.ManagedObject.idl`
(the base every `.idl`-defined class ultimately includes) declares
`@nativeStub native DistributedObjectServant getServant()` -- this is
the mechanism by which *every* `ManagedObject` subclass inherits
Stub/Servant/Adapter dispatch through the base class alone, with zero
opt-in required from feature code (ties directly into section 338's
codegen pipeline). `DistributedObjectAdapter::invokeMethod()` is the
single dispatch point every generated method call routes through
regardless of whether the target is local or remote, confirming calls
are architecturally always indirected through the adapter.

**Practical impact for new feature code: none, by design.** A
developer writing new `.idl`-backed code never opts into cross-process
transparency or needs to think about "is this object local or
remote" -- it's baked into the base class. No latency/performance
documentation exists anywhere in the `engine/orb` tree (confirmed via
exhaustive grep) -- this remains genuinely undocumented, not
something to assume either way.

## 355. Build System -- Grounded in This Project's Own Rebuild History (extends section 14)

CMake generates Ninja build files (no direct `make`-based compile);
the top-level `MMOCoreORB/Makefile` wraps this, but this project's own
real rebuild passes (documented in `NOTES.md`) use `cmake -G Ninja
-DRUN_GIT=ON -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug` from `build/unix/ninja-debug`
followed by `ninja -C build/unix/ninja-debug core3`. The build requires
`clang++`, Lua 5.3/MySQL dev headers, C++14, and treats warnings as
errors by default.

**The real, already-hit new-`.idl`-file bug, worth internalizing:**
`src/CMakeLists.txt`'s `BUILD_IDL` branch does `file(GLOB_RECURSE
idls "src/*.idl")` at **configure time only**, emitting one build rule
per file found at that moment. On 2026-07-13 two brand-new `.idl`
files broke the entire build (an umbrella-header include failure, jumping
from a normal ~250-target incremental build to 881 targets) because
Ninja's own re-run can never add a rule for a file its graph doesn't
know exists -- and CMake's "reconfigure if CMakeLists.txt changed"
safety net doesn't fire, since no CMakeLists.txt actually changed.
**Editing an existing `.idl` only needs `ninja`** (its own per-file
`idlc.jar` rule reruns automatically on mtime change); **a genuinely
new `.idl` or `.cpp` file anywhere under `src/` needs a real `cmake`
reconfigure first** -- safe and non-destructive, it reuses the
existing cache and doesn't wipe object files.

**No working automated test suite exists in practice.** `src/tests/`
matches zero real source files today despite `COMPILE_TESTS` being on
by default; Googletest is vendored but this project has only ever used
it as an include-path aid for a syntax-only sanity check, never to run
real tests. The actual, consistently-used verification loop
throughout this project's own history is: rebuild, then manually test
live in-game with a real client -- not automated testing.

## 356. Error Handling / Logging Conventions

The base is `engine::log::Logger` (`engine/log/Logger.h:136`), composed
via the IDL layer rather than always plain C++ inheritance: nearly
every `SceneObject`-family class declares `implements Logger` in its
`.idl` (`SceneObject.idl:76`), and the compiler generates delegating
`info()`/`error()`/`debug()`/`warning()` methods that forward to an
internal `Logger` member -- this is why game-object code calls
`error("...")` as a bare method with no explicit logger reference.
Many non-game-object classes (managers, `TaskScheduler`,
`DatabaseManager`, `ConfigManager` -- 186 files) use true C++
inheritance instead. A global static `Logger::console` exists as a
fallback for code with no natural per-object logger.

**Real severity levels:** `NONE=-1, FATAL=0, ERROR=1, WARNING=2,
LOG=3, INFO=4, DEBUG=5` (`fatal()` is `[[noreturn]]`, aborts).
Observed convention: `error()`/`fatal()` for real bugs/unrecoverable
conditions worth investigating; `warning()` for rejected/anomalous-
but-handled situations; `info()`/`log()` for routine diagnostic trace,
often gated behind a `forcedLog` flag so it's silent unless
explicitly enabled; `debug()` is compiled out entirely in release
builds.

**Output and filtering are real, not cosmetic.** A global file sink is
wired at boot (`Core3.LogFile`, default `log/core3.log`;
`Core3.LogFileLevel`, default `INFO`), and severity filtering is
enforced per-call via `hasToLog()` against both the per-object and
global level -- a live admin `loglevel <n>` console command can change
the global threshold at runtime. The `[Name]` bracket prefix seen in
output (e.g. `[CompanionSystem] ERROR - ...`) comes from a genuine
per-class subsystem tag set once via `Logger.setLoggingName(...)` in
the object's `.idl` constructor, not a hand-typed prefix on every
call -- though developers commonly *also* add a manual text prefix
matching the subsystem inside the message itself for easier
grep-ability in raw log files, confirmed as a real project-wide habit
across unrelated subsystems (spatial indexing, the DB layer, and the
companion system all follow this same dual-prefix pattern).

## 357. Deed / Control-Device Pattern -- The General "Summon a Thing" Architecture

A `Deed` (extends `TangibleObject`) sits in inventory/datapad; using
it creates two new server objects -- an intangible control device and
the real world object -- then permanently links them via
`controlDevice->setControlledObject(worldObj)`. Confirmed across
Vehicle, Pet, Droid, and Ship deeds. Vehicle and Pet control devices
share a real common base class, `ControlDevice extends
IntangibleObject`, holding the link field and the abstract
`storeObject`/`generateObject`/`callObject` contract -- this project's
own companion system deliberately extends `IntangibleObject` directly
instead of `ControlDevice` (an intentional, documented choice so the
companion system doesn't cross-recognize with pet/vehicle code), so it's
a parallel instance of the same *pattern*, not the same *class
hierarchy*.

**The device stores the spawned object's persistent reference exactly
once, at creation time, never reassigned afterward.**
Re-summoning reuses the same object rather than creating a new one:
`spawnObject()` pulls the stored reference and transfers it back into
the world; `storeObject()` calls `destroyObjectFromWorld(true)` --
removing it from the active zone/quadtree but **not** the database, so
it survives to be re-transferred later. This exactly matches this
project's own companion `getCompanionObject()`/`spawnObject()`/
`storeObject()` cycle, confirming the companion system correctly
mirrored the established precedent.

**Structures diverge, but only in follow-up behavior, not the deed
layer itself.** `StructureDeed` is also a `Deed` subclass using the
same `handleObjectMenuSelect()` entry point, but has no control device
at all -- `placeStructure()` delegates to `PlaceStructureComponent`,
places once, and the deed is consumed. There's no store/re-summon
cycle because a structure isn't meant to vanish; the divergence is
that structures skip the `ControlDevice` link-back/store-summon
lifecycle entirely, not that the deed mechanism itself differs.

**Minimum pieces for a new "summon a thing" feature**, per this
project's own already-built companion example: an intangible
link-back class holding a persistent reference to the live object; a
`spawnObject(player)`/`storeObject(player, force)` method pair that
transfers the existing linked object into/out of the zone (never
recreates it); a one-time link field set at creation/grant time; and a
`handleObjectMenuSelect` radial handler wired to Summon/Store IDs.

## 358. Generic DataTable/.iff Parsing System (extends the skills.iff-specific `docs/companion_system` tooling)

Base classes live under `src/templates/datatables/`:
`DataTableCell`/`DataTableRow`/`DataTableIff` (extends `IffTemplate`).
The read API is dual -- rows are fetched by index
(`DataTableIff::getRow(int)`, `DataTableRow::getCell(int)`), and a
column **name** resolves to an index via a linear-scan
`getColumnIndexByName()` (there's no direct "get cell by column name"
one-liner; callers resolve the name once, then index). Values pull out
through a templated `getValue<V>(idx, V& out)` that dispatches to the
cell's typed overload and throws on a type mismatch.

**The DTII binary format this project's own Python tooling
(`docs/companion_system/tools/iff_datatable.py`) reverse-engineered is
confirmed to match the real C++ reader exactly** --
`DataTableIff::readObject()` parses the identical structure:
outer `FORM 'DTII'` -> version sub-form -> `COLS` chunk (count +
null-terminated names) -> `TYPE` chunk (type-char strings) -> `ROWS`
chunk, dispatching each cell on its type char (`f`=float, `s`=string,
`h`=hex uint32, `b`=bool-as-int, everything else including
`i`/`I`/`c`/`p`/`e`/`z`=signed int). No divergence found between the
project's own Python reimplementation and the real engine parser.

**There is no `DataTableManager` singleton or generic shared-table
cache** despite the naming convention elsewhere in the engine.
Instead, each subsystem manager opens its own `.iff` once at boot via
`TemplateManager`/`DataArchiveStore::openIffFile()`, constructs a
**stack-local** `DataTableIff`, calls `readObject()` once, iterates
rows into the manager's own long-lived domain containers (e.g.
`SkillManager::loadClientData()` builds `skillMap` from
`skills.iff`), and lets the `DataTableIff` itself go out of scope --
the parsed *domain objects* are what's cached, not the raw table.

**Other real `.iff` datatables read via this exact system**, beyond
`skills.iff`/`badge_map.iff` -- confirming how widely reused it is:
`datatables/faction/rank.iff` (`FactionManager`), `datatables/chat/
social_types.iff`/`spatial_chat_types.iff`/`mood_types.iff`
(`ChatManagerImplementation`), `datatables/space/ship_chassis.iff`/
`ship_components.iff`/`missiles.iff`/`countermeasures.iff`
(`ShipManager`), `datatables/crafting/component.iff`
(`ComponentMap`), `datatables/xp/species.iff`/`datatables/creation/
starting_locations.iff`/`datatables/player/quests.iff`
(`PlayerManagerImplementation`), `datatables/resource/
resource_tree.iff` (`ResourceTree`), `datatables/performance/
performance.iff`/`perform_effect.iff` (`PerformanceManager`).

## 359. XP -> Skill-Point Spend -> Skill Grant -- Full Pipeline (extends section 44)

**XP award** (already documented in section 68's group/combat XP
formula) funnels every source -- combat, crafting, entertaining --
through `PlayerManager::awardExperience(player, xpType, amount, ...)`.

**Real player-initiated trainer spend** goes through
`trainerConvHandler.lua::handleConfirmLearnScreen()` (distinct from
the companion system's own free, no-skill-point training path): it
checks credits, calls `LuaSkillManager:canLearnSkill()` as a UX
pre-check, then `LuaSkillManager:awardSkill()` -- the identical
`SkillManager::awardSkill()` this project's own companion research
already partially documented for the badge-award branch.

**Inside `awardSkill()` (`SkillManager.cpp:329-568`), beyond the
already-documented badge branch, the full step list is:** recursively
grant any missing required prerequisite skills, then **re-validate
`canLearnSkill()` server-side** (the authoritative gate -- the Lua
pre-check is UX-only and cannot be relied on for security); an
idempotency guard if already owned; withdraw skill points and XP as a
linked transaction pair; `creature->addSkill()` (adds to `skillList`,
recalculates speed/acceleration mods, one-time-spawns a helper droid
for a brand-new base profession); apply every `SKILL_MODS` entry via
`creature->addSkillMod(SkillModManager::SKILLBOX, ...)`; grant
`COMMANDS` via `addAbilities()` (section 346); grant draft schematic
groups; recompute XP caps and max Force power; a self-healing skill-
point-budget recheck that logs and corrects any drift; and special-
case hooks for Jedi FS-tree completion, bounty-list updates, squad-
leader group-mod refresh, and (this project's own addition) the
one-time `companion_master_novice` control-device grant.

**Spend enforcement is doubly checked, not just UX-gated.** The
Lua-side `canLearnSkill()` call is purely for UX (routes to a
"nsf_skill_points" screen on failure); the actual authority is
`awardSkill()`'s own internal `canLearnSkill()` re-check, run before
any SP/XP/skillList mutation, validating ownership, prerequisites,
XP sufficiency, and skill-point sufficiency independently of whatever
the client/Lua UI already checked.

## 360. Faction / GCW Manager Architecture -- A Mental Map (extends sections 10, 76, 86, 89, 96, 115, 154, 158, 233, 274, 282)

Three managers divide GCW-adjacent responsibility with **no direct
cross-calls between `FactionManager` and `GCWManager`** (confirmed:
zero grep hits either direction) -- they are architecturally
independent siblings that both happen to read/write overlapping player
state directly on `CreatureObject`/`PlayerObject`, rather than through
each other.

**`FactionManager`** is pure per-player reputation bookkeeping --
`awardFactionStanding`/`awardSpaceFactionPoints`/
`awardPvpFactionPoints` all just adjust `ghost->increaseFactionStanding()`/
`decreaseFactionStanding()`, plus it owns static faction taxonomy data
(ally/enemy lists, rank costs, loaded from `faction_manager.lua`/
`rank.iff`). It has zero knowledge of bases, planets, or combat
mechanics.

**`GCWManagerImplementation`** (3800+ lines) is base-siege/planetary-
control machinery: base registration, vulnerability-window scheduling,
the hacking minigame, base destruction, turret/minefield/scanner
defense donation, crackdown contraband scanning, and planet-control
aggregation. It never touches the faction-standing data structures at
all.

**`CombatManager`** is the gate between them, but only loosely --
`checkForTefs()` reads faction/status directly off the combatants and
stamps TEF timers, but writes nothing to reputation or GCW score
itself (zero direct calls into either manager, confirmed by grep). The
actual connective tissue is `PlayerManagerImplementation`'s
death-resolution routine, which queries `CombatManager::areInDuel()`
to exclude duels, then explicitly calls
`FactionManager::instance()->awardPvpFactionPoints(...)` on a
confirmed kill, and separately consults `GCWManager` only for an
XP-bonus multiplier -- not for score writes.

**Mental map for "which manager do I call":** call `FactionManager`
for anything about moving a specific player's standing/points for a
specific faction; call `GCWManager` for anything about a physical
base's lifecycle or planetary control aggregation; `CombatManager`
decides *whether* an exchange counts as PvP-flaggable at all but
delegates the actual bookkeeping elsewhere -- and the code that
actually chains combat outcomes into faction/GCW effects lives in
`PlayerManagerImplementation`'s death handler, not in any of the three
managers themselves.

## 361. Screenplay/Quest Scripting Framework (extends sections 34, 103)

The C++ counterpart is `DirectorManager`, a singleton owning the
shared `Lua*` engine, a flat `screenPlays` registry, and roughly 100
Lua-callable static functions (`spawnMobile`, `createLoot`,
`createObserver`, `sendMail`, etc.). A screenplay's real entry points
are called by name via Lua function lookup, not C++ virtual dispatch.
Confirmed real hook names beyond `onPlayerCreated`: `onPlayerLoggedIn`,
`onPlayerLoggedOut`, `onFSTreeCompleted`, `onSkillRevoked`, and a
generic `start()`.

**Manager screenplays and generic quest screenplays are the identical
underlying mechanism** -- `scripts/screenplays/screenplay.lua` defines
the base `ScreenPlay = Object:new{...}` table every screenplay
extends, and Jedi-manager files literally `require("screenplays.
screenplay")` and `:new{}`-extend it with extra fields. The only real
difference is C++-side wiring: Jedi content gets a dedicated thin
singleton (`JediManager`) that picks one active screenplay by
configured name and calls its hooks from fixed C++ lifecycle call
sites; generic quest/theme-park screenplays have no dedicated
per-subsystem manager and instead register into `DirectorManager`'s
flat table directly, triggered by conversation handlers or observers.
This confirms the "New Player Theme Park" content documented in
section 103 is built on the same generic mechanism, not a separate
quest engine.

**Triggering happens three ways, all through `DirectorManager`:**
global auto-start (`registerScreenPlay(name, true)`, run for every such
entry at boot via `startGlobalScreenPlays()`); on-demand
(`registerScreenPlay(name, false)`, something else must call
`startScreenPlay()` explicitly); and manager-hook dispatch
(Jedi-style managers invoked from fixed C++ lifecycle points
regardless of registration state). Nothing is registered "against a
zone" directly -- NPC/zone binding happens indirectly through
conversation templates and spawn tables embedded in the screenplay's
own Lua data.

**Authoring workflow for new quest/NPC content:** write a new `.lua`
file under `scripts/screenplays/<category>/` extending
`ScreenPlay:new{...}`, call `registerScreenPlay("Name", true/false)`
at file scope, add an `includeFile()`/`require()` line into the
manifest (`scripts/screenplays/screenplays.lua`) so it's actually
loaded, and reference NPC templates/conversation handlers by string
name inside the screenplay's own data tables -- no C++ recompilation
or `.idl` changes needed anywhere in this workflow.

## 362. Radial/Object Menu Architecture -- The Generic Right-Click System (extends the companion system's own radial-menu additions)

`fillObjectMenuResponse()` is declared `native abstract` on
`SceneObject.idl`, but real dispatch forwards to a pluggable
`ObjectMenuComponent*` member resolved by name from the object's
template (the same component-swap pattern documented in section 353
for containers) -- not a per-`SceneObject`-subclass virtual override.
The base `ObjectMenuComponent` provides universal options (Pick Up/
Move/Rotate for structure admins); `TangibleObjectMenuComponent` calls
the base first to inherit those, then layers on tangible-specific
options; every specialized component (`CompanionMenuComponent`,
pet/trainer/event-actor menu components) follows the same
override-and-extend chain.

**Radial IDs are one flat global enum with a real, confirmed
collision risk.** `RadialOptions.h` is explicitly commented "do not
modify, matches `datatables/player/radial_menu.iff`" -- IDs are global
across the entire game, not scoped per object type. This project's own
companion equip/pick-up radials use raw integer literals `82`/`83`
instead of named constants, and those exact values are already claimed
by the enum as `SERVER_OBSERVE`/`SERVER_STOP_OBSERVING`, actively used
elsewhere for event-perk actors and spawn eggs. It only works today
because a companion-inventory tangible object is never simultaneously
one of those other types -- a latent, not active, collision. The
companion system's own `CompanionMenuComponent` avoids this correctly
elsewhere by using the enum's dedicated `SERVER_MENU1-4` reserved pool
instead of bare numbers. **Rule for any new radial option: always use
the named `RadialOptions::` constant, never a literal int, and prefer
the `SERVER_MENU*`/`SERVER_*` reserved slots.**

**`handleObjectMenuSelect()` is two-tier dispatch, not one big
chain.** Tier 1 is the same component-registration routing as
`fillObjectMenuResponse()`; tier 2, within a single component, is a
plain switch/if-else on `selectedID` with an explicit fallthrough to
the parent component's handler for anything not locally recognized --
no reflection or per-ID handler registry exists.

**Gating pattern, confirmed as the idiomatic shape project-wide (not
just in the companion system):** resolve the relevant object ->
ownership/permission check -> state check, done **twice** -- once in
`fillObjectMenuResponse()` to decide visibility, once again in
`handleObjectMenuSelect()` to re-validate before acting, since a
client's cached menu can go stale between render and click. This
double-check recurs in the base `ObjectMenuComponent` (admin-list
checks for building Pick Up/Move/Rotate) and the Slicing gate
(skill + inventory-location checks) -- confirming it's a genuine
project convention worth following for any new radial-driven feature,
not something the companion system invented.

# General Engine Architecture -- Batch 2 (Sections 363-377)

Second architecture research pass, filling in the remaining
foundational systems not yet touched: the real main-loop/tick model,
memory management, generic data structures, full session lifecycle,
the missing baseline-message half of the network protocol, RPC
marshaling, packet threading, cross-zone transfer, exceptions,
strings, telemetry, config propagation, shutdown, zone lifecycle, and
atomics. Together with sections 337-362 this is now the practical
ceiling of "backend architecture" knowledge short of reading every
file directly -- what's left beyond this is depth-on-demand for
specific features, not foundational gaps.

## 363. Server Main Loop -- Confirmed Fully Reactive/Task-Driven, No Central Simulation Tick Exists

**There is no discrete "world tick."** `main()` constructs `ServerCore`
and calls `core.start()`
(`Core::start()`, `MMOEngine/src/engine/core/Core.cpp:172-177`), which
runs `ServerCore::initialize()` asynchronously on a task-pool thread
and then, on the **main thread itself**, synchronously calls `run()`.
`ServerCore::run()` (`ServerCore.cpp:857-861`) is just
`handleCommands(); shutdown();` -- and `handleCommands()`
(`ServerCore.cpp:1075-1122`) is a `while(handleCmds) { Thread::sleep(
500); read a line from the admin console pipe; process it; }`. **This
is purely a GM/admin console poll loop** -- it never touches zones,
objects, or AI. There is no `zoneServer->tick()`, no object-update
pass, no central AI poll anywhere in the codebase's main thread.

**Confirmed: the entire simulation is emergent from the task-scheduling
system (section 348), not a central loop.** The clearest proof is
creature AI "thinking": `AiAgentImplementation::activateAiBehavior()`
creates/reschedules an `AiBehaviorEvent` (a `Task` subclass); its
`run()` executes the behavior tree and, rather than the loop
re-polling it, the state-change logic itself calls
`activateAiBehavior(true)` again, which re-`schedule()`s the same
event after a variable interval (10ms up to a max, shorter while
`WATCHING`, longer while `PATROLLING`/`RESTING`). **Each creature
drives its own "tick" by re-scheduling its own task on the shared
`TaskManager`, rather than being polled by anything central** -- the
identical self-rescheduling pattern documented in section 348 for
object saves, maintenance decay, and buff expiry is the same mechanism
underneath AI "thought," weather changes (section 375), and every
other time-driven system in this engine.

**No signal-based shutdown exists.** No `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` handler is
wired anywhere near server lifecycle. Shutdown is entirely
command-driven: an admin `shutdown` console command calls
`zoneServer->timedShutdown()`, which eventually broadcasts a
`Condition` variable (`signalShutdown()`) that wakes the blocked
console thread, breaking `handleCommands()`'s loop and falling through
to `ServerCore::shutdown()` (see section 375 for the full sequence).
The Linux `service`-mode process wrapper (`main.cpp`'s
`while(true){ CoreProcess core(...); core.start(); core.wait(); }`) is
purely a crash-recovery supervisor that restarts the whole process on
exit/crash -- not a simulation tick either.

**Practical takeaway:** there is no "per-frame game logic" hook to add
new time-driven behavior into. Any new feature needing periodic
behavior must use the task-scheduling system directly (section 348) --
either a one-shot/delayed `executeTask()`/`scheduleTask()` call, or a
`Task` subclass that reschedules itself, exactly like `AiBehaviorEvent`
and `WeatherChangeEvent` already do. There is no other mechanism.

## 364. Reference-Counting Model -- `Reference<T>` / `ManagedReference<T>` / `WeakReference<T>`

Every `Object`-derived instance carries a lazily-allocated, atomic
intrusive reference counter (`system/lang/Object.h`'s
`AtomicReference<StrongAndWeakReferenceCount*>`), incremented/
decremented via `acquire()`/`release()` on copy/assign/destruct --
classic CAS-based intrusive smart-pointer semantics, confirmed
zero-overhead (`static_assert(sizeof(Reference<Object*>) ==
sizeof(Object*))`). `Object::release()` destroys the object once the
count hits zero.

**`Reference<T>` vs `ManagedReference<T>` -- same counting engine,
different persistence awareness.** `ManagedReference<T>` literally
`: public Reference<O>`, inheriting all acquire/release logic
unchanged. Its addition is ORB/ODB awareness: it caches the object's
database ID alongside the pointer and supports serializing/
deserializing by that ID via `Core::getObjectBroker()->lookUp()` --
i.e. it's what lets a member field survive a save/load round-trip
through the persistence layer (section 341) or a cross-process ORB
call (section 354). `Reference<T>` is the same mechanism without that
persistence-ID tracking, for plain non-distributed `Object` types.

**`WeakReference<T>` does NOT participate in the strong count at
all.** It resolves via `Object::requestWeak()` against a separately
reference-counted weak-count control block; calling `get()` checks
whether the target has already been destroyed and returns a genuinely
null `Reference<O>` if so -- this project's own
`CompanionThreatObserver` deliberately holds only a weak reference to
its target companion for exactly this reason (a separate, independently-
lockable `ManagedObject` that must never be kept artificially alive by
an observer registration, and must never be assumed valid without
re-resolving). `ManagedWeakReference<O>` layers a saved object ID on
top, so even a dead in-memory weak pointer can lazily re-resolve by ID
via a fresh lookup.

**No garbage collection, no cycle detection exists anywhere in this
system** -- confirmed by an exhaustive grep for "cycle"/"circular" in
the reference-counting sources (zero hits). This is pure deterministic
reference counting: a cycle between two `ManagedReference`s will leak
permanently, exactly like `std::shared_ptr`.

**Practical rule of thumb:** `ManagedReference<T>` is the default for
any `ManagedObject`-derived member field (anything persisted or
crossing the ORB boundary -- this is what every companion-system class
already uses). `Reference<T>` for shared ownership of plain,
non-distributed types. `WeakReference<T>`/`ManagedWeakReference<T>`
for back-references and observer/parent-child links where a strong
reference would create a cycle or artificially extend lifetime --
always re-resolve and null-check before use, never trust an old
snapshot. Raw pointers only for same-stack-frame temporaries whose
lifetime is provably bounded by an already-held strong reference --
never as a class member for anything with independent lifetime.

## 365. Generic Engine Data Structures -- `SortedVector`, `VectorMap`, `HashTable`

Distinct from `std::` containers, these are the engine's own,
serialization-aware collection classes used throughout the codebase.

**`SortedVector<E>`** is genuinely sorted, not sort-on-demand -- `put()`
does a binary-search insert directly into a contiguous backing array,
keeping it ordered after every insert (O(log n) find, O(n) insert due
to shifting). Default ordering comes from a `TypeInfo<E>::compare()`
trait (operator-based), overridable per subclass. Duplicate-key policy
is configurable (`ALLOW_DUPLICATE`/`NO_DUPLICATE`/`ALLOW_OVERWRITE`).

**`VectorMap<K,V>`** is literally `class VectorMap : public
SortedVector<VectorMapEntry<K,V>>`, forcing overwrite-on-duplicate
semantics -- confirmed to be exactly the "sorted flat array of
key-value pairs" pattern (not a hash table or tree): `get()`/`find()`
both binary-search the flat array. This gives O(log n) lookup backed
by one contiguous, cache-friendly array -- good for iteration and
moderate-size collections (the `containerObjects`/`slottedObjects`
maps documented in section 353 are exactly this), poor for very
frequent inserts/removes into large collections.

**`HashTable<K,V>`** is a real hash table -- bucket array with
singly-linked-list chaining, dynamic rehashing past a 0.75 load
factor. Its hash function dispatches through the same generic
`TypeInfo<T>::hashCode()` trait mechanism that backs `String::hashCode()`
(section 371) -- the identical hashing infrastructure used for packet
opcodes and STF lookups also backs this container's bucket indexing.

**None of the three has any internal locking.** Confirmed by full
header reads -- no mutex member, no synchronization anywhere. All
three rely entirely on the caller already holding the owning object's
lock, consistent with the engine's per-object `Locker` discipline
(section 349).

**Practical idiom:** `VectorMap` for small-to-medium, iteration-heavy,
key-lookup collections (slot maps, per-object small registries).
`HashTable` where N is large and lookup/insert/remove dominates over
iteration (global object tables, large ID-keyed registries) -- O(1)
average regardless of size, no O(n) shift cost. `SortedVector` for a
sorted sequence of plain values, not key/value pairs. `std::map`/
`std::unordered_map` are rarely used in core engine code -- the
codebase consistently reaches for its own containers since they plug
directly into `TypeInfo` comparison/hashing and binary
serialization (`toBinaryStream`/`parseFromBinaryStream`) that `std::`
containers don't natively support.

## 366. Full Session Lifecycle -- Login to Spawn to Logout (extends section 30)

Section 30's login<->zone handshake stops at "client now has
permission + a character list" -- it never covers character
selection, loading, or spawning. This section picks up from there.

**Character selection:** `SelectCharacterCallback::run()` validates
the client actually owns the requested character
(`client->hasCharacter(characterID, galaxyID)`), then loads it via
`zoneServer->getObject(characterID, true)` -- the `true` flag triggers
an ODB load if the object isn't already resident in memory. No further
zone-handoff packet exists; the client is already connected directly
to the zone server chosen from the login server's galaxy list, so
selection happens entirely inside that already-open connection.

**Character load:** `characterID` is the root `CreatureObject`'s
object ID. `PlayerObject` (the "ghost") is not loaded separately -- it's
a slotted child under the `CreatureObject`, so loading the
`CreatureObject` recursively loads its contained/slotted subtree via
the generic container persistence model (section 353); the code simply
calls `player->getPlayerObject()` to get the already-populated child.

**Zone-in/spawn:** `connectPlayer()`/`connectApprovedPlayer()`
branches on the saved parent (ship/cell/vehicle/open zone) and places
the player via `transferObject()`, using floor-collision detection for
Z placement when returning to raw terrain. `transferObject`/`sendTo`
sends a `SceneObjectCreateMessage`, calls `sendBaselinesTo()` (section
367) and `link()`, which triggers `notifyInsert`/`notifyInsertToZone`
-- this is what actually populates the QuadTree/close-objects cache
documented in section 342. The client-side completion trigger is
`CmdSceneReady`, which calls `notifySceneReady()` -- clearing loading-
screen state, sending buffs, joining guild/planet chat, and spawning
the helper droid. Only after this is the character fully interactive.

**Logout:** disconnect triggers a scheduled `PlayerDisconnectEvent`
roughly 2-3 seconds later (a real linger period, not instant), which
stores pets/vehicles, removes the creature from the zone, and leaves
chat/groups -- but does **not** force an immediate database write. It
relies on the same runtime dirty-flag + periodic 5-minute ODB sweep
documented in section 341, meaning a character's very last actions
before logout are protected by the WAL (section 341) but not
necessarily flushed to the `.db` file until the next sweep or a
graceful shutdown's forced save (section 375).

## 367. Baseline Network Messages -- The Full-State Counterpart to Delta Messages (extends section 350)

Section 350 documented `DeltaMessage` (incremental field updates to an
object the client already knows about). **`BaseLineMessage` is a
genuinely separate class family**, also extending `BaseMessage`
directly (not `DeltaMessage`) -- it writes a fixed header (object ID, a
4-char type CRC like `'CREO'`, a baseline-group number, and a field
count) followed by a **curated, hand-picked field list for that
group**, not a raw memory dump. Concrete classes are named
`<Type>ObjectMessage<N>` -- e.g. `CreatureObjectMessage3/4/6`,
`PlayerObjectMessage3/6/8/9`, `TangibleObjectMessage3/6/7/8/9`.

**Group numbers line up with delta-group numbers, but per-class, not a
universal fixed sequence.** `CreatureObjectImplementation::
sendBaselinesTo()` sends groups 3 and 6 to *every* observer but groups
1 and 4 **only to the owning client** -- exactly matching which delta
groups (`CreatureObjectDeltaMessage3/4/6`) exist and confirming why
deltas require a non-null `owner` (section 350's finding). Each object
type defines its own baseline-group set via its own override; there is
no server-wide fixed sequence.

**The trigger is the QuadTree membership diff, not a generic "known
objects" registry.** Each object's own `CloseObjectsVector` (section
342) IS the per-observer "known objects" set. When
`TreeEntryImplementation::addInRangeObject()` adds a genuinely new
member (not already present), it fires `notifyInsert()`, which calls
`sendTo(observer, true, false)` -- sending a `SceneObjectCreateMessage`
then the full baseline set then contents. An already-known object
instead gets `notifyPositionUpdate` (cheap deltas only). This entire
chain fires synchronously from the same `zone->inRange()`/QuadTree
walk documented in section 342 -- there's no separate baseline
subsystem, it's a direct consequence of spatial-index membership
changing.

**No batching or rate-limiting exists at the game-logic layer.** A
baseline burst (create message + 2-4 grouped baselines with full
equipment/HAM/skill-mod lists) is many times larger than a single
delta update, and `notifyInsert` fires per newly-in-range pair inside
the QuadTree walk with no throttling -- meaning zoning into a crowded
area can burst many full baseline sets essentially at once. Any
pacing happens only at the SOE transport layer's ack/resend/
compression (section 350), never in game logic.

## 368. RPC / `DistributedMethod` Argument Marshaling (extends sections 351, 354)

The byte-level mechanics underneath the Stub/Servant/Adapter machinery
already documented in sections 351 (IDL codegen) and 354 (ORB
clustering).

**`DistributedMethod` is a thin facade, not itself a packet class.**
It holds an `InvokeMethodMessage*` (the real wire buffer, which does
extend the same `Packet` chain as `BaseMessage`) and hand-writes a
header (`objectID`, `methodID`, `invocationID`, `async` flag) via the
identical primitive-insert idiom (`insertLong`/`insertInt`/etc.)
documented for normal packets in section 350. Every
`addXParameter()` call on the Stub side just appends onto that same
buffer, in call order -- argument order in the generated Stub method
**is** the wire format, exactly like a normal packet's constructor
field order.

**Generated Adapter dispatch** (`Foo::Adapter::invokeMethod(methid,
inv)`) is a plain `switch(methid)`: each case reads arguments back off
the incoming buffer in the same order the Stub wrote them, calls the
real native method, and for non-void methods writes the return value
onto the same buffer for the reply. Unmatched IDs fall through to the
parent class's Adapter for inherited methods.

**Caller side is synchronous blocking, not a future/promise.** A Stub
method that detects `_getImplementation()==NULL` (object is remote)
builds a stack-local `DistributedMethod`, adds parameters, and calls
`execute()`, which sends the request and blocks on a per-message
`Condition` with a 10-second timeout until the receive thread matches
the reply by sequence number and signals it. Non-void calls then parse
the return value straight off the response buffer.

**Method dispatch is by numeric ID, class-seeded then sequential.**
Each generated class's enum shows the **first** method getting an
explicit large literal (idlc.jar hashing the mangled method signature
at generation time), with every subsequent method in that same class
being a plain auto-incrementing enum value from that seed -- confirmed
by reading two different generated classes with two different seed
values. idlc.jar's own source isn't in-tree (compiled jar only), so
the exact hash algorithm on that first constant couldn't be traced
further, but the switch-based numeric dispatch mechanism itself is
fully confirmed.

## 369. Packet-Receive Thread Architecture (extends sections 348, 350)

Section 350 documented the send path (a raw UDP socket under a session
abstraction); this covers the receive side.

**One dedicated receive thread per listening port, not a pool.**
`DatagramServiceThread` is a single OS thread whose `run()` loops on
one non-blocking UDP socket via epoll (`pollEvents`). The zone server,
login server, and ping server each instantiate exactly one such
thread -- there is no thread-pool at the socket layer, ever.

**The first-stage handoff after `recvfrom()` is synchronous, on that
single receive thread** -- despite going through something called
