`MessageReceiverTask`, `Task::executeInThread()` just calls `run()`
directly on the calling thread rather than routing through
`TaskManager`. This means the SOE reliability layer (ack/resend,
fragment reassembly, CRC validation, already documented in section
350) executes entirely on that one receive thread per port, not on a
worker pool.

**The real queue-off-thread point is per-client, not per-packet.**
Once a full logical message is assembled, its resulting task is handed
to `client->executeOrderedTask(task)`, which pushes it onto a
lock-free **per-client** queue. If nothing is already pending for that
client, the task goes straight to the shared `TaskManager` worker pool
(section 348); if something is already in flight, the new task waits
and is picked up automatically once the prior one finishes. This
guarantees **one client's packets always execute in strict order**,
but never pins that client to a fixed worker thread.

**Practical concurrency implication:** the receive thread itself is
not the locking risk -- it never touches game objects, only recv/
parse/enqueue. The real exposure is that while one client's own
command stream is serialized, *different* clients' ordered-task
chains run fully concurrently across the shared worker pool. **Any
object reachable from more than one player's packet stream (a shared
NPC, a vendor, a guild/manager singleton) can legitimately be entered
by as many concurrent threads as the configured worker-pool size** --
not just one or two -- which is exactly why the `Locker` discipline in
section 349 is load-bearing correctness, not defensive boilerplate.

## 370. Cross-Zone Object Transfer -- Confirms the Companion "Stranded on Travel" Finding (extends sections 342, 348)

Section 342 documented the quadtree WITHIN one zone. This covers what
happens when an object actually moves BETWEEN zones (shuttle travel,
GM teleport, cloning).

**The real entry point is `SceneObject::switchZone()`**, invoked by
every discontinuous move (shuttle boarding, teleport commands,
cloning, hyperspace). It does a genuine remove-then-reinsert, not a
pointer reassignment: `destroyObjectFromWorld(false)` fully unlinks
the object from the old zone's quadtree (including close-objects cache
cleanup), then the new zone's `transferObject()` reinserts it -- the
object's `Zone*` updates as a side effect of that reinsertion.

**No diff optimization on the resulting resend** -- switching zones
resets the player's "on load screen" state and unloads spawned
children, and insertion into the destination zone's quadtree triggers
the identical full-baseline-burst `notifyInsert()` path documented in
section 367 for every object newly in range. A zone transfer is, from
the network's perspective, functionally equivalent to a fresh login
spawn.

**The companion-stranding finding from `docs/companion_system/
HANDOFF.md` is CONFIRMED, with the exact root cause identified.**
`switchZone()` operates purely on the single object passed in --
nothing in the call chain queries nearby creatures. There IS a real
"bring owned things along" mechanism
(`PlayerObjectImplementation::unloadSpawnedChildren()`), but it only
walks the player's datapad and force-stores objects where
`isControlDevice()` is true -- which resolves true for
`PetControlDevice`/`VehicleControlDevice`/`ShipControlDevice` (all
`extends ControlDevice`, section 357) but is **false** for a companion,
because `CompanionControlDevice` deliberately `extends
IntangibleObject` directly rather than `ControlDevice` (an intentional
architectural isolation, documented in its own source comment, so the
two systems can't cross-recognize). Because of that one class-hierarchy
choice, a summoned companion is silently skipped by the "bring my
stuff along" logic and left alive, ownerless, in the old zone's
quadtree -- neither auto-stored nor teleported along. This fully
corroborates the companion system's own earlier finding and pins it to
a specific, fixable root cause: `unloadSpawnedChildren()`'s
`isControlDevice()` check simply needs a companion-aware branch
alongside it.

**Cell transitions (walking through a building door) are
architecturally distinct from cross-zone transfers** -- they don't
call `switchZone()` at all, instead using a lightweight same-zone
reparent (a `CellObject` is just a child of a `BuildingObject` inside
the same zone/quadtree). `switchZone()` internally branches on
same-zone vs. different-zone, taking a lighter parent-transfer path for
same-zone teleports into a cell and the full destroy/reinsert path
only for genuine cross-`Zone` moves.

## 371. Exception Handling Conventions

Distinct from the logging conventions already documented (section
356) -- this covers real C++ `throw`/`catch`.

The base `Exception` class (`system/lang/Exception.h`) is a plain
value type (not `std::exception`-derived) holding a message string and
a real captured stack trace, with `printStackTrace()`/`getMessage()`
accessors. Real subclasses span the engine: `DatabaseException`
(DB layer), `ObjectNotDeployedException`/`ObjectAlreadyDeployedException`/
`ObjectNotLocalException` (ORB clustering), `LuaCallbackException`/
`LuaPanicException` (scripting bridge), several `.iff`-parsing
exceptions, and generic ones (`ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`,
`IllegalArgumentException`, `FileNotFoundException`, `SocketException`).
Notably, `ObjectNotDeployedException` isn't meant to be recovered from
at all -- its constructor prints a trace and raises `SIGSEGV`
deliberately, used as an intentional crash-and-core-dump for
unrecoverable ORB corruption.

**Genuine catch-alls exist at every major entry point, so an uncaught
exception normally cannot take the whole process down.** Every
scheduled task's execution (`TaskWorkerThread`, and `Task::run()`
itself) is wrapped in `try { ... } catch (const Exception&) { ... }
catch (...) { ... }`; packet dispatch catches exceptions at the
handler level; and critically, every queued player command's
`activateCommand()` call (`CommandQueue.cpp`) is individually wrapped
so one bad command can't crash the server -- it just logs and the
player's next command proceeds normally.

**Honest read: exception usage is sparse and inconsistent, not a
deliberate layered error-handling architecture.** `throw` appears only
around 69 times across all of `server/zone` (versus pervasive
`error()`/bool-return usage per section 356), almost always as a
bare `throw Exception()` with no message inside GM/debug command
argument parsing, functioning as a "bail out of this command" escape
hatch that relies on the `CommandQueue` catch site to absorb it. There
is no documented or consistently-followed rule for when new code
should throw versus log-and-return -- the honest practical guidance is
to default to the already-established logging convention (section
356) for ordinary error conditions, and reserve throwing for genuinely
exceptional, hard-to-otherwise-signal conditions where an existing
catch-all (task execution, packet dispatch, command queue) will
reasonably absorb it.

## 372. String / Unicode Internals (extends sections 350, 359)

Sections 350 and 359 already lean on `String::hashCode()` and
`UnicodeString` as usage; this documents the implementation
underneath.

**`String` is a genuinely custom class, not a `std::string` wrapper.**
It's small-string-optimized (an inline buffer for short strings,
`malloc` for longer ones) with no copy-on-write and no reference
counting -- every copy deep-copies. `std::string` only appears as a
convenience conversion at the boundary, never as the internal
representation.

**`String::hashCode()` and the compile-time `STRING_HASHCODE()`/
`""_hashCode` variant are confirmed to always produce IDENTICAL
results, by construction -- there is no possibility of divergence.**
The runtime method is a direct call into the same `constexpr` function
the compile-time macro invokes; there is only one algorithm
implementation, runtime just isn't guaranteed to fold at compile
time. It's a genuine CRC32-style table-driven hash. This matters
because the same hash backs packet opcodes (section 350), STF text
keys (section 351), and `HashTable` bucket indexing (section 365) --
a divergence here would have been a systemic, silent bug class, and
none exists.

**`UnicodeString` is UTF-16 code-unit storage, and the two conversion
directions are asymmetric.** The wire path (`Packet::insertUnicode`/
`parseUnicode`) is genuine UTF-16 round-tripping, matching what the
client sends for typed chat/names -- safe for non-ASCII. But
`String`-to-`UnicodeString` conversion (`asciitowide()`) is a **naive
1:1 byte-widen, not real UTF-8 decoding** -- a proper `mbsrtowcs` call
exists in the source but is commented out. Any UTF-8 multi-byte
sequence (accented Latin, CJK, etc.) held in a `String` gets each raw
byte promoted to its own bogus UTF-16 code unit if converted this way.
The reverse direction (`UnicodeString`-to-`String`) does use a real
UTF-8/UTF-16 codec, so the two directions are NOT symmetric or lossless
as a round-trip.

**Practical boundary rule:** use `String` for internal/ASCII
identifiers, hashed keys, template/file paths, and command names. Use
`UnicodeString` specifically for player-facing text traveling to/from
the client wire (chat, character names, mail, SUI arguments), where
the client already speaks real UTF-16. **Never construct a
`UnicodeString` directly from a `String`/`const char*` that might
contain non-ASCII bytes** -- that's the one place international text
can silently corrupt in this codebase.

## 373. Metrics/Telemetry Interface -- Confirmed Built But Entirely Unused

Section 337 noted `SceneObject.idl` declares `implements Logger,
Metrics` -- the `Logger` half is fully documented (section 356); this
confirms what `Metrics` actually is.

`server::metrics::Metrics` is a lightweight StatsD-style publishing
mixin -- any class inheriting it gets `publishGauge`/`publishCounter`/
`publishTimer`/`publishHist`/`publishMeter` one-liners that route
through a global `MetricsManager` sending UDP StatsD packets, gated
entirely off if `Core3.UseMetrics` (default `false`) isn't set.

**Confirmed: real usage is zero.** An exhaustive grep for calls to any
of the five publish methods across all of `server/zone` returns
matches only inside the `Metrics.h` definitions themselves -- no game
object, including `SceneObject` and everything that inherits it, ever
actually calls these methods. The capability is fully wired end-to-end
(config flag, UDP transport, publishing API) but completely unexercised
-- vestigial infrastructure. No broader profiler/performance-monitoring
system exists anywhere else in the codebase either (confirmed by grep
for "profiler"/"benchmark"/"perfmon"); `Metrics` is the entire extent
of this engine's built-in telemetry, and nothing uses it.

**Practical note:** a developer wanting real runtime metrics for a new
feature would need to actually call `publishCounter()`/`publishGauge()`
etc. themselves and flip `Core3.UseMetrics` on -- the pipe exists and
works, it's just never been plumbed into any actual game code.

## 374. Config Value Propagation -- From `config.lua` Text to a Live Manager Variable (extends section 25)

Section 25 covers parsing `config.lua` into a flattened dotted-key
map; this covers how a Manager actually consumes a value from it.

**Confirmed on-demand, not cached by the calling Manager.**
`ConfigManager::getInt/getBool/etc.` does a real map lookup under a
read lock on every single call -- no manager-side caching. The
dominant pattern across 164 grepped call sites is a bare inline call
at the exact point of use, re-fetching fresh every time with the
default value hardcoded at the call site, not stored in a member
field. The one caching mechanism that exists lives inside
`ConfigManager` itself, in a handful of hot-path accessors using a
`static` value + version-counter idiom -- that's ConfigManager's own
optimization, not something calling code does.

**No general live-reload for `config.lua` exists.** Admin commands
exist for individual value changes (e.g. `setpvpmode`) and for
dumping the current config, but nothing re-runs `config.lua` at
runtime -- file edits require a restart to take effect. Any of the
individual setter commands bumps the internal version counter, so the
handful of cached hot-path accessors pick up the change immediately,
but that's distinct from a general config-reload.

**Adding a new config key requires no registration or schema step.**
The parser just walks whatever tables exist under the config file's
top-level namespace at load time -- there's no fixed schema to update
elsewhere. Minimum work for a new feature's config value: add the
key/value to `config.lua`, then call `ConfigManager::instance()->
getX("Core3.YourKey", defaultValue)` directly wherever it's needed --
the default-value argument even means the code works correctly before
the key exists in the Lua file at all. The only established
convention for hot-loop values is to add a cached accessor to
`ConfigManager` itself following its existing static+version-counter
pattern, rather than calling the raw getter every tick.

## 375. Server Shutdown / Save-All Sequence (extends section 341)

Section 341 documented the periodic ODB save sweep and crash-recovery
WAL; this covers the graceful shutdown path specifically.

**No OS signal handler is wired to shutdown at all** -- confirmed by
exhaustive grep. The only graceful paths are admin console commands:
an immediate `exit`, or a `shutdown {minutes}` that schedules a
per-minute broadcast countdown before converging on the same shutdown
function.

**Confirmed real order of operations:** (1) stop accepting new work --
the zone server's state flips to `SHUTTINGDOWN`, which is checked
pervasively (30+ call sites) to reject new logins and short-circuit AI/
maintenance tasks immediately, before anything else happens; (2) wait
for any save already in progress to finish (unbounded wait); (3)
cancel background tasks, stop the login server; (4) disconnect all
connected players, with a **bounded** wait (max 10 seconds) for
connections to actually drop; (5) stop remaining services, then an
unconditional fixed 5-second grace sleep; (6) a **forced full save**
of every dirty object right now, reusing the exact same dirty-object
collection mechanism as the periodic sweep (section 341) but running
it immediately in full-serialization mode instead of waiting for the
next 5-minute tick -- critically, this does **not** bypass the
dirty-flag gate, so an object that was never marked dirty in the first
place still won't be saved here either; (7) wait again (unbounded) for
that save to finish; (8) close zones, ORB, task manager, and finally
the database environment.

**No timeout or forced-kill fallback exists anywhere in this
sequence** -- two of the wait loops are genuinely unbounded, meaning a
stuck database commit or deadlocked save thread would hang the
shutdown process indefinitely with nothing to force it through.

**Practical implication for a hard kill (`kill -9`, OOM, crash) versus
graceful shutdown, directly extending section 341's WAL
conclusion:** since BDB's transaction log already durably persists
every *committed* transaction and replays it automatically on next
boot, a hard kill loses essentially nothing that the WAL doesn't
already protect. The real difference is narrower than "data loss" --
a hard kill skips the player-facing graceful steps (no warning
countdown, ungraceful disconnects) and forgoes the chance to force an
*immediate* write of whatever was dirty but hadn't yet hit the
5-minute periodic sweep. In practice that's a small, bounded window
(at most ~5 minutes) of dirty-but-uncommitted in-memory state that a
graceful shutdown flushes early but a crash simply leaves for the next
sweep after restart to catch -- not a WAL/durability failure.

## 376. Zone/Planet Lifecycle -- Creation, Recurring Maintenance, Teardown (extends sections 340, 342)

Section 340 covered manager boot wiring (including Zone creation as a
byproduct); this covers the `Zone` object's own lifecycle as a
first-class thing.

**Creation does more than spin up managers.** Beyond allocating its
quadtrees (section 342) and per-zone task queue,
`PlanetManagerImplementation`'s initialization loads sub-planet
region/city-limit/PvP data, conditionally constructs `WeatherManager`/
`GCWManager`, loads travel points and shuttleport timing data, loads
the client's static World Snapshot geometry, spawns static planet
objects/terminals from Lua, loads badge-trigger areas, builds
navmeshes, and loads that zone's player-owned structures -- NPC spawn
tables are a separate `CreatureManager` responsibility (already
documented in sections 38/42).

**Each zone genuinely owns real recurring maintenance, distinct from
generic per-object task scheduling.** `WeatherManager` self-reschedules
a `WeatherChangeEvent` task after each weather pattern's duration
expires -- a real, per-zone recurring timer, following the identical
self-rescheduling `Task` pattern documented in section 348 (and the
same mechanism underlying AI "thinking" in section 363). NPC respawn is
handled per-lair via its own scheduled tasks rather than one global
zone-wide tick.

**No runtime teardown path exists for an individual zone.** Zone
destruction methods (`stopManagers()`, `clearZone()`) are meaningfully
implemented, but their only call site is the whole-server shutdown
sequence (section 375) -- there is no "take one planet offline while
the server keeps running" capability anywhere in the codebase. Zones
are created once at boot and live for the server's entire process
lifetime.

**Scale, for calibration:** a full deployment's `config.lua` lists
roughly a dozen real ground zones (corellia, dantooine, dathomir,
dungeon1, endor, lok, naboo, rori, talus, tatooine, tutorial, yavin4)
plus ten real space zones, with a further set of dev/test zones present
but commented out. A running server has on the order of **~22 real
`Zone` objects total** -- dozens, not hundreds -- which matters for
reasoning about the practical cost of any per-zone maintenance work a
new feature might add.

## 377. Thread-Safe Primitives -- When an Atomic Is Enough vs. When You Need a Full `Locker` (extends section 349)

Section 349 documented the full per-object `Locker`/mutex model for
coordinating compound state. This documents the lighter-weight
alternative for single-value shared state.

**`AtomicInteger`/`AtomicBoolean`/`AtomicLong` wrap genuine hardware
atomics (`std::atomic`), not a disguised mutex** -- confirmed by
reading all three headers: every mutation goes through real atomic
compare-exchange/load/store operations, with zero `Lockable`/`Locker`
involvement anywhere in the class.

**Real usages span the engine, confirming this is a deliberate,
recurring idiom, not a one-off:** version/hot-reload counters (the
already-known `masterScreenPlayVersion` for live Lua screenplay
reloading, and `ConfigManager`'s own version counter backing its
cached hot-path accessors from section 374); connection/session
counters (`ZoneServer`'s `currentPlayers`/`totalPlayers`, bumped on
every login/logout with no compound invariant to protect); cross-thread
statistics aggregation (`StatisticsManager`'s block of counters bumped
concurrently from worker threads across the whole server); and
ready/in-flight flags (`Zone`'s `managersStarted` boolean,
`spawnedAiAgents` counter).

**The line between "atomic is enough" and "you need a full `Locker`"
is exactly: does this value have any invariant relating it to another
field, or does mutating it require touching another object?** A pure
independent counter or flag (player count, a version number, a stat
total) is correctly an atomic. The moment two-or-more fields must
change together, or the operation reaches into another object's state,
`Locker` is required -- this is precisely the class of bug documented
in sections 348/349's real SIGABRTs, where code that should have
deferred to a locked task instead tried to get away with lighter-weight
coordination. `Zone`'s own source shows both sides of this line
side-by-side: `spawnedAiAgents` is a plain atomic counter, but it sits
next to a separate real `Mutex` used specifically whenever spawn
bookkeeping needs more than a single counter bump.

**Lock-free object-ID generation is real and is the pattern new code
needing unique IDs should follow:** `DOBObjectManager`'s
`nextObjectID` is an `AtomicLong`; ID generation is a bare
fetch-and-increment with zero locking, and uniqueness across
concurrent threads/objects is guaranteed purely by the atomic
increment itself -- a database/table identifier gets OR'd into the
high bits separately, outside the atomic operation, so no coordination
is needed there either.

# General Engine Architecture -- Batch 3 (Sections 378-417)

Third architecture research pass (40 parallel agents), pushing past
the foundational engine-mechanics layer (batches 1-2) into the
IMPLEMENTATION internals of specific subsystems already documented at
the mechanics/feature level elsewhere in this guide -- crafting,
loot, weather, missions, chat, guilds, groups, structures, AI -- plus
a few genuinely new surfaces (REST API, status/ping servers, MySQL,
Recast/Detour navmesh). Each section below builds on and cross-cites
its mechanics-level counterpart rather than repeating it.

## 378. REST API Server -- A Real, Off-by-Default Remote Admin API

`server::web3::RESTServer` (built on Microsoft cpprestsdk) exposes an
HTTPS admin API: object inspection/mutation (`/v1/object/{oid}/`),
live config read/write (`/v1/admin/config/{key}/`), stats
(`/v1/admin/stats/`), **remote console command injection**
(`POST /v1/admin/console/{command}/`), player/account admin actions,
character/guild lookups, and mail/chat dispatch. Auth is a `Bearer`
token matched against `Core3.RESTServer.APIToken` (min 15 chars) --
fails closed if unconfigured. Gated behind the `WITH_REST_API`
compile flag (default off) **and** a nonzero `Core3.RESTServerPort`
config value, so it must be explicitly opted into twice. The console
endpoint reuses the exact same command-injection pipe
(`ServerCore::queueConsoleCommand()`) as local operator input and
section 13's admin-command system -- it's a remote front-end, not a
parallel command system.

## 379. Status/Ping Servers -- Deliberately Simpler Protocols Than the Game Wire Format

Neither uses `BaseMessage`/SOE framing (section 350). **`PingServer`**
is a raw 4-byte UDP echo -- no parsing, pure RTT/reachability check.
**`StatusServer`** is one-shot TCP: on connect it writes a plain XML
document (galaxy name, connected/cap/max/total/deleted player counts,
uptime) and closes -- the classic "galaxy status" feed a
launcher/server-list page scrapes, cached 60s server-side so repeated
hits don't hammer `ZoneServer`. Both instantiated alongside Login/Zone
servers in `ServerCore.cpp`, on `Core3.StatusPort`(44455)/
`Core3.PingPort`(44462).

## 380. Dynamic Mission Generation Algorithm (extends sections 20, 80)

`MissionManagerImplementation`'s terminal-mission generator is the
only real procedural-content generator in the codebase (badges/quests
per section 361 are 100% hand-authored, zero randomization). It
doesn't create fresh `MissionObject`s per roll -- it pre-pads a
player's mission bag with empty shells, then **re-rolls each shell's
type/content** via `randomizeGeneralTerminalMissions()` and friends.
Destroy missions pick a random `SpawnGroup` lair entry (level-filtered
±5) from a static per-zone data table and place the mission at a
random offset *relative to the player*, not a real spatial query.
Deliver/crafting missions use a dedicated `MissionNpcSpawnMap` (a
separate spatial lookup of pre-placed NPC spawn points, **not** the
general QuadTree). Reward is a formula (base + difficulty*level +
jitter), never a loot-table roll. Bounty missions (sections 20/80) are
architecturally different again -- drawn from a live player-target
list, closer to matchmaking than world-content generation.

## 381. Weather Pattern Generation Algorithm (extends sections 60, 376)

Not a weighted datatable roll. `createNewWeatherPattern()` uses a
per-planet `weatherStability` (0-100) scalar from
`weather_manager.lua` to build an implicit cumulative-threshold curve
over 5 severity states (CLEAR..EXTREMESTORM) each cycle -- a fresh
uniform roll every time, **no exclusion of the current weather and no
seasonal factor**, so immediate repeats can and do happen. Duration is
inversely scaled by severity. Within one weather window, severity also
varies by *location* via Simplex noise (`WeatherMap::getWeatherAt(x,y)`)
plus a time-based intensity ramp -- so two players in the same zone can
see different conditions. Delivery is pull-based per player (section
416), not a zone broadcast.

## 382. City Government Persistent Data Structure (extends section 54)

The real object is `CityRegion` (`extends ManagedObject`, not
`ActiveArea`) -- a city *owns* one or more `Region extends ActiveArea`
trigger objects for its geographic footprint rather than being one
itself. Persists treasury, mayor OID, citizen/militia/ban lists (as
plain OID vectors, not embedded objects), zoning rights/data,
specialization, the five-tax-type array, city hall reference, and
election state -- an ordinary ODB-persisted object (section 341's
model applies directly, `persistObject(city, 1, "cityregions")`).
`CityManager` is per-`ZoneServer` (not a true global singleton),
holding a `transient` in-memory `VectorMap<string, CityRegion>`
rebuilt at boot by scanning the `"cityregions"` BDB table -- durability
lives entirely in the individual `CityRegion` rows, `CityManager` is
just a runtime index.

## 383. Resource Spawning Algorithm Internals (extends sections 15, 358)

`ResourceSpawner::createResourceSpawn()` rolls each stat within its
type's min/max range, but it's not flat-uniform: a server-tunable
`spawnThrottling` breakpoint plus a ~10% coin-flip push most spawns
toward a quality band with occasional extremes. Procedural naming
(`NameManager::generateResourceName()`) is a real syllable-grammar
generator per resource class, retried against a profanity filter and
a collision check -- confirmed not player input. Despawn time is a
randomized multi-day window per instance. Despite that per-resource
randomness, the sweep cadence is a **single global self-rescheduling
`ResourceShiftTask` every 2 hours** (not one task per type/planet, a
deviation from the usual section 348 per-entity pattern) that walks
every resource pool and replaces any expired slot with a freshly
rolled resource of the same pool-configured type.

## 384. Vendor NPC Restocking -- Confirmed: No Restock Mechanism Exists At All

Direct source verification (zero `restock` hits anywhere in
`MMOCoreORB/src` or `bin/`) confirms section 214's finding at the code
level: there is no self-rescheduling restock `Task` and no periodic
sweep, because **there is nothing to restock**. Traced the real cantina
bartender example: drink purchases just `giveItem()` a brand-new
instance straight from a hardcoded per-zone Lua price/name table on
every buy, with no quantity counter anywhere. "Infinite stock, fresh
instance per purchase" is the entire mechanism -- a real restock system
would be genuinely new content, not an extension of anything present.

## 385. MySQL Usage Alongside Berkeley DB -- Two Fully Separate Persistence Domains (extends section 341)

BDB ODB (section 341) is the sole source of truth for game-object
state. MySQL (`ServerDatabase`, real connection pool) is used purely
for account/credential/session/ban data (the `accounts`/`sessions`/
`account_bans` tables -- confirms the `sessions` table referenced in
section 30's login handshake) and a lightweight cross-galaxy
character-name-to-OID index (`characters` table) so login/admin
tooling can resolve a name without opening BDB. The only coupling is
that `characters.character_oid` values must match real BDB object
IDs -- no transactional/FK relationship exists. A `WITH_SWGREALMS_API`
build variant can swap out direct MySQL account queries for a remote
API entirely, confirming MySQL itself is treated as optional/swappable
infrastructure, not a hard dependency.

## 386. NavMeshManager / Recast-Detour Pipeline (extends section 3)

A genuine boot-time Recast bake, not a precomputed-file load --
`buildRegionNavAreas()`/`buildCityNavMeshes()` enqueue jobs that
gather static geometry and run a real rasterize/contour/mesh build
(comment in source: "This will take a very long time to complete").
Storage is **not** plain files in the normal path -- the whole
`dtNavMesh` tile set serializes into the `NavArea` object's own field
and rides along with ordinary ODB persistence into a dedicated
`"navareas"` BDB table, loaded at boot and only rebuilt if missing or
if the region's position/radius changed. A separate admin-triggered
export-to-file path exists purely for debugging. AI pathing
(`AiAgentImplementation`) makes genuine `dtNavMeshQuery::findPath()`
Detour calls via a thread-local query object -- see section 411 for
the vendored library itself.

## 387. AiAgent Behavior Tree Class Architecture (extends sections 52, 363)

Real node classes exist under `ai/bt/`: `Composite` base with
`Selector`/`ParallelSelector`/`RandomSelector` (short-circuit OR
variants) and `Sequence`/`ParallelSequence`/`RandomSequence`
(short-circuit AND), `Decorator` wrappers (`AlwaysFail`,
`AlwaysSucceed`, `If`, `Not`, `UntilFailure`/`UntilSuccess`,
`LookForAllies`/`LookForPlayer`/`LookForTarget`), leaf condition
checks (`Checks.h`, ~70 `CheckType` entries), and action leaves. Trees
are **fully data-driven from Lua**, not fixed C++ -- flat tables in
`bin/scripts/ai/*.lua` (`{id, name=ClassName, pid=parent, args={...}}`)
registered via `addAiTemplate()`. A `TreeSocket` node resolves its
subtree at execute-time by slot ID (`agent->getBehaviorTree(slotID)`),
letting each creature type compose a *set* of named subtrees (move,
attack, heal, idle, etc.) rather than one monolithic tree -- confirmed
via the real `rootDefault` composition wiring 8+ named subtrees
together. `runBehaviorTree()` (the tree-walk) is distinct from
`AiBehaviorEvent`'s self-rescheduling wrapper already documented in
section 363.

## 388. Building Interior Cell/Portal Architecture (extends section 342)

`CellObject extends SceneObject` directly (a container *child* of a
`BuildingObject`, not a subclass of it -- corrects an imprecision in
section 370). Cells are built once at building-load time, one per
portal-layout floor mesh from the client `.iff` data
(`createCellObjects()`). **Server-side collision/LOS through walls is
real, not a client-only illusion**: `CollisionManager::
checkLineOfSightInBuilding()`/`checkLineOfSightWorldToCell()` perform
genuine triangle-mesh raycasts against each cell's `AppearanceTemplate`
geometry, walk the real portal-connectivity graph between adjacent
cells, and fail closed if a cell has no world-facing portal --
multi-story floor-height resolution is also per-cell via
`getCellFloorCollision()`. LOS across two different buildings is an
automatic `false`.

## 389. SpaceZone vs. GroundZone Architecture (extends sections 342, 376)

Sibling implementations of the same `Zone` base, not a
subclass-of-each-other relationship. `SpaceZone` owns a real 3D
**`Octree`** (cubic bounds, `MAX_DEPTH=4`) while `GroundZone` owns the
2D **`QuadTree`** (section 342) -- confirmed as genuinely different
C++ classes, not a coordinate-rescaled reuse, reflecting that space has
no terrain height plane. `SpaceZone` swaps `PlanetManager`/
`CreatureManager` (ground's NPC-population bookkeeping) for a single
`SpaceManager`, which in turn drives the `ShipManager` singleton for
ship AI -- `ShipManager` is not a direct `SpaceZone` member.

## 390. ShipAiAgent vs. Ground AiAgent Divergence (extends sections 337, 363)

Genuinely separate class trees with no shared ancestry: `ShipAiAgent
extends FighterShipObject extends ShipObject`, versus ground `AiAgent
extends CreatureObject` -- ships are the one major object type that
doesn't descend from `CreatureObject`/`TangibleObject` at all. Space AI
still uses the identical self-rescheduling `Task` pattern (section
363) via its own `ShipAiBehaviorEvent`, with the same
shutdown-short-circuit check. Pathing is architecturally distinct,
however: **zero navmesh usage anywhere under `ship/`** -- space AI
computes straight-line/intercept target points via real vector math
(`getInterceptPosition()`) rather than any obstacle-avoidance
structure, since open space has nothing to avoid.

## 391. CraftingManager Session Architecture (extends sections 45, 65, 88, 220)

There's no `CraftingManager`-owned session table -- each session is a
`CraftingSession` `Facade` object registered onto both the crafter and
the tool via the generic per-object session-slot mechanism
(`addActiveSession(SessionFacadeType::CRAFTING, ...)`). Station/tool
resolution happens once at session start (`findCraftingTool()`/
`getNearbyCraftingStation()`, a 7m proximity gate), and a station's
real effect is **binary capability-gating** (unlocks a higher
`complexityLevel` and enables the experimentation UI at all,
`setExperimentationEnabled(craftingStation != nullptr)`) -- confirmed
it contributes **zero bonus to the actual roll math**, which pulls
exclusively from skill mods and the handheld tool's own effectiveness
stat, matching section 88's finding at the exact call-site level. The
full stage sequence (session start -> select schematic -> add
ingredients -> assembly -> experiment -> create) is a real `state`-int
dispatch inside `CraftingSessionImplementation`, ending in a scheduled
`CreateObjectTask` that does the actual inventory transfer.

## 392. LootManager Internal Algorithm Architecture (extends section 55)

Layered class structure: `LootManager` (an ORB-distributed
`ManagedService`) owns one `LootGroupMap` singleton, itself two
`HashTable`s (`itemTemplates`/`groupTemplates`); a `LootGroupTemplate`
is a weighted pool (`VectorMap<name, weight>`, cumulative-sum roll);
`LootItemTemplate` is pure Lua-authored but cross-references the
target item's own compiled `.iff` template for stat-range metadata.
**Loading is pure Lua, not the general `.iff`-datatable pattern**
(section 358) -- loot tables have no `.iff` form at all. Per-mob
wiring is entirely static: each `CreatureTemplate` gets its own
`LootGroupCollection` parsed at boot; `LootManager` never does a
runtime lookup keyed on creature type. Real call chain confirmed:
creature death -> `CreatureManagerImplementation::notifyDestruction()`
-> `lootManager->createLoot()` -> resolves nested groups up to 32 deep
-> instantiates the real item via the standard CRC-template spawn path
(section 343) -> transfers into the corpse container.

## 393. Auction/Bazaar Backend Search Implementation (extends section 50)

One central in-memory registry (`AuctionsMap`), never per-vendor
queries. A two-tier structure: a flat `VectorMap<oid, AuctionItem>`
for by-ID lookup, plus a nested `VectorMap` tree
(galaxy->planet->region->vendor) of `SortedVector`-backed item lists
per vendor -- the same generic `VectorMap`/`SortedVector` container
idiom documented in section 365. Every search is a genuine live tree
walk and nested filtering scan (status/expiry/category/price/name),
capped at 100 results, offloaded to a scheduled task 100ms after the
request rather than answered synchronously on the network thread --
**no cached/precomputed result set exists**, every search recomputes
from current live state.

## 394. ChatManager Internal Room/Channel Implementation (extends section 188)

Every channel type (galaxy chat, auction spam, planet rooms, group,
guild, player-created custom rooms) is the **same concrete `ChatRoom`
class**, differentiated purely by a `roomType` enum and permission
flags/lists -- not a class hierarchy per channel type. Membership is a
real per-room `VectorMap<string, CreatureObject>`, and broadcast is a
straightforward O(members) fan-out iterating just that room's list
(never a global player scan), so routing cost scales with room size.
Planet rooms are built once at zone boot and are transient (rebuilt
every restart); group/guild rooms are created on demand and torn down
with their owning object; only player-created custom rooms are
genuinely ODB-persisted (`chatrooms.db`). A single flat
`ChatRoomMap` (`HashTable<uint32, ChatRoom*>`) is the global registry
across all types.

## 395. Buff/Debuff Timer Implementation (extends sections 6, 137)

Each `Buff` owns a real scheduled `Task` (`BuffDurationEvent`) that
fires exactly at expiration -- **no periodic sweep of active buffs
exists**, expiration is push-driven per instance, matching the section
348 pattern. The timer holds only weak references to the creature/buff
so a buff can never keep a dead creature artificially alive. Remaining
duration for UI purposes isn't tracked as separate mutable state --
`getTimeLeft()` derives it live by asking the task manager for the
event's actual next-execution time, so it can never drift out of sync.
Client sync is a **single fixed duration value pushed once** on
activation/renewal (`AddBuffMessage`), not a recurring tick packet --
the client counts down locally from that one value.

## 396. Structure Maintenance Decay Tick Implementation (extends section 30)

One self-rescheduling `StructureMaintenanceTask` per structure
(matching section 348's per-entity pattern, not a global sweep),
dynamically computing its next fire time from
`surplusMaintenance*3600/maintenanceRate` (clamped 1s-24h, randomized
to spread server load). Maintenance pool decrement happens
continuously via `updateStructureStatus()` based on real elapsed time,
mirroring the deficit directly into condition damage. "Condemned" is
**not a stored flag** -- it's simply `getDecayPercentage() == 0`
computed on demand. **Confirmed persistence gap, extending section
341's known bug class**: none of the maintenance-decrement or
condition-damage mutations call `_setUpdated(true)`/
`updateObjectToDatabase()` anywhere -- a maintenance tick does not
itself mark the structure dirty for the next save sweep, so its
durability depends entirely on some unrelated mutation on the same
object happening to trigger a save first.

## 397. Structure Placement Validation Algorithm (extends section 35)

The real geometric check is a **coarse axis-aligned bounding-box
corner-containment test**, not a mesh or radius check -- candidates
are gathered via the QuadTree (section 342, 128-unit query radius),
then each candidate's footprint (shrunk by a 0.1-unit inset) is tested
for whether it contains any of the new structure's 4 corners or
vice versa; rotated footprints are approximated as boxes. **Slope/
terrain-flatness validation is confirmed genuinely absent, not merely
simple** -- the real height-lookup line in `isBuildingPermittedAt()` is
literally commented out (`//targetPos.setZ(zone->getHeight(x,y)); not
needed`), and a codebase-wide grep for "slope" turns up nothing in
structure placement at all. Separately-checked gates: zone boundaries,
no-build zones, in-water, and POI-proximity exclusion.

## 398. GCW Score Persistent Data Structure (extends sections 86, 360)

**No per-player GCW score field exists anywhere** -- `FactionManager`'s
per-player `factionStanding` (section 360) is a different number
entirely. Planetary score lives directly on `GCWManager` itself (one
instance per zone): `rebelScore`/`imperialScore`/`rebelBases`/
`imperialBases`/`winningFaction`, all explicitly declared **`transient`**
-- excluded from ODB persistence at the field level, not just by
design convention. Recompute is a **full sweep, not incremental
accumulation**: an hourly self-rescheduling task zeroes and rebuilds
both scores from every live GCW base's per-template point value --
destroying or adding a base doesn't touch the score directly, it just
changes what the next hourly sweep counts.

## 399. HAM Regen Tick Implementation (extends section 61)

Two parallel self-rescheduling `Task` implementations, both on a flat
**1-second tick**: `PlayerRecoveryEvent` for players (always
reschedules, regardless of combat state) and `AiRecoveryEvent` for
NPCs (only reschedules while there's still an active defender/DoT/HAM
deficit/wound, otherwise the chain stops until combat restarts it).
Shared base formula: `ceil(currentHAM * 13/2100 * modifier)` per pool,
where **posture directly scales the modifier** -- kneeling is 1.25x,
sitting is 1.75x, applied uniformly to all three pools (not
mind-specific). Players are NOT gated out of regen while in combat
(only non-player creatures are); mounted players get the plain 1.0x
modifier since mounting precludes kneel/sit. AI agents use a separate,
simpler formula with no posture modifiers at all. A parallel wound-
healing accumulator runs every tick alongside the HAM regen,
independently gated by `private_med_wound_*` skill mods.

## 400. CraftingStation Object Interaction Internals (extends sections 65, 88)

Proximity (7m) is checked **continuously, not just once** --
`CraftingSessionImplementation::validateSession()` re-runs the range
check at every subsequent session action (stage advance, experiment
roll, prototype creation), so walking away does cancel a session, but
reactively on the player's next action rather than via a background
idle timer. Confirms and pins down section 88's finding at the exact
call-site level: the station contributes to `complexityLevel` (schematic
filtering) and toggles experimentation on/off, but is **never passed
into the actual roll functions** at all -- `calculateAssemblySuccess()`'s
`effectiveness` parameter comes from the handheld tool's own stat, not
the station's stored-but-unread `effectiveness` field.

## 401. Combat Queue Threading Model (extends sections 339, 349, 369)

No special combat-specific threading or serialization layer exists
beyond the generic per-client ordered-task queue (section 369) and
per-object `Locker` discipline (section 349) -- confirmed by reading
`CombatManager::doCombatAction()`'s actual locking calls. Concurrent-
defender safety when two different attackers target the same creature
simultaneously is handled entirely by the standard `Locker(defender,
attacker)` cross-lock/backoff primitive, re-acquired independently at
each contention point (`startCombat()`, `doTargetCombatAction()`,
armor/PSG mitigation sub-objects) -- there is no combat-manager mutex,
zone-wide combat lock, or per-encounter queue anywhere. Area/cone
attacks use a non-blocking `tryWLock()` on secondary targets and simply
skip any target already locked by another thread for that swing,
rather than retrying.

## 402. NPC Conversation State Machine Implementation (extends sections 34, 112)

Conversation state is **per-player, not per-NPC**, and **not durable
across logout**. The shared `ConversationObserver` (one per template)
holds no mutable state itself; "current screen" lives in an in-memory-
only `ConversationSession` facade attached to the *player's*
`CreatureObject` via the generic session-slot mechanism (section 391
uses the identical pattern for crafting). Screen resolution on option-
click is pure C++ table lookup (`getOptionLink()`), not a Lua branching
walk -- Lua supplies only the static screen shape/text, C++ owns
dispatch and dynamic content injection via non-mutating clone-and-fill.
Unlike durable quest state (which has a real ODB save hook), the
mid-dialogue screen pointer has no such hook and is simply lost on
logout -- a player resumes at the conversation's entry point, not
where they left off.

## 403. Bio-Engineer Creature Template Generation Algorithm (extends sections 33, 244, 343)

**No new template is ever fabricated at runtime.** The crafting
schematic author picks an existing, already-boot-registered
`CreatureTemplate` "skin" at content-authoring time (a plain Lua field
on `PetDeedTemplate`); DNA-derived stats (HAM, armor, resists, damage,
level) are computed by the Genetics/crafting-experimentation system and
stored as ordinary fields directly **on the deed object itself**, not
in any template. At spawn time the standard CRC-template spawn path
(section 343) runs completely unmodified. The trick is downstream:
nearly every stat getter on `AiAgent` branches `if (petDeed) return
petDeed.getX(); else return npcTemplate.getX()` -- the same
override-getter pattern documented for droids in section 33, letting a
stock template's spawnable identity carry custom, deed-owned stats
transparently.

## 404. Guild Persistent Data Structure Architecture (extends sections 16, 134, 337, 364)

`GuildObject extends SceneObject` directly (section 337). Confirmed
absent: **no treasury field, no guild-hall reference field, no
emblem/insignia field anywhere** -- guild hall is a derived label (any
building with a Guild Terminal), and identity is text-only. Member
records (`GuildMemberList : VectorMap<uint64, GuildMemberInfo>`) store
a per-member **permission bitmask**, not a role enum -- "leader" is
just whoever holds the ALL-permissions bit, no separate leader field
exists. `GuildManager` holds all guilds in a `DeltaSet` keyed by a
composite `"guildID:abbrev"` string, one instance per zone process (not
a true cross-process singleton). A player's guild reference on
`CreatureObject` is a genuine `@weakReference`, re-resolved and
null-checked on every access -- confirming section 364's reference-
counting discipline in a second real, independent case beyond the
companion system's own usage.

## 405. Packet Opcode Catalog -- Breadth Survey (extends section 350)

332 packet/message header files across ~26 subdirectories under
`server/zone/packets/`. Largest buckets: `object/` (~62, generic
cross-object messages -- combat, command queue, crafting callbacks,
radial menu), `chat/` (44), `player/` (27), `ui/` (26, SUI/tickets/
console), `auction/` (19). Most subdirectories mirror a SceneObject
subtype and hold a `*ObjectMessage{N}.h` (baseline, section 367) +
`*ObjectDeltaMessage{N}.h` (delta, section 350) pair per client "view"
tier. For a new packet, check the subdirectory matching the target
object type first for baseline/delta precedent, or `object/`/`ui/` for
a one-off action/UI message resembling the new one.

## 406. TreeEntry Class -- Full Interface, Shared by Both Spatial Trees (extends section 342)

Beyond `coordinates`/`node`/`closeobjects`, `TreeEntry` also carries
`worldCoordinates` (a second, world-relative mirror kept in sync for
cross-zone queries), parent/root-parent linkage, and geometry-test
methods for all 8 quadrant/octant divisions (`isInSWArea`...`NE2Area`,
the "2" variants handling the octree's extra Z-split). **Confirmed:
the identical `TreeEntry` base backs both the ground `QuadTree` and the
space `Octree`** (section 389) -- dual-structure support is an internal
`nodeType` tag branch inside `TreeEntryImplementation`, not
polymorphism against an abstract spatial contract. `ActiveAreaQuadTree`
is a wholly separate, `TreeEntry`-independent structure indexing
`ActiveArea` directly. There is no swappable spatial-index abstraction
-- a genuinely different structure would require modifying `TreeEntry`/
`TreeNode` themselves.

## 407. Vehicle/Ship Collision Detection Implementation (extends section 249)

Real mesh-level collision machinery exists
(`CollisionManager::checkMovementCollision()`, raycasting against
NavArea navmeshes plus true bounding-sphere/`AppearanceTemplate`
intersection tests) -- but **its only call site is inside a commented-
out code block** in `DataTransform.h`, specifically gated on vehicle/
mount movement. The only *live* server-side check on vehicle position
updates today is `checkSpeedHackTests()` -- a flat distance/time
threshold, no geometry at all. Since section 249 already confirms no
ramming/damage code path exists, there's no "was this a collision"
question being asked server-side in the first place: the server
largely trusts client-reported vehicle transforms, consistent with the
companion system's own client-authoritative-vehicle-movement finding.

## 408. StructureManager Internal Object Bookkeeping (extends sections 341, 342)

**No central in-memory registry exists** -- `StructureManager` holds
only a `ZoneServer*`/`TemplateManager*`, zero structure-keyed
containers. The real "registry" is a **Berkeley DB secondary index**
(`"playerstructuresindex"`), auto-maintained by BDB's own associate
callback whenever a record is written to the primary
`"playerstructures"` database -- deserializing each record's zone field
into the index key. `loadPlayerStructures(zoneName)` at zone boot walks
this index to find and instantiate every structure for that zone.
Runtime placement has **no push notification to StructureManager** at
all -- writing the new object into the `"playerstructures"` database
(via `ObjectManager::createObject(..., "playerstructures")`) is itself
what triggers BDB's index maintenance; there's no explicit
`registerStructure()` call or observer pattern involved.

## 409. PlayerManager Internal Architecture (extends sections 44, 64, 68, 359)

At ~7,490 lines/~130 methods, one of the largest single manager
implementations in the codebase -- not a thin facade. Holds no
object-pointer registry keyed by OID; its one identity structure is a
plain **name<->OID lookup** (`CharacterNameMap`), with actual live
object references always fetched fresh via `ZoneServer::getObject()`.
A second real structure, `OnlineZoneClientMap`, is keyed by **account
ID** (session/connection tracking), distinct from character OID.
Best characterized as the session/identity/economy bookkeeping layer
sitting between `ZoneServer` (owns the real object table) and the
per-zone QuadTree (owns spatial presence) -- a large surface of
stateless orchestration methods that mutate objects passed in as
arguments, never duplicating either underlying registry.

## 410. Instance/Heroic Zones -- Confirmed: No Instancing Mechanism Exists At All (extends sections 22, 219, 376)

Independent re-verification confirms the prior finding: zero hits for
`InstanceManager`/`createInstance`/`cloneZone`/`privateZone` anywhere
in the codebase. `Zone` objects (both `GroundZone` and `SpaceZone`) are
constructed **exactly once at server boot**, one per `config.lua`
entry (~22 total per section 376), and every other call site in the
engine (teleports, hyperspace, mission objectives, ~15+ call sites in
`DirectorManager`) exclusively fetches an *existing* zone by name --
none ever construct one at runtime. Neither the "real dynamic zone per
instance" model nor the "flagged region in a shared zone" model is
implemented; this engine has no instancing concept whatsoever.
"Dungeons" are ordinary shared world-space content on the standard
lair/spawn-group system, simultaneously fightable by any number of
unrelated groups -- matching original SWG's non-instanced design.

## 411. Recast/Detour Library Integration (extends section 386)

Vendored in-tree under `src/pathfinding/recast/` (24 files), largely
unmodified upstream (no project-specific markers found), a fairly
recent snapshot based on internal version constants -- and
deliberately trimmed (no `DetourCrowd`, `DetourTileCache`, debug-draw,
or demo tooling, just the core build+query pipeline). Integration is
**not hidden behind an adapter** -- two thin purpose-built wrapper
classes (`RecastNavMesh`, `RecastTileBuilder`) handle build/
persistence, but the query hot path (`PathFinderManager`,
`AiAgentImplementation`, `CollisionManager`) calls raw `dtNavMeshQuery`/
`dtQueryFilter` Detour types directly.

## 412. Group/Raid Internal Data Structure Architecture (extends sections 47, 62, 296, 308, 337, 364)

`GroupObject extends SceneObject` directly (no HAM/damage state, like
`GuildObject`/`CellObject`). Members are stored in a
`DeltaVector<GroupMember>` (not a bare `Vector` of references) --
`DeltaVector` is what turns member add/remove into proper baseline/
delta network sync (section 350/367) rather than full resends; each
`GroupMember` wraps one real `ManagedReference<CreatureObject*>`
internally. **No dedicated leader field exists** -- leadership is
purely positional (index 0 of the member list), contrasting with
`GuildObject`'s hard-stored leader field (section 404). Confirmed:
**no raid/ops sub-grouping container exists** -- large groups are
still one flat 20-cap list (section 308). Broadcast is plain iteration:
clone-and-send to each member individually, no batching.

## 413. Mail/PersistentMessage Delivery Pipeline (extends sections 21, 290, 337)

Since `PersistentMessage extends ManagedObject` (not world-placed,
section 337), delivery is **pull-on-query with an online-push
shortcut**, not true push notification. A message is persisted to the
ODB `"mail"` database immediately regardless of recipient state; if the
recipient is online, a genuine live push happens over their session --
otherwise the mail OID goes into a separate `PendingMessageList`
keyed by recipient, drained into the player's own message-ID list on
next login (`checkPendingMessages()`), then lazily resolved via a
standard ODB lookup when the mailbox is actually opened. **Item/credit
attachments are confirmed absent by design, not unfinished plumbing**
-- `PersistentMessage.idl` has no container/credit field at all, and no
wire-format field carries one in either direction; real item/credit-
by-mail only exists via the architecturally separate structure/vendor
COD mailbox (section 232).

## 414. WorldSnapshot Static Geometry Loading Pipeline (extends section 69)

A `.ws` file is the same client-authored format the SOE client itself
uses to render static world props -- a recursive node tree (building
-> interior cells -> furniture/loot-crate placements), parsed by a
dedicated snapshot parser distinct from the generic DataTable/.iff
system (section 358). Critically, the server instantiates **real,
individually-addressable, ODB-persisted `SceneObject`s** for every
snapshot entry (using the file's baked object ID verbatim as the live
database ID) -- not a lightweight collision-only shadow. Each is
flagged `setClientObject(true)`, which only suppresses network sync to
players (since the client already renders its own copy from the same
file) -- screenplay-authored content routinely looks these objects up
by their fixed snapshot IDs to spawn population inside them. A noted
open risk: snapshot object IDs share the same ID space as the runtime
allocator, a real collision hazard for anyone authoring new snapshot
content.

## 415. Admin/GM Command Permission-Level Architecture (extends sections 13, 339, 346)

A real tiered numeric system, not a boolean. `PlayerObject.adminLevel`
(0-15) is mirrored from the login `Account` object at character
creation, with threshold helpers (`hasGodMode()` >0, `isPrivileged()`
>6, `isStaff()` >10, `isAdmin()` ==15) used directly in gameplay code
beyond command dispatch (city management, forced structure demolition,
forced despawns). The real level catalog (`intern`, `qa_basilisk`,
`cc`, `csr`, `admin`, etc.) is data-driven Lua, each tier mapping to a
distinct **granted skill/ability set** -- command dispatch's actual
per-command gate is `hasGodMode() && hasAbility(commandName)`, so a
junior tier genuinely cannot invoke commands outside its granted
ability set. The `GODLEVEL` datatable column exists in
`command_table.iff`'s schema but is confirmed **never actually read**
by the loader -- vestigial. Granting/changing tiers goes through
`/setGodMode`, itself gated so only a full admin (level 15) can assign
a new permission tier to someone else.

## 416. Zone Weather Broadcast Pipeline (extends sections 60, 345, 367, 381)

A dedicated packet type (`ServerWeatherMessage`), but **not part of the
baseline message set** (section 367) and **not a zone broadcast** --
weather has no broadcast call anywhere in the codebase. Delivery is a
lazy, per-player pull: on zone-in, a sentinel value forces an
immediate send so a player logging in mid-storm sees it right away;
thereafter, the same per-player HAM-regen recovery tick (section 399,
every 3 seconds) also checks and re-sends weather if it changed for
that player's specific position (weather varies spatially per section
381's noise-based `WeatherMap`). Net effect: each player's client
updates independently on its own cadence, not simultaneously
zone-wide.

## 417. CraftingManager Batch/Mass-Production Task Architecture (extends sections 179, 264, 341, 348)

A real self-rescheduling `Task` per factory (`CreateFactoryObjectTask`,
matching section 348's pattern), producing **exactly one unit per
invocation** then calling `reschedule()` on itself with a
`complexity*8`-second delay -- genuine one-tick-per-unit real-time
pacing, not an instantly-computed batch with a simulated client-side
delay. **Player presence is not required** -- the task is owned by the
installation object itself and keeps firing on the server's task
threads regardless of the initiating player's session; production only
halts on power/maintenance exhaustion or schematic depletion. Restart
persistence is partial: overall progress (run count, schematic's
remaining-use counter) is stored as ordinary persisted fields and
survives a restart exactly, but the live scheduled `Task` itself is
`transient` (section 337's persistence model) -- on reload the factory
just restarts its per-unit countdown at a full fresh duration, losing
only the in-flight unit's partial progress.
